NAMES.name: faraday_angle
NAMES.short: Angular rotation of the polarization plane of a polarimeter probe beam induced by circular birefringence of the magnetized plasma, proportional to the line-integrated product of electron density and the parallel magnetic field.
NAMES.long:
The Faraday rotation angle is the net signed angular displacement of the plane of linear polarization of a probe beam that accumulates as the beam traverses a magnetized plasma along a polarimeter line of sight. Left- and right-hand circularly polarized components of the beam propagate at different phase velocities in the magnetized medium, producing a rotation whose magnitude and sign depend on the line-integrated product of electron number density and the magnetic-field component parallel to the beam.

The defining relation is:

$$
\Psi_F = \frac{e^3 \lambda^2}{8\pi^2 \varepsilon_0 m_e^2 c^3} \int n_e B_\parallel \, dl
$$

where $e$ is the elementary charge, $\lambda$ is the vacuum probing wavelength, $\varepsilon_0$ is the permittivity of free space, $m_e$ is the electron mass, $c$ is the speed of light, $n_e$ is the local electron number density, $B_\parallel$ is the component of the equilibrium magnetic field along the beam propagation direction, and the integral is taken along the line of sight through the plasma.

This quantity represents the variation induced by the plasma alone, excluding any initial polarization offset or instrumental offset at launch. It is sensitive to $\int n_e B_\parallel \, dl$, combining constraints from both the magnetic geometry and the electron density, and complements [line_averaged_electron_density](name:line_averaged_electron_density) in equilibrium reconstruction by adding explicit magnetic-field sensitivity.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the net line-integrated product $\int n_e B_\parallel \, dl$ is positive, with $B_\parallel$ taken as the projection of the magnetic field onto the beam propagation direction.

NAMES.name: first_local_tangential_coordinate_of_reflectometer_antenna
NAMES.short: Signed position of a reflectometer-antenna aperture-outline vertex along the first local tangential axis of the antenna’s in-plane frame.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the signed first local tangential coordinate of a vertex on the reflectometer antenna aperture outline. It defines the vertex position in the antenna-local tangential frame.

$$
x_1 = (\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}_0) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}_1
$$

where $x_1$ is the first local tangential coordinate, $\mathbf{r}$ is the position of the aperture-outline vertex, $\mathbf{r}_0$ is the origin of the local frame, and $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_1$ is its first local tangential unit vector. The right-handed local basis $(\hat{\mathbf{e}}_1, \hat{\mathbf{e}}_2, \hat{\mathbf{e}}_3)$ uses the more-horizontal in-plane tangent toward increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame; $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_3$ is the plasma-facing normal and $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_2 = \hat{\mathbf{e}}_3 \times \hat{\mathbf{e}}_1$.

Each value locates one aperture-outline vertex and is not the aperture width or a global cylindrical coordinate. The complementary coordinate along the second local tangent is the [second local tangential coordinate of the reflectometer antenna](name:second_local_tangential_coordinate_of_reflectometer_antenna).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the outline vertex lies in the direction of $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_1$ from $\mathbf{r}_0$.

NAMES.name: frequency_at_measurement_position
NAMES.short: Frequency at measurement position is the local temporal rate of an oscillation, wave, or characteristic plasma response evaluated at the spatial point where the measurement is defined. It is a generic parent for specific local frequencies, not a definition of any one frequency species.
NAMES.long:
Frequency at measurement position is the local cyclic frequency of an oscillatory process, wave, or characteristic plasma response evaluated at the spatial point where the measurement is defined. It denotes ordinary frequency rather than angular frequency, and the mechanism that determines the value is specified only by a more specialized child quantity.

For a periodic process with local period $T$, the cyclic frequency is defined by

$$
f = \frac{1}{T}
$$

where $f$ is the frequency at measurement position and $T$ is the local period of the oscillation or response.

This parent name does not identify the physical origin of the frequency. Specializations include local characteristic frequencies such as the [plasma frequency at measurement position](name:plasma_frequency_at_measurement_position), but the parent itself does not imply an electron plasma frequency, cyclotron frequency, wave frequency, cutoff frequency, or any other specific frequency species.

NAMES.name: frequency_of_diagnostic_antenna
NAMES.short: Temporal frequency of the coherent electromagnetic wave associated with a diagnostic antenna channel, whether transmitted, received, or selected for tuning.
NAMES.long:
This quantity specifies the oscillation rate of the coherent electromagnetic wave associated with a diagnostic antenna channel. It applies to the channel's transmitted, received, or selected wave and does not by itself identify a plasma location.

The temporal frequency $f$ is related to angular frequency by

$$
f = \frac{\omega}{2\pi}
$$

where $\omega$ is the wave angular frequency in radians per second and $f$ is the temporal frequency in hertz.

This channel-associated frequency is distinct from the local electron plasma frequency, which is determined by electron density at a measurement position as described by [frequency at measurement position](name:frequency_at_measurement_position). It is also distinct from the launch-referenced spectral framework of [launched wave frequency](name:launched_wave_frequency) and from the general [wave frequency](name:wave_frequency).

NAMES.name: launched_wave_duration
NAMES.short: Duration of a single frequency sweep during which a probing electromagnetic wave is launched.
NAMES.long:
Launched wave duration is the time interval of one complete swept-frequency launch of a probing electromagnetic wave. It is defined by the start and end times of the same launched-wave sweep, independent of how any received signal is analyzed.

For a sweep beginning at $t_{\mathrm{start}}$ and ending at $t_{\mathrm{end}}$, the launched wave duration is:

$$
\Delta t_{\mathrm{lw}} = t_{\mathrm{end}} - t_{\mathrm{start}}
$$

where $\Delta t_{\mathrm{lw}}$ is the launched wave duration, and $t_{\mathrm{start}}$ and $t_{\mathrm{end}}$ are the sweep start and end times, all measured in seconds.

The corresponding launched frequency during this interval is described by [launched_wave_frequency](name:launched_wave_frequency). This quantity specifies only the duration of the complete sweep; it does not define the detailed frequency waveform, dwell time at individual frequencies, received-wave interval, or signal-analysis interval.

NAMES.name: length_of_electron_cyclotron_beam
NAMES.short: Curvilinear distance measured along an electron-cyclotron beam-tracing ray, providing the propagation coordinate from its launch point to the evaluated point.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the cumulative arclength along an electron-cyclotron beam-tracing ray from its launch point to a specified point on the propagation path. It parameterizes the ray independently of the arbitrary parameter used to trace it.

The arclength is defined by

$$
s(\lambda)=\int_{\lambda_0}^{\lambda}\left\lvert\frac{d\mathbf{r}}{d\lambda'}\right\rvert\,d\lambda'
$$

where $\mathbf{r}(\lambda')$ is the ray position in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $\lambda'$ is an arbitrary path parameter, and $\lambda_0$ denotes the launch point. The arclength is non-negative and increases in the chosen propagation direction. It is a local path coordinate; the complete trajectory length represented by [length of beam-tracing beam](name:length_of_beam_tracing_beam) is a distinct endpoint quantity.

sources.enhanced_context: Curvilinear arc length along the ray or beam path in ECE beam-tracing calculations. Parameterizes the propagation distance from the launcher to the emission or absorption region along the beam trajectory.
sources.leaf_definition: Ray/beam curvilinear length
sources.parent_definition: Set of rays/beams describing the wave propagation

NAMES.name: length_of_fiber_optic_current_sensor
NAMES.short: Total physical arclength of the optical fiber centerline in a fiber-optic current sensor, defining its optical propagation distance and distributed magneto-optic interaction length.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the total arclength of the optical fiber centerline forming the fiber-optic current sensor. It includes the complete winding path and is not the straight-line distance between endpoints or the length of the sensor outline.

For a centerline parameterized by an arbitrary parameter $u$, the fiber length is defined by

$$
L = \int_{u_0}^{u_1} \left|\frac{d\mathbf{r}}{du}\right|\,du
$$

where $L$ is the total fiber arclength, $\mathbf{r}(u)$ is the centerline position, and $u_0$ and $u_1$ delimit the fiber path. The length sets the optical propagation distance; accumulated Faraday rotation additionally depends on the magnetic-field projection along the winding and the [Verdet constant](name:verdet_constant_of_fiber_optic_current_sensor).

sources.enhanced_context: Total length of the spun optical fibre wound on the vacuum vessel for the Fiber Optic Current Sensor (FOCS) diagnostic. A key geometric parameter determining the sensitivity and integration path length for the Faraday-effect current measurement.
sources.leaf_definition: Spun fibre length on the vacuum vessel

NAMES.name: normalized_toroidal_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam
NAMES.short: Dimensionless toroidal direction cosine of an electromagnetic wave vector along a beam-tracing ray in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The normalized toroidal wave-vector component is the signed direction cosine of the electromagnetic wave vector along a beam-tracing ray. It gives the projection of the propagation direction onto the geometric toroidal direction, rather than the unnormalized toroidal wavenumber.

$$
n_\phi = \frac{k_\phi}{\lVert\mathbf{k}\rVert} = \frac{\mathbf{k}\cdot\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}{\sqrt{k_R^2+k_\phi^2+k_Z^2}}
$$

Here $n_\phi$ is the normalized toroidal wave-vector component, $\mathbf{k}$ is the wave vector, $\lVert\mathbf{k}\rVert$ is its magnitude, $k_R$, $k_\phi$, and $k_Z$ are its components in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, and $\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle. The quantity lies between $-1$ and $1$. The same normalization is used for the [radial normalized wave-vector component](name:radial_normalized_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam) and [vertical normalized wave-vector component](name:vertical_normalized_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the wave vector has a component in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

sources.enhanced_context: Normalized toroidal wave vector component (k_phi/|k|) of an ECE beam or ray along its propagation path in cylindrical coordinates. Represents the toroidal direction cosine of the unit wave vector in beam tracing calculations for ECE diagnostics.
sources.leaf_definition: Normalized wave vector component in the toroidal direction = k_phi / norm(k)
sources.parent_definition: Wave vector of the ray/beam along its path

NAMES.name: parallel_normalized_power_of_beam_tracing_beam
NAMES.short: Signed fraction of a beam’s local time-averaged electromagnetic power flow parallel to the local magnetic field, normalized to the launched beam power.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the signed local fraction of electromagnetic power carried by a coherent beam-tracing beam in the direction parallel to the local magnetic field. It is evaluated along the beam’s ray path and referenced to the beam’s initial launched power.

The normalized parallel fraction is defined by

$$
f_\parallel = \frac{P_\parallel}{P_0} = \frac{\int_{\mathcal{A}} \langle\mathbf{S}\rangle \cdot \hat{\mathbf{b}}\,\mathrm{d}A}{P_0}
$$

where $P_\parallel$ is the local parallel power flow, $\langle\mathbf{S}\rangle$ is the time-averaged electromagnetic Poynting vector, $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$ is the unit vector along the local magnetic field, $\mathcal{A}$ is the beam cross-section, and $P_0$ is the [initial power of the beam-tracing beam](name:initial_power_of_beam_tracing_beam). This signed projection is distinct from the non-negative [perpendicular normalized power of the beam-tracing beam](name:perpendicular_normalized_power_of_beam_tracing_beam).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the local electromagnetic power flow has a component in the direction of the local magnetic field.

sources.parent_definition: Normalised power flow

NAMES.name: period_of_fiber_optic_current_sensor
NAMES.short: Period of a fiber optic current sensor is the repeat arclength along the sensing fiber of a specified spatially periodic optical or geometrical state. Specialized names identify which state repeats, such as optical-axis twist.
NAMES.long:
Period of a fiber optic current sensor is the repeat arclength along the sensing fiber centerline of a specified spatially periodic optical or geometrical state of the sensor. It identifies the longitudinal spacing of repetition; the specialized standard name supplies the repeating state.

For a state $Q(s)$ that is periodic along the fiber, the period $L_p$ is the smallest positive arclength satisfying:

$$
Q(s + L_p) = Q(s)
$$

where $s$ is arclength along the fiber centerline and $Q$ is the periodic state specified by the specialized name.

This parent quantity is intentionally generic across fiber-sensor periods. The [twist period of a fiber optic current sensor](name:twist_period_of_fiber_optic_current_sensor) is one specialization, with $Q$ the effective birefringent-axis orientation; the parent does not itself specify twist, manufacturing spin, the total [length of the fiber optic current sensor](name:length_of_fiber_optic_current_sensor), or the [polarization beat length](name:polarization_beat_length).

NAMES.name: perpendicular_normalized_power_of_beam_tracing_beam
NAMES.short: Non-negative fraction of a beam’s local time-averaged electromagnetic power flow perpendicular to the local magnetic field, normalized to its initial launch power.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the magnitude of the local time-averaged electromagnetic power-flow component perpendicular to the local magnetic-field direction, normalized by the beam’s initial launch power. It measures transverse power flow and is not a signed projection onto a selected perpendicular direction.

$$
p_{\perp} = \frac{\left\lVert \mathbf{P} - (\mathbf{P}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{b}})\hat{\mathbf{b}}\right\rVert}{P_0}
$$

where $\mathbf{P}$ is the local beam power-flow vector, $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$ is the unit vector along the local magnetic field, and $P_0$ is the initial launch power. The magnitude makes $p_{\perp}$ non-negative. Together with the signed [parallel normalized beam power](name:parallel_normalized_power_of_beam_tracing_beam), it characterizes the local power-flow decomposition relative to the magnetic field; [initial beam power](name:initial_power_of_beam_tracing_beam) supplies the normalization reference.

NAMES.name: plasma_frequency_at_measurement_position
NAMES.short: Local electron plasma frequency at the measurement position, set by free-electron number density and defining the ordinary-mode electromagnetic cutoff.
NAMES.long:
The electron plasma frequency is the natural electrostatic oscillation frequency of the local free-electron population at the measurement position. It is a plasma property, not the carrier frequency of a diagnostic source.

For the cold-electron response, the frequency is defined by

$$
f_{pe} = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{n_e e^2}{\varepsilon_0 m_e}}
$$

where $f_{pe}$ is the electron plasma frequency, $n_e$ is the local free-electron number density, $e$ is the elementary charge, $\varepsilon_0$ is the vacuum permittivity, and $m_e$ is the electron mass.

This quantity is the local cutoff scale for ordinary-mode electromagnetic-wave propagation. It differs from the externally selected [diagnostic antenna frequency](name:frequency_of_diagnostic_antenna), while serving as the physical component of [frequency at measurement position](name:frequency_at_measurement_position).

sources.parent_definition: Set of channels, e.g. different reception antennas or frequency bandwidths of the reflectometer

NAMES.name: poloidal_perturbed_suprathermal_electron_angle_at_measurement_position
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Poloidal angular offset estimate of the electron cyclotron emission measurement position due to the presence of suprathermal electrons, relative to the thermal-electron emission reference.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal angular offset estimate of the electron cyclotron emission measurement position due to the presence of suprathermal electrons is the signed change in the assigned poloidal coordinate of that position relative to the thermal-electron emission reference. The poloidal angle $\theta$ is measured about the magnetic axis in a constant-$\phi$ cross-section of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height; $\theta=0$ is at the outboard midplane and $\theta$ increases from larger $R$ toward $+Z$.

The offset is the difference between the poloidal coordinate assigned when suprathermal emission is included and the thermal-electron reference coordinate:

$$
\Delta\theta_\mathrm{supra} = \theta_\mathrm{meas,supra} - \theta_\mathrm{meas,thermal}
$$

where $\theta_\mathrm{meas,supra}$ is the assigned measurement-position poloidal angle with the suprathermal-electron contribution included, $\theta_\mathrm{meas,thermal}$ is the corresponding thermal-electron reference angle, and $\Delta\theta_\mathrm{supra}$ is this quantity; all angular quantities are in radians.

This quantity is only the poloidal angular component of the suprathermal-electron offset at the measurement position; it is not a radial displacement, toroidal angular offset, or full spatial correction. It is distinguished from [poloidal_suprathermal_electron_perturbed_angle_of_ece_channel_emission_position](name:poloidal_perturbed_suprathermal_electron_angle_at_measurement_position), which applies to the ECE-channel emission position. No universal signed range, magnitude, or sign is implied by the name; the value is zero when the presence of suprathermal electrons leaves the assigned measurement position unchanged.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $\Delta\theta_\mathrm{supra}$ shifts the assigned electron cyclotron emission measurement position in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$, from the outboard midplane toward $+Z$ in the constant-$\phi$ cross-section of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

sources.leaf_definition: Poloidal angle (oriented clockwise when viewing the poloidal cross section on the right hand side of the tokamak axis of symmetry, with the origin placed on the plasma magnetic axis)
sources.parent_definition: Simple estimate of the difference in position induced by the presence of suprathermal electrons. Position without corrections = position - delta_position_suprathermal

NAMES.name: radial_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam
NAMES.short: Radial (major-radius) component of the local wave vector along the beam tracing ray path.
NAMES.long:
The wave vector $\mathbf{k}$ characterizes the local spatial frequency and propagation direction of an electromagnetic wave at each point along a beam tracing ray. Its radial component $k_R = \mathbf{k} \cdot \hat{R}$ quantifies how rapidly the wave phase advances in the major-radius direction $\hat{R}$ of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, the wave vector decomposes as:

$$
\mathbf{k} = k_R \hat{R} + k_\phi \hat{\phi} + k_Z \hat{Z}
$$

where $k_\phi = n_\phi / R$ with $n_\phi$ the toroidal mode number and $R$ the major radius in meters, and $k_Z$ is the [vertical wave vector component](name:vertical_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam). Together with [toroidal_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam](name:toroidal_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam), these three components fully specify the local wave propagation geometry consistent with the local dispersion relation $D(\mathbf{k}, \omega, \mathbf{x}) = 0$.

This component is computed by beam tracing along the ray path for electron cyclotron heating, current drive, and electron cyclotron emission diagnostic beams. For electron cyclotron waves near 170 GHz, the vacuum wavenumber $|\mathbf{k}_0| = \omega/c$ is approximately 3600 m$^{-1}$; in-plasma values of $k_R$ vary along the ray according to plasma geometry and the local dispersion relation.

The dimensionless counterpart [radial_normalized_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam](name:radial_normalized_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam) gives the direction cosine $k_R / |\mathbf{k}|$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the radial wave vector component points in the direction of increasing major radius $R$.

NAMES.name: radiative_temperature
NAMES.short: Blackbody-equivalent brightness temperature inferred from electron cyclotron emission, approaching the local electron temperature when the resonant layer is optically thick.
NAMES.long:
Electron-cyclotron radiative temperature is the energy-equivalent blackbody temperature whose thermal radiation has the observed electron-cyclotron spectral radiance. It characterizes the radiation field and is not necessarily the local electron temperature.

At frequency $\nu$, the brightness temperature is defined by the Planck relation:

$$
I_\nu = \frac{2 h \nu^3}{c^2}\left[\exp\left(\frac{h\nu}{T_{\mathrm{rad}}}\right)-1\right]^{-1}
$$

where $I_\nu$ is the electron-cyclotron spectral radiance, $h$ is Planck's constant, $c$ is the speed of light, and $T_{\mathrm{rad}}$ is the brightness temperature expressed as thermal energy.

For an optically thick, thermalized resonant layer, $T_{\mathrm{rad}}$ approaches the local electron temperature. At finite optical depth, it instead represents the radiation emerging from the emitting and absorbing plasma along the observation path and can differ from the local value. The axis-specific counterpart is [radiative temperature at the magnetic axis](name:radiative_temperature_at_magnetic_axis).

NAMES.name: refractive_index
NAMES.short: Dimensionless ratio of an electromagnetic wave’s phase-gradient vector to its vacuum wavenumber, retaining propagation direction and signed components.
NAMES.long:
The refractive-index vector describes electromagnetic phase propagation relative to propagation in vacuum. It preserves the direction of the wave phase gradient while expressing its magnitude relative to the vacuum reference.

The defining relation is

$$
\mathbf{n} = \frac{\mathbf{k}}{k_0}, \qquad k_0 = \frac{\omega}{c}
$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ is the refractive-index vector, $\mathbf{k}$ is the [wave vector](name:wave_vector), $k_0$ is the vacuum wavenumber, $\omega$ is the wave angular frequency, and $c$ is the speed of light in vacuum.

Directional representations include the projection parallel to the local magnetic field, represented by [parallel_refractive_index](name:parallel_refractive_index), and the magnitude of the perpendicular projection, represented by [perpendicular_refractive_index](name:perpendicular_refractive_index). The same normalized phase-propagation concept applies to propagation through an [optical element](name:refractive_index_of_optical_element).
NAMES.sign: Positive when a signed component indicates phase propagation in its declared positive geometric direction; in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ basis, these directions are increasing major radius $R$, toroidal angle $\phi$, and vertical coordinate $Z$.

NAMES.name: parallel_refractive_index
NAMES.short: Projection of the refractive-index vector onto the local equilibrium magnetic field direction, equal to the wave vector component parallel to the magnetic field normalized by the vacuum wave number.
NAMES.long:
The parallel refractive index $N_\parallel$ is the component of the refractive-index vector $\mathbf{N} = \mathbf{k}/k_0$ projected along the local equilibrium magnetic field unit vector $\hat{b} = \mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$, where $k_0 = \omega/c$ is the vacuum wave number at angular frequency $\omega$ and $c$ is the speed of light in vacuum. It governs the phase velocity of a wave along the field line and controls parallel resonance effects including Landau damping and transit-time magnetic pumping.

The defining relation is:

$$
N_\parallel = \mathbf{N} \cdot \hat{b} = \frac{\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{B}}{k_0 |\mathbf{B}|}
$$

where $\mathbf{k}$ is the local wave vector and $\mathbf{B}$ is the background magnetic field.

Together with [perpendicular_refractive_index](name:perpendicular_refractive_index), $N_\parallel$ fully decomposes the parent [refractive_index](name:refractive_index) vector into its field-aligned and cross-field components. In beam-tracing or ray-tracing calculations, $N_\parallel$ is evaluated at each point along the ray path; for lower hybrid current drive it is a primary launch parameter controlled by the phasing between antenna straps, and for electron cyclotron emission diagnostics it determines the Doppler shift of the resonance layer.

For lower hybrid waves, $N_\parallel$ at launch lies in the range 1.5–3.5 to satisfy the wave accessibility condition in the core plasma. For nearly perpendicular electron cyclotron beams, $|N_\parallel|$ is well below unity.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the wave vector projected onto the magnetic field $\mathbf{B}$ points in the same direction as $\mathbf{B}$.

NAMES.name: perpendicular_refractive_index
NAMES.short: Projection magnitude of the refractive-index vector onto the plane perpendicular to the local equilibrium magnetic field, equal to the perpendicular wave-vector magnitude normalized by the vacuum wave number.
NAMES.long:
The perpendicular refractive index $N_\perp$ is the magnitude of the component of the refractive-index vector projected onto the plane perpendicular to the local equilibrium magnetic field direction. It is the field-normal part of the dimensionless wave-propagation vector used to describe electromagnetic waves in a magnetized plasma.

The defining relation is:

$$
N_\perp = \left|\mathbf{N} - (\mathbf{N}\cdot\hat{b})\hat{b}\right|, \qquad \mathbf{N}=\frac{\mathbf{k}}{k_0}, \qquad k_0=\frac{\omega}{c}
$$

where $\mathbf{N}$ is the refractive-index vector, $\mathbf{k}$ is the local wave vector, $k_0$ is the vacuum wave number, $\omega$ is angular frequency, $c$ is the speed of light in vacuum, and $\hat{b}=\mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$ is the unit vector along the local equilibrium magnetic field.

This scalar is the nonnegative magnitude of the perpendicular projection, not a signed projection along a chosen transverse basis direction. Together with the [parallel refractive index](name:parallel_refractive_index) $N_\parallel=\mathbf{N}\cdot\hat{b}$, it satisfies $N_\perp^2+N_\parallel^2=|\mathbf{N}|^2$; the corresponding unnormalized quantity is the [perpendicular wave-vector magnitude](name:perpendicular_wave_vector_magnitude).

NAMES.name: second_local_tangential_coordinate_of_reflectometer_antenna
NAMES.short: Coordinate of each reflectometer antenna aperture-outline vertex along the second local tangential axis of the antenna’s orthogonal (X1, X2) frame.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the signed position of a reflectometer antenna aperture-outline vertex along the second local tangential direction in the antenna-local orthogonal $(X_1, X_2)$ frame.

$$
x_2 = \mathbf{r} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}_2
$$

where $x_2$ is the second local tangential coordinate, $\mathbf{r}$ is the vertex displacement from the local frame origin, and $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_2$ is the second local tangential unit vector. The local orientation is defined by $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_2 = \hat{\mathbf{e}}_3 \times \hat{\mathbf{e}}_1$, with $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_1$ the first local tangential unit vector and $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_3$ the plasma-facing normal.

Together with the [first local tangential coordinate of the reflectometer antenna](name:first_local_tangential_coordinate_of_reflectometer_antenna), this coordinate specifies the aperture-outline geometry. It is not a vertical coordinate or a coordinate in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the vertex displacement has a positive projection onto the second local tangential direction $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_2$.

NAMES.name: tilt_angle_of_beam_tracing_beam
NAMES.short: Signed rotation of an elliptical beam cross-section’s principal axis relative to the local transverse basis attached to a beam-tracing propagation path.
NAMES.long:
The tilt angle specifies the orientation of a selected principal axis of the elliptical cross-section associated with a beam-tracing beam, relative to the beam’s transverse basis. It describes ellipse orientation rather than the beam’s propagation direction, which is characterized separately by the [poloidal angle of the beam-tracing beam](name:poloidal_angle_of_beam_tracing_beam).

The principal-axis direction is defined by

$$
\hat{\mathbf a} = \cos\alpha\,\hat{\mathbf e}_1 + \sin\alpha\,\hat{\mathbf e}_2
$$

where $\alpha$ is the tilt angle, $\hat{\mathbf a}$ is the selected principal-axis unit vector, and $(\hat{\mathbf e}_1,\hat{\mathbf e}_2,\hat{\mathbf e}_\parallel)$ is the local right-handed beam frame, with $\hat{\mathbf e}_\parallel$ aligned with propagation. Because an ellipse is unchanged when a principal axis is reversed, the angle is defined modulo $\pi$; selecting the other principal axis changes the reference by $\pi/2$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the selected principal axis rotates from $\hat{\mathbf e}_1$ toward $\hat{\mathbf e}_2$ according to the right-handed orientation about $\hat{\mathbf e}_\parallel$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_normalized_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam
NAMES.short: Toroidal normalized wave vector of a beam-tracing beam is the signed toroidal direction cosine k_phi/|k| of the electromagnetic wave vector at the beam launch point in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal normalized wave vector of a beam-tracing beam is the signed toroidal direction cosine of the electromagnetic wave vector at the beam launch point. It is the projection of the local unit wave vector onto the toroidal basis direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The normalized toroidal component is defined by

$$
k_{\phi,\mathrm{norm}} = \frac{\mathbf{k}\cdot\hat{\phi}}{\lvert\mathbf{k}\rvert} = \frac{k_\phi}{\lvert\mathbf{k}\rvert}
$$

where $\mathbf{k}$ is the electromagnetic wave vector at the beam launch point, $\hat{\phi}$ is the toroidal unit vector in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ basis with $\hat{R}\times\hat{\phi}=\hat{Z}$, $k_\phi=\mathbf{k}\cdot\hat{\phi}$ is the [toroidal wave vector of a beam-tracing beam](name:toroidal_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam), and $\lvert\mathbf{k}\rvert$ is the wave-vector magnitude.

This is a launch-point quantity, not an integral or average over a beam path. It is distinct from the [normalized toroidal wave vector of a beam-tracing beam](name:normalized_toroidal_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam), which denotes the same toroidal direction cosine evaluated along a traced beam rather than specifically at launch. For real nonzero $\mathbf{k}$ it satisfies $-1 \leq k_{\phi,\mathrm{norm}} \leq 1$; together with the [radial normalized wave vector of a beam-tracing beam](name:radial_normalized_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam) and the [vertical normalized wave vector of a beam-tracing beam](name:vertical_normalized_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam), the cylindrical direction cosines obey $k_{R,\mathrm{norm}}^2+k_{\phi,\mathrm{norm}}^2+k_{Z,\mathrm{norm}}^2=1$. The [poloidal normalized wave vector of a beam-tracing beam] is instead a related projection in the meridional plane spanned by $\hat{R}$ and $\hat{Z}$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the projection of $\mathbf{k}$ onto $\hat{\phi}$ is along the local $+\hat{\phi}$ direction, the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam
NAMES.short: Signed projection of the electromagnetic wave vector of a beam-tracing beam onto the toroidal direction in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame at the evaluated point along the ray.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal wave vector of a beam-tracing beam is the physical component of the local electromagnetic wave vector along $\hat{\phi}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It represents the local toroidal wave-number component of the propagating beam.

The component is defined by the orthonormal projection of the local wave vector:

$$
k_\phi = \mathbf{k} \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $k_\phi$ is the toroidal wave-vector component, $\mathbf{k}$ is the local electromagnetic wave vector, both have units of inverse length, and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

This is the orthonormal physical component along $\hat{\phi}$, not the canonical phase-gradient component conjugate to the toroidal angle; the corresponding canonical factor is $R k_\phi$. The corresponding normalized toroidal wave-vector component is the signed direction cosine $k_\phi / |\mathbf{k}|$, not a normalization by a vacuum wave number.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the wave vector component points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: twist_period_of_fiber_optic_current_sensor
NAMES.short: Repeat arclength along the sensing-fiber centerline at which the effective birefringent-axis orientation completes one spatial cycle.
NAMES.long:
The twist period is the repeat arclength along the sensing-fiber centerline for the effective birefringent-axis orientation to return to the same state.

Let $s$ denote arclength along the fiber centerline and $Q(s)$ denote the specified effective birefringent-axis state. The twist period $L_{\rm tw}$ is defined by

$$
Q(s + L_{\rm tw}) = Q(s)
$$

where $L_{\rm tw}$ is the smallest positive repeat arclength.

This is the twist-specific member of the [fiber optic current sensor period](name:period_of_fiber_optic_current_sensor). It describes spatial repetition of the optical anisotropy, not the total fiber arclength, the [initial twist phase](name:initial_twist_phase_of_fiber_optic_current_sensor), or the [polarization beat length](name:polarization_beat_length).

sources.enhanced_context: Twist period of the spun optical fibre used in a Fiber Optic Current Sensor (FOCS). Characterizes the helical twist rate of the fibre, which determines its sensitivity to the Faraday magneto-optic effect and its rejection of linear birefringence.

sources.parent_definition: Intrinsic properties of the fibre installed on the vacuum vessel

NAMES.name: verdet_constant_of_fiber_optic_current_sensor
NAMES.short: Verdet constant of a fiber-optic current sensor is the sensing fiber's Faraday-effect coefficient for its optical wavelength and material state. It sets the polarization rotation per path length caused by the magnetic-field component parallel to the oriented optical path.
NAMES.long:
Verdet constant of a fiber-optic current sensor is the scalar Faraday-effect coefficient of the sensing fiber for a specified optical wavelength and material state. It relates the magnetic-field component parallel to the oriented guided-light path to the incremental rotation of the optical polarization.

For an oriented path $C$, the Faraday rotation produced in the sensing fiber is defined by

$$
\Delta \chi = \int_C V(s)\,\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{r}(s))\cdot\hat{\mathbf{t}}(s)\,ds
$$

where $\Delta\chi$ is the change in polarization angle, $V(s)$ is the Verdet constant along the path, $s$ is arc length, $\mathbf{r}(s)$ is the position on the path, $\hat{\mathbf{t}}(s)$ is the unit tangent in the positive optical propagation direction, and $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field. For a uniform fiber segment, $V(s)$ reduces to a constant $V$.

This coefficient is distinct from geometrical quantities such as [length of a fiber-optic current sensor](name:length_of_fiber_optic_current_sensor) and [period of a fiber-optic current sensor](name:period_of_fiber_optic_current_sensor); those quantities determine the path $C$ and tangent $\hat{\mathbf{t}}$, not the local material response. Nonmagnetic phase retardance, including linear birefringence, is not part of the Verdet constant.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $\mathbf{B}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{t}}>0$ produces $d\chi/ds>0$, with $\chi$ measured in the co-propagating transverse basis from $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_1$ toward $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_2$ where $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_1 \times \hat{\mathbf{e}}_2 = \hat{\mathbf{t}}$.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_diagnostic_antenna
NAMES.short: Vertical Z coordinate of the geometric center of a diagnostic antenna in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate $Z$ locates the geometric center of a diagnostic antenna along the machine symmetry axis within the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major radius measured from the symmetry axis and $Z$ is the vertical height, both in meters, with the nominal midplane at $Z = 0$.

This coordinate, together with the corresponding major radius, specifies the spatial position from which electromagnetic wave diagnostics launch or receive signals. Applications include reflectometer emission and detection channels, electron cyclotron emission receivers, and X-ray and UV spectrometer optical components. Beam-tracing and ray-tracing algorithms use the antenna center position as the boundary condition for the launch or detection point of the propagating wave. The analogous geometric reference for related diagnostic hardware is captured by [vertical_coordinate_of_diagnostic_aperture](name:vertical_coordinate_of_diagnostic_aperture), [vertical_coordinate_of_optical_element](name:vertical_coordinate_of_optical_element), and [vertical_coordinate_of_antenna_strap](name:vertical_coordinate_of_antenna_strap).

Values span the full height range of the machine port system; in medium-sized tokamaks this is approximately $-2$ to $+2$ m depending on port access geometry and the plasma region targeted by the diagnostic.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the antenna center is located above the device midplane in the direction of increasing $Z$.

NAMES.name: vertical_magnetic_field_at_wall
NAMES.short: Z component of the total magnetic field vector at a vacuum-vessel wall position in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, positive in the direction of increasing vertical height.
NAMES.long:
Vertical magnetic field at the wall is the $Z$ component of the total magnetic-field vector evaluated at a specified point on the vacuum-vessel wall. It is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle increasing counter-clockwise when viewed from $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height measured relative to the machine midplane.

The defining projection is

$$
B_Z(R, \phi, Z) = \mathbf{B}(R, \phi, Z) \cdot \hat{Z}
$$

where $\mathbf{B}$ is the total magnetic-field vector at the wall point, $\hat{Z}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing vertical height, and $B_Z$ is its vertical component.

The specified wall point is a geometric locus on the vacuum-vessel wall; its vertical coordinate uses the same $Z$ reference as coordinate quantities such as [vertical coordinate of a poloidal magnetic-field probe](name:vertical_coordinate_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe). This quantity is a local vector component, not the magnetic-field magnitude, not a magnetic flux, and not the [radial](name:radial_magnetic_field) or [toroidal](name:toroidal_magnetic_field) magnetic-field component.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $B_Z$ points in the direction of increasing $Z$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

sources.enhanced_context: Vertical component (Bz) of the magnetic field at each point along the FOCS fibre outline on the vacuum vessel. Used together with the fibre geometry to derive the total enclosed toroidal plasma current via Ampère's law.
sources.leaf_definition: Vertical component of the magnetic field on each point of the FOCS outline

NAMES.name: vertical_normalized_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam
NAMES.short: Direction cosine of the electromagnetic wave vector along the vertical Z-direction, equal to k_Z divided by the total wave-vector magnitude, evaluated pointwise along a beam-tracing ray path.
NAMES.long:
The normalized vertical wave vector component is the direction cosine of the local electromagnetic wave propagation direction projected onto the vertical $Z$-axis of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, computed pointwise along a beam-tracing or ray-tracing path. It encodes the fraction of the propagation direction aligned with the vertical direction at each position along the ray.

The defining relation is:

$$
k_{Z,\mathrm{norm}} = \frac{k_Z}{|\mathbf{k}|}
$$

where $k_Z$ is the [vertical wave vector component](name:vertical_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam) and $|\mathbf{k}|$ is the total wave-vector magnitude. Together with [radial_normalized_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam](name:radial_normalized_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam) and [toroidal_normalized_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam](name:toroidal_normalized_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam), it fully specifies the unit propagation direction in the cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, satisfying $k_{R,\mathrm{norm}}^2 + k_{\phi,\mathrm{norm}}^2 + k_{Z,\mathrm{norm}}^2 = 1$.

This quantity is computed during beam-tracing or ray-tracing simulations for RF wave propagation and ECE diagnostics, where the Hamiltonian ray equations simultaneously advance the spatial position and wave vector along the ray. The normalized form characterizes the instantaneous propagation direction independently of the local wave number magnitude.

As a direction cosine, values are bounded to $[-1, 1]$. Values near zero indicate nearly horizontal propagation, while values near $\pm 1$ correspond to strongly oblique launch geometries or wave turning near a vertical reflection layer.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $k_Z$ points in the direction of increasing $Z$.

sources.enhanced_context: Normalised vertical component of the wave vector (k_z/|k|) along the ECE beam or ray path. Represents the direction cosine of the wave vector in the vertical (z) direction during beam tracing propagation.
sources.leaf_definition: Normalized wave vector component in the vertical direction = k_z / norm(k)
sources.parent_definition: Wave vector of the ray/beam along its path

sources.enhanced_context: Normalised vertical component of the wave vector (k_z/|k|) along the beam or ray path in beam tracing calculations. Represents the direction cosine of the wave vector in the vertical (Z) direction for RF wave propagation.
sources.leaf_definition: Normalized wave vector component in the vertical direction = k_z / norm(k)

NAMES.name: vertical_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam
NAMES.short: Signed spatial phase gradient of an electromagnetic wave along the vertical direction in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame at each point on a beam-tracing ray.
NAMES.long:
The vertical wave-vector component is the signed projection of the local electromagnetic-wave vector onto the vertical direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame. It gives the local spatial phase gradient along $Z$ at each point of a beam-tracing ray, rather than a launch-point-only value.

Using the phase convention $\mathbf{k}=\nabla S$, it is defined by

$$
k_Z = \mathbf{k}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{Z}} = \frac{\partial S}{\partial Z}
$$

where $\mathbf{k}$ is the local wave vector, $\hat{\mathbf{Z}}$ is the vertical unit vector, $S$ is the spatial phase, and $Z$ is vertical height. Unlike the direction cosine [vertical normalized wave vector of a beam-tracing beam](name:vertical_normalized_wave_vector_of_beam_tracing_beam), this component retains the wave-number scale; [vertical wave vector](name:vertical_wave_vector) denotes the corresponding launch-point quantity.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the local wave vector has a component in the $+Z$ direction, so the phase increases with increasing vertical height $Z$.

sources.leaf_definition: Wave vector component in the vertical direction
sources.parent_definition: Wave vector of the ray/beam along its path

NAMES.name: voltage_of_diagnostic_antenna
NAMES.short: Voltage of a diagnostic antenna is the signed electrical potential difference at the antenna port between its signal terminal and reference conductor. It denotes the antenna terminal quantity, not a downstream receiver, detector, spectrometer-channel, or calibrated radiometric signal.
NAMES.long:
Voltage of a diagnostic antenna is the electrical terminal voltage across the antenna port. The antenna port is the pair of conductors forming the antenna feed connection to external circuitry; the voltage is the potential difference between the signal terminal and the reference conductor at that port.

The terminal voltage is defined by the port potential difference:

$$
V_\mathrm{ant}(t) = \Phi_\mathrm{sig}(t) - \Phi_\mathrm{ref}(t)
$$

where $V_\mathrm{ant}$ is the antenna terminal voltage in volts, $t$ is time, and $\Phi_\mathrm{sig}$ and $\Phi_\mathrm{ref}$ are the signal-terminal and reference-conductor potentials in volts.

This quantity is bounded at the antenna electrical port. It excludes voltages produced after transmission-line propagation, receiver gain, frequency conversion, detection, digitization, or spectrometer-channel processing, which are distinct channel or electronics quantities such as [voltage_of_spectrometer_channel](name:voltage_of_spectrometer_channel) and [measured_voltage_of_spectrometer_channel](name:measured_voltage_of_spectrometer_channel). It is also not the electromagnetic electric-field waveform in space.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the signal-terminal potential is greater than the reference-conductor potential.

NAMES.name: voltage_of_reflectometer_antenna
NAMES.short: Voltage of a reflectometer antenna is the peak amplitude of a calibrated narrow-band microwave voltage at a reflectometer antenna terminal or specified electrical reference plane. It is the generic terminal amplitude, not only the plasma-reflected component.
NAMES.long:
Voltage of a reflectometer antenna is the peak amplitude of a narrow-band microwave voltage associated with a reflectometer antenna terminal or specified electrical reference plane. It is a calibrated voltage amplitude, meaning the value is referred to that terminal or reference plane after applying the gain, attenuation, and reference-plane convention that define the reported electrical amplitude.

For a narrow-band waveform represented by the complex voltage phasor $\tilde V(t)$ through $v(t)=\Re\{\tilde V(t)e^{-i\omega_0 t}\}$, the antenna voltage is defined by:

$$
V_\mathrm{ant}(t)=|\tilde V(t)|
$$

where $v(t)$ is the real microwave voltage waveform in volts, $\tilde V(t)$ is the slowly varying complex voltage phasor in volts at the reference plane, $\omega_0$ is the carrier angular frequency in radians per second, and $V_\mathrm{ant}(t)$ is the reported peak voltage amplitude in volts. For a pure sinusoid, the corresponding root-mean-square voltage is $V_\mathrm{ant}/\sqrt{2}$; this standard name denotes the peak amplitude.

As a generic reflectometer-antenna terminal amplitude, this quantity can include launched-wave leakage, plasma-reflected or scattered components, antenna coupling, standing-wave effects, and receiver-chain response unless a component has been separated by definition. It is the reflectometer-specific counterpart of [voltage of a diagnostic antenna](name:voltage_of_diagnostic_antenna) and is broader than [reflected voltage of a reflectometer antenna](name:reflected_voltage_of_reflectometer_antenna), which denotes only the reflected-wave component; it is not a reflection coefficient, cutoff position, or plasma density.

NAMES.name: wave_phase_of_wave_beam
NAMES.short: Fringe-jump-corrected phase angle of a probing electromagnetic signal at a selected wavelength, retaining the channel’s defined phase reference.
NAMES.long:
The wave phase is the angular position of the complex probing-signal amplitude associated with a selected wavelength. Fringe-jump correction removes artificial integer-cycle discontinuities while preserving the physical phase evolution.

The corrected phase is represented by

$$
\phi_{\mathrm{corr}}(\lambda)=\operatorname{unwrap}\!\left[\arg \tilde{S}(\lambda)\right]
$$

where $\lambda$ is the selected probing wavelength, $\tilde{S}$ is the complex signal amplitude, $\arg$ gives its angular argument, and $\operatorname{unwrap}$ applies the integer-cycle correction.

The phase origin and reference are those defined for the wavelength channel; this quantity is not necessarily a phase difference relative to launch. Phase variation along the probing chord provides information related to line-integrated electron density and [line-averaged electron density](name:line_averaged_electron_density).

Phase convention: Positive phase denotes increasing argument of the complex signal under the adopted phasor convention; the phase is defined modulo $2\pi$ before fringe-jump correction.

sources.leaf_definition: Phase of the envelope of the probing signal, relative to the phase at launch

NAMES.name: width_of_reflectometer_antenna
NAMES.short: Width of a reflectometer antenna is the full non-negative transverse extent of a rectangular antenna aperture along the X1 direction of the local aperture frame (X1, X2, X3), where X1 and X2 lie in the aperture plane and X3 is normal to it.
NAMES.long:
Width of a reflectometer antenna is the full non-negative transverse extent of a rectangular antenna aperture along the $X_1$ direction of the local aperture frame $(X_1, X_2, X_3)$, where $X_1$ and $X_2$ are tangent to the aperture plane and $X_3$ is normal to that plane. It describes the physical aperture size, not the antenna position, pointing direction, or orientation of the aperture frame.

For an aperture region $A$ expressed in the local aperture frame $(X_1, X_2, X_3)$, the width $w$ is the span of the $X_1$ coordinate over the aperture:

$$
w = \max_{\mathbf{r} \in A} X_1(\mathbf{r}) - \min_{\mathbf{r} \in A} X_1(\mathbf{r})
$$

where $\mathbf{r}$ is a point of the aperture and $X_1(\mathbf{r})$ is its coordinate along the $X_1$ axis.

Only the span parallel to $X_1$ is the width; the span parallel to $X_2$ is the orthogonal aperture-plane dimension when the two local tangential directions are distinguished. The quantity is a full side-to-side extent, not a half-width, radius, aperture area, or individual boundary coordinate such as the [first local tangential coordinate of a reflectometer antenna](name:first_local_tangential_coordinate_of_reflectometer_antenna).

NAMES.name: electron_absorbed_power_of_beam_tracing_beam
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Wave power absorbed by the electron population from a single coherent beam-tracing beam, representing the electron contribution to total path-integrated wave energy deposition.
NAMES.long:
The electron absorbed power of a beam-tracing beam is the total wave power transferred from a single traced coherent electromagnetic beam to the electron population over its computed propagation path. It represents the electron contribution to wave energy deposition and sums with the ion species contributions — ion_absorbed_power_of_beam_tracing_beam and ion_state_absorbed_power_of_beam_tracing_beam — to give the species-summed [absorbed_power_of_beam_tracing_beam](name:absorbed_power_of_beam_tracing_beam).

The path-integrated electron absorbed power is determined by the local electron damping coefficient $\alpha_e(s)$ and the evolving beam power $P(s)$:

$$
P_{e,\mathrm{abs}} = \int_{\mathrm{path}} 2\,\alpha_e(s)\,P(s)\,ds
$$

where $s$ is the arc length along the ray and $\alpha_e$ derives from the electron contribution to the anti-Hermitian part of the plasma dielectric tensor. For electron cyclotron resonance heating and ECE diagnostics, $\alpha_e$ peaks near the resonance layer where the wave frequency satisfies $\omega = n\,\Omega_{ce}$, with $\Omega_{ce} = eB/m_e$ the local electron cyclotron frequency and $n$ a harmonic integer.

This quantity is computed by beam-tracing solvers that propagate ray equations through a plasma equilibrium and evaluate the electron dielectric response at each point along the path. The ratio $P_{e,\mathrm{abs}} / P_0$ — where $P_0$ is the [initial_power_of_beam_tracing_beam](name:initial_power_of_beam_tracing_beam) — characterizes single-pass absorption efficiency, which approaches unity in strongly absorbing scenarios such as fundamental or second-harmonic electron cyclotron resonance heating.

sources.enhanced_context: Power absorbed along the beam or ray path by the electron population during ECE beam tracing calculations. Quantifies local electron absorption of the probing electromagnetic wave as a function of position along the ray.
sources.leaf_definition: Power absorbed along the beam by the species
sources.parent_definition: Quantities related to the electrons

sources.enhanced_context: Wave power absorbed along a beam or ray path by the electron species, as computed by beam tracing. Represents the cumulative power deposition profile for electron heating from RF or EC waves along the propagation path.
sources.leaf_definition: Power absorbed along the beam by the species

NAMES.name: initial_power_of_beam_tracing_beam
NAMES.short: Electromagnetic wave power assigned to a single beam-tracing beam at launch, providing the reference for evaluating attenuation and plasma absorption along its trajectory.
NAMES.long:
The electromagnetic power associated with a single coherent-wave beam propagated through the plasma by beam-tracing methods at its launch point. It is the initial forward wave-power reference for the beam trajectory.

$$
P_{\mathrm{launch}} = P(0)
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{launch}}$ is the launch power and $P(s)$ is the beam power at arc length $s$ from the launch point. Along the trajectory, local absorption gives $dP/ds = -\alpha(\mathbf{r})P(s)$, where $\alpha(\mathbf{r})$ is the local wave power absorption coefficient at position $\mathbf{r}$. The launch value supplies the normalization for [power_of_beam_tracing_beam](name:power_of_beam_tracing_beam) and is distinct from [absorbed_power_of_beam_tracing_beam](name:absorbed_power_of_beam_tracing_beam), which is the net power transferred to the plasma. It is also distinct from [launched_power_of_wave_beam](name:launched_power_of_wave_beam), which denotes power entering the vacuum vessel rather than the beam-tracing launch-point quantity.

sources.enhanced_context: Initial power of a ray or beam at the starting point of beam-tracing calculations for an ECE channel. Represents the wave power carried at the launch point of the ray or beam propagation.
sources.leaf_definition: Initial power in the ray/beam
sources.parent_definition: Set of rays/beams describing the wave propagation

NAMES.name: launched_wave_frequency
NAMES.short: Launched wave frequency is the non-negative temporal carrier frequency of a coherent electromagnetic wave at launch. It is the absolute launch reference used when forming launch-referenced spectral frequency differences, not the frequency difference itself.
NAMES.long:
Launched wave frequency is the non-negative temporal carrier frequency of a coherent electromagnetic wave at the launching reference before any comparison with a returned or observed spectrum. It identifies the launched component used as the reference wave in launch-referenced spectral quantities.

For a coherent component with temporal phase $\varphi_\mathrm{launch}(t)$, the launch frequency is defined by the phase-rate magnitude:

$$
f_\mathrm{launch}(t) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\left|\frac{d\varphi_\mathrm{launch}}{dt}\right|
$$

where $\varphi_\mathrm{launch}(t)$ is the phase of the launched electric or magnetic field component and $t$ is time. For a steady sinusoidal component with period $T_\mathrm{launch}$, this reduces to $f_\mathrm{launch}=1/T_\mathrm{launch}$.

This quantity excludes the frequency of a received, reflected, or observed spectral feature and excludes any difference between such a feature and the launch reference. A launch-referenced offset such as [difference of reflected-wave spectral-peak frequency and launched-wave frequency](name:difference_of_reflected_wave_spectral_peak_frequency_and_launched_wave_frequency) is a separate signed quantity formed using $f_\mathrm{launch}$ as the reference operand.

sources.enhanced_context: Wave frequency (f) of a coherent electromagnetic wave in the plasma. Determines resonance conditions for wave-particle interactions and selects the relevant heating regime (EC, IC, LH).
sources.leaf_definition: Wave frequency
sources.parent_definition: Global quantities for various time slices

NAMES.name: line_averaged_electron_density
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Number density of free electrons per unit volume averaged along a plasma chord, obtained by dividing the electron-density path integral by chord length.
NAMES.long:
Number density of free electrons per unit volume averaged along a specified chord through a plasma is the path-length mean of the local unbound-electron density.

For a chord coordinate $l$ extending from $0$ to its total length $L$, the line-averaged electron density is defined by:

$$
\bar{n}_e = \frac{1}{L}\int_0^L n_e(l)\,dl
$$

where $n_e(l)$ is the local electron number density, [electron_density](name:electron_density), $l$ is distance along the chord in m, $L$ is the chord length in m, and $\bar{n}_e$ is the resulting line average. The quantity is distinct from the unnormalized line integral and from the local density; it represents their path-length-normalized value. The same averaging operation can be applied to other local plasma quantities, such as [line-averaged_electron_temperature](name:line_averaged_electron_temperature).

sources.enhanced_context: Line-average electron density (n̄e), the line-integrated electron density along the full interferometer chord divided by the chord length. May combine multiple wavelengths for dispersion correction.
sources.leaf_definition: Line average density, possibly obtained by a combination of multiple interferometry wavelengths. Corresponds to the density integrated along the full line-of-sight and then divided by the length of the line-of-sight
sources.parent_definition: Set of channels (lines-of-sight)

sources.enhanced_context: Line-averaged electron density (ne), the electron density averaged along a representative chord through the plasma. A standard global density measure used for density feedback control and confinement scaling.
sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Electron density

NAMES.name: normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.short: Dimensionless radial flux-surface label based on normalized toroidal magnetic flux, evaluated at the magnetic axis; it equals zero at this reference surface.
NAMES.long:
The normalized toroidal flux coordinate at the magnetic axis is the dimensionless radial label assigned to the magnetic-axis reference surface. It is the [normalized toroidal flux coordinate](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate) evaluated at the origin of the nested-flux-surface labeling, where the coordinate is zero and the outer normalization reference is the plasma boundary or last closed flux surface.

The coordinate is defined from the toroidal flux difference between the magnetic-axis surface and the boundary:

$$
\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}(\mathrm{axis}) = \sqrt{\frac{\Phi_0 - \Phi_0}{\Phi_b - \Phi_0}} = 0
$$

where $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ is the normalized toroidal flux coordinate, $\Phi_0$ is the toroidal magnetic flux at the magnetic axis, and $\Phi_b$ is the toroidal magnetic flux at the plasma boundary or last closed flux surface. This reference value is distinct from the coordinate evaluated at a displaced locus, such as the [normalized toroidal flux coordinate at the measurement position](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_measurement_position), and from the corresponding [normalized poloidal flux coordinate](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate).

NAMES.name: normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_measurement_position
NAMES.short: Dimensionless radial flux-surface label based on normalized toroidal magnetic flux, evaluated at a measurement position to identify its corresponding nested flux surface.
NAMES.long:
The normalized toroidal flux coordinate at a measurement position is the dimensionless radial label assigned to the nested flux surface passing through that position. It is the [normalized toroidal flux coordinate](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate) evaluated at the measurement position, with the origin at the magnetic axis and the outer normalization reference at the plasma boundary or last closed flux surface.

The coordinate is defined from the toroidal flux of the flux surface passing through the measurement position:

$$
\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{meas}}) = \sqrt{\frac{\Phi(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{meas}}) - \Phi_0}{\Phi_b - \Phi_0}}
$$

where $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{meas}}$ identifies the measurement position, $\Phi(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{meas}})$ is the toroidal magnetic flux of the corresponding flux surface, $\Phi_0$ is the magnetic-axis toroidal magnetic flux, and $\Phi_b$ is the boundary toroidal magnetic flux. The square root gives a nonnegative radial coordinate that runs from zero at the magnetic axis toward unity at the boundary.

This quantity is a flux-surface coordinate evaluated at a measurement position, not a measurement signal or a toroidal-flux value. It is distinct from the [normalized toroidal flux coordinate at the magnetic axis](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_magnetic_axis), which is exactly zero by definition.

NAMES.name: perpendicular_wave_vector
NAMES.short: Perpendicular wave-vector component describing spatial phase variation transverse to the local equilibrium magnetic field and the cross-field scale of wave-plasma coupling.
NAMES.long:
The perpendicular wave vector is the part of the local wave vector associated with phase variation transverse to the local equilibrium magnetic field. Its magnitude sets the cross-field spatial scale relevant to wave–plasma coupling and density-fluctuation backscattering.

For wave vector $\mathbf{k}$ and unit vector $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$ parallel to the local equilibrium magnetic field, the perpendicular wave-vector magnitude is defined by:

$$
k_\perp = \left|\mathbf{k} - (\mathbf{k}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{b}})\hat{\mathbf{b}}\right|
$$

where $k_\perp$ is the perpendicular wavenumber, $\mathbf{k}$ is the wave vector, and $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$ is dimensionless. This quantity excludes the component parallel to the equilibrium magnetic field. It specializes the spatial phase-gradient information carried by the [wave vector](name:wave_vector); the [perpendicular wave-vector magnitude](name:perpendicular_wave_vector_magnitude) is its explicit magnitude form. It differs from the [vertical wave vector](name:vertical_wave_vector), which is resolved along the geometric vertical direction rather than relative to the magnetic field.

NAMES.name: perpendicular_wave_vector_magnitude
NAMES.short: Non-negative magnitude of the wave vector transverse to the local equilibrium magnetic field, setting the inverse cross-field phase scale.
NAMES.long:
The perpendicular wave-vector magnitude is the non-negative length of the part of a local electromagnetic wave vector transverse to the equilibrium magnetic field. It characterizes cross-field phase variation and is the scalar magnitude associated with the [perpendicular wave vector](name:perpendicular_wave_vector).

For wave vector $\mathbf{k}$ and magnetic-field unit vector $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$, the perpendicular magnitude is defined by

$$
k_\perp = \left|\mathbf{k} - (\mathbf{k}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{b}})\hat{\mathbf{b}}\right|
$$

where $k_\perp$ and $\mathbf{k}$ have units of inverse length, and $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$ is tangent to the local equilibrium magnetic-field direction. The quantity excludes the wave-vector component parallel to the magnetic field and is non-negative by definition.

NAMES.name: poloidal_angle_of_measurement_position
NAMES.short: Poloidal angle of a diagnostic measurement position in the poloidal cross-section of the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, measured clockwise from the outward radial direction about the magnetic axis.
NAMES.long:
The poloidal angle of a diagnostic measurement position is the angular coordinate of that point about the magnetic axis in a poloidal cross-section of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It is the measurement-position form of [poloidal angle](name:poloidal_angle).

For a measurement position with coordinates $(R,Z)$ and magnetic-axis coordinates $(R_\mathrm{ax},Z_\mathrm{ax})$, the angle is

$$
\theta=\operatorname{atan2}(Z_\mathrm{ax}-Z,\,R-R_\mathrm{ax})\pmod{2\pi}
$$

where $\theta$ is the poloidal angle, $R$ and $R_\mathrm{ax}$ are major-radius coordinates in meters, $Z$ and $Z_\mathrm{ax}$ are vertical coordinates in meters, and $\operatorname{atan2}$ returns the quadrant-resolved angle. Unlike [poloidal angle of a flux-surface point](name:poloidal_angle_of_flux_surface), this quantity applies to a diagnostic measurement position and does not require the position to be identified as a point on a flux surface.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the measurement position lies clockwise from the outward $+R$ direction when viewed from the $+\phi$ direction.

NAMES.name: radiative_temperature_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.short: Radiative temperature at the magnetic axis is the blackbody-equivalent brightness temperature of electron cyclotron emission from the resonance layer nearest the magnetic axis.
NAMES.long:
Radiative temperature at the magnetic axis is the local blackbody-equivalent brightness temperature assigned to electron cyclotron emission from the resonance layer nearest the central singular point of the confined plasma. It is the radiative component of [temperature_at_magnetic_axis](name:temperature_at_magnetic_axis), rather than a direct definition of the local kinetic electron temperature.

The energy-equivalent brightness temperature is defined by the blackbody relation

$$
I_\nu = \frac{2h\nu^3}{c^2\left[\exp\left(h\nu/\Theta_{\rm rad}\right)-1\right]}
$$

where $I_\nu$ is the specific intensity, $\nu$ is frequency, $h$ is Planck's constant, $c$ is the speed of light, and $\Theta_{\rm rad}$ is the radiative temperature expressed as energy. The magnetic-axis locus is defined by $\nabla\psi=0$, where $\psi$ is poloidal magnetic flux.

For optically thick thermal emission, this quantity approaches the local electron kinetic temperature represented by [electron_temperature_at_magnetic_axis](name:electron_temperature_at_magnetic_axis); it remains a brightness-temperature proxy and can differ when the emission is not optically thick. The corresponding non-local radiative quantity is [radiative_temperature](name:radiative_temperature).

NAMES.name: wave_electric_field
NAMES.short: Complex vector phasor of a coherent electromagnetic-wave electric field, capturing its local amplitude, phase, and polarization as the oscillatory contribution to the total electric field.
NAMES.long:
The wave electric field is the complex vector phasor representing the oscillatory electromagnetic-wave contribution to the local [electric field](name:electric_field). It retains the wave amplitude, phase, and polarization before any spatial projection or spectral mode decomposition.

For a single angular frequency, the physical wave field is defined by

$$
\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{wave}}(\mathbf{r},t)=\operatorname{Re}\left\{\widetilde{\mathbf{E}}_{\mathrm{wave}}(\mathbf{r},\omega)e^{-i\omega t}\right\}
$$

where $\widetilde{\mathbf{E}}_{\mathrm{wave}}$ is the complex wave-electric-field phasor, $\mathbf{r}$ is position, $t$ is time, and $\omega$ is angular frequency. Its projections include the [parallel wave electric field](name:parallel_wave_electric_field) and [vertical wave electric field](name:vertical_wave_electric_field); its toroidal Fourier components are represented by the [per-toroidal-mode electric field](name:per_toroidal_mode_electric_field). The quantity excludes electrostatic and non-wave contributions unless they are explicitly part of the identified electromagnetic wave.

NAMES.name: left_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field
NAMES.short: Complex phasor of the E-plus left-hand circular polarization component of an electromagnetic-wave electric field in a magnetized plasma.
NAMES.long:
The left-hand circularly polarized wave electric field is the E-plus complex phasor obtained by projecting the electromagnetic-wave electric-field phasor onto the circular polarization basis transverse to the local equilibrium magnetic field. It retains both polarization amplitude and phase and is a component of the [wave electric field](name:wave_electric_field).

Using the negative-time-harmonic convention, the component is defined by

$$
E_{+}=\mathbf{E}_{w}\cdot\mathbf{e}_{+}^{*},\qquad \mathbf{e}_{+}=\frac{\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{1}+i\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{2}}{\sqrt{2}},\qquad \hat{\mathbf{e}}_{1}\times\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{2}=\hat{\mathbf{b}},\qquad \hat{\mathbf{b}}=\frac{\mathbf{B}_{0}}{|\mathbf{B}_{0}|}
$$

where $\mathbf{E}_{w}$ is the complex wave-electric-field phasor, $\mathbf{B}_{0}$ is the local background magnetic field, $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$ is its unit direction, the transverse unit vectors $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{1}$ and $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{2}$ form a right-handed basis, and the asterisk denotes complex conjugation. The associated physical field uses $\exp(-i\omega t)$, so this component carries phase information rather than representing a field magnitude. Its real-part sibling [left-hand circularly polarized wave electric field real part](name:left_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_real_part) provides one quadrature, while the [right-hand circularly polarized wave electric field](name:right_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field) represents the opposite circular polarization.

NAMES.name: left_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_real_part
NAMES.short: Signed in-phase real quadrature of the E-plus wave electric-field phasor in the left-hand circular polarization basis.
NAMES.long:
Signed in-phase real quadrature of the $E_+$ wave electric-field phasor in the left-hand circular polarization basis is the real component of the complex coefficient obtained by projecting the wave electric-field phasor onto the normalized left-hand circular basis perpendicular to the local background magnetic field. It retains the phase-relative sign of that coefficient and is distinct from the non-negative modulus $|E_+|$.

With harmonic time dependence $\tilde{\mathbf{E}}\exp(-i\omega t)$ and $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_+=(\hat{\mathbf{e}}_1+i\hat{\mathbf{e}}_2)/\sqrt{2}$, this quantity is defined by the Hermitian projection

$$
E_{+,\mathrm{re}} = \operatorname{Re}\!\left[\hat{\mathbf{e}}_+^{\,*}\cdot\tilde{\mathbf{E}}\right]
$$

where $\tilde{\mathbf{E}}$ is the complex wave electric-field phasor, $\operatorname{Re}$ denotes the real-part operator, the star denotes complex conjugation, $\hat{\mathbf{b}}=\mathbf{B}_0/|\mathbf{B}_0|$ is the local background magnetic-field direction, and $(\hat{\mathbf{e}}_1,\hat{\mathbf{e}}_2,\hat{\mathbf{b}})$ is an orthonormal triad with $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_1\times\hat{\mathbf{e}}_2=\hat{\mathbf{b}}$.

Together with the [left-hand circularly polarized wave electric-field imaginary part](name:left_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_imaginary_part), it forms the complex coefficient $E_+=E_{+,\mathrm{re}}+iE_{+,\mathrm{im}}$. The complete local phasor in the circular-and-parallel basis is reconstructed as $\tilde{\mathbf{E}}=E_+\hat{\mathbf{e}}_+ + E_-\hat{\mathbf{e}}_- + E_\parallel\hat{\mathbf{b}}$, where $E_-$ is the right-hand circular coefficient and $E_\parallel$ is the field-aligned coefficient.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the reference-phase left-hand circularly polarized phasor corresponds, for $E_-=E_\parallel=0$, to an electric field pointing along $+\hat{\mathbf{e}}_1$ and rotating toward $+\hat{\mathbf{e}}_2$ about $+\hat{\mathbf{b}}$ under the $\exp(-i\omega t)$ time dependence.

NAMES.name: parallel_wave_electric_field
NAMES.short: Complex phasor of the wave electric field projected along the local equilibrium magnetic-field direction in a magnetized plasma.
NAMES.long:
The parallel wave electric field is the complex phasor obtained by projecting the electromagnetic-wave electric-field phasor onto the local equilibrium magnetic-field direction. It retains both amplitude and phase and is a component of the [wave electric field](name:wave_electric_field).

The parallel component is defined by

$$
E_{\parallel}=\mathbf{E}_{w}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{b}},\qquad \hat{\mathbf{b}}=\frac{\mathbf{B}_{0}}{|\mathbf{B}_{0}|}
$$

where $\mathbf{E}_{w}$ is the complex wave-electric-field phasor, $\mathbf{B}_{0}$ is the local equilibrium magnetic field, and $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$ is its unit direction. The phasor carries the phase of the harmonic field under the selected time convention.

This quantity is the complex component rather than its magnitude. Its modulus gives the [parallel wave electric field amplitude](name:parallel_wave_electric_field_amplitude), while its quadratures include the [parallel wave electric field imaginary part](name:parallel_wave_electric_field_imaginary_part) and the corresponding real part.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the electric-field component is directed along the local equilibrium magnetic-field direction $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$.

NAMES.name: parallel_wave_electric_field_imaginary_part
NAMES.short: Imaginary quadrature component of the complex wave electric-field phasor projected along the local equilibrium magnetic-field direction.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the signed imaginary quadrature component of the parallel electromagnetic wave electric-field phasor. It retains phase information and is not the field amplitude or magnitude.

$$
\tilde E_\parallel = \tilde{\mathbf E}\cdot\hat{\mathbf b} = E_{\parallel,R}+iE_{\parallel,I},\qquad E_{\parallel,I}=\operatorname{Im}(\tilde E_\parallel)
$$

Here $\tilde{\mathbf E}$ is the complex wave electric-field phasor, $\hat{\mathbf b}$ is the unit vector along the local equilibrium magnetic field, and $E_{\parallel,R}$ and $E_{\parallel,I}$ are its real and imaginary quadrature components. The imaginary component, together with the [parallel wave electric field](name:parallel_wave_electric_field), specifies the complex parallel field; its algebraic sign follows the selected temporal phasor convention. It is distinct from the [parallel wave electric field amplitude](name:parallel_wave_electric_field_amplitude).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the imaginary quadrature electric-field component points along the local equilibrium magnetic-field direction.

NAMES.name: parallel_wave_electric_field_real_part
NAMES.short: Real, in-phase coefficient of the wave electric-field phasor projected along the local equilibrium magnetic-field direction, complementing its quadrature coefficient.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the in-phase coefficient of the complex [parallel wave electric field](name:parallel_wave_electric_field) phasor, resolved along the local equilibrium magnetic-field direction. It represents the component aligned with the chosen phasor phase reference, not the field magnitude or instantaneous electric field.

$$
E_{parallel,mathrm{R}} = operatorname{Re}\!\left(E_{parallel}\right)
$$

where $E_{parallel}$ is the complex parallel wave-electric-field phasor, $E_{parallel,mathrm{R}}$ is its real coefficient, and $\operatorname{Re}$ denotes the real-part operator. The phase reference is the same one used for the corresponding [parallel wave electric field imaginary part](name:parallel_wave_electric_field_imaginary_part); together, the two coefficients specify the complex phasor. The coefficient is signed according to projection onto the selected local magnetic-field direction.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the in-phase electric-field coefficient points along the chosen local equilibrium magnetic-field direction.

NAMES.name: right_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field
NAMES.short: Complex phasor of the right-hand circularly polarized (E-minus) component of the wave electric field, projected onto the circular polarization basis constructed from the transverse plane perpendicular to the local equilibrium magnetic field.
NAMES.long:
The right-hand circularly polarized wave electric field is the E-minus component of the transverse wave electric field in a magnetized plasma, obtained by projecting the full [wave electric field](name:left_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field) phasor onto the right-hand circular polarization basis. In the local orthonormal frame $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{b})$, where $\hat{b}$ is the unit vector along the equilibrium magnetic field and $\hat{x} \times \hat{y} = \hat{b}$, the component is defined as

$$
E_- = \frac{E_x - i E_y}{\sqrt{2}}
$$

where $E_x$ and $E_y$ are the complex transverse Cartesian components of the wave electric field phasor.

The full complex phasor encodes both amplitude and phase. Its real and imaginary quadrature components are individually given by [right_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_real_part](name:right_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_real_part) and [right_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_imaginary_part](name:right_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_imaginary_part), while the nonnegative modulus $|E_-|$ is provided by right_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_amplitude. The complementary left-hand circular component (E+) is documented under [left_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field](name:left_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field). In ion-cyclotron-range-of-frequencies heating, the relative magnitude of $E_-$ characterizes the right-hand polarization fraction of the wave and governs coupling to electron-cyclotron and right-hand-cutoff resonances along the wave propagation path.
