NAMES.name: right_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_imaginary_part
NAMES.short: Imaginary quadrature component of the complex E-minus wave electric-field phasor in the right-hand circular polarization basis.
NAMES.long:
The imaginary quadrature coefficient is the component of the [right-hand circularly polarized wave electric field](name:right_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field) that is 90 degrees out of phase with its real component.

$$
E_{-,I} = \operatorname{Im}(\widetilde{E}_{-}), \qquad \widetilde{E}_{-} = E_{-,R} + iE_{-,I}
$$

Here, $\widetilde{E}_{-}$ is the complex E-minus phasor, $E_{-,I}$ is its imaginary quadrature coefficient, $E_{-,R}$ is its real coefficient, and $i$ is the imaginary unit. The decomposition uses the adopted time-harmonic phasor convention; the imaginary coefficient is not the field magnitude and must be combined with the real component to recover the phasor amplitude and phase. The corresponding [real part](name:right_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_real_part) provides the in-phase coefficient.

NAMES.name: right_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_real_part
NAMES.short: Signed in-phase real quadrature of the E-minus electric-field phasor in the right-hand circular polarization basis.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the in-phase real quadrature of the complex right-hand circularly polarized, or E-minus, wave electric-field phasor. It preserves the signed field component relative to the phase reference of the parent [right-hand circularly polarized wave electric field](name:right_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field), rather than representing the field magnitude.

It is defined by

$$
E_{-,R} = \operatorname{Re}(E_-)
$$

where $E_-$ is the parent complex E-minus phasor, $E_{-,R}$ is its real quadrature, and $\operatorname{Re}$ denotes the real-part operator.

The complementary quadrature is [the imaginary part of the right-hand circularly polarized wave electric field](name:right_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_imaginary_part); together, the real and imaginary quadratures reconstruct the parent complex phasor.

NAMES.name: toroidal_wave_electric_field
NAMES.short: Complex phasor component of the electromagnetic-wave electric field projected onto the toroidal φ direction at the evaluation point in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame. It represents the signed toroidal polarization component, not an instantaneous field value.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal wave electric field $E_\phi$ is the complex phasor component of an electromagnetic-wave electric-field vector along $\hat{\phi}$, the toroidal basis vector of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It is a coordinate component of the [wave electric field](name:wave_electric_field), retaining both amplitude and phase.

Using the negative-time-harmonic convention, the component is defined by

$$
E_\phi(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{E}_{w}(\mathbf{x}) \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\mathbf{E}_{w}$ is the complex wave-electric-field phasor in volts per meter, $\mathbf{x}$ is the evaluation point, and $\hat{\phi}$ points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The associated physical field uses $\operatorname{Re}[\mathbf{E}_{w}\exp(-i\omega t)]$, so $E_\phi$ is a phase-referenced phasor component rather than an instantaneous real field value.

This quantity is the toroidal coordinate component, distinct from the non-wave [toroidal electric field](name:toroidal_electric_field), from the vertical coordinate component [vertical wave electric field](name:vertical_wave_electric_field), and from components defined relative to magnetic geometry such as the [parallel wave electric field](name:parallel_wave_electric_field) or [radial wave electric field](name:radial_wave_electric_field).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the real toroidal component of the wave electric field points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_wave_electric_field
NAMES.short: Complex phasor of the wave electric field projected onto the vertical Z direction in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, preserving local amplitude, phase, and vertical polarization.
NAMES.long:
The vertical wave electric field is the complex phasor component of an electromagnetic-wave electric-field vector along the vertical direction. It preserves the local amplitude and phase of the vertical polarization of the [wave electric field](name:wave_electric_field), distinct from its parallel and flux-surface-normal components.

The vertical projection is defined by:

$$
\tilde{E}_Z(\mathbf{r}) = \tilde{\mathbf{E}}(\mathbf{r}) \cdot \hat{Z}
$$

where $\tilde{E}_Z$ is the vertical wave-electric-field phasor in V m$^{-1}$, $\tilde{\mathbf{E}}$ is the full wave-electric-field phasor in V m$^{-1}$, $\mathbf{r}$ is position in m, and $\hat{Z}$ is the vertical unit vector of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The component is a wave phasor, not an instantaneous field value or a magnitude; the equilibrium or slowly varying contribution represented by [vertical electric field](name:vertical_electric_field) is excluded.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the projected phasor component is oriented along the $+Z$ direction, toward increasing vertical height in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: wavelength_of_wave_beam
NAMES.short: Wavelength of a wave beam is the spectral coordinate, expressed as vacuum wavelength, that identifies one phase period of a probing electromagnetic beam along its propagation direction.
NAMES.long:
Wavelength of a wave beam is the spectral coordinate, expressed as vacuum wavelength, that identifies one phase period of a probing electromagnetic beam along its propagation direction. It is a property of the launched or incident wave component and not of a detector response that may observe radiation produced by the beam interaction.

For a monochromatic plane-wave component in vacuum, wavelength is related to vacuum wave-vector magnitude and frequency by

$$
\lambda_0 = \frac{2\pi}{|\mathbf{k}_0|} = \frac{c}{\nu}
$$

where $\lambda_0$ is the vacuum wavelength, $\mathbf{k}_0$ is the vacuum wave vector, $|\mathbf{k}_0|$ is its magnitude, $c$ is the speed of light in vacuum, and $\nu$ is the ordinary frequency. The angular frequency satisfies $\omega = 2\pi\nu = c|\mathbf{k}_0|$ for the same wave component.

For finite-bandwidth or pulsed beams, this quantity denotes the specified central or carrier vacuum wavelength. Propagation through plasma or material media changes the local wavelength through the refractive index, but does not change this vacuum reference wavelength. It is the wavelength counterpart of [launched_wave_frequency](name:launched_wave_frequency), is related to [wave_vector](name:wave_vector) and [wave_phase_of_wave_beam](name:wave_phase_of_wave_beam), and is distinct from detection-side spectral coordinates such as [wavelength_of_spectrometer_channel](name:wavelength_of_spectrometer_channel).

NAMES.name: current_density
NAMES.short: Current density is the vector flux density of conventional electric charge, equal to electric current per unit area normal to the flow. It points in the direction of positive charge transport and includes all charged-particle contributions unless a narrower current-density quantity is specified.
NAMES.long:
Current density $\mathbf{J}$ is the vector density of conventional electric charge flux at a point. It represents the signed flow of electric charge carried by charged particles, with direction defined by positive charge transport.

A kinetic definition is the charge-weighted first velocity moment of the particle distribution functions:

$$
\mathbf{J}(\mathbf{x},t) = \sum_s q_s \int \mathbf{v}\, f_s(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v},t)\, d^3v
$$

where $\mathbf{x}$ is position, $t$ is time, $s$ indexes charged species, $q_s$ is the species charge, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity, and $f_s$ is the velocity-space distribution function. In quasistatic equilibrium it is the source term in Ampere's law, $\nabla \times \mathbf{B} = \mu_0 \mathbf{J}$ when displacement current is neglected, and steady charge conservation gives $\nabla \cdot \mathbf{J}=0$.

This quantity excludes displacement-current density and is distinct from a scalar electric current, which is the flux of $\mathbf{J}$ through a specified surface. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, the geometric components are the projections along $(\hat{R}, \hat{\phi}, \hat{Z})$: radial_current_density, [toroidal_current_density](name:toroidal_current_density), and [vertical_current_density](name:vertical_current_density). The full vector has direction rather than a single scalar sign; scalar components and projections inherit the positive direction of their defining basis vector or unit vector.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the stated component or scalar projection of $\mathbf{J}$ is aligned with the positive direction of the basis vector or unit vector defining that component or projection.

NAMES.name: current_of_passive_structure
NAMES.short: Net conventional electric current circulating toroidally in a passive conducting structure, induced electromagnetically rather than driven by an external power supply.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the net conventional electric current circulating in a passive conducting structure. It represents an induced current caused by changing magnetic flux linked with the structure, including contributions from the plasma, active coils, and neighboring conducting structures, rather than an intentionally supplied drive current.

For an oriented cross-section $S$ of the structure, the net current is defined by

$$
I_{\mathrm{passive}} = \int_S \mathbf{J} \cdot d\mathbf{S}
$$

where $\mathbf{J}$ is the conventional electric-current density and $d\mathbf{S}$ is the oriented area element normal to the toroidal current path.

This is a structure-level net current. [Current of a passive loop](name:current_of_passive_loop) is the corresponding quantity for one identified passive loop, while [toroidal current of the vacuum vessel](name:toroidal_current_of_vacuum_vessel) is the vessel-specific case.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the net current flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: current_of_plasma_filament
NAMES.short: Electric current carried by a single discrete plasma-filament element in an axisymmetric filamentary representation of the distributed plasma current.
NAMES.long:
In the filamentary model of an axisymmetric plasma, the spatially distributed plasma current is represented as an array of discrete annular current-carrying elements, each called a filament. The current of each element is its individual contribution to the net toroidal plasma current, and the ensemble of filament currents constitutes a discrete model of the plasma current density distribution across the poloidal cross-section.

The total plasma current $I_p$ is recovered by summing the contributions from all filament elements:

$$
I_p = \sum_k I_k
$$

where $I_k$ is the current of the $k$-th filament element and the sum runs over all elements in the filamentary array.

Filament currents are determined during equilibrium reconstruction or electromagnetic circuit-equation integration, treating the plasma as a collection of discrete current sources. Each filament element is fully characterized by its current together with its geometric descriptors — including area_of_plasma_filament, [inner_radius_of_plasma_filament](name:inner_radius_of_plasma_filament), and [outer_radius_of_plasma_filament](name:outer_radius_of_plasma_filament) — which together define the local current-density contribution. The analogous quantity for the conducting vessel structure is [toroidal_current_of_vacuum_vessel](name:toroidal_current_of_vacuum_vessel).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the current flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$).

NAMES.name: current_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Conventional electrical current through a poloidal-field coil winding, with sign set by winding orientation and distinct from the winding’s ampere-turn product.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the conventional current carried by the conductor forming a poloidal-field coil winding. It describes the circuit current itself, independent of the number of turns in the winding, and is the poloidal-field-coil counterpart of [current of a toroidal-field coil](name:current_of_toroidal_field_coil).

The current is defined by the rate of conventional charge flow:

$$
I = \frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

where $I$ is the winding current, $Q$ is the net transported electric charge, and $t$ is time. For a winding with $N$ series-connected turns, its magnetomotive effect is proportional to the ampere-turn product $NI$; $N$ is the dimensionless number of turns. This quantity is not the coil resistance or the resulting voltage drop, which is related to [poloidal-field-coil resistance](name:resistance_of_poloidal_field_coil).
NAMES.sign: Positive when conventional current follows the positive reference direction assigned around the poloidal-field-coil winding.

NAMES.name: electron_density
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Number density of free electrons per physical volume for the local continuum plasma state, excluding spatial averages that have distinct standard names.
NAMES.long:
Number density of free electrons per physical volume is the local continuum count density of electrons not bound to atoms, molecules, or ions. Unless a population qualifier is present, it denotes the unqualified local free-electron density at a point, not a line-averaged or volume-averaged quantity.

For a representative physical volume surrounding the point, the defining ratio is:

$$
n_e = \frac{N_e}{V}
$$

where $n_e$ is the electron density, $N_e$ is the number of free electrons in the representative volume, and $V$ is that physical volume. The continuum value is understood for volumes small on macroscopic plasma scales but large enough to contain many particles.

Population-specific quantities are distinct: [thermal_electron_density](name:thermal_electron_density) and [fast_electron_density](name:fast_electron_density) denote component densities, while [total_electron_density](name:total_electron_density) denotes the explicit aggregate over the free-electron populations in a decomposition, for example $n_{e,\mathrm{tot}} = n_{e,\mathrm{thermal}} + n_{e,\mathrm{fast}}$ when those are the only components. Spatially averaged quantities such as [line_averaged_electron_density](name:line_averaged_electron_density) and [volume_averaged_electron_density](name:volume_averaged_electron_density) are separate from this local density.

NAMES.name: elongation_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short: Dimensionless vertical-to-horizontal aspect ratio of a nested magnetic flux-surface cross-section, defining its poloidal elongation independently of overall size.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal elongation is the aspect ratio of a nested magnetic flux-surface cross-section, comparing its vertical extent with its radial extent. It describes plasma shaping independently of the surface's absolute size.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height, the elongation of the surface labeled by $\psi$ is defined by

$$
\kappa(\psi) = \frac{a_Z(\psi)}{a_R(\psi)}
$$

where $a_Z$ and $a_R$ are the vertical and radial semi-extents of that flux surface, and $\psi$ is its magnetic-flux label.

This parent quantity applies to every nested magnetic flux surface; the boundary-specific case is [elongation of the plasma boundary](name:elongation_of_plasma_boundary). Its radial variation is described by [radial derivative of elongation of the flux surface](name:radial_derivative_of_elongation_of_flux_surface).

sources.enhanced_context: Elongation (κ) of nested magnetic flux surfaces as a 1D radial profile in the MHD equilibrium, defined as the ratio of the vertical to horizontal semi-axis of each flux surface. Characterizes plasma shape as a function of the poloidal flux coordinate.
sources.leaf_definition: Elongation
sources.parent_definition: Equilibrium profiles (1D radial grid) as a function of the poloidal flux

NAMES.name: elongation_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Dimensionless ratio of the full vertical extent to the full radial extent of the last closed magnetic-flux-surface cross-section.
NAMES.long:
Plasma-boundary elongation measures the vertical stretching of the last closed magnetic-flux-surface cross-section relative to its radial width. It is evaluated at fixed toroidal angle in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height.

The defining ratio is

$$
\kappa_b = \frac{Z_{\max}-Z_{\min}}{R_{\max}-R_{\min}}
$$

where $Z_{\max}$ and $Z_{\min}$ are the maximum and minimum vertical coordinates of the boundary, and $R_{\max}$ and $R_{\min}$ are its maximum and minimum radial coordinates.

This full-extent boundary measure is distinct from [elongation_of_flux_surface](name:elongation_of_flux_surface), which characterizes individual nested flux surfaces, and from [minor_radius_of_plasma_boundary](name:minor_radius_of_plasma_boundary), which characterizes radial half-width.

NAMES.name: external_loop_voltage
NAMES.short: Electromotive-force contribution to the plasma loop voltage caused by changing externally generated poloidal magnetic flux, including flux linked through active coils and passive conducting structures.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the inductive electromotive-force contribution to the plasma loop voltage produced by time-varying poloidal magnetic flux generated by active coil circuits and magnetically coupled passive conducting structures. It excludes resistive voltage drops and other non-inductive contributions.

The contribution is defined by Faraday's law:

$$
V_{\mathrm{ext}}(t) = -\frac{d\Phi_{\mathrm{ext}}(t)}{dt}
$$

where $\Phi_{\mathrm{ext}}$ is the externally generated poloidal magnetic flux linked by the considered toroidal plasma circuit and $t$ is time. It contributes to the total [loop voltage at the plasma boundary](name:loop_voltage_at_plasma_boundary); currents in passive conductors are represented by the linked-flux response of structures such as those described by [current of passive structure](name:current_of_passive_structure).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the induced electromotive force has a positive line integral in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

sources.enhanced_context: External voltage (V_ext), defined as the negative time derivative of the externally applied average poloidal flux (−dψ_ext/dt). Represents the inductive voltage from external poloidal field coils driving plasma current.

NAMES.name: gap_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Gap at the plasma boundary is the geometric distance from the closest-wall point to the plasma boundary. It quantifies the clearance between the nearest wall location and the outermost closed flux surface.
NAMES.long:
Gap at the plasma boundary is the geometric distance from the closest-wall point to the plasma boundary. The plasma boundary is the outermost closed flux surface that bounds the confined plasma.

Let $W$ be the wall surface from which the closest-wall point is selected and let $\Gamma_b$ denote the plasma-boundary surface. The gap $g$ is defined as the minimum Euclidean separation between these surfaces:

$$
g = \min_{\mathbf{x}_w \in W,\ \mathbf{x}_b \in \Gamma_b} \left\lVert \mathbf{x}_w - \mathbf{x}_b \right\rVert
$$

where $\mathbf{x}_w$ and $\mathbf{x}_b$ are physical position vectors on the wall and plasma-boundary surfaces, respectively, and the norm is the Euclidean distance in physical space. A minimizing point on $W$ is the closest-wall point, and the corresponding line segment to $\Gamma_b$ is the geometric separation whose length is $g$.

The value is non-negative and is zero only when the closest-wall point lies on the plasma boundary. It denotes wall-plasma clearance, not the coordinates of the closest-wall point, a flux-coordinate difference, a prescribed wall-normal or flux-surface-normal projection, or the [radius of plasma boundary](name:radius_of_plasma_boundary).

sources.enhanced_context: Distance from the nearest first-wall point to the reconstructed plasma boundary. Quantifies the plasma-wall gap at the closest wall location, a key geometric parameter for limiter and confinement margin assessment.
sources.leaf_definition: Distance to the plasma boundary
sources.parent_definition: Position and distance to the plasma boundary of the point of the first wall which is the closest to plasma boundary

NAMES.name: height_of_plasma_filament
NAMES.short: Full vertical extent of the rectangular cross-section of a discrete plasma current-carrying filament element, measured along the machine’s vertical axis.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the full vertical dimension of the rectangular cross-section associated with one discrete plasma current-carrying filament. It is a geometric extent, not the filament current or its current density.

The height $H$ is defined by the difference between the upper and lower vertical coordinates:

$$
H = Z_{\mathrm{upper}} - Z_{\mathrm{lower}}
$$

where $Z_{\mathrm{upper}}$ and $Z_{\mathrm{lower}}$ are the upper and lower coordinates in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, with $Z$ denoting vertical height and $\hat{Z}$ the vertical basis direction.

This quantity applies only to the vertical dimension of the rectangular filament cross-section. The horizontal full width is defined separately by [plasma filament width](name:plasma_filament_width), while the in-plane thickness is defined by [thickness of plasma filament](name:thickness_of_plasma_filament).

sources.leaf_definition: Vertical full height
sources.parent_definition: Rectangular description of the element

NAMES.name: inner_squareness_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short: Dimensionless Luce shape coefficient quantifying how much the high-field-side (inner) corners of a nested magnetic flux surface deviate from a reference ellipse; positive values indicate a boxier corner, negative values a more diamond-like or indented corner.
NAMES.long:
The inner squareness of a flux surface is the dimensionless Luce (2013) shape coefficient that characterizes how much the high-field-side (inboard, smaller major radius) corners of a nested toroidal magnetic flux surface depart from a reference ellipse sharing the same center, horizontal half-width, and [elongation](name:elongation_of_flux_surface). It is the inboard counterpart within the [squareness_of_flux_surface](name:squareness_of_flux_surface) family, complementing the outboard variants [upper_outer_squareness_of_flux_surface](name:upper_outer_squareness_of_flux_surface) and [lower_outer_squareness_of_flux_surface](name:lower_outer_squareness_of_flux_surface). This parent quantity abstracts over the quadrant-resolved coefficients [upper_inner_squareness_of_flux_surface](name:upper_inner_squareness_of_flux_surface) and [lower_inner_squareness_of_flux_surface](name:lower_inner_squareness_of_flux_surface), which independently describe the upper and lower high-field-side corners.

The coefficient $\zeta$ enters the parametric flux-surface shape model as an additional harmonic beyond elongation $\kappa$ and triangularity $\delta$, evaluated at the high-field-side corners of the poloidal cross-section in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height. A value of zero recovers the reference ellipse precisely; deviations capture corner shaping not expressible through $\kappa$ and $\delta$ alone.

The inner squareness is inferred from equilibrium reconstruction by fitting closed flux-surface contours to a multi-parameter shape model. Asymmetry between upper and lower inner quadrants can arise in vertically asymmetric or diverted configurations, motivating the quadrant-resolved child quantities.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the high-field-side corner of the flux-surface cross-section extends outward beyond the reference ellipse (boxy shape); negative when the corner is indented inward relative to the reference ellipse (diamond-like shape).

NAMES.name: length_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Geometric perimeter of the last closed magnetic-flux-surface contour in a poloidal cross-section at fixed toroidal angle.
NAMES.long:
The plasma-boundary arc length is the geometric perimeter of the closed last-closed-flux-surface contour in a poloidal cross-section at fixed toroidal angle. It measures the boundary curve itself, not the area it encloses or the area of the full toroidal surface.

For a boundary curve $C$ at fixed $phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, the arc length is defined by:

$$
L_C = \oint_C ds = \oint_C \sqrt{(dR)^2 + (dZ)^2}
$$

where $L_C$ is the arc length, $s$ is differential curve length, $R$ is major-radius coordinate, $Z$ is vertical coordinate, and $\phi$ is toroidal angle. The curve is traversed once around the plasma boundary. The enclosed region is characterized separately by the [poloidal cross-sectional area of the plasma boundary](name:poloidal_cross_sectional_area_of_plasma_boundary), while the corresponding three-dimensional surface measure is the [surface area of a flux surface](name:surface_area_of_flux_surface).

sources.enhanced_context: Poloidal arc length of the magnetic flux surface boundary contour in the poloidal plane (length_pol). A geometric property of the equilibrium flux surface used in flux-surface-averaged quantities.
sources.leaf_definition: Poloidal length of the magnetic surface
sources.parent_definition: 0D parameters of the equilibrium

NAMES.name: lower_inner_squareness_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short: Dimensionless Luce (2013) squareness coefficient for the lower-inner, high-field-side quadrant of a nested magnetic flux surface, measuring signed departure from a reference ellipse.
NAMES.long:
The lower-inner squareness of a flux surface is the dimensionless Luce (2013) shape coefficient that characterizes how the lower, high-field-side quadrant of a nested toroidal magnetic flux surface departs from a reference ellipse sharing the same center, horizontal half-width, and [elongation](name:elongation_of_flux_surface). It is the lower-quadrant component of [inner squareness of a flux surface](name:inner_squareness_of_flux_surface), complementary to [upper-inner squareness of a flux surface](name:upper_inner_squareness_of_flux_surface).

The reference ellipse is parameterized in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame by

$$
\mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{ref}}(\theta)=\left(R_0+a\cos\theta,\;Z_0+\kappa a\sin\theta\right)
$$

where $R$ is major radius, $Z$ is vertical height, $\theta$ is a poloidal parameter, $(R_0,Z_0)$ is the ellipse center, $a$ is its horizontal half-width, and $\kappa$ is its elongation. Within the Luce model, $\zeta_{\mathrm{li}}=0$ represents no additional lower-inner corner shaping; positive values indicate an outward, boxier corner and negative values an inward, more indented corner.

This coefficient describes only the lower high-field-side quadrant and is not an average of the upper and lower inner coefficients.

sources.enhanced_context: Lower inner squareness (ζ_li) of a flux surface, quantifying the deviation of the inner lower quadrant from an elliptical boundary following the Luce (PPCF 55, 2013) definition. Part of the flux-surface shape characterization in the 1D equilibrium profile.
sources.leaf_definition: Lower inner squareness (definition from T. Luce, Plasma Phys. Control. Fusion 55 (2013) 095009)
sources.parent_definition: Equilibrium profiles (1D radial grid) as a function of the poloidal flux

NAMES.name: magnetic_field
NAMES.short: Magnetic induction vector representing the local magnetic field before specifying its physical contribution, perturbation, spatial projection, or magnitude.
NAMES.long:
The magnetic induction vector $\mathbf{B}$ is the local magnetic flux density, carrying both field strength and direction. This parent quantity does not by itself select an equilibrium state, source region, perturbation, component, or evaluation locus.

In terms of the [magnetic vector potential](name:magnetic_vector_potential) $\mathbf{A}$, the field is defined by

$$
\mathbf{B} = \nabla \times \mathbf{A}
$$

where $\mathbf{A}$ is the magnetic vector potential and $\nabla \times$ is the curl operator. The potential representation is gage-dependent, whereas the resulting magnetic induction vector is physical.

Qualifiers distinguish contributions such as the [vacuum magnetic field](name:vacuum_magnetic_field), [plasma magnetic field](name:plasma_magnetic_field), and [perturbed magnetic field](name:perturbed_magnetic_field). Projections such as the [toroidal magnetic field](name:toroidal_magnetic_field) are signed components, while field-strength extrema such as the [maximum magnetic field](name:maximum_magnetic_field) are scalar reductions rather than vector fields.
NAMES.sign: Positive when a resolved component of $\mathbf{B}$ points along the corresponding positive direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame: increasing $R$, increasing $\phi$, or increasing $Z$.

sources.enhanced_context: Magnetic field (B) values at the non-linear response calibration points of a toroidal field probe, used alongside the linear-response reference to characterise the full non-linear input-output relationship. Relevant for Hall probes where the response deviates from linearity at higher fields.
sources.leaf_definition: Magnetic field value taking into account the non-linear response of the probe

NAMES.name: magnetic_flux
NAMES.short: Family of magnetic flux quantities in tokamak equilibrium, spanning poloidal and toroidal projections and contributions from external coils, resistive dissipation, and plasma diamagnetism.
NAMES.long:
Magnetic flux is the surface integral of the magnetic field over a bounded area, quantifying the total field lines threading a specified surface. In tokamak equilibrium, the vector quantity encompasses several physically distinct components: [poloidal magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux) threading horizontal disks centered on the toroidal symmetry axis serves as the canonical radial flux-surface coordinate, while [toroidal magnetic flux](name:toroidal_magnetic_flux) threads the poloidal cross-section enclosed by each flux surface and increases monotonically outward from the magnetic axis.

The defining surface integral is:

$$
\Phi = \int_S \mathbf{B} \cdot d\mathbf{A}
$$

where $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic-field vector and $d\mathbf{A}$ is the oriented area element of the bounding surface $S$.

Beyond the geometric poloidal and toroidal projections, the equilibrium flux budget includes contributions from external coil systems such as the central solenoid and poloidal-field coils, and flux consumed by resistive dissipation within the plasma. The [poloidal current weighted average external magnetic flux](name:poloidal_current_weighted_average_external_magnetic_flux) is one such derived quantity combining external-source flux with current weighting. Flux quantities are measured by saddle loops, flux loops, and diamagnetic loops distributed around the vacuum vessel, and are reconstructed from equilibrium solvers that invert the Grad-Shafranov equation in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the enclosed magnetic flux is directed in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: magnetic_shear_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.short: Magnetic shear evaluated at the magnetic axis, defined as the limiting normalized logarithmic derivative of the safety factor with respect to normalized toroidal flux radius.
NAMES.long:
Magnetic shear at the magnetic axis is the limiting value of [magnetic shear](name:magnetic_shear) as the flux-surface label approaches the magnetic axis.

Using the [normalized toroidal flux coordinate](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate) $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ as the radial label, with $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}=0$ at the magnetic axis, the defining relation is

$$
s_{\mathrm{axis}} = \lim_{\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}\to 0} \frac{\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}}{q}\frac{dq}{d\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}}
$$

where $q$ is the safety factor and $s_{\mathrm{axis}}$ is the magnetic-shear limit. For a smooth equilibrium with finite [safety factor at the magnetic axis](name:safety_factor_at_magnetic_axis), this limit is zero. It therefore differs from evaluations on finite-radius surfaces such as [magnetic shear at the plasma boundary](name:magnetic_shear_at_plasma_boundary).
NAMES.sign: Positive when $q^{-1}dq/d\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ is positive as the normalized toroidal flux radius increases outward from the magnetic axis.

NAMES.name: major_radius
NAMES.short: Nonnegative perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis to a point or defined location, serving as the major-radius coordinate in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Major radius is the nonnegative perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis to a geometric point or specified location. It is the radial coordinate $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame and is independent of toroidal angle.

Using a right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$ basis with $\hat{z}=\hat{Z}$ along the toroidal symmetry axis, it is defined by:

$$
R = \sqrt{X^2 + Y^2}
$$

where $X$ and $Y$ are the Cartesian coordinates perpendicular to the axis, and $R$ is the resulting distance. The cylindrical basis satisfies $\hat{R}\times\hat{\phi}=\hat{Z}$; $\phi$ is toroidal angle and $Z$ is vertical height.

For an extended or derived quantity, major radius may be evaluated pointwise, averaged over a flux surface, fixed at a reference location, or combined algebraically with another quantity. Thus [flux-surface-averaged major radius](name:flux_surface_averaged_major_radius) is an average, whereas [reference major radius](name:reference_major_radius) identifies a fixed normalization location; products, ratios, and differences of major radii are derived quantities rather than alternate definitions of $R$.

NAMES.name: flux_surface_averaged_major_radius
NAMES.short: Flux-surface average of the major radius coordinate R on each nested magnetic flux surface, yielding the mean distance from the toroidal symmetry axis weighted by the inverse poloidal field strength.
NAMES.long:
The flux-surface averaged major radius $\langle R \rangle$ is the mean value of the cylindrical major radius coordinate $R$ over a closed toroidal magnetic flux surface, weighted by the local inverse poloidal magnetic field magnitude. It belongs to the family of geometric metric coefficients (sometimes denoted $gm8$ in neoclassical transport literature) that enter the flux-surface-averaged forms of transport and equilibrium equations, and is the flux-surface-averaging transformation of the parent quantity [major_radius](name:major_radius).

The defining expression is:

$$
\langle R \rangle = \frac{\oint R \, \frac{dl}{B_p}}{\oint \frac{dl}{B_p}}
$$

where $l$ is the poloidal arc length along the flux surface and $B_p$ is the poloidal magnetic field magnitude, with integrals taken over one complete poloidal circuit. Because $B_p$ is smaller on the outboard low-field side, field lines dwell longer there, and $\langle R \rangle$ is shifted toward larger $R$ relative to a simple geometric centroid; it lies between the inner_major_radius_of_flux_surface and the outer_major_radius_of_flux_surface.

This coefficient is computed directly from the magnetic geometry obtained in equilibrium reconstruction, and is closely related to flux_surface_average_magnetic_field and flux_surface_averaged_curvature, which are derived from the same surface-averaging procedure.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $R$ is measured outward from the toroidal symmetry axis in the $+\hat{R}$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: maximum_magnetic_field
NAMES.short: The maximum magnetic field is the scalar upper extremum of total magnetic-field strength over a specified magnetic locus, with qualifiers selecting the locus or concrete realization. It is not a signed vector component and is paired with the minimum magnetic field in mirror-ratio concepts.
NAMES.long:
The maximum magnetic field $B_{\max}$ is the largest value of the total [magnetic induction](name:magnetic_field) strength selected by the quantity's qualifying context. It is a scalar upper extremum of $|\mathbf{B}|$, not a magnetic-field vector and not a signed component.

For a specified evaluation set $S$, the abstract extremum is

$$
B_{\max}(S) = \sup_{\mathbf{x}\in S} |\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{x})|
$$

where $S$ is the selected magnetic locus, $\mathbf{x}$ is position on that locus, and $\mathbf{B}$ is the total magnetic induction vector.

A concrete child such as the [maximum magnetic-field magnitude](name:maximum_magnetic_field_magnitude) fixes the selected locus to a nested toroidal magnetic flux surface and realizes the value as a surface extremum. The paired [minimum magnetic field](name:minimum_magnetic_field) is the corresponding lower extremum; mirror-ratio quantities derived from the two are not part of this definition.

NAMES.name: maximum_magnetic_field_magnitude
NAMES.short: Maximum magnetic-field magnitude is the largest total magnetic-field magnitude attained on one nested toroidal magnetic flux surface. It is a surface extremum of field strength, not a maximum of any signed magnetic-field component.
NAMES.long:
Maximum magnetic-field magnitude is the largest total magnetic-field magnitude attained on one nested toroidal magnetic flux surface. It is a scalar surface extremum of the norm of the magnetic-field vector.

For a surface $S(\lambda)$ labeled by scalar flux-surface label $\lambda$, the quantity is defined by the surface maximum:

$$
B_{\max}(\lambda) = \max_{\mathbf{x} \in S(\lambda)} \lVert \mathbf{B}(\mathbf{x}) \rVert
$$

where $\lambda$ is any scalar label constant on each nested toroidal magnetic flux surface, $S(\lambda)$ is the surface with that label, $\mathbf{x}$ is position restricted to that surface, $\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{x})$ is the magnetic-field vector at that position, and $\lVert \mathbf{B}(\mathbf{x}) \rVert$ is magnetic-field magnitude.

This quantity is the explicit-magnitude spelling of [maximum_magnetic_field](name:maximum_magnetic_field), which denotes the same surface maximum of $\lVert \mathbf{B} \rVert$. Together with [minimum_magnetic_field_magnitude](name:minimum_magnetic_field_magnitude), it defines the field-strength interval on the same flux surface; in magnetic-mirror dynamics, for particle kinetic energy $E$ and magnetic moment $\mu$, the condition $E = \mu B_{\max}$ marks the boundary between orbits that can reach the highest-field point and those reflected before it. It must not be interpreted as the maximum of any signed component of the magnetic-field vector.

NAMES.name: minimum_magnetic_field
NAMES.short: The minimum magnetic field is the smallest total magnetic-field strength attained on a given nested toroidal flux surface. It is paired with the maximum magnetic field and defines the weak-field endpoint used in magnetic-mirror and trapped-particle conditions.
NAMES.long:
The minimum magnetic field $B_{\min}$ is the smallest value of the total [magnetic_field](name:magnetic_field) strength attained anywhere on a specified nested toroidal flux surface. It is a scalar extremum of $|\mathbf{B}|$ on that surface, not a signed component of the magnetic-field vector.

For a flux surface $S_\lambda$ labeled by a scalar flux label $\lambda$, the defining relation is

$$
B_{\min}(\lambda) = \min_{\mathbf{x} \in S_\lambda} |\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{x})|
$$

where $\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{x})$ is the total magnetic-field vector at position $\mathbf{x}$ and $S_\lambda$ is the corresponding closed toroidal flux surface.

This quantity is the lower field-strength bound paired with [maximum_magnetic_field](name:maximum_magnetic_field), and the two extrema define mirror-ratio quantities such as $B_{\max}/B_{\min}$. The explicitly magnitude-named form [minimum_magnetic_field_magnitude](name:minimum_magnetic_field_magnitude) refers to this same flux-surface minimum of $|\mathbf{B}|$.

NAMES.name: minimum_magnetic_field_magnitude
NAMES.short: Smallest value of total magnetic field magnitude on each nested toroidal flux surface, used in determining the magnetic trapping condition for charged particles in bounce motion.
NAMES.long:
The minimum magnetic field magnitude $B_\mathrm{min}(\psi)$ is the smallest value of $|\mathbf{B}|$ over all points on the flux surface labeled by poloidal flux $\psi$. In tokamaks with a dominant toroidal field satisfying $B_\phi \propto 1/R$, the minimum occurs near the outboard (low-field-side) midplane, where the major radius $R$ reaches its largest value on the flux surface.

The ratio $B_\mathrm{min}/B_\mathrm{max}$ governs magnetic trapping of charged particles bouncing along field lines. A particle with normalized parallel velocity $\xi = v_\parallel/v$ is magnetically trapped when

$$
\xi^2 < 1 - \frac{B_\mathrm{min}}{B_\mathrm{max}}
$$

where $v_\parallel$ is the velocity component along the magnetic field and $v$ is the total particle speed. The resulting trapped particle fraction enters neoclassical transport coefficients, bootstrap current models, and bounce-averaged kinetic equations.

$B_\mathrm{min}$ is obtained from MHD equilibrium reconstruction by minimizing the total field strength $|\mathbf{B}(\psi, \theta)|$ over the poloidal angle $\theta$ on each flux surface. Together with [maximum_magnetic_field_magnitude](name:maximum_magnetic_field_magnitude) and flux_surface_average_magnetic_field, it fully characterizes the field-strength variation on a flux surface that is relevant for classifying particle orbits.

NAMES.name: non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field
NAMES.short: Toroidally varying part of the external-coil vacuum magnetic-field vector, with its toroidally averaged component removed; it represents non-axisymmetric error and resonant perturbation fields.
NAMES.long:
The non-axisymmetric magnetic field designates the toroidally varying part of the vacuum magnetic-field vector produced by external coil currents, after removal of its toroidally averaged component. It is a non-axisymmetric component of the total [magnetic field](name:magnetic_field), excluding the axisymmetric vacuum contribution and plasma-response field.

At fixed major radius and vertical height, the field is defined by

$$
\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{na}}(R,\phi,Z)=\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{vac}}(R,\phi,Z)-\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{vac}}(R,\phi',Z)\,d\phi'
$$

where $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{na}}$ is the non-axisymmetric field, $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{vac}}$ is the vacuum field, $R$ and $Z$ are the major-radius and vertical coordinates in meters, $\phi$ and $\phi'$ are toroidal angles in radians, and $\phi'$ is the integration variable. Its cylindrical projections include the [radial non-axisymmetric magnetic field](name:radial_non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field), [toroidal non-axisymmetric magnetic field](name:toroidal_non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field), and [vertical non-axisymmetric magnetic field](name:vertical_non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field).
NAMES.sign: Positive when a resolved component points along the corresponding positive direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(\hat{R},\hat{\phi},\hat{Z})$ basis.

NAMES.name: normalized_minor_radius_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short: Dimensionless minor-radius label of a magnetic flux surface, obtained by normalizing its major-radius half-width to a specified positive reference length.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the dimensionless minor-radius label assigned to a magnetic flux surface from its radial extent in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

$$
\rho_{\mathrm{minor}} = \frac{R_{\max}-R_{\min}}{2L_{\mathrm{ref}}}
$$

where $R_{\max}$ and $R_{\min}$ are the maximum and minimum major-radius coordinates of the surface, each in m, and $L_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the specified positive reference length in m.

The label is a geometric normalization of the surface half-width; it is not a magnetic-flux normalization and therefore is distinct from the [normalized toroidal flux coordinate](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate). Its numerical value depends on the chosen reference length.

NAMES.name: normalized_plasma_internal_inductance
NAMES.short: Normalized plasma internal inductance is the li_3 equilibrium parameter formed from the plasma-volume integral of squared poloidal magnetic field, normalized by total plasma current and the reference major-radius position in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame. It measures spatial concentration of poloidal-field energy associated with the plasma current, not a boundary-field ratio.
NAMES.long:
Normalized plasma internal inductance is the $l_i(3)$ equilibrium parameter that characterizes the spatial concentration of the poloidal magnetic field generated by the plasma current. It is a global measure of how the current-density distribution stores poloidal magnetic-field energy within the plasma, not a local boundary-field ratio.

The defining normalization is

$$
l_i(3) = \frac{2}{R_0 \mu_0^2 I_p^2} \int_{V_p} B_p^2 \, dV
$$

where $V_p$ is the plasma volume; $B_p$ is the magnitude of the poloidal magnetic field, in tesla; $dV$ is the volume element, in cubic meters; $I_p$ is the total toroidal plasma current, in amperes; $\mu_0$ is the permeability of free space, in henries per meter; and $R_0$ is the major-radius coordinate, in meters, of the geometric center of the plasma boundary, taken as the midpoint between the innermost and outermost boundary major-radius positions in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

This quantity is the normalized internal-inductance convention denoted $l_i(3)$ or $li_3$. It is distinct from a dimensional plasma internal inductance and from [poloidal_beta](name:poloidal_beta), which normalizes plasma pressure by poloidal magnetic-field energy; here the numerator weights $B_p^2$ throughout the plasma volume. Through Ampere's law, changes in the spatial distribution of [current density](name:current_density) change $B_p$ and therefore this parameter, while the factor $I_p^2$ makes it insensitive to reversal of the total plasma-current direction.

NAMES.name: normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_minimum_safety_factor
NAMES.short: Dimensionless radial flux-surface label based on normalized toroidal magnetic flux, evaluated at the minimum-safety-factor surface. It identifies the nested flux surface where the magnitude of the safety factor is minimized, with 0 at the magnetic axis and 1 at the plasma boundary.
NAMES.long:
The normalized toroidal flux coordinate at the minimum-safety-factor surface is the dimensionless radial label assigned to the nested flux surface where the magnitude of the safety factor is globally minimized. It is the [normalized toroidal flux coordinate](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate) evaluated at that surface, with the origin at the magnetic axis and the outer normalization reference at the plasma boundary or last closed flux surface.

The coordinate is defined from the toroidal flux difference between the minimum-safety-factor flux surface and the magnetic-axis flux:

$$
\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}(q_{\min}) = \sqrt{\frac{\Phi_{q_{\min}} - \Phi_0}{\Phi_b - \Phi_0}}
$$

where $q_{\min}$ identifies the global minimum of $|q|$ over the nested-flux-surface domain, $\Phi_{q_{\min}}$ is the toroidal magnetic flux of the flux surface on which that minimum occurs, $\Phi_0$ is the magnetic-axis toroidal magnetic flux, and $\Phi_b$ is the boundary toroidal magnetic flux. The square root makes this a nonnegative radial coordinate; for a valid nested-flux-surface mapping the numerator and denominator have the same flux orientation, so the ratio is nonnegative and increases outward from the magnetic axis.

This quantity is the radial coordinate of the minimum-safety-factor surface, not the safety-factor value itself. It is the toroidal-flux-based counterpart of [normalized poloidal flux coordinate at minimum safety factor](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_at_minimum_safety_factor) and is distinct from [normalized toroidal flux coordinate at the sawtooth inversion radius](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_sawtooth_inversion_radius), which identifies a sawtooth-crash inversion surface rather than the global minimum of $|q|$.

NAMES.name: outer_squareness_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short: Dimensionless Luce shape coefficient for the outboard corners of nested magnetic flux surfaces, measuring signed departure from a co-centered reference ellipse across upper and lower quadrants.
NAMES.long:
The outer squareness of a flux surface is the dimensionless Luce (2013) shape coefficient that characterizes how much the outboard (larger major radius) corners of a nested toroidal magnetic flux surface depart from a reference ellipse sharing the same center, horizontal half-width, and [elongation](name:elongation_of_flux_surface). It is the outboard counterpart within the [squareness_of_flux_surface](name:squareness_of_flux_surface) family, complementing the [inner squareness](name:inner_squareness_of_flux_surface), and abstracts over the quadrant-resolved coefficients [upper outer squareness](name:upper_outer_squareness_of_flux_surface) and [lower outer squareness](name:lower_outer_squareness_of_flux_surface).

At the modeled outboard corners, the reference condition is

$$
\zeta_{\rm out}=0 \Longleftrightarrow \mathcal{C}_{\rm out}=\mathcal{E}_{\rm out}
$$

where $\zeta_{\rm out}$ is the outer squareness coefficient, $\mathcal{C}_{\rm out}$ is the modeled outboard corner of the flux-surface cross-section, and $\mathcal{E}_{\rm out}$ is the corresponding reference ellipse. The cross-section is described in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

This quantity does not select either the upper or lower outboard quadrant; those quadrant-specific coefficients may differ for an up-down asymmetric flux surface. Positive values describe boxier outward corners, while negative values describe corners indented relative to the reference ellipse.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the modeled outboard corner extends toward increasing $R$ beyond the corresponding reference ellipse in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: lower_outer_squareness_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short: Dimensionless Luce shape coefficient for the lower outboard quadrant of nested magnetic flux surfaces, measuring signed departure from a reference ellipse with the same center, horizontal half-width, and elongation.
NAMES.long:
The lower outer squareness $\zeta_{\rm lo}$ is the dimensionless Luce (2013) shape coefficient for the lower outboard ($-Z$, larger-$R$) corner of each nested magnetic flux surface, measuring its departure from a reference ellipse sharing the same center, horizontal half-width, and elongation.

At the modeled lower outboard corner, the reference condition is

$$
\zeta_{\rm lo}=0 \Longleftrightarrow \mathcal{C}_{\rm lo}=\mathcal{E}_{\rm lo}
$$

where $\zeta_{\rm lo}$ is the lower outer squareness coefficient, $\mathcal{C}_{\rm lo}$ is the modeled lower outboard corner, and $\mathcal{E}_{\rm lo}$ is the corresponding reference ellipse. The cross-section is described in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

This coefficient selects the lower outboard quadrant and is the lower component of [outer squareness](name:outer_squareness_of_flux_surface), complementing [upper outer squareness](name:upper_outer_squareness_of_flux_surface). Up-down asymmetry allows the two quadrant-specific coefficients to differ; positive values describe boxier outward corners, while negative values describe corners indented relative to the reference ellipse.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the modeled lower outboard corner extends toward increasing $R$ beyond the corresponding reference ellipse in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: parallel_flux_surface_averaged_current_density_at_constraint_position
NAMES.short: Flux-surface averaged parallel current density at a constraint position is the flux-surface average of the current-density vector projected along the local magnetic-field direction on the closed magnetic surface selected by the constraint position.
NAMES.long:
Flux-surface averaged parallel current density at a constraint position is the flux-surface average of the current-density vector projected onto the unit vector along the local magnetic field, evaluated on the closed magnetic flux surface selected by the constraint position. The constraint position is a specified value of the normalized toroidal flux radius $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$, with $0$ on the magnetic axis and $1$ at the last closed flux surface.

For a constraint at $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm},c}$, let $\psi_c$ be the value of a monotonic flux label $\psi$ on the same magnetic surface. The volume-derivative flux-surface average is

$$
\langle j_\parallel \rangle_c =
\frac{\oint_{\psi=\psi_c} \mathbf{j}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{b}} \, dS/|\nabla\psi|}
{\oint_{\psi=\psi_c} dS/|\nabla\psi|}
$$

where $\mathbf{j}$ is the current-density vector, $\hat{\mathbf{b}}=\mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$ is the unit vector along the local magnetic field $\mathbf{B}$, $dS$ is an element of the magnetic surface, and $dS/|\nabla\psi|$ gives the volume-derivative weighting of the flux-surface average.

The definition applies only on closed magnetic flux surfaces for which the flux-surface average is defined. It uses the local unit-field projection before averaging; it is not a $|\mathbf{B}|$-weighted measure such as $\langle\mathbf{j}\cdot\mathbf{B}\rangle/B_\mathrm{ref}$, where $B_\mathrm{ref}$ is a reference magnetic flux density. It is distinct from [flux-surface averaged toroidal current density at a constraint position](name:toroidal_flux_surface_averaged_current_density_at_constraint_position), which averages the $\hat{\phi}$ component in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $\phi$ is toroidal angle.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the flux-surface averaged current-density projection is along the local magnetic-field direction.

NAMES.name: plasma_current
NAMES.short: Plasma current is the net toroidal electric current carried by the plasma column, defined by integrating toroidal current density over the full poloidal cross-section in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Plasma current is the net toroidal electric current carried by the plasma column in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It is the cross-sectional integral of the toroidal component of the [total current density](name:total_current_density) over the plasma region.

The defining integral over a poloidal cross-section is

$$
I_p = \int_{\mathcal{S}} j_\phi \, dA
$$

where $I_p$ is plasma current, $j_\phi$ is the [toroidal current density](name:toroidal_current_density), $\mathcal{S}$ is the full poloidal cross-section at fixed toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame and bounded by the plasma boundary, and $dA$ is the positive scalar poloidal area element, not an oriented vector surface element.

The integral includes all toroidal current contributions carried by the plasma, including inductive, bootstrap, and non-inductive driven currents, and excludes currents outside the plasma boundary. For an axisymmetric equilibrium the value is independent of the chosen toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame and is the global current associated with the [poloidal magnetic field].
NAMES.sign: Positive when the net plasma current flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, counterclockwise when viewed from the $+\hat{Z}$ direction.

NAMES.name: plasma_pressure
NAMES.short: Isotropic scalar pressure of the plasma fluid in a continuum description, serving as the parent concept for both the bulk thermal equilibrium pressure and first-order perturbative pressure deviations in linear MHD stability analysis.
NAMES.long:
Plasma pressure in the fluid (MHD) description is the isotropic part of the pressure tensor, entering the radial force balance $\nabla p = \mathbf{j} \times \mathbf{B}$, where $\mathbf{j}$ is the current density and $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field. This parent abstracts over two physically distinct realizations: [thermal_plasma_pressure](name:thermal_plasma_pressure), which sums the kinetic contributions from bulk thermal electron and ion populations while excluding fast or suprathermal particles, and [perturbed_plasma_pressure](name:perturbed_plasma_pressure), which represents the complex-amplitude linear eigenfunction $\delta p$ arising in stability analysis about a magnetohydrostatic equilibrium.

In the thermal regime the pressure is given by the equation of state:

$$
p = n_e k_B T_e + \sum_i n_i k_B T_i
$$

where $n_e$ and $n_i$ are the electron and ion number densities, $T_e$ and $T_i$ are their respective temperatures, and $k_B$ is the Boltzmann constant. In linear MHD stability analysis the equilibrium profile $p_0$ is perturbed as $p = p_0 + \delta p$, where $\delta p$ is the pressure eigenfunction resolved per toroidal Fourier mode.

Pressure profiles are inferred from equilibrium reconstruction by enforcing the radial force-balance constraint against magnetic diagnostic data and a finite set of kinetic pressure measurements. The volume integral of the thermal pressure, scaled by $3/2$, yields the stored thermal energy [thermal_plasma_energy](name:thermal_plasma_energy), while a pointwise sum of electron and ion contributions is captured by [total_thermal_pressure](name:total_thermal_pressure).

NAMES.name: plasma_resistance
NAMES.short: Effective resistance of the plasma column, defined by irreversible ohmic power divided by the square of the total plasma current.
NAMES.long:
The effective plasma-column resistance is the circuit-level coefficient relating irreversible electrical dissipation in the plasma to the total plasma current. It is distinct from local electrical resistivity and from inductive contributions to the plasma voltage.

$$
R_{\rm pl} = \frac{P_{\rm ohm}}{I_{\rm p}^{2}}
$$

where $R_{\rm pl}$ is the effective resistance, $P_{\rm ohm}$ is the [power due to ohmic dissipation](name:power_due_to_ohmic_dissipation) in W, and $I_{\rm p}$ is the total conventional plasma current in A. The quantity is non-negative for irreversible ohmic dissipation. It represents only the resistive part of the plasma circuit response; inductive electromotive-force contributions are included in the [loop voltage at the plasma boundary](name:loop_voltage_at_plasma_boundary), not in this resistance.

NAMES.name: polarization_angle_at_constraint_position
NAMES.short: Motional Stark effect polarization angle evaluated at a discrete spatial location designated as a measurement constraint in tokamak equilibrium reconstruction.
NAMES.long:
The polarization angle at a constraint position is the angle of linear polarization of Stark-split Balmer-alpha emission from fast neutral beam ions traversing the plasma, evaluated at a discrete spatial site where this measurement serves as an input constraint in equilibrium reconstruction. The motional Stark effect (MSE) diagnostic exploits the Lorentz electric field experienced by injected beam neutrals to align the polarization plane of the emitted light in a direction encoding the local magnetic-field pitch angle.

The MSE polarization angle $\gamma$ is related to the local magnetic field components by:

$$
\tan(\gamma) = \frac{B_Z}{A_1 B_R + A_2 B_\phi}
$$

where $B_Z$ is the vertical field component, $B_R$ is the radial field component, $B_\phi$ is the toroidal field component, and $A_1$, $A_2$ are dimensionless geometric weighting factors determined by the beam trajectory and sightline orientation.

During equilibrium reconstruction, the measured value at each constraint position is compared against the corresponding reconstructed [polarization_angle](name:polarization_angle_at_constraint_position) to form residuals that enter the least-squares cost functional. The motional_stark_radiance provides complementary spectral intensity data from the same beam-emission event. MSE polarization angles in conventional-aspect-ratio tokamak configurations span a few degrees to roughly 20 degrees, varying with local field pitch, beam geometry, and viewing-sightline angle.

NAMES.name: poloidal_angle_at_plasma_boundary_gap_reference_point
NAMES.short: Poloidal angle of a plasma-boundary-gap reference point in the poloidal cross-section of the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, measured clockwise from the outward radial direction about the magnetic axis.
NAMES.long:
The poloidal angle of a plasma-boundary-gap reference point is the angular coordinate of that point about the magnetic axis in a poloidal cross-section of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It locates the reference point used to define the [gap at plasma boundary](name:gap_at_plasma_boundary), using the geometric convention of [poloidal angle](name:poloidal_angle).

For reference-point coordinates $(R_\mathrm{g},Z_\mathrm{g})$ and magnetic-axis coordinates $(R_\mathrm{ax},Z_\mathrm{ax})$, the angle is

$$
\theta_\mathrm{g}=\operatorname{atan2}(Z_\mathrm{ax}-Z_\mathrm{g},\,R_\mathrm{g}-R_\mathrm{ax})\pmod{2\pi}
$$

where $R_\mathrm{g}$ and $R_\mathrm{ax}$ are major radii in meters, $Z_\mathrm{g}$ and $Z_\mathrm{ax}$ are vertical heights in meters, and $\operatorname{atan2}$ returns a quadrant-resolved angle. The reference point is distinct from the boundary itself and from the gap distance; [poloidal angle of a measurement position](name:poloidal_angle_of_measurement_position) applies the same construction to a measurement location.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the reference point lies clockwise from the outward $+R$ direction when viewed from the $+\phi$ direction.

NAMES.name: poloidal_angle_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short: Poloidal angle of a flux-surface point in the poloidal cross-section of the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, measured clockwise from the outward radial direction about the magnetic axis.
NAMES.long:
The poloidal angle of a flux-surface point is the angular coordinate of that point about the magnetic axis in a poloidal cross-section of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It parameterizes points on a surface of constant poloidal magnetic flux and is the flux-surface form of [poloidal angle](name:poloidal_angle).

For a surface point with coordinates $(R,Z)$ and magnetic-axis coordinates $(R_\mathrm{ax},Z_\mathrm{ax})$, the angle is

$$
\theta=\operatorname{atan2}(Z_\mathrm{ax}-Z,\,R-R_\mathrm{ax})\pmod{2\pi}
$$

where $\operatorname{atan2}$ returns the quadrant-resolved angle. The flux surface identifies the set of valid points, but does not define one unique angle; each point has its own value. Unlike [poloidal angle of a measurement position](name:poloidal_angle_of_measurement_position), this quantity applies to points on a flux surface rather than to a diagnostic location.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the point lies clockwise from the outward $+R$ direction when viewed from the $+\phi$ direction.

NAMES.name: poloidal_beta
NAMES.short: Poloidal beta is a dimensionless global equilibrium ratio of volume-averaged plasma pressure to the magnetic-pressure scale of the plasma-current-generated poloidal field. The reference poloidal-field scale is fixed by total toroidal plasma current, reference major radius, and confined plasma volume.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal beta is a global equilibrium pressure-normalization parameter for the confined plasma. It compares the volume-averaged scalar plasma pressure with the magnetic-pressure scale of the poloidal magnetic field generated by the total toroidal plasma current.

The volume-integral definition closes the reference poloidal-field scale:

$$
\beta_p = \frac{2\mu_0 \langle p\rangle_V}{B_{p,\mathrm{ref}}^2}
= \frac{4\int_V p\,dV}{\mu_0 R_0 I_p^2},\qquad
\langle p\rangle_V = \frac{1}{V}\int_V p\,dV,\qquad
B_{p,\mathrm{ref}}^2 = \frac{\mu_0^2 R_0 I_p^2}{2V}
$$

where $V$ is the confined plasma volume in cubic meters, $p$ is the scalar plasma pressure in pascals, $dV$ is a volume element in cubic meters, $\langle p\rangle_V$ is the volume average of $p$, $\mu_0$ is the permeability of free space in henries per meter, $R_0$ is a reference major radius in meters measured from the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, $I_p$ is the total toroidal plasma current in amperes, and $B_{p,\mathrm{ref}}$ is the reference poloidal magnetic field in teslas.

The pressure $p$ is the scalar kinetic pressure entering the equilibrium force balance; it excludes the magnetic pressure used in the normalization. Poloidal beta differs from [toroidal beta], which is normalized to toroidal-field magnetic pressure, and from [normalized plasma internal inductance](name:normalized_plasma_internal_inductance), which characterizes poloidal-field energy associated with the spatial distribution of toroidal current. The use of $I_p^2$ makes poloidal beta independent of the sign of the toroidal plasma current.

NAMES.name: poloidal_cross_sectional_area_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Geometric area enclosed by the last closed magnetic-flux-surface contour in a fixed-toroidal-angle poloidal cross-section.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the area enclosed by the last closed magnetic-flux-surface contour in a poloidal cross-section at fixed toroidal angle. It characterizes the plasma cross-sectional size in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ coordinate frame with basis $(\hat{R},\hat{\phi},\hat{Z})$.

The enclosed area is defined by

$$
A = \iint_{\Omega_{\rm LCFS}} dR\,dZ
$$

where $A$ is the cross-sectional area, $\Omega_{\rm LCFS}$ is the region inside the last closed flux-surface contour, $R$ is major radius measured in meters, and $Z$ is vertical height measured in meters; $\phi$ is the fixed toroidal angle.

This poloidal area is distinct from the boundary perimeter, given by the [length of the plasma boundary](name:length_of_plasma_boundary), and from the three-dimensional [surface area of a flux surface](name:surface_area_of_flux_surface).

NAMES.name: poloidal_current_function
NAMES.short: Poloidal current function is the signed product of major radius and the toroidal magnetic-field component in an axisymmetric equilibrium. It is a flux function associated with the net poloidal current linked by magnetic flux surfaces.
NAMES.long:
The poloidal current function is the flux-surface quantity equal to the major-radius-weighted toroidal magnetic field in an axisymmetric equilibrium. It is constant on nested surfaces of constant [poloidal_magnetic_flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux), so it may be expressed as a function of that flux label.

The defining relationship is

$$
F(\psi) = R B_\phi
$$

where $F$ is the poloidal current function, $\psi$ is [poloidal_magnetic_flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux), $R$ is major radius measured from the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, and $B_\phi$ is the toroidal magnetic-field component in that frame.

By Ampère's law, $F$ is proportional to the net poloidal current linked by a toroidal Amperian contour on the same magnetic flux surface; this proportionality gives the quantity its current-function interpretation. It is distinct from $B_\phi$, which equals $F/R$ and therefore generally varies around a flux surface; in vacuum it reduces to [vacuum_poloidal_current_function](name:vacuum_poloidal_current_function). In the Grad-Shafranov equation its current-gradient contribution appears through [product_of_poloidal_current_function_and_derivative_with_respect_to_poloidal_magnetic_flux_coordinate_of_poloidal_current_function](name:product_of_poloidal_current_function_and_derivative_with_respect_to_poloidal_magnetic_flux_coordinate_of_poloidal_current_function).
NAMES.sign: Positive when $B_\phi$ points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: poloidal_current_weighted_average_external_magnetic_flux
NAMES.short: Current-density-weighted mean of external poloidal magnetic flux over the plasma cross-section, including active and passive circuits but excluding the plasma’s self-generated flux.
NAMES.long:
External poloidal magnetic flux is the flux generated by all external circuits, including central-solenoid and poloidal-field coils, eddy currents, and in-vessel coils; the plasma self-flux is excluded. This quantity is its toroidal-current-density-weighted mean over the plasma poloidal cross-section.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, the defining average is

$$
\psi_{\mathrm{ext,avg}} = \frac{\displaystyle\int_A \psi_{\mathrm{ext}}(R,Z)\,j_\phi(R,Z)\,dS}{I_p}
$$

where $A$ is the plasma poloidal cross-section, $\psi_{\mathrm{ext}}$ is the external poloidal magnetic flux, $j_\phi$ is the toroidal plasma-current-density component, $dS$ is the poloidal area element, and $I_p=\int_A j_\phi\,dS$ is the signed total plasma current. The quantity is an externally generated member of the [magnetic flux](name:magnetic_flux) family and is distinct from a total poloidal flux that includes the plasma contribution.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the external vertical magnetic-field component $B_Z$ through the defining horizontal disk points in the $+Z$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_constraint_position
NAMES.short: Value of the poloidal magnetic-flux function at a location where an equilibrium constraint is applied, identifying the magnetic flux surface passing through that location.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal magnetic flux at a constraint position is the value of the equilibrium poloidal-flux function at a location designated for an equilibrium constraint. It identifies the magnetic flux surface passing through that location.

For an axisymmetric equilibrium, the poloidal-flux function is defined by:

$$
\psi(R,Z) = \int_0^R B_Z(R',Z)\,2\pi R'\,dR'
$$

where $\psi$ is poloidal magnetic flux, $R$ and $R'$ are major-radius coordinates in m, $Z$ is vertical height in m, and $B_Z$ is the vertical magnetic-field component in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, with $\phi$ the toroidal angle. At the constraint location $(R_c,Z_c)$, the value is $\psi(R_c,Z_c)$.

This locus-specific value complements [poloidal magnetic flux at a flux surface](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_flux_surface) and differs from the reference value at [the magnetic axis](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_magnetic_axis).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the vertical magnetic field on the integration disk points in the $+Z$ direction.

NAMES.name: poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_flux_surface
NAMES.short: Poloidal magnetic flux ψ at a point in the poloidal cross-section of an axisymmetric equilibrium, constant on each nested flux surface and serving as a natural radial coordinate between the magnetic axis and the plasma boundary.
NAMES.long:
The poloidal magnetic flux $\psi$ is the total magnetic flux threading a horizontal disk of radius $R$ centered on the toroidal symmetry axis at height $Z$:

$$
\psi(R, Z) = \int_0^R B_Z(R', Z)\, 2\pi R' \, dR'
$$

where $B_Z$ is the vertical component of the magnetic field in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame and $R$ is the major radius from the symmetry axis. Because $\psi$ is constant on each nested flux surface, it provides a natural radial coordinate for axisymmetric equilibria, varying monotonically between its value at the [magnetic axis](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_magnetic_axis) and its value at the [plasma boundary](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary). At topological critical points of the poloidal flux map — O-points (local extrema of $\psi$, including the primary magnetic axis) and X-points (saddle points where $\nabla\psi = 0$ but $\psi$ is not a local extremum, including the separatrix X-point) — the value of $\psi$ identifies the flux level of that node within the equilibrium topology, characterizing the connectivity structure of the poloidal flux contours.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the net vertical magnetic flux threading the horizontal integration disk points in the $+Z$ direction.

NAMES.name: poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.short: Poloidal magnetic flux evaluated at the magnetic axis, providing the inner reference for normalized poloidal-flux coordinates.
NAMES.long:
The poloidal magnetic flux at the magnetic axis is the value of the equilibrium flux function at the interior extremum that defines the magnetic axis. It is the inner reference for the [normalized poloidal flux coordinate](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate), complementary to the value at the [plasma boundary](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary).

$$
\psi_{\mathrm{axis}} = \psi(R_{\mathrm{axis}}, Z_{\mathrm{axis}})
$$

Here $\psi$ is poloidal magnetic flux, and $R_{\mathrm{axis}}$ and $Z_{\mathrm{axis}}$ are the major-radius and vertical coordinates of the magnetic axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The magnetic axis is the interior point where the gradient of $\psi$ vanishes.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the vertical magnetic field through the defining horizontal disk points in the $+Z$ direction.

NAMES.name: poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_minimum_safety_factor
NAMES.short: Poloidal magnetic flux evaluated on the closed flux surface where the magnitude of the safety factor is minimized, providing a dimensional label for that surface.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the signed poloidal magnetic-flux function evaluated on the closed flux surface where the magnitude of the safety factor is smallest. It provides a dimensional, non-normalized flux label for that surface.

The selected value is defined by

$$
\psi_{q_{\min}}=\psi(\chi_\ast),\qquad \chi_\ast\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\chi\in\mathcal{D}}|q(\chi)|
$$

where $\psi$ is the poloidal magnetic-flux function, $q$ is the safety factor, $\chi$ is any monotonic label of the nested closed flux surfaces, and $\mathcal{D}$ is the selected closed-flux-surface domain. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, $\psi(R,Z)=\int_0^R B_Z(R',Z)\,2\pi R'\,dR'$, where $B_Z$ is the vertical magnetic-field component.

The minimizing surface may be the magnetic axis, an interior surface, or the domain boundary. An additive constant in $\psi$ is a gage choice, so only flux differences are invariant; its normalized location is given by [normalized poloidal flux coordinate at minimum safety factor](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_at_minimum_safety_factor).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the poloidal magnetic flux through the enclosed horizontal disk centered on the toroidal symmetry axis is oriented along $+\hat{Z}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Poloidal magnetic flux assigned to the last closed magnetic flux surface, providing the outer reference for normalized radial flux coordinates.
NAMES.long:
The boundary value of the poloidal flux function is the flux label of the last closed magnetic flux surface (LCFS), the outermost closed surface of the equilibrium. It is constant along the LCFS.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, the boundary value is defined by

$$
\psi_b = \psi(R,Z) \quad \text{for } (R,Z) \in \mathrm{LCFS}
$$

where $\psi_b$ is the boundary poloidal magnetic flux, $\psi(R,Z)$ is the axisymmetric poloidal flux function, $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The value provides the outer endpoint for normalized poloidal-flux coordinates, together with the magnetic-axis value [poloidal magnetic flux at the magnetic axis](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_magnetic_axis); it therefore defines the boundary reference used by the [normalized poloidal flux coordinate](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the vertical magnetic field through the oriented horizontal disk points in the $+Z$ direction.

NAMES.name: poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_sensor_attachment_point
NAMES.short: Poloidal magnetic flux at a sensor attachment point is the signed value of the equilibrium poloidal magnetic flux function at the physical point where the sensor is attached. It preserves the global flux function's additive reference and is not a magnetic-axis-referenced flux difference.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal magnetic flux at a sensor attachment point is the point value of the equilibrium [poloidal magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux) function at the physical attachment point of a magnetic flux sensor. The quantity retains the additive reference of that global flux function.

The point value is defined by evaluating the flux function at the attachment-point coordinates:

$$
\psi_\mathrm{attach} = \psi(R_\mathrm{attach}, Z_\mathrm{attach})
$$

where $\psi_\mathrm{attach}$ is the poloidal magnetic flux at the sensor attachment point, $\psi(R, Z)$ is the equilibrium [poloidal magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux) function, and $R_\mathrm{attach}$ and $Z_\mathrm{attach}$ are the major radius and vertical height of the attachment point in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, with $R$ the major radius, $\phi$ the toroidal angle, and $Z$ the vertical height. For an axisymmetric equilibrium, $\psi$ is independent of $\phi$.

This is a local value of the same scalar flux function, not the flux linked by the finite [area of a flux loop](name:area_of_flux_loop) and not a magnetic-axis-subtracted quantity. Subtracting the [poloidal magnetic flux at the magnetic axis](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_magnetic_axis) from this value gives a magnetic-axis-referenced flux difference; if the attachment point lies on a magnetic flux surface, its value equals the [poloidal magnetic flux at that flux surface](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_flux_surface).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the sensor attachment point lies on a level set of $\psi$ whose signed flux label is greater than the chosen additive zero of the same equilibrium flux function.

sources.enhanced_context: Measured value of flux loop.
