NAMES.name: vacuum_magnetic_field
NAMES.short: Magnetic field in current-free regions, generalizing over equilibrium and perturbed configurations generated by external coil currents with plasma-current contributions omitted.
NAMES.long:
The vacuum magnetic field designates the magnetic-induction vector generated by external coil currents when plasma-current contributions are omitted. It is the current-free counterpart of the total [magnetic field](name:magnetic_field), covering both equilibrium and perturbation fields.

In any region containing no modeled current density, the vacuum field satisfies

$$
\nabla \times \mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{vac}} = \mathbf{0}
$$

where $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{vac}}$ is the vacuum magnetic induction, $\nabla$ is the spatial differential operator, and $\mathbf{0}$ is the zero vector. The field is also solenoidal, so $\nabla \cdot \mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{vac}} = 0$. Its toroidal component is represented by [toroidal vacuum magnetic field](name:toroidal_vacuum_magnetic_field), while a first-order vacuum perturbation is represented by [perturbed vacuum magnetic field](name:perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field). The corresponding [vacuum magnetic vector potential](name:vacuum_magnetic_vector_potential) is gage-dependent, but its curl yields this field.
NAMES.sign: Positive when a resolved component of $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{vac}}$ points along the corresponding positive basis vector in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ increases in the toroidal direction, and $Z$ is vertical height.

NAMES.name: toroidal_vacuum_magnetic_field
NAMES.short: The toroidal vacuum magnetic field is the toroidal component of the external-coil equilibrium magnetic field at the reference major radius in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, excluding plasma-current contributions.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal vacuum magnetic field $B_{0,\mathrm{vac}}$ is the $\hat{\phi}$ component of the external-coil contribution to the equilibrium [vacuum magnetic field](name:vacuum_magnetic_field), evaluated at the [reference major radius](name:reference_major_radius) $R_0$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It represents the toroidal field that would be present from the external coil system with plasma-current contributions excluded.

For an axisymmetric current-free vacuum region, the toroidal vacuum field is related to the [vacuum poloidal current function](name:vacuum_poloidal_current_function) by:

$$
B_{0,\mathrm{vac}} = B_{\phi,\mathrm{vac}}(R_0) = \frac{F_\mathrm{vac}}{R_0}
$$

where $B_{\phi,\mathrm{vac}}$ is the $\hat{\phi}$ component of the vacuum magnetic field, $R_0$ is the reference major radius, and $F_\mathrm{vac} = R B_{\phi,\mathrm{vac}}(R)$ in the current-free axisymmetric vacuum region.

This quantity is the vacuum external-coil contribution only. It is distinct from the [toroidal reference magnetic field](name:toroidal_reference_magnetic_field) when that quantity denotes the total reference toroidal field including plasma-current, diamagnetic, or paramagnetic contributions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $B_{\phi,\mathrm{vac}}$ points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $\phi$ increases counter-clockwise viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_active_limiter_point
NAMES.short: Signed vertical Z coordinate of the point where a limited plasma boundary contacts the active limiter, expressed in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The active limiter point is the geometric contact point between a limited plasma boundary and the limiter. This quantity is the signed vertical coordinate of that point, rather than a coordinate of the limiter-tile outline.

$$
Z_{\mathrm{active}} = Z(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{active}})
$$

where $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{active}}$ is the active limiter-point position and $Z(\mathbf{x})$ is its vertical coordinate in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, whose basis is $(\hat{R}, \hat{\phi}, \hat{Z})$ with $\hat{R} \times \hat{\phi} = \hat{Z}$. The quantity applies only when the plasma is limited by an active limiter. It is distinct from the [vertical outline of the limiter tile](name:vertical_outline_of_limiter_tile) and from the [vertical coordinate of the plasma boundary](name:vertical_coordinate_of_plasma_boundary).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the active limiter point lies in the $+Z$ direction.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_closest_wall_point
NAMES.short: Signed vertical Z coordinate of the first-wall point with minimum geometric distance to the plasma boundary or separatrix in the right-handed cylindrical frame.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the vertical position of the first-wall location closest to the plasma boundary or separatrix. It identifies a wall point geometrically, rather than a point on the boundary itself or the [vertical coordinate of the plasma boundary](name:vertical_coordinate_of_plasma_boundary).

$$
\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{fw}}=\underset{\mathbf{p}\in\mathcal{W}}{\operatorname{arg\,min}}\,d(\mathbf{p},\mathcal{B}),\qquad Z_{\mathrm{fw}}=Z(\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{fw}})
$$

Here, $\mathcal{W}$ is the first-wall surface, $\mathcal{B}$ is the relevant plasma boundary or separatrix, $d$ is geometric distance, and $Z$ is vertical height in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $\phi$ is toroidal angle. The quantity is distinct from [gap at plasma boundary](name:gap_at_plasma_boundary), which gives the corresponding minimum separation rather than its vertical location.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the closest first-wall point lies in the $+Z$ direction, above the machine midplane.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_constraint_position
NAMES.short: Vertical Z coordinate of the physical location where an equilibrium constraint is applied, expressed in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Vertical Z coordinate of the physical location where an equilibrium constraint is applied in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. Here $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height; the coordinate is the height of the constraint point relative to the chosen $Z=0$ reference plane.

The constraint position is the physical point in the equilibrium domain at which a prescribed condition on the equilibrium solution is imposed. Together with the [major radius of the constraint position], this coordinate specifies the constraint point in the axisymmetric poloidal cross-section and is distinct from the [vertical coordinate of a measurement position](name:vertical_coordinate_of_measurement_position).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the constraint position lies in the $+\hat{Z}$ direction from the $Z=0$ reference plane in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_control_surface
NAMES.short: Vertical Z coordinate of points on the control surface in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, specifying their height for non-axisymmetric magnetic-field analysis.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the vertical coordinate $Z$ of a point belonging to the control surface, measured in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It identifies the height at which the control surface serves as a geometric locus for evaluating non-axisymmetric magnetic fields; it is not the surface-normal component itself.

$$
Z_{\mathrm{cs}} = \mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{cs}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{Z}}
$$

Here $\mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{cs}}$ is the position vector of the selected control-surface point and $\hat{\mathbf{Z}}$ is the vertical unit vector. The associated $R$ and $\phi$ coordinates are the major-radius and toroidal-angle coordinates of that same point. Unlike the [vertical coordinate of the plasma boundary](name:vertical_coordinate_of_plasma_boundary), this quantity is defined on the control surface and does not imply that the control surface is the plasma boundary. Its toroidal counterpart is the [toroidal angle of the control surface](name:toroidal_angle_of_control_surface).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the point lies in the $+Z$ direction from the $Z=0$ reference plane.

sources.enhanced_context: Vertical (Z) coordinate of normal vector.
sources.leaf_definition: Height
sources.parent_definition: Components of the normal vector to the surface, given on each point of the surface

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_current_center
NAMES.short: Signed vertical position of the plasma-current centroid, obtained by weighting the toroidal current distribution by height in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate of the plasma-current center is the current-density-weighted centroid height of the plasma current distribution in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

$$
Z_{\mathrm{c}} = \frac{\int_{\mathcal{A}} Z\,j_{\phi}(R,Z)\,dA}{\int_{\mathcal{A}} j_{\phi}(R,Z)\,dA}
$$

where $Z_{\mathrm{c}}$ and $Z$ are vertical coordinates in m, $R$ is major radius in m, $j_{\phi}$ is toroidal current density in A m$^{-2}$, $dA$ is differential poloidal cross-sectional area in m$^{2}$, and $\mathcal{A}$ is the region carrying plasma current. The current-weighted center is distinct from the geometric axis; its radial counterpart is the [radial coordinate of the current center](name:radial_coordinate_of_current_center).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the plasma-current centroid lies in the $+Z$ direction from the coordinate origin.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_geometric_axis
NAMES.short: Signed vertical coordinate of the geometric axis in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, defined as the midpoint of the last closed flux surface’s maximum and minimum Z positions.
NAMES.long:
The geometric axis is the vertical shape center of the last closed flux surface, distinct from the magnetic axis. Its vertical coordinate is determined from the extrema of the plasma-boundary contour, whose vertical position is described by [vertical coordinate of plasma boundary](name:vertical_coordinate_of_plasma_boundary).

The geometric-axis coordinate is defined by

$$
Z_{\mathrm{geo}} = \frac{Z_{\max} + Z_{\min}}{2}
$$

where $Z_{\mathrm{geo}}$, $Z_{\max}$, and $Z_{\min}$ are vertical coordinates in m, and $Z_{\max}$ and $Z_{\min}$ are respectively the maximum and minimum values of $Z$ on the last closed flux-surface boundary. Together with the [radial coordinate of geometric axis](name:radial_coordinate_of_geometric_axis), it locates the geometric axis in the poloidal cross-section.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the geometric-axis coordinate points in the $+Z$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, upward from the machine midplane.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_magnetic_axis
NAMES.short: Signed Z coordinate of the magnetic axis, the interior poloidal-flux extremum around which nested magnetic flux surfaces are organized.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the signed vertical coordinate of the magnetic axis in an equilibrium. The magnetic axis is the O-point of the nested poloidal-flux surfaces, located at an interior extremum of poloidal magnetic flux in the poloidal cross-section.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, it is defined by

$$
Z_{\rm axis}=Z(\mathbf{x}_{\rm axis}), \qquad \nabla_{R,Z}\psi(\mathbf{x}_{\rm axis})=\mathbf{0}
$$

where $\mathbf{x}_{\rm axis}$ is the magnetic-axis position, $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, $Z$ is vertical height, and $\psi$ is poloidal magnetic flux. The gradient is taken in the poloidal $(R,Z)$ plane.

This coordinate refers to the magnetic-axis O-point, not the separatrix X-point described by the [vertical coordinate of the X-point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_x_point).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the magnetic axis lies above the $Z=0$ reference plane in the direction of increasing $Z$.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_measurement_position
NAMES.short: Signed vertical coordinate of a diagnostic measurement position in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, referenced to the machine midplane.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate of a diagnostic measurement position is the signed location of that point along the vertical $Z$ direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, whose basis is $(\hat{R}, \hat{\phi}, \hat{Z})$. The coordinate origin is the machine midplane.

$$
Z_{\rm mp} = \mathbf{r}_{\rm mp} \cdot \hat{Z}
$$

where $Z_{\rm mp}$ is the vertical coordinate, $\mathbf{r}_{\rm mp}$ is the position vector from the frame origin to the measurement position, and $\hat{Z}$ is the vertical unit vector. The associated [poloidal angle of the measurement position](name:poloidal_angle_of_measurement_position) specifies angular location in the poloidal cross-section and does not replace this signed coordinate.

This quantity applies to the measurement position itself, not to the geometric center of a diagnostic aperture, antenna, or optical element.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Signed vertical Z coordinate of points on the plasma-boundary contour in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the vertical position coordinate of a point on the plasma-boundary contour, evaluated in a poloidal cross-section at the specified toroidal angle. It locates the boundary relative to the machine midplane and is distinct from the boundary's total vertical extent or elongation.

The coordinate is defined by the vertical projection of the boundary position:

$$
Z_{\mathrm{b}}(\theta,\phi)=\mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{b}}(\theta,\phi)\cdot\hat{Z}
$$

where $\mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{b}}$ is the boundary position vector, $\theta$ parameterizes the contour, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle, and $\hat{Z}$ is the vertical unit vector of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The associated boundary geometry includes the [length of the plasma boundary](name:length_of_plasma_boundary) and [elongation of the plasma boundary](name:elongation_of_plasma_boundary).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the point lies in the direction of increasing vertical coordinate $Z$, above the machine midplane.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_primary_x_point
NAMES.short: Vertical coordinate of the primary X-point is the signed Z position of the boundary-defining poloidal magnetic null where separatrix branches meet, expressed in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Vertical coordinate of the primary X-point is the $Z$ coordinate of the boundary-defining poloidal magnetic null at which separatrix branches meet in an axisymmetric equilibrium. The coordinate is expressed in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The primary X-point position is the saddle point of the poloidal magnetic flux in the poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame:

$$
\nabla_{R,Z}\psi(R_{X,\mathrm{p}}, Z_{X,\mathrm{p}}) = \left(\frac{\partial \psi}{\partial R}, \frac{\partial \psi}{\partial Z}\right)_{(R_{X,\mathrm{p}}, Z_{X,\mathrm{p}})} = (0,0)
$$

where $\psi(R,Z)$ is the axisymmetric poloidal magnetic flux, and $R_{X,\mathrm{p}}$ and $Z_{X,\mathrm{p}}$ are the major-radius and vertical coordinates of the primary X-point. The saddle topology distinguishes an X-point from the magnetic axis.

This quantity is the primary-X-point specialization of [vertical coordinate of an X-point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_x_point). When more than one X-point exists, primary denotes the null whose separatrix branches define the principal plasma-boundary separatrix; vertical coordinates of secondary X-points or nulls not assigned to that primary separatrix are excluded.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the primary X-point lies in the $+\hat{Z}$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame relative to the chosen vertical origin.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_strike_point
NAMES.short: Signed vertical (Z) coordinate of the strike point, where the plasma separatrix intersects a divertor target plate or limiter surface in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The strike-point vertical coordinate is the signed height of the intersection between the plasma separatrix and a divertor target plate or limiter surface. It identifies the strike-point location along the vertical direction, while excluding its radial coordinate.

The coordinate is defined by

$$
Z_{\mathrm{sp}} = \mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{sp}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{Z}}
$$

where $\mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{sp}}$ is the strike-point position vector and $\hat{\mathbf{Z}}$ is the vertical unit vector of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The upstream null is represented separately by the [vertical coordinate of the X point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_x_point), while limiter-contact geometry is represented by the [vertical coordinate of the active limiter point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_active_limiter_point).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the strike point lies in the direction of increasing $Z$.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_x_point
NAMES.short: Signed vertical coordinate of the poloidal magnetic null where separatrix branches meet, expressed as Z in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate of an X-point is the signed value $Z_X$ locating a poloidal magnetic-field null where separatrix branches meet in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

At the X-point, the poloidal magnetic-field components satisfy

$$
B_R(R_X,Z_X)=B_Z(R_X,Z_X)=0
$$

where $R_X$ and $Z_X$ are the major-radius and vertical coordinates of the null, and $B_R$ and $B_Z$ are the radial and vertical magnetic-field components. The quantity identifies the selected X-point and is distinct from the [vertical coordinate of the primary X-point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_primary_x_point) when another X-point is selected.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the X-point lies in the direction of increasing $Z$ from the origin of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_magnetic_field
NAMES.short: Z component of the magnetic field vector in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, where Z is vertical height. It includes contributions from plasma currents, external coil systems, and any non-axisymmetric field perturbations.
NAMES.long:
The vertical magnetic field $B_Z$ is the projection of the [magnetic_field](name:magnetic_field) vector onto the vertical unit direction $\hat{Z}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It is one component of the poloidal magnetic field in axisymmetric equilibria, and it may also include toroidally varying contributions; the non-axisymmetric part is represented by [vertical_non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field](name:vertical_non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field). The same component evaluated at material boundary locations is [vertical_magnetic_field_at_wall](name:vertical_magnetic_field_at_wall).

In an axisymmetric equilibrium, $B_Z$ is related to the radial derivative of the [poloidal_magnetic_flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux) function $\psi(R, Z)$:

$$
B_Z = \frac{1}{R}\frac{\partial \psi}{\partial R}
$$

where $R$ is major radius in meters, $Z$ is vertical height, and $\psi$ is the poloidal magnetic flux per radian. Axis and boundary reference values such as [poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_magnetic_axis](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_magnetic_axis) and poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_boundary set flux-surface normalization, while the local derivative of $\psi$ determines the vertical magnetic-field component.

$B_Z$ is computed in equilibrium reconstruction from magnetic measurements, plasma-current constraints, and, when available, internal magnetic-field constraints such as motional Stark effect polarimetry. It can also be obtained directly from magnetic-field calculations by projecting the vector field onto $\hat{Z}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

Representative values are highly device- and location-dependent. In tokamak plasma regions, $|B_Z|$ is commonly much smaller than the toroidal magnetic field, often in the range $10^{-3}$-$10^{-1}$ T, with larger local values possible near strong poloidal-field coils, divertor regions, or X-point shaping fields.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $B_Z$ points in the $+Z$ direction.

NAMES.name: vertical_magnetization_of_iron_core_segment
NAMES.short: Vertical component of an iron-core segment’s magnetization, expressed as the equivalent magnetic flux density μ0MZ in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the vertical component of the magnetization assigned to an iron-core segment, expressed as an equivalent magnetic flux density. The segment magnetization is treated as uniform, and this quantity is distinct from the total magnetic field produced by the plasma, coils, currents, and magnetized materials.

$$
B_{M,Z} = \mu_0 M_Z
$$

where $B_{M,Z}$ is the equivalent vertical magnetization flux density, $M_Z = \mathbf{M} \cdot \hat{Z}$ is the vertical component of the magnetization vector, and $\mu_0$ is the vacuum permeability. The vertical direction is $\hat{Z}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The corresponding radial component is [radial magnetization of an iron-core segment](name:radial_magnetization_of_iron_core_segment).
NAMES.sign: Positive when $M_Z$ points in the direction of increasing vertical coordinate $Z`.

NAMES.name: vertical_non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field
NAMES.short: Vertical non-axisymmetric magnetic field is the signed Z component of the toroidally varying external-coil vacuum field after its toroidally averaged component is removed.
NAMES.long:
Vertical non-axisymmetric magnetic field is the vertical component of the toroidally varying part of the external-coil vacuum magnetic field in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame. It is the signed Z-directed projection of the [non-axisymmetric magnetic field](name:non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field), not the total magnetic field.

At fixed major radius and vertical height, its defining toroidal-mean subtraction is

$$
B_{\mathrm{na},Z}(R,\phi,Z)=B_{\mathrm{vac},Z}(R,\phi,Z)-\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}B_{\mathrm{vac},Z}(R,\phi',Z)\,d\phi'
$$

where $B_{\mathrm{na},Z}$ is the vertical non-axisymmetric component, $B_{\mathrm{vac},Z}$ is the vertical vacuum-field component, $R$ and $Z$ are major-radius and vertical coordinates measured in meters, and $\phi$ and $\phi'$ are toroidal angles measured in radians.

The quantity excludes the toroidally averaged vacuum field and any plasma-response field. It is distinct from the [radial non-axisymmetric magnetic field](name:radial_non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field), which is the corresponding radial projection.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $B_{\mathrm{na},Z}$ points in the $+Z$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(\hat{R},\hat{\phi},\hat{Z})$ basis.

NAMES.name: vertical_velocity_at_current_center
NAMES.short: Vertical velocity of the plasma-current centroid, defined by the rate of change of its vertical position.
NAMES.long:
The vertical velocity at the current center is the kinematic velocity of the centroid of the plasma current distribution, describing motion along the vertical direction rather than a local fluid velocity sampled at that point.

$$
v_{Z,c}(t)=\frac{dZ_c(t)}{dt}
$$

where $Z_c$ is the vertical coordinate of the current center in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $t$ is time, and $v_{Z,c}$ is the corresponding signed velocity. The position $Z_c$ is defined by the [vertical coordinate of the current center](name:vertical_coordinate_of_current_center).

This quantity describes motion of the current-density-weighted plasma-current centroid and is distinct from the local [vertical plasma velocity](name:vertical_plasma_velocity) evaluated at that location.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the current center moves toward increasing $Z$.

NAMES.name: volume_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short: Volume enclosed by a nested toroidal magnetic flux surface, increasing from zero at the magnetic axis to the plasma volume at the last closed flux surface.
NAMES.long:
The enclosed volume is the three-dimensional region inside a nested toroidal magnetic flux surface, bounded by that surface and containing the magnetic axis.

For a surface labeled by poloidal magnetic flux \(\psi\), the enclosed volume is defined by

$$
V(\psi) = \int_{\Omega(\psi)} d^3\mathbf{x}
$$

where \(V\) is the enclosed volume, \(\Omega(\psi)\) is the region inside the flux surface, and \(\mathbf{x}\) is the position vector. The label \(\psi\) is the [poloidal magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux) associated with the surface.

The volume is zero at the magnetic axis and increases outward through nested surfaces; at the last closed flux surface it equals the confined plasma volume. It excludes regions outside that surface and is distinct from the [surface area of the flux surface](name:surface_area_of_flux_surface).

NAMES.name: minimum_safety_factor
NAMES.short: Minimum safety factor is the signed value of the safety-factor function on the closed magnetic flux surface where its magnitude is smallest. It is the scalar minimum value, not the surface location, and differs from fixed-locus values such as the magnetic-axis or edge safety factor.
NAMES.long:
The minimum safety factor is the value of the [safety factor](name:safety_factor) on the nested closed magnetic flux surface where the magnitude of the safety factor is globally minimal. It characterizes magnetic-field-line winding: the signed toroidal-angle advance per poloidal circuit in flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, with $\phi$ the toroidal angle of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The quantity is defined by evaluating the signed safety-factor function at the surface where its absolute value is smallest:

$$
q_\mathrm{min} = q(\rho_\ast), \qquad \rho_\ast \in \operatorname*{arg\,min}_{0 \le \rho \le 1} |q(\rho)|
$$

where $\rho$ is a monotonic flux-surface label normalized to 0 at the magnetic axis and 1 at the last closed flux surface, $q(\rho)$ is the signed safety-factor function, and $\rho_\ast$ labels a surface of minimum $|q|$. The result is independent of the particular monotonic label used, provided the same set of nested closed flux surfaces is covered.

This is the scalar safety-factor value at the minimum, not the position of that surface; the corresponding flux-surface location is represented by [poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_minimum_safety_factor](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_minimum_safety_factor). It differs from [safety_factor_at_magnetic_axis](name:safety_factor_at_magnetic_axis) and [safety_factor_at_normalized_poloidal_magnetic_flux_equal_to_0_95](name:safety_factor_at_normalized_poloidal_magnetic_flux_equal_to_0_95), which evaluate the same safety-factor function at specified loci rather than minimizing it over the closed-surface domain.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the toroidal angle advance of a magnetic field line is in the direction of increasing $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame as the poloidal angle $\theta$ increases in flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$.

sources.enhanced_context: Minimum q value and position.

NAMES.name: normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_at_minimum_safety_factor
NAMES.short: Radial flux-surface location of the surface of minimum safety-factor magnitude within the confined plasma, expressed by the normalized poloidal flux coordinate.
NAMES.long:
The normalized poloidal flux coordinate at minimum safety factor is the value of the [normalized poloidal flux coordinate](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate) $\rho_{\mathrm{pol,norm}}$ on the closed flux surface where the magnitude of the [safety factor](name:safety_factor) $|q|$ reaches its global minimum within the confined plasma. It locates the minimum-$|q|$ surface relative to the magnetic axis and the last closed flux surface, independent of the dimensional scale of [poloidal magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux).

The coordinate is defined by minimizing the safety-factor magnitude as a function of $\rho_{\mathrm{pol,norm}}$ and by applying the square-root normalization of poloidal magnetic flux between the magnetic axis and the last closed flux surface:

$$
\rho_{\mathrm{pol,norm},q_{\min}} = \operatorname*{arg\,min}_{0 \le \rho_{\mathrm{pol,norm}} \le 1} |q(\rho_{\mathrm{pol,norm}})|, \qquad \rho_{\mathrm{pol,norm}} = \sqrt{\frac{\psi - \psi_{\mathrm{axis}}}{\psi_{\mathrm{LCFS}} - \psi_{\mathrm{axis}}}}
$$

where $\rho_{\mathrm{pol,norm},q_{\min}}$ is the coordinate of the minimum-safety-factor-magnitude surface, $q(\rho_{\mathrm{pol,norm}})$ is the safety factor on the closed flux surface labeled by $\rho_{\mathrm{pol,norm}}$, $\psi$ is the poloidal magnetic flux of that surface, $\psi_{\mathrm{axis}}$ is the value at the magnetic axis, and $\psi_{\mathrm{LCFS}}$ is the value at the last closed flux surface.

The minimization is over the closed-flux-surface interval of the confined plasma, including the magnetic-axis limit and the last closed flux surface and excluding open-field-line regions. If more than one flux surface has the same minimum value of $|q|$, the coordinate is not uniquely determined without an additional tie-breaking convention. Because the locus is defined by $|q|$ rather than signed $q$, changing the sign assigned to $q$ does not change this coordinate; [normalized toroidal flux coordinate at minimum safety factor](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_minimum_safety_factor) gives the corresponding toroidal-flux coordinate, and [poloidal magnetic flux at minimum safety factor](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_minimum_safety_factor) gives the poloidal flux on the same surface.

NAMES.name: safety_factor_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.short: Safety factor at the magnetic axis is the limiting field-line winding number on nested closed flux surfaces, giving toroidal turns per poloidal turn as the magnetic-axis limit is approached.
NAMES.long:
The safety factor at the magnetic axis is the value of the [safety factor](name:safety_factor) on nested closed flux surfaces approaching the magnetic axis. It characterizes field-line winding by the number of toroidal turns per complete poloidal turn in the limiting surface.

The magnetic-axis value is defined by

$$
q_{\mathrm{axis}} = \lim_{\psi \to \psi_{\mathrm{axis}}} \frac{d\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}}{d\left(\Phi_{\mathrm{pol}}/2\pi\right)}
$$

where $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is toroidal magnetic flux, $\Phi_{\mathrm{pol}}$ is poloidal magnetic flux, and $\psi$ is a flux-surface label approaching its magnetic-axis value $\psi_{\mathrm{axis}}$.

It is a flux-surface limit, not a local magnetic pitch angle or local field-direction component. Unlike the [minimum safety factor](name:minimum_safety_factor), it is selected by the magnetic-axis locus rather than by the minimum of the safety-factor function; its local radial variation is related to [magnetic shear at the magnetic axis](name:magnetic_shear_at_magnetic_axis).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the toroidal magnetic-field direction and the toroidal plasma-current direction are parallel in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

sources.enhanced_context: Safety factor (q) at the magnetic axis, the value of q at the innermost closed flux surface. A key MHD stability parameter — values near rational numbers indicate potential for core-resonant modes such as sawteeth.
sources.leaf_definition: q at the magnetic axis
sources.parent_definition: 0D parameters of the equilibrium

sources.enhanced_context: Safety factor.
sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Safety factor

NAMES.name: safety_factor_at_normalized_poloidal_magnetic_flux_equal_to_0_95
NAMES.short: Safety factor at normalized poloidal magnetic flux equal to 0.95; it is the toroidal-to-poloidal magnetic-flux increment ratio on that closed flux surface and gives the number of toroidal turns in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame per poloidal turn.
NAMES.long:
The safety factor at normalized poloidal magnetic flux equal to 0.95 is the value of the [safety factor](name:safety_factor) on the closed magnetic flux surface where the normalized poloidal magnetic-flux label $\psi_N$ equals $0.95$. It characterizes magnetic-field-line winding: the number of toroidal turns in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame per complete poloidal turn on that surface.

The value is defined by evaluating the safety-factor function at the specified normalized poloidal magnetic-flux label:

$$
q_{95} = q(\psi_N = 0.95)
$$

where $q(\psi_N)$ is the safety-factor function, $\psi_N$ equals $0$ at the magnetic axis and $1$ at the plasma boundary, and the underlying safety factor is the flux-surface derivative $d\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}/d(\Phi_{\mathrm{pol}}/2\pi)$ across neighboring nested flux surfaces. Here $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}$ and $\Phi_{\mathrm{pol}}$ are respectively toroidal and poloidal magnetic fluxes expressed in webers.

This is a fixed-flux-label value near the edge of the closed-flux-surface region. It is distinct from the boundary value [safety_factor_at_plasma_boundary](name:safety_factor_at_plasma_boundary), from locus-defined values such as [safety_factor_at_pedestal_top](name:safety_factor_at_pedestal_top), and from extrema of the function such as [minimum_safety_factor](name:minimum_safety_factor); it is not a local magnetic pitch angle or a local field-direction component.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the toroidal magnetic-field direction and the toroidal plasma-current direction are parallel in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: safety_factor_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Safety factor at the plasma boundary is the field-line winding number on the boundary flux surface, giving toroidal turns during one complete poloidal turn.
NAMES.long:
The safety factor at the plasma boundary is the value of the [safety factor](name:safety_factor) on the outermost closed magnetic flux surface, identified with the plasma boundary. It characterizes magnetic-field-line winding by the number of toroidal turns per complete poloidal turn.

The boundary value is defined from neighboring nested flux surfaces by

$$
q_{\mathrm{b}} = \left.\frac{d\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}}{d\left(\Phi_{\mathrm{pol}}/2\pi\right)}\right|_{\mathrm{plasma\ boundary}}
$$

where $q_{\mathrm{b}}$ is the boundary safety factor, $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the toroidal magnetic flux enclosed by a flux surface, $\Phi_{\mathrm{pol}}$ is the poloidal magnetic flux linked by that surface, and the derivative is taken across the nested-flux-surface label.

This is a flux-surface boundary value, not a local magnetic pitch angle or field-direction component. Unlike the [safety factor at the magnetic axis](name:safety_factor_at_magnetic_axis), it is evaluated at the outermost closed surface; it is the reciprocal of rotational transform on the same surface.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the toroidal magnetic-field direction and the toroidal plasma-current direction are parallel in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_angle_of_line_of_sight
NAMES.short: Toroidal angle locating the designated point on a diagnostic line of sight in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the toroidal angular coordinate of the point designated on a line of sight. It locates that point azimuthally around the symmetry axis and is the line-of-sight-specific counterpart of the general [toroidal angle](name:toroidal_angle).

For Cartesian coordinates of the designated point, with the $chat{x}$ axis along the $phi=0$ reference and $hat{z}=hat{Z}$, the toroidal angle is defined by:

$$
\phi = \operatorname{atan2}(y,x) \pmod{2\pi}
$$

where $x$ and $y$ are the horizontal Cartesian coordinates and $\operatorname{atan2}$ returns the azimuthal angle. This is the $\phi$ coordinate in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, whose basis $(\hat{R},\hat{\phi},\hat{Z})$ satisfies $\hat{R}\times\hat{\phi}=\hat{Z}$.

The value applies to the designated point of the line of sight, not to the line-of-sight direction, angular width, or an integral along the path. For a multi-point path, the designated point is the one specified by the associated geometry.
NAMES.sign: Positive when measured counter-clockwise about $+\hat{Z}$ from the $\phi=0$ reference direction when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$.

NAMES.name: area_of_flux_loop
NAMES.short: The effective area of a flux loop is the non-negative field-to-flux sensitivity area of the sensor, including the aperture enclosed by each turn, the number of turns, and calibration factors. It converts a spatially averaged magnetic-field component normal to the loop aperture into total linked magnetic flux.
NAMES.long:
The effective area of a flux loop is the non-negative field-to-flux sensitivity factor of the sensor. It represents the aperture area enclosed by each turn, the number of turns, and calibration corrections that make the total linked magnetic flux equivalent to a spatially averaged magnetic-field component normal to the loop aperture.

The effective area $A_\mathrm{eff}$ is defined by the relation between linked flux and averaged normal field:

$$
A_\mathrm{eff} = \frac{\Phi}{\bar{B}_n}
$$

where $\Phi$ is the signed magnetic flux threading the loop and $\bar{B}_n$ is the spatial average of the magnetic-field component along the chosen loop normal.

For a specified loop normal and terminal polarity, Faraday's law gives $V = -d\Phi/dt = -A_\mathrm{eff}\,d\bar{B}_n/dt$ when $A_\mathrm{eff}$ is constant. Reversing the winding direction or terminal polarity reverses the signed quantities $\Phi$ and $V$, not the non-negative effective area.

This quantity is the flux-loop analog of [area_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe](name:area_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe) for magnetic-field probes. It differs from [area_of_rogowski_coil](name:area_of_rogowski_coil), which describes coupling to enclosed current rather than linked magnetic flux; the corresponding signed circuit response is [voltage_of_flux_loop](name:voltage_of_flux_loop).

sources.enhanced_context: Effective area of a flux loop sensor, defined as the ratio of the magnetic flux through the loop to the average magnetic field over the loop. Used to convert measured flux to equivalent field in magnetics diagnostics.
sources.leaf_definition: Effective area (ratio between flux and average magnetic field over the loop)
sources.parent_definition: Flux loops; partial flux loops can be described

NAMES.name: area_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe
NAMES.short: Geometric area enclosed by one turn of a poloidal magnetic-field probe coil, setting the winding’s flux sensitivity together with its turn count.
NAMES.long:
The poloidal magnetic-field probe area is the geometric surface area enclosed by one sensing turn of the coil. It determines the magnetic flux coupled to that turn when the field is approximately uniform and normal to the enclosed surface.

The area is defined by

$$
A_p = \int_{S_p} dS
$$

where $S_p$ is the surface bounded by one coil turn and $dS$ is its differential area element. For a uniform normal poloidal field, the linked flux is proportional to $N A_p B_p$, where $N$ is the dimensionless turn count and $B_p$ is the poloidal magnetic-field component normal to the turn surface.

This is a one-turn geometric area and does not include the turn-count factor or other calibration factors. It is the area parameter underlying the induced [voltage of a poloidal magnetic field probe](name:voltage_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe) and is analogous to the one-turn area of a [toroidal magnetic field probe](name:area_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe).

sources.enhanced_context: Cross-sectional area of each turn of a poloidal field (Bp) probe coil. Used together with the number of turns to compute the effective flux-sensing area of the magnetic pick-up coil for converting measured voltage to magnetic field.
sources.leaf_definition: Area of each turn of the coil
sources.parent_definition: Poloidal field probes

NAMES.name: area_of_rogowski_coil
NAMES.short: Area of a Rogowski coil is the effective cross-sectional area linked by one sensing turn of the closed winding. It is a geometric area factor; with winding turn density it determines the ideal current-sensing sensitivity.
NAMES.long:
Area of a Rogowski coil is the effective cross-sectional area linked by one sensing turn of a closed Rogowski winding. It is a scalar geometry factor of the winding, not the signed current threaded by the coil or the measured coil voltage.

In the ideal uniformly wound limit, the area appears as the non-negative sensitivity factor in the linear constitutive relation between coil voltage and enclosed-current time derivative:

$$
V_R(t) = \sigma \mu_0 n A \frac{d I_\mathrm{enc}}{dt}
$$

where $A$ is the Rogowski-coil area, $n$ is the winding turn density along the closed winding path, $\mu_0$ is the vacuum permeability, $I_\mathrm{enc}$ is the signed [Rogowski-coil current](name:current_of_rogowski_coil) threaded by the coil, $V_R$ is the [Rogowski-coil voltage], and $\sigma$ is the sign set by winding orientation and terminal polarity.

The effective area may represent a calibrated equivalent for a real winding with finite pitch or nonuniform cross-section, but it remains a per-turn area factor. It is in the same geometric-coil-area family as [area of a poloidal magnetic field probe](name:area_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe) and [area of a toroidal magnetic field probe](name:area_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe); multiplying by turn density, turn number, or path length gives related sensitivity factors, not this quantity.

sources.enhanced_context: Effective cross-sectional area of a Rogowski coil loop wound around a current-carrying conductor. For multi-layer coils, this is the sum of individual layer areas, determining the coil's sensitivity to enclosed current.
sources.leaf_definition: Effective area of the loop wrapped around the guiding center. In case of multiple layers, sum of the areas of each layer
sources.parent_definition: Set of Rogowski coils

NAMES.name: area_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe
NAMES.short: Cross-sectional area enclosed by one turn of a toroidal magnetic-field probe coil, determining its flux sensitivity with the winding turn count.
NAMES.long:
The per-turn cross-sectional area of a toroidal magnetic-field probe is the geometric area enclosed by one sensing turn and threaded by the local toroidal magnetic-field component. It is a non-negative geometric parameter, distinct from the total effective area of the complete winding.

For $N$ identical turns, the ideal effective flux-pickup area is

$$
A_{\mathrm{eff}} = N A_{\mathrm{turn}}
$$

where $A_{\mathrm{turn}}$ is the area enclosed by one turn, $N$ is the dimensionless number of turns, and $A_{\mathrm{eff}}$ is the total linked area. The induced [voltage of the toroidal magnetic-field probe](name:voltage_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe) is proportional to the time derivative of the magnetic flux coupled through this effective area. The quantity is analogous to the per-turn area of a [poloidal magnetic-field probe](name:area_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe), but applies to toroidal-field sensing.

sources.enhanced_context: Physical cross-sectional area of a single turn of a toroidal field (B_φ) probe coil in the magnetics diagnostic. Multiplied by the number of turns, yields the effective area for converting measured voltage to magnetic field.
sources.leaf_definition: Area of each turn of the sensor; becomes effective area when multiplied by the turns
sources.parent_definition: Toroidal field probes

NAMES.name: breakdown_stray_magnetic_field_magnitude
NAMES.short: Breakdown stray magnetic field magnitude is the scalar Euclidean magnitude of the stray magnetic-field vector at the plasma position during plasma initiation. It includes residual field in all spatial directions and carries no directional information.
NAMES.long:
Breakdown stray magnetic field magnitude is the scalar Euclidean magnitude of the stray magnetic-field vector at the plasma position during plasma initiation. It represents the local residual magnetic field at the breakdown location without retaining vector direction.

For a stray magnetic-field vector $\mathbf{B}_\mathrm{stray}$ with components in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame with basis $(\hat{R}, \hat{\phi}, \hat{Z})$, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, the magnitude is defined by:

$$
B_\mathrm{stray} = |\mathbf{B}_\mathrm{stray}| = \sqrt{B_R^2 + B_\phi^2 + B_Z^2}
$$

where $B_R$, $B_\phi$, and $B_Z$ are respectively the $\hat{R}$, $\hat{\phi}$, and $\hat{Z}$ components of the stray magnetic-field vector, and $B_\mathrm{stray}$ is the scalar magnitude.

This quantity is the breakdown-specific counterpart of [stray_magnetic_field_magnitude](name:breakdown_stray_magnetic_field_magnitude) and the scalar magnitude corresponding to breakdown_stray_magnetic_field. It differs from poloidal_breakdown_stray_magnetic_field_magnitude, which uses only the projection onto the $(\hat{R}, \hat{Z})$ poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame; it also differs from directional component quantities because it contains no sign or orientation information.

sources.enhanced_context: Stray magnetic field (Bstray) at the plasma position during plasma initiation. Residual fields from imperfect cancellation of external coil fields can inhibit electron avalanche breakdown.
sources.leaf_definition: Stray magnetic field at plasma position
sources.parent_definition: Global quantities

NAMES.name: current_of_rogowski_coil
NAMES.short: Signed conventional current threading a Rogowski-coil winding contour, with orientation set by the coil's assigned normal.
NAMES.long:
Signed conventional current threading a Rogowski-coil winding contour is the net conventional electric current crossing an oriented surface bounded by that contour. The surface orientation is specified by the coil's assigned normal and the associated right-hand rule for the contour.

The enclosed current is defined by the surface integral of conventional current density:

$$
I_{\mathrm{enc}} = \int_S \mathbf{J} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}\, dS
$$

where $S$ is any surface whose boundary is the Rogowski-coil contour, $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ is the assigned unit normal to that surface, and $\mathbf{J}$ is the conventional electric current density.

This is an enclosed-current quantity, not the electrical current carried by the Rogowski-coil sensor winding. In the Rogowski-coil principle, the induced winding voltage is proportional to $dI_{\mathrm{enc}}/dt$; $I_{\mathrm{enc}}$ is the current whose time variation drives that signal.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the net conventional current crosses the oriented surface in the direction of the assigned normal.

sources.enhanced_context: Measured current enclosed within a Rogowski coil contour, used to determine the net current (e.g., plasma current) threading the coil loop. The sign convention follows the right-hand rule relative to the coil's normal direction.
sources.leaf_definition: Measured current inside the Rogowski coil contour. The normal direction to the Rogowski coil is defined by the order of points in the list of guiding centre positions. The current is positive when oriented in the same direction as the normal.
sources.parent_definition: Set of Rogowski coils

NAMES.name: length_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe
NAMES.short: Physical length of the poloidal magnetic field probe coil along its normal vector axis. Geometric calibration parameter used with coil cross-sectional area and turn count to characterize the sensor geometry and effective sensing volume.
NAMES.long:
Physical length of the poloidal magnetic field probe coil along its normal vector axis is the non-negative axial extent of the winding that contributes to the probe's effective sensing volume. It is a geometric calibration parameter of the poloidal magnetic-field pickup coil.

This quantity is an extent of the probe coil, not a directed displacement, position, or signed projection. It excludes the coil cross-sectional area, the number of turns, lead lengths, support structures, and any calibration factor that combines geometry with electromagnetic response; the corresponding quantity for a toroidal magnetic-field probe is [length_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe](name:length_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe).

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_flux_loop
NAMES.short: Radial coordinate of a flux loop is the major-radius coordinate of the flux-loop center in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, equal to its non-negative perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis.
NAMES.long:
Radial coordinate of a flux loop is the major-radius coordinate of the flux-loop center in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It is the non-negative perpendicular distance of the loop center from the toroidal symmetry axis.

For a flux-loop center with Cartesian coordinates in a right-handed Cartesian basis $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ with $\hat{z}=\hat{Z}$ and origin on the toroidal symmetry axis, the radial coordinate is

$$
R_\mathrm{loop} = \sqrt{x_\mathrm{loop}^2 + y_\mathrm{loop}^2}
$$

where $R_\mathrm{loop}$ is the radial coordinate of the flux-loop center, and $x_\mathrm{loop}$ and $y_\mathrm{loop}$ are its transverse Cartesian coordinates.

This coordinate is distinct from [vertical_coordinate_of_flux_loop](name:vertical_coordinate_of_flux_loop) and toroidal_angle_of_flux_loop. It locates the loop center associated with flux-loop electromagnetic quantities, but does not denote the magnetic flux, terminal voltage, effective sensing area, or local orientation of the loop.

sources.enhanced_context: Major radius (R) coordinate of position.
sources.leaf_definition: Major radius
sources.parent_definition: List of (R,Z,phi) points defining the position of the loop (see data structure documentation FLUXLOOPposition.pdf)

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_rogowski_coil
NAMES.short: Major-radius coordinate of the Rogowski-coil reference point, measured as its perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the major-radius coordinate of the geometric reference point assigned to a Rogowski coil. It locates the coil relative to the toroidal symmetry axis, independently of the coil's toroidal angle.

The defining relation is

$$
R_{\mathrm{coil}} = \operatorname{dist}(\mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{coil}},\mathcal{A})
$$

where $R_{\mathrm{coil}}$ is the major-radius coordinate, $\mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{coil}}$ is the position vector of the reference point, and $\mathcal{A}$ is the toroidal symmetry axis. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $R$ is the perpendicular distance from that axis.

The reference point is the designated geometric location for the coil and is distinct from the coil's area, winding length, or electrical current. Together with the [vertical coordinate of the Rogowski coil](name:vertical_coordinate_of_rogowski_coil), it specifies the coil position in the poloidal plane.

sources.enhanced_context: Major radius (R) coordinate of position.
sources.leaf_definition: Major radius
sources.parent_definition: List of (R,Z,phi) points defining the position of the coil guiding center

NAMES.name: toroidal_angle_of_magnetic_field_probe
NAMES.short: Toroidal angle of a magnetic-field probe is the signed azimuthal orientation of the probe sensitive-axis normal in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal angle of a magnetic-field probe is the signed azimuthal angle of the probe sensitive-axis normal about the toroidal symmetry axis. It is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame with basis $(\hat{R}, \hat{\phi}, \hat{Z})$, where $\hat{R} \times \hat{\phi}=\hat{Z}$, $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ increases counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The angle is defined by the principal branch of the two-argument arctangent applied to the radial and toroidal components of that normal:

$$
\alpha_\phi = \operatorname{atan2}(n_\phi, n_R)
$$

where $\alpha_\phi$ is the scalar angle represented by this standard name, $\hat{\mathbf n}$ is the dimensionless unit vector along the probe sensitive-axis normal, $n_R=\hat{\mathbf n}\cdot\hat{R}$, $n_\phi=\hat{\mathbf n}\cdot\hat{\phi}$, and $\operatorname{atan2}(y,x)$ returns the signed principal angle from $+x$ toward $+y$.

This quantity is a probe-geometry orientation coordinate, distinct from magnetic-field components and from probe-position coordinates such as [vertical coordinate of a poloidal magnetic-field probe](name:vertical_coordinate_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe). The more specific [toroidal angle of a toroidal magnetic-field probe](name:toroidal_angle_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe) uses the same azimuthal definition for a probe classified by its intended field component. If $n_R=n_\phi=0$, the sensitive-axis normal is parallel to $\hat{Z}$ and this azimuthal angle is undefined.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the projection of the probe sensitive-axis normal onto the plane spanned by $\hat{R}$ and $\hat{\phi}$ rotates from $+\hat{R}$ toward $+\hat{\phi}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

sources.enhanced_context: Toroidal angle of the sensitive axis of a poloidal field (Bp) probe coil, describing the deviation of the coil orientation from a purely poloidal plane. Used to project the measured field component onto the correct direction.
sources.leaf_definition: Toroidal angle of coil orientation (0 if fully in the poloidal plane)
sources.parent_definition: Poloidal field probes

NAMES.name: toroidal_angle_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe
NAMES.short: Signed azimuthal orientation of a toroidal magnetic-field probe’s horizontal sensitive-axis normal, measured from the outward radial direction toward increasing toroidal angle.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the signed azimuthal orientation of the horizontal projection of a toroidal magnetic-field probe’s sensitive-axis normal vector. It describes probe orientation rather than the probe’s spatial location or its poloidal tilt.

The angle is defined from the radial and toroidal components of the normal vector:

$$
\alpha_\phi = \operatorname{atan2}(n_\phi,n_R)
$$

where $\alpha_\phi$ is the toroidal orientation angle, and $n_R$ and $n_\phi$ are the radial and toroidal components of the sensitive-axis normal vector in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame. The angle convention is complementary to the [poloidal angle of the toroidal magnetic-field probe](name:poloidal_angle_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe) and differs from the [toroidal angle](name:toroidal_angle), which locates a point rather than specifying an orientation.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the horizontal projection rotates from the outward radial direction toward increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

sources.enhanced_context: Toroidal angle of the projection of a toroidal field (B_φ) probe's normal vector onto the horizontal plane, measured counter-clockwise from the outward major radius direction. Defines the in-plane orientation of the probe sensor.
sources.leaf_definition: Angle of the projection of the sensor normal vector (n) in the horizontal plane with the increasing R direction (i.e. grad(R)) (angle is counter-clockwise from above as in cocos=11 phi-like angle). Values should be taken modulo pi with values within (-pi/2,pi/2]. Zero if projected sensor normal is parallel to grad(R), pi/2 if it is parallel to grad(phi).
sources.parent_definition: Toroidal field probes

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_flux_loop
NAMES.short: Signed vertical position of the flux-loop reference point in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, measured relative to the machine midplane.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate of a flux loop is the height of its reference point along the machine symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It locates the loop geometrically and does not describe its enclosed area, orientation, or induced voltage.

$$
Z_{\mathrm{loop}} = \mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{loop}} \cdot \hat{Z}
$$

where $Z_{\mathrm{loop}}$ is the vertical coordinate, $\mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{loop}}$ is the position vector of the flux-loop reference point relative to the coordinate origin, and $\hat{Z}$ is the upward vertical unit vector. The corresponding radial location is given by the [radial coordinate of the flux loop](name:radial_coordinate_of_flux_loop).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the flux-loop reference point lies in the $+Z$ direction, above the machine midplane.

sources.enhanced_context: Vertical (Z) coordinate of position.
sources.leaf_definition: Height
sources.parent_definition: List of (R,Z,phi) points defining the position of the loop (see data structure documentation FLUXLOOPposition.pdf)

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe
NAMES.short: Vertical Z coordinate of a poloidal magnetic-field probe position in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, locating the probe above or below the machine midplane.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate of a poloidal magnetic-field probe is the signed height of the probe position relative to the machine midplane. It describes the probe location, not the orientation of its sensitive axis or the measured magnetic-field component.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, the coordinate is defined by

$$
Z_{\mathrm{probe}} = \mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{probe}} \cdot \hat{Z}
$$

where $\mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{probe}}$ is the probe position vector and $\hat{Z}$ is the vertical unit vector. The coordinate is the positional counterpart of the [vertical coordinate of a toroidal magnetic-field probe](name:vertical_coordinate_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe) and is distinct from the [vertical coordinate of a flux loop](name:vertical_coordinate_of_flux_loop).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the probe position lies above the machine midplane in the $+Z$ direction.

sources.enhanced_context: Vertical (Z) coordinate of position.
sources.leaf_definition: Height
sources.parent_definition: R, Z, Phi position of the coil centre

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_rogowski_coil
NAMES.short: Vertical Z coordinate of the Rogowski coil position in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, measured along the machine symmetry axis.
NAMES.long:
The vertical Z coordinate locates the Rogowski coil along the machine symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $Z$ measures height above the $Z = 0$ reference plane. Together with the major radius given by [radial_coordinate_of_rogowski_coil](name:radial_coordinate_of_rogowski_coil), it fully specifies the coil's position in a poloidal cross-section, which is required to associate the enclosed-current measurement with the correct plasma geometry and to provide geometric inputs for magnetic equilibrium reconstruction.

This coordinate is a fixed geometric parameter established from engineering metrology of the installed coil. The same vertical-coordinate convention is applied to [vertical_coordinate_of_flux_loop](name:vertical_coordinate_of_flux_loop) and [vertical_coordinate_of_coil_conductor](name:vertical_coordinate_of_coil_conductor) across the magnetic diagnostics family.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the coil is located above the $Z = 0$ reference plane, in the upward direction along the machine symmetry axis.

sources.enhanced_context: Vertical (Z) coordinate of position.
sources.leaf_definition: Height
sources.parent_definition: List of (R,Z,phi) points defining the position of the coil guiding center

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe
NAMES.short: Vertical coordinate of a toroidal magnetic-field probe is the Z position of the probe in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, measured above or below the machine midplane.
NAMES.long:
Vertical coordinate of a toroidal magnetic-field probe is the $Z$ position of the probe in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It locates the probe along the vertical direction relative to the machine midplane.

For a probe position vector $\mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{probe}}$ and the vertical unit vector $\hat{Z}$, the coordinate is the signed projection onto $\hat{Z}$:

$$
Z_{\mathrm{probe}} = \mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{probe}} \cdot \hat{Z}
$$

where $Z_{\mathrm{probe}}$ is the vertical coordinate of the toroidal magnetic-field probe.

Together with the [radial coordinate of a toroidal magnetic-field probe] and the [toroidal angle of a toroidal magnetic-field probe](name:toroidal_angle_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe), this coordinate specifies the probe position in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. This quantity is a position coordinate, not a magnetic-field component or a probe response; the corresponding coordinate for a poloidal magnetic-field probe is [vertical coordinate of a poloidal magnetic-field probe](name:vertical_coordinate_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the probe is located above the machine midplane in the $+Z$ direction.

sources.enhanced_context: Vertical (Z) coordinate of position.
sources.leaf_definition: Height
sources.parent_definition: R, Z, Phi position of the coil centre

NAMES.name: vertical_outline_of_fiber_optic_current_sensor
NAMES.short: Signed vertical Z coordinate of a contour point defining the geometric boundary of a fiber-optic current sensor in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The vertical outline coordinate is the signed height of a point on the geometric boundary of a fiber-optic current sensor, represented in a poloidal cross-section. It describes the sensor boundary geometry, not the sensed current or the optical path.

$$
Z = \mathbf{r} \cdot \hat{Z}
$$

where $\mathbf{r}$ is the point position relative to the coordinate origin and $\hat{Z}$ is the vertical unit vector of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The quantity is geometrically analogous to the contour coordinate used for [vertical outline of wall material](name:vertical_outline_of_wall_material), but applies to the fiber-optic current sensor boundary.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the outline point lies in the direction of increasing vertical coordinate $Z$.

sources.enhanced_context: Vertical (Z) coordinate of outline.
sources.leaf_definition: Height
sources.parent_definition: FOCS outline

NAMES.name: voltage_of_flux_loop
NAMES.short: Voltage of a flux loop is the direct, unintegrated terminal voltage measured across the sensor. It is induced by the time rate of change of the oriented magnetic flux threading the loop and is related to that flux by Faraday's law.
NAMES.long:
Voltage of a flux loop is the signed terminal potential difference produced when the magnetic flux linked by a conducting loop changes in time. It is the direct, unintegrated sensor output: the measured voltage itself, before conversion to magnetic flux by time integration, offset removal, or calibration.

For an oriented surface $S$ bounded by the loop, the flux-loop voltage is defined by Faraday's law:

$$
V(t) = -\frac{d\Phi(t)}{dt}, \qquad \Phi(t)=\int_S \mathbf{B}(\mathbf{x},t)\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}}\,dA
$$

where $V$ is the terminal voltage in volts, $t$ is time in seconds, $\Phi$ is the oriented magnetic flux in webers, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic flux density in tesla, $\mathbf{x}$ is position, $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ is the chosen unit normal to the surface, and $dA$ is an area element in square meters. The chosen $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ defines positive flux; the corresponding positive circulation around the loop is given by the right-hand rule, and reversing $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ or swapping the terminal polarity reverses the reported sign.

The voltage is measured with a high-impedance differential input across the two loop terminals so that the sensor minimally loads the induced electromotive force. Recovering flux requires choosing the polarity and an integration constant: with the equation's polarity, $\Phi(t)=\Phi(t_0)-\int_{t_0}^{t} V(t')\,dt'$, where $t_0$ is the reference time and $\Phi(t_0)$ is the integration constant. For equilibrium or shape constraints, this integrated flux may be used as a local constraint on [poloidal magnetic flux at a sensor attachment point](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_sensor_attachment_point); the [area of the flux loop](name:area_of_flux_loop) sets the scale for converting a flux change to an average normal-field change.

The magnitude scales with linked area and field slew rate, approximately as $|V|\sim A_\mathrm{eff}|dB_n/dt|$ for a nearly uniform normal field over effective area $A_\mathrm{eff}$, where $A_\mathrm{eff}$ is in square meters and $B_n$ is the magnetic field component along $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ in tesla. Representative operating amplitudes are often 10^-3-10 V, but near-zero values occur during slowly varying field intervals and larger voltages can occur for large loops or rapid magnetic changes; the usable range is normally set by sensor area, bandwidth, and digitizer range.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the designated positive terminal is at higher electric potential than the designated negative terminal; with the chosen loop normal defining positive magnetic flux by the right-hand rule, this corresponds through $V=-d\Phi/dt$ to a decreasing positive flux through the loop.

sources.enhanced_context: Measured voltage between the terminals of a flux loop sensor in the magnetics diagnostic. This raw signal is time-integrated to obtain the magnetic flux (Φ) through the loop, used in equilibrium reconstruction and plasma shape control.
sources.leaf_definition: Measured voltage between the loop terminals
sources.parent_definition: Flux loops; partial flux loops can be described

NAMES.name: voltage_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe
NAMES.short: Terminal voltage induced at the terminals of a poloidal magnetic field probe coil by the time variation of the local poloidal magnetic field component threading the coil windings.
NAMES.long:
The terminal voltage of a poloidal magnetic field probe is the raw inductive electrical signal generated when the poloidal magnetic field component at the sensor location changes with time. It is the primary electrical observable from which the local poloidal field is derived during post-processing.

For a coil with $N$ turns and effective cross-sectional area $A$ per turn, Faraday's law gives:

$$
V = -N A \frac{dB_p}{dt}
$$

where $B_p$ is the poloidal magnetic field component along the probe's sensitive axis, $N$ is the algebraic turn count encoding the winding direction, and $A$ is the effective [area of each turn](name:area_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe).

The raw voltage is time-integrated in post-processing to recover the instantaneous $B_p$, with corrections for resistive losses and signal drift. Arrays of poloidal field probes distributed around the vacuum vessel provide the boundary field measurements essential for equilibrium reconstruction and real-time plasma shape control. The directly analogous signal for probes oriented to sense the toroidal field is [voltage_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe](name:voltage_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe); the complement for flux-enclosed measurements is [voltage_of_flux_loop](name:voltage_of_flux_loop). The probe's spatial location entering the field derivation is given by major_radius_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the poloidal magnetic flux threading the coil in the direction of the probe's positive sensitive-axis normal is decreasing with time.

sources.enhanced_context: Voltage measured at the terminals of a poloidal field (Bp) probe coil. The raw electrical signal from which the local magnetic field is derived after accounting for coil geometry and turns.
sources.leaf_definition: Voltage on the coil terminals
sources.parent_definition: Poloidal field probes

NAMES.name: voltage_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe
NAMES.short: Terminal voltage of a toroidal magnetic field probe coil, induced by the time variation of the local toroidal magnetic field component threading the coil windings.
NAMES.long:
A toroidal magnetic field probe is a pickup coil wound to sense the toroidal component of the magnetic field at a specific location. The terminal voltage is the raw inductive signal produced as the local toroidal field $B_\phi$ evolves in time.

The coil voltage follows from Faraday's law of induction:

$$
V = -N A \frac{dB_\phi}{dt}
$$

where $N$ is the number of turns and $A$ is the effective cross-sectional area per turn. Time-integrating the voltage signal and dividing by the coil sensitivity $NA$ recovers the local toroidal field value; the geometric parameters are provided by count_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe and [area_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe](name:area_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe).

Probes are mounted on the vacuum vessel wall or plasma-facing surfaces and sampled on fast analog-to-digital converters to capture the full temporal evolution of the toroidal field. The analogous measurement for the poloidal field component is given by [voltage_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe](name:voltage_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe).
NAMES.sign: Positive when $dB_\phi/dt > 0$ for a coil wound in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

sources.enhanced_context: Voltage measured at the terminals of a toroidal magnetic field (B_φ) probe coil in the magnetics diagnostic. The raw coil voltage is integrated and calibrated to derive the local toroidal magnetic field component.
sources.leaf_definition: Voltage on the coil terminals
sources.parent_definition: Toroidal field probes

NAMES.name: poloidal_angle_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe
NAMES.short: Poloidal angle of a toroidal magnetic-field probe’s sensitive-axis normal in the poloidal cross-section of the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, measured clockwise from the outward radial direction.
NAMES.long:
The poloidal angle of a toroidal magnetic-field probe is the angular coordinate of its sensitive-axis normal in a poloidal cross-section of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It is the orientation form of [poloidal angle](name:poloidal_angle), not the spatial angle of the probe location.

For the probe's sensitive-axis unit normal vector $\hat{\mathbf n}$, the angle is

$$
\theta_n=\operatorname{atan2}(-n_Z,n_R)\pmod{2\pi}
$$

where $\theta_n$ is the poloidal angle, and $n_R$ and $n_Z$ are the components of $\hat{\mathbf n}$ along the cylindrical $\hat{R}$ and $\hat{Z}$ directions.

This quantity defines the coil orientation used to relate the probe's normal to the local magnetic field. Unlike [poloidal angle of a measurement position](name:poloidal_angle_of_measurement_position), it does not locate the probe; together with [toroidal angle of a toroidal magnetic-field probe](name:toroidal_angle_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe), it specifies the angular orientation of the sensitive-axis normal.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the sensitive-axis normal is tilted clockwise from the outward $+R$ direction toward $-Z$ when viewed from the $+\phi$ direction.

sources.enhanced_context: Poloidal angle of the normal vector of a toroidal field (B_φ) probe sensor with respect to the horizontal plane, defining the coil orientation. Used to project the measured magnetic signal onto the correct vector component for equilibrium reconstruction.
sources.leaf_definition: Angle of the sensor normal vector (vector parallel to the the axis of the coil, n on the diagram) with respect to horizontal plane (clockwise theta-like angle). Zero if sensor normal vector fully in the horizontal plane and oriented towards increasing major radius. Values in [0 , 2Pi]
sources.parent_definition: Toroidal field probes

NAMES.name: angle_of_iron_core_segment
NAMES.short: Signed orientation angle of a slanted side in a poloidal cross-section, measured from the outward major-radius direction in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is a signed inclination angle for an oriented slanted side or edge in a poloidal cross-section. It characterizes orientation relative to the outward major-radius direction and is independent of the side's length. The representative [alpha angle of an iron core segment](name:alpha_angle_of_iron_core_segment) is a concrete instance.

The inclination $\theta$ is defined from the oriented side unit vector $\hat{s}$ by

$$
\theta = \operatorname{atan2}(\hat{s}\cdot\hat{Z},\hat{s}\cdot\hat{R})
$$

where $\hat{R}$ and $\hat{Z}$ are the outward radial and upward vertical unit vectors in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, and $\hat{s}$ is the oriented unit vector along the side. The toroidal unit vector is $\hat{\phi}$, completing the basis. This angle describes cross-sectional orientation rather than the side length, for which [major length of an iron core segment](name:major_length_of_iron_core_segment) is a distinct quantity.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the oriented side direction is rotated from the outward $+\hat{R}$ direction toward $+\hat{Z}$.

NAMES.name: alpha_angle_of_iron_core_segment
NAMES.short: Signed inclination of the alpha-side edge of an iron core segment cross-section, measured from the outward major-radius direction toward increasing vertical height.
NAMES.long:
The alpha angle is the signed orientation of the designated alpha-side edge of an iron core segment in the poloidal cross-section of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It identifies the alpha-side orientation and is independent of the edge length.

For an oriented alpha-side vector with signed radial and vertical components $\Delta R$ and $\Delta Z$, the angle is defined by

$$
\alpha = \operatorname{atan2}(\Delta Z,\Delta R)
$$

where $\alpha$ is the alpha angle, $\Delta R$ is the component along the outward major-radius direction, and $\Delta Z$ is the component along the vertical direction. This quantity is the alpha-side specialization of the general [iron core segment orientation angle](name:angle_of_iron_core_segment), not a length or cross-sectional dimension.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the oriented alpha-side vector is inclined from the outward $+R$ direction toward increasing $Z$.

sources.enhanced_context: First inclination angle (α) of the oblique (trapezoidal/parallelogram) cross-sectional geometry of an iron core segment, measured counter-clockwise from a reference axis. Part of the geometric parametrisation of transformer core elements.
sources.leaf_definition: Inclination of first angle TBD
sources.parent_definition: Trapezoidal description of the element

NAMES.name: area_of_correction_coil
NAMES.short: Non-negative full geometric area of the conducting material in one correction-coil cross-section, taken perpendicular to the local conductor path and treated as constant along the coil length.
NAMES.long:
Non-negative full geometric area of the conducting material in one correction-coil cross-section is the cross-sectional measure of the electrical conductor on a plane normal to the local conductor path. It is a property of one correction-coil conductor element, not a sum over separate turns or parallel conductor elements.

The area includes the conducting material in that cross-section and excludes voids, insulation, coolant channels, nonconducting supports, and any winding-pack or coil-footprint area outside the conductor material. For hollow or compound conductors, only regions that are part of the electrical conductor are included.

It is distinct from [radius_of_correction_coil](name:radius_of_correction_coil), [inner_radius_of_correction_coil](name:inner_radius_of_correction_coil), and [width_of_correction_coil](name:width_of_correction_coil), which specify particular dimensions of a cross-section; different cross-sectional shapes can have the same area.

sources.enhanced_context: Cross-sectional area of a non-axisymmetric coil conductor, derived from its geometric contour. Characterizes the conductor cross-section, assumed constant along the conductor length, for ELM control, error field, or RMP coils.
sources.leaf_definition: Area of the conductor cross-section, derived from the above geometric data
sources.parent_definition: The cross-section perpendicular to the conductor contour is described by a series of contour points, given by their relative position with respect to the start point of the first element. This cross-section is assumed constant for all elements.

NAMES.name: area_of_passive_loop
NAMES.short: Area of a passive loop is the non-negative cross-sectional area of conducting material in a passive loop element, taken on a section normal to the local current path. It excludes the aperture enclosed by the loop.
NAMES.long:
Area of a passive loop is the non-negative cross-sectional area of the solid conducting material of a passive conducting loop element, evaluated on a surface normal to the local current path. It is a material cross-section of the conductor, not the aperture enclosed by the loop or the area swept out by the loop centerline.

The general geometric definition is the area of the conducting region $\mathcal{S}$ in that normal cross-section:

$$
A = \int_{\mathcal{S}} dS
$$

where $A$ is the passive-loop conductor area, $\mathcal{S}$ is the subset of the section occupied by conducting material, and $dS$ is the scalar surface-area element.

For an annular cross-section, this definition gives $A = \pi(r_o^2-r_i^2)$, where $r_i$ and $r_o$ are the [inner](name:inner_radius_of_passive_loop) and [outer](name:outer_radius_of_passive_loop) radii measured from the annulus center to the conducting boundaries. For a non-annular cross-section, $\mathcal{S}$ is the bounded conducting region defined by the conductor geometry; parameters such as [thickness](name:thickness_of_passive_loop), width, or height describe that boundary but are not themselves the area.

sources.enhanced_context: Cross-sectional area of an individual passive conductor loop element. Used in electromagnetic circuit modelling of the tokamak passive conducting structures for eddy current and vertical stability analysis.
sources.leaf_definition: Cross-sectional areas of the element
sources.parent_definition: Each loop is comprised of a number of cross-section elements described  individually

NAMES.name: area_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Non-negative full geometric area of the conducting cross section of one poloidal-field-coil element in a poloidal plane at fixed toroidal angle φ of the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, where R is major radius and Z is vertical height.
NAMES.long:
Non-negative full geometric area of the conducting cross section of one poloidal-field-coil element is the surface measure of the conductor region enclosed by that element boundary. It is defined in a poloidal plane at fixed toroidal angle $\phi$ of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

For an arbitrary conductor cross-section, the area is the integral of the differential surface measure over the conductor region $\mathcal{S}$:

$$
A = \int_{\mathcal{S}} dS
$$
