where $A$ is the area of the poloidal-field-coil element, $\mathcal{S}$ is the conductor region in the poloidal plane, and $dS$ is the differential surface measure on that plane.

The quantity is per coil element, not a sum over multiple elements or over a complete coil. For a rectangular cross-section aligned with the $R$ and $Z$ directions of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $A = W H$, where $W$ is [width_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:width_of_poloidal_field_coil) and $H$ is [height_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:height_of_poloidal_field_coil); [thickness_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:thickness_of_poloidal_field_coil) is a separate geometric extent and is not the radial width in this relationship. For an annular cross-section, $A = \pi(r_\mathrm{out}^2-r_\mathrm{in}^2)$, where $r_\mathrm{out}$ is [outer_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:outer_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil) and $r_\mathrm{in}$ is [inner_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:inner_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil). An insulation envelope, winding-pack envelope, or effective conducting area is a distinct quantity unless it is defined by the same boundary as $\mathcal{S}$.

sources.enhanced_context: Cross-sectional area of an individual element of a poloidal field (PF) coil, describing the conductor cross-section geometry used in electromagnetic and structural modelling of the coil assembly.
sources.leaf_definition: Cross-sectional areas of the element
sources.parent_definition: Each PF coil is comprised of a number of cross-section elements described  individually

NAMES.name: area_of_toroidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Non-negative geometric area of the conducting material within a toroidal-field-coil conductor’s cross-sectional boundary, measured normal to its local centerline.
NAMES.long:
The area of a toroidal-field-coil conductor is the geometric area occupied by conducting material in a cross-section normal to the conductor’s local centerline. It excludes any void, bore, insulation, or surrounding aperture.

The area is defined by

$$
A_{\mathrm{cond}} = \iint_{S_{\mathrm{cond}}} dS
$$

where $A_{\mathrm{cond}}$ is the conductor cross-sectional area, $S_{\mathrm{cond}}$ is the region enclosed by the conductor boundary, and $dS$ is its differential area element.

This quantity complements the conductor dimensions represented by the [width of the toroidal field coil](name:width_of_toroidal_field_coil) and [height of the toroidal field coil](name:height_of_toroidal_field_coil); it is not the area enclosed by a winding or loop.

sources.enhanced_context: Cross-sectional area of a TF coil conductor, derived from the conductor cross-section geometry. Used in electromagnetic and structural analyses of the toroidal field coil system.
sources.leaf_definition: Area of the conductor cross-section, derived from the above geometric data
sources.parent_definition: The cross-section perpendicular to the TF conductor contour is described by a series of contour points, given by their relative position with respect to the start point of the first element. This cross-section is assumed constant for all elements.

NAMES.name: binormal_coordinate_of_correction_coil
NAMES.short: Signed displacement of a correction-coil conductor outline vertex along the local Frenet–Serret binormal, measured from the conductor centerline.
NAMES.long:
The binormal coordinate specifies the signed position of a correction-coil conductor cross-section outline vertex along the local Frenet–Serret binormal direction. Together with the [normal coordinate of the correction coil](name:normal_coordinate_of_correction_coil), it defines the vertex position in the cross-sectional plane.

For vertex position $\mathbf{r}_v$ and corresponding centerline position $\mathbf{r}_c$, the coordinate is

$$
b_v = (\mathbf{r}_v - \mathbf{r}_c) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{b}}
$$

where $b_v$ is the binormal coordinate in m, $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$ is the local unit binormal, and $\mathbf{r}_v$ and $\mathbf{r}_c$ are positions in m. The local Frenet–Serret triad is oriented so that $\hat{\mathbf{b}} = \hat{\mathbf{t}} \times \hat{\mathbf{n}}$, with $\hat{\mathbf{t}}$ the tangent and $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ the normal unit vector. This coordinate is a signed vertex displacement, not the full conductor cross-section height represented by the [height of the correction coil](name:height_of_correction_coil).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the vertex displacement from the conductor centerline points in the direction of the local unit binormal $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$.

sources.enhanced_context: Coordinates of the conductor cross-section outline vertices along the binormal axis of the local Frenet-Serret frame. Defines the polygonal shape of the non-axisymmetric coil conductor cross-section perpendicular to the conductor contour.
sources.leaf_definition: Coordinates along the binormal axis
sources.parent_definition: Polygonal outline of the cross section in the (normal, binormal) coordinate system. Do NOT repeat the first point.

NAMES.name: binormal_coordinate_of_toroidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Signed displacement of each toroidal-field-coil conductor cross-section outline vertex along the local Frenet–Serret binormal from the conductor centerline.
NAMES.long:
The binormal coordinate specifies the signed local displacement of a toroidal-field-coil conductor cross-section outline vertex from the conductor centerline in the direction perpendicular to both the local tangent and normal.

$$
b_v = (\mathbf{r}_v-\mathbf{r}_c)\cdot\hat{\mathbf{b}}
$$

where $b_v$ is the binormal coordinate, $\mathbf{r}_v$ is the vertex position in m, $\mathbf{r}_c$ is the corresponding centerline position in m, and $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$ is the unit binormal of the local Frenet–Serret frame. Together with the [normal coordinate of the toroidal field coil](name:normal_coordinate_of_toroidal_field_coil), it defines the conductor cross-section outline in the local normal–binormal plane; it is not a global vertical coordinate.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the vertex displacement has a component in the direction of the local Frenet–Serret binormal.

sources.enhanced_context: Coordinates of the TF conductor cross-section outline vertices along the binormal axis of the local Frenet–Serret frame, defining the polygonal shape of the conductor cross-section perpendicular to the conductor contour.
sources.leaf_definition: Coordinates along the binormal axis
sources.parent_definition: Polygonal outline of the cross section in the (normal, binormal) coordinate system. Do NOT repeat the first point.

NAMES.name: count_of_toroidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Count of discrete toroidal-field-coil modules forming the device’s toroidal magnetic-field system; conductor turns within a module are not counted separately.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal-field-coil module count is the number of distinct coil modules forming the device’s toroidal magnetic-field system. Each module is counted once, regardless of how many conductor turns or conductor elements it contains.

This count is an inventory of coil modules, not a winding-turn count and not a measure of electrical excitation or conductor geometry. Those properties are described separately by the [current of a toroidal field coil](name:current_of_toroidal_field_coil) and the [area of a toroidal field coil](name:area_of_toroidal_field_coil).

sources.enhanced_context: Data field in tf.
sources.leaf_definition: Number of coils around the torus, in case is_periodic = 1

NAMES.name: current_of_correction_coil
NAMES.short: Signed conventional current circulating through a non-axisymmetric correction-coil winding and determining its electromagnetic excitation.
NAMES.long:
Correction-coil current is the signed rate of charge transport through the winding circuit. It represents the net circuit current driving the magnetic field generated by the correction coil, rather than the local current density within its conductor.

The current is defined by

$$
I = \frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

where $I$ is conventional current, $Q$ is transported electric charge in coulombs, and $t$ is time in seconds. Its electrical behavior is related to the coil's [resistance](name:resistance_of_correction_coil), while the conductor geometry is characterized by its [cross-sectional area](name:area_of_correction_coil). It is distinct from [passive-loop current](name:current_of_passive_loop), which is induced in a passive conducting loop rather than deliberately driven through a correction-coil winding.
NAMES.sign: Positive when conventional current flows in the designated positive direction around the correction-coil winding; reversing the winding traversal reverses the sign.

sources.enhanced_context: Electrical current flowing through a non-axisymmetric coil element, such as an ELM control or error field correction coil. Time-resolved waveform used to compute the resulting 3D perturbed magnetic field.
sources.leaf_definition: Current in the coil
sources.parent_definition: Set of coils

NAMES.name: current_of_passive_loop
NAMES.short: Current of a passive loop is the signed toroidal current flowing in one passive conducting loop identified by a passive-loop index. It is an eddy current induced by changes in linked magnetic flux from plasma currents, active coils, and mutual coupling to other passive conductors.
NAMES.long:
Current of a passive loop is the signed toroidal electric current flowing in one identified closed passive conducting loop with no applied power supply. Each value is per passive-loop index, where the index denotes a distinct conducting circuit; it is not the aggregate current of a passive structure.

For lumped passive circuit $k$, Faraday's law and Ohm's law give the source-free circuit equation:

$$
\mathcal{R}_k I_k + \frac{d}{dt}\left(L_k I_k + \sum_{j \ne k} M^{pp}_{kj} I_j + \sum_a M^{pa}_{ka} I_a + \Psi^{\mathrm{pl}}_k\right) = 0
$$

where $I_k$ is the current of passive loop $k$, $\mathcal{R}_k$ is its [resistance_of_passive_loop](name:resistance_of_passive_loop), $L_k$ is its self-inductance, $M^{pp}_{kj}$ couples it to passive loop $j$, $M^{pa}_{ka}$ couples it to active coil circuit $a$, $I_j$ and $I_a$ are the corresponding currents, and $\Psi^{\mathrm{pl}}_k$ is the plasma-linked magnetic flux. The mutual-inductance terms represent coupling to neighboring passive loops and active coils; they are not included in $\Psi^{\mathrm{pl}}_k$. All flux-linkage terms are signed by the right-hand rule for the loop orientation corresponding to positive $I_k$.

This quantity is distinct from [current_of_passive_structure](name:current_of_passive_structure), which denotes an aggregate or structure-level passive current rather than the current assigned to one passive-loop index. It is also distinct from voltage_of_passive_loop and [voltage_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe](name:voltage_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe), which denote loop voltages rather than conduction currents in a passive loop.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the loop current circulates in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height.

sources.enhanced_context: Induced current flowing in a passive conducting loop as a function of time. Arises from inductive coupling during plasma current changes, active coil transients, and disruptions, and plays a key role in vertical stability.
sources.leaf_definition: Passive loop current
sources.parent_definition: Passive axisymmetric conductor description in the form of non-connected loops; any connected loops are expressed as active coil circuits with no power supply attached.

NAMES.name: current_of_toroidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Current of a toroidal-field coil is the signed conventional electric current carried by one toroidal-field-coil winding. Its sign is defined by the toroidal magnetic-field component produced by that coil.
NAMES.long:
Current of a toroidal-field coil is the signed conventional electric current carried by one toroidal-field-coil winding. It represents the coil current that sources that coil's contribution to the toroidal magnetic field.

The signed current is the current-density flux through an oriented cross-section of the winding conductor:

$$
I = \int_S \mathbf{J} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}\, dA
$$

where $I$ is the coil current, $\mathbf{J}$ is the conventional current density, $S$ is the oriented cross-section, $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ is its unit normal, and $dA$ is the surface area element.

This quantity is an individual coil or coil-circuit current. It excludes multiplication by the number of turns, summation over a toroidal-field-coil set, and currents induced in passive conducting structures such as [current of passive structure](name:current_of_passive_structure). It is distinct from terminal [voltage of a toroidal-field coil](name:voltage_of_toroidal_field_coil) and from [resistance of a toroidal-field coil](name:resistance_of_toroidal_field_coil).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the toroidal component of the magnetic-field contribution from the coil is positive, $B_\phi > 0$, in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

sources.enhanced_context: Current flowing in a toroidal field (TF) coil. Together with coil turns and geometry, determines the vacuum toroidal magnetic field strength (B0) used to confine the plasma.
sources.leaf_definition: Current in the coil
sources.parent_definition: Set of coils around the tokamak

NAMES.name: flux_of_toroidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Particle flux of neutrons produced by fusion reactions, giving the number of neutrons crossing a unit surface area per unit time at a specified location in or around the device.
NAMES.long:
Neutron flux $\Phi_n$ quantifies the intensity of neutron radiation at a given point as the number of neutrons traversing a unit area per unit time, integrated over all directions and energies. It is related to the local neutron number density $n_n$ and mean neutron speed $v_n$ by

$$
\Phi_n = n_n \, v_n
$$

where $n_n$ is in m$^{-3}$ and $v_n$ is in m s$^{-1}$, so that $\Phi_n$ carries units of m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$. More generally, $\Phi_n$ is the zeroth angular moment of the neutron angular flux, obtained by integrating the directional neutron current over all solid angles.

In tokamaks, neutrons arise primarily from deuterium-tritium reactions releasing 14.1 MeV neutrons and deuterium-deuterium reactions releasing 2.45 MeV neutrons; the flux peaks near the plasma core where fusion power density is highest and attenuates through blanket and structural materials. Neutron flux is detected using fission chambers, activation foils, or scintillation detectors placed at various radial and poloidal positions around the vacuum vessel. The specific instance [neutron_flux_of_toroidal_field_coil](name:neutron_flux_of_toroidal_field_coil) characterizes the flux reaching the toroidal field coils, which governs radiation damage accumulation and coil lifetime.

NAMES.name: force_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Signed electromagnetic force on an individual poloidal field coil, formed from radial and vertical Lorentz force components, used to define structural load limits and engineering bounds for coil system design.
NAMES.long:
The force on a poloidal field coil arises from the Lorentz interaction between the energized coil conductors and the total magnetic field contributed by the plasma current and all electromagnets in the device. It is a signed scalar representing a projection or combination of force components resolved in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, with radial contributions along $\hat{R}$ (increasing major radius) and vertical contributions along $\hat{Z}$.

The net electromagnetic force along a given direction is obtained by integrating the Lorentz body force over the conductor volume:

$$
F = \int_V (\mathbf{J} \times \mathbf{B}) \cdot \hat{n} \, dV
$$

where $\mathbf{J}$ is the current density in the conductor, $\mathbf{B}$ is the total magnetic field, and $\hat{n}$ is the unit vector of the projection direction. This force scalar underlies the engineering bounds expressed by [maximum_force_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:maximum_force_of_poloidal_field_coil) and [minimum_force_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:minimum_force_of_poloidal_field_coil), which set the upper and lower structural limits used in coil system design and scenario optimization. For spatially resolved component forces, see [radial_force_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:radial_force_of_poloidal_field_coil) and [vertical_force_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:vertical_force_of_poloidal_field_coil); for the global coil-system resultants, see radial_force and vertical_force.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the vertical force component is directed upward along $+Z$ and the radial force component is directed outward along increasing major radius $R$.

sources.enhanced_context: Mechanical force on the poloidal field (PF) coil system, with positive sign defined as upward for vertical forces and outward for radial forces. Used in structural integrity assessment and coil scenario optimisation.
sources.leaf_definition: Force (positive when upwards for a vertical force, positive when outwards for a radial force)
sources.parent_definition: Description of force limits on the axisymmetric PF coil system

NAMES.name: height_of_correction_coil
NAMES.short: Full non-negative extent of a rectangular correction-coil conductor cross-section measured along the local Frenet–Serret binormal.
NAMES.long:
The correction-coil height is the full external-envelope dimension of its rectangular conductor cross-section along the binormal direction of the local Frenet–Serret frame $(\hat{\mathbf t}, \hat{\mathbf n}, \hat{\mathbf b})$. It is distinct from the transverse dimension measured along the local normal direction, defined by the [width of a correction coil](name:width_of_correction_coil).

$$
h = b_{\max} - b_{\min}
$$

where $h$ is the conductor height and $b_{\max}$ and $b_{\min}$ are the signed binormal coordinates of the opposing outer faces, consistent with the [binormal coordinate of a correction coil](name:binormal_coordinate_of_correction_coil). The quantity is the full extent, not a half-height, centerline offset, or cross-sectional area.

sources.enhanced_context: Full height of the rectangular cross-section of a non-axisymmetric coil conductor in the binormal direction, applicable when the cross-section geometry type is rectangular (index = 3).
sources.leaf_definition: Full height of the rectangle in the binormal direction, used only if geometry_type/index = 3
sources.parent_definition: The cross-section perpendicular to the conductor contour is described by a series of contour points, given by their relative position with respect to the start point of the first element. This cross-section is assumed constant for all elements.

NAMES.name: height_of_iron_core_segment
NAMES.short: Full non-negative vertical extent of an iron-core segment’s rectangular cross-section, measured parallel to Z in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The height of an iron-core segment is the full separation between its upper and lower boundaries in the vertical direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It describes the segment’s rectangular cross-section and is distinct from its radial width and transverse thickness.

$$
H = Z_{\mathrm{upper}} - Z_{\mathrm{lower}}
$$

where $H$ is the segment height and $Z_{\mathrm{upper}}$ and $Z_{\mathrm{lower}}$ are the vertical coordinates of the upper and lower cross-section boundaries, respectively. The height is non-negative and is measured independently of the segment’s position or orientation in the toroidal direction. It is the vertical counterpart to [width of iron core segment](name:width_of_iron_core_segment) and differs from [thickness of iron core segment](name:thickness_of_iron_core_segment), which measures the transverse face-to-face dimension.

sources.enhanced_context: Vertical full height of the rectangular cross-section used in the axisymmetric representation of a ferritic object. Defines the vertical geometric extent for electromagnetic modelling of ferromagnetic components.
sources.leaf_definition: Vertical full height
sources.parent_definition: Rectangular description of the element

sources.enhanced_context: Vertical full height of the rectangular cross-section of an iron core segment in the tokamak magnetic circuit. Defines the vertical extent of the rectangular geometry element used to model the transformer core.
sources.leaf_definition: Vertical full height
sources.parent_definition: Rectangular description of the element

NAMES.name: height_of_passive_structure
NAMES.short: Full vertical extent of a rectangular cross-section of a passive conducting structure element, measured parallel to Z in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The height is the full vertical extent of a rectangular cross-section of a passive conducting structure element, measured along the vertical direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

It is defined by the difference between the upper and lower vertical coordinates:

$$
H = Z_{\max} - Z_{\min}
$$

where $H$ is the full height, and $Z_{\max}$ and $Z_{\min}$ are the vertical coordinates of the upper and lower cross-section boundaries, respectively.

This quantity is the full height, not a half-height, local thickness, or horizontal width. Its corresponding horizontal dimension is the [full horizontal width of a passive conducting structure element](name:width_of_passive_structure).

sources.enhanced_context: Vertical full height of the rectangular cross-section of a passive conducting loop element. Specifies the geometric extent of the conductor cross-section in the vertical direction.
sources.leaf_definition: Vertical full height
sources.parent_definition: Rectangular description of the element

NAMES.name: height_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Full vertical extent of a rectangular poloidal-field-coil conductor cross-section, measured parallel to the Z direction in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the complete vertical extent of an individual poloidal-field-coil conductor element with a rectangular cross-section. It measures the separation between the lower and upper boundaries parallel to the vertical coordinate $Z$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

$$
H = Z_{\max} - Z_{\min}
$$

where $H$ is the full height, and $Z_{\max}$ and $Z_{\min}$ are the upper and lower boundary coordinates of the conductor cross-section. The quantity is distinct from the radial cross-sectional extent, represented by the [width of a poloidal field coil](name:width_of_poloidal_field_coil), and from the height of a passive conducting structure, represented by [height of a passive structure](name:height_of_passive_structure).

sources.enhanced_context: Vertical full height of the rectangular cross-section of an active PF coil element. Defines the vertical dimension of the conductor cross-section for electromagnetic and structural modelling.
sources.leaf_definition: Vertical full height
sources.parent_definition: Rectangular description of the element

sources.enhanced_context: Vertical full height of the rectangular cross-section of a poloidal field (PF) coil conductor element. A geometric parameter defining the winding pack dimensions in the vertical direction.
sources.leaf_definition: Vertical full height
sources.parent_definition: Rectangular description of the element

NAMES.name: height_of_toroidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Full binormal extent of a rectangular toroidal-field-coil conductor cross-section, measured across its external envelope in the local Frenet–Serret frame.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the full dimension of a rectangular toroidal-field-coil conductor cross-section along the binormal direction of its local right-handed Frenet–Serret frame. The frame consists of tangent, normal, and binormal unit vectors, with the binormal perpendicular to the conductor centerline and the other two directions.

For opposing cross-section boundaries, the full binormal height is defined by

$$
h_b = b_{\max} - b_{\min}
$$

where $b_{\max}$ and $b_{\min}$ are the extreme signed binormal coordinates of the external cross-section envelope. The coordinate convention is consistent with the [binormal coordinate of the toroidal field coil](name:binormal_coordinate_of_toroidal_field_coil), which describes individual outline vertices.

This is a gross geometric envelope dimension; it is not the net current-carrying material thickness, insulation thickness, or a local signed coordinate.

sources.enhanced_context: Full height of the TF coil conductor cross-section in the binormal direction, applicable when the cross-section geometry is rectangular (geometry_type=3). Specifies a conductor dimension for detailed coil modelling.
sources.leaf_definition: Full height of the rectangle in the binormal direction, used only if geometry_type/index = 3
sources.parent_definition: The cross-section perpendicular to the TF conductor contour is described by a series of contour points, given by their relative position with respect to the start point of the first element. This cross-section is assumed constant for all elements.

NAMES.name: inner_radius_of_ferritic_element
NAMES.short: Inner radial boundary of the annular cross-section of a ferritic element in the axisymmetric equivalent geometry, defining the bore of the annulus centered at a reference point in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The inner radius specifies the hollow bore of the annular cross-section used to represent a ferritic element in the axisymmetric thick-line equivalent geometry. Ferritic elements are ferromagnetic inserts employed in some fusion devices to reduce toroidal magnetic-field ripple; each element is modeled as an axisymmetric body whose cross-section is an annulus centered at a reference point $(R_0, Z_0)$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major radius from the toroidal symmetry axis and $Z$ is the vertical height.

For an annular cross-section with inner radius $r_\mathrm{in}$ and outer radius $r_\mathrm{out}$, the enclosed area is

$$
A = \pi\bigl(r_\mathrm{out}^2 - r_\mathrm{in}^2\bigr)
$$

with the geometric constraint $0 \leq r_\mathrm{in} < r_\mathrm{out}$. The inner radius is a design parameter supplied directly to the geometry model and is not inferred from in-situ measurements. Together with [outer_radius_of_ferritic_element](name:outer_radius_of_ferritic_element), it fully characterizes the radial extent of the annular cross-section, while the overall radial placement of the element is given by [radius_of_ferritic_element](name:radial_coordinate_of_ferritic_element_centroid). The analogous quantity for iron core segments is [inner_radius_of_iron_core_segment](name:inner_radius_of_iron_core_segment).
NAMES.sign: Positive as a non-negative radial distance from the annulus center to the inner surface in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame where $R \geq 0$.

sources.enhanced_context: Inner radius of an annular axisymmetric element used in the equivalent geometry representation of a ferritic object. Defines the inner boundary of the annulus centred at (R, Z).
sources.leaf_definition: Inner radius
sources.parent_definition: The element is an annulus of centre R, Z, with inner radius radius_inner and outer radius radius_outer

NAMES.name: length_of_ferritic_element
NAMES.short: Euclidean length of a designated inclined side of an oblique parallelogram cross-section, measured in the poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the Euclidean length of a designated inclined side of an oblique parallelogram cross-section of a physical component. [Major length of a ferritic element](name:major_length_of_ferritic_element) is a component-specific instance of this geometric quantity.

For endpoints $(R_1,Z_1)$ and $(R_2,Z_2)$ of the side at a common toroidal angle $[1m\phi[0m$, its length is defined by

$$
L = \sqrt{(R_2-R_1)^2 + (Z_2-Z_1)^2}
$$

where $L$ is the side length, $R_i$ are major-radius coordinates, and $Z_i$ are vertical coordinates in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame; $\phi$ is the toroidal angle. The quantity is nonnegative and describes geometric extent only; it does not encode the side's signed inclination or orientation.

NAMES.name: length_of_iron_core_segment
NAMES.short: Euclidean length of a designated side of an iron-core segment’s oblique cross-section in the poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the non-negative Euclidean length of a designated side of an iron-core segment’s oblique parallelogram cross-section. It applies to either inclined side selected by the geometry, including the alpha-side specialization defined by [major length of iron-core segment](name:major_length_of_iron_core_segment).

The side length is defined by

$$
L = \sqrt{(\Delta R)^2 + (\Delta Z)^2}
$$

where $L$ is the side length, and $\Delta R$ and $\Delta Z$ are the major-radius and vertical-coordinate differences between the side’s endpoints in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame; the side lies in a poloidal plane at fixed $\phi$.

This is the length of one oblique side, not the full perimeter, cross-sectional area, vertical height, or radial width of the segment. The corresponding side angle determines the relationship between $\Delta R$, $\Delta Z$, and $L$.

sources.enhanced_context: Length of the parallelogram side inclined at angle β in the oblique (trapezoidal) cross-sectional description of an iron core segment. Defines the extent of the segment along the β-inclined direction.
sources.leaf_definition: Length of the parallelogram side inclined with angle beta with respect to the height axis
sources.parent_definition: Trapezoidal description of the element

NAMES.name: length_of_passive_structure
NAMES.short: Length of a passive conducting structure is the Euclidean length of its beta-side inclined edge in an oblique parallelogram cross-section, evaluated in a constant-φ poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, where R is major radius and Z is vertical height.
NAMES.long:
Length of a passive conducting structure is the Euclidean length of its beta-side inclined edge in an oblique parallelogram cross-section representing a passive conducting structure element. The edge is evaluated in a constant-$\phi$ poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

For endpoints $P_1=(R_1,Z_1)$ and $P_2=(R_2,Z_2)$ on the beta-side edge, the length is defined by the planar Euclidean distance:

$$
L_\beta = \sqrt{(R_2-R_1)^2 + (Z_2-Z_1)^2}
$$

where $L_\beta$ is the beta-side length and $R_i$ and $Z_i$ are the major-radius and vertical-height coordinates of endpoint $P_i$ in the same constant-$\phi$ plane.

This quantity is the beta-side member of the inclined-edge pair for an oblique passive-structure cross-section; the complementary side is a distinct specialization. It is distinct from major_length_of_passive_structure and [width_of_passive_structure](name:width_of_passive_structure), which describe other side lengths or rectangular limiting geometry, and from [height_of_passive_structure](name:height_of_passive_structure) and cross_section_area_of_passive_structure, which are separate geometric descriptors of the same cross-section. As a Euclidean distance, it is not a signed projection along $R$ or $Z$.

sources.enhanced_context: Length of the inclined side (alpha side) of the parallelogram cross-section of a passive conductor element, where this side makes angle alpha with the major radius axis. Part of the oblique trapezoidal geometry parameterisation.
sources.leaf_definition: Length of the parallelogram side inclined with angle alpha with respect to the major radius axis
sources.parent_definition: Trapezoidal description of the element

sources.enhanced_context: Length of the inclined side (beta side) of a parallelogram-shaped cross-section element of a passive conducting loop. Defines the geometry of an oblique (trapezoidal) conductor element used in passive structure modelling.
sources.leaf_definition: Length of the parallelogram side inclined with angle beta with respect to the height axis
sources.parent_definition: Trapezoidal description of the element

NAMES.name: length_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Euclidean length of an inclined side of an oblique parallelogram cross-section of a magnetic component, defining one of its oblique geometric dimensions.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the Euclidean length of a designated inclined side of an oblique parallelogram cross-section of a magnetic component. It defines one oblique geometric dimension independently of the component's particular identity or side-label convention.

The edge length is defined in the poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame by

$$
L = \sqrt{(R_2-R_1)^2 + (Z_2-Z_1)^2}
$$

where $L$ is the edge length, $R_1$ and $R_2$ are the major-radius coordinates of the endpoints, and $Z_1$ and $Z_2$ are their vertical-height coordinates; all length coordinates are in meters. The endpoints share the same toroidal angle $\phi$.

The selected edge may be distinguished by its inclination or geometric role. [major_length_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:major_length_of_poloidal_field_coil) is a concrete poloidal-field-coil instance, while [length_of_passive_structure](name:length_of_passive_structure) and [major_length_of_iron_core_segment](name:major_length_of_iron_core_segment) apply the same geometric concept to other magnetic components. This quantity is distinct from a cross-sectional height, width, or area.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the Euclidean edge length is represented as a non-negative magnitude.

sources.enhanced_context: Length of the parallelogram side inclined at angle beta with respect to the height axis in the oblique (trapezoidal) cross-section of an active PF coil element. Defines one oblique dimension of the coil geometry.
sources.leaf_definition: Length of the parallelogram side inclined with angle beta with respect to the height axis
sources.parent_definition: Trapezoidal description of the element

NAMES.name: major_length_of_ferritic_element
NAMES.short: Euclidean length of the alpha-side of a ferritic element’s oblique parallelogram cross-section, measured in the poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the non-negative Euclidean length of the alpha-side, the designated inclined edge of a ferritic element’s oblique parallelogram cross-section. It is the alpha-side-specific component of [length of a ferritic element](name:length_of_ferritic_element), rather than the length of an unspecified cross-sectional edge.

For endpoints $(R_1,Z_1)$ and $(R_2,Z_2)$ of the alpha-side in the poloidal plane,

$$
L_\alpha = \sqrt{(R_2-R_1)^2+(Z_2-Z_1)^2}
$$

where $R_i$ are major-radius coordinates and $Z_i$ are vertical coordinates, both in meters, in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame. The toroidal coordinate is fixed for this poloidal cross-sectional length. The quantity is a magnitude and is therefore non-negative.

sources.enhanced_context: Length of the parallelogram side inclined at angle alpha with respect to the major radius axis, used in the axisymmetric oblique parallelogram representation of a ferritic object's cross-section geometry.
sources.leaf_definition: Length of the parallelogram side inclined with angle alpha with respect to the major radius axis
sources.parent_definition: Parallelogram description of the element

NAMES.name: major_length_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Length of the parallelogram side inclined at the alpha angle from the major-radius direction, defining the alpha-edge of the oblique cross-section of a poloidal field coil.
NAMES.long:
In the oblique parallelogram model of a poloidal field coil cross-section, the full shape in the poloidal $(R, Z)$ plane is described by two inclined side lengths and their respective angles from the outward major-radius direction $+\hat{R}$. The major length $L_\alpha$ is the Euclidean length of the side whose orientation is inclined at the alpha angle from $+\hat{R}$, complementing the beta-side length given by [length_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:length_of_poloidal_field_coil).

For a parallelogram cross-section with alpha-side $L_\alpha$, beta-side $L_\beta$, and interior angle $\theta$ between the two sides, the cross-sectional area satisfies:

$$
A = L_\alpha \, L_\beta \, \sin\theta
$$

where $\theta$ is set by the combination of the alpha and beta inclination angles.

This side length, together with [radial_angle_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:radial_angle_of_poloidal_field_coil) and [length_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:length_of_poloidal_field_coil), fully parameterizes the oblique cross-section and enters coil flux and inductance calculations. The same alpha-side naming convention is used for iron core segments in major_length_of_iron_core_segment and for individual conductor elements in major_length_of_coil_conductor_element.
NAMES.sign: Positive as a geometric side length in the poloidal $(R, Z)$ plane; this quantity is invariant under reversal of plasma current or toroidal field direction.

sources.enhanced_context: Length of the parallelogram side inclined at angle alpha with respect to the major radius axis, used to define the oblique (trapezoidal) cross-sectional geometry of a PF coil element.
sources.leaf_definition: Length of the parallelogram side inclined with angle alpha with respect to the major radius axis
sources.parent_definition: Trapezoidal description of the element

sources.enhanced_context: Length of the parallelogram side inclined at angle alpha with respect to the major radius axis, defining the oblique (parallelogram) cross-section geometry of an active PF coil. Used in flux and inductance calculations for the coil conductor.
sources.leaf_definition: Length of the parallelogram side inclined with angle alpha with respect to the major radius axis
sources.parent_definition: Parallelogram description of the element

NAMES.name: maximum_force_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Upper allowable value of a signed electromagnetic force resultant for a poloidal-field coil, with magnitude and sign defined by one force-combination-matrix row.
NAMES.long:
Maximum force of a poloidal-field coil is the upper allowable value of a signed electromagnetic force resultant acting on the coil. It bounds the resultant derived from radial and vertical Lorentz-force components and is distinct from the actual [force of a poloidal-field coil](name:force_of_poloidal_field_coil).

For matrix row $m$, the associated force resultant is defined by

$$
F_m = a_m F_R + b_m F_Z
$$

where $F_R$ is the [radial force of a poloidal-field coil](name:radial_force_of_poloidal_field_coil), $F_Z$ is the [vertical force of a poloidal-field coil](name:vertical_force_of_poloidal_field_coil), and $a_m$ and $b_m$ are the row-specific force-combination weights. The maximum-force quantity is the upper allowable value assigned to the selected resultant; it is not a separate Lorentz-force component.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the weighted combination of outward radial force and upward vertical force, resolved in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, is positive.

sources.enhanced_context: Maximum force limit for each constraint in the PF coil force combination matrix. An unbounded limit is indicated by the EMPTY_FLT sentinel value. Used in coil current optimisation to enforce structural integrity of the PF system.
sources.leaf_definition: Maximum force limit, for each limit (line of the combination matrix). EMPTY_FLT value means unbounded
sources.parent_definition: Description of force limits on the axisymmetric PF coil system

NAMES.name: minimum_force_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Lower allowable value of a signed electromagnetic force resultant for poloidal-field coils, with its magnitude and sign defined by one row of the force-combination matrix.
NAMES.long:
Minimum force of a poloidal-field coil is the lower allowable value of a signed electromagnetic force resultant acting on the poloidal-field coil system. Each row of the force-combination matrix defines one resultant by weighting the radial and vertical components of the [force of a poloidal-field coil](name:force_of_poloidal_field_coil).

For combination row $k$, the resultant is defined by

$$
F_{\mathrm{comb},k}=w_{kR}F_R+w_{kZ}F_Z
$$

where $F_R$ and $F_Z$ are the radial and vertical electromagnetic-force components, $w_{kR}$ and $w_{kZ}$ are the row weights, and $k$ identifies the combination row. The minimum value satisfies $F_{\min,k}\leq F_{\mathrm{comb},k}$ for the applicable row. Unlike the [maximum force of a poloidal-field coil](name:maximum_force_of_poloidal_field_coil), this quantity specifies the lower structural bound rather than the upper bound.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the vertical force component is directed upward along $+Z$ and the radial force component is directed outward along increasing major radius $R$.

sources.enhanced_context: Minimum allowable force on the poloidal field (PF) coil system for each constraint defined in the force combination matrix. An unbounded lower limit is indicated by an EMPTY_FLT value.
sources.leaf_definition: Minimum force limit, for each limit (line of the combination matrix). EMPTY_FLT value means unbounded
sources.parent_definition: Description of force limits on the axisymmetric PF coil system

NAMES.name: neutron_flux_of_correction_coil
NAMES.subject: neutron
NAMES.short: Neutron number flux incident on a correction-coil surface, measuring the rate at which neutrons cross each unit area.
NAMES.long:
Neutron number flux is the local rate of neutron crossings through a surface on a correction coil. It quantifies the incident neutron radiation field at the coil surface and provides the neutron-specific content of the broader [correction-coil flux](name:flux_of_correction_coil).

The differential neutron flux is defined by

$$
\Phi_n = \frac{dN_n}{dA\,dt}
$$

where $N_n$ is the number of neutrons crossing surface area $A$ and $t$ is time. The unqualified quantity includes the neutron population without an energy selection; [fast-neutron flux of a correction coil](name:fast_neutron_flux_of_correction_coil) is its energy-restricted instance. Flux is distinct from neutron fluence, which is the time integral of flux.

NAMES.name: fast_neutron_flux_of_correction_coil
NAMES.subject: neutron
NAMES.short: Incident crossing rate of fast neutrons per unit area on the inboard-facing surface of a non-axisymmetric correction coil.
NAMES.long:
Fast neutron number flux is the incident crossing rate of the fast-neutron population per unit area on the inboard-facing surface of a non-axisymmetric correction coil. It is the fast-neutron component of [neutron flux of correction coil](name:neutron_flux_of_correction_coil).

The differential number flux is defined by

$$
\Phi_{\mathrm{fast}} = \frac{dN_{\mathrm{fast}}}{dA\,dt}
$$

where $N_{\mathrm{fast}}$ is the number of fast neutrons incident on surface area $A$ and $t$ is time; $A$ is measured in m$^2$ and $t$ in s.

The inboard-facing surface is the side directed toward decreasing major radius $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. This quantity includes only incident fast-neutron crossings and excludes outgoing crossings and the energy-integrated neutron flux.

sources.enhanced_context: Fast neutron flux incident on the inboard side of a non-axisymmetric coil. A time-resolved quantity used to assess radiation exposure and material degradation of coil components.
sources.leaf_definition: Fast neutron flux arriving on the inboard side of this coil
sources.parent_definition: Set of coils

NAMES.name: neutron_flux_of_toroidal_field_coil
NAMES.subject: neutron
NAMES.short: Total neutron flux incident on a toroidal field coil, giving the number of neutrons from all energy groups crossing a unit area of the coil structure per unit time.
NAMES.long:
The neutron flux $\Phi_n$ at a toroidal field coil quantifies the total radiation loading from all fusion-born neutrons on the coil structure, expressed as the number of neutrons of all energies crossing a unit surface area per unit time. This encompasses both thermal and fast neutron components and provides the broadest measure of radiation exposure relevant to activation inventory, cumulative dose, and gas-production in coil structural materials and superconducting windings.

The energy-integrated flux is defined as

$$
\Phi_n = \int_0^\infty n_n(\mathbf{r}, E)\, v_n(E)\, dE
$$

where $n_n(\mathbf{r}, E)$ is the energy-dependent neutron number density at position $\mathbf{r}$ and $v_n(E)$ is the neutron speed at kinetic energy $E$. The fast-neutron sub-spectrum, which governs atomic displacement damage and insulation degradation, is resolved separately by [fast_neutron_flux_of_toroidal_field_coil](name:fast_neutron_flux_of_toroidal_field_coil).

Flux levels are estimated from neutronics transport calculations driven by the fusion plasma neutron source distribution, and can be benchmarked against activation foil or dosimetry measurements on coil structural samples. The parent concept covering general particle flux on the toroidal field coil is defined in [flux_of_toroidal_field_coil](name:flux_of_toroidal_field_coil); a corresponding quantity for non-axisymmetric correction coils is given by [neutron_flux_of_correction_coil](name:neutron_flux_of_correction_coil).

NAMES.name: fast_neutron_flux_of_toroidal_field_coil
NAMES.subject: neutron
NAMES.short: Fast neutron flux incident on the inboard side of a toroidal field coil, providing a measure of radiation exposure relevant to material activation, radiation damage, and conductor insulation lifetime assessment.
NAMES.long:
Fast neutron flux at a toroidal field coil quantifies the number of energetic neutrons crossing unit area per unit time at the inboard-facing surface of the coil structure. In deuterium-tritium burning plasmas, 14.1 MeV fusion neutrons are the dominant source; these are attenuated and scattered by the blanket and shield, but a residual fast population reaches the coil and constitutes the primary radiation load on the superconducting windings and their organic insulation.

The quantity is the energy-integrated fluence rate above a fast-neutron threshold:

$$
\Phi_n = \int_{E_\mathrm{th}}^{\infty} \Phi(E)\, dE
$$

where $\Phi(E)$, in m$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$ eV$^{-1}$, is the differential neutron flux spectrum and $E_\mathrm{th}$ is the fast-neutron energy threshold adopted in the transport model.

This flux drives radiation damage processes including atomic displacement damage in conductor structural materials, helium bubble formation, and degradation of organic insulation resins — all of which set operational lifetime limits for the coil. It is assessed using Monte Carlo or deterministic neutron transport codes, validated against activation foil and threshold detector measurements. The analogous quantity for non-axisymmetric correction coils is [fast_neutron_flux_of_correction_coil](name:fast_neutron_flux_of_correction_coil).

sources.enhanced_context: Fast neutron flux incident on the inboard side of a toroidal field (TF) coil. Quantifies the neutron radiation load relevant for radiation damage, material activation, and insulation lifetime assessment.
sources.leaf_definition: Fast neutron flux arriving on the inboard side of this coil
sources.parent_definition: Set of coils around the tokamak

NAMES.name: normal_coordinate_of_correction_coil
NAMES.short: Coordinate of the correction-coil conductor cross-section outline vertices along the normal axis of the local Frenet–Serret frame.
NAMES.long:
The normal coordinate locates each vertex of the polygonal outline bounding a correction-coil conductor cross-section along the principal normal basis vector $\hat{n}$ of the Frenet–Serret moving frame. In that frame, $\hat{t}$ is the unit tangent along the conductor centerline, $\hat{n}$ points toward the instantaneous center of curvature, and $\hat{b} = \hat{t} \times \hat{n}$ is the binormal. Paired with the complementary [binormal coordinate](name:binormal_coordinate_of_correction_coil), the two coordinates fully specify each outline vertex in the plane perpendicular to the centerline.

For an outline vertex at position $\mathbf{r}$ relative to the centerline reference point $\mathbf{r}_0$, the normal coordinate is:

$$
n = (\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}_0) \cdot \hat{n}
$$

where $\hat{n}$ is the Frenet–Serret principal normal unit vector at the corresponding centerline location.

The outline vertices are defined from engineering drawings or CAD models of the correction-coil winding pack. The closed polygon formed by the normal and binormal vertex pairs encloses the [cross-sectional area] of the conductor. The analogous quantity for toroidal field coils is [normal_coordinate_of_toroidal_field_coil](name:normal_coordinate_of_toroidal_field_coil).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the vertex displacement is in the direction of the principal normal $\hat{n}$, pointing toward the center of curvature of the conductor centerline.

sources.enhanced_context: Coordinate of the conductor cross-section outline vertices along the normal axis of the local Frenet–Serret frame. Defines normal-direction positions of the polygonal cross-section boundary for a non-axisymmetric coil conductor.
sources.leaf_definition: Coordinate along the normal axis
sources.parent_definition: Polygonal outline of the cross section in the (normal, binormal) coordinate system. Do NOT repeat the first point.

NAMES.name: normal_coordinate_of_toroidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Signed coordinate of each toroidal-field-coil conductor cross-section outline vertex along the local Frenet–Serret normal, perpendicular to the conductor centerline and binormal directions.
NAMES.long:
The normal coordinate is the signed location of a toroidal-field-coil conductor cross-section outline vertex along the local Frenet–Serret normal. The cross-section lies in the plane perpendicular to the conductor centerline, so this coordinate resolves displacement along one local transverse direction.

For a vertex at centerline position $s$, the defining relation is:

$$
x_n(s) = \left[\mathbf{r}_v - \mathbf{r}_c(s)\right] \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}(s)
$$

where $x_n$ is the normal coordinate in m, $s$ is centerline arc length in m, $\mathbf{r}_v$ and $\mathbf{r}_c(s)$ are the vertex and centerline position vectors in m, and $\hat{\mathbf{n}}(s)$ is the local Frenet–Serret normal unit vector.

Together with the [binormal coordinate of the toroidal field coil](name:binormal_coordinate_of_toroidal_field_coil), this coordinate specifies the conductor outline in the local cross-sectional plane. It is distinct from a radial coordinate in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame and has the same geometric role as the [normal coordinate of the correction coil](name:normal_coordinate_of_correction_coil).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the vertex displacement has a positive projection onto the local Frenet–Serret normal unit vector $\hat{\mathbf{n}}(s)$.

sources.enhanced_context: Coordinates of the TF conductor cross-section outline polygon along the normal axis of the local Frenet-Serret frame. Defines the conductor shape in the direction perpendicular to the centreline and to the binormal axis.
sources.leaf_definition: Coordinate along the normal axis
sources.parent_definition: Polygonal outline of the cross section in the (normal, binormal) coordinate system. Do NOT repeat the first point.

NAMES.name: outer_radius_of_ferritic_element
NAMES.short: Outer radial boundary of the annular cross-section of a ferritic element in the axisymmetric equivalent geometry, defining the external extent of the annulus centered at a reference point in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The outer radius specifies the external boundary of the annular cross-section used to represent a ferritic element in the axisymmetric thick-line equivalent geometry. Ferritic elements are ferromagnetic inserts, and each element is represented by an axisymmetric body whose cross-section is an annulus centered at a reference point $(R_0, Z_0)$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius from the toroidal symmetry axis and $Z$ is vertical height.

For an annular cross-section with inner radius $r_\mathrm{in}$ and outer radius $r_\mathrm{out}$, the enclosed area is

$$
A = \pi\bigl(r_\mathrm{out}^2 - r_\mathrm{in}^2\bigr)
$$

where $A$ is the cross-sectional area and $r_\mathrm{in}$ and $r_\mathrm{out}$ are radial distances from the annulus center. The constraint is $0 \leq r_\mathrm{in} < r_\mathrm{out}$. Together with [inner radius of the ferritic element](name:inner_radius_of_ferritic_element), this quantity defines the annular cross-section; [radius of the ferritic element](name:radial_coordinate_of_ferritic_element_centroid) specifies its radial placement rather than its outer boundary.

sources.enhanced_context: Outer radius of an axisymmetric annular element representing ferritic material in the equivalent axisymmetric geometry. Together with the inner radius, defines the radial extent of the annulus used in equilibrium solvers.
sources.leaf_definition: Outer radius
sources.parent_definition: The element is an annulus of centre R, Z, with inner radius radius_inner and outer radius radius_outer

NAMES.name: permeability_of_ferritic_element
NAMES.short: Absolute magnetic permeability of a ferritic structural element, quantifying the local slope of its nonlinear B-H characteristic that relates magnetic flux density to applied field strength at a given operating point.
NAMES.long:
The absolute magnetic permeability of a ferritic element characterizes how the magnetic flux density $B$ responds to the applied magnetic field strength $H$ in the ferromagnetic material, capturing its nonlinear magnetization behavior at any point along the B-H curve. Because ferritic steels are strongly nonlinear, the permeability is field-dependent and must be specified at the relevant operating point.

The tangent permeability at a given field amplitude is defined as:

$$
\mu = \frac{dB}{dH}
$$

where $B$ is the local magnetic flux density and $H$ is the magnetic field strength at the operating point.

This permeability enters electromagnetic models of fusion devices because ferritic structural elements can significantly distort the equilibrium magnetic field configuration, particularly in the context of non-axisymmetric field correction and passive ferromagnetic compensation. Values are extracted from B-H characterization curves measured for the specific ferritic steel alloy used. In the high-field regime where magnetization has largely reached its saturation value, the tangent permeability converges to a reduced residual slope captured specifically by [saturated_permeability_of_ferritic_element](name:saturated_permeability_of_ferritic_element). The local field driving magnetization at the element's centroid is given by [radial_magnetic_field_at_ferritic_element_centroid](name:radial_magnetic_field_at_ferritic_element_centroid), and the resulting induced magnetization is described by [toroidal_magnetization_of_ferritic_element](name:toroidal_magnetization_of_ferritic_element).

NAMES.name: radial_angle_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: First inclination angle (alpha) of the oblique parallelogram or trapezoidal cross-section of a poloidal field coil element, measured in the poloidal plane from the outward major-radius direction.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal field coil conductors are frequently designed with non-rectangular cross-sections modeled as parallelograms or trapezoids in the poloidal $(R, Z)$ plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The radial angle $\alpha$ defines the inclination of one pair of parallel sides (the alpha-sides) relative to the outward major-radius direction $+\hat{R}$, characterizing how much the conductor winding departs from a purely radial orientation.

The oblique cross-section is fully parameterized by two inclination angles and two side lengths. The radial angle $\alpha$ pairs with the [vertical angle](name:vertical_angle_of_poloidal_field_coil) $\beta$ — measured from the vertical $+\hat{Z}$ direction — to define both side orientations, while [major_length_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:major_length_of_poloidal_field_coil) and [length_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:length_of_poloidal_field_coil) give the corresponding alpha-side and beta-side lengths.

This angle is a fixed geometric design parameter derived from coil engineering drawings and used in computing cross-sectional area, mutual inductance, and electromagnetic force distributions in poloidal field coil systems. The analogous first inclination angle for iron core segments is described by [alpha_angle_of_iron_core_segment](name:alpha_angle_of_iron_core_segment).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the alpha-side of the cross-section is inclined counter-clockwise from $+\hat{R}$ (toward $+\hat{Z}$) in the poloidal $(R, Z)$ plane.

sources.enhanced_context: First inclination angle (alpha, α) of the oblique (trapezoidal/parallelogram) cross-sectional geometry of an active PF coil element. Part of the oblique geometry parameterisation for non-rectangular conductor cross-sections.
sources.leaf_definition: Inclination of first angle TBD
sources.parent_definition: Trapezoidal description of the element

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_ferritic_element_centroid
NAMES.short: Non-negative major-radius coordinate locating a ferritic-element geometric centroid in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the non-negative major-radius coordinate $R$ of the geometric centroid of a ferritic element. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, $R$ is measured from the machine symmetry axis and identifies the centroid's radial location.

For the same centroid, the radial coordinate is related to its Cartesian coordinates by:

$$
R = \sqrt{x^2+y^2}
$$

where $x$ and $y$ are the signed Cartesian coordinates of the centroid in the right-handed Cartesian $(x,y,z)$ frame. The corresponding [x coordinate of the ferritic-element centroid](name:x_coordinate_of_ferritic_element_centroid), [y coordinate of the ferritic-element centroid](name:y_coordinate_of_ferritic_element_centroid), and [z coordinate of the ferritic-element centroid](name:z_coordinate_of_ferritic_element_centroid) locate the same geometric point.

This is an absolute major-radius coordinate, not a signed local offset, radial extent, outer radius, or curvature radius.

sources.enhanced_context: Curvature radius of each arc-of-circle segment defining the axisymmetric contour of a ferritic object. Used to describe the shape of axisymmetric ferritic components such as iron core segments in electromagnetic modelling.
sources.leaf_definition: Curvature radius of each arc of circle
sources.parent_definition: Description of the element contour by a set of arcs of circle. For each of these, the position of the start point is given together with the curvature radius. The end point is given by the start point of the next arc of circle.

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_iron_core_segment
NAMES.short: Non-negative major-radius coordinate of an arc-of-circle defining point on an iron-core-segment boundary in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The major-radius coordinate $R$ of an arc-of-circle defining point on an iron-core-segment boundary is its perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis. It locates the point in the poloidal cross-section in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, [1m\phi[0m, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

$$
R = \sqrt{x^2+y^2}
$$

where $x$ and $y$ are horizontal Cartesian coordinates in the right-handed Cartesian basis $(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$, with $\hat{z}=\hat{Z}$, measured from the toroidal symmetry axis and expressed in meters.

This quantity applies to a boundary point defined by the arc geometry. It is distinct from the [radius of the iron-core segment](name:radius_of_iron_core_segment), which is the curvature radius of the arc, and from the [radial coordinate of a measurement position](name:radial_coordinate_of_measurement_position), which applies the same major-radius definition at a measurement location.

sources.enhanced_context: Major radius (R) coordinate of arcs of circle.
sources.leaf_definition: Major radii of the start point of each arc of circle
sources.parent_definition: Description of the element contour by a set of arcs of circle. For each of these, the position of the start point is given together with the curvature radius. The end point is given by the start point of the next arc of circle.

NAMES.name: radial_force_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Signed radial component of the net electromagnetic Lorentz force on an individual poloidal-field coil, resolved along increasing major radius.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the net electromagnetic force on an individual poloidal-field coil projected onto the radial direction. It describes the resultant coil load, not the local electromagnetic body-force density.

The radial force is defined by

$$
F_R = \int_{V_\mathrm{coil}} (\mathbf{J} \times \mathbf{B}) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{R}}\,dV
$$

where $V_\mathrm{coil}$ is the conductor volume, $\mathbf{J}$ is the current-density vector, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic-field vector, $\hat{\mathbf{R}}$ is the radial unit vector, and $dV$ is the volume element. The radial and vertical components together determine the [electromagnetic force of a poloidal-field coil](name:force_of_poloidal_field_coil); the corresponding vertical component is given by the [vertical force of a poloidal-field coil](name:vertical_force_of_poloidal_field_coil). It is distinct from [radial volumetric force](name:radial_volumetric_force), which is a local force density rather than a net force.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the force points toward increasing major radius $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

sources.enhanced_context: Radial force (F_R) applied on a poloidal field (PF) coil, with positive values indicating the outward (centrifugal) direction. A critical structural loading parameter for coil and support design assessment.
sources.leaf_definition: Radial force applied on this coil (positive when outwards)
sources.parent_definition: Active PF coils

NAMES.name: radial_magnetic_field_at_ferritic_element_centroid
NAMES.short: Radial magnetic-field component at the geometric centroid of a ferritic element, projected onto the outward major-radius direction in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the magnetic-field component evaluated at a ferritic element’s geometric centroid and projected along the cylindrical major-radius direction. It describes the applied magnetic field, not the ferritic element’s magnetization.

The radial component is defined by

$$
B_R = \mathbf{B} \cdot \hat{R}
$$

where $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic-field vector and $\hat{R}$ is the outward major-radius unit vector in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The evaluation point is the ferritic-element centroid; its radial location is given by the [radial coordinate of the ferritic element centroid](name:radial_coordinate_of_ferritic_element_centroid). Together with the [vertical magnetic field at the ferritic element centroid](name:vertical_magnetic_field_at_ferritic_element_centroid) and [toroidal magnetic field at the ferritic element centroid](name:toroidal_magnetic_field_at_ferritic_element_centroid), it specifies the local field vector.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $B_R$ points toward increasing major radius $R$.

sources.enhanced_context: Radial (R) component of the magnetic field (B_R) evaluated at the centroid of each ferritic object element. Part of the local magnetic field vector used to evaluate magnetization and field perturbations from ferromagnetic materials.
sources.leaf_definition: R component of the magnetic field at each centroid
sources.parent_definition: Dynamic quantities, per time slice

NAMES.name: radial_magnetization_of_ferritic_element
NAMES.short: Signed radial component of the effective magnetization vector assigned to a ferritic element in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Radial magnetization of a ferritic element is the projection of its effective magnetization vector onto the cylindrical major-radius direction. It describes the element's magnetization, not the radial component of the surrounding magnetic field.

$$
M_R = \mathbf{M} \cdot \hat{R}
$$

where $M_R$ is the radial magnetization, $\mathbf{M}$ is the effective magnetization vector assigned to the ferritic element, and $\hat{R}$ is the outward radial unit vector in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The [vertical magnetization of the ferritic element](name:vertical_magnetization_of_ferritic_element) and [toroidal magnetization of the ferritic element](name:toroidal_magnetization_of_ferritic_element) are the corresponding projections onto the other cylindrical directions. This quantity is distinct from the [radial magnetic field at the ferritic element centroid](name:radial_magnetic_field_at_ferritic_element_centroid), which describes magnetic flux density rather than magnetization.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the effective magnetization points toward increasing major radius $R$.

sources.enhanced_context: Major radius (R) component of the magnetic moment vector of each ferritic element as a function of time. Characterises the radial projection of the local magnetization state of individual ferritic objects in the tokamak structure.
sources.leaf_definition: R component of the magnetic moment of each element
sources.parent_definition: Dynamic quantities, per time slice

NAMES.name: radial_outline_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Non-negative major-radius coordinate of a point on a poloidal cross-sectional outline of a poloidal-field coil conductor in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The radial outline coordinate gives the major-radius position of a point on the poloidal cross-sectional outline of a poloidal-field coil conductor. It is the absolute distance from the toroidal symmetry axis, not a signed local offset or a cross-sectional extent.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, the coordinate is defined from Cartesian coordinates by

$$
R = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}
$$

where $x$ and $y$ are Cartesian lengths in the right-handed $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ basis, with $\hat{z}=\hat{Z}$, and $R$ is the non-negative distance from the toroidal symmetry axis.

The quantity applies to outline points and is distinct from the conductor [height](name:height_of_poloidal_field_coil), [cross-sectional area](name:area_of_poloidal_field_coil), and the analogous outline coordinate for a generic [coil conductor element](name:radial_outline_of_coil_conductor_element).

sources.enhanced_context: Major radius (R) coordinate of arcs of circle.
sources.leaf_definition: Major radii of the start point of each arc of circle
sources.parent_definition: Description of the element contour by a set of arcs of circle. For each of these, the position of the start point is given together with the curvature radius. The end point is given by the start point of the next arc of circle.

NAMES.name: radius_of_correction_coil
NAMES.short: Radial dimension from the center of a correction-coil conductor’s annular cross-section to a specified conductor boundary.
NAMES.long:
The radius of a correction-coil conductor is the non-negative distance from the center of its annular cross-section to a specified inner or outer conductor boundary. It is a geometric boundary location, not the conductor thickness, transverse width, or cross-sectional area.

For a specified boundary point, the radius is defined by

$$
r_b = \left\lVert \mathbf{x}_b - \mathbf{x}_c \right\rVert
$$

where $r_b$ is the boundary radius, $\mathbf{x}_b$ is the boundary-point position, and $\mathbf{x}_c$ is the annulus-center position; the position vectors and radius are measured in meters.

The boundary designation identifies the specific quantity: [inner radius of the correction coil](name:inner_radius_of_correction_coil) is the inner-boundary case and defines the conductor bore size. The radius is non-negative and is distinct from annular thickness, conductor width, and cross-sectional area.

NAMES.name: inner_radius_of_correction_coil
NAMES.short: Inner radius of the annular cross-section of a non-axisymmetric correction coil conductor, defining the bore size of the hollow conductor or winding pack.
NAMES.long:
The inner radius defines the bore boundary of the annular cross-section used to model a correction coil conductor or winding pack. Together with the outer radius given by radius_of_correction_coil, it fully specifies the hollow circular geometry, with conductor material occupying the annular region between $r_{\rm in}$ (this quantity) and $r_{\rm out}$.

The cross-sectional area enclosed by the conductor annulus is

$$
A = \pi \left( r_{\rm out}^2 - r_{\rm in}^2 \right)
$$

where $r_{\rm out}$ is the outer radius and $r_{\rm in}$ is the inner radius, both in meters.

This parameter enters electromagnetic and structural models of non-axisymmetric coils used for error field correction or ELM suppression. The area_of_correction_coil is computed directly from the inner and outer radii. An analogous bore parameter for poloidal field coils is given by [inner_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:inner_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil).
NAMES.sign: Positive when measured as a radial distance from the conductor bore axis to the inner conducting surface.

sources.enhanced_context: Inner radius of an annular conductor cross-section for a non-axisymmetric coil, applicable when the geometry type is set to annulus. Defines the hole radius of the annular conductor shape.
sources.leaf_definition: Inner radius of the annulus, used only if geometry_type/index = 5
sources.parent_definition: The cross-section perpendicular to the conductor contour is described by a series of contour points, given by their relative position with respect to the start point of the first element. This cross-section is assumed constant for all elements.

NAMES.name: radius_of_iron_core_segment
NAMES.short: Radius of an iron-core segment is the non-negative geometry radius used to define that segment’s boundary in the poloidal cross-section of the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, where R is major radius and Z is vertical height. It is axis-referenced only for boundary geometry defined about the toroidal symmetry axis; otherwise it is the radius about the specified arc center.
NAMES.long:
Radius of an iron-core segment is the non-negative geometry radius that defines an axis-centered boundary or a circular-arc boundary of the segment. The relevant cross-section is the plane spanned by $R$ and $Z$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius measured from the toroidal symmetry axis and $Z$ is vertical height. The reference is the toroidal symmetry axis only for boundary geometry specified about that axis; when an explicit arc center is specified in the poloidal cross-section, that center is the reference.

The defining distance is selected by the reference geometry:

$$
r = \begin{cases}
R_b, & \text{for boundary geometry referenced to the toroidal symmetry axis}, \\
\sqrt{(R_b - R_c)^2 + (Z_b - Z_c)^2}, & \text{for boundary geometry referenced to an explicit arc center}.
\end{cases}
$$

where $r$ is the radius, $(R_b, Z_b)$ is the boundary point, and $(R_c, Z_c)$ is the explicit circular-arc center; $r$, $R_b$, $Z_b$, $R_c$, and $Z_c$ are expressed in meters. In the axis-referenced case, $R_b$ is the shortest distance from the boundary point to the toroidal symmetry axis.

This quantity is a boundary-geometry radius, not the [radial coordinate of an iron-core segment](name:radial_coordinate_of_iron_core_segment), which is the $R$ coordinate of a point in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It is distinct from the [outer radius of an iron-core segment](name:outer_radius_of_iron_core_segment), which is the outermost axis-referenced radial extent of the segment; a local or specified radius of an iron-core segment need not be that maximum. The radius alone does not specify the boundary point, arc endpoints, angular sweep, or traversal orientation.

sources.enhanced_context: Curvature radius of each arc of circle used to describe the cross-sectional contour of an iron core segment via a piecewise arc representation. Together with start positions, these radii fully define the segment boundary shape.
sources.leaf_definition: Curvature radius of each arc of circle
sources.parent_definition: Description of the element contour by a set of arcs of circle. For each of these, the position of the start point is given together with the curvature radius. The end point is given by the start point of the next arc of circle.

NAMES.name: inner_radius_of_iron_core_segment
NAMES.short: Non-negative radial distance from the toroidal symmetry axis to the inner boundary of an annular iron-core segment. Together with the outer radius, it fixes the radial extent of the hollow cross section.
NAMES.long:
The inner radius of an iron-core segment is the non-negative major-radius distance from the toroidal symmetry axis to the inner boundary of an annular iron region. It is expressed in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height.

For an annular cross-section, the inner radius $R_{\rm in}$ is the radial location of the inner boundary, and it is smaller than the corresponding outer radius $R_{\rm out}$:

$$
0 \le R_{\rm in} < R_{\rm out}
$$

The quantity specifies the hollow-bore boundary and radial extent, not the position along the toroidal direction, vertical height, boundary thickness, or local curvature of an arc. Unlike the curvature radius represented by [radius of an iron-core segment](name:radius_of_iron_core_segment), it is a radial boundary dimension. Together with the [outer radius of an iron-core segment](name:outer_radius_of_iron_core_segment), it defines the annular radial interval.

sources.enhanced_context: Inner radius of an annular cross-section element belonging to an iron core segment in the tokamak magnetic circuit. Together with radius_outer, defines the annulus geometry for electromagnetic modelling of the iron core.
sources.leaf_definition: Inner radius
sources.parent_definition: The element is an annulus of  center r, z, with inner radius radius_inner and outer radius radius_outer

NAMES.name: outer_radius_of_iron_core_segment
NAMES.short: Radius of an iron-core segment is the non-negative geometry radius used to define its outer boundary in the poloidal cross-section of the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame about the toroidal symmetry axis.
NAMES.long:
Radius of an iron-core segment is the non-negative geometry radius that defines the outer boundary of an annular iron-core region. This member specializes [radius of an iron-core segment](name:radius_of_iron_core_segment) to the outermost boundary measured from the toroidal symmetry axis. The relevant cross-section is the plane spanned by $R$ and $Z$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius measured from the toroidal symmetry axis and $Z$ is vertical height.

The outer radius is the maximum major-radius coordinate on the cross-sectional boundary:

$$
r_{\rm out} = \max_{(R,Z)\in\partial A} R
$$

where $r_{\rm out}$ is the outer radius, $A$ is the iron-core cross-sectional region, and $\partial A$ is its boundary; $R$, $Z$, and $r_{\rm out}$ are expressed in meters.

For annular geometry, the outer radius together with the [inner radius of an iron-core segment](name:inner_radius_of_iron_core_segment) determines the radial thickness through $r_{\rm out}-r_{\rm in}$. It is an axis-referenced outer extent, not the radius of a local circular arc about an explicit off-axis center or the full rectangular extent described by the [width of an iron-core segment](name:width_of_iron_core_segment).

sources.enhanced_context: Outer radius of an annular cross-section segment of the tokamak iron core. Together with the inner radius, defines the radial extent of this annular element in the iron core geometry description.
sources.leaf_definition: Outer radius
sources.parent_definition: The element is an annulus of  center r, z, with inner radius radius_inner and outer radius radius_outer

NAMES.name: radius_of_passive_loop
NAMES.short: Radius of the annular cross-section of a passive conducting loop element is the Euclidean distance from the cross-section center to a specified conducting boundary. It is nonnegative and does not denote the loop center's major-radius position.
NAMES.long:
Radius of the annular cross-section of a passive conducting loop element is the Euclidean distance, in the $(R,Z)$ plane at fixed toroidal angle $phi$ of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, phi, Z)$ frame, from the center of the annular conductor cross-section to a specified conducting boundary of that annulus. Here $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height.

The boundary radius is defined by the poloidal-plane distance from the cross-section center to the selected boundary point:

$$
r = \sqrt{(R_b - R_c)^2 + (Z_b - Z_c)^2}
$$

where $(R_c,Z_c)$ is the center position of the annular cross-section and $(R_b,Z_b)$ is the selected boundary position in the same fixed-$phi$ plane; all coordinate components in the equation are expressed in meters.

This parent quantity abstracts over [inner_radius_of_passive_loop](name:inner_radius_of_passive_loop) and [outer_radius_of_passive_loop](name:outer_radius_of_passive_loop). It satisfies $r \ge 0$ and is a size of the conductor cross-section, not a signed component along $\hat{R}$, $\hat{\phi}$, or $\hat{Z}$ and not the major-radius coordinate of the loop center. For a circular annulus, [area_of_passive_loop](name:area_of_passive_loop) is related by $A=\pi(r_\mathrm{outer}^2-r_\mathrm{inner}^2)$, and [thickness_of_passive_loop](name:thickness_of_passive_loop) is $r_\mathrm{outer}-r_\mathrm{inner}$.

NAMES.name: inner_radius_of_passive_loop
NAMES.short: Inner radius of the annular cross-section of a passive conducting loop element is the Euclidean distance from the cross-section center to its inner conducting boundary. It is nonnegative.
NAMES.long:
Inner radius of the annular cross-section of a passive conducting loop element is the Euclidean distance, in the $(R,Z)$ plane at fixed toroidal angle $phi$ of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,phi,Z)$ frame, from the center of the annular conductor cross-section to its inner conducting boundary. Here $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height.

The inner boundary radius is defined by the poloidal-plane distance from the cross-section center to the selected inner-boundary point:

$$
r_\mathrm{inner} = \sqrt{(R_i - R_c)^2 + (Z_i - Z_c)^2}
$$

where $(R_c,Z_c)$ is the annular cross-section center and $(R_i,Z_i)$ is the inner-boundary position in the same fixed-$\phi$ plane; all coordinate components in the equation are expressed in meters.
