This quantity specializes [radius_of_passive_loop](name:radius_of_passive_loop) to the inner conducting boundary and complements [outer_radius_of_passive_loop](name:outer_radius_of_passive_loop). For a circular annulus, the conductor thickness is the outer radius minus this inner radius, and [area_of_passive_loop](name:area_of_passive_loop) is determined by the difference of the squared outer and inner radii. It is a cross-sectional size, not the loop center's major-radius coordinate or a signed cylindrical component.

sources.enhanced_context: Inner radius of an annular cross-section element of a passive conducting loop (e.g., vacuum vessel segment). Together with the outer radius, defines the radial extent of the annular geometry used to compute electromagnetic and resistive properties.
sources.leaf_definition: Inner radius
sources.parent_definition: The element is an annulus of  center r, z, with inner radius radius_inner and outer radius radius_outer

NAMES.name: outer_radius_of_passive_loop
NAMES.short: Outer radius of the annular cross-section of a passive conducting loop element is the Euclidean distance from the cross-section center to its outer conducting boundary.
NAMES.long:
Outer radius of the annular cross-section of a passive conducting loop element is the Euclidean distance, in the $(R,Z)$ plane at fixed toroidal angle $phi$ of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, phi, Z)$ frame, from the center of the annular conductor cross-section to its outer conducting boundary. Here $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height.

The outer boundary radius is defined by the poloidal-plane distance from the cross-section center to the selected outer-boundary point:

$$
r_\mathrm{outer} = \sqrt{(R_\mathrm{outer} - R_c)^2 + (Z_\mathrm{outer} - Z_c)^2}
$$

where $(R_c,Z_c)$ is the annulus-center position and $(R_\mathrm{outer},Z_\mathrm{outer})$ is the outer-boundary position in the same fixed-$\phi$ plane; all coordinate components in the equation are measured in meters.

This quantity is the outer member of the [radius of a passive loop](name:radius_of_passive_loop) family. Together with the [inner radius of a passive loop](name:inner_radius_of_passive_loop), it defines the conducting annulus; for a circular annulus, the cross-sectional area is $A=\pi(r_\mathrm{outer}^2-r_\mathrm{inner}^2)$ and the radial thickness is $r_\mathrm{outer}-r_\mathrm{inner}$. It is nonnegative and is not the loop center's major-radius coordinate or a signed cylindrical component.

sources.enhanced_context: Outer radius of an annular cross-sectional element of a passive conducting loop (e.g., vacuum vessel segment). Defines the outer radial boundary of the annulus geometry used in electromagnetic circuit modelling.
sources.leaf_definition: Outer radius
sources.parent_definition: The element is an annulus of  center r, z, with inner radius radius_inner and outer radius radius_outer

NAMES.name: radius_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Non-negative curvature radius of one arc-of-circle segment used to approximate the cross-sectional contour of a poloidal field coil. The contour lies in a poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, where R is major radius and Z is vertical height.
NAMES.long:
Radius of a poloidal-field-coil arc is the non-negative circle radius of a single circular segment of the coil cross-sectional contour, taken in a poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height. The conductor or winding-pack boundary is approximated by connected circular arcs, and this quantity sets the local radius of curvature of one such arc.

For a circular contour segment, the curvature radius $\rho$ (in m) is the inverse magnitude of the planar curvature $\kappa$ (in m$^{-1}$) of the boundary curve in the $(R, Z)$ cross-section:

$$
\rho = \frac{1}{|\kappa|}
$$

where a finite physical arc has $\rho > 0$, and as $\rho$ grows the segment approaches a straight line ($\kappa \to 0$). Each arc is anchored by a start point in the poloidal plane: its major-radius coordinate is given by major_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil and its vertical coordinate by [height_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:height_of_poloidal_field_coil); both together with $\rho$ are needed to locate and shape one arc, with the end of each arc coinciding with the start of the next.

The value is determined from the designed circular-arc contour, from CAD geometry, or by fitting circular arcs to surveyed boundary points. Small radii represent tightly rounded corners and compact winding-pack features, while larger radii represent gently curved coil sides; the magnitude scales with coil aperture, winding-pack dimensions, and mechanical-clearance requirements. An analogous arc-of-circle convention applies to iron core segment boundaries via [radius_of_iron_core_segment](name:radius_of_iron_core_segment).

sources.enhanced_context: Curvature radius of each arc of circle used to describe the cross-sectional contour of a PF coil element via a piecewise arc representation. Each arc is defined by its start point (R, Z) and this radius, with the end given by the start of the next arc.
sources.leaf_definition: Curvature radius of each arc of circle
sources.parent_definition: Description of the element contour by a set of arcs of circle. For each of these, the position of the start point is given together with the curvature radius. The end point is given by the start point of the next arc of circle.

NAMES.name: inner_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Inner radius of the annular cross-section of a poloidal field coil, defining the size of the conductor bore in the poloidal plane.
NAMES.long:
The inner radius is the smaller of the two radial dimensions characterizing the annular conductor cross-section of a poloidal field coil, measured from the center of the annulus to its inner conducting boundary in a poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major radius and $Z$ is the vertical height.

Together with [outer_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:outer_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil) and the annulus center position, the inner radius completely specifies the annular cross-section geometry required for electromagnetic calculations including inductance and field-map computations. The annular cross-sectional area relates to both radii via:

$$
A = \pi \left( r_\mathrm{out}^2 - r_\mathrm{in}^2 \right)
$$

where $r_\mathrm{in}$ is the inner radius and $r_\mathrm{out}$ is the outer radius; this area corresponds to [area_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:area_of_poloidal_field_coil). The physical constraint $0 \le r_\mathrm{in} < r_\mathrm{out}$ must hold; when $r_\mathrm{in} = 0$ the annular cross-section degenerates to a solid disk.

The inner radius is taken directly from engineering design specifications and serves as a geometric input to electromagnetic and structural modeling of PF coil systems. The analogous quantity for non-axisymmetric correction coils is [inner_radius_of_correction_coil](name:inner_radius_of_correction_coil).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the inner conductor boundary is displaced radially outward from the annulus center, as measured in the poloidal cross-section of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

sources.enhanced_context: Inner radius of the annular cross-section of an active PF coil element. Together with the outer radius and centre position, fully specifies the annular conductor geometry for electromagnetic modelling.
sources.leaf_definition: Inner radius
sources.parent_definition: The element is an annulus of  center r, z, with inner radius radius_inner and outer radius radius_outer

sources.enhanced_context: Inner radius of the annular cross-section of a PF coil conductor element. Together with the outer radius and centre position, fully defines the annulus geometry for electromagnetic calculations.
sources.leaf_definition: Inner radius

NAMES.name: outer_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Outer radius of the annular cross-section of a poloidal field coil, measured from its annulus center to the outer conducting boundary in a poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The outer radius is the larger of the two radial dimensions characterizing the annular conductor cross-section of a poloidal field coil, measured from the center of the annulus to its outer conducting boundary in a poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height. It defines the external radial envelope of the conductor cross-section.

The outer radius is defined by

$$
r_{\mathrm{out}} = \max_{\mathbf{x} \in C_{\mathrm{out}}} \left\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_{c}\right\|
$$

where $\mathbf{x}=(R,Z)$ is a point on the outer conducting boundary $C_{\mathrm{out}}$, $\mathbf{x}_{c}=(R_c,Z_c)$ is the annulus center, and the norm is the Euclidean distance in the poloidal $(R,Z)$ plane.

The quantity is non-negative and characterizes the cross-sectional envelope, not the local curvature of its boundary. Together with the [inner radius](name:inner_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil), it bounds the annular conductor region; unlike the [radius of a poloidal field coil](name:radius_of_poloidal_field_coil), it is not the curvature radius of an individual contour arc.

sources.parent_definition: The element is an annulus of  center r, z, with inner radius radius_inner and outer radius radius_outer

NAMES.name: radius_of_toroidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Non-negative radial dimension of a toroidal field coil conductor cross-section, abstracting over distinct radial boundary positions — such as the bore-side inner boundary — of the annular winding pack.
NAMES.long: The radius of a toroidal field coil is a characteristic radial measurement of the coil's conductor or winding pack cross-section, measured from the geometric center of the annular cross-section to a specified boundary of the conducting material. For an annular winding pack, the principal instance attested is the bore-side boundary distance, captured by [inner_radius_of_toroidal_field_coil](name:inner_radius_of_toroidal_field_coil), which represents the non-negative distance from the annulus center to the inward, plasma-facing edge of the conducting material. The radial thickness of the winding pack follows from the difference between the outer and inner boundary radii, and together with the [area_of_toroidal_field_coil](name:area_of_toroidal_field_coil) and coil current, these dimensions support estimates of average engineering current density and structural load analysis. Radial dimensions are defined in the plane perpendicular to the local coil centerline, consistent with the Frenet-Serret frame used for [binormal_coordinate_of_toroidal_field_coil](name:binormal_coordinate_of_toroidal_field_coil) and related cross-section geometry. An analogous radial boundary quantity for non-axisymmetric error-field coils is [inner_radius_of_correction_coil](name:inner_radius_of_correction_coil).

NAMES.name: inner_radius_of_toroidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Inner radius of a toroidal field coil is the bore-side radius of an annular conductor or winding-pack cross-section, measured from the geometric center of that cross-section to its inner boundary.
NAMES.long:
Inner radius of a toroidal field coil is the non-negative radial distance in the local cross-sectional plane normal to the local conductor or winding-pack centerline, from the geometric center of an annular toroidal-field-coil cross-section to its bore-side inner boundary. It defines the bore size of the annular cross-section, not the spatial location of the coil.

For an annular cross-section with circular inner and outer boundaries, the conducting or winding-pack cross-sectional area satisfies:

$$
A = \pi\left(r_\mathrm{outer}^2 - r_\mathrm{inner}^2\right)
$$

where $A$ is the annular cross-sectional area in square meters, $r_\mathrm{inner}$ is this inner radius in meters, and $r_\mathrm{outer}$ is the corresponding outer radius in meters.

The quantity is defined for hollow annular conductor or winding-pack cross-sections and obeys $0 \le r_\mathrm{inner} < r_\mathrm{outer}$; the limiting value $r_\mathrm{inner}=0$ represents a solid circular cross-section treated as an annulus with no bore. It is the inner-boundary member of the toroidal-field-coil cross-section radius family: outer_radius_of_toroidal_field_coil gives the outer boundary, while [radius_of_toroidal_field_coil](name:radius_of_toroidal_field_coil) denotes a generic non-negative cross-section radius not tied specifically to the bore-side boundary.

sources.enhanced_context: Inner radius of an annular conductor cross-section in a TF coil, applicable when the geometry type is set to annulus. Defines the bore boundary of the TF coil conductor cross-section geometry.

NAMES.name: resistance_of_correction_coil
NAMES.short: Ohmic resistance of a non-axisymmetric correction-coil conductor, relating its current to the voltage drop and dissipated resistive power.
NAMES.long:
The resistance of a non-axisymmetric correction-coil conductor is the proportionality between its steady conventional current and the associated ohmic voltage drop. It describes dissipation in the conductor rather than inductive or other reactive voltage contributions.

For a uniform conductor, the resistance is defined by

$$
R = \rho \frac{L}{A}
$$

where $R$ is resistance in ohms, $\rho$ is electrical resistivity in ohm-meters, $L$ is the effective conductor length in meters, and $A$ is the cross-sectional area in square meters. The terminal relation is $V = IR$, where $V$ is the ohmic voltage drop and $I$ is the current; the corresponding resistive power is $P = I^2R$. The current is the [current of the correction coil](name:current_of_correction_coil), and the conductor area is represented by the [area of the correction coil](name:area_of_correction_coil).

sources.leaf_definition: Coil resistance
sources.parent_definition: Set of coils

NAMES.name: resistance_of_passive_loop
NAMES.short: Ohmic resistance of one passive conducting loop, relating its induced current to the resistive voltage drop and determining dissipation during electromagnetic transients.
NAMES.long:
The electrical resistance of a passive conducting loop is the proportionality between its current and the voltage drop caused by ohmic dissipation. It represents irreversible conversion of electrical energy into heat in the conducting path.

$$
V_R = R_{\rm loop} I_{\rm loop}
$$

where $V_R$ is the resistive voltage drop in volts, $I_{\rm loop}$ is the loop current in amperes, and $R_{\rm loop}$ is the resistance in ohms. For a uniform conductor, the resistance is governed by $R_{\rm loop}=\rho\ell/A$, where $\rho$ is electrical resistivity, $\ell$ is conductor length, and $A$ is cross-sectional area. The current is the [current of a passive loop](name:current_of_passive_loop). This quantity excludes inductive voltage and describes only the ohmic contribution; together with the loop self-inductance, it determines the resistive electromagnetic decay timescale. It is the loop-level counterpart of the [resistance of a vacuum vessel](name:resistance_of_vacuum_vessel) and depends on the conductor material described by its [resistivity](name:resistivity_of_wall_material).

sources.enhanced_context: Electrical resistance of a passive conducting loop in the tokamak, characterizing its resistive dissipation. Together with the loop inductance, determines the L/R time constant governing the decay of induced eddy currents during plasma transients.
sources.leaf_definition: Passive loop resistance
sources.parent_definition: Passive axisymmetric conductor description in the form of non-connected loops; any connected loops are expressed as active coil circuits with no power supply attached.

NAMES.name: resistance_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Ohmic resistance of an individual poloidal-field coil winding, relating its resistive voltage drop to current and determining Joule dissipation.
NAMES.long:
The ohmic resistance characterizes the opposition to electrical current in an individual poloidal-field coil winding and the associated conversion of electrical energy into heat.

For coil current $I$ and resistive voltage drop $V_R$, the resistance is defined by

$$
V_R = R I
$$

where $R$ is the ohmic resistance, $I$ is the signed winding current in amperes, and $V_R$ is the resistive voltage drop in volts.

This quantity excludes inductive back-EMF and other transient voltage contributions represented by the [voltage of the poloidal field coil](name:voltage_of_poloidal_field_coil). Its value may depend on the conductor state, including the [temperature of the poloidal field coil](name:temperature_of_poloidal_field_coil), and is conceptually analogous to the [resistance of the toroidal field coil](name:resistance_of_toroidal_field_coil).

sources.enhanced_context: Electrical resistance of a poloidal field (PF) coil winding. Used in circuit models to compute Ohmic dissipation, voltage requirements, and thermal loading of the coil.
sources.leaf_definition: Coil resistance
sources.parent_definition: Active PF coils

NAMES.name: resistance_of_toroidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Ohmic resistance of a toroidal-field-coil winding, relating its current to the resistive voltage drop and Joule power dissipation.
NAMES.long:
The resistance of a toroidal-field-coil winding is the proportionality coefficient between its current and the voltage component produced by ohmic conduction in the winding. It is a conductor property that may vary with the winding temperature.

The defining relation is

$$
V_R = R I
$$

where $V_R$ is the resistive voltage in volts, $R$ is the winding resistance, and $I$ is the signed coil current in amperes. The associated resistive power is $P_R = I^2R$. The [terminal voltage of the toroidal field coil](name:voltage_of_toroidal_field_coil) can also contain an inductive component and therefore is not identical to $V_R$; external circuit and contact resistances are excluded.

NAMES.name: resistivity_of_passive_structure
NAMES.short: Effective isotropic electrical resistivity of passive conducting-structure material, relating local electric field to induced current density and distinct from lumped resistance.
NAMES.long:
Effective isotropic electrical resistivity characterizes the local ohmic response of material in a passive conducting structure carrying induced eddy currents. It is a material property and is nonnegative.

The constitutive relation is

$$
\mathbf{E} = \rho\,\mathbf{J}
$$

where $\mathbf{E}$ is the local electric-field vector, $\mathbf{J}$ is the induced current-density vector, and $\rho$ is the electrical resistivity. Isotropy requires the same $\rho$ for every current direction.

This quantity applies to the conducting material of passive structures, including the material represented by [resistivity of the vacuum vessel](name:resistivity_of_vacuum_vessel). It excludes geometry-dependent lumped resistance, such as [resistance of the cryostat](name:resistance_of_cryostat), which also depends on current-path length and cross-sectional geometry.

sources.enhanced_context: Electrical resistivity of a passive conducting loop (axisymmetric passive structure), characterizing the material property per unit length. Used with geometry to compute total loop resistance and induced current dynamics during transient plasma events.
sources.leaf_definition: Passive loop resistivity
sources.parent_definition: Passive axisymmetric conductor description in the form of non-connected loops; any connected loops are expressed as active coil circuits with no power supply attached.

NAMES.name: thickness_of_iron_core_segment
NAMES.short: Full non-negative toroidal extent of a rectangular iron-core segment between its pair of opposite faces, measured along the toroidal direction φ in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame. It is perpendicular to the segment's radial width along R and vertical height along Z.
NAMES.long:
Full non-negative toroidal extent of a rectangular iron-core segment between its pair of opposite faces, measured along the toroidal direction $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major radius from the machine symmetry axis, $\phi$ increases counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is the vertical height.

The thickness is the face-to-face separation of paired points on the two opposite toroidal-facing faces along the local toroidal unit vector:

$$
t = \left| (\mathbf{x}_+ - \mathbf{x}_-) \cdot \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}} \right|
$$

where $t$ is the segment thickness in m, $\mathbf{x}_-$ and $\mathbf{x}_+$ are position vectors in m of paired points on the two opposite faces lying on the same line parallel to $\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}$, and $\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}$ is the local toroidal unit vector of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

Together with the [width of the iron-core segment](name:width_of_iron_core_segment), the radial extent along $R$, and the [height of the iron-core segment](name:height_of_iron_core_segment), the vertical extent along $Z$, the thickness completes the mutually orthogonal triplet of extents describing the segment as a rectangular block whose cross section lies in the poloidal $(R, Z)$ plane and is extruded along $\phi$. It excludes any diagonal, chordwise, or arc-length measure across the segment.

sources.enhanced_context: Thickness of the thick-line rectangular element representing an iron core segment geometry, measured perpendicular to the segment centerline. Defines the cross-sectional extent of the segment in the magnetic circuit model.
sources.leaf_definition: Thickness
sources.parent_definition: The element is approximated by a rectangle defined by a central segment and a thickness in the direction perpendicular to the segment

NAMES.name: thickness_of_passive_loop
NAMES.short: Non-negative thickness of a passive conducting loop element measured between parallel bounding sides in its poloidal cross-section.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the shortest distance between the two parallel bounding sides of a passive conducting loop element's cross-section in the poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It defines the loop's transverse geometric thickness.

The thickness $w$ is defined by

$$
w = \left|\left(\mathbf{r}_2-\mathbf{r}_1\right)\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}}\right|
$$

where $\mathbf{r}_1$ and $\mathbf{r}_2$ are position vectors of points on the two opposing sides, and $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ is a unit vector normal to those sides within the poloidal plane. The absolute value makes the thickness non-negative.

This linear dimension is distinct from the conducting cross-sectional [area of the passive loop](name:area_of_passive_loop) and from the inner and outer radii that describe an annular cross-section.

sources.enhanced_context: Thickness of the passive conductor loop element perpendicular to the central segment in the thick-line (rectangular) cross-section approximation. Defines one dimension of the rectangular cross-section geometry for passive structure modelling.
sources.leaf_definition: Thickness
sources.parent_definition: The element is approximated by a rectangle defined by a central segment and a thickness in the direction perpendicular to the segment

NAMES.name: thickness_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Thickness of a poloidal field coil is the non-negative full conductor-cross-section extent measured normal to the coil reference centerline in the poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, where R is major radius and Z is vertical height. It is distinct from radial width and vertical height.
NAMES.long:
Thickness of a poloidal field coil is the non-negative full extent of the coil conductor cross-section measured along the direction normal to the local poloidal-field-coil reference centerline. The direction is evaluated in the poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

For a conductor cross-section with gross-envelope points $\mathbf{x}$ in the poloidal plane, a reference point $\mathbf{x}_c$ on the local coil centerline, and a unit normal $\hat{n}$ in that plane perpendicular to the centerline, the thickness $t$ is the full projected extent:

$$
t = \max_{\mathbf{x}}\left[(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}_c)\cdot\hat{n}\right] - \min_{\mathbf{x}}\left[(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}_c)\cdot\hat{n}\right]
$$

where the extrema are taken over the gross conductor-cross-section envelope. This definition fixes the signed projection coordinate relative to the centerline point $\mathbf{x}_c$; the resulting thickness is invariant under reversal of $\hat{n}$ and satisfies $t \ge 0$.

The gross envelope includes insulation, stabilizer, casing, and internal voids that are part of the conductor cross-section, and excludes material outside that conductor-cross-section envelope. Thickness is distinct from [width_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:width_of_poloidal_field_coil), which is a radial extent, and from [height_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:height_of_poloidal_field_coil), which is a vertical extent; together with the cross-section shape these dimensions determine [area_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:area_of_poloidal_field_coil).

NAMES.name: tilt_angle_of_passive_loop
NAMES.short: Signed inclination of a passive conducting loop element’s overall geometric reference axis in the poloidal plane, distinct from oblique cross-section shape angles.
NAMES.long:
The tilt angle specifies the orientation of a passive conducting loop element’s directed geometric reference axis in the poloidal plane. It describes the overall orientation of the element, not an inclination parameter defining the shape of an oblique cross-section, and is analogous to the orientation defined for a [tilt angle of a plasma filament](name:tilt_angle_of_plasma_filament).

Let the reference-axis direction have components $t_R$ and $t_Z$ along the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height. The tilt angle is defined by

$$
\theta_{\mathrm{tilt}} = \operatorname{atan2}(t_Z,t_R)
$$

where $\operatorname{atan2}$ returns the directed angle from the outward $+R$ direction toward the upward $+Z$ direction.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the reference axis rotates from $+R$ toward $+Z$.

NAMES.name: tilt_angle_of_plasma_filament
NAMES.short: Signed beta inclination of the beta-angle side of a plasma-filament parallelogram cross-section in the poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, measured counterclockwise from +Z toward decreasing R.
NAMES.long:
The tilt angle of a plasma filament is the signed inclination $\beta$ of the beta-angle side of a plasma-filament parallelogram cross-section. The angle lies in the poloidal $(R,Z)$ plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height, and is referenced to the upward $+Z$ direction.

For the ordered parallelogram, let $\mathbf{u}_\beta = u_R\hat{R}+u_Z\hat{Z}$ be the unit vector along the beta-angle side, directed from the reference vertex shared with the base side toward the adjacent beta-side vertex. The signed angle is defined by:

$$
\beta = \operatorname{atan2}(-u_R, u_Z)
$$

where $u_R$ and $u_Z$ are the components of $\mathbf{u}_\beta$ along $\hat{R}$ and $\hat{Z}$, and $\operatorname{atan2}(y,x)$ returns the principal branch $-\pi < \beta \le \pi$.

The beta-angle side terminology follows the same angle-labeled parallelogram convention as [length of iron-core segment](name:length_of_iron_core_segment), identifying a side by its inclination angle rather than by an ordinal label. The directed-edge and branch conventions make $\beta$ unique: translating to the opposite parallel edge leaves the value unchanged, while reversing the side direction is excluded. This angle complements cross-section size quantities such as [plasma-filament width](name:plasma_filament_width) and [thickness of plasma filament](name:thickness_of_plasma_filament); it is not a filament-current direction or a magnetic-field pitch angle.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the directed beta-angle side is rotated counterclockwise from the upward $+Z$ direction in the poloidal $(R,Z)$ plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, drawn with $R$ increasing to the right.

sources.enhanced_context: Inclination angle beta (β) of the second parallelogram side, measured counter-clockwise from the vertically upward direction. Defines the tilt of the second side of the parallelogram cross-section used in the discrete filamentary plasma current element representation.
sources.leaf_definition: Inclination of second angle measured counter-clockwise from vertically upwards directed vector (grad Z). If both alpha and beta are zero (rectangle) then the simpler rectangular elements description should be used.

NAMES.name: toroidal_angle_of_coil_conductor_element
NAMES.short: Toroidal azimuthal coordinate locating a coil conductor element around the symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal angle $\phi$ specifies the azimuthal location of a coil conductor element about the machine symmetry axis. It is the object-specific counterpart of the [toroidal angle](name:toroidal_angle) coordinate and does not specify the element's radial or vertical position.

With the Cartesian $x$ axis chosen at $\phi=0$, the angle is defined by

$$
\phi = \operatorname{atan2}(y,x) \pmod{2\pi}
$$

where $x$ and $y$ are the horizontal Cartesian coordinates in the right-handed $(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$ basis, with $\hat{z}=\hat{Z}$. The corresponding cylindrical frame is the right-handed $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $\phi$ increases counter-clockwise when viewed from above the $+\hat{Z}$ direction.

NAMES.name: toroidal_magnetic_field_at_ferritic_element_centroid
NAMES.short: Signed projection of the magnetic-field vector onto the toroidal direction at a ferritic element’s geometric centroid.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal magnetic-field component at a ferritic element’s geometric centroid is the projection of the local magnetic-field vector onto the toroidal direction. The projection is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

$$
B_\phi(\mathbf r_c) = \mathbf B(\mathbf r_c) \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\mathbf B$ is the magnetic-field vector, $\mathbf r_c$ is the ferritic-element centroid position, and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle.

This quantity is the toroidal counterpart of the [radial magnetic field at a ferritic element centroid](name:radial_magnetic_field_at_ferritic_element_centroid) and [vertical magnetic field at a ferritic element centroid](name:vertical_magnetic_field_at_ferritic_element_centroid). It describes magnetic field, not the material magnetization represented by [toroidal magnetization of a ferritic element](name:toroidal_magnetization_of_ferritic_element).
NAMES.sign: Positive when $B_\phi$ points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

sources.enhanced_context: Toroidal (phi) component of the magnetic field (B_phi) evaluated at the centroid of each ferritic object element. Used in modelling the magnetic response of ferromagnetic in-vessel components to the ambient field.
sources.leaf_definition: Toroidal component of the magnetic field at each centroid
sources.parent_definition: Dynamic quantities, per time slice

NAMES.name: toroidal_magnetization_of_ferritic_element
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the ferritic-element magnetization vector: the signed projection of the effective magnetization assigned to a discrete ferritic element onto the positive toroidal direction in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame. This is the element-level convention, not a pointwise bulk-material magnetization field.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal component of the ferritic-element magnetization vector is the signed projection of the effective magnetization assigned to a discrete ferritic element onto the toroidal basis direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The projection is defined by:

$$
M_\phi^{\mathrm{fe}} = \mathbf{M}^{\mathrm{fe}} \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\mathbf{M}^{\mathrm{fe}}$ is the ferritic-element magnetization vector assigned to the element, $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle, and $M_\phi^{\mathrm{fe}}$ is this toroidal component.

In this family, ferritic-element magnetization denotes the effective magnetization attributed to the individual ferritic element for its magnetic source strength. It is not the pointwise bulk magnetization field inside the material, and it is distinct from material properties such as magnetic permeability. Together with the [radial component](name:radial_magnetization_of_ferritic_element) and [vertical component](name:vertical_magnetization_of_ferritic_element), it forms the three cylindrical components of the same effective ferritic-element magnetization vector.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $M_\phi^{\mathrm{fe}}$ points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ (counter-clockwise viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$).

sources.enhanced_context: Toroidal (phi) component of the magnetic dipole moment of ferritic material elements, describing the magnetization response of ferromagnetic components in the toroidal direction. Used in electromagnetic modelling of field perturbations.
sources.leaf_definition: Toroidal component of the magnetic moment of each element
sources.parent_definition: Dynamic quantities, per time slice

NAMES.name: vertical_angle_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Signed inclination of the second oblique side of a poloidal-field-coil parallelogram cross-section, measured counterclockwise from upward +Z in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the signed orientation angle of the second oblique side of a poloidal field coil parallelogram cross-section. It is defined in a constant-$\phi$ poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It is the beta-side counterpart to the first inclination angle [radial angle of the poloidal field coil](name:radial_angle_of_poloidal_field_coil).

Let $\hat{\mathbf{s}}_\beta$ be the unit vector directed along the second oblique side, $\hat{\mathbf{Z}}$ the upward vertical unit vector, and $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{\rm ccw}$ the in-plane unit vector toward counterclockwise rotation from $+Z$. The signed angle is defined by:

$$
\beta = \operatorname{atan2}\left(\hat{\mathbf{s}}_\beta \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}_{\rm ccw},\, \hat{\mathbf{s}}_\beta \cdot \hat{\mathbf{Z}}\right)
$$

Here, $\operatorname{atan2}$ returns the oriented angle from the upward direction to the directed side. The quantity describes orientation only; it is not the side length, cross-sectional area, or first oblique side inclination.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the directed second oblique side is counterclockwise from the upward $+Z$ direction in the poloidal plane.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_passive_structure
NAMES.short: Signed vertical position of a reference point on a passive conducting structure, measured from the machine midplane in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the signed vertical displacement of a designated reference point on a passive conducting structure from the machine midplane. It uses the vertical coordinate $Z$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, rather than the structure's vertical extent.

The reference-point coordinate is defined by

$$
Z_{\mathrm{ref}} = Z(P_{\mathrm{ref}}) - Z_{\mathrm{mid}}
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the designated reference point, $Z(P_{\mathrm{ref}})$ is its vertical coordinate, and $Z_{\mathrm{mid}}$ is the vertical coordinate of the machine midplane. The coordinate $Z$ is measured along the vertical direction of the cylindrical frame.

This quantity identifies a position and is distinct from [height of a passive structure](name:height_of_passive_structure), which describes the structure's full vertical extent. It is analogous to the [vertical coordinate of a conductor cross-section](name:vertical_coordinate_of_conductor_cross_section) when the reference point is a cross-sectional center.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the reference point lies toward increasing $Z$ from the machine midplane.

sources.parent_definition: Description of the element contour by a set of arcs of circle. For each of these, the position of the start point is given together with the curvature radius. The end point is given by the start point of the next arc of circle.

NAMES.name: vertical_force_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Signed vertical component of the net electromagnetic Lorentz force on one poloidal-field coil, resolved along increasing Z in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the net electromagnetic Lorentz force on an individual poloidal-field-coil conductor projected onto the vertical axis of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

The force component is defined by

$$
F_Z = \int_{V_{\mathrm{coil}}} (\mathbf{J} \times \mathbf{B}) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{Z}}\,\mathrm{d}V
$$

where $F_Z$ is the vertical force component, $V_{\mathrm{coil}}$ is the conductor volume, $\mathbf{J}$ is the current-density vector, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic-field vector acting on the conductor, $\hat{\mathbf{Z}}$ is the vertical unit vector, and $\mathrm{d}V$ is a differential volume element.

This is a signed component rather than the force magnitude or resultant. The radial component is represented separately by [radial force of a poloidal-field coil](name:radial_force_of_poloidal_field_coil), while [force of a poloidal-field coil](name:force_of_poloidal_field_coil) represents the coil’s electromagnetic force resultant.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the net force points toward increasing $Z$.

sources.enhanced_context: Vertical force (Fz) applied on a poloidal field (PF) coil, positive upward. Represents the net electromagnetic force in the vertical direction on the coil, critical for structural integrity assessment and coil support design.

sources.parent_definition: Active PF coils

NAMES.name: vertical_magnetic_field_at_ferritic_element_centroid
NAMES.short: Signed vertical component of the magnetic-field vector at a ferritic element’s centroid in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The vertical magnetic field at a ferritic element’s geometric centroid is the projection of the local magnetic-field vector onto the vertical direction. The centroid location is identified by the [vertical coordinate of the ferritic element centroid](name:z_coordinate_of_ferritic_element_centroid), while this quantity describes the field component there, not the element’s magnetization.

$$
B_Z(\mathbf r_c)=\mathbf B(\mathbf r_c)\cdot\hat{\mathbf Z}
$$

where $\mathbf r_c$ is the centroid position, $\mathbf B$ is the local magnetic-field vector, and $\hat{\mathbf Z}$ is the vertical unit vector in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The radial, vertical, and toroidal components together describe the local field; the corresponding radial and toroidal quantities are [radial magnetic field at ferritic element centroid](name:radial_magnetic_field_at_ferritic_element_centroid) and [toroidal magnetic field at ferritic element centroid](name:toroidal_magnetic_field_at_ferritic_element_centroid).
NAMES.sign: Positive when $B_Z$ points in the direction of increasing vertical coordinate $Z$.

sources.enhanced_context: Vertical (Z) component of the magnetic field (B_Z) at the centroid of each ferritic object element. Part of the local field vector characterizing the magnetic state of ferromagnetic in-vessel components.
sources.leaf_definition: Z component of the magnetic field at each centroid
sources.parent_definition: Dynamic quantities, per time slice

NAMES.name: vertical_magnetization_of_ferritic_element
NAMES.short: Signed vertical component of the effective magnetization vector assigned to a ferritic element in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Vertical magnetization of a ferritic element is the signed projection of its assigned effective magnetization vector onto the vertical direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

The defining projection is:

$$
M_Z^{\mathrm{eff}} = \mathbf{M}^{\mathrm{eff}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{Z}}
$$

where $M_Z^{\mathrm{eff}}$ is the vertical magnetization component, $\mathbf{M}^{\mathrm{eff}}$ is the effective magnetization vector assigned to the ferritic element, and $\hat{\mathbf{Z}}$ is the unit vector toward increasing vertical height. The corresponding radial projection is [radial magnetization of a ferritic element](name:radial_magnetization_of_ferritic_element); neither quantity is the magnetic field at the element centroid, such as the [vertical magnetic field at a ferritic element centroid](name:vertical_magnetic_field_at_ferritic_element_centroid).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the effective magnetization vector has a component toward increasing vertical height $Z$.

sources.leaf_definition: Z component of the magnetic moment of each element
sources.parent_definition: Dynamic quantities, per time slice

NAMES.name: voltage_of_correction_coil
NAMES.short: Signed terminal voltage of a correction coil, including the resistive voltage drop and the inductive voltage associated with changes in coil currents.
NAMES.long:
Signed terminal voltage of a correction coil is the electric potential difference across the terminals of a correction-coil winding, evaluated with a specified terminal polarity. A correction coil is a winding used to correct or control magnetic-field errors or perturbations; this quantity does not assume a particular spatial symmetry or toroidal mode number.

For a lumped coupled-circuit representation, the terminal voltage of coil $k$ is

$$
V_k = R_k I_k + L_k \frac{d I_k}{dt} + \sum_{j \ne k} M_{kj} \frac{d I_j}{dt}
$$

where $V_k$ is the terminal voltage, $R_k$ is the [resistance of the correction coil](name:resistance_of_correction_coil), $I_k$ and $I_j$ are coil currents, $L_k$ is the self-inductance of coil $k$, $M_{kj}$ is the signed mutual inductance coupling circuit $j$ to coil $k$, and $t$ is time.

This quantity is a circuit terminal voltage, not a magnetic-field amplitude or a measure of the imposed perturbation. It excludes voltage drops in external leads, feedthroughs, or power-supply elements unless the reference terminals are defined to include those elements.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the electric potential at the terminal where positive current enters the coil in the chosen winding orientation is greater than the electric potential at the terminal where it leaves.

sources.enhanced_context: Voltage measured across the terminals of a non-axisymmetric coil conductor. Time-resolved electrical parameter used to characterise the coil drive circuit and cross-check current waveforms in 3D field-shaping coil systems.
sources.leaf_definition: Voltage on the conductor terminals
sources.parent_definition: Set of conductors inside the coil. The structure can be used with size 1 for a simplified description as a single conductor. A conductor is composed of several elements, serially connected, i.e. transporting the same current.

sources.enhanced_context: Terminal voltage of a non-axisymmetric coil, time-resolved. Used for monitoring and control of 3D field-shaping coil systems such as ELM control coils or error field correction coils.
sources.leaf_definition: Voltage on the coil terminals
sources.parent_definition: Set of coils

NAMES.name: voltage_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Signed terminal voltage across a poloidal-field-coil winding, equal to its resistive voltage drop plus the voltage induced by changing magnetic flux linkage.
NAMES.long:
The terminal voltage is the total voltage drop across a poloidal-field-coil winding. It combines the ohmic voltage drop in the conductor with the inductive voltage associated with changing magnetic flux linkage.

Using a consistent winding orientation, the voltage is defined by

$$
V_{\mathrm{term}} = R_{\mathrm{w}} I + \frac{d\Phi_{\mathrm{link}}}{dt}
$$

where $V_{\mathrm{term}}$ is the terminal voltage, $R_{\mathrm{w}}$ is the winding resistance represented by the [poloidal-field-coil resistance](name:resistance_of_poloidal_field_coil), $I$ is the conventional current in the winding, $\Phi_{\mathrm{link}}$ is its signed total magnetic flux linkage, and $t$ is time.

This quantity applies to the complete active winding and includes both self-field and externally produced flux linkage. It is distinct from the induced terminal voltage of a separate [poloidal magnetic-field probe](name:voltage_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe) and is analogous to the [toroidal-field-coil terminal voltage](name:voltage_of_toroidal_field_coil).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the terminal potential drop is measured in the direction of the winding's defined positive conventional-current direction.

sources.enhanced_context: Voltage measured at the terminals of an active poloidal field (PF) coil. A time-resolved electrical quantity used in power supply modelling, circuit simulation, and plasma shape control.
sources.leaf_definition: Voltage on the coil terminals
sources.parent_definition: Active PF coils

NAMES.name: voltage_of_toroidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Terminal voltage across a toroidal-field-coil winding, combining the resistive drop with the inductive voltage caused by changing winding current.
NAMES.long:
Terminal voltage across a toroidal-field-coil winding is the sum of the ohmic voltage drop and the inductive voltage associated with changing winding current.

For constant winding inductance, it is defined by

$$
V = R I + L\frac{dI}{dt}
$$

where $V$ is terminal voltage in volts, $R$ is winding resistance in ohms, $I$ is signed conventional current in amperes, $L$ is self-inductance in henries, and $t$ is time in seconds. The resistive contribution uses the winding [resistance](name:resistance_of_toroidal_field_coil), and the current is the signed quantity defined by [current](name:current_of_toroidal_field_coil).

This quantity applies across the coil winding terminals and excludes voltage drops in external leads, power supplies, or other circuit elements.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the terminal where the positive conventional current enters is at higher electric potential than the other terminal; positive current produces a toroidal magnetic-field component toward increasing $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

sources.enhanced_context: Voltage measured across the terminals of a TF coil conductor (V). Time-resolved electrical potential difference applied to or developed across the conductor within the toroidal field coil system.

sources.parent_definition: Set of conductors inside the coil. The structure can be used with size 1 for a simplified description as a single conductor. A conductor is composed of several elements, serially connected, i.e. transporting the same current.

NAMES.name: volume_of_ferritic_element
NAMES.short: Geometric volume enclosed by the boundaries of a ferritic in-vessel element, representing its complete material extent rather than a cross-sectional dimension.
NAMES.long:
The volume of a ferritic in-vessel element is the non-negative geometric measure of the material region bounded by the element’s physical boundary. It represents the element as a whole, rather than a single cross-sectional dimension such as its [ferritic-element width](name:width_of_ferritic_element).

The volume is defined by

$$
V = \int_{\Omega} d^3x
$$

where $V$ is the element volume, $\Omega$ is the region occupied by the ferritic element, and $d^3x$ is the differential volume element. The quantity excludes surrounding plasma, vacuum, and unrelated neighboring structures.

sources.enhanced_context: Volume of each element of a ferritic object, characterizing the spatial extent of ferromagnetic components such as test blanket modules or structural inserts that perturb the magnetic field configuration.
sources.leaf_definition: Volume of each element of this object
sources.parent_definition: Set of n objects characterized by a list of centroids, volumes, and permeabilities. Optionally a full 3D description of the n volumes may be given in ../grid_ggd. Here the index for each element given in the grid_ggd should be referenced by the object set.

NAMES.name: width_of_correction_coil
NAMES.short: Full transverse dimension of a non-axisymmetric correction-coil conductor cross-section, measured along the local normal axis; for circular or annular sections it equals the outer diameter.
NAMES.long:
Width of a correction coil is the full transverse extent of its conductor cross-section measured along the local normal axis, in the plane perpendicular to the conductor centerline. In the local right-handed conductor frame $(\hat{t}, \hat{n}, \hat{b})$, $\hat{t}$ is tangent to the conductor centerline, $\hat{n}$ is the normal direction that defines the width, and $\hat{b}=\hat{t}\times\hat{n}$ is the binormal direction that defines the complementary height.

For a cross-section $C$ taken at centerline point $\mathbf{r}_0$, the width is the full outer extent along $\hat{n}$:

$$
w \equiv \max_{\mathbf{r}\in C} \left[(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}_0)\cdot\hat{n}\right] - \min_{\mathbf{r}\in C} \left[(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}_0)\cdot\hat{n}\right]
=\begin{cases}
a_n, & \text{rectangular or square conductor},\\
D, & \text{solid circular conductor},\\
D_{\mathrm{out}}, & \text{annular conductor},
\end{cases}
$$

where $a_n$ is the outer rectangular dimension along $\hat{n}$, $D$ is the diameter of a solid circular conductor, and $D_{\mathrm{out}}$ is the outer diameter of an annular conductor. This quantity is the direct analog, for non-axisymmetric error-field and edge-localized-mode control coils, of [width_of_toroidal_field_coil](name:width_of_toroidal_field_coil), and is complementary to the binormal-direction [height_of_correction_coil](name:height_of_correction_coil).

The value is taken from the conductor engineering geometry, the manufacturing drawing, or dimensional inspection of the outer conductor envelope. It is a gross outer-envelope dimension that bounds the full conductor footprint, including any jacket, insulation, or cooling channel; it is therefore generally larger than the net current-carrying region implied by the conductor area_of_correction_coil. Width should be used consistently with the binormal height: solid circular conductors have equal width and height, whereas annular conductors use the outer diameter here rather than the bore diameter set by [inner_radius_of_correction_coil](name:inner_radius_of_correction_coil).

Representative correction-coil conductor widths are design dependent, commonly about 0.005-0.1 m for individual conductors and up to roughly 0.2-0.3 m for large external conductor assemblies. The chosen width is governed by required current capacity, cooling channel layout, structural support, and the space available around the coil path.

sources.enhanced_context: Characteristic transverse dimension of a non-axisymmetric coil conductor cross-section: full width for rectangular/square geometries, diameter for circular, or outer diameter for annular cross-sections.
sources.leaf_definition: Full width of the rectangle or square in the normal direction, when geometry_type/index = 3 or 4. Diameter of the circle when geometry_type/index = 2. Outer diameter of the annulus in case geometry_type/index = 5
sources.parent_definition: The cross-section perpendicular to the conductor contour is described by a series of contour points, given by their relative position with respect to the start point of the first element. This cross-section is assumed constant for all elements.

NAMES.name: width_of_ferritic_element
NAMES.short: Full non-negative radial extent of a ferritic element’s rectangular cross-section, measured along major radius in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the full non-negative radial extent of a ferritic element’s rectangular cross-section, measured along the major-radius direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It spans the inner and outer radial boundaries of the cross-section.

$$
w_R = R_{\mathrm{out}} - R_{\mathrm{in}}
$$

where $w_R$ is the radial extent, and $R_{\mathrm{out}}$ and $R_{\mathrm{in}}$ are the outer and inner major-radius coordinates, respectively, measured in meters.

This is a geometric width, not the radial coordinate of the [ferritic element centroid](name:radial_coordinate_of_ferritic_element_centroid), the outer boundary radius of an annular representation, or the extent in the vertical direction. It is analogous to the [width of an iron core segment](name:width_of_iron_core_segment).

sources.enhanced_context: Horizontal full width of the rectangular cross-section used in the axisymmetric representation of a ferritic object. Defines the radial dimension of ferromagnetic components for electromagnetic and equilibrium modelling.
sources.leaf_definition: Horizontal full width
sources.parent_definition: Rectangular description of the element

NAMES.name: width_of_iron_core_segment
NAMES.short: Full non-negative radial extent of an iron core segment’s rectangular cross-section, measured along major radius in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The iron core segment width is the complete radial span between the inner and outer faces of its rectangular cross-section. It is a geometric extent, not the radial position of the segment or the curvature radius of an arc boundary.

The width is defined by

$$
w_{\rm iron} = R_{\rm outer} - R_{\rm inner}
$$

where $R_{\rm outer}$ and $R_{\rm inner}$ are the major-radius coordinates in meters of the outer and inner radial faces, respectively, and $w_{\rm iron}$ is the resulting full extent. The width complements the [height of the iron core segment](name:height_of_iron_core_segment), while the [outer radius of the iron core segment](name:outer_radius_of_iron_core_segment) identifies a boundary position rather than a cross-sectional span.

sources.enhanced_context: Horizontal full width of the rectangular cross-section of an iron core segment in the tokamak magnetic circuit. A geometric parameter defining the segment shape in 2D cross-section for neutronics and electromagnetic modelling.
sources.leaf_definition: Horizontal full width
sources.parent_definition: Rectangular description of the element

NAMES.name: width_of_passive_structure
NAMES.short: Full radial extent of a rectangular passive conducting structure element in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The radial width is the full major-radius extent of a rectangular passive conducting structure element, measured between its inner and outer radial boundaries.

$$
W = R_{\mathrm{outer}} - R_{\mathrm{inner}}
$$

where $W$ is the radial width, and $R_{\mathrm{outer}}$ and $R_{\mathrm{inner}}$ are the major-radius coordinates in meters of the outer and inner boundaries in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

The quantity is non-negative and describes radial extent only; it is distinct from the full vertical extent given by [height of passive structure](name:height_of_passive_structure) and from the element length given by [length of passive structure](name:length_of_passive_structure).

sources.enhanced_context: Horizontal full width of a rectangular cross-section element of a passive conducting loop, used to define the geometry of passive conductors in the tokamak electromagnetic model.
sources.leaf_definition: Horizontal full width
sources.parent_definition: Rectangular description of the element

NAMES.name: width_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Width of a poloidal field coil is the non-negative scalar full radial extent of a rectangular conductor cross-section. It is a length measured along the major-radius direction, not a directed displacement.
NAMES.long:
Width of a poloidal field coil is the full radial extent of a rectangular conductor cross-section. It is a non-negative scalar length in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

For a rectangular cross-section with radial bounds $R_\mathrm{in}$ and $R_\mathrm{out}$, the width is

$$
w = R_\mathrm{out} - R_\mathrm{in} = \max(R) - \min(R)
$$

where $w$ is the coil width, $R_\mathrm{out}$ and $R_\mathrm{in}$ are the larger and smaller radial bounds of the conductor cross-section, and all lengths are measured in meters.

The width is determined from the conductor geometry, for example from the radial bounds represented by the [radial_outline_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:radial_outline_of_poloidal_field_coil). Together with the [height_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:height_of_poloidal_field_coil), it defines the rectangular cross-section used in electromagnetic and structural calculations; for a rectangle, the [area_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:area_of_poloidal_field_coil) satisfies the inline relation $A = w h$, where $h$ is in meters and $A$ is in square meters.

Valid values satisfy $w \ge 0$. A strictly positive value represents a finite conductor cross-section, while $w = 0$ is a degenerate geometric limit rather than a physical coil width.

sources.enhanced_context: Horizontal full width of the rectangular cross-section element of an active PF coil conductor, defining the radial extent of the element geometry. Used in electromagnetic modelling of the poloidal field coil system.
sources.leaf_definition: Horizontal full width
sources.parent_definition: Rectangular description of the element

sources.enhanced_context: Horizontal full width of the rectangular cross-section of a PF coil conductor element. Defines the extent of the rectangle in the horizontal (radial) direction for coil geometry specification.
sources.leaf_definition: Horizontal full width
sources.parent_definition: Rectangular description of the element

NAMES.name: width_of_toroidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Full geometric width of a toroidal-field-coil conductor cross-section, measured as the boundary-to-boundary transverse extent along the normal direction of the local Frenet-Serret frame. It is an unsigned extent, not a centerline location or coil radius.
NAMES.long:
Full geometric width of a toroidal-field-coil conductor cross-section, measured along the normal axis of the local right-handed Frenet-Serret frame $(\hat{t}, \hat{n}, \hat{b})$. The tangent $\hat{t}$ follows the conductor centerline, the normal $\hat{n}$ lies in the cross-section plane, and the binormal $\hat{b} = \hat{t} \times \hat{n}$; the corresponding extent along $\hat{b}$ is [height_of_toroidal_field_coil](name:height_of_toroidal_field_coil).

The width is the boundary-to-boundary span of the outer conductor boundary $\partial S$ projected onto $\hat{n}$:

$$
w = \max_{\mathbf{r} \in \partial S} (\mathbf{r} \cdot \hat{n}) - \min_{\mathbf{r} \in \partial S} (\mathbf{r} \cdot \hat{n})
$$

where $\mathbf{r}$ is the position of a boundary point in the cross-section plane and $\hat{n}$ is the unit normal. Reversing the sense of $\hat{n}$ leaves $w$ unchanged, so it is an unsigned extent.

For a rectangular or square section this is the full side length along $\hat{n}$; for a circular section it is the diameter; for an annular section it is the outer diameter, not the bore diameter or wall thickness. It is a geometric extent of the outer cross-section and is distinct from a centerline location or from a coil radius such as [radius_of_toroidal_field_coil](name:radius_of_toroidal_field_coil) or [inner_radius_of_toroidal_field_coil](name:inner_radius_of_toroidal_field_coil).

sources.enhanced_context: Characteristic width of a TF coil conductor cross-section: full width for rectangular/square geometries, diameter for circular, or outer diameter for annular cross-sections, depending on the geometry type index.
sources.leaf_definition: Full width of the rectangle or square in the normal direction, when geometry_type/index = 3 or 4. Diameter of the circle when geometry_type/index = 2. Outer diameter of the annulus in case geometry_type/index = 5
sources.parent_definition: The cross-section perpendicular to the TF conductor contour is described by a series of contour points, given by their relative position with respect to the start point of the first element. This cross-section is assumed constant for all elements.

NAMES.name: x_coordinate_of_ferritic_element_centroid
NAMES.short: Signed Cartesian x coordinate of a ferritic element’s geometric centroid in the right-handed (x, y, z) frame, with z aligned with the vertical Z direction.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the signed Cartesian x position of the geometric centroid of a ferritic element. It gives the element’s absolute position in the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ basis, with $\hat{z}$ aligned with the vertical direction; it is not a radial coordinate or a local displacement.

For an element occupying volume $V$, the centroid coordinate is defined by

$$
x_c = \frac{1}{V}\int_V x\,\mathrm{d}V
$$

where $x_c$ and $x$ are Cartesian x coordinates in meters, $V$ is the element volume, and $\mathrm{d}V$ is a volume element. Together with the [y coordinate of the ferritic element centroid](name:y_coordinate_of_ferritic_element_centroid) and [z coordinate of the ferritic element centroid](name:z_coordinate_of_ferritic_element_centroid), it locates the same geometric centroid; it is distinct from the [radial coordinate of the ferritic element centroid](name:radial_coordinate_of_ferritic_element_centroid).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the centroid lies in the $+x$ direction from the Cartesian origin.

sources.enhanced_context: X coordinate of centroid.
sources.leaf_definition: List of X coordinates
sources.parent_definition: List of positions of the centroids, in Cartesian coordinates

NAMES.name: z_coordinate_of_ferritic_element_centroid
NAMES.short: Vertical Z coordinate of the geometric centroid of a ferritic element in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, where Z increases upward from the machine midplane.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate $Z_\mathrm{cent}$ specifies the height of the geometric centroid of a ferritic element along the $Z$-axis of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major radius from the symmetry axis, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle increasing counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is the vertical height measured from the machine midplane.

Ferritic elements are passive ferromagnetic components installed in some tokamak configurations to reduce toroidal magnetic field ripple generated by discrete toroidal field coils. The centroid position serves as the representative reference point for each element in electromagnetic field models that compute the perturbed equilibrium field arising from the ferromagnetic material. Together with [radial_coordinate_of_ferritic_element_centroid](name:radial_coordinate_of_ferritic_element_centroid), this coordinate fully determines the axisymmetric centroid location in the poloidal $(R, Z)$ plane.

For configurations requiring the full three-dimensional centroid location, the Cartesian counterparts [x_coordinate_of_ferritic_element_centroid](name:x_coordinate_of_ferritic_element_centroid) and [y_coordinate_of_ferritic_element_centroid](name:y_coordinate_of_ferritic_element_centroid) provide the transverse displacement when the element's toroidal position is also needed. Centroid coordinates are derived from the engineering design geometry of the device and used as inputs to equilibrium reconstruction and ripple-compensation analyzes.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the centroid lies above the machine midplane in the $+Z$ direction.

sources.enhanced_context: Vertical (Z) coordinate of centroid.
sources.leaf_definition: List of Z coordinates
sources.parent_definition: List of positions of the centroids, in Cartesian coordinates

NAMES.name: vacuum_magnetic_vector_potential
NAMES.short: Gage-dependent vacuum magnetic vector potential generated by external current sources; its curl gives the magnetic induction when plasma-current contributions are excluded.
NAMES.long:
The vacuum magnetic vector potential is a gage-dependent vector field representing the external-source contribution to the [magnetic vector potential](name:magnetic_vector_potential). It excludes the contribution generated by plasma currents while retaining the gage dependence of the full potential.

The defining relation between this potential and the corresponding vacuum magnetic induction is:

$$
\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{vac}} = \nabla \times \mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{vac}}
$$

where $\mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{vac}}$ is the vacuum magnetic vector potential, $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{vac}}$ is the magnetic induction produced by the external sources alone, and $\nabla \times$ is the curl operator. Replacing $\mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{vac}}$ by $\mathbf{A}_{\mathrm{vac}} + \nabla \chi$, where $\chi$ is an arbitrary scalar gage function, leaves $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{vac}}$ unchanged.

The vector may be resolved into components in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. Its radial and vertical projections are represented by the [radial vacuum magnetic vector potential](name:radial_vacuum_magnetic_vector_potential) and [vertical vacuum magnetic vector potential](name:vertical_vacuum_magnetic_vector_potential), respectively.
NAMES.sign: Positive when a component of the vector points along its corresponding positive basis direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: radial_vacuum_magnetic_vector_potential
NAMES.short: Radial (R) component of the vacuum magnetic vector potential produced by toroidal-field coil currents, evaluated in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The radial component $A_R$ of the vacuum magnetic vector potential is the projection of $\mathbf{A}_\mathrm{vac}$ onto the major-radius direction $\hat{R}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It represents the $R$-directed contribution of the vector field generated exclusively by toroidal-field coil conductor currents in the absence of any plasma contribution, forming part of the complete [vacuum magnetic vector potential](name:vacuum_magnetic_vector_potential) vector $(A_R, A_\phi, A_Z)$.

The vacuum magnetic field is related to the vector potential by $\mathbf{B}_\mathrm{vac} = \nabla \times \mathbf{A}_\mathrm{vac}$, so the poloidal field components follow from the cylindrical curl of $(A_R, A_\phi, A_Z)$. Because only $\nabla \times \mathbf{A}_\mathrm{vac}$ is gage-invariant, $A_R$ individually depends on the chosen gage; the Coulomb gage $\nabla \cdot \mathbf{A} = 0$ is standard for static TF coil computations.

This component is calculated numerically via Biot-Savart integration over the TF coil conductor geometry and current distribution, and is used in equilibrium reconstruction and MHD stability analysis on both structured and unstructured spatial grids. The complementary vertical component is provided by [vertical_vacuum_magnetic_vector_potential](name:vertical_vacuum_magnetic_vector_potential), while the analogous quantity incorporating full plasma and coil contributions is [radial_magnetic_vector_potential](name:radial_magnetic_vector_potential).
NAMES.sign: Positive when $A_R$ points in the direction of increasing major radius $R$.

sources.enhanced_context: Array of values for a field r.
sources.leaf_definition: One scalar value is provided per element in the grid subset.
sources.parent_definition: R component of the vacuum vector potential, given on various grid subsets

NAMES.name: vertical_vacuum_magnetic_vector_potential
NAMES.short: Vertical (Z) component of the vacuum magnetic vector potential produced solely by toroidal-field coil currents in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The vertical component $A_Z$ of the vacuum magnetic vector potential is the projection of $\mathbf{A}_\mathrm{vac}$ onto the vertical direction $\hat{Z}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It represents the $Z$-directed contribution of the vector field generated exclusively by toroidal-field coil currents in the absence of plasma and eddy-current contributions, forming part of the complete [vacuum magnetic vector potential](name:vacuum_magnetic_vector_potential) vector $(A_R, A_\phi, A_Z)$.

The vacuum magnetic field is related to the vector potential by

$$
\mathbf{B}_\mathrm{vac} = \nabla \times \mathbf{A}_\mathrm{vac}
$$

where $\mathbf{B}_\mathrm{vac}$ is the vacuum magnetic field, $\mathbf{A}_\mathrm{vac}$ is the vacuum magnetic vector potential, and $\nabla \times$ is the curl operator. The curl is gage-invariant, whereas $A_Z$ depends on the selected gage and is not itself a magnetic-field component. The complementary radial component is [radial_vacuum_magnetic_vector_potential](name:radial_vacuum_magnetic_vector_potential); unlike [vertical_magnetic_vector_potential](name:vertical_magnetic_vector_potential), this quantity excludes plasma and eddy-current contributions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $A_Z$ points in the direction of increasing vertical height $Z$.

sources.enhanced_context: Array of values for a field z.
sources.leaf_definition: One scalar value is provided per element in the grid subset.
sources.parent_definition: Z component of the vacuum vector potential, given on various grid subsets

NAMES.name: vacuum_poloidal_current_function
NAMES.short: Vacuum poloidal current function equal to major radius times the toroidal magnetic field generated solely by external coil currents; it is spatially constant in an axisymmetric current-free region.
NAMES.long:
The vacuum poloidal current function is the contribution to the poloidal current function from the magnetic field of external coil currents alone. It excludes contributions from plasma currents and induced currents in conducting structures.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, it is defined by

$$
F_{\mathrm{vac}}(R,Z) = R B_{\phi}^{\mathrm{vac}}(R,Z)
$$

where $R$ is the major radius measured from the toroidal symmetry axis in meters, $Z$ is vertical height, and $B_{\phi}^{\mathrm{vac}}$ is the vacuum magnetic-field component in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$, in teslas. In an axisymmetric current-free region, $F_{\mathrm{vac}}$ is spatially constant and represents the vacuum part of the [poloidal current function](name:poloidal_current_function). The associated field is the toroidal component of the [vacuum magnetic field](name:vacuum_magnetic_field).
NAMES.sign: Positive when $B_{\phi}^{\mathrm{vac}}$ points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

sources.enhanced_context: Vacuum toroidal field product (B0·R0), the product of the vacuum toroidal magnetic field and the reference major radius. This structure groups the time-dependent B0·R0 quantity used as the primary normalization reference across plasma physics IDSs.
sources.leaf_definition: Vacuum field times major radius in the toroidal field magnet. Positive sign means anti-clockwise when viewed from above

NAMES.name: accumulated_radiated_energy_due_to_impurity_radiation
NAMES.short: Cumulative energy emitted through electron–impurity radiation over the disruption interval, obtained by integrating the corresponding radiated power in time.
NAMES.long:
Accumulated impurity-radiation energy is the total energy carried away by photons produced through electron interactions with impurity ions over the disruption interval. It is a cumulative quantity, distinct from the instantaneous [impurity-radiation power](name:power_due_to_impurity_radiation).

$$
E_{\mathrm{imp}}(t_0,t_1)=\int_{t_0}^{t_1}P_{\mathrm{imp}}(t)\,dt
$$

where $E_{\mathrm{imp}}$ is the accumulated radiated energy, $P_{\mathrm{imp}}(t)$ is the total radiative power attributed to electron–impurity interactions in W, and $t$, $t_0$, and $t_1$ are times in s. The integration interval spans the defined disruption duration. The quantity includes the impurity-radiation channels represented in $P_{\mathrm{imp}}$ and excludes radiation not attributed to impurity interactions; it is therefore not equivalent to [total plasma radiated power](name:total_plasma_radiated_power).

sources.enhanced_context: Total cumulative energy radiated by electrons interacting with impurity ions during a disruption (E_rad_imp), integrated over the disruption duration. A key metric for assessing impurity-driven radiative collapse and thermal quench energy balance.
sources.leaf_definition: Total cumulated energy (integral of the power over the disruption duration) radiated by electrons on impurities
sources.parent_definition: Global quantities

sources.enhanced_context: Cumulative energy radiated by electrons colliding with impurity ions in the halo region during a disruption. Represents the time-integrated radiative power from electron-impurity interactions specifically in the halo current zone.
sources.leaf_definition: Cumulated energy (integral of the power over the disruption duration) radiated by electrons on impurities in the halo region
sources.parent_definition: Global quantities

NAMES.name: alfven_frequency
NAMES.short: Alfvén frequency at a given radial position for a single toroidal mode number is the complex local shear-Alfvén continuum angular frequency; its real part gives oscillation and its imaginary part gives growth or damping for the stated time dependence.
NAMES.long:
Alfvén frequency at a given radial position for a single toroidal mode number is the complex local shear-Alfvén continuum angular frequency for perturbations propagating along the magnetic field on the flux surface at that radial position. Its [real part](name:alfven_frequency_real_part) is the oscillatory component, and its [imaginary part](name:alfven_frequency_imaginary_part) is the temporal growth or damping component.

The ideal shear-Alfvén continuum relation defining the underlying continuum frequency is

$$
\omega_A = |k_\parallel| v_A
$$

where $\omega_A$ is the real continuum angular frequency, $k_\parallel$ is the component of the wave vector parallel to the magnetic field, and $v_A$ is the Alfvén speed, $B/\sqrt{\mu_0\rho_m}$ with $B$ the magnetic-field magnitude, $\mu_0$ the vacuum permeability, and $\rho_m$ the plasma mass density.

This quantity denotes the full complex frequency $\Omega_A=\operatorname{Re}(\Omega_A)+i\operatorname{Im}(\Omega_A)$, not either component alone, and it is an angular frequency rather than a cyclic frequency. The radial position is a flux-surface label in explicitly named flux coordinates such as $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$ or $(\psi,\theta,\phi)$, not a cylindrical vector component in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame. At fixed [toroidal mode number], $k_\parallel$ is determined by field-line pitch, magnetic geometry, and poloidal harmonic content, with the [safety factor](name:safety_factor) entering common single-harmonic specializations.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $\operatorname{Im}(\Omega_A)$ makes perturbations proportional to $\exp(-i\Omega_A t)$ grow exponentially in time.

NAMES.name: alfven_frequency_imaginary_part
NAMES.short: Damping rate when negative or growth rate when positive, the imaginary part of the complex shear Alfvén continuum frequency, for a single toroidal mode number at a given radial position.
NAMES.long:
The imaginary part of the complex shear Alfvén continuum frequency, $\gamma = \operatorname{Im}(\omega_A)$, sets how fast a shear Alfvén perturbation grows or decays at a given radial position for a chosen toroidal mode number $n$. Together with the oscillation frequency [alfven_frequency_real_part](name:alfven_frequency_real_part) it fixes the full time dependence, which under the $e^{-i\omega_A t}$ convention evolves as

$$
\delta f(t) \propto e^{\gamma t}\, e^{-i\omega_r t}
$$

so a positive $\gamma$ marks an unstable, growing response and a negative $\gamma$ a linearly damped one. A linear MHD calculation resolves $\gamma$ as a function of minor radius and toroidal mode number. The continuum is purely real in ideal MHD, and a finite $\gamma$ arises from resistive, kinetic, or energetic-particle effects, the same drives that excite the discrete Alfvén eigenmodes occupying the continuum gaps. The full complex value is the [alfven_frequency](name:alfven_frequency).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the mode amplitude grows exponentially in time under the $e^{-i\omega_A t}$ convention.

sources.enhanced_context: Imaginary part of the local shear Alfvén frequency spectrum as a function of radius and root index in linear MHD stability analysis. Represents the damping or growth rate component of Alfvén continuum eigenfrequencies.
sources.leaf_definition: Imaginary part of the frequency, for a given radial position and every root found at this position
sources.parent_definition: Local shear Alfvén spectrum as a function of radius (only in case grid/dim1 is a radial coordinate)

NAMES.name: alfven_frequency_real_part
NAMES.short: Oscillation frequency, the real part of the complex frequency, of the local shear Alfvén continuum at a given radial position for a single toroidal mode number.
NAMES.long:
The shear Alfvén continuum is the set of frequencies at which shear Alfvén waves resonate on each flux surface, and its real part gives the local oscillation frequency for a chosen toroidal mode number $n$. A linear MHD calculation returns one frequency for every root of the local continuum equation at each radial position, so the spectrum varies continuously with minor radius. In the cylindrical limit the continuum frequency for poloidal harmonic $m$ is

$$
\operatorname{Re}(\omega_A) = \frac{|n - m/q|}{R}\, v_A
$$

where $q$ is the safety factor, $R$ the major radius in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, and $v_A = B/\sqrt{\mu_0 \rho}$ the Alfvén speed for total field magnitude $B$ and mass density $\rho$. Toroidal coupling of neighboring poloidal harmonics opens frequency gaps in which discrete Alfvén eigenmodes, such as the toroidicity-induced and reversed-shear modes, can form. The companion damping or growth rate is the [alfven_frequency_imaginary_part](name:alfven_frequency_imaginary_part), the two together forming the complex [alfven_frequency](name:alfven_frequency), and the associated timescale is the [alfven_time](name:alfven_time).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the wave phase advances in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.
