NAMES.name: alfven_time
NAMES.short: Reference shear-Alfvén transit time across the magnetic-axis major-radius scale, used to normalize ideal-magnetohydrodynamic dynamics.
NAMES.long:
The Alfvén time is the shear-Alfvén transit time across the magnetic-axis major-radius scale. It is a nonnegative reference timescale for ideal-magnetohydrodynamic dynamics, distinct from the oscillation period or damping time of a particular mode.

$$
\tau_A = \frac{R_{\rm axis}}{v_A} = \frac{R_{\rm axis}\sqrt{\mu_0\rho_i}}{\left|B_{\phi,\rm axis}\right|}
$$

where $R_{\rm axis}$ is the magnetic-axis major radius, $v_A$ is the reference shear-Alfvén speed, $\mu_0$ is the vacuum permeability, $\rho_i$ is the ion mass density at the specified reference location, and $B_{\phi,\rm axis}$ is the toroidal magnetic-field component on the magnetic axis. The magnitude makes the timescale independent of magnetic-field orientation. The resulting reference timescale is distinct from the local complex [Alfvén frequency](name:alfven_frequency).

sources.enhanced_context: Alfvén time (τ_A) as a function of radial coordinate, defined as τ_A = R0·√(m_i·n_i(ρ))/B0. This local MHD timescale characterises shear Alfvén wave propagation speed and normalises MHD growth rates.

sources.parent_definition: MHD modes in the confined plasma

NAMES.name: alpha_parameter
NAMES.short: Alpha parameter is the dimensionless normalized plasma pressure-gradient drive entering local ideal-MHD ballooning stability theory.
NAMES.long:
Alpha parameter is the dimensionless normalized plasma pressure-gradient drive entering local ideal-MHD ballooning stability theory. It represents the destabilizing pressure-gradient contribution relative to magnetic-field-line bending and curvature in a local equilibrium description.

For a local minor radius $r$ increasing from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary, the ballooning normalization is:

$$
\alpha = -\frac{2\mu_0 q^2 R}{B_\phi^2}\frac{dp}{dr}
$$

where $p$ is the scalar plasma pressure entering the ideal-MHD equilibrium, $q$ is the safety factor, $R$ is major radius in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $B_\phi$ is the toroidal magnetic-field component in that frame, and $\mu_0$ is the vacuum permeability.

The normalization makes $\alpha$ dimensionless. This quantity is the pressure-gradient drive itself, not a marginal-stability threshold; a critical alpha parameter is a threshold for the same drive, and [ratio of critical alpha parameter to alpha parameter at pedestal](name:ratio_of_critical_alpha_parameter_to_alpha_parameter_at_pedestal) is a distinct stability-margin quantity.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the plasma pressure decreases in the outward direction of the chosen local minor radius $r$ ($dp/dr < 0$).

NAMES.name: decay_time_due_to_disruption
NAMES.short: Decay time due to disruption is a characteristic timescale for the disruption-driven reduction of a specified plasma quantity. The specialized quantity defines the decaying variable and whether the time is an exponential e-folding time or another effective decay interval.
NAMES.long:
Decay time due to disruption is the characteristic time associated with the decrease of a specified plasma quantity during the disruptive phase of a plasma discharge. It represents the temporal scale of disruption-driven loss or removal of that quantity, independent of which plasma population or state variable is being described.

The defining decay convention belongs to the specialized quantity. An exponential decay time is an e-folding time only when that specialized definition assumes exponential behavior, while other specialized disruption decay times may be effective intervals between defined levels; this parent quantity does not impose a universal single-exponential law. A representative specialization is the [runaway-electron decay time due to disruption](name:runaway_electron_decay_time_due_to_disruption).

NAMES.name: effective_charge
NAMES.short: Dimensionless effective ionic charge of an ion mixture, equal to the electron-density-normalized sum of squared ionic charge numbers.
NAMES.long:
Effective ionic charge characterizes the charge composition of an ion mixture through the second moment of its ionic charge distribution. It is defined locally and may subsequently be averaged along a viewing path or over a plasma volume.

For a quasineutral plasma, the effective ionic charge is

$$
Z_{\mathrm{eff}} = \frac{\sum_s n_s Z_s^2}{n_e}
$$

where $n_s$ is the number density of ion species $s$, $Z_s$ is the positive ionic charge number of that species, and $n_e$ is the electron number density. Quasineutrality gives $n_e = \sum_s n_s Z_s$ when electron inertia and charge separation are negligible.

The quantity is distinct from a first-moment mean ionic charge because it weights each species by the square of its charge. Path and volume reductions are represented by [line-averaged effective charge](name:line_averaged_effective_charge) and [volume-averaged effective charge](name:volume_averaged_effective_charge), respectively.

NAMES.name: electron_temperature
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Energy-equivalent measure of the mean random kinetic energy of the bulk electron population, defined locally or after a prescribed spatial average.
NAMES.long:
Electron temperature is the energy-equivalent measure of the mean random kinetic energy of the bulk electron population. It characterizes the second moment of the electron velocity distribution and may be defined locally or after a prescribed spatial average.

For an isotropic electron population, the defining relation is

$$
\langle E_e \rangle = \frac{3}{2} T_e
$$

where $\langle E_e \rangle$ is the mean random kinetic energy per electron and $T_e$ is the energy-equivalent electron temperature.

The definition applies to local values and to specified line or volume averages, including the [line-averaged electron temperature](name:line_averaged_electron_temperature) and [volume-averaged electron temperature](name:volume_averaged_electron_temperature). A ratio of two such temperatures, such as the [ratio of electron temperature to volume-averaged electron temperature](name:ratio_of_electron_temperature_to_volume_averaged_electron_temperature_over_inside_flux_surface), is a derived comparison rather than a separate temperature definition. A separately defined fast or suprathermal population is excluded unless explicitly included in the population being characterized.

NAMES.name: electrostatic_potential
NAMES.short: Voltage-valued electrostatic potential giving the electric potential energy per unit positive charge relative to a chosen electrical reference.
NAMES.long:
Electrostatic potential is the electric potential energy per unit positive test charge at a specified plasma, probe, or surface location, relative to a chosen electrical reference. It includes equilibrium values, localized values such as the [midplane electrostatic potential](name:electrostatic_potential_at_midplane) and [wall electrostatic potential](name:electrostatic_potential_at_wall), floating values, and perturbations such as the [perturbed electrostatic potential](name:perturbed_electrostatic_potential).

The electrostatic contribution to the electric field is defined by

$$
\mathbf{E}_{\rm es} = -\nabla \Phi
$$

where $\Phi$ is the electrostatic potential expressed in volts, $\mathbf{E}_{\rm es}$ is the electrostatic electric field expressed in volts per meter, and $\nabla$ is the spatial gradient. The full [electric field](name:electric_field) may additionally contain an inductive contribution.

Only potential differences are gage-independent. A floating value is distinguished by the zero-net-current condition at an electrically isolated probe or surface, and is not the material wall voltage or an applied wall bias.
NAMES.sign: Positive when a positive test charge has greater electrostatic potential energy at the specified location than at the chosen electrical reference.

NAMES.name: mode_number
NAMES.short: Dimensionless mode-number vector labeling the radial branch and poloidal and toroidal periodicities of a linear magnetohydrodynamic perturbation.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the collection of discrete mode labels that identifies a linear magnetohydrodynamic perturbation across its radial, poloidal, and toroidal structure. It is a mode-index vector, not a spatial wavevector or a physical displacement vector.

$$
\mathbf{N} = (n_r, m, n_\phi)
$$

where $n_r$ is the non-negative radial branch index, $m$ is the integer poloidal Fourier harmonic, and $n_\phi$ is the integer toroidal Fourier harmonic. The radial component is defined by the number of radial nodes, as described by the [radial mode number](name:radial_mode_number); the angular components label periodicity and correspond to the [poloidal mode number](name:poloidal_mode_number) and [toroidal MHD mode number](name:toroidal_mhd_mode_number). Coupled poloidal harmonics may belong to one eigenmode, so the vector identifies the mode labels rather than requiring a single separable spatial harmonic.

NAMES.name: momentum_due_to_avalanche
NAMES.short: Electron momentum scale associated with avalanche runaway dynamics, including thresholds separating collisional drag-dominated electrons from those accelerated into the runaway population.
NAMES.long:
This quantity denotes a momentum scale associated with avalanche runaway-electron dynamics. It covers momentum-space thresholds that distinguish electrons remaining drag-dominated from electrons that can be accelerated into the runaway population; it is not a particle source rate.

The relativistic electron momentum magnitude is defined by

$$
p = \frac{m_e v}{\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}}
$$

where $p$ is momentum magnitude, $m_e$ is the electron rest mass in kg, $v$ is electron speed in m s$^{-1}$, and $c$ is the speed of light in m s$^{-1}$. An avalanche threshold is a selected value of $p$ determined by the balance between collisional drag and electric-field acceleration.

The representative [critical avalanche momentum](name:critical_momentum_due_to_avalanche) is the boundary used to evaluate avalanche multiplication, including contributions from seed populations. Its acceleration context is related to the [critical electric field](name:critical_electric_field), but this quantity is a momentum scale rather than an electric-field threshold.

NAMES.name: critical_momentum_due_to_avalanche
NAMES.short: Critical momentum due to avalanche is the scalar electron momentum threshold that separates electrons slowed by collisional drag from electrons accelerated by the parallel electric field into runaway avalanche multiplication. It is a magnitude, not a signed field-aligned momentum.
NAMES.long:
Critical momentum due to avalanche is the scalar electron momentum threshold that separates electrons slowed by collisional drag from electrons accelerated by the parallel electric field into runaway avalanche multiplication. It is a local electron momentum magnitude and does not encode the sign of field-aligned motion.

The defining balance is between the electric force magnitude and the collisional slowing-down force at the threshold momentum:

$$
e\,|E_\parallel| = F_\mathrm{drag}\!\left(p_{c,\mathrm{av}}\right)
$$

where $p_{c,\mathrm{av}}$ is the critical momentum due to avalanche, $e$ is the elementary charge in coulombs, $E_\parallel$ is the electric-field component parallel to the magnetic field in volts per meter, and $F_\mathrm{drag}(p)$ is the magnitude of the collisional drag force on an electron with momentum magnitude $p$ in newtons.

A finite threshold requires an accelerating field strong enough for the force-balance equation to have a solution; in the usual Coulomb-drag limit this corresponds to $|E_\parallel|$ exceeding the [critical electric field](name:critical_electric_field). This quantity is the threshold itself, not [momentum due to avalanche](name:momentum_due_to_avalanche) or an avalanche growth rate, and it differs from [volume-averaged runaway-electron critical momentum due to avalanche](name:volume_averaged_runaway_electron_critical_momentum_due_to_avalanche), which is a volume average of the same local threshold.

NAMES.name: neoclassical_tearing_mode_phase
NAMES.short: Angular phase of a neoclassical tearing-mode magnetic island, specifying its helical orientation on the resonant flux surface at a given time.
NAMES.long:
The phase $\varphi(t)$ is the angular offset that specifies the instantaneous helical orientation of a neoclassical tearing-mode magnetic island on its resonant flux surface.

The associated island rotation frequency is the time derivative of the phase:

$$
\omega_{\rm NTM}(t)=\frac{d\varphi(t)}{dt}
$$

where $\omega_{\rm NTM}$ is the angular rotation frequency and $t$ is time. The phase $\varphi$ is defined modulo $2\pi$; its zero and increasing direction must remain consistent with the adopted helical mode representation.

This quantity denotes the island phase, not the [rotation frequency of the neoclassical tearing mode](name:rotation_frequency_of_neoclassical_tearing_mode), its radial width, or the torque acting on it.

NAMES.short: Linear exponential growth rate of a single MHD eigenmode resolved per toroidal mode number, equal to the imaginary part of the complex eigenfrequency from linear stability analysis.
NAMES.long:
The per-toroidal-mode growth rate is the linear growth rate $\gamma$ of a plasma MHD instability eigenmode for a specific toroidal Fourier mode number $n_\phi$. It is the imaginary part of the complex eigenfrequency $\omega = \omega_r + i\gamma$, where the real part $\omega_r$ is the mode oscillation frequency given by mode_frequency.

The eigenmode amplitude $A$ evolves in time as:

$$
A(t) \propto e^{(\gamma + i\omega_r)\,t}
$$

where $t$ is time. A positive $\gamma$ signals exponential growth of the perturbation (instability), while a negative $\gamma$ indicates a damped or stable mode.

The growth rate is obtained by solving the linearized MHD equations as an eigenvalue problem, treating each toroidal mode number $n_\phi$ independently under the assumption of an axisymmetric background equilibrium. The complementary per_toroidal_mode_perturbed_energy characterizes the energy content of the same eigenmode, and [alfven_frequency_imaginary_part](name:alfven_frequency_imaginary_part) provides an analogous growth or damping rate for the shear Alfvén continuum.

Ideal kink ($n_\phi = 1$) instabilities in high-normalized-pressure plasmas can reach $10^3$–$10^5$ Hz, while resistive tearing modes grow on slower timescales, $\gamma \sim 1$–$10^3$ Hz.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the eigenmode amplitude grows exponentially in time, indicating instability; negative when the mode is stable or damped.

sources.enhanced_context: Linear growth rate (γ) of an MHD toroidal mode, characterizing the exponential growth timescale of the instability. A primary output of linear MHD stability analysis codes such as MARS, MISHKA, or KINX.
sources.leaf_definition: Linear growthrate of the mode
sources.parent_definition: Vector of toroidal modes

NAMES.name: perturbed_electrostatic_potential
NAMES.short: Perturbed electrostatic potential is the voltage-valued scalar potential perturbation of the quasineutral plasma about an equilibrium state and electrical reference. Its negative spatial gradient defines the electrostatic contribution to the perturbed electric field, distinct from inductive electric-field contributions.
NAMES.long:
Perturbed electrostatic potential is the voltage-valued scalar potential perturbation of the quasineutral plasma about an equilibrium state. It is the first-order variation of [electrostatic_potential](name:electrostatic_potential) evaluated relative to the same electrical reference as the equilibrium potential. It encodes only the electrostatic part of the linear electric perturbation.

The first-order decomposition of the plasma electrostatic potential is:

$$
\Phi(\mathbf{x}, t) = \Phi_0(\mathbf{x}) + \epsilon\,\delta\Phi(\mathbf{x}, t) + O(\epsilon^2)
$$

where $\Phi$ is the total electrostatic potential, $\Phi_0$ is the equilibrium electrostatic potential, $\delta\Phi$ is the perturbed electrostatic potential, $\epsilon$ is an ordering parameter, and $\mathbf{x}$ is position. For a single toroidal Fourier mode, a complex representation of $\delta\Phi$ uses the amplitude $\hat{\Phi}(R,Z)$ multiplying $e^{i(n\phi-\omega t)}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle, $Z$ is vertical height, $n$ is toroidal mode number, and $\omega$ is complex angular frequency.

The electrostatic contribution to the perturbed electric field is $-\nabla\delta\Phi$; terms such as $-\partial\delta\mathbf{A}/\partial t$ are inductive contributions and are excluded from this scalar potential. In complex modal notation, [perturbed_electrostatic_potential_real_part](name:perturbed_electrostatic_potential_real_part) and [perturbed_electrostatic_potential_imaginary_part](name:perturbed_electrostatic_potential_imaginary_part) denote the real and imaginary components of the complex amplitude, while [normalized_perturbed_electrostatic_potential](name:normalized_perturbed_electrostatic_potential) denotes a normalized form rather than this unnormalized perturbation.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the perturbation increases the local plasma electrostatic potential above the equilibrium value for the same electrical reference.

sources.enhanced_context: Imaginary part of the perturbed electrostatic potential (δφ) eigenfunction for a given toroidal mode number in linear MHD analysis within the confined plasma. Together with the real part, it defines the complex electrostatic component of the MHD perturbation.
sources.leaf_definition: Imaginary part
sources.parent_definition: Perturbed electrostatic potential for given toroidal mode number

NAMES.name: perturbed_plasma_mass_density_real_part
NAMES.short: In-phase component of the complex first-order plasma mass-density eigenfunction for one toroidal Fourier harmonic in linear MHD stability theory.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the real, in-phase component of the complex first-order plasma mass-density perturbation eigenfunction associated with one toroidal Fourier harmonic in linear MHD stability theory. The complete complex quantity is [perturbed plasma mass density](name:perturbed_plasma_mass_density).

The real component is defined by

$$
\widetilde{\rho}_{n,\mathrm{real}}(\mathbf{x}) = \operatorname{Re}\!\left[\widetilde{\rho}_n(\mathbf{x})\right]
$$

where $\widetilde{\rho}_n$ is the complex first-order mass-density eigenfunction, $n$ is the toroidal Fourier mode number, and $\mathbf{x}$ denotes position. The decomposition is relative to the phase convention of the complex eigenfunction.

This quantity excludes the imaginary quadrature component and must not be interpreted as the magnitude of the complex perturbation. Its meaning parallels the real component of the corresponding temperature eigenfunction, [perturbed plasma temperature real part](name:perturbed_plasma_temperature_real_part).

sources.enhanced_context: Real part of the perturbed mass density (ρ̃) eigenfunction for a given toroidal MHD mode in linear stability analysis, representing the in-phase amplitude of the mass density perturbation in the poloidal plane.
sources.leaf_definition: Real part
sources.parent_definition: Perturbed mass density for given toroidal mode number

NAMES.name: plasma_temperature
NAMES.short: Effective temperature of the plasma in a fluid or MHD description, representing the average thermal kinetic energy per degree of freedom of the combined charged particle population.
NAMES.long:
The plasma temperature is a fundamental thermodynamic state variable in fluid and single-fluid MHD models, quantifying the mean random kinetic energy of the charged particle population. In a single-fluid description it is linked to [thermal pressure] via the equation of state

$$
p = n k_B T
$$

where $p$ is the scalar pressure, $n$ is the total particle number density, and $k_B$ is the Boltzmann constant.

In multi-species plasmas an effective plasma temperature may be obtained as a density-weighted combination of electron and ion contributions; applications requiring species resolution use explicitly qualified forms such as particle_temperature or [neutral_temperature](name:neutral_internal_state_temperature). This quantity also appears as the equilibrium background in linear MHD stability analysis, where its first-order perturbation is represented by the complex eigenfunction [perturbed_plasma_temperature](name:perturbed_plasma_temperature), encoding the amplitude and phase of the temperature fluctuation for a specified toroidal Fourier harmonic. The total isotropic pressure of the plasma, including contributions summed over all species, is captured by [plasma_pressure](name:plasma_pressure).

NAMES.name: perturbed_plasma_temperature
NAMES.short: Complex first-order eigenfunction of the plasma temperature perturbation in linear MHD stability analysis, encoding the amplitude and phase of the temperature fluctuation for a specified toroidal Fourier harmonic.
NAMES.long:
In linear MHD stability analysis, the plasma temperature is expanded about a background equilibrium as $T = T_0 + \delta T\,e^{i(n\phi - \omega t)}$, where $T_0$ is the equilibrium temperature, $n$ is the toroidal mode number, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle, and $\omega$ is the complex eigenfrequency. The quantity $\delta T$ is a complex-valued eigenfunction that simultaneously encodes the local amplitude and spatial phase of the temperature fluctuation across the plasma cross-section.

The principal decomposition is:

$$
T(\mathbf{r}, t) = T_0(\mathbf{r}) + \delta T(\mathbf{r})\,e^{i(n\phi - \omega t)}
$$

where $\delta T(\mathbf{r})$ is the complex position-dependent eigenfunction. Its in-phase and quadrature components are resolved by [perturbed_plasma_temperature_real_part](name:perturbed_plasma_temperature_real_part) and [perturbed_plasma_temperature_imaginary_part](name:perturbed_plasma_temperature_imaginary_part), respectively.

Because eigenfunction normalization is arbitrary up to a complex scale factor, absolute magnitudes carry no independent physical significance; only ratios among perturbed-field components or the spatial mode structure are physically meaningful. The perturbation is evaluated from equilibrium-based linear MHD stability calculations using the background described by [plasma_temperature](name:plasma_temperature), with toroidal periodicity indexed by the [toroidal_mhd_mode_number](name:toroidal_mhd_mode_number).

NAMES.name: perturbed_plasma_temperature_imaginary_part
NAMES.short: Quadrature (out-of-phase) component of the complex first-order plasma-temperature eigenfunction for one toroidal Fourier harmonic in linear MHD stability analysis.
NAMES.long:
The imaginary component of the complex first-order plasma-temperature eigenfunction for a single toroidal Fourier harmonic in linear MHD. It is the quadrature component relative to the real component under the selected Fourier phase convention.

The defining decomposition is:

$$
\delta T = \delta T_R + i\,\delta T_I
$$

where $\delta T$ is the complex temperature amplitude, $\delta T_R$ is its real component, $\delta T_I$ is the imaginary component represented by this quantity, and $i$ is the imaginary unit.

Together with the [real component of the perturbed plasma temperature](name:perturbed_plasma_temperature_real_part), this quantity reconstructs the complex [perturbed plasma temperature](name:perturbed_plasma_temperature). In the perturbation $T=T_0+\delta T e^{i(n\phi-\omega t)}$, $T_0$ is the equilibrium temperature, $n$ is the toroidal mode number, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, $\omega$ is the complex eigenfrequency, and $t$ is time. Its value depends on the selected Fourier phase origin and does not by itself represent the complete physical temperature perturbation.

sources.enhanced_context: Imaginary part of the complex perturbed plasma temperature (T̃) eigenfunction for a given toroidal mode number in linear MHD stability analysis. Together with the real part, it defines the full complex temperature perturbation associated with the MHD mode.
sources.leaf_definition: Imaginary part
sources.parent_definition: Perturbed temperature for given toroidal mode number

NAMES.name: perturbed_plasma_temperature_real_part
NAMES.short: In-phase component of the complex first-order plasma-temperature eigenfunction for a specified toroidal Fourier harmonic in linear MHD stability analysis.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the real, in-phase component of the first-order plasma-temperature perturbation associated with one toroidal Fourier harmonic. It is a component of the complex eigenfunction represented by [perturbed plasma temperature](name:perturbed_plasma_temperature).

The in-phase component is defined from the complex perturbation amplitude by

$$
\delta T_{\mathrm{R}} = \operatorname{Re}\!\left(\delta T\right)
$$

where $\delta T_{\mathrm{R}}$ is the real temperature-perturbation component and $\delta T$ is the full complex first-order temperature eigenfunction. The result depends on the phase reference chosen for the harmonic and excludes the quadrature component represented by the imaginary part. It is not the equilibrium temperature or the complete complex perturbation.

sources.enhanced_context: Real part of the complex perturbed plasma temperature eigenfunction (T̃) for a toroidal MHD mode in linear stability analysis. Together with the imaginary part, it defines the full complex temperature perturbation eigenfunction.
sources.leaf_definition: Real part
sources.parent_definition: Perturbed temperature for given toroidal mode number

NAMES.name: plasma_velocity
NAMES.short: Mass-weighted bulk center-of-mass velocity vector of the plasma fluid, whose projections onto the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) coordinate directions provide the radial, toroidal, vertical, and parallel flow components.
NAMES.long:
The plasma velocity is the local center-of-mass (barycentric) flow velocity of the bulk plasma, representing the momentum per unit mass carried collectively by all plasma species. It is the primary kinematic quantity in single-fluid and multi-fluid magnetohydrodynamic descriptions of plasma transport, rotation, and momentum confinement.

The center-of-mass velocity vector is defined as:

$$
\mathbf{v}_\mathrm{cm} = \frac{\sum_s m_s n_s \mathbf{v}_s}{\sum_s m_s n_s}
$$

where the sum runs over all contributing plasma species $s$, $m_s$ is the species mass, $n_s$ is the number density, and $\mathbf{v}_s$ is the mean fluid velocity of species $s$.

The full velocity vector decomposes into projections along the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame: the [radial component](name:radial_plasma_velocity) along $\hat{R}$, the [toroidal component](name:toroidal_center_of_mass_velocity) along $\hat{\phi}$, the [vertical component](name:vertical_plasma_velocity) along $\hat{Z}$, and the [parallel component](name:parallel_plasma_velocity) along the local magnetic-field unit vector $\hat{b}$. Individual projections are inferred from Doppler spectroscopy, charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, and motional-Stark-effect diagnostics; Mach probes provide parallel-flow access in the scrape-off layer.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the velocity vector component points in the direction of increasing $R$ (outward), increasing $\phi$ (counter-clockwise viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$), or increasing $Z$ (upward) for the respective cylindrical projections.

NAMES.name: parallel_plasma_velocity
NAMES.short: Parallel component of the bulk plasma center-of-mass velocity, projected onto the local magnetic-field direction and representing field-aligned mass transport of all contributing species.
NAMES.long:
The parallel plasma velocity $v_\parallel$ is the projection of the [plasma velocity](name:plasma_velocity) vector onto the local magnetic-field unit vector $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$. It represents the field-aligned component of the mass-weighted bulk center-of-mass flow of all contributing plasma species, not the velocity of one selected species.

The projection is defined by:

$$
v_\parallel = \mathbf{v}_\mathrm{cm} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{b}}
$$

where $v_\parallel$ is the parallel plasma velocity, $\mathbf{v}_\mathrm{cm}$ is the [plasma velocity](name:plasma_velocity) vector, $\hat{\mathbf{b}} = \mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$ is the local magnetic-field unit vector, and $\mathbf{B}$ is the local magnetic field.

This quantity is synonymous with [parallel center-of-mass velocity](name:parallel_center_of_mass_velocity): both denote the field-aligned projection of the mass-weighted plasma center-of-mass flow. It differs from [radial plasma velocity](name:radial_plasma_velocity), [toroidal center-of-mass velocity](name:toroidal_center_of_mass_velocity), and [vertical plasma velocity](name:vertical_plasma_velocity), which are projections onto the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height; it is also not the speed magnitude $|\mathbf{v}_\mathrm{cm}|$ or a flux-surface-normal component. The quantity is defined only where the local magnetic-field direction is defined.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the plasma center-of-mass velocity has a component in the direction of the local magnetic-field vector $\mathbf{B}$.

NAMES.name: poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_halo_boundary
NAMES.short: Poloidal magnetic flux evaluated on the outermost flux surface of the halo-current region during a disruption. This is the wall-side halo boundary of the halo-current domain, not the inner confined-plasma interface.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal magnetic flux at the halo boundary is the value of the [poloidal magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux) function on the outermost magnetic flux surface of the halo-current region during a disruption. The halo boundary is the wall-side flux-surface limit of the halo-current domain, not the inner interface between that domain and any confined-plasma core.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, with $R$ the major radius, $\phi$ the toroidal angle, and $Z$ the vertical height, the value on a halo-boundary point $(R_h, Z_h)$ is defined by the flux of the vertical magnetic field through the horizontal disk centered on the toroidal symmetry axis:

$$
\psi_h = \psi(R_h, Z_h) = \int_0^{R_h} B_Z(R', Z_h)\,2\pi R'\,dR'
$$

where $\psi_h$ is the poloidal magnetic flux at the halo boundary, $\psi(R_h, Z_h)$ is the poloidal magnetic flux function evaluated on that boundary, and $B_Z$ is the vertical component of the magnetic field.

This quantity is the poloidal-flux counterpart of the [toroidal magnetic flux at the halo boundary](name:toroidal_magnetic_flux_at_halo_boundary). It is a flux-surface value and does not denote the total magnetic flux through the halo-current volume or the halo current itself.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $B_Z$ on the integration disk points in the $+Z$ direction.

NAMES.name: poloidal_mode_number
NAMES.short: Dimensionless integer Fourier harmonic labeling the poloidal periodicity of a linear MHD perturbation; coupled poloidal harmonics may form one eigenmode.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal mode number is a dimensionless integer Fourier harmonic that specifies the variation of a linear MHD perturbation with poloidal angle. It is one component of the [mode number](name:mode_number), alongside the toroidal mode number and the radial mode number.

The angular phase of a Fourier component is represented by

$$
\delta X(\rho,\theta,\phi) \propto \exp\!\bigl(i(m\theta-n\phi)\bigr)
$$

where $\delta X$ is a complex perturbation amplitude, $m$ is the poloidal mode number, $n$ is the toroidal mode number, and $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$ are flux coordinates. The angle $\phi$ is the toroidal angle in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, with $R$ the major radius and $Z$ the vertical height.

A single eigenmode can contain several coupled poloidal harmonics; this quantity identifies one harmonic rather than the complete mode vector. Its radial branch is identified separately by the [radial mode number](name:radial_mode_number).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the perturbation phase advances as the poloidal angle $\theta$ increases.

NAMES.name: poloidal_perturbed_plasma_velocity_imaginary_part
NAMES.short: Quadrature poloidal velocity component of a complex first-order plasma-velocity perturbation eigenfunction for a specified toroidal Fourier harmonic. It is the imaginary part of the projection onto the positive poloidal direction, paired with the in-phase real part.
NAMES.long:
Quadrature poloidal velocity component of a complex first-order plasma-velocity perturbation eigenfunction is the imaginary part of the poloidal projection of that eigenfunction for a specified toroidal Fourier harmonic. The poloidal direction is the unit vector $\hat{\mathbf e}_\theta$ toward increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in a flux-coordinate basis $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, with $\phi$ the toroidal angle of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height.

The projected component and its imaginary part are defined by

$$
v_{\theta,\mathrm{im}} = \operatorname{Im}\!\left(\tilde v_\theta\right), \qquad \tilde v_\theta = \tilde{\mathbf v}\cdot\hat{\mathbf e}_\theta
$$

where $\tilde{\mathbf v}$ is the complex first-order plasma-velocity perturbation eigenfunction, $\tilde v_\theta$ is its poloidal component, and $v_{\theta,\mathrm{im}}$ is the coefficient of the imaginary term when $\tilde v_\theta = v_{\theta,\mathrm{re}} + i v_{\theta,\mathrm{im}}$.

This quantity is the quadrature component paired with the [poloidal perturbed plasma velocity real part](name:poloidal_perturbed_plasma_velocity_real_part); together they specify the complex [poloidal perturbed plasma velocity](name:poloidal_perturbed_plasma_velocity) for the chosen harmonic and phase convention. It is distinct from the corresponding [toroidal perturbed plasma velocity imaginary part](name:toroidal_perturbed_plasma_velocity_imaginary_part), which projects the same complex velocity perturbation onto the toroidal direction.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the quadrature component of $\tilde{\mathbf v}\cdot\hat{\mathbf e}_\theta$ is aligned with $+\hat{\mathbf e}_\theta$, toward increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in the flux-coordinate basis $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$.

sources.enhanced_context: Imaginary part of the second (poloidal) component of the perturbed velocity eigenvector (ṽ) in linear MHD stability analysis. Represents the out-of-phase poloidal fluid velocity perturbation amplitude for a given toroidal mode number.
sources.leaf_definition: Imaginary part
sources.parent_definition: Second coordinate (poloidal)

NAMES.name: poloidal_perturbed_plasma_velocity_real_part
NAMES.short: Real part of the poloidal perturbed plasma velocity is the in-phase component of the complex first-order plasma-velocity amplitude for toroidal mode number n, resolved tangent to increasing poloidal angle in the flux-coordinate basis (ρ, θ, φ). The toroidal angle φ is that of the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame; equilibrium flow and the quadrature component are excluded.
NAMES.long:
Real part of the poloidal perturbed plasma velocity is the in-phase component of the complex first-order plasma-velocity perturbation amplitude for one toroidal Fourier harmonic with mode number $n$. The poloidal component is resolved along the local basis direction tangent to increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in a specified flux-coordinate basis $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, with $\phi$ the toroidal angle of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame where $R$ is major radius, $Z$ is vertical height, and $\phi$ increases counterclockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$. It is distinct from equilibrium plasma flow.

For a complex poloidal amplitude in that flux-coordinate basis, the real part is defined by:

$$
v_{\theta,1}^{\mathrm{Re}}(\rho,\theta;n) = \operatorname{Re}\!\left[\tilde{v}_{\theta,1}(\rho,\theta;n)\right]
$$

where $v_{\theta,1}^{\mathrm{Re}}$ is this real poloidal perturbation amplitude, $\tilde{v}_{\theta,1}$ is the [poloidal perturbed plasma velocity](name:poloidal_perturbed_plasma_velocity), $\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_1$ is the complex first-order plasma-velocity perturbation eigenfunction for harmonic $n$, $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_\theta$ is the local normalized direction tangent to increasing $\theta$ with $\tilde{v}_{\theta,1}=\tilde{\mathbf{v}}_1\cdot\hat{\mathbf{e}}_\theta$, $\rho$ is the radial flux label, and $n$ is the toroidal Fourier mode number.

Together with [poloidal perturbed plasma velocity imaginary part](name:poloidal_perturbed_plasma_velocity_imaginary_part), this quantity specifies the complex poloidal velocity amplitude for the selected harmonic. It is not the full real-space poloidal velocity at a particular toroidal angle; the dependence on $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame is supplied by the chosen Fourier harmonic convention. Multiplication of the complex eigenfunction by a constant phase factor changes the split between real and imaginary parts without changing the underlying linear mode, so a fixed phase reference is required for this real component.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the real first-order velocity perturbation component projects along $+\hat{\mathbf{e}}_\theta$, the local direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in the flux-coordinate basis $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, after the complex eigenmode phase reference is fixed.

sources.enhanced_context: Real part of the poloidal component (coordinate2) of the perturbed velocity eigenvector (ṽ) in linear MHD stability analysis. Together with the imaginary part, specifies the complex-valued poloidal velocity perturbation for a given toroidal mode number.
sources.leaf_definition: Real part
sources.parent_definition: Second coordinate (poloidal)

NAMES.name: poloidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_real_part
NAMES.short: Real part of the single-toroidal-mode poloidal perturbed vacuum magnetic field, equal to the in-phase projection of the complex first-order vacuum magnetic-field perturbation onto the poloidal unit tangent outside the plasma.
NAMES.long:
Real part of the single-toroidal-mode poloidal perturbed vacuum magnetic field is the in-phase scalar component of the complex first-order vacuum magnetic-field perturbation projected onto the poloidal unit tangent outside the plasma. The poloidal unit tangent is defined in a specified flux-coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$ as the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ at fixed $\rho$ and $\phi$, where $\phi$ is the toroidal angle in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame with basis $(\hat{R},\hat{\phi},\hat{Z})$. This poloidal direction is a local flux-coordinate tangent, not a cylindrical-basis direction.

The real poloidal vacuum perturbation amplitude is defined by projecting the complex vacuum perturbation onto the poloidal unit tangent and taking the real part:

$$
\delta B_{\theta,\mathrm{real}}^{\mathrm{vac}}(\rho,\theta;n) = \operatorname{Re}\!\left[\delta\mathbf{B}^{\mathrm{vac}}(\rho,\theta;n) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}_{\theta}\right]
$$

where $\delta B_{\theta,\mathrm{real}}^{\mathrm{vac}}$ is this real poloidal vacuum perturbation amplitude, $\delta\mathbf{B}^{\mathrm{vac}}$ is the complex first-order [perturbed vacuum magnetic field](name:perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field) amplitude, $n$ is the integer toroidal mode number, and $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{\theta}$ is the poloidal unit tangent defined above.

The vacuum qualifier restricts the quantity to the current-free region exterior to the plasma, where the first-order perturbation satisfies $\nabla\times\delta\mathbf{B}^{\mathrm{vac}}=0$ and $\nabla\cdot\delta\mathbf{B}^{\mathrm{vac}}=0$. For a single toroidal mode, the complex poloidal amplitude is reconstructed as $\delta B_{\theta}^{\mathrm{vac}}=\delta B_{\theta,\mathrm{real}}^{\mathrm{vac}}+i\,\delta B_{\theta,\mathrm{imag}}^{\mathrm{vac}}$ and enters the toroidal dependence through the factor $\exp(i n\phi)$; this quantity is the real part of that mode amplitude, not a poloidal Fourier coefficient. It is distinct from the [imaginary-part counterpart](name:poloidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_imaginary_part), the [radial](name:radial_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_real_part) and [toroidal](name:toroidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_real_part) vacuum projections, and the corresponding [plasma-region component](name:poloidal_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field_real_part).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the in-phase magnetic-field perturbation component points along $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{\theta}$, the unit tangent toward increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ at fixed $\rho$ and $\phi$ in the specified flux-coordinate system $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$.

sources.enhanced_context: Real part of the second (poloidal) component of the perturbed magnetic field (δB) eigenfunction in the vacuum region, from linear MHD stability analysis for a given toroidal mode number.
sources.leaf_definition: Real part
sources.parent_definition: Second coordinate (poloidal)

NAMES.name: power_due_to_impurity_radiation
NAMES.short: Power due to impurity radiation is the instantaneous electromagnetic power radiated by impurity species through electron-impurity radiation processes in the plasma volume. It includes impurity line emission, recombination continuum, and the impurity contribution to bremsstrahlung, summed over impurity species and charge states.
NAMES.long:
Power due to impurity radiation is the instantaneous electromagnetic power emitted by impurity species through electron-impurity radiation processes in a plasma volume. It represents a non-negative radiative loss from the electron energy population, summed over all impurity species and over all charge states included in that volume.

The defining volume integral is the integral of the impurity-radiation volumetric emissivity over the emitting plasma volume:

$$
P_{\mathrm{imp\,rad}} = \int_V \epsilon_{\mathrm{imp\,rad}}(\mathbf{x})\, dV
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{imp\,rad}}$ is the impurity-radiation power, $V$ is the emitting plasma volume, $dV$ is a volume element, $\mathbf{x}$ is position, and $\epsilon_{\mathrm{imp\,rad}}$ is the local volumetric emissivity attributable to electron-impurity radiation.

The included channels are impurity bound-bound line emission, recombination and other impurity continuum emission, and the part of bremsstrahlung produced by electron interactions with impurity ions. Radiation from main-ion or neutral-fuel species is excluded unless those species are treated as impurity species for the quantity being defined.

This quantity is narrower than [total plasma radiated power](name:total_plasma_radiated_power), which includes all plasma radiating species and processes. It is distinct from [power due to line radiation](name:power_due_to_line_radiation), which denotes total bound-bound line emission by plasma atoms and ions rather than the impurity-only line contribution; it overlaps [bremsstrahlung power](name:bremsstrahlung_power) only through the impurity-attributable bremsstrahlung component. Its interval integral is [accumulated radiated energy due to impurity radiation](name:accumulated_radiated_energy_due_to_impurity_radiation), with $E_{\mathrm{imp\,rad}}(t_2)-E_{\mathrm{imp\,rad}}(t_1)=\int_{t_1}^{t_2} P_{\mathrm{imp\,rad}}(t)\,dt$.

NAMES.name: power_due_to_ohmic_dissipation
NAMES.short: Irreversible electrical power converted into heat by finite resistivity, obtained by integrating Joule heating over the relevant conducting plasma or material domain.
NAMES.long:
Ohmic-dissipation power is the irreversible conversion of electromagnetic work into heat by finite electrical resistivity in a conducting plasma or material domain. It is nonnegative for passive resistive media.

$$
P_{\mathrm{ohm}} = \int_{\mathcal{V}} \mathbf{J} \cdot \mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{res}}\,dV = \int_{\mathcal{V}} \eta |\mathbf{J}|^2\,dV
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{ohm}}$ is the total dissipated power, $\mathbf{J}$ is current density in A m$^{-2}$, $\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{res}}$ is the resistive electric field in V m$^{-1}$, $\eta$ is scalar resistivity in Ω m, and $\mathcal{V}$ is the included conducting volume. The second equality applies when $\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{res}}=\eta\mathbf{J}$.

The integration domain sets the scope: the wall contribution is [power at the wall due to ohmic dissipation](name:power_at_wall_due_to_ohmic_dissipation), while a plasma-column contribution is related to [plasma resistance](name:plasma_resistance) by $P_{\mathrm{ohm}}=R_{\mathrm{p}}I_{\mathrm{p}}^2$ when a lumped resistance $R_{\mathrm{p}}$ and total current $I_{\mathrm{p}}$ are defined. Reversible electromagnetic energy storage and externally delivered power are excluded.

sources.enhanced_context: Total ohmic power (P_ohm) deposited in the plasma during a disruption, representing resistive heating from the plasma current. Contributes to thermal energy deposition during the thermal and current quench phases.
sources.leaf_definition: Total ohmic power
sources.parent_definition: Global quantities

sources.enhanced_context: Ohmic power dissipated in the halo region (P_ohm,halo) during a disruption, arising from resistive heating by halo currents. Contributes to thermal loads on plasma-facing components during the current quench.
sources.leaf_definition: Ohmic power in the halo region
sources.parent_definition: Global quantities

sources.enhanced_context: Ohmic heating power (P_ohm), the resistive power dissipated in the plasma by the toroidal plasma current flowing through the plasma resistance. A primary intrinsic heating channel in tokamak operation.
sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Ohmic power

NAMES.name: radial_mode_number
NAMES.short: Dimensionless non-negative integer labeling the radial branch of a linear MHD eigenmode by its number of radial nodes between the magnetic axis and plasma boundary.
NAMES.long:
Radial mode number is a dimensionless integer branch index that specifies the radial branch of a linear MHD perturbation. It identifies radial structure rather than periodicity in either angular direction.

The radial branch index is defined by

$$
n_r = N_{\mathrm{nodes}}[\xi(\rho)]
$$

where $n_r$ is the radial mode number, $\xi(\rho)$ is the radial eigenfunction, $N_{\mathrm{nodes}}$ counts its interior zeros, and $\rho$ is the radial coordinate within the flux-coordinate set $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$; the count is taken between the magnetic axis and the plasma boundary.

The radial mode number is one component of the [mode number](name:mode_number), distinct from the angular harmonics represented by the [poloidal mode number](name:poloidal_mode_number) and [toroidal MHD mode number](name:toroidal_mhd_mode_number).

sources.enhanced_context: Radial mode number of a linear MHD eigenmode, characterizing the radial oscillation structure of the perturbation within the plasma. Complements the toroidal mode number (n) and dominant poloidal mode number (m) in classifying the mode structure.
sources.leaf_definition: Radial mode number
sources.parent_definition: Vector of toroidal modes

NAMES.name: radial_perturbed_plasma_velocity_imaginary_part
NAMES.short: Imaginary part of the complex amplitude of the radial plasma-velocity perturbation for toroidal harmonic index n in linear MHD stability analysis. Radial denotes the component along the R direction in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Imaginary part of the complex amplitude of the radial plasma-velocity perturbation is the quadrature component of the cylindrical $R$ projection of the first-order plasma velocity eigenfunction for a specified toroidal harmonic index $n$. The radial projection is along $\hat{R}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame with basis $(\hat{R},\hat{\phi},\hat{Z})$, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The complex radial perturbation amplitude and its contribution to the single-mode physical perturbation are represented by

$$
\delta v_R^{\mathrm{phys},(n)}(\mathbf{x},t)
=
\operatorname{Re}\!\left[
\left(\delta v_{R,\mathrm{re}}^{(n)}(\mathbf{x})
+i\,\delta v_{R,\mathrm{im}}^{(n)}(\mathbf{x})\right)
e^{i(n\phi-\omega t)}
\right]
$$

where $\delta v_{R,\mathrm{im}}^{(n)}$ is this quantity, $\delta v_{R,\mathrm{re}}^{(n)}$ is [radial_perturbed_plasma_velocity_real_part](name:radial_perturbed_plasma_velocity_real_part), $\delta v_R^{\mathrm{phys},(n)}$ is the corresponding real physical perturbation component, $\mathbf{x}$ is position, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle of that position, $t$ is time, $\omega$ is the complex mode angular frequency under the chosen temporal phase convention, $n$ is the integer toroidal harmonic index, and $i$ is the imaginary unit.

The real and imaginary parts together reconstruct the complex radial amplitude [radial_perturbed_plasma_velocity](name:radial_perturbed_plasma_velocity). A change of the arbitrary global eigenmode phase rotates these two parts, so this imaginary part is meaningful only with the same phase reference and eigenfunction normalization as the other perturbation components. It is the cylindrical $R$ component, not a flux-surface-normal component and not a component perpendicular to the magnetic field.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $\delta v_{R,\mathrm{im}}^{(n)}$ points in the $+\hat{R}$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

sources.enhanced_context: Imaginary part of the first (radial) component of the perturbed velocity eigenfunction (ṽ) in linear MHD stability analysis. Together with the real part, defines the complex-valued radial velocity perturbation for a given toroidal mode number.
sources.leaf_definition: Imaginary part
sources.parent_definition: First coordinate (radial)

NAMES.name: radial_plasma_velocity
NAMES.short: Radial component of the bulk plasma center-of-mass velocity, projected onto the outward major-radius direction in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The radial plasma velocity $v_R$ is the projection of the [plasma_velocity](name:plasma_velocity) vector onto the $\hat{R}$ unit vector of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major radius measured from the machine symmetry axis. It represents the inward or outward bulk mass flow of the plasma and is a key quantity for radial transport analysis in MHD descriptions of magnetized plasmas.

The defining relation is:

$$
v_R = \mathbf{v}_\mathrm{plasma} \cdot \hat{R}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_\mathrm{plasma}$ is the mass-weighted mean velocity of all plasma species and $\hat{R}$ points in the direction of increasing major radius $R$.

Radial flows arise from pressure-gradient-driven forces, $\mathbf{E}\times\mathbf{B}$ convection, and MHD instability dynamics. The quantity is evaluated from time-dependent MHD simulations on unstructured spatial grids and can be inferred experimentally through charge exchange recombination spectroscopy combined with magnetic equilibrium reconstruction. The complementary cylindrical velocity components are [toroidal_plasma_velocity](name:toroidal_impurity_ion_velocity_at_measurement_position) and [vertical_plasma_velocity](name:vertical_plasma_velocity); for the projection along the local magnetic-field direction, see [parallel_plasma_velocity](name:parallel_plasma_velocity).
NAMES.sign: Positive when directed in the direction of increasing major radius $R$, i.e., outward from the machine symmetry axis.

sources.enhanced_context: Array of values for velocity r.
sources.leaf_definition: One scalar value is provided per element in the grid subset.
sources.parent_definition: R component of the plasma velocity, given on various grid subsets

NAMES.name: radial_vector_potential
NAMES.short: R-component of the magnetic vector potential in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, where R is major radius directed outward from the symmetry axis.
NAMES.long:
R-component of the magnetic vector potential is the projection of the magnetic vector potential onto the outward major-radius direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It is a signed scalar component of the vector potential whose curl gives the magnetic field.

The component is defined by the vector projection:

$$
A_R = \mathbf{A} \cdot \hat{R}
$$

where $A_R$ is the R-component of the magnetic vector potential, $\mathbf{A}$ is the magnetic vector potential, and $\hat{R}$ is the outward major-radius basis vector of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

This quantity is gage-dependent: a transformation $\mathbf{A} \mapsto \mathbf{A} + \nabla\chi$, where $\chi$ is a scalar gage function, can change $A_R$ without changing the magnetic field. It is a vector-potential component, not the [R-component of the magnetic field](name:radial_magnetic_field).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the magnetic vector potential has a component in the $+\hat{R}$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

sources.enhanced_context: Array of values for a field r.
sources.leaf_definition: One scalar value is provided per element in the grid subset.
sources.parent_definition: R component of the magnetic vector potential, given on various grid subsets

NAMES.name: radial_width_of_neoclassical_tearing_mode
NAMES.short: Radial width of a neoclassical tearing mode is the nonnegative full extent of its magnetic island along the major-radius coordinate R in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, measured between separatrix crossings through the resonant rational surface.
NAMES.long:
Radial width of a neoclassical tearing mode is the full cross-island extent of the associated magnetic island along the major-radius coordinate $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It is evaluated across the island separatrix through the resonant rational surface and is a nonnegative full width, not a signed displacement of the island center.

The full-width convention is represented by the separation of the outer and inner separatrix crossings along $R$:

$$
w = R_\mathrm{out} - R_\mathrm{in}
$$

where $w$, $R_\mathrm{in}$, and $R_\mathrm{out}$ are lengths in meters, and $R_\mathrm{in}$ and $R_\mathrm{out}$ are the inner and outer separatrix crossing positions on the same island cross-section, ordered so that $R_\mathrm{out} \ge R_\mathrm{in}$.

This quantity uses a full-width convention; an island half-width is half of this value and is not the same quantity. The generic [mode width](name:mode_width) uses the same full-island-width convention without the neoclassical-tearing-mode specialization, while [time derivative of mode width](name:time_derivative_of_mode_width) denotes the temporal rate of change of the width. The position of the island center may be specified by the [toroidal flux coordinate of the neoclassical tearing mode center](name:toroidal_flux_coordinate_of_neoclassical_tearing_mode_center).

NAMES.name: ratio_of_upper_bound_plasma_current_to_initial_plasma_current_due_to_disruption
NAMES.short: Ratio of upper-bound plasma current to initial plasma current during a disruption is the higher-current fractional threshold used with a lower threshold to define a custom linear current-quench decay interval.
NAMES.long:
Ratio of upper-bound plasma current to initial plasma current during a disruption is the higher-current threshold $X_2$ formed from the signed [plasma current](name:plasma_current) relative to its signed pre-disruption reference value. It identifies the earlier, higher-current crossing that bounds a custom linear plasma-current quench interval.

Let $t_2$ be the earlier crossing time selected for the upper endpoint of that interval. The threshold is defined by:

$$
X_2 = \frac{I_p(t_2)}{I_{p,0}}
$$

where $I_p(t_2)$ is the signed [plasma current](name:plasma_current) at the upper-endpoint crossing and $I_{p,0}$ is the signed pre-disruption reference [plasma current](name:plasma_current).

Together with the corresponding lower-bound threshold $X_1$, [ratio of lower-bound plasma current to initial plasma current during a disruption], the valid ordering for a decreasing-current interval is $0 < X_1 < X_2 \le 1$. The reference current must be nonzero, and the threshold applies to intervals in which the current at the crossings has the same sign as the pre-disruption reference current. The associated [linear plasma-current decay time during a disruption] uses $\tau_\mathrm{lin} = (t_2 - t_1)/(X_1 - X_2)$, where $t_1$ is the lower-threshold crossing time; for monotonic decay across the interval, $t_2 < t_1$ and the decay time is positive. This plasma-current threshold is distinct from analogous disruption-quench definitions for other current populations, such as the [linear runaway-electron decay time during a disruption](name:linear_runaway_electron_decay_time_due_to_disruption).

sources.enhanced_context: User-defined upper fractional threshold X2 for the custom linear plasma current (Ip) decay time during a disruption current quench. Used with X1 to compute the decay time as (t(X2)−t(X1))/(X1−X2) relative to the pre-disruptive value.
sources.leaf_definition: User-defined value, see description of linear_custom
sources.parent_definition: Decay time defined as (t(X2)-t(X1))/(X1-X2), where t(Xj) corresponds to the time where this quantity reaches Xj*100% of its pre-disruptive value

NAMES.name: rotation_frequency_of_neoclassical_tearing_mode
NAMES.short: Angular rate at which a neoclassical tearing-mode magnetic island advances or regresses in helical phase on its resonant flux surface.
NAMES.long:
The angular rotation frequency of a neoclassical tearing-mode magnetic island describes the instantaneous evolution of its helical phase. The phase identifies the island's orientation on the resonant flux surface, while its first derivative gives the rotation rate.

$$
\omega_{\mathrm{NTM}}(t) = \frac{d\phi_{\mathrm{NTM}}(t)}{dt}
$$

where $\omega_{\mathrm{NTM}}$ is the angular rotation frequency, $\phi_{\mathrm{NTM}}$ is the island's helical phase, and $t$ is time. The phase may advance or regress, so the frequency can have either sign. Its time derivative is the angular acceleration represented by [tendency of rotation frequency of a neoclassical tearing mode](name:tendency_of_rotation_frequency_of_neoclassical_tearing_mode). The phase itself is defined by [neoclassical tearing mode phase](name:neoclassical_tearing_mode_phase).

sources.enhanced_context: Time derivative of the phase (dφ/dt) of a neoclassical tearing mode (NTM), equivalent to the instantaneous angular rotation frequency of the mode. Part of the detailed NTM temporal evolution record.
sources.leaf_definition: Time derivative of the phase of the mode
sources.parent_definition: Detailed NTM evolution on a finer timebase than the time_slice array of structure

sources.leaf_definition: Frequency of the mode
sources.parent_definition: Detailed NTM evolution on a finer timebase than the time_slice array of structure

sources.enhanced_context: Time derivative of the phase of a neoclassical tearing mode (NTM) magnetic island (dφ/dt), equivalent to the mode's instantaneous angular rotation frequency. Captures the phase evolution dynamics of the rotating island.

NAMES.name: runaway_electron_decay_time_due_to_disruption
NAMES.subject: runaway_electron
NAMES.short: Characteristic decay time for the disruption-driven decrease of the runaway-electron current. It abstracts over the convention used to assign a time scale, such as an exponential e-folding time or a fractional-level linear decay time.
NAMES.long:
Runaway-electron decay time due to disruption is the characteristic time scale associated with the decrease of the runaway-electron current during a disruption. It fixes the decaying quantity as the runaway-electron current while leaving the specific decay-time convention to the more specialized quantity.

This parent quantity includes decay times defined from different idealizations of the same current decrease, such as an exponential e-folding time or the fractional-level convention used by the [linear runaway-electron decay time due to disruption](name:linear_runaway_electron_decay_time_due_to_disruption). It is not a decay time for total plasma current, thermal current, or an unspecified plasma quantity.

sources.enhanced_context: Exponential decay time constant (τ) characterizing the decay of runaway electron current during a disruption, describing the process as exp(-(t-t0)/τ). Quantifies how rapidly the runaway current diminishes after onset.
sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Exponential decay time (tau) used when the process is described by an exponential function (exp(-(t-t0)/tau))). Here "t" is time and "t0" is the time where the decay process starts

NAMES.name: sawtooth_period
NAMES.short: Time interval between successive sawtooth crash events, representing the duration of one complete sawtooth oscillation cycle in a tokamak plasma.
NAMES.long:
The sawtooth period is the elapsed time from one sawtooth crash to the next consecutive crash, including the intervening growth and relaxation phases.

For successive crash times $t_k$ and $t_{k+1}$, the period is defined by

$$
T_{\mathrm{st}} = t_{k+1} - t_k
$$

where $T_{\mathrm{st}}$ is the sawtooth period and $t_k$ is the time of the $k$th crash. The quantity refers to the temporal spacing of consecutive crash events, not the duration of the crash itself or the duration of the preceding growth phase alone.

sources.enhanced_context: Period of the previous sawtooth oscillation cycle, defined as the time between two consecutive sawtooth crash events. Used to characterize sawtooth repetition frequency and validate sawtooth trigger models.
sources.leaf_definition: Previous sawtooth period
sources.parent_definition: Detailed information about the sawtooth characteristics

NAMES.name: thermal_energy_decay_time_due_to_disruption
NAMES.short: Thermal energy decay time due to disruption is the effective linear time scale for loss of thermal plasma energy between two normalized-energy thresholds during the thermal quench, with X2 the upper fraction and X1 the lower fraction. It is not an exponential e-folding time.
NAMES.long:
Thermal energy decay time due to disruption is the threshold-normalized linear time scale for the decrease of thermal plasma energy during the thermal quench of a disruption. It is defined from the elapsed time required for the normalized thermal energy to fall from an upper fraction to a lower fraction of its pre-disruptive value.

Let $W_\mathrm{th}(t)$ be the thermal plasma energy and $W_{\mathrm{th},0}$ its pre-disruptive reference value. For dimensionless thresholds $X_2$ and $X_1$ satisfying $0 \le X_1 < X_2 \le 1$, with $X_2$ the upper fraction and $X_1$ the lower fraction, let $t(X)$ be the earliest downward crossing time on the thermal-quench interval at which $W_\mathrm{th}(t)/W_{\mathrm{th},0}$ reaches $X$. The decay time is defined by

$$
\tau_{W_\mathrm{th}} = \frac{t(X_1)-t(X_2)}{X_2-X_1}
$$

where $\tau_{W_\mathrm{th}}$ and $t(X)$ are times in seconds, $W_\mathrm{th}$ and $W_{\mathrm{th},0}$ are thermal energies in joules, and $X_1$ and $X_2$ are dimensionless fractions. For a monotonic decrease, $t(X_1) \ge t(X_2)$, so the defined decay time is non-negative; if both thresholds are not crossed in this order, the quantity is undefined for that event.

The threshold pair is part of the definition of a particular value: energy_upper_fraction_due_to_disruption specifies $X_2$ and energy_lower_fraction_due_to_disruption specifies $X_1$ when custom thresholds are used; an 80-to-20 convention has $X_2=0.8$ and $X_1=0.2$. Here $W_\mathrm{th}$ is [thermal_plasma_energy](name:thermal_plasma_energy), which for an isotropic plasma is related to [thermal_plasma_pressure](name:thermal_plasma_pressure) by the volume integral of $3p_\mathrm{th}/2$. This quantity applies only to the thermal-energy component and excludes magnetic-energy, kinetic-energy, radiated-energy, and total-disruption energy decay times such as energy_decay_time_due_to_disruption.

sources.enhanced_context: Linear decay time of thermal plasma energy content (Wth) during a disruption, defined as (t(0.2)−t(0.8))/0.6 using the times at which the quantity reaches 20% and 80% of its pre-disruptive value. Characterizes the thermal quench timescale.
sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Decay time defined as (t(0.2)-t(0.8))/0.6, where t(X) corresponds to the time where this quantity reaches X*100% of its pre-disruptive value

sources.enhanced_context: Custom linear decay time of the thermal plasma energy (Wth) during a disruption, defined as (t(X2)−t(X1))/(X1−X2) relative to the pre-disruptive value. Characterizes the thermal quench timescale using user-specified threshold levels X1 and X2.
sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Decay time

NAMES.name: time_derivative_of_mode_width
NAMES.short: Time derivative of mode width is the signed instantaneous temporal derivative of the full radial magnetic-island width for a tearing or neoclassical tearing mode. It is a width-evolution rate, distinct from the island width itself and from mode phase rotation.
NAMES.long:
Time derivative of mode width is the signed instantaneous temporal derivative of the full radial width of a magnetic island associated with a tearing or neoclassical tearing mode. The width being differentiated is the full island width described by [radial_width_of_neoclassical_tearing_mode](name:radial_width_of_neoclassical_tearing_mode), not an island half-width or a phase quantity.

The derivative is defined with respect to physical time:

$$
\dot W(t) = \frac{dW(t)}{dt}
$$

where $W(t)$ is the full radial magnetic-island width and $\dot W(t)$ is its time derivative.

This quantity is distinct from [rotation_frequency_of_neoclassical_tearing_mode](name:rotation_frequency_of_neoclassical_tearing_mode), which describes temporal advance of the mode phase rather than change of island width. Model-specific stability factors or drive terms, including quantities such as [coefficient_of_neoclassical_tearing_mode](name:coefficient_of_neoclassical_tearing_mode), may enter an island-evolution equation but are not themselves this derivative.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the full magnetic-island width increases with time.

sources.enhanced_context: Time derivative of the full magnetic island width (dW/dt) of a neoclassical tearing mode (NTM), characterising the instantaneous rate of change of island size on the detailed evolution timebase.
sources.leaf_definition: Time derivative of the full width of the mode
sources.parent_definition: Detailed NTM evolution on a finer timebase than the time_slice array of structure

sources.enhanced_context: Time derivative of the full magnetic island width (dw/dt) for a neoclassical tearing mode (NTM). Quantifies the island growth or decay rate, a key quantity in the generalized Rutherford equation for NTM evolution.
sources.leaf_definition: Time derivative of the full width of the mode
sources.parent_definition: List of the various NTM modes appearing during the simulation. If a mode appears several times, use several indices in this array of structure with the same m,n values.

NAMES.name: toroidal_flux_coordinate_of_neoclassical_tearing_mode_center
NAMES.short: Toroidal-flux radius of the rational magnetic surface at the center of a neoclassical tearing-mode island.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal-flux radius at a neoclassical tearing-mode center is the nonnegative radial flux-surface coordinate of the resonant rational surface about which the magnetic island is centered. It identifies the island location and is distinct from the island's radial width.

The coordinate is defined by

$$
\rho_{\mathrm{tor}} = \sqrt{\frac{\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}}{\pi B_0}}
$$

where $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the toroidal magnetic flux enclosed by the resonant surface, and $B_0$ is the reference toroidal magnetic-field strength used for the flux-radius definition. The value is evaluated at the neoclassical tearing-mode center and is measured outward from the magnetic axis through nested magnetic flux surfaces. It is the locus-specific counterpart of the general [toroidal flux radius](name:toroidal_flux_radius), whereas [radial width of a neoclassical tearing mode](name:radial_width_of_neoclassical_tearing_mode) describes the island's radial extent.

sources.enhanced_context: Toroidal flux coordinate (ρ_tor) giving the radial position of the neoclassical tearing mode (NTM) island centre on the detailed evolution timebase. Locates the mode on the flux surface grid.
sources.leaf_definition: Flux coordinate on which the mode is centred
sources.parent_definition: Detailed NTM evolution on a finer timebase than the time_slice array of structure

sources.enhanced_context: Toroidal flux coordinate (ρ_tor) of the flux surface on which a neoclassical tearing mode (NTM) is centred. Specifies the radial location of the magnetic island in real-space flux coordinates.
sources.leaf_definition: Flux coordinate on which the mode is centred
sources.parent_definition: List of the various NTM modes appearing during the simulation. If a mode appears several times, use several indices in this array of structure with the same m,n values.

NAMES.name: toroidal_halo_current
NAMES.subject: halo
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the electric current carried by halo plasma on open magnetic field lines between the last closed flux surface and first wall during a disruption.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal halo current is the toroidal component of the electric-current vector carried by halo plasma on open magnetic field lines between the last closed flux surface and the first wall during a disruption. It is the toroidal member of the vector quantity [halo current](name:halo_current).

The component is defined by

$$
I_{\phi} = \mathbf{I}_{\mathrm{halo}} \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\mathbf{I}_{\mathrm{halo}}$ is the integrated halo-current vector and $\hat{\phi}$ is the toroidal unit vector in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. Unlike [poloidal halo current](name:poloidal_halo_current), this component measures current along the direction of increasing toroidal angle and excludes the poloidal component.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the halo current flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

sources.enhanced_context: Toroidal component of the halo current (I_phi,halo) flowing in the halo plasma region during a disruption, where plasma contacts the first wall. A key quantity for assessing electromagnetic loads on plasma-facing components.
sources.leaf_definition: Toroidal halo current
sources.parent_definition: Global quantities

NAMES.name: toroidal_impurity_ion_velocity_at_measurement_position
NAMES.subject: impurity_ion
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the bulk-flow velocity of an impurity-ion population, evaluated at a specified measurement position.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the impurity-ion bulk-flow velocity projected onto the toroidal direction at the specified measurement position. It is a signed velocity component in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

$$
v_\phi(\mathbf{x}_m)=\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{imp}}(\mathbf{x}_m)\cdot\hat{\phi}
$$

where $v_\phi$ is the toroidal velocity component, $\mathbf{x}_m$ is the measurement position, $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{imp}}$ is the bulk velocity of the impurity-ion population, and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

For an impurity population combined over charge states, the bulk velocity is the density-weighted mean over the included charge states. The species and charge-state aggregation must be interpreted from the defined population; the related [toroidal ion velocity](name:toroidal_ion_velocity) provides the corresponding generic ion quantity.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the impurity-ion flow points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.
