NAMES.name: toroidal_linear_mhd_mode_reference_phase
NAMES.short: Signed angular offset that fixes the complex phase of a linear MHD perturbation’s toroidal Fourier mode relative to its zero-phase reference.
NAMES.long:
The reference phase is the angular offset assigned to the complex eigenfunction of a linear MHD perturbation with a specified toroidal harmonic. It fixes the mode’s phase origin and is not a spatial displacement or amplitude.

Using the complex-amplitude convention, the toroidal dependence of a perturbation quantity is written as:

$$
\widetilde{Q}(R,Z,\phi)=\widehat{Q}(R,Z)\exp\!\left[i\left(n\phi+\phi_{\mathrm{ref}}\right)\right]
$$

where $\widetilde{Q}$ is the complex perturbation, $\widehat{Q}$ is its complex amplitude, $n$ is the dimensionless integer toroidal mode number, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $\phi_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the reference phase. $R$ and $Z$ are the major-radius and vertical coordinates in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame. The toroidal harmonic is identified by [mode number](name:mode_number), while its phase is carried by quantities such as the [toroidal perturbed plasma magnetic field](name:toroidal_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field).

The reference phase does not specify perturbation amplitude, growth rate, oscillation frequency, or temporal phase.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the complex mode phase advances in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

sources.enhanced_context: Additional phase offset (φ) of a linear MHD toroidal mode eigenfunction. Defines the angular phase shift applied to the mode structure in the representation of the perturbation.
sources.leaf_definition: Additional phase offset of mode
sources.parent_definition: Vector of toroidal modes

NAMES.name: toroidal_magnetic_flux_at_halo_boundary
NAMES.short: Signed toroidal magnetic flux through the poloidal cross-section bounded by the outermost flux surface of the halo-current region during a disruption.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal magnetic flux function evaluated on the outermost flux surface bounding the halo-current region during a disruption is the net toroidal magnetic-field flux through the enclosed poloidal cross-section. It is distinct from the [toroidal halo current](name:toroidal_halo_current), which describes current rather than magnetic flux.

The flux is defined by

$$
\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}(\mathcal{A}_h)=\int_{\mathcal{A}_h}\mathbf{B}\cdot\hat{\phi}\,dA=\int_{\mathcal{A}_h}B_{\phi}\,dA
$$

where $\mathcal{A}_h$ is the poloidal area enclosed by the halo boundary, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field in tesla, $\hat{\phi}$ is the toroidal unit vector, $B_{\phi}$ is its toroidal component, and $dA$ is the poloidal area element. The boundary value is the halo-region counterpart of [toroidal magnetic flux at the plasma boundary](name:toroidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the toroidal magnetic field points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

sources.enhanced_context: Toroidal magnetic flux (Φ) at the boundary of the halo current region during a disruption. Defines the flux surface enclosing the halo zone for characterizing current and energy deposition during disruption events.
sources.leaf_definition: Toroidal flux at halo region boundary
sources.parent_definition: Global quantities

NAMES.name: toroidal_magnetic_flux_at_halo_boundary_due_to_poloidal_current
NAMES.short: Toroidal magnetic flux at the halo boundary due to poloidal current is the signed flux through the poloidal cross-section bounded by the outermost halo-region flux surface, retaining only the toroidal magnetic-field contribution generated by poloidal halo current. It excludes contributions from all other current systems.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal magnetic flux at the halo boundary due to poloidal current is the signed toroidal magnetic flux through the poloidal cross-section bounded by the outermost halo-region flux surface. It contains only the magnetic-field contribution generated by the [poloidal_halo_current](name:poloidal_halo_current), the poloidal component of halo current.

Let $S_h$ be the area enclosed by the halo-boundary contour in a plane of constant toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ increases counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height. With the oriented surface element $d\mathbf{S}=+\hat{\phi}\,dA$, the flux is

$$
\Phi_{\mathrm{tor},h}^{(\mathrm{pol})} = \int_{S_h} \mathbf{B}_h^{(\mathrm{pol})}\cdot d\mathbf{S} = \int_{S_h} B_{\phi,h}^{(\mathrm{pol})}\,dA
$$

where $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor},h}^{(\mathrm{pol})}$ denotes this quantity, $\mathbf{B}_h^{(\mathrm{pol})}$ is the magnetic-field contribution from poloidal halo current, $B_{\phi,h}^{(\mathrm{pol})}$ is its component along $+\hat{\phi}$ in tesla, $d\mathbf{S}$ is the oriented surface element in square meters, and $dA$ is the corresponding scalar area element in square meters.

This quantity is the poloidal-current source component of [toroidal_magnetic_flux_at_halo_boundary](name:toroidal_magnetic_flux_at_halo_boundary), which includes all magnetic-field sources. It excludes toroidal flux contributions generated by any current other than poloidal halo current and is distinct from [poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_halo_boundary](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_halo_boundary), which concerns poloidal magnetic flux at the same halo boundary.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the magnetic-field contribution generated by the poloidal halo current crosses $S_h$ in the $+\hat{\phi}$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

sources.enhanced_context: Toroidal magnetic flux (Φ) at the halo region boundary generated by the plasma poloidal current during a disruption. Characterizes the electromagnetic state of the halo boundary relevant to vessel interaction and structural loading.
sources.leaf_definition: Toroidal flux at halo region boundary generated by the plasma poloidal current
sources.parent_definition: Global quantities

NAMES.name: toroidal_perturbed_plasma_velocity_imaginary_part
NAMES.short: Imaginary part of the complex amplitude of the mode-n toroidal plasma-velocity perturbation in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame. It is the φ component of a single toroidal Fourier harmonic and is not the equilibrium toroidal flow.
NAMES.long:
The imaginary part of the complex amplitude of the mode-$n$ toroidal plasma-velocity perturbation is the coefficient of $i$ in the toroidal component of the first-order plasma velocity perturbation for a single toroidal Fourier harmonic. The toroidal component is the projection onto $\hat{\phi}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It is a perturbation eigenfunction component, not the equilibrium toroidal flow.

For a harmonic with phase dependence proportional to $e^{i(n\phi-\omega t)}$, the full complex toroidal component combines this quantity with the matched real part [toroidal_perturbed_plasma_velocity_real_part](name:toroidal_perturbed_plasma_velocity_real_part):

$$
\delta \hat{v}_{\phi,n}(R,Z) = \delta \hat{\mathbf{v}}_n(R,Z)\cdot\hat{\phi} = \operatorname{Re}\!\left[\delta \hat{v}_{\phi,n}(R,Z)\right] + i\,\operatorname{Im}\!\left[\delta \hat{v}_{\phi,n}(R,Z)\right]
$$

where $\delta \hat{\mathbf{v}}_n$ is the complex first-order velocity amplitude for toroidal mode number $n$, $\delta \hat{v}_{\phi,n}$ is its toroidal projection, $\omega$ is the mode angular frequency in the phase factor, and $i$ is the imaginary unit.

This quantity is defined for one specified toroidal mode number $n$; contributions from other toroidal harmonics are excluded. A global phase rotation of the eigenfunction changes the split between real and imaginary parts, so this component must be interpreted with the matched real part and the chosen eigenfunction phase reference.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the imaginary coefficient of the toroidal velocity perturbation is directed along $\hat{\phi}$, the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

sources.enhanced_context: Imaginary part of the toroidal component (coordinate 3) of the perturbed velocity eigenvector (ṽ) in the confined plasma, from linear MHD stability analysis for a given toroidal mode number.
sources.leaf_definition: Imaginary part
sources.parent_definition: Third coordinate (toroidal)

NAMES.name: toroidal_perturbed_plasma_velocity_real_part
NAMES.short: Toroidal perturbed plasma velocity real part is the real part of the complex amplitude of the toroidal component of the first-order plasma velocity perturbation for a single toroidal Fourier harmonic with mode number n in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame. It is the in-phase eigenfunction component relative to the chosen complex phase, not the equilibrium toroidal flow.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal perturbed plasma velocity real part is the real part of the complex amplitude of the toroidal component of the first-order plasma velocity perturbation for a single toroidal Fourier harmonic with mode number $n$. The toroidal component is the projection along $\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}$, the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height. It represents the in-phase part of the linear magnetohydrodynamic perturbation eigenfunction relative to the chosen complex phase, not the equilibrium toroidal flow.

The component is defined by projecting the complex velocity eigenfunction for the selected harmonic onto the toroidal basis direction and taking the real part:

$$
v_{\phi,\mathrm{Re},n}(R,Z) = \operatorname{Re}\!\left[\widetilde{\mathbf v}_n(R,Z)\cdot\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}\right]
$$

where $v_{\phi,\mathrm{Re},n}$ is this quantity, $\widetilde{\mathbf v}_n$ is the complex first-order plasma velocity eigenfunction for toroidal mode number $n$, $\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}$ is the toroidal unit vector, and $\operatorname{Re}$ denotes the real part. With toroidal dependence proportional to $\exp(i n\phi)$, $i$ is the imaginary unit.

Together with [toroidal perturbed plasma velocity imaginary part](name:toroidal_perturbed_plasma_velocity_imaginary_part), this quantity forms the complex toroidal perturbed velocity amplitude. Because a linear eigenfunction may be multiplied by an arbitrary complex constant, the division into real and imaginary parts depends on the selected normalization and phase; the quadrature component is the linked imaginary part, not a separate physical velocity direction.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the real toroidal velocity component points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

sources.enhanced_context: Real part of the toroidal (coordinate 3) component of the perturbed plasma velocity eigenvector (ṽ) from linear MHD stability analysis. Part of the complex velocity perturbation field associated with a given toroidal MHD mode.
sources.leaf_definition: Real part
sources.parent_definition: Third coordinate (toroidal)

NAMES.name: toroidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_imaginary_part
NAMES.short: Imaginary part of the complex toroidal component of the first-order magnetic-field perturbation eigenfunction in the current-free vacuum region, for a specified toroidal mode number in linear MHD stability analysis.
NAMES.long:
In linear MHD stability analysis for a specified toroidal mode number $n$, the first-order magnetic-field perturbation $\delta\mathbf{B}$ in the current-free vacuum region surrounding the plasma is a complex eigenfunction satisfying $\nabla \times \delta\mathbf{B} = 0$ and $\nabla \cdot \delta\mathbf{B} = 0$. This name gives the imaginary part of the toroidal projection of that eigenfunction:

$$
\delta B_\phi^\mathrm{vac} = \delta\mathbf{B}^\mathrm{vac} \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, so that $\delta B_\phi^\mathrm{vac} = \mathrm{Re}(\delta B_\phi^\mathrm{vac}) + i\,\mathrm{Im}(\delta B_\phi^\mathrm{vac})$.

The real part is given by [toroidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_real_part](name:toroidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_real_part), and together they constitute the parent complex eigenfunction [toroidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field](name:toroidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field). Boundary conditions at the plasma–vacuum interface link this vacuum eigenfunction to the corresponding plasma-region toroidal component [toroidal_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field_imaginary_part](name:toroidal_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field_imaginary_part); the radial vacuum counterpart is [radial_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_imaginary_part](name:radial_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_imaginary_part). Absolute eigenfunction amplitudes are normalization-convention-dependent in linear stability calculations.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $\mathrm{Im}(\delta B_\phi^\mathrm{vac})$ is directed in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

sources.enhanced_context: Imaginary part of the toroidal (coordinate3) component of the perturbed magnetic field (δB) eigenfunction in the vacuum region, from linear MHD stability analysis for a given toroidal mode number. Forms the complex eigenfunction together with the corresponding real part.
sources.leaf_definition: Imaginary part
sources.parent_definition: Third coordinate (toroidal)

NAMES.name: vertical_plasma_velocity
NAMES.short: Z-direction component of the plasma center-of-mass bulk fluid velocity in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, capturing net vertical mass transport of the plasma.
NAMES.long:
The vertical plasma velocity is the projection of the plasma center-of-mass bulk fluid velocity onto the vertical direction $\hat{Z}$ of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major radius from the symmetry axis and $Z$ is the height above the midplane. It captures net vertical mass transport — relevant to equilibrium vertical stability, edge flows near magnetic X-points, and the onset or evolution of vertical displacement events.

The component is defined as:

$$
v_Z = \mathbf{v}_\mathrm{cm} \cdot \hat{Z}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_\mathrm{cm}$ is the [plasma_velocity](name:plasma_velocity) center-of-mass bulk velocity vector, a mass-weighted mean of all contributing plasma species.

Together with [radial_plasma_velocity](name:radial_plasma_velocity) and [toroidal_plasma_velocity](name:toroidal_impurity_ion_velocity_at_measurement_position), this component fully decomposes the bulk plasma flow in the cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The [parallel_plasma_velocity](name:parallel_plasma_velocity) gives the field-aligned projection, which combines contributions from all three cylindrical directions. In tokamak near-equilibrium conditions, vertical velocities are generally much smaller than toroidal rotation speeds but become significant near magnetic X-points, in scrape-off layer flows, or during vertical stability transients.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the plasma flow is directed in the $+Z$ direction (vertically upward).

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_runaway_electron_critical_momentum_due_to_avalanche
NAMES.subject: runaway_electron
NAMES.short: Volume-averaged momentum threshold for runaway-electron avalanche multiplication, separating collisional drag-dominated electrons from those capable of net acceleration and secondary runaway production.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the plasma-volume average of the local critical momentum threshold for avalanche-driven runaway-electron generation. It characterizes the boundary between collisional drag-dominated and net-accelerated electron dynamics.

The volume average is defined by

$$
p_{c,\mathrm{av}} = \frac{1}{V}\int_V p_c(\mathbf{r})\,dV
$$

where $p_{c,\mathrm{av}}$ is the averaged threshold, $V$ is the plasma volume, $dV$ is a differential volume element, and $p_c(\mathbf{r})$ is the local [critical momentum due to avalanche](name:critical_momentum_due_to_avalanche) at position $\mathbf{r}$.

This quantity is an unweighted volume average, not the momentum carried by the runaway-electron population and not a volume average of electron momentum. It is the spatially aggregated form of the local avalanche threshold and is distinct from the broader [momentum due to avalanche](name:momentum_due_to_avalanche), which need not denote a critical threshold.

sources.enhanced_context: Volume-averaged critical momentum (p_c,av) for runaway electron avalanche generation, above which electrons undergo net acceleration via avalanche, Compton, or tritium decay mechanisms. The threshold separating runaway from drag-dominated electron dynamics.
sources.leaf_definition: Critical momentum for avalanche, Compton and tritium
sources.parent_definition: Volume average runaways parameters

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_runaway_electron_kinetic_energy_density
NAMES.subject: runaway_electron
NAMES.short: Mean relativistic kinetic energy per unit volume of the runaway electron population, obtained by averaging the local kinetic energy density over the confined plasma volume.
NAMES.long:
The volume-averaged runaway electron kinetic energy density is a global scalar characterizing the mean suprathermal energy stored per unit volume in the runaway electron (RE) population. It is obtained by integrating the local relativistic kinetic energy density over the total confined plasma volume $V$ and dividing by $V$.

The underlying local quantity is the relativistic kinetic energy moment of the RE distribution function:

$$
u_\mathrm{RE}(\mathbf{r}) = \int f_\mathrm{RE}(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{p})\,(\gamma - 1)\,m_e c^2 \, d^3p
$$

where $f_\mathrm{RE}$ is the runaway electron phase-space distribution function, $\gamma = (1 + p^2 / m_e^2 c^2)^{1/2}$ is the Lorentz factor, $m_e$ is the electron rest mass, $c$ is the speed of light, and $\mathbf{p}$ is the relativistic momentum. The volume average is then $\langle u_\mathrm{RE} \rangle = V^{-1} \int_V u_\mathrm{RE}\,dV$.

This quantity is evaluated from kinetic or reduced-fluid runaway electron models, particularly in disruption current-quench simulations where RE populations can reach energies of several to tens of MeV per particle. Multiplying by the plasma volume $V$ recovers the total stored relativistic energy given by [runaway_electron_kinetic_energy](name:runaway_electron_kinetic_energy). The local non-averaged counterpart is runaway_electron_kinetic_energy_density, and the corresponding global particle number density is [volume_averaged_runaway_electron_density](name:volume_averaged_runaway_electron_density).

sources.enhanced_context: Volume-averaged kinetic energy density of the runaway electron (RE) population. Represents the mean kinetic energy per unit volume stored in suprathermal runaway electrons averaged over the plasma volume.
sources.leaf_definition: Runaways kinetic mean energy density
sources.parent_definition: Volume average runaways parameters

NAMES.name: vorticity
NAMES.short: Curl of the plasma bulk velocity field measuring local angular rotation of fluid elements; parent quantity generalizing over directional projections including radial, toroidal, poloidal, and field-aligned components.
NAMES.long:
Plasma vorticity characterizes the rotational nature of bulk plasma flow and plays a central role in MHD dynamics, entering the momentum equation through nonlinear advection and governing the evolution of shear layers and vortex structures. It resolves into components along the coordinate axes of the plasma geometry, each describing a distinct aspect of rotational fluid motion.

The defining relation is:

$$
\boldsymbol{\omega} = \nabla \times \mathbf{v}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}$ is the local plasma bulk flow velocity. Projections in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame are provided by [radial_vorticity](name:radial_vorticity), [toroidal_vorticity](name:toroidal_vorticity), and [vertical_vorticity](name:vertical_vorticity); the field-aligned projection is [parallel_vorticity](name:parallel_vorticity).

Vorticity is evaluated from velocity fields obtained via ion Doppler spectroscopy or charge exchange recombination spectroscopy, or computed self-consistently in MHD simulations through curl operations applied to the discrete velocity field on the computational mesh.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the plasma velocity field rotates in the right-hand sense about the positive direction of the relevant coordinate axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: critical_temperature_at_pedestal_top
NAMES.short: Critical temperature at the pedestal top is the threshold kinetic temperature at the pedestal top at which an H-mode edge pedestal is marginal to ideal magnetohydrodynamic peeling-ballooning stability, representing a stability-limit quantity distinct from the measured or fitted pedestal temperature.
NAMES.long:
Critical temperature at the pedestal top is the threshold kinetic temperature of a plasma species or population evaluated at the top of the H-mode edge transport barrier at which the pedestal is marginally stable to ideal magnetohydrodynamic peeling-ballooning modes. The pedestal top is the fitted transition location where the steep edge temperature gradient relaxes toward the core region, following the convention of the [temperature_at_pedestal_top](name:temperature_at_pedestal_top) family. This critical temperature is a stability-limit quantity, not the measured or fitted kinetic temperature of the edge pedestal.

The critical temperature $T_\mathrm{crit,ped}$ at the fitted pedestal-top normalized poloidal flux coordinate $\psi_{N,\mathrm{ped}}$ is defined by the marginal peeling-ballooning stability condition:

$$
\gamma_\mathrm{peel-bal}(T_\mathrm{crit,ped},\, \psi_{N,\mathrm{ped}}) = 0
$$

where $\gamma_\mathrm{peel-bal}$ is the ideal-MHD peeling-ballooning mode growth rate evaluated at pedestal-top parameters and $\psi_{N,\mathrm{ped}}$ is the normalized poloidal flux coordinate at the pedestal top.

The representative species specialization is [electron_critical_temperature_at_pedestal_top](name:electron_critical_temperature_at_pedestal_top); other species-resolved members are defined analogously. This quantity is distinct from [electron_temperature_at_pedestal_top](name:electron_temperature_at_pedestal_top), which gives the measured kinetic temperature at the pedestal top rather than the stability threshold.

NAMES.name: electron_critical_temperature_at_pedestal_top
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Electron critical temperature at the pedestal top is the electron kinetic-temperature threshold at the top of an H-mode edge transport barrier for marginal ideal peeling-ballooning stability. It is distinct from the fitted electron temperature at the same pedestal-top locus.
NAMES.long:
Electron critical temperature at the pedestal top is the electron kinetic-temperature threshold at the top of an H-mode edge transport barrier for marginal ideal peeling-ballooning stability. It is the pedestal-top electron temperature that, with the specified accompanying pedestal density, ion temperature, impurity content, pedestal width, current-profile, and equilibrium-shape parameters, places the pedestal pressure-gradient and edge-current state on the ideal magnetohydrodynamic stability boundary.

The threshold is defined by the marginality condition:

$$
\mathcal{M}(T_{e,\mathrm{crit}}; \mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{ped}}, \mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{eq}}) = 0
$$

where $T_{e,\mathrm{crit}}$ is the electron critical temperature at the pedestal top, $\mathcal{M}$ is the ideal peeling-ballooning marginality condition whose zero level is the stability boundary, $\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{ped}}$ denotes the accompanying pedestal kinetic, composition, gradient, and width parameters, and $\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{eq}}$ denotes the associated equilibrium, shaping, magnetic-shear, and current-density parameters.

The value is conditioned on the joint pedestal/equilibrium parameter set; changing those companion parameters changes the threshold being named. It is the electron-specific counterpart of [critical_temperature_at_pedestal_top](name:critical_temperature_at_pedestal_top), not the fitted [electron_temperature_at_pedestal_top](name:electron_temperature_at_pedestal_top) at the same locus, and it does not by itself define a total pedestal temperature or pressure.

sources.enhanced_context: Critical electron temperature (Te) at the pedestal top, determined from self-consistent MHD stability runs using the Hager bootstrap current formula. Represents the Te value at which the pedestal reaches the peeling-ballooning stability boundary.

sources.parent_definition: Critical electron temperature at pedestal top determined with self-consistent runs with an MHD stability code. Details of the method for scanning parameters in the series of runs must be described in the 'source' node

This threshold value marks the stability boundary in parameter scans coupling pedestal profiles to peeling-ballooning mode analysis.

NAMES.name: magnetic_shear_at_sawtooth_inversion_radius
NAMES.short: Magnetic shear evaluated at the sawtooth inversion radius, defined as the normalized logarithmic derivative of the safety factor with respect to normalized toroidal flux radius.
NAMES.long:
Magnetic shear at the sawtooth inversion radius is the value of [magnetic shear](name:magnetic_shear) on the flux surface where the sawtooth-crash electron-temperature perturbation changes sign.

Using the [normalized toroidal flux coordinate at the sawtooth inversion radius](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_sawtooth_inversion_radius) $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ as the radial label, the defining relation is

$$
s_{\mathrm{inv}} = \left.\frac{\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}}{q}\frac{dq}{d\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}}\right|_{\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}=\rho_{\mathrm{inv}}}
$$

where $q$ is the safety factor, $\rho_{\mathrm{inv}}$ is the normalized toroidal flux radius of the inversion surface, and $s_{\mathrm{inv}}$ is the corresponding magnetic shear.

This is a point evaluation at the inversion surface, not a flux-surface average or a volume average. The inversion surface is not defined by $q=1$ and differs from [magnetic shear at the magnetic axis](name:magnetic_shear_at_magnetic_axis).
NAMES.sign: Positive when $q^{-1}dq/d\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ is positive as the normalized toroidal flux radius increases outward from the magnetic axis.

sources.enhanced_context: Magnetic shear (s) at the q=1 rational surface, defined as (rho_tor/q)·(dq/drho_tor) evaluated where the safety factor equals unity. A key parameter for sawtooth trigger models and MHD stability analysis.
sources.leaf_definition: Magnetic shear at surface q = 1, defined as rho_tor/q . dq/drho_tor
sources.parent_definition: Detailed information about the sawtooth characteristics

NAMES.name: normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_sawtooth_inversion_radius
NAMES.short: Dimensionless radial flux-surface label based on normalized toroidal magnetic flux, evaluated at the sawtooth inversion radius where a crash-induced electron-temperature perturbation changes sign.
NAMES.long:
The normalized toroidal flux coordinate at the sawtooth inversion radius is the dimensionless radial label assigned to the nested flux surface where a crash-induced electron-temperature perturbation changes sign. It is the [normalized toroidal flux coordinate](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate) evaluated at that surface, with the origin at the magnetic axis and the outer normalization reference at the plasma boundary or last closed flux surface.

The coordinate is defined from the toroidal magnetic flux difference between the sawtooth inversion surface and the magnetic axis:

$$
\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}(r_{\mathrm{inv}}) = \sqrt{\frac{\Phi_{\mathrm{inv}} - \Phi_0}{\Phi_b - \Phi_0}}
$$

where $r_{\mathrm{inv}}$ identifies the sawtooth inversion radius, $\Phi_{\mathrm{inv}}$ is the toroidal magnetic flux of its flux surface, $\Phi_0$ is the magnetic-axis toroidal magnetic flux, and $\Phi_b$ is the boundary toroidal magnetic flux. The square root gives a nonnegative radial label that spans from zero at the magnetic axis to unity at the normalization boundary.

This quantity identifies the sawtooth inversion surface rather than the temperature perturbation or its amplitude. It is distinct from the [normalized toroidal flux coordinate at the magnetic axis](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_magnetic_axis), which is the zero-valued reference coordinate, and from [magnetic shear at the sawtooth inversion radius](name:magnetic_shear_at_sawtooth_inversion_radius), which describes the safety-factor gradient at the same surface.

sources.enhanced_context: Normalized toroidal flux coordinate (ρ_tor_norm) at the sawtooth inversion radius, the radial location where the electron temperature perturbation changes sign during a sawtooth crash. Characterizes the spatial extent of the sawtooth-affected region.
sources.leaf_definition: Normalised toroidal flux coordinate at inversion radius
sources.parent_definition: Detailed information about the sawtooth characteristics

sources.enhanced_context: Normalised toroidal flux coordinate (ρ_tor_norm) at the q=1 rational surface, marking the radial location of the sawtooth inversion surface. Used to characterize the extent of the sawtooth-affected zone and validate trigger models.
sources.leaf_definition: Normalised toroidal flux coordinate at surface q = 1
sources.parent_definition: Detailed information about the sawtooth characteristics

NAMES.name: normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_sawtooth_mixing_radius
NAMES.short: Dimensionless radial flux-surface label based on normalized toroidal magnetic flux, evaluated at the sawtooth mixing radius. It identifies the outer boundary of the region homogenized during a sawtooth crash, with 0 at the magnetic axis and 1 at the plasma boundary.
NAMES.long:
The normalized toroidal flux coordinate at the sawtooth mixing radius is the dimensionless radial label assigned to the nested flux surface defining the outer boundary of the region homogenized during a sawtooth crash. It is the [normalized toroidal flux coordinate](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate) evaluated at that surface, with the origin at the magnetic axis and the outer normalization reference at the plasma boundary or last closed flux surface.

The coordinate is defined from the toroidal magnetic flux at the sawtooth mixing radius:

$$
\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}(r_{\mathrm{mix}}) = \sqrt{\frac{\Phi_{\mathrm{mix}} - \Phi_0}{\Phi_b - \Phi_0}}
$$

where $r_{\mathrm{mix}}$ is the sawtooth mixing radius, $\Phi_{\mathrm{mix}}$ is the toroidal magnetic flux of its flux surface, $\Phi_0$ is the magnetic-axis toroidal flux, and $\Phi_b$ is the boundary toroidal flux. The square root gives a nonnegative radial label that increases outward for a valid nested-flux-surface mapping.

This quantity identifies the mixing boundary, not the sawtooth inversion surface, where the crash-induced electron-temperature perturbation changes sign; that distinct locus is represented by the [normalized toroidal flux coordinate at the sawtooth inversion radius](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate_at_sawtooth_inversion_radius).

NAMES.name: perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field
NAMES.short: Complex first-order magnetic-field perturbation vector in the current-free vacuum region outside the plasma, forming a single-toroidal-mode eigenfunction in linear MHD stability analysis.
NAMES.long:
The perturbed vacuum magnetic field $\delta\mathbf{B}_\mathrm{vac}$ is the complex first-order perturbation of the magnetic-field vector in the exterior current-free domain surrounding the plasma, arising in linear MHD stability analysis when the plasma undergoes a small displacement from equilibrium relative to the background [vacuum_magnetic_field](name:vacuum_magnetic_field). In this region all plasma currents are absent, so the perturbation obeys the source-free Maxwell conditions $\nabla \times \delta\mathbf{B}_\mathrm{vac} = 0$ and $\nabla \cdot \delta\mathbf{B}_\mathrm{vac} = 0$.

Because the vacuum perturbation is curl-free, it derives from a scalar magnetic potential $\delta\Phi$:

$$
\delta\mathbf{B}_\mathrm{vac} = -\nabla\delta\Phi
$$

where $\nabla^2\delta\Phi = 0$ in the vacuum domain, expanded for a single toroidal harmonic of mode number $n$ (see [toroidal_mhd_mode_number](name:toroidal_mhd_mode_number)). The eigenfunction is obtained by matching the normal component of the perturbation at the plasma–vacuum interface, with $|\delta\mathbf{B}_\mathrm{vac}| \to 0$ in the far field.

The full complex vector is resolved in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame into the [radial](name:radial_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field) component $\delta B_R$, [poloidal](name:poloidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field) component $\delta B_\theta$, and [toroidal](name:toroidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field) component $\delta B_\phi$. The complex representation encodes both amplitude and spatial phase of the mode; the real and imaginary parts of each component form two orthogonal phase quadratures, accessible via quantities such as the [real part of the toroidal component](name:toroidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_real_part).
NAMES.sign: Positive for each cylindrical component when directed along $+R$, $+\phi$, or $+Z$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $\phi$ increases counter-clockwise viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$.

NAMES.name: radial_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field
NAMES.short: Complex first-order radial component of the magnetic-field perturbation eigenfunction in the current-free vacuum outside the plasma, forming part of a single-toroidal-mode linear MHD perturbation.
NAMES.long:
The radial component of the perturbed vacuum magnetic field is the projection of the complex first-order magnetic-field eigenfunction onto the cylindrical radial direction in the current-free exterior region. It is one component of the full [perturbed vacuum magnetic field](name:perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field), which satisfies source-free Maxwell conditions in the vacuum.

The component is defined by

$$
\delta B_R = \delta\mathbf{B}_\mathrm{vac} \cdot \hat{R}
$$

where $\delta\mathbf{B}_\mathrm{vac}$ is the perturbed vacuum magnetic-field vector, $\hat{R}$ is the radial unit vector, and $\delta B_R$ is its radial projection in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame. The radial direction means increasing major radius $R$, not the normal to a magnetic flux surface.

The complex value retains the eigenfunction amplitude and phase; its in-phase and quadrature coefficients are represented by the [real radial component](name:radial_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_real_part) and [imaginary radial component](name:radial_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_imaginary_part). In the current-free vacuum, the perturbation obeys $\nabla\times\delta\mathbf{B}_\mathrm{vac}=0$ and $\nabla\cdot\delta\mathbf{B}_\mathrm{vac}=0$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the radial component is directed along increasing major radius $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: radial_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_real_part
NAMES.short: Real part of the radial perturbed vacuum magnetic field is the in-phase coefficient of the R component in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame for a complex vacuum magnetic-field perturbation eigenfunction of one toroidal Fourier harmonic.
NAMES.long:
Real part of the radial perturbed vacuum magnetic field is the in-phase coefficient of the radial component of a complex magnetic-field perturbation eigenfunction in the current-free vacuum region outside the plasma for one toroidal Fourier harmonic. Radial means projection onto $\hat R$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height; it is not projection onto the equilibrium flux-surface-normal direction.

For a complex harmonic amplitude $\delta\tilde{\mathbf B}^{\mathrm{vac}}_n(\mathbf{x})$, with physical perturbation represented by $\operatorname{Re}\{\delta\tilde{\mathbf B}^{\mathrm{vac}}_n(\mathbf{x}) e^{i(n\phi-\omega t)}\}$, this quantity is defined by:

$$
\delta B^{\mathrm{vac,Re}}_{R,n}(\mathbf{x}) = \operatorname{Re}\!\left[\delta\tilde{\mathbf B}^{\mathrm{vac}}_n(\mathbf{x}) \cdot \hat R\right]
$$

where $\operatorname{Re}$ denotes real part, $n$ is the toroidal mode number, $\omega$ is the angular frequency associated with the chosen complex representation, $\mathbf{x}$ is position, and $\hat R$ is the radial basis vector of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

The [imaginary counterpart](name:radial_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_imaginary_part) is the quadrature coefficient of the same complex radial component, and the two together specify the [complex radial vacuum perturbation amplitude](name:radial_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field) for the chosen eigenfunction phase. This vacuum-region quantity is distinct from the corresponding plasma-region perturbation; a linear eigenfunction amplitude is defined only up to an overall complex normalization unless a separate normalization condition is imposed.
NAMES.sign: Positive when, at Fourier phase $n\phi-\omega t=0$ for the representation above, the vacuum magnetic-field perturbation has a component in the $+\hat R$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: plasma_magnetic_field
NAMES.short: Magnetic field in the confined plasma interior, generalizing over equilibrium and perturbed configurations arising from MHD modes or non-axisymmetric fields, and distinct from equivalent field definitions in the surrounding vacuum region.
NAMES.long:
The plasma magnetic field designates the magnetic-field vector evaluated within the confined plasma volume, where both the equilibrium field from external coil systems and plasma-current-driven contributions are present, together with first-order departures driven by MHD instabilities or applied non-axisymmetric perturbations. This quantity serves as the conceptual parent for field quantities that are explicitly localized to the plasma interior, as opposed to vacuum-region counterparts that satisfy $\nabla \times \mathbf{B} = 0$.

In the linearized MHD framework the total field decomposes as

$$
\mathbf{B} = \mathbf{B}_0 + \delta\mathbf{B}
$$

where $\mathbf{B}_0$ is the axisymmetric equilibrium field and $\delta\mathbf{B}$ is the first-order perturbation. Inside the plasma, $\delta\mathbf{B}$ couples to the perturbed current density $\delta\mathbf{J}$ and pressure gradient through the linearized MHD force balance, a physical constraint absent in the vacuum region.

The concrete vector realization of the first-order plasma-interior perturbation is [perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field](name:perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field), which carries the eigenfunction field in tesla and is explicitly distinguished from perturbation fields defined in the vacuum region. For the scalar amplitude of the equilibrium departure without the plasma-interior qualification, the sibling quantity perturbed_magnetic_field applies. Measurement of the perturbation field inside the plasma relies on Mirnov coil arrays for edge fluctuations, polarimetry for line-integrated signals, and MHD eigenfunction reconstruction from equilibrium data.

NAMES.name: perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field
NAMES.short: Perturbed plasma magnetic field is the complex linear-MHD eigenfunction, or corresponding real perturbation, of the magnetic-field deviation carried by the confined-plasma response about an equilibrium field. It excludes externally imposed vacuum perturbations when those are represented separately.
NAMES.long:
Perturbed plasma magnetic field is the complex linear-MHD eigenfunction, or corresponding real perturbation, of the magnetic-field deviation carried by the confined-plasma response about an equilibrium magnetic field. It represents magnetic-field bending and current perturbations inside the confined plasma and excludes any externally imposed vacuum perturbation that is retained as a separate field.

The plasma-response perturbation is defined by subtracting the equilibrium field and any separately represented vacuum perturbation from the total field in the confined plasma region:

$$
\delta\mathbf{B}_\mathrm{pl}(\mathbf{x},t) = \mathbf{B}(\mathbf{x},t) - \mathbf{B}_0(\mathbf{x}) - \delta\mathbf{B}_\mathrm{vac}(\mathbf{x},t)
$$

where $\delta\mathbf{B}_\mathrm{pl}$ is this quantity, $\mathbf{x}$ is position, $t$ is time, $\mathbf{B}$ is the total magnetic field, $\mathbf{B}_0$ is the equilibrium magnetic field, and $\delta\mathbf{B}_\mathrm{vac}$ is the externally imposed vacuum magnetic perturbation that would exist without plasma response. If no separate vacuum perturbation is present or retained, set $\delta\mathbf{B}_\mathrm{vac}=0$; the field satisfies $\nabla\cdot\delta\mathbf{B}_\mathrm{pl}=0$.

Externally imposed vacuum-field quantities, including [perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field](name:perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field), [radial_non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field](name:radial_non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field), and non_axisymmetric_magnetic_field_at_control_surface, can drive the plasma response but are not included in $\delta\mathbf{B}_\mathrm{pl}$ when represented separately. Fourier harmonic amplitudes, eigenfunction components, and spatial projections must carry their stated phase, harmonic, and direction definitions; they are not interchangeable with the unrestricted vector. The related component quantities [radial_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field](name:radial_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field), [poloidal_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field](name:poloidal_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field), and [toroidal_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field](name:toroidal_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field) describe resolved quantities: radial is the $\hat{R}$ projection in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, poloidal requires an explicitly defined poloidal projection direction such as the tangent to increasing $\theta$ in flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, and the toroidal entry denotes the single-harmonic $\hat{\phi}$-resolved quantity specified by that standard name.
NAMES.sign: Positive when a real resolved component of $\delta\mathbf{B}_\mathrm{pl}$, or the real part of a complex resolved component after applying its stated phase convention, is directed along the positive basis direction; in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame with $\hat{R}\times\hat{\phi}=\hat{Z}$, $+\hat{R}$ is toward increasing major radius $R$, $+\hat{\phi}$ is toward increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $+\hat{Z}$ is toward increasing vertical height $Z$.

NAMES.name: poloidal_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field
NAMES.short: Poloidal perturbed plasma magnetic field is the poloidal component of the complex linear-MHD eigenfunction, or corresponding real perturbation, of the magnetic-field deviation carried by the confined-plasma response about equilibrium.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal perturbed plasma magnetic field is the poloidal component of the complex linear-MHD eigenfunction, or corresponding real perturbation, of the magnetic-field deviation carried by the confined-plasma response about an equilibrium magnetic field. It is the poloidal projection of the [perturbed plasma magnetic field](name:perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field), rather than the unrestricted magnetic-field vector.

$$
\delta B_{\mathrm{pol}}(\mathbf{x},t)=\hat{\mathbf e}_{\mathrm{pol}}(\mathbf{x})\cdot\delta\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{pl}}(\mathbf{x},t)
$$

Here, $\delta B_{\mathrm{pol}}$ is the poloidal component, $\hat{\mathbf e}_{\mathrm{pol}}$ is the chosen poloidal unit vector in the poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, and $\delta\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{pl}}$ is the plasma-response perturbation after subtracting the equilibrium field and any separately represented externally imposed vacuum perturbation. The complex quantity includes the [poloidal real part](name:poloidal_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field_real_part) and [poloidal imaginary part](name:poloidal_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field_imaginary_part); the [toroidal perturbed plasma magnetic field](name:toroidal_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field) is its complementary toroidal projection.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the perturbed magnetic field points in the direction of increasing poloidal angle within the poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: radial_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field
NAMES.short: Radial perturbed plasma magnetic field is the R component of the complex linear-MHD plasma-response perturbation in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The radial perturbed plasma magnetic field is the major-radius-directed component of the complex linear-MHD magnetic-field perturbation eigenfunction, or of its corresponding real perturbation, carried by the confined plasma. It is the radial projection of the [perturbed plasma magnetic field](name:perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field). The right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame has $R$ as major radius, $\phi$ as toroidal angle, and $Z$ as vertical height.

The plasma-response component is defined by

$$
\delta B_{R,\mathrm{pl}}(\mathbf{x},t) = \delta\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{pl}}(\mathbf{x},t) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{R}}
$$

where $\delta B_{R,\mathrm{pl}}$ is the radial component, $\delta\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{pl}}$ is the plasma-response magnetic perturbation, $\mathbf{x}$ is position, $t$ is time, and $\hat{\mathbf{R}}$ is the cylindrical major-radius unit vector. For a Fourier-resolved eigenfunction, the projection applies to the specified complex harmonic coefficient.

Here radial means the cylindrical $R$ direction, not the normal to an equilibrium magnetic flux surface. The component excludes the equilibrium field and any separately represented externally imposed vacuum perturbation. Together with the [toroidal perturbed plasma magnetic field](name:toroidal_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field), it describes directional components of the plasma response; its in-phase component is represented by the [radial perturbed plasma magnetic field real part](name:radial_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field_real_part).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the magnetic perturbation points toward increasing major radius $R$.

NAMES.name: radial_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field_real_part
NAMES.short: Radial perturbed plasma magnetic field real part is the in-phase radial component of the complex first-order plasma magnetic-field perturbation for one toroidal Fourier harmonic. The radial direction is the R component in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Radial perturbed plasma magnetic field real part is the real part of the cylindrical radial component of a complex first-order plasma magnetic-field perturbation for a selected toroidal Fourier harmonic. The radial direction is the $+\hat{\mathbf{R}}$ basis direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The defining component is

$$
\delta B_{R,n}^{\mathrm{re}} = \operatorname{Re}\!\left(\widetilde{\delta\mathbf{B}}_n \cdot \hat{\mathbf{R}}\right)
$$

where $\delta B_{R,n}^{\mathrm{re}}$ is this real component, $\widetilde{\delta\mathbf{B}}_n$ is the complex first-order plasma magnetic-field perturbation for toroidal Fourier mode number $n$, $\operatorname{Re}$ takes the real part, and $\hat{\mathbf{R}}$ is the radial basis vector.

Together with [radial perturbed plasma magnetic field imaginary part], it determines the complex [radial perturbed plasma magnetic field](name:radial_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field); changing the chosen complex phase of the harmonic rotates the real and imaginary parts without changing the represented perturbation. It is the radial component counterpart of [toroidal perturbed plasma magnetic field](name:toroidal_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field) and is distinct from a flux-surface-normal projection, which would use a unit normal to a specified flux coordinate rather than $\hat{\mathbf{R}}$.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the in-phase radial perturbation component points in the $+\hat{\mathbf{R}}$ direction of increasing major radius $R$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field
NAMES.short: Toroidal perturbed plasma magnetic field is the toroidal component of the complex linear-MHD magnetic-field perturbation carried by the confined-plasma response about equilibrium.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal perturbed plasma magnetic field is the toroidal component of the complex linear-MHD eigenfunction, or corresponding real perturbation, of the magnetic-field deviation carried by the confined-plasma response about an equilibrium field. It is the toroidal projection of the [perturbed plasma magnetic field](name:perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field) and excludes separately represented externally imposed vacuum perturbations.

The toroidal component is defined by

$$
\delta B_{\mathrm{pl},\phi}(\mathbf{x},t) = \delta\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{pl}}(\mathbf{x},t) \cdot \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}
$$

where $\delta B_{\mathrm{pl},\phi}$ is the toroidal component, $\delta\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{pl}}$ is the plasma-response perturbation, $\mathbf{x}$ is position, $t$ is time, and $\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}$ is the toroidal unit vector in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame with oriented basis $(\hat{\mathbf{R}},\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}},\hat{\mathbf{Z}})$. Here $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The response field is $\delta\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{pl}}=\mathbf{B}-\mathbf{B}_0-\delta\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{vac}}$, where $\mathbf{B}$ is total field, $\mathbf{B}_0$ is equilibrium field, and $\delta\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{vac}}$ is a separately represented vacuum perturbation. For a specified toroidal Fourier harmonic, the [real part](name:toroidal_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field_real_part) and [imaginary part](name:toroidal_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field_imaginary_part) are phase components of this same toroidal quantity.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the corresponding real-valued perturbation points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field_real_part
NAMES.short: Toroidal perturbed plasma magnetic-field real part is the in-phase φ component, in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, of the complex first-order plasma magnetic-field perturbation eigenfunction for one specified toroidal Fourier harmonic. In this frame, R is major radius, φ is toroidal angle, and Z is vertical height.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal perturbed plasma magnetic-field real part is the real component of the toroidal projection of the complex first-order plasma magnetic-field perturbation eigenfunction in the plasma region for one specified toroidal Fourier harmonic. The toroidal projection is the component along $\hat{\phi}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle increasing counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The physical toroidal perturbation associated with the complex eigenfunction is represented by

$$
\delta B_\phi(R,\phi,Z,t) = \operatorname{Re}\!\left[\delta\tilde{B}_\phi(R,Z)\exp\!\left(i(n\phi-\omega t)\right)\right]
$$

where $\delta B_\phi$ is the physical first-order toroidal magnetic-field perturbation, $\delta\tilde{B}_\phi$ is the complex toroidal eigenfunction amplitude, $\operatorname{Re}$ denotes the real-part operator, $n$ is the toroidal mode number, $\omega$ is the mode angular frequency, and $t$ is time. This quantity is $\operatorname{Re}[\delta\tilde{B}_\phi(R,Z)]$.

Together with [toroidal_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field_imaginary_part](name:toroidal_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field_imaginary_part), this quantity specifies the complex toroidal perturbation component [toroidal_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field](name:toroidal_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field) for the selected harmonic. It is distinct from the radial and poloidal real-part components [radial_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field_real_part](name:radial_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field_real_part) and [poloidal_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field_real_part](name:poloidal_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field_real_part), from the equilibrium toroidal magnetic field, and from the vacuum-region counterpart [toroidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_real_part](name:toroidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_real_part). A global complex phase rotation of the eigenfunction changes the split between real and imaginary parts while leaving the reconstructed physical perturbation unchanged when the same Fourier convention is used.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $\operatorname{Re}[\delta\tilde{B}_\phi]$ is directed along increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: plasma_mass_density
NAMES.short: Local plasma mass per unit volume, forming the inertial term in the MHD momentum equation and appearing in contexts from equilibrium transport profiles to linear MHD stability perturbations.
NAMES.long:
The plasma mass density is the local plasma mass per unit volume, forming the inertial term in the MHD momentum balance and the compressibility term in the plasma continuity equation. This parent concept subsumes both equilibrium-profile and linear-perturbation contexts: the equilibrium total value summed over all charged species, and the complex first-order perturbation amplitude used in linear MHD eigenvalue problems.

In the equilibrium formulation, the mass density is defined by:

$$
\rho = \sum_s m_s n_s
$$

where $m_s$ is the particle mass and $n_s$ the number density of charged species $s$, summed over electrons, main-ion isotopes, and impurity charge states; neutral atoms are excluded. Ion contributions dominate because $m_i \gg m_e$.

In deuterium-dominated fusion plasmas at core electron densities of order $10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$, the mass density is approximately $3 \times 10^{-7}$ kg m$^{-3}$, scaling directly with ion density and average ion mass. The mass density sets the local Alfvén speed $v_A = B / \sqrt{\mu_0 \rho}$, where $B$ is the local magnetic-field magnitude and $\mu_0$ is the permeability of free space, governing the [alfven_time](name:alfven_time) and ideal-MHD wave dynamics. It enters inertial_current_density through the plasma-fluid acceleration term and is inferred from electron_number_density measurements combined with plasma composition analysis. This quantity is closely related to [mass_density](name:total_plasma_mass_density), which covers the same physical concept without explicit species qualification.

NAMES.name: product_of_current_density_and_major_radius
NAMES.short: Product of current density and major radius is the major-radius-weighted toroidal current-density component in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Product of current density and major radius is the scalar major-radius-weighted toroidal current density at a point. It combines the major radius with the $\hat{\phi}$ component of current density in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is distance from the toroidal symmetry axis, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The defining relation is:

$$
K_\phi(R, \phi, Z) = R\,j_\phi(R, \phi, Z)
$$

where $K_\phi$ denotes the product of current density and major radius, $j_\phi$ is [toroidal current density](name:toroidal_current_density), and $R$ is [major radius](name:major_radius).

In axisymmetric MHD equilibrium, $Rj_\phi$ is the toroidal-current source term in the Grad-Shafranov balance for [poloidal magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux): with $\Delta^* = R^2 \nabla \cdot (R^{-2}\nabla)$, $\Delta^*\psi = -\mu_0 Rj_\phi$, where $\psi$ is poloidal magnetic flux and $\mu_0$ is the vacuum permeability. With pressure $p(\psi)$ and [poloidal current function](name:poloidal_current_function) $F(\psi)=R B_\phi$, the same source satisfies $\mu_0 Rj_\phi = \mu_0 R^2 dp/d\psi + F dF/d\psi$, where $B_\phi$ is the toroidal magnetic-field component.

This quantity is a local density-radius product rather than the total toroidal current. Relations to enclosed current or flux arise only after integration with the appropriate geometric measure, which defines a distinct quantity.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $j_\phi$ points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_magnetic_vector_potential
NAMES.short: Z-component of the magnetic vector potential in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, where the full potential satisfies the curl relation giving the magnetic induction B.
NAMES.long:
The vertical component $A_Z$ is the projection of the magnetic vector potential $\mathbf{A}$ onto the vertical axis $\hat{Z}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major radius, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle, and $Z$ is the vertical height. The full potential satisfies $\mathbf{B} = \nabla \times \mathbf{A}$, making $\mathbf{A}$ gage-dependent but essential in canonical particle momentum, gyrokinetic formulations, and MHD perturbation theory.

The projection is formally defined as:

$$
A_Z = \mathbf{A} \cdot \hat{Z}
$$

where $\hat{Z}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing height. Through the curl relation, $A_Z$ couples to the radial magnetic-field component as $B_R = R^{-1}\partial A_Z/\partial\phi - \partial A_\phi/\partial Z$ and to the toroidal component as $B_\phi = \partial A_R/\partial Z - \partial A_Z/\partial R$, where $A_R$ and $A_\phi$ are the radial and toroidal components of $\mathbf{A}$.

Computed from MHD equilibria or electromagnetic simulations covering the full plasma domain, including edge and wall-adjacent regions. The companion toroidal_vector_potential gives the $\phi$-projection of $\mathbf{A}$, while [vertical_vacuum_magnetic_vector_potential](name:vertical_vacuum_magnetic_vector_potential) isolates the vacuum contribution to $A_Z$ arising from external coil currents. The corresponding magnetic-field component is [vertical_magnetic_field](name:vertical_magnetic_field).
NAMES.sign: Positive when $A_Z$ points in the direction of increasing $Z$.

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_runaway_electron_source_rate
NAMES.subject: runaway_electron
NAMES.short: Volume-averaged production rate of runaway-electron number density over the confined plasma, including all active generation mechanisms and excluding runaway-electron losses.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the confined-plasma volume average of the local runaway-electron number-density production rate. It represents a production contribution to the runaway-electron balance, not a loss rate.

The volume average is defined by

$$
\langle S_{\rm RE} \rangle_V = \frac{1}{V_c} \int_{V_c} S_{\rm RE}(\mathbf{x})\,dV
$$

where $S_{\rm RE}(\mathbf{x})$ is the local volumetric source rate, $V_c$ is the confined-plasma volume, $\mathbf{x}$ is position, and $dV$ is the volume element. The integrand is the total [runaway electron source rate](name:runaway_electron_source_rate), including all active generation mechanisms. Sink and loss terms are excluded. This quantity is distinct from the volume-averaged runaway-electron density, which describes the population rather than its production rate.

NAMES.name: displacement_of_passive_structure
NAMES.short: Displacement of a passive structure is the signed linear displacement of a selected point or defined surface target on a passive component relative to a reference configuration, projected along a defined positive direction.
NAMES.long:
Displacement of a passive structure is the signed scalar component of the motion of a selected material point, attachment point, or defined reference point on a passive structural component relative to a reference configuration. It is the passive-structure instance of mechanical displacement, not an absolute position, velocity, acceleration, or strain.

The signed projected displacement is defined by

$$
u(t) = \left[\mathbf{r}(t) - \mathbf{r}_\mathrm{ref}\right] \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}_u
$$

where $u(t)$ is the scalar displacement, $\mathbf{r}(t)$ is the current position vector of the selected point, $\mathbf{r}_\mathrm{ref}$ is the position vector of the same point in the reference configuration, and $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_u$ is the unit vector defining the positive direction of the displacement component. All vectors and the unit direction are expressed in the same right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ frame, with $\hat{z}$ vertical.

The selected point, reference configuration, and positive direction are part of the semantic definition of any instance. An undeformed, surveyed, calibrated, initial, or previous-time configuration may serve as $\mathbf{r}_\mathrm{ref}$ only if that choice is fixed; changing it changes the displacement, and using a previous-time reference defines an incremental displacement over the interval. A single value describes one projected local displacement; deformation or strain requires spatial variation of displacement or a separate deformation measure.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the selected point is displaced from $\mathbf{r}_\mathrm{ref}$ in the direction of $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_u$.

sources.enhanced_context: Displacement (length) measured by a displacement sensor for structural health monitoring of tokamak components. Provides time-resolved positional or deformation data complementing acceleration, strain, and temperature measurements from co-located sensors.

NAMES.name: neutral_pressure
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Neutral pressure is the scalar kinetic pressure of a neutral-particle population, defined as one third of the trace of its central second velocity moment. It is the general neutral-pressure quantity before any thermal, fast, or internal-state partition is specified.
NAMES.long:
Neutral pressure is the scalar kinetic pressure of a neutral-particle population. It is the isotropic scalar obtained from the central second velocity moment of the neutral velocity distribution, independent of any decomposition into thermal, fast, or internal-state populations.

For a neutral distribution function $f_n(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})$ that is a number density per velocity-space volume, the pressure tensor and associated scalar pressure are defined by:

$$
\mathbf{P}_n = m_n \int (\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{u}_n)(\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{u}_n) f_n(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\,d^3v,\qquad p_n = \frac{1}{3}\operatorname{tr}\mathbf{P}_n
$$

where $m_n$ is the neutral particle mass, $\mathbf{x}$ is position, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity, $n_n=\int f_n\,d^3v$ is the neutral number density, and $\mathbf{u}_n=n_n^{-1}\int \mathbf{v}f_n\,d^3v$ is the mean neutral flow velocity.

This is the parent neutral-pressure concept: it does not specify a split into [thermal neutral pressure](name:thermal_neutral_pressure) and [fast neutral pressure](name:fast_neutral_pressure), nor a selected [neutral internal state pressure](name:neutral_internal_state_pressure). When internal states are not explicitly resolved, their distributions are included in $f_n$ before the central moment is taken. [Total neutral pressure](name:total_neutral_pressure) denotes an explicitly aggregated pressure over named neutral populations. For anisotropic or gyrotropic neutral distributions, neutral pressure denotes the trace scalar $p_n$, not an individual tensor component.

sources.enhanced_context: Neutral gas pressure measured by a barometry gauge within the vacuum vessel or surrounding vacuum system. Characterizes local gas inventory and vacuum conditions relevant to plasma fuelling, recycling, and neutral gas modelling.
sources.leaf_definition: Pressure
sources.parent_definition: Set of gauges

NAMES.name: x_coordinate_of_sensor_attachment_point
NAMES.short: Signed Cartesian x coordinate locating the point where a sensor is mechanically attached to a device component.
NAMES.long:
This quantity gives the x-coordinate of a sensor's mechanical attachment point relative to the origin of the right-handed Cartesian $(x, y, z)$ frame.

The coordinate is defined by

$$
x_{\rm att} = \mathbf{r}_{\rm att} \cdot \hat{x}
$$

where $\mathbf{r}_{\rm att}$ is the position vector of the attachment point relative to the Cartesian origin and $\hat{x}$ is the unit vector along the positive x-axis. Together with the [y coordinate of the sensor attachment point](name:y_coordinate_of_sensor_attachment_point) and [z coordinate of the sensor attachment point](name:z_coordinate_of_sensor_attachment_point), it specifies the attachment location. A displacement sensor may have two mechanical attachment points; other sensor types have one.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the attachment point lies in the positive x direction from the Cartesian origin.

NAMES.name: x_first_measurement_direction_unit_vector_of_strain_gauge
NAMES.short: X-axis component of the unit vector along the first measurement direction of a strain gage, giving the signed direction cosine in the right-handed Cartesian (x, y, z) basis.
NAMES.long:
Signed x-axis direction cosine of the first measurement-direction unit vector of a strain gage is the scalar projection of that unit vector onto the positive $\hat{x}$ basis vector of the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ frame. The first measurement direction is one sensing axis of the strain gage, distinct from its second measurement direction.

The direction cosine is defined by the dot product:

$$
u_{1x} = \hat{\mathbf{u}}_{1} \cdot \hat{x}
$$

where $\hat{\mathbf{u}}_{1}$ is the unit vector along the first measurement direction of the strain gage, $\hat{x}$ is the positive x-axis basis vector of that frame, and $u_{1x}$ is this signed direction cosine.

Together with the direction cosines along the remaining two axes it fixes the orientation of the first measurement direction, satisfying $u_{1x}^2 + u_{1y}^2 + u_{1z}^2 = 1$, with each value bounded between $-1$ and $1$. It is not a strain reading, a gage factor, or a spatial coordinate of the gage.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the first measurement-direction unit vector projects onto the positive $\hat{x}$ direction of the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ frame.

NAMES.name: x_second_measurement_direction_unit_vector_of_strain_gauge
NAMES.short: Signed x-axis direction cosine of the second measurement direction unit vector of a strain gage in the right-handed Cartesian (x-hat, y-hat, z-hat) basis.
NAMES.long:
Signed x-axis direction cosine of the second measurement direction unit vector of a strain gage is the scalar projection of that unit vector onto the positive $\hat{x}$ basis vector of the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ frame. The second measurement direction is one sensing axis of the strain gage, distinct from its first measurement direction.

The direction cosine is defined by the dot product:

$$
u_{2x} = \hat{\mathbf{u}}_2 \cdot \hat{x}
$$

where $\hat{\mathbf{u}}_2$ is the unit vector along the second measurement direction of the strain gage, $\hat{x}$ is the positive x-axis basis vector, and $u_{2x}$ is this signed direction cosine.

Together with the [y-axis direction cosine] and [z-axis direction cosine], it specifies the orientation of the second measurement direction, with $u_{2x}^2 + u_{2y}^2 + u_{2z}^2 = 1$ and each component bounded between $-1$ and $1$. It is distinct from the [first-measurement x-axis direction cosine] and is not a strain value, gage factor, or spatial coordinate of the gage.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the second measurement-direction unit vector has a component along the positive $\hat{x}$ direction of the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ frame.

NAMES.name: y_coordinate_of_sensor_attachment_point
NAMES.short: Y coordinate of the point where a sensor is physically attached to a device component, in the right-handed Cartesian (x, y, z) machine frame.
NAMES.long:
The $y$ coordinate of a sensor attachment point specifies the location along the $y$ axis of the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ machine frame at which a sensor is physically mounted to a structural component, where $\hat{z}$ is the vertical axis and $\phi = 0$ is defined by the facility convention.

Together with [x_coordinate_of_sensor_attachment_point](name:x_coordinate_of_sensor_attachment_point) and [vertical_coordinate_of_sensor_attachment_point](name:z_coordinate_of_sensor_attachment_point), this coordinate fully determines the three-dimensional position of the mechanical attachment point in the machine reference frame. Attachment point coordinates are established from engineering drawings or direct metrology surveys of the as-built device; accurate knowledge of these positions is essential for relating sensor signals to plasma geometry and for alignment corrections in field or current reconstructions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the attachment point lies in the $+\hat{y}$ direction from the machine Cartesian origin.

NAMES.short: Signed y-axis component of the unit vector along a strain gage's second measurement direction in the right-handed Cartesian (x, y, z) frame. It is the direction cosine given by the projection of that oriented local sensing direction onto the y basis direction.

NAMES.name: z_coordinate_of_sensor_attachment_point
NAMES.short: Z coordinate of the point where a sensor is mechanically attached to a device component, expressed in the right-handed Cartesian (x, y, z) frame with z vertical.
NAMES.long:
Z coordinate of the point where a sensor is mechanically attached to a device component is the signed vertical Cartesian coordinate of the fixed mechanical attachment point in the right-handed Cartesian $(x, y, z)$ frame. The $hat{z}$ direction is vertical and is aligned with $hat{Z}$ of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

Let $\mathbf{r}_a$ be the position vector of the attachment point and $\mathbf{r}_0$ the origin of the right-handed Cartesian $(x, y, z)$ frame. The coordinate is the projection on the vertical basis vector of that frame:

$$
z_a = (\mathbf{r}_a - \mathbf{r}_0) \cdot \hat{z}
$$

where $z_a$ is the sensor-attachment-point z coordinate and $\hat{z}$ is the vertical unit vector of the right-handed Cartesian $(x, y, z)$ frame.

Together with [x_coordinate_of_sensor_attachment_point](name:x_coordinate_of_sensor_attachment_point) and [y_coordinate_of_sensor_attachment_point](name:y_coordinate_of_sensor_attachment_point), this quantity locates the same mechanical attachment reference point. It is not the sensor sensitive point, line-of-sight reference point, or orientation vector. The zero level is the plane $z=0$ through the origin of the right-handed Cartesian $(x, y, z)$ frame; for a midplane-centered frame this plane is the machine midplane.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the attachment point lies in the $+\hat{z}$ direction from the plane $z=0$ of the right-handed Cartesian $(x, y, z)$ frame.
