NAMES.name: area_of_langmuir_probe
NAMES.short: Total geometric surface area of a Langmuir probe collector, characterizing the probe's physical extent independent of plasma exposure fraction or magnetic-field projection.
NAMES.long:
The area of a Langmuir probe is the total geometric surface area of the probe collector, representing its full physical size as a fixed hardware property independent of local plasma conditions or magnetic-field geometry. It is the parent area concept from which two operationally distinct sub-areas are derived: the [wetted area](name:wetted_area_of_langmuir_probe), which captures only the portion of the collector surface directly exposed to plasma, and the [effective collection area](name:effective_area_of_langmuir_probe), which is the projection onto the plane perpendicular to the local magnetic field that governs ion collection in a magnetized sheath.

For probes oriented at a grazing angle to the magnetic field — quantified by the [field-aligned incident angle] — the effective collection area can be substantially smaller than the total geometric area. Conflating the two when normalizing the [ion saturation current] to obtain the [ion saturation current density] introduces systematic errors in the inferred plasma density and particle flux at the probe surface.

Probe areas are treated as fixed diagnostic geometry parameters, determined from engineering drawings or direct measurement of the fabricated collector prior to installation.

sources.enhanced_context: Area of the probe surface exposed to the plasma for an embedded Langmuir probe. Used to convert ion saturation current to current density, directly affecting derived quantities such as electron density (ne) and parallel heat flux.
sources.leaf_definition: Area of the probe surface exposed to the plasma
sources.parent_definition: Set of embedded (in a plasma facing component) probes or probe pins

sources.enhanced_context: Area of the collector surface exposed to the plasma for each reciprocating Langmuir probe pin. Used for computing current density and ion saturation current density from raw probe current measurements.
sources.leaf_definition: Area of the surface exposed to the plasma of each collector (constant assuming negligible dependence on e.g. the magnetic field line angle)
sources.parent_definition: Set of reciprocating probes or probe pins

NAMES.name: area_of_neutron_detector
NAMES.short: Geometric area of a particle-detector sensitive surface that can intercept the relevant particles, independent of projection, solid-angle weighting, and detector response.
NAMES.long:
Geometric surface area is the physical extent of the detector surface designated as sensitive to the relevant particles. It applies to planar, curved, or segmented sensitive surfaces, with segmented areas combined into one total.

$$
A = \int_{S_{\mathrm{sens}}} dS
$$

where $A$ is the geometric surface area, $S_{\mathrm{sens}}$ is the sensitive-surface domain, and $dS$ is its differential area element. The area includes only the sensitive surface and excludes passive housing, shielding, supports, and electronics. It is not projected area, solid-angle-weighted area, or response-weighted effective area. The representative [neutron-detector surface area](name:surface_area_of_neutron_detector) is an instance of this quantity.

NAMES.name: beryllium_density
NAMES.subject: beryllium
NAMES.short: Local number density of beryllium impurity ions per unit plasma volume, summed over all ionization states from singly ionized to fully stripped (Be1+ through Be4+), excluding neutral beryllium atoms.
NAMES.long:
Beryllium (atomic number $Z = 4$) enters the plasma primarily through sputtering or evaporation from beryllium first-wall surfaces. The local beryllium ion number density $n_\mathrm{Be}$ aggregates contributions from all four charged ionization stages:

$$
n_\mathrm{Be} = \sum_{z=1}^{4} n_{\mathrm{Be}^{z+}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{Be}^{z+}}$ is the number density of beryllium ions in charge state $z+$, with $z$ running from 1 (singly ionized) to 4 (fully stripped). Neutral beryllium atoms are excluded from this sum.

Beryllium impurity content is inferred from passive spectroscopy of beryllium emission lines or from active charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, with spatially resolved profiles reconstructed by tomographic inversion of chord-integrated measurements. Spatially averaged representations include [line_averaged_beryllium_density](name:line_averaged_beryllium_density) along a diagnostic chord and [volume_averaged_beryllium_density](name:volume_averaged_beryllium_density) integrated over the confined plasma volume. The relative impurity abundance with respect to the electron population is characterized by the ratio_of_beryllium_density_to_electron_density.
NAMES.sign: Positive when beryllium ions are present in the plasma volume.

NAMES.name: current_of_mass_spectrometer_channel
NAMES.short: Electric current generated by transport or collection of positive ions across a defined surface or through a circuit element.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the conventional electric current associated with positive-ion charge transport or collection. It represents the net rate at which ion charge crosses a defined surface or enters a circuit element.

$$
I = \frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

where $I$ is electric current, $Q$ is the net positive-ion charge transported, and $t$ is time. The aggregation over ion species, charge states, or mass-selected populations is determined by the physical boundary or collection process; detector gain and voltage are not part of the current itself.

The mass-discriminated detector measurement [ion current of a mass spectrometer channel](name:ion_current_of_mass_spectrometer_channel) is a specialized instance of this quantity, while [ion current](name:ion_current) expresses the broader ion-charge transport concept.
NAMES.sign: Positive when positive ion charge crosses the chosen surface in the defined positive direction.

NAMES.name: diameter_of_diagnostic_aperture
NAMES.short: Full transverse diameter of a circular diagnostic aperture, measured across its center between opposite points on the circumferential boundary.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the full transverse extent of the clear circular opening at the diagnostic entrance pupil, measured between opposite points on its circumferential boundary.

The diameter is defined by

$$
D = 2r
$$

where $D$ is the aperture diameter and $r$ is the geometric radius given by the [radius of the diagnostic aperture](name:radius_of_diagnostic_aperture).

The quantity describes the opening geometry only; it excludes aperture thickness, housing dimensions, and the width of a noncircular aperture. The diameter determines the geometric area and contributes to the solid-angle acceptance together with the aperture-to-source distance.

sources.enhanced_context: Diameter of the base of the optical cone at the entrance pupil of a CXRS channel. A geometric parameter characterizing the light collection optics of the charge exchange recombination spectroscopy diagnostic.
sources.leaf_definition: Diameter of the base of the optical cone at the entrance pupil
sources.parent_definition: Set of channels (lines-of-sight). The line-of-sight is defined by the centre of the collimating aperture and the position of the measurements.

NAMES.name: difference_of_fast_neutral_beam_motional_stark_wavelength_and_fast_neutral_beam_reference_wavelength_of_spectral_line
NAMES.short: Signed wavelength displacement of a selected fast-neutral-beam spectral-line component from its reference wavelength, caused by the motional Stark electric field.
NAMES.long:
The motional-Stark wavelength displacement is the signed separation between a selected spectral-line component from fast neutral beam particles and its unshifted reference wavelength. It represents the Lorentz shift produced by the electric field arising from particle motion across the magnetic field.

$$
\Delta\lambda_{\mathrm{MS}} = \lambda_{\mathrm{component}} - \lambda_{\mathrm{reference}}
$$

where $\Delta\lambda_{\mathrm{MS}}$ is the motional-Stark wavelength displacement, $\lambda_{\mathrm{component}}$ is the wavelength of the selected component, and $\lambda_{\mathrm{reference}}$ is the corresponding unshifted wavelength. The motional electric field is $\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{motional}} = \mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B}$, where $\mathbf{v}$ is the fast-neutral velocity and $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field.

This quantity is distinct from the Doppler wavelength difference caused by line-of-sight motion, represented by [difference of neutral-beam Doppler wavelength and neutral-beam reference wavelength](name:difference_of_neutral_beam_doppler_wavelength_and_neutral_beam_reference_wavelength). Positive displacement denotes a component at a longer wavelength than the reference.

sources.enhanced_context: Lorentz shift of the BES spectral line due to the motional Stark electric field (v×B) acting on fast diagnostic neutral beam particles. Used as a wavelength correction in beam emission spectroscopy and CXRS spectral analysis.
sources.leaf_definition: Lorentz shift due to the Lorentz electric field (vxB) in the frame of the diagnostic neutral beam particles moving with a velocity v across the magnetic field B
sources.parent_definition: Derived Beam Emission Spectroscopy (BES) parameters

NAMES.name: effective_area_of_langmuir_probe
NAMES.short: Effective collection area of a Langmuir probe, obtained by projecting its plasma-facing collector surface onto the plane normal to the local magnetic field.
NAMES.long:
The effective area of a Langmuir probe is the plasma-facing collector surface area projected onto the plane perpendicular to the local magnetic-field direction. It represents the area governing particle collection when the sheath is magnetized.

$$
A_{\mathrm{eff}} = \int_{S_{\mathrm{w}}} \left|\hat{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{b}}\right|\,dA
$$

where $A_{\mathrm{eff}}$ is the effective collection area, $S_{\mathrm{w}}$ is the plasma-exposed collector surface, $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ is the local outward unit normal, $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$ is the local magnetic-field unit vector, and $dA$ is an element of collector surface area. The absolute dot product gives the geometrical projection factor.

Unlike the total [area of a Langmuir probe](name:area_of_langmuir_probe), this quantity accounts for magnetic-field orientation; unlike the [wetted area of a Langmuir probe](name:wetted_area_of_langmuir_probe), it is not the unprojected plasma-exposed surface area.

sources.enhanced_context: Effective collection area of an embedded Langmuir probe, which varies with time as the magnetic field line incidence angle changes. Determines the effective ion collection area for accurate ion saturation current and heat flux measurements.
sources.leaf_definition: Effective collection area of the probe surface, varying with time due to e.g. changes in the magnetic field line incidence angle
sources.parent_definition: Set of embedded (in a plasma facing component) probes or probe pins

NAMES.name: efficiency_of_neutron_detector
NAMES.short: Probability that a neutron incident on the detector’s sensitive surface within the selected energy band produces an accepted registered count event.
NAMES.long:
Detection efficiency is the conditional probability that an incident neutron within the selected energy band produces an accepted registered count event. It characterizes the detector response, not the incident neutron flux or the geometric area of the sensitive surface.

For an energy band $\mathcal{B}$, the efficiency is defined by

$$
\eta_{\mathcal{B}} = \frac{N_{\mathrm{registered},\mathcal{B}}}{N_{\mathrm{incident},\mathcal{B}}}
$$

where $N_{\mathrm{registered},\mathcal{B}}$ is the number of accepted neutron-induced count events and $N_{\mathrm{incident},\mathcal{B}}$ is the number of neutrons incident on the sensitive surface within $\mathcal{B}$. The incident population is related to the [neutron flux of the neutron detector](name:neutron_flux_of_neutron_detector), while the registered events contribute to the [neutron rate of the neutron detector](name:neutron_rate_of_neutron_detector). The efficiency excludes counts unrelated to incident neutrons and does not itself represent detector area.

sources.enhanced_context: Detection efficiency of a neutron detector energy band as a function of incident neutron energy. Gives the probability that a neutron impacting the detector within the specified energy interval is recorded as a count.
sources.leaf_definition: Probability of detection of a photon impacting the detector as a function of its energy
sources.parent_definition: Set of energy bands in which neutrons are counted by the detector

NAMES.name: energy_at_launching_position
NAMES.short: Energy at launching position is the total energy carried by a launched beam or pulse at its launch reference position, before downstream interaction, absorption, or transport loss changes that energy.
NAMES.long:
Energy at launching position is the total energy carried by a launched beam, pulse, or directed emission at the specified launching locus along its trajectory. It is defined at the launch reference position, not after propagation through or interaction with a target medium.

When represented through the instantaneous power carried through the launch reference position, the launch energy is

$$
E_\mathrm{launch} = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} P_\mathrm{launch}(t)\,dt
$$

where $E_\mathrm{launch}$ is the energy at launching position, $P_\mathrm{launch}(t)$ is the instantaneous power carried by the launched beam or pulse through that position, and $t_1$ and $t_2$ bound the launch interval.

This parent quantity is independent of the physical carrier or beam species. The [wave-beam energy at launching position](name:wave_beam_energy_at_launching_position) is the specialization for coherent electromagnetic wave beams; this parent also excludes energy stored in the source, energy absorbed in the target, and energy evaluated at downstream positions.

NAMES.name: energy_of_neutron_detector
NAMES.short: Energy threshold defining a boundary of a neutron detector spectral energy band, such that only neutrons with kinetic energy within the bounded interval register as counts.
NAMES.long:
Neutron detectors used in fusion diagnostics operate over discrete spectral energy bands, each delimited by lower and upper kinetic-energy thresholds. These thresholds define the interval of neutron kinetic energies to which a given detector channel responds, determining which reaction products are distinguished and how the detector partitions the measured neutron emission spectrum.

The registered count rate $\dot{N}$ for a band with lower threshold $E_{\min}$ and upper threshold $E_{\max}$ is:

$$
\dot{N} = \int_{E_{\min}}^{E_{\max}} \epsilon(E) \, \Phi(E) \, A \, dE
$$

where $\epsilon(E)$ is the energy-dependent detection efficiency, $\Phi(E)$ is the incident neutron energy spectrum per unit area per unit energy, and $A$ is the active detector area.

In deuterium–deuterium burning plasmas the primary neutron peak falls near 2.45 MeV, while deuterium–tritium fusion produces neutrons near 14.1 MeV; detector energy bands are selected to bracket these peaks or to isolate background contributions. The [lower_bound_energy_of_neutron_detector](name:lower_bound_energy_of_neutron_detector) specifies the minimum kinetic energy of a given band, while [neutron_maximum_energy_of_neutron_detector](name:neutron_maximum_energy_of_neutron_detector) specifies its upper limit. Detection efficiency over the band is captured by [efficiency_of_neutron_detector](name:efficiency_of_neutron_detector), and the resulting event rate by [neutron_rate_of_neutron_detector](name:neutron_rate_of_neutron_detector).

NAMES.name: fast_ion_radiance_of_spectral_line_due_to_charge_exchange
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Fast-ion charge-exchange spectral-line radiance is photon radiance in a selected transition emitted by charge-exchange products of fast ions, integrated along a viewing path. It is counted per projected area perpendicular to the viewing direction, per solid angle, and per time.
NAMES.long:
Fast-ion charge-exchange spectral-line radiance is the photon radiance of a specified atomic transition emitted by the excited product formed when a fast ion undergoes charge exchange with a neutral atom. It is integrated along the viewing path and over the selected spectral line, and is defined per projected area perpendicular to the viewing direction, per solid angle, and per time. Physical values are non-negative.

The defining relation is the line integral of the local photon emissivity for that transition along the viewing path:

$$
\mathcal{R}_{\ell} = \int_{\Gamma} \varepsilon_{\ell}^{\mathrm{FICX}}\bigl(\mathbf{r}(l), \hat{\mathbf{n}}\bigr)\, dl
$$

where $\mathcal{R}_{\ell}$ is the radiance of transition $\ell$ with photon-radiance units, $\Gamma$ is the viewing path, $l$ is path length along $\Gamma$ with length units, $\mathbf{r}(l)$ is position on that path, $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ is the dimensionless unit viewing direction, and $\varepsilon_{\ell}^{\mathrm{FICX}}$ is the local photon emissivity of transition $\ell$ from radiating charge-exchange products with photon-emissivity units. The emissivity includes the relevant relative-velocity-dependent charge-exchange or excitation rates and the radiative branching for the selected transition.

The selected-line qualifier means the photon radiance is integrated over the transition's spectral line and is not a wavelength-differential radiance. This quantity is the spectral-line counterpart of [fast-ion radiance due to charge exchange](name:fast_ion_radiance_of_spectral_line_due_to_charge_exchange) and is equivalent in meaning to [line-integrated fast-ion emissivity of a spectral line due to charge exchange](name:fast_ion_radiance_of_spectral_line_due_to_charge_exchange) when expressed as a path-integrated emissivity. It is distinct from [Motional Stark radiance at a spectral line](name:motional_stark_radiance_at_spectral_line), which describes radiation from beam-neutral Motional Stark emission rather than fast-ion charge-exchange products.

sources.enhanced_context: Calibrated radiance of the fast ion charge exchange (FICX) spectrum, integrated over the sightline crossing the neutral beam. The spectral shape is assumed pre-defined, e.g., by the Fokker-Planck slowing-down function.
sources.leaf_definition: Calibrated radiance of the fast ion charge exchange spectrum assuming the shape is pre-defined (e.g. by the Fokker-Planck slowing-down function). Note: radiance is integrated over the sightline crossing the neutral beam

NAMES.name: first_local_tangential_coordinate_of_neutron_detector
NAMES.short: Signed coordinate of a neutron-detector outline vertex along the first local tangential axis of the right-handed local basis (e1, e2, e3), paired with the second coordinate to define the detector cross section.
NAMES.long:
Signed coordinate of a neutron-detector outline vertex along the first local tangential axis is the scalar displacement of that vertex from the detector cross-section local origin projected onto $\hat{e}_1$. The right-handed local detector basis $(\hat{e}_1,\hat{e}_2,\hat{e}_3)$ has $\hat{e}_3$ as the plasma-facing normal to the detector cross section, $\hat{e}_1$ as the tangential axis whose positive sense is toward increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, and $\hat{e}_2 = \hat{e}_3 \times \hat{e}_1$.

The coordinate is defined by the local tangent-plane projection:

$$
\ell_1 = (\mathbf{r}_v - \mathbf{r}_0) \cdot \hat{e}_1
$$

where $\ell_1$ is this first local tangential coordinate, $\mathbf{r}_v$ is the position vector of the outline vertex, $\mathbf{r}_0$ is the position vector of the detector cross-section local origin, and $\hat{e}_1$ is the first local tangential unit vector.

Together with the [second local tangential coordinate of the neutron detector](name:second_local_tangential_coordinate_of_neutron_detector), this coordinate specifies the in-plane position of an outline vertex of the detector cross section. It is not a cylindrical $R$, $\phi$, or $Z$ position in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame and does not denote displacement normal to the detector cross section.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the outline vertex is displaced from the local origin in the $+\hat{e}_1$ direction.

sources.enhanced_context: Positions of the neutron detector or aperture outline vertices along the X1 axis of the local (X1, X2) coordinate system. Used to specify the cross-sectional geometry of the detector for neutron diagnostic systems.
sources.leaf_definition: Positions along x1 axis
sources.parent_definition: Irregular outline of the detector/aperture in the (X1, X2) coordinate system. Do NOT repeat the first point.

NAMES.name: flux_of_neutron_detector
NAMES.short: Rate at which fusion neutrons cross a specified surface per unit area, providing the local intensity of neutron transport through that surface.
NAMES.long:
Neutron number flux is the rate at which fusion neutrons cross a specified surface, normalized by the surface area. It describes neutron transport through the surface rather than neutron production within a volume.

$$
\Phi_n = \frac{dN_n}{dA\,dt}
$$

where $\Phi_n$ is the neutron number flux, $dN_n$ is the number of neutrons crossing the surface element $dA$ during time interval $dt$, and $dA$ is the relevant surface-area element. The detector-specific quantity [neutron flux incident on a detector surface](name:neutron_flux_of_neutron_detector) is an instance evaluated on an active detector surface. This quantity is distinct from the [local volumetric neutron production rate](name:emissivity_due_to_fusion), which describes neutron creation per unit volume and time.

NAMES.name: fraction_of_neutron_detector_converter
NAMES.short: Fraction of neutron detector converter is the part-to-whole composition ratio of a specified constituent within the total neutron-detector converter material. The constituent and total are evaluated on the same composition basis, such as atom count, mass, volume, or amount of substance.
NAMES.long:
Fraction of neutron detector converter is the part-to-whole composition ratio for a specified constituent of the material that converts incident neutrons into detectable secondary particles or radiation in a neutron detector. It compares that constituent with the full converter material over the same converter composition domain and on one non-negative extensive composition basis, such as atom count, mass, volume, or amount of substance.

For constituent $c$, the converter composition fraction is defined by

$$
f_c = \frac{Q_c}{Q_{\mathrm{tot}}}
$$

where $Q_c$ is the amount of constituent $c$ in the converter material on the selected composition basis, and $Q_{\mathrm{tot}} = \sum_j Q_j$ is the corresponding total over all constituents $j$ included in the same converter material. Both $Q_c$ and $Q_{\mathrm{tot}}$ must have the same physical dimension: particle count for an atomic fraction, mass for a mass fraction, volume for a volume fraction, or amount of substance for a mole fraction.

This generic fraction does not by itself impose atom-count weighting; [atomic fraction of neutron detector converter](name:atomic_fraction_of_neutron_detector_converter) is the specialized case in which the basis is atom count. For mutually exclusive constituents that exhaust the defined converter composition domain, the fractions sum to unity and each fraction lies between zero and one; the quantity excludes surrounding detector structures and detector response quantities such as conversion efficiency.

NAMES.name: atomic_fraction_of_neutron_detector_converter
NAMES.short: Atomic fraction characterizing the composition of a neutron detector converter, the material that transforms incident neutrons into detectable secondary charged particles.
NAMES.long:
A neutron detector converter is a material placed within or adjacent to the active detection medium to transform incident neutrons — electrically neutral particles that interact weakly with most matter — into secondary charged particles (alpha particles, protons, or tritons) that produce measurable ionization or scintillation signals. The compositional fractions of the converter govern the macroscopic neutron absorption cross-section and hence the detection sensitivity for a given neutron energy range.

The most diagnostically specific instance of this quantity is the target atomic fraction, which gives the share of converter atoms that are the reactive nuclei for the neutron-capture or neutron-scattering channel of interest. For boron-based converters this corresponds to the B-10 enrichment fraction; for helium-3 proportional detectors it is the He-3 purity. Converter fractions are dimensionless and bounded between 0 and 1, with values close to unity for highly enriched materials used in high-sensitivity fusion diagnostics.

Converter composition fractions are manufacturing parameters determined from isotopic enrichment specifications and chemical analysis of the converter material. They enter the detector response model alongside the [efficiency_of_neutron_detector](name:efficiency_of_neutron_detector) to relate measured count rates to absolute neutron fluxes during fusion plasma diagnostics.

NAMES.name: height_of_neutron_detector
NAMES.short: Full physical extent of a rectangular neutron-detector aperture along its second local tangential direction, the X2 axis of the detector-local Cartesian frame.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the full end-to-end extent of a rectangular neutron-detector aperture along its second local tangential direction. This direction is the $X_2$ axis of the detector-local Cartesian basis $(\hat{X}_1, \hat{X}_2)$.

The extent is defined by the separation of the two boundary coordinates along $X_2$:

$$
H_2 = X_{2,\max} - X_{2,\min}
$$

where $X_{2,\max}$ and $X_{2,\min}$ are the maximum and minimum aperture-boundary coordinates along $X_2$, and $H_2$ is the resulting length.

This quantity describes the second local tangential dimension and is distinct from the [width of the neutron detector](name:width_of_neutron_detector), which measures the corresponding first local tangential dimension. For a circular aperture, the radial size is instead characterized by the [radius of the neutron detector](name:radius_of_neutron_detector).

NAMES.name: helium_3_density
NAMES.subject: helium_3
NAMES.short: Local number density of charged helium-3 ions, obtained by summing their populations over all included ionization states at a plasma location.
NAMES.long:
Helium-3 ion number density is the local count of charged helium-3 ions per unit plasma volume at a specified plasma location. It is summed over the singly ionized and fully stripped charge states and excludes neutral helium-3 atoms.

$$
n_{{}^{3}\mathrm{He}}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{Z=1}^{2} n_{{}^{3}\mathrm{He},Z}(\mathbf{x})
$$

where $\mathbf{x}$ is the plasma location, $Z$ is the ionic charge state, and $n_{{}^{3}\mathrm{He},Z}$ is the number density of helium-3 ions in charge state $Z$, expressed in m$^{-3}$. The [volume-averaged helium-3 density](name:volume_averaged_helium_3_density) and [line-averaged helium-3 density](name:line_averaged_helium_3_density) are spatial averages of this local quantity over their respective domains.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the counted charged helium-3 ion population contributes positively to the number-density measure.

NAMES.name: helium_4_density
NAMES.subject: helium_4
NAMES.short: Local number density of helium-4 ions per unit plasma volume, the principal measure of fusion ash concentration in deuterium-tritium burning plasmas.
NAMES.long:
The helium-4 ion number density $n_{{}^4\text{He}}$ quantifies the local concentration of ${}^4\text{He}$ nuclei at a given point in the plasma. At fusion-relevant temperatures (several keV), helium-4 is fully stripped to He$^{2+}$, and in deuterium-tritium burning plasmas it accumulates as the primary fusion ash product of the reaction ${}^2\text{H} + {}^3\text{H} \rightarrow {}^4\text{He} + n$; its buildup dilutes the fuel and reduces the fusion reaction rate if not exhausted by the divertor system.

The time evolution of $n_{{}^4\text{He}}$ is governed by the particle continuity equation

$$
\frac{\partial n_{{}^4\text{He}}}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{{}^4\text{He}} = S_{{}^4\text{He}}
$$

where $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{{}^4\text{He}}$ is the helium-4 particle flux and $S_{{}^4\text{He}}$ is the volumetric source rate from fusion reactions and ionization of recycled helium neutrals at the plasma edge.

The helium-4 density is measured primarily via charge exchange recombination spectroscopy, where injected neutral beam atoms undergo charge exchange with He$^{2+}$ ions to produce line emission from excited helium atoms; passive spectroscopy of edge recycling emission provides a complementary approach. Chord-averaged and volume-averaged forms are provided by [line_averaged_helium_4_density](name:line_averaged_helium_4_density) and [volume_averaged_helium_4_density](name:volume_averaged_helium_4_density) respectively, while [helium_4_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:flux_surface_averaged_helium_4_density_at_plasma_boundary) gives the boundary value.

In D-T burning plasmas, central He-4 densities are in the range $10^{18}$-$10^{19}$ m$^{-3}$, with the helium-to-electron density ratio — captured by [fraction](name:ratio_of_volume_averaged_helium_4_density_to_volume_averaged_electron_density) — kept below approximately 5-10% in steady state to avoid excessive fuel dilution.

NAMES.name: ion_current
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Electric current carried by positive ions, representing the net charge transport attributable to ion species flow across a defined surface or through a circuit element.
NAMES.long:
Ion current is the net charge transport rate due to positive ions. For a multi-species plasma the ion current through a surface $S$ is

$$
I_i = \sum_s Z_s e \int_S n_s \mathbf{v}_s \cdot d\mathbf{A}
$$

where $Z_s$ is the charge number of species $s$, $e$ is the elementary charge, $n_s$ is the number density, and $\mathbf{v}_s$ is the mean drift velocity of species $s$. In probe diagnostics, progressively increasing the negative bias on a collector reduces the electron current until only the ion contribution remains; this limiting value is the [saturated_ion_current](name:saturated_ion_current), reached when electron collection is fully suppressed.
NAMES.sign: Positive when positive ions flow from the plasma toward the collecting surface, constituting conventional current in the direction of ion transport.

NAMES.name: ion_current_of_mass_spectrometer_channel
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Ion current of a mass spectrometer channel is the signed electrical current attributable to ions within the acceptance of one mass-discriminated channel, with magnitude set by the charge and arrival rate of those ions.
NAMES.long:
Ion current of a mass spectrometer channel is the electrical current carried by ions whose mass-to-charge ratio lies within that channel's acceptance. The channel acceptance defines which ions contribute; unresolved ion species or charge states admitted by the same channel contribute together according to their charge arrival rates.

The defining charge-rate relation is:

$$
I_{\mathrm{ion},\mathrm{ch}} = \sum_{s \in \mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{ch}}} q_s \, \dot{N}_s
$$

where $I_{\mathrm{ion},\mathrm{ch}}$ is the ion current of the channel, $\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{ch}}$ is the set of ion species or charge states admitted by the channel, $q_s$ is the electric charge of ion type $s$, and $\dot{N}_s$ is its collection rate at the channel detector.

This quantity excludes neutral pressure or partial-pressure quantities derived from spectrometer sensitivity factors and excludes detector offset, dark current, leakage current, and displacement current. For positive-ion collection, [current_of_mass_spectrometer_channel](name:current_of_mass_spectrometer_channel) denotes the corresponding channel current without separating the ion carrier explicitly; it is not a total of ion and non-ion residual currents.
NAMES.sign: Positive when positive ion charge admitted by the channel is collected at the channel detector.

NAMES.name: krypton_density
NAMES.subject: krypton
NAMES.short: Number density of krypton ions at a point in the plasma, summed over all ionized charge states from Kr1+ through fully stripped Kr36+ and excluding neutral krypton atoms.
NAMES.long:
Number density of krypton ions at a point in the plasma, summed over all ionized charge states from Kr$^{1+}$ through fully stripped Kr$^{36+}$; neutral krypton atoms are excluded.

With krypton atomic number $Z_\mathrm{Kr}=36$, the ion density is the charge-state sum:

$$
n_\mathrm{Kr} = \sum_{q=1}^{36} n_\mathrm{Kr}^{(q)}
$$

where $n_\mathrm{Kr}^{(q)}$ is the number density of krypton ions in charge state $q$ and the neutral state $q=0$ is omitted from the sum.

This is an extensive, charge-state-summed species density, not a density-weighted mean over charge states and not the charge-state-resolved [ion charge-state density](name:ion_charge_state_density), which retains the individual $n_\mathrm{Kr}^{(q)}$ terms. It is an absolute density, distinct from the relative [krypton fraction](name:ratio_of_volume_averaged_krypton_density_to_volume_averaged_electron_density) normalized to the electron density. The locus-specific values [krypton_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:krypton_density_at_magnetic_axis), krypton_density_at_pedestal, and [krypton_density_at_divertor_target](name:krypton_density_at_divertor_target) share this ions-only charge-state scope. In contrast, [volume_averaged_krypton_density](name:volume_averaged_krypton_density) includes all krypton charge states from neutral through fully stripped, so its charge-state scope differs from this ions-only local quantity; the [line_averaged_krypton_density](name:line_averaged_krypton_density) likewise carries its own averaging definition.

NAMES.name: line_averaged_beryllium_density
NAMES.subject: beryllium
NAMES.short: Chord-average of the beryllium ion number density along a diagnostic line of sight, equal to the path integral of the local beryllium density divided by the chord length.
NAMES.long:
The line-averaged beryllium ion number density quantifies the mean beryllium ion content along a plasma diagnostic chord, normalized by chord length. It is the chord-integrated analog of the local [beryllium_density](name:beryllium_density) and is the most directly accessible measure of beryllium impurity concentration from line-of-sight diagnostics.

The quantity is defined as:

$$
\bar{n}_{Be} = \frac{1}{L} \int_0^L n_{Be}(l) \, dl
$$

where $n_{Be}(l)$ is the local beryllium ion number density at path coordinate $l$ along the chord and $L$ is the total chord length.

Inferred from passive spectroscopy of beryllium emission lines by inverting chord-integrated emission intensities using atomic emissivity coefficients; the result aggregates contributions from all beryllium ionization states present along the chord. The [volume_averaged_beryllium_density](name:volume_averaged_beryllium_density) provides a complementary global volume average, while [beryllium_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:beryllium_density_at_magnetic_axis) gives the local on-axis value.
NAMES.sign: Positive when beryllium ions populate the measurement chord.

NAMES.name: line_averaged_helium_3_density
NAMES.subject: helium_3
NAMES.short: Line-averaged helium-3 density is the chord-length average of local ionized helium-3 density along a specified viewing path, excluding neutral atoms.
NAMES.long:
Line-averaged helium-3 density is the chord-length average of the local helium-3 ion number density along a specified path. It includes singly ionized $^3\mathrm{He}^{+}$ and fully stripped $^3\mathrm{He}^{2+}$ ions, while excluding neutral helium-3 atoms.

The line average is defined by

$$
\overline{n}_{^3\mathrm{He}} = \frac{1}{L}\int_{0}^{L} n_{^3\mathrm{He}}(s)\,\mathrm{d}s
$$

where $\overline{n}_{^3\mathrm{He}}$ is the line-averaged density, $n_{^3\mathrm{He}}(s)$ is the local charge-state-summed density at path coordinate $s$, and $L$ is the chord length. Unlike the volume average in [volume-averaged helium-3 density](name:volume_averaged_helium_3_density), this quantity weights each position uniformly by distance along the path. It is a path-integrated representation of [helium-3 density](name:helium_3_density), not a separate charge-state population.

NAMES.name: line_averaged_helium_4_density
NAMES.subject: helium_4
NAMES.short: Chord-averaged helium-4 ion number density along a specified line of sight through the plasma, representing the path mean of local fusion-ash concentration.
NAMES.long:
The line-averaged helium-4 ion number density is the path average of the local helium-4 ion density along a specified chord through the plasma. It represents an effective density for that chord, not the local value at a point or a volume-wide mean.

The line average is defined by

$$
\overline{n}_{{}^4\mathrm{He}} = \frac{1}{L}\int_{0}^{L} n_{{}^4\mathrm{He}}(l)\,dl
$$

where $n_{{}^4\mathrm{He}}(l)$ is the local helium-4 ion number density from [helium_4_density](name:helium_4_density), $l$ is distance along the chord, and $L$ is the chord length; $l$ and $L$ are measured in m.

The average includes the local helium-4 ion density along the specified path and uses uniform path-length weighting. Unlike [volume_averaged_helium_4_density](name:volume_averaged_helium_4_density), it is not averaged over the confined plasma volume.

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Helium isotope with 4 nucleons

NAMES.name: line_averaged_krypton_density
NAMES.subject: krypton
NAMES.short: Line-averaged krypton density is the chord-length average of the total local krypton number density, summed over all charge states from neutral krypton through fully stripped krypton.
NAMES.long:
Line-averaged krypton density is the chord-length average of the total local krypton number density. It includes every krypton charge state, so it measures elemental krypton abundance along a specified line of sight rather than the density of one particular ionization state.

For a chord parameterized by path length, the line average is defined by:

$$
\langle n_\mathrm{Kr} \rangle_\mathrm{line} = \frac{1}{L}\int_0^L \sum_{q=0}^{36} n_\mathrm{Kr}^{(q)}(\ell)\,d\ell = \frac{1}{L}\int_0^L n_\mathrm{Kr}(\ell)\,d\ell
$$

where $\langle n_\mathrm{Kr} \rangle_\mathrm{line}$ has units of $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, $L$ is the chord length in meters, $\ell$ is distance along the chord in meters, $q$ is the integer charge-state index with $q=0$ for neutral krypton and $q=36$ for fully stripped krypton, $n_\mathrm{Kr}^{(q)}$ is the local density of charge state $q$ in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, and $n_\mathrm{Kr}=\sum_{q=0}^{36} n_\mathrm{Kr}^{(q)}$ is the charge-state-summed local [krypton_density](name:krypton_density).

This quantity is a normalized path mean, not an unnormalized line integral. It differs from [volume_averaged_krypton_density](name:volume_averaged_krypton_density), which averages the same charge-state-summed local density over a plasma volume rather than along a chord.

NAMES.name: lower_bound_energy_of_neutron_detector
NAMES.short: Lower kinetic-energy boundary of a neutron detector spectral band, defining the minimum neutron energy assigned to that band.
NAMES.long:
The lower neutron energy threshold is the low-energy endpoint of one spectral band assigned to a neutron detector. It defines the minimum neutron kinetic energy included in the band described by [energy_of_neutron_detector](name:energy_of_neutron_detector).

$$
E_{\mathrm{lower}} = \inf \mathcal{B}
$$

where $\mathcal{B}$ is the set of neutron kinetic energies assigned to the band and $E_{\mathrm{lower}}$ is its lower boundary. The band’s corresponding upper boundary is given by [neutron_maximum_energy_of_neutron_detector](name:neutron_maximum_energy_of_neutron_detector). This threshold specifies spectral selection; it is not a detection probability or an event rate, which are represented by [efficiency_of_neutron_detector](name:efficiency_of_neutron_detector) and [neutron_rate_of_neutron_detector](name:neutron_rate_of_neutron_detector), respectively.

NAMES.name: neutral_beam_mass
NAMES.subject: neutral_beam
NAMES.short: Mass of one neutral atom in the injected beam species, determined by its isotope and including the bound-electron contribution.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the isotope-dependent inertial mass assigned to one neutral atom in the injected beam species. It describes an individual beam particle, not the total beam mass or mass flow.

The atomic mass is expressed as

$$
m_b = M_b u
$$

where $m_b$ is the mass of one beam atom, $M_b$ is its numerical atomic mass in atomic mass units, and $u$ is the atomic mass unit. The neutral-atom convention includes the nucleus and bound electrons.

The quantity applies before beam-particle ionization and is distinct from [fast-ion atomic number](name:fast_ion_atomic_number), which identifies nuclear proton count rather than particle mass.

NAMES.name: neutron_flux_of_neutron_detector
NAMES.subject: neutron
NAMES.short: Fusion-neutron number flux incident on the neutron detector’s active surface, giving the rate at which neutrons cross each unit of that surface.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the incident fusion-neutron number flux on the neutron-sensitive active surface of the detector. It is the surface-crossing flux, not the neutron production rate or the registered detection-event rate described by [rate of neutron detector](name:rate_of_neutron_detector). The parent quantity [flux of neutron detector](name:flux_of_neutron_detector) expresses the same surface-transport concept.

The defining relation is

$$
\Phi_n = \frac{dN_n}{dA\,dt}
$$

where $\Phi_n$ is the incident neutron number flux, $N_n$ is the number of neutrons crossing the active surface, $A$ is active surface area, and $t$ is time. The surface is the neutron-sensitive area characterized by [area of neutron detector](name:area_of_neutron_detector); passive housing, shielding, supports, and electronics are excluded. Registered event rates additionally depend on detector response and efficiency.

NAMES.name: neutron_maximum_energy_of_neutron_detector
NAMES.subject: neutron
NAMES.short: High-energy endpoint of the neutron kinetic-energy interval assigned to a neutron detector energy band.
NAMES.long:
The maximum neutron energy of a detector band is the upper kinetic-energy boundary used to classify energy-resolved neutron counts. It is an instrumental band limit, not the maximum energy present in the neutron population.

The selected energy interval is bounded by

$$
E_{\min} \leq E_n \leq E_{\max}
$$

where $E_n$ is neutron kinetic energy, $E_{\min}$ is the lower band boundary, and $E_{\max}$ is this quantity. The lower boundary is represented by [lower-bound neutron-detector energy](name:lower_bound_energy_of_neutron_detector); [neutron-detector energy](name:energy_of_neutron_detector) denotes a band boundary without specifying which edge.

sources.enhanced_context: Upper energy bound of a neutron detector energy band. Defines the high-energy edge of the detection interval used for energy-resolved neutron counting in fusion neutron spectroscopy.

NAMES.name: nitrogen_density
NAMES.subject: nitrogen
NAMES.short: Number density of nitrogen nuclei is the local count of nitrogen atomic nuclei per plasma volume, summed over all charge states from neutral through fully stripped nitrogen.
NAMES.long:
Number density of nitrogen nuclei is the local count of nitrogen atomic nuclei per plasma volume. It is a species-level elemental density, so neutral nitrogen and every ionized nitrogen charge state are included.

The charge-state aggregation is defined by

$$
n_N = \sum_{z=0}^{7} n_{N,z}
$$

where $n_N$ is the nitrogen density, $n_{N,z}$ is the number density of nitrogen nuclei in charge state $z$, $z=0$ denotes neutral nitrogen, and $z=7$ denotes fully stripped nitrogen because nitrogen has atomic number $7$.

This quantity is local and is distinct from [line-averaged nitrogen density](name:line_averaged_nitrogen_density) and [volume-averaged nitrogen density](name:volume_averaged_nitrogen_density), which are spatial averages of the same charge-state-summed species density. In the absence of a population qualifier, the density includes thermal, fast, and other nonthermal nitrogen nuclei.

NAMES.name: line_averaged_nitrogen_density
NAMES.subject: nitrogen
NAMES.short: Line-averaged number density of all nitrogen nuclei along a specified plasma chord, summed over every ionization state from neutral through fully stripped nitrogen.
NAMES.long:
Line-averaged nitrogen density is the chord-length average of the local number density of all nitrogen nuclei, including every nitrogen ionization state from neutral nitrogen through fully stripped nitrogen.

The line average is defined by

$$
\overline{n}_N = \frac{1}{L}\int_0^L n_N(\ell)\,d\ell
$$

where $n_N(\ell)$ is the local charge-state-summed nitrogen density defined by [nitrogen density](name:nitrogen_density), $\ell$ is distance along the specified chord, and $L$ is the total chord length.

This quantity is the chord-integrated nitrogen inventory divided by chord length, so it preserves the density dimension while removing variation along the chord. It is distinct from the spatially averaged [volume-averaged nitrogen density](name:volume_averaged_nitrogen_density), which averages over the plasma volume rather than a chord.

NAMES.name: oxygen_density
NAMES.subject: oxygen
NAMES.short: Total number density of oxygen atoms and ions across all charge states, from neutral to fully stripped, giving the local oxygen impurity concentration at a point in the plasma.
NAMES.long:
The local oxygen number density $n_\mathrm{O}$ quantifies the total concentration of oxygen impurity per unit plasma volume, encompassing neutral atomic oxygen and all ionic charge states up to fully stripped O$^{8+}$. Oxygen is a ubiquitous low-Z impurity in fusion devices, entering through wall outgassing and vessel conditioning; it contributes to radiative power losses and dilutes the hydrogenic fuel inventory.

The total oxygen density is defined as the sum over all ionization states:

$$
n_\mathrm{O} = \sum_{Z=0}^{8} n_{\mathrm{O}^{Z+}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{O}^{Z+}}$ is the number density of oxygen in charge state $Z^+$, with $Z$ ranging from 0 (neutral) to 8 (fully stripped).

The local density is inferred from passive extreme-ultraviolet spectroscopy, charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, and soft X-ray emission tomography. Spatially averaged forms include [line_averaged_oxygen_density](name:line_averaged_oxygen_density) (chord integral divided by chord length) and [volume_averaged_oxygen_density](name:volume_averaged_oxygen_density) (integral over the plasma volume). The dimensionless oxygen_fraction relates this local density to the electron density as an impurity concentration measure.

In well-conditioned fusion plasmas the core oxygen density is a small fraction of the electron density; edge concentrations of $10^{15}$–$10^{17}$ m$^{-3}$ are representative of limiter and divertor configurations.
NAMES.sign: Positive when oxygen atoms or ions are present in the plasma volume element.

NAMES.name: line_averaged_oxygen_density
NAMES.subject: oxygen
NAMES.short: Line-of-sight average of the total oxygen impurity number density, encompassing all charge states from neutral to fully stripped, divided by the chord length.
NAMES.long:
The line-averaged oxygen density is the chord-mean of the local oxygen number density—summed over all charge states from neutral O$^0$ through fully stripped O$^{8+}$—along a measurement path through the plasma. It characterizes the mean impurity concentration of oxygen along a given line of sight and is directly related to the local [oxygen_density](name:oxygen_density) integrated along the chord.

The defining relation is:

$$
\langle n_O \rangle_\ell = \frac{1}{L} \int_0^L n_O(\ell) \, d\ell
$$

where $n_O(\ell)$ is the local oxygen number density at position $\ell$ along the chord and $L$ is the chord length in m.

Line-averaged impurity densities are extracted from chord-integrated spectroscopic measurements of oxygen emission lines combined with ionization balance models. Passive spectroscopy of ultraviolet oxygen transitions or charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy of helium-like and hydrogen-like oxygen lines provides the chord-integrated signal from which the line-averaged density is inferred. As a chord-averaged observable, spatial resolution is inherently limited, and tomographic inversion or profile modeling is required to recover local distributions.

Oxygen is a low-concentration impurity in fusion plasmas under normal operating conditions; line-averaged values fall several orders of magnitude below the electron density, with representative ranges of $10^{15}$–$10^{17}$ m$^{-3}$ depending on wall conditioning and impurity seeding. The [volume_averaged_oxygen_density](name:volume_averaged_oxygen_density) provides the plasma-volume–weighted counterpart, while analogous chord-averaged densities for other impurity species include [line_averaged_nitrogen_density](name:line_averaged_nitrogen_density) and [line_averaged_carbon_density](name:line_averaged_carbon_density).
NAMES.sign: Positive when oxygen impurity particles are present along the measurement chord at nonzero concentration.

NAMES.name: pressure_of_mass_spectrometer_channel
NAMES.short: Calibrated pressure-equivalent assigned to a resolved measurement channel, representing a channel-specific gas-pressure contribution without requiring a unique neutral species.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is a calibrated pressure-equivalent associated with one resolved channel response. It represents the gas-pressure contribution assigned to that channel from detected ions, while remaining an instrument-response quantity rather than necessarily the partial pressure of a unique neutral species.

The channel-specific calibration maps the detected ion response to a pressure-equivalent value; the calibration convention defines that mapping and no universal kinetic-pressure equation applies. Accordingly, this quantity must not be interpreted as the charge-state-resolved kinetic pressure [ion_charge_state_pressure](name:ion_charge_state_pressure) unless the calibration explicitly establishes that equivalence.

The representative channel-resolved instance is [neutral_pressure_of_mass_spectrometer_channel](name:neutral_pressure_of_mass_spectrometer_channel). Contributions may be compared with the associated [ion_current_of_mass_spectrometer_channel](name:ion_current_of_mass_spectrometer_channel), but the pressure-equivalent is not itself an ion-current measurement.

NAMES.name: neutral_pressure_of_mass_spectrometer_channel
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Neutral pressure of a mass-spectrometer channel is the calibrated neutral-gas pressure equivalent assigned to a selected mass-to-charge channel. It denotes a channel-resolved neutral contribution and does not require correspondence to a unique neutral species.
NAMES.long:
Neutral pressure of a mass-spectrometer channel is the calibrated neutral-gas pressure equivalent assigned to one mass-discriminated channel of a mass spectrometer. The channel denotes a response in mass-to-charge space after ionization, so the quantity is a pressure equivalent for neutrals that can contribute to that channel, not a pressure of the detected ions.

This quantity is neutral in scope: it excludes charged-particle plasma pressure, electron pressure, and any pressure contribution not represented as neutral gas before ionization. It is the neutral-specific counterpart of [pressure of a mass-spectrometer channel](name:pressure_of_mass_spectrometer_channel).

A channel value need not be the thermodynamic partial pressure of a single species, because fragmentation, isotopologues, charge states of produced ions, and isobaric species can overlap in the same mass-to-charge channel. Summing channel values represents [total neutral pressure](name:total_neutral_pressure) only when the calibrated channels are non-overlapping, span the neutral mixture being represented, and treat cross-sensitivities consistently.

NAMES.name: radius_of_diagnostic_aperture
NAMES.short: Geometric radius of a circular diagnostic aperture, measured from its center to the circumferential boundary and defining the opening size for optical acceptance.
NAMES.long:
The diagnostic-aperture radius is the common distance from the center of a circular opening to any point on its circumferential boundary. It describes the physical opening size, not the aperture's radial position in the machine.

For a circular aperture, the radius is defined by

$$
r_{\mathrm{ap}} = \left\lVert \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{b}} - \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{c}} \right\rVert
$$

where $r_{\mathrm{ap}}$ is the aperture radius, $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{c}}$ is the aperture-center position, $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{b}}$ is any position on the circumferential boundary, and $\lVert\cdot\rVert$ is the Euclidean distance. The corresponding full opening width is twice this radius, as defined by [diameter of diagnostic aperture](name:diameter_of_diagnostic_aperture). The quantity applies only to circular aperture geometry and contributes to optical acceptance, solid angle, and etendue calculations.
NAMES.sign: Positive when measured from the aperture center toward its circumferential boundary.

NAMES.name: radius_of_neutron_detector
NAMES.short: Radius of a circular neutron-detector aperture, measured from the aperture center to its circumferential boundary, characterizing the transverse opening size of the neutron detector.
NAMES.long:
Radius of a circular neutron-detector aperture, measured from the aperture center to its circumferential boundary, is the scalar length parameter of the circular aperture associated with a neutron detector. It applies to a circular sensitive entrance or circular collimating opening of that detector.

For a circular aperture, the associated geometric area is

$$
A = \pi r^2
$$

where $A$ is the circular aperture area in square meters and $r$ is the radius of the neutron-detector aperture in meters.

The physical scalar range is $r \ge 0$; $r=0$ represents a vanishing circular opening, and negative values are outside the geometry. This quantity is the neutron-detector-specific aperture radius, distinct from the generic [radius_of_diagnostic_aperture](name:radius_of_diagnostic_aperture), from the corresponding [diameter_of_diagnostic_aperture](name:diameter_of_diagnostic_aperture), and from the total [area_of_neutron_detector](name:area_of_neutron_detector). For noncircular neutron-detector openings, transverse aperture dimensions are described by [width_of_neutron_detector](name:width_of_neutron_detector) and [height_of_neutron_detector](name:height_of_neutron_detector); [solid_angle_of_neutron_detector](name:solid_angle_of_neutron_detector) is a separate geometric quantity that also depends on source position, aperture orientation, distance, and surrounding collimation.

NAMES.name: rate_of_neutron_detector
NAMES.short: Temporal rate of accepted detection events in a counting process, distinct from incident particle flux, detection efficiency, and total source emission.
NAMES.long:
An event rate is the temporal frequency of accepted discrete events in a defined counting process. For the detector family represented here, the events are registered neutron-induced detection events; [neutron rate of a neutron detector](name:neutron_rate_of_neutron_detector) is a concrete instance.

The rate is defined by

$$
r = \frac{dN}{dt}
$$

where $N$ is the cumulative number of accepted events and $t$ is elapsed time.

This quantity counts accepted registered events, not the incident particle flux, the probability of detection, or the total number of particles emitted by the source. The corresponding incident neutron flux is a surface-crossing rate density, while [efficiency of a neutron detector](name:efficiency_of_neutron_detector) describes the probability that an incident neutron produces a registered event.

NAMES.name: neutron_rate_of_neutron_detector
NAMES.subject: neutron
NAMES.short: Neutron rate of a neutron detector is the rate of accepted neutron-induced detection events registered by the detector, distinct from incident neutron flux, detector efficiency, and total neutron source emission.
NAMES.long:
Neutron rate of a neutron detector is the time rate of individually accepted neutron-induced detection events registered by that detector.

It is defined from the cumulative accepted neutron-event count:

$$
R_n(t) = \frac{dN_\mathrm{det}(t)}{dt}
$$

where $R_n(t)$ is the neutron detection rate and $N_\mathrm{det}(t)$ is the cumulative number of accepted neutron-induced detector events up to time $t$.

This quantity is a detector response count rate. It excludes non-neutron events and is distinct from the incident [neutron flux of a neutron detector](name:neutron_flux_of_neutron_detector), the [efficiency of a neutron detector](name:efficiency_of_neutron_detector), and the total neutron emission rate of the source.

NAMES.name: requested_voltage_of_neutron_detector
NAMES.short: Commanded bias potential difference applied between a neutron-detector module's bias terminal and electrical return, not its raw output signal.
NAMES.long:
The commanded bias voltage is the electrical potential difference specified for energizing a neutron-detector module between its bias terminal and return or reference terminal. It is a setpoint, distinct from the instantaneous detector waveform represented by [voltage of neutron detector].

$$
V_{\mathrm{bias,set}} = \phi_{\mathrm{bias}} - \phi_{\mathrm{ref}}
$$

where $V_{\mathrm{bias,set}}$ is the commanded bias voltage, and $\phi_{\mathrm{bias}}$ and $\phi_{\mathrm{ref}}$ are the electrical potentials of the bias and return/reference terminals, respectively, expressed in volts.

The quantity specifies the intended applied potential and excludes the measured supply output, detector signal amplitude, pulse waveform, and derived neutron count rate. Its setpoint meaning distinguishes it from the detector bias voltage represented by [voltage of mass spectrometer](name:voltage_of_mass_spectrometer) and the spectrometer supply command [requested voltage of spectrometer](name:requested_voltage_of_spectrometer).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the bias terminal is at higher electrical potential than the return or reference terminal.

NAMES.name: saturated_ion_current
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Ion charge flux collected by a Langmuir probe at the ion-saturation limit, expressed as the non-negative magnitude of the area-integrated ion current when electron collection is suppressed.
NAMES.long:
Ion charge flux collected by a Langmuir probe at the ion-saturation limit is the non-negative magnitude of the current due to ions reaching the collecting surface when the probe bias is sufficiently negative that electron collection is suppressed and the ion branch is in its saturation regime. It represents the area-integrated counterpart of the local saturated ion current density.

The saturated ion current is defined by integration of the saturated ion current density over the effective collecting surface:

$$
I_{\mathrm{sat},i} = \int_{A_{\mathrm{eff}}} j_{\mathrm{sat},i}(\mathbf{x})\, dA
$$

where $j_{\mathrm{sat},i}$ is the [saturated ion current density](name:saturated_ion_current_density), $A_{\mathrm{eff}}$ is the [effective area of a Langmuir probe](name:effective_area_of_langmuir_probe), $\mathbf{x}$ labels position on the collecting surface, and $dA$ is a surface-area element.

Any sheath-expansion factor, incidence-angle correction, ion-species assumption, or Bohm-speed estimate is model dependent and belongs to the evaluation of $j_{\mathrm{sat},i}$ or $A_{\mathrm{eff}}$, not to the definition of this quantity. This quantity excludes electron current and does not encode a signed electrode-current convention.

NAMES.name: solid_angle_of_neutron_detector
NAMES.short: Geometric acceptance of a neutron detector aperture as viewed from a neutron emission point, independent of detector efficiency and material response.
NAMES.long:
The solid angle is the geometric measure of the aperture’s apparent extent from a neutron emission point. It is nonnegative and depends only on the aperture geometry, its orientation, and the source-point location; detector efficiency and converter response are excluded.

For a point source, the solid angle is defined by

$$
\Omega = \int_A \frac{\cos\theta}{r^2}\,dA
$$

where $A$ is the aperture surface, $r$ is the distance from the source point to an aperture element, and $\theta$ is the angle between the aperture normal and the line from the source point to that element. For a finite source region, the quantity denotes the specified volume average of this point-source solid angle; it does not imply weighting by the neutron emission profile. The geometric aperture dimensions described by [area of neutron detector](name:area_of_neutron_detector) and [radius of neutron detector](name:radius_of_neutron_detector) can determine the acceptance but do not include detector efficiency, which is a separate quantity described by [efficiency of neutron detector](name:efficiency_of_neutron_detector).

sources.enhanced_context: Average solid angle subtended by a neutron detector within each voxel of the voxelized plasma field-of-view. Used to weight neutron emission contributions from each plasma volume element seen by the detector.
sources.leaf_definition: Average solid angle that the detector covers within the voxel
sources.parent_definition: Field of view associated to this detector. The field of view is described by a voxelized plasma volume. Each voxel, with indexes i_R, i_Z, and i_phi, has an associated solid angle scalar and a detector direction vector.

NAMES.name: surface_area_of_neutron_detector
NAMES.short: Geometric area of the neutron-sensitive detector surface, excluding passive housing, shielding, supports, electronics, projection effects, and solid-angle weighting.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the geometric area of the neutron-sensitive active surface of the detector. It includes the physical sensitive face, including contributions from segmented or curved surfaces, and excludes passive detector structures.

The area is defined by integration over the neutron-sensitive surface:

$$
A = \int_{S_{\rm active}} dS
$$

where $S_{\rm active}$ is the neutron-sensitive surface and $dS$ is an element of geometric surface area. This is the active-surface component represented by [area of neutron detector](name:area_of_neutron_detector); it is not an effective area weighted by detection efficiency, neutron incidence angle, projection, or solid angle.

NAMES.name: target_atomic_fraction_of_neutron_detector_converter
NAMES.short: Target atomic fraction of a neutron detector converter is the fraction of all atoms in the converter material that are atoms of the target species for the primary neutron-induced detection reaction.
NAMES.long:
Target atomic fraction of a neutron detector converter is the fraction of all atoms in the converter material that are atoms of the target species for the primary neutron-induced detection reaction. It identifies the converter composition factor associated with the active target nuclide, not the total amount of converter material.

For a representative amount of converter material, the fraction is defined by the atom-count ratio:

$$
f_t = \frac{N_t}{N_\mathrm{tot}}
$$

where $N_t$ is the count of target-species atoms, $N_\mathrm{tot}$ is the count of all atoms in the same converter material amount, and $N_\mathrm{tot} > 0$. The admissible range is $0 \le f_t \le 1$.

This quantity is the target-species specialization of [atomic fraction of a neutron detector converter](name:atomic_fraction_of_neutron_detector_converter) and is equivalent in scope to [nuclear target atomic fraction of a neutron detector converter](name:nuclear_target_atomic_fraction_of_neutron_detector_converter). In compounds or mixtures, $N_\mathrm{tot}$ includes chemically bound and non-target atoms, so the value is not the isotopic enrichment of the target element alone unless the converter material contains only atoms of that element. If $n_\mathrm{tot}$ denotes the total atomic number density of the converter material, then $f_t n_\mathrm{tot}$ is the target-species number density relevant to [nuclear density of a neutron detector converter] and to the normalized converter nuclear-response quantity [nuclear rate of a neutron detector converter].

NAMES.name: nuclear_target_atomic_fraction_of_neutron_detector_converter
NAMES.short: Dimensionless fraction of all converter atoms that are nuclei of the target species for the primary neutron-induced detection reaction.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the normalized composition factor for target nuclei in the converter material of a neutron detector. It identifies the share of converter atoms belonging to the nuclear species that produces the intended neutron-induced detection reaction.

The target atomic fraction is defined by

$$
f_{\mathrm{target}} = \frac{N_{\mathrm{target}}}{N_{\mathrm{all}}}
$$

where $N_{\mathrm{target}}$ is the number of target-species nuclei and $N_{\mathrm{all}}$ is the total number of atoms in the converter material. It is the nuclear-target realization of [target atomic fraction of a neutron detector converter](name:target_atomic_fraction_of_neutron_detector_converter), rather than a fraction based on converter volume, mass, or detector efficiency. The fraction is bounded between zero and one.

NAMES.name: temperature_of_neutron_detector
NAMES.short: Absolute thermodynamic temperature of a neutron detector assembly or converter material, describing its thermal state independently of neutron-counting response.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the thermodynamic temperature of the neutron detector assembly or neutron-conversion material, characterizing its thermal state rather than the detector's electrical response or neutron-counting behavior.

The temperature is defined thermodynamically by

$$
\frac{1}{T}=\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial U}\right)_{V,N}
$$

where $T$ is thermodynamic temperature, $S$ is entropy, $U$ is internal energy, $V$ is volume, and $N$ is the amount of material or particle number held fixed in the derivative. The quantity applies to the specified detector or converter material and is distinct from the local material temperature at a [sensor attachment point](name:temperature_at_sensor_attachment_point). It is not the neutron-energy threshold represented by [energy of a neutron detector](name:energy_of_neutron_detector).

NAMES.name: toroidal_plasma_momentum_at_measurement_position
NAMES.short: Toroidal plasma momentum at a measurement position is the local mechanical angular-momentum density of the plasma about the toroidal symmetry axis. It equals the major radius in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame multiplied by the total toroidal particle linear-momentum density.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal plasma momentum at a measurement position is the local mechanical angular-momentum density of the plasma about the toroidal symmetry axis at the specified point. It is the major-radius lever arm multiplying the toroidal component of the total particle linear-momentum density in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

For a measurement position $\mathbf{x}_m$, the defining relation is:

$$
\ell_\phi(\mathbf{x}_m) = R_m \sum_s n_s(\mathbf{x}_m)\, m_s\, V_{\phi,s}(\mathbf{x}_m)
$$

where $\mathbf{x}_m$ is the point of evaluation, $\ell_\phi$ is the local toroidal plasma momentum, $R_m = R(\mathbf{x}_m)$ is the major radius of that point, $s$ indexes electrons and all ion species and charge states, $n_s$ is the particle number density, $m_s$ is the particle mass, and $V_{\phi,s}$ is the toroidal component of the species flow velocity.

In this definition, toroidal denotes angular momentum about the symmetry axis, not the toroidal component of linear momentum alone; the linear-momentum density is the species sum before multiplication by $R_m$. The quantity is mechanical particle angular-momentum density and excludes canonical toroidal momentum, electromagnetic-field angular momentum, and spatially integrated toroidal angular momentum.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the total toroidal particle linear-momentum density points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_beam_tracing_point
NAMES.short: Vertical Z coordinate of a beam-tracing point in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame; it is the signed height relative to the machine equatorial plane.
NAMES.long:
Vertical $Z$ coordinate of a beam-tracing point is the signed height of that point relative to the machine equatorial plane in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. A beam-tracing point is a point on an electromagnetic wave-beam or ray trajectory; this quantity identifies only the point position, not the wave vector or deposited energy.

Together with the corresponding major-radius and toroidal-angle coordinates of the same beam-tracing point, this coordinate specifies its spatial location in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. At a trajectory point identified with the launching position, it is the same vertical coordinate as [vertical coordinate of launching position](name:vertical_coordinate_of_launching_position); it shares the same vertical-coordinate convention as [vertical coordinate of aperture](name:vertical_coordinate_of_aperture) and [z coordinate of divertor target](name:z_coordinate_of_divertor_target).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the beam-tracing point lies in the $+\hat{Z}$ direction from the machine equatorial plane in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: voltage_of_mass_spectrometer
NAMES.short: Detector bias voltage of a mass spectrometer is the potential difference applied between the detector electrode or electron-multiplying stage and its bias reference, setting collection efficiency or gain for ion-current measurement. It is a device-level setting; voltage_of_mass_spectrometer_channel denotes a channel-specific detector bias.
NAMES.long:
The detector bias voltage of a mass spectrometer is the electrical potential difference applied by the detector bias circuit to the detector electrode or electron-multiplying detector stage. It sets the electric-field conditions that affect ion collection efficiency and detector gain for converting mass-selected ions into a measured current or pulse signal. This is a device-level detector setting, distinct from the channel-specific [voltage_of_mass_spectrometer_channel](name:voltage_of_mass_spectrometer_channel).

With a specified bias reference node, the detector bias voltage is defined as the detector bias-node potential relative to that reference:

$$
V_\mathrm{det} = \Phi_\mathrm{det} - \Phi_\mathrm{ref}
$$

where $\Phi_\mathrm{det}$ is the electric potential of the detector electrode or detector-stage bias node, and $\Phi_\mathrm{ref}$ is the potential of the reference node chosen by the detector bias circuit, such as the supply return, detector housing, or another designated electrode.

The value is normally set and monitored by the detector high-voltage or bias supply and is interpreted together with detector calibration, gain setting, and measured [ion_current_of_mass_spectrometer_channel](name:ion_current_of_mass_spectrometer_channel). In operation it is chosen to provide adequate sensitivity for the expected ion flux while avoiding detector overloading or operation outside the rated bias range.

Representative setpoints are strongly instrument- and detector-dependent: an unbiased or disabled detector may be near 0 V, while high-voltage electron-multiplying detector stages commonly use hundreds of volts to a few kilovolts. The allowable range should be interpreted from the detector and power-supply ratings rather than from a universal physical limit.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the detector electrode or detector-stage bias node is at a higher electric potential than the bias reference node.

sources.enhanced_context: Bias voltage applied to the detector (e.g., microchannel plate) of the mass spectrometer, controlling detector gain for ion current measurement.
sources.leaf_definition: Voltage applied on the microchannel plate detector

NAMES.name: voltage_of_mass_spectrometer_channel
NAMES.short: Voltage of mass spectrometer channel is the signed detector-bias potential difference between the electron-multiplying detector electrode of one mass-discriminated channel and that channel's electronics reference. It establishes the channel-specific ion-signal gain.
NAMES.long:
Voltage of mass spectrometer channel is the signed detector-bias potential difference between the electron-multiplying detector electrode assigned to one mass-discriminated channel and that channel's electronics reference. It sets the channel-specific detector gain that converts collected ions into an electron signal.

The channel bias voltage is defined by the electrode potential difference:

$$
V_\mathrm{ch} = \Phi_{\mathrm{det},\mathrm{ch}} - \Phi_{\mathrm{ref},\mathrm{ch}}
$$

where $V_\mathrm{ch}$ is the channel voltage, $\Phi_{\mathrm{det},\mathrm{ch}}$ is the electric potential of the biased detector electrode, and $\Phi_{\mathrm{ref},\mathrm{ch}}$ is the electric potential of the electronics reference for the same channel.

This quantity is channel-specific and excludes the instrument-level detector bias [voltage_of_mass_spectrometer](name:voltage_of_mass_spectrometer). It also excludes the resulting signal [ion_current_of_mass_spectrometer_channel](name:ion_current_of_mass_spectrometer_channel), which denotes the channel ion current rather than the applied detector potential difference.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the detector-bias electrode of the channel is at a higher electric potential than the channel's electronics reference.

sources.enhanced_context: Voltage applied to the photomultiplier detector of a mass spectrometer channel. An instrumental operating parameter that sets the detector gain for ion current measurement in residual gas analysis.
sources.leaf_definition: Voltage applied to the photomultiplier
sources.parent_definition: Set of mass channels, each corresponding to a given atomic mass measured continuously by the spectrometer

NAMES.name: voltage_of_temperature_sensor
NAMES.short: Electrical potential difference produced by a temperature sensor associated with a neutron-detector module and referenced to the sensor electronics return.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the electrical potential difference delivered by a temperature sensor thermally associated with a neutron-detector module. It is the sensor signal associated with the module's thermal state, distinct from the detector temperature itself and from a commanded detector bias.

The sensor voltage is defined by

$$
V_s = \phi_s - \phi_{\mathrm{ref}}
$$

where $V_s$ is the sensor output voltage, $\phi_s$ is the electric potential of the sensor signal terminal, and $\phi_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the potential of the designated electronics reference; $V_s$ is expressed in volts.

This quantity represents the sensor's electrical output and is not a calibrated value of [temperature of neutron detector](name:temperature_of_neutron_detector) or the applied bias represented by [requested voltage of neutron detector](name:requested_voltage_of_neutron_detector).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the sensor signal terminal is at higher electric potential than the designated electronics reference.
