NAMES.name: power_at_wall_due_to_conduction
NAMES.short: Thermal power deposited on all plasma-facing wall and divertor surfaces by parallel electron and ion heat conduction along open scrape-off-layer magnetic field lines, excluding convective, radiative, and neutral-particle channels.
NAMES.long:
The power at the wall due to conduction is the thermal energy deposited on all plasma-facing wall and divertor surfaces by electron and ion heat conduction along open scrape-off-layer magnetic field lines. It excludes convective particle enthalpy, absorbed radiation, and neutral-particle energy deposition.

The defining surface integral is:

$$
P_{\mathrm{wall,cond}} = \int_{S_{\mathrm{wall}}} \left(\mathbf{q}_{e,\parallel}^{\mathrm{cond}} + \mathbf{q}_{i,\parallel}^{\mathrm{cond}}\right) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}\,\mathrm{d}A
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{wall,cond}}$ is the deposited conductive power, $S_{\mathrm{wall}}$ is the union of all plasma-facing wall and divertor surfaces, $\mathbf{q}_{e,\parallel}^{\mathrm{cond}}$ and $\mathbf{q}_{i,\parallel}^{\mathrm{cond}}$ are the electron and ion conductive heat-flux vectors along open magnetic field lines, $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ is the unit normal directed from the plasma toward the material, and $\mathrm{d}A$ is a surface-area element.

This quantity is the all-wall member of [power due to conduction](name:power_due_to_conduction). Restricting the selected surfaces to all divertor targets gives [power of divertor due to conduction](name:power_of_divertor_due_to_conduction), while a single target contribution is represented by [power at divertor target due to conduction](name:power_at_divertor_target_due_to_conduction).

sources.enhanced_context: Power conducted by the plasma onto the first wall and divertor surfaces, representing the conductive heat flux channel in the plasma–wall power balance. Distinct from convected, radiated, recombination, and neutral power channels tracked in the same structure.
sources.leaf_definition: Power conducted by the plasma onto the wall
sources.parent_definition: Simple 0D description of plasma-wall interaction

NAMES.name: power_at_wall_due_to_convection
NAMES.short: Power deposited on plasma-facing wall and divertor surfaces by convective plasma particle flux, comprising thermal enthalpy and directed kinetic energy carried by streaming ions and electrons from the scrape-off layer.
NAMES.long:
Convective power at plasma-facing wall and divertor surfaces quantifies the energy transported by bulk plasma-particle flow from the scrape-off layer into the material surfaces. It comprises thermal enthalpy and directed kinetic-energy contributions and is the surface-integrated component of [power due to convection](name:power_due_to_convection).

$$
P_{\mathrm{conv,wall}} = \int_{A_{\mathrm{wall}}} q_{\mathrm{conv}}(\mathbf{x})\,\mathrm{d}A
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{conv,wall}}$ is the total convective power, $q_{\mathrm{conv}}(\mathbf{x})$ is the local convective energy flux density at surface position $\mathbf{x}$, and $A_{\mathrm{wall}}$ is the combined plasma-facing wall and divertor surface area included in the quantity.

Only convective particle-energy transport is included; conductive and radiative deposition are excluded. [Power at a single divertor target due to convection](name:power_at_divertor_target_due_to_convection) isolates one target, while [convective power summed over divertor targets](name:power_of_divertor_due_to_convection) includes only the divertor-target subset. The conductive counterpart is [power at the wall due to conduction](name:power_at_wall_due_to_conduction).

sources.enhanced_context: Power convected by the plasma onto the first wall and divertor surfaces, representing the kinetic energy flux carried by plasma particles striking plasma-facing components. A component of the total wall power load alongside conducted and radiated power.
sources.leaf_definition: Power convected by the plasma onto the wall
sources.parent_definition: Simple 0D description of plasma-wall interaction

NAMES.name: power_at_wall_due_to_ohmic_dissipation
NAMES.short: Irreversible electrical power converted into heat within conducting wall and vessel structures by induced eddy currents and plasma-connected currents closed through the wall.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the ohmic-dissipation power deposited within conducting wall, plasma-facing, and vessel structures. It is the wall-specific component of [power due to ohmic dissipation](name:power_due_to_ohmic_dissipation), resolved by the conducting domain in which resistive currents flow.

The deposited power is defined by

$$
P_{\mathrm{wall,ohm}} = \int_{\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{wall}}} \mathbf{J} \cdot \mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{res}}\,dV
$$

where $\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{wall}}$ is the conducting wall and vessel volume, $\mathbf{J}$ is the electrical current density, $\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{res}}$ is the resistive electric field, and $dV$ is the differential volume element.

The quantity includes Joule heating from induced eddy currents and from plasma-connected currents that close through the wall. It is a volume-integrated deposited power, distinct from the surface energy flux at the wall and from thermal power subsequently removed by coolant circuits; passive resistive media give a nonnegative value.

sources.enhanced_context: Power deposited on the wall due to electric currents flowing in vessel structures, representing resistive Joule heating from induced or halo currents. Positive values indicate power deposition on the wall.
sources.leaf_definition: Power deposited on the wall due to electric currents (positive means power is deposited on the target)
sources.parent_definition: Simple 0D description of plasma-wall interaction

NAMES.name: power_at_wall_due_to_recombination
NAMES.short: Total power deposited on plasma-facing wall surfaces by all recombination processes, encompassing both plasma-ion recombination and surface recombination of incident neutral particles into molecules.
NAMES.long:
The total recombination power at the wall aggregates two distinct heat-load channels: the plasma-ion channel, in which ions arriving at the surface capture free electrons and release their recombination energy into the wall material, and the neutral surface-recombination channel, in which incident hydrogen-isotope atoms combine into diatomic molecules on the material surface and deposit the molecular binding energy as heat.

This quantity is the wall-surface component of the broader [power due to recombination](name:power_due_to_recombination), which encompasses volumetric recombination throughout the plasma volume. The two contributing channels are resolved separately: [plasma_power_at_wall_due_to_recombination](name:plasma_power_at_wall_due_to_recombination) carries the ion-channel contribution and [neutral_power_at_wall_due_to_recombination](name:neutral_power_at_wall_due_to_recombination) carries the neutral surface-recombination contribution, their sum giving:

$$
P_{\mathrm{rec,wall}} = P_{\mathrm{rec,wall}}^{\mathrm{ion}} + P_{\mathrm{rec,wall}}^{\mathrm{neutral}}
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{rec,wall}}^{\mathrm{ion}}$ is the integrated plasma-ion recombination power and $P_{\mathrm{rec,wall}}^{\mathrm{neutral}}$ is the neutral surface-recombination power, both summed over all plasma-facing surfaces.

In edge plasma models, this quantity is evaluated from particle-balance calculations coupled to surface-interaction models, with each channel weighted by the recombination energy per event and the incident particle flux to the wall.

NAMES.name: neutral_power_at_wall_due_to_recombination
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Power deposited on plasma-facing wall surfaces when incident neutral hydrogen-isotope particles recombine at the material surface, primarily through molecular formation and release of binding energy.
NAMES.long:
Neutral surface-recombination power at the wall is the rate at which recombination energy from incident neutral particles is deposited in plasma-facing wall material. It represents the neutral-channel contribution to the wall heat load from recombination.

The deposited power is defined by

$$
P_{\mathrm{rec,wall}}^{\mathrm{neutral}} = \int_{A_{\mathrm{wall}}} \sum_r \Gamma_r Q_r \, \mathrm{d}A
$$

where $A_{\mathrm{wall}}$ is the set of plasma-facing wall surfaces, $r$ indexes neutral surface-recombination channels, $\Gamma_r$ is the corresponding recombination-event rate per unit area, and $Q_r$ is the energy deposited per event. The quantity is the neutral component of [power at wall due to recombination](name:power_at_wall_due_to_recombination), complementary to [plasma power at wall due to recombination](name:plasma_power_at_wall_due_to_recombination); plasma-ion electron-capture recombination is excluded.

sources.enhanced_context: Net power deposited on the wall by neutrals, representing the thermal load from neutral particle bombardment of plasma-facing components. Positive sign convention indicates energy deposition on the wall.
sources.leaf_definition: Net power from neutrals on the wall  (positive means power is deposited on the wall)
sources.parent_definition: Simple 0D description of plasma-wall interaction

sources.enhanced_context: Power deposited on the wall due to recombination of neutral particles, such as molecule formation at the surface. Contributes to the overall plasma-wall interaction power balance at the vessel first wall.
sources.leaf_definition: Power deposited on the wall due to recombination of neutrals into a ground state (e.g. molecules)
sources.parent_definition: Simple 0D description of plasma-wall interaction

NAMES.name: plasma_power_at_wall_due_to_recombination
NAMES.short: Power deposited on plasma-facing wall surfaces when incident plasma ions recombine at the material boundary, representing the ion-channel contribution to total wall recombination power.
NAMES.long:
Plasma-ion recombination power at the wall is the rate at which recombination energy from incident plasma ions is deposited in plasma-facing wall material. It is the ion-channel contribution to the total wall heat load from recombination.

The contribution is defined by

$$
P_{\mathrm{rec,wall}}^{\mathrm{plasma}} = \sum_s \int_A \Gamma_s^{\mathrm{ion}} E_{\mathrm{rec},s}\,\mathrm{d}A
$$

where $s$ indexes the contributing plasma-ion species and charge states, $\Gamma_s^{\mathrm{ion}}$ is the incident particle flux, $E_{\mathrm{rec},s}$ is the recombination energy deposited per event, and $A$ is the total plasma-facing wall area.

This quantity excludes surface recombination of incident neutral particles into molecules, represented by [neutral recombination power at the wall](name:neutral_power_at_wall_due_to_recombination). Together, the two channels form [total recombination power at the wall](name:power_at_wall_due_to_recombination), which is distinct from volumetric [power due to recombination](name:power_due_to_recombination).

sources.enhanced_context: Power deposited on the wall due to recombination of plasma ions, as a time-resolved global quantity. Represents the energy released when ions recombine at the wall surface, contributing to the total plasma-wall energy transfer.
sources.leaf_definition: Power deposited on the wall due to recombination of plasma ions
sources.parent_definition: Simple 0D description of plasma-wall interaction

NAMES.name: ratio_of_volume_averaged_beryllium_density_to_volume_averaged_electron_density
NAMES.short: Dimensionless global beryllium impurity abundance defined by the charge-state-summed volume-averaged beryllium ion density relative to volume-averaged electron density.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the global abundance of ionized beryllium relative to the electron population in the confined plasma volume enclosed by the last closed flux surface. It compares the charge-state-summed beryllium content with the corresponding global electron content.

The abundance is defined by

$$
a_{\mathrm{Be}} = \frac{\langle n_{\mathrm{Be}} \rangle_V}{\langle n_e \rangle_V}
$$

where $\langle n_{\mathrm{Be}} \rangle_V$ is the [volume-averaged beryllium density](name:volume_averaged_beryllium_density), summed over included beryllium ionization states, and $\langle n_e \rangle_V$ is the [volume-averaged electron density](name:volume_averaged_electron_density).

The numerator represents ionized beryllium rather than total plasma particle density or local beryllium density. Consequently, this ratio is not an atomic fraction of all particles; it is normalized specifically to the global electron population.

sources.leaf_definition: Value

NAMES.name: ratio_of_volume_averaged_boron_density_to_volume_averaged_electron_density
NAMES.short: Dimensionless elemental-boron abundance formed by dividing the plasma-volume-averaged boron number density by the plasma-volume-averaged electron number density.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the global elemental-boron abundance relative to the electron population. The boron numerator includes neutral boron atoms and all ionic charge states, while both numerator and denominator refer to the same plasma volume and state.

The ratio is defined by

$$
f_B = \frac{\overline{n}_B}{\overline{n}_e}
$$

where $\overline{n}_B$ is the [volume-averaged boron density](name:volume_averaged_boron_density) and $\overline{n}_e$ is the volume-averaged electron number density. This is a composition ratio, distinct from the local [boron density](name:boron_density), and is dimensionless.

NAMES.name: ratio_of_volume_averaged_carbon_density_to_volume_averaged_electron_density
NAMES.short: Dimensionless carbon abundance ratio formed by dividing the plasma-volume-averaged total elemental carbon density by the corresponding plasma-volume-averaged electron density.
NAMES.long:
This quantity expresses the abundance of elemental carbon relative to electrons over the confined plasma volume. It is derived from [volume-averaged carbon density](name:volume_averaged_carbon_density) and is not a local carbon-to-electron density ratio.

The defining ratio is

$$
f_C = \frac{\langle n_C \rangle_V}{\langle n_e \rangle_V}
$$

where $f_C$ is the carbon abundance ratio, $\langle n_C \rangle_V$ is the [volume-averaged carbon density](name:volume_averaged_carbon_density), $\langle n_e \rangle_V$ is the corresponding plasma-volume-averaged electron number density, and $V$ denotes the confined plasma volume. The numerator includes neutral carbon and all ionic charge states through fully stripped C6+, as specified for [carbon density](name:carbon_density). It is not a fraction of total particle density or an ion-only carbon abundance.

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Carbon (C)

NAMES.name: ratio_of_volume_averaged_oxygen_density_to_volume_averaged_electron_density
NAMES.short: Ratio of volume-averaged oxygen ion density to electron density, summing O1+ through O8+ and excluding neutral oxygen.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the oxygen ion contribution to the volume-averaged plasma composition, expressed relative to the volume-averaged electron density. It is the ionized-oxygen component of [volume-averaged oxygen density](name:volume_averaged_oxygen_density), which also includes neutral oxygen.

$$
f_{O} = \frac{\frac{1}{V}\int_V \sum_{q=1}^{8} n_{O^{q+}}\,dV}{\frac{1}{V}\int_V n_e\,dV}
$$

where $V$ is the confined plasma volume bounded by the last closed flux surface, $n_{O^{q+}}$ is the local number density of oxygen in charge state $q$, and $n_e$ is the local electron number density. Neutral oxygen is excluded from the numerator; the ratio is evaluated at the time of peak electron density.

sources.enhanced_context: Oxygen (O).
sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Oxygen (O)

NAMES.name: ratio_of_volume_averaged_tungsten_density_to_volume_averaged_electron_density
NAMES.short: Dimensionless tungsten impurity abundance equal to the charge-state-summed, plasma-volume-averaged tungsten-ion density divided by the corresponding volume-averaged electron density.
NAMES.long:
This quantity measures the abundance of tungsten ions relative to electrons in the plasma volume enclosed by the last closed flux surface. Its numerator is the [volume-averaged tungsten-ion density](name:volume_averaged_tungsten_density), and its denominator is the volume-averaged electron density over the same volume.

$$
a_W = \frac{\langle n_W \rangle_V}{\langle n_e \rangle_V}
$$

where $a_W$ is the tungsten abundance, $\langle n_W \rangle_V$ is the charge-state-summed volume average of the local [tungsten-ion density](name:tungsten_density), and $\langle n_e \rangle_V$ is the volume-averaged electron density. The tungsten numerator includes all positive tungsten ionization states and excludes neutral tungsten. This is a global abundance ratio, distinct from a local tungsten density or an effective-charge measure.

NAMES.name: reference_wavelength_of_filter
NAMES.short: Reference wavelength of the passband transmitted by a diagnostic filter window. It is the nominal center or designated peak-transmission wavelength of the filter-window transmission band.
NAMES.long:
The reference wavelength of a filter, $\lambda_\mathrm{ref}$, is the nominal center or designated peak-transmission wavelength of the passband transmitted by a filter window. It is the wavelength used as the central spectral marker of the filter-window transmission criterion and therefore locates the passband without specifying its width or edge roll-off.

For a peak-defined filter reference, the reference wavelength is determined from the nominal spectral transmittance by:

$$
\lambda_\mathrm{ref} = \operatorname*{arg\,max}_{\lambda} T_\mathrm{nom}(\lambda)
$$

where $T_\mathrm{nom}(\lambda)$ is the nominal spectral transmittance as a function of wavelength $\lambda$.

If the passband maximum is flat, multi-peaked, or defined by an edge-based centering rule rather than by a unique transmittance maximum, $\lambda_\mathrm{ref}$ is the specified scalar reference point of that passband. It is distinct from the passband boundaries [lower_wavelength_of_filter](name:lower_wavelength_of_filter) and [upper_wavelength_of_filter](name:upper_wavelength_of_filter), and from the passband width [width_of_filter](name:width_of_filter); together these quantities characterize the passband but do not by themselves define the full spectral response.

sources.enhanced_context: Central wavelength of the optical filter used in an IR camera frame, defining the nominal spectral band centre for the measurement. Key parameter for identifying the spectral sensitivity of the filter assembly.
sources.leaf_definition: Central wavelength of the filter
sources.parent_definition: Set of filters

NAMES.name: absorptivity_of_filter
NAMES.short: Dimensionless fraction of the incident photon flux absorbed by a diagnostic filter material, bounded between 0 and 1.
NAMES.long:
Absorptivity of a diagnostic filter is the dimensionless ratio of the absorbed photon flux to the total incident photon flux at the filter surface. It is bounded on the interval $[0, 1]$, where $\alpha = 0$ indicates no absorption and $\alpha = 1$ indicates complete absorption of incident photons.

Conservation of energy at the filter interface constrains absorptivity $\alpha$, transmissivity $T$, and reflectivity $R$ through

$$
\alpha + T + R = 1
$$

where scattering contributions are subsumed into reflectivity or treated as a separate loss term, depending on the optical model.

The wavelength-resolved instance [spectral_absorptivity_of_filter](name:spectral_absorptivity_of_filter) extends this quantity as a function of photon wavelength, capturing the spectral selectivity of the filter material. The overall filter detection probability, which combines absorptivity with downstream optical and detector efficiencies, is quantified separately by [efficiency_of_filter](name:efficiency_of_filter).

NAMES.name: angular_width_of_bragg_crystal
NAMES.short: The Bragg diffraction angle of the crystal in an X-ray crystal spectrometer channel, fixing the central X-ray wavelength selected for diffraction according to Bragg's law.
NAMES.long:
The Bragg angle $\theta_B$ is the angle between the incident X-ray beam and the crystal lattice planes at which constructive interference produces wavelength-selective Bragg diffraction. It is the primary parameter governing the central wavelength of a measurement channel in an X-ray crystal spectrometer.

The selected X-ray wavelength $\lambda$ is determined by Bragg's law:

$$
n\lambda = 2d\sin\theta_B
$$

where $n$ is a positive integer diffraction order and $d$ is the crystal lattice plane spacing of the diffracting crystal. For a crystal with known $d$-spacing, $\theta_B$ uniquely determines the central wavelength of the spectral channel.

In X-ray crystal spectrometer systems used for fusion plasma diagnostics, the Bragg angle is established by the geometric orientation of the crystal relative to the plasma X-ray source and the detector. It is a key configuration parameter for selecting specific resonance lines used in impurity transport studies and ion temperature measurements via Doppler line-broadening analysis. Complementary crystal geometry parameters include the [radius of curvature of the diffracting surface in the toroidal direction](name:toroidal_curvature_of_bragg_crystal) and the [aperture radius of the crystal](name:radius_of_bragg_crystal), while the physical transverse extent of the crystal along the first axis is given by [bragg_crystal_width](name:bragg_crystal_width).

sources.enhanced_context: Bragg angle (θB) of the crystal in an X-ray crystal spectrometer channel. Determines the X-ray wavelength selected for diffraction according to Bragg's law (nλ = 2d sinθB), fixing the central wavelength of the measurement.
sources.leaf_definition: Bragg angle of the crystal
sources.parent_definition: Characteristics of the crystal used

NAMES.name: area_of_filter
NAMES.short: Geometric area of a radiation-filter surface that intercepts incoming radiation, measured over the true material surface rather than its planar projection.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the geometric area of a surface associated with a radiation filter and participating in interception or transmission of incoming radiation. It refers to the actual surface geometry, including curvature, rather than a projected aperture area.

The area is defined by integrating the differential surface-area element over the relevant surface:

$$
A = \int_S dA
$$

where $A$ is the total area, $S$ is the specified filter surface, and $dA$ is an infinitesimal element of true surface area. For the concrete specialization [surface area of filter](name:surface_area_of_filter), $S$ is the material surface of the filter window.

NAMES.name: bragg_crystal_width
NAMES.short: Bragg crystal width is the full physical extent of a rectangular Bragg crystal along its first local tangential direction, corresponding to the crystal-local X1 tangent axis.
NAMES.long:
Bragg crystal width is the full physical extent of a rectangular Bragg crystal along its first local tangential direction. The direction is the first in-surface axis of the crystal-local right-handed Cartesian frame $(\hat{t}_1, \hat{t}_2, \hat{n})$, with $\hat{t}_1$ corresponding to the crystal-local $X_1$ tangent axis and $\hat{n}$ normal to the diffracting surface.

For a rectangular crystal whose two opposing edges perpendicular to $\hat{t}_1$ have first local tangential coordinates $u_{1,-}$ and $u_{1,+}$, the width $w$ is

$$
w = |u_{1,+} - u_{1,-}|
$$

where $w$, $u_{1,+}$, and $u_{1,-}$ are expressed in meters.

This quantity is an extent, not a signed outline-vertex coordinate. [first_local_tangential_coordinate_of_bragg_crystal](name:first_local_tangential_coordinate_of_bragg_crystal) and [second_local_tangential_coordinate_of_bragg_crystal](name:second_local_tangential_coordinate_of_bragg_crystal) denote coordinates of points on the crystal outline in the two local tangential directions; bragg_crystal_height is the corresponding extent along $\hat{t}_2$, and [thickness_of_bragg_crystal](name:thickness_of_bragg_crystal) is the extent along the local normal.

sources.enhanced_context: Full width of the X-ray crystal spectrometer crystal in the X1 direction, applicable only for rectangular crystal geometry (geometry_type = 3). Defines the physical extent of the diffracting crystal along the first transverse axis.
sources.leaf_definition: Full width of the object in the X1 direction, used only if geometry_type/index = 3
sources.parent_definition: Characteristics of the crystal used

NAMES.name: bremsstrahlung_power
NAMES.short: Total electromagnetic power emitted by free-free bremsstrahlung as electrons accelerate in the Coulomb fields of plasma ions.
NAMES.long:
Bremsstrahlung power is the total electromagnetic power emitted by free-free radiation from electron acceleration in the Coulomb fields of plasma ions. It is integrated over the emitting plasma volume and the full photon-frequency range.

$$
P_{\mathrm{brem}} = \int_V \int_0^\infty \varepsilon_{\mathrm{brem}}(\mathbf{x},\omega)\,d\omega\,d^3\mathbf{x}
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{brem}}$ is the total bremsstrahlung power, $V$ is the emitting plasma volume, $\mathbf{x}$ is position, $\omega$ is photon angular frequency, and $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{brem}}$ is the spectral volumetric bremsstrahlung emissivity. This quantity is a contribution to [total plasma radiated power](name:total_plasma_radiated_power) and excludes discrete [line radiation](name:power_due_to_line_radiation) and [synchrotron radiation](name:power_due_to_synchrotron_radiation).

sources.enhanced_context: Total radiated power from Bremsstrahlung emission, the continuum radiation arising from electron-ion Coulomb collisions in the plasma. Scales as ne² Zeff Te^(1/2) and represents a key power loss channel.
sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Radiated power from Bremsstrahlung

NAMES.name: brightness_of_visible_camera
NAMES.short: Visible-camera brightness is band-integrated photon radiance along a specified viewing direction over the wavelengths admitted by a visible passband. It gives the photon rate per projected collecting area and accepted solid angle, with the spectral dependence integrated over that band.
NAMES.long:
Visible-camera brightness is the photon radiance of a radiation field along a specified viewing direction after integration over a visible wavelength interval or passband. It is normalized to projected collecting area, observation time, and accepted solid angle, and counts photons rather than radiant energy.

The band-integrated photon radiance is defined by integrating the spectral photon radiance over the visible passband:

$$
B_\mathrm{vis} = \int_{\lambda_1}^{\lambda_2} L_\lambda^{(\gamma)}(\lambda)\, d\lambda
$$

where $B_\mathrm{vis}$ is the visible-camera brightness, $L_\lambda^{(\gamma)}(\lambda)$ is the spectral photon radiance at wavelength $\lambda$, and $[\lambda_1,\lambda_2]$ is the wavelength interval defining the visible passband.

The quantity is non-negative because spectral photon radiance is non-negative over the passband. It is distinct from [spectral radiance](name:spectral_radiance), which retains wavelength dependence, and from [radiance at spectral line](name:radiance_at_spectral_line), which refers to an individual spectral line or narrow line interval; it also differs from energy radiance because photons are counted without weighting by photon energy.

NAMES.name: curvature_of_optical_element
NAMES.short: Signed local radius of curvature of an optical-element surface, defined along a specified tangent direction and applicable to spherical, cylindrical, and toroidal geometries.
NAMES.long:
The signed local radius of curvature characterizes how an optical-element surface bends in a specified tangent direction at a surface point. It is a surface-shape property, distinct from the aperture size represented by [radius of optical element](name:radius_of_optical_element).

For unit tangent direction $\hat{t}$, the radius is defined by the reciprocal of the signed normal curvature:

$$
R_c(\hat{t}) = \frac{1}{\kappa_n(\hat{t})}
$$

where $R_c$ is the signed radius of curvature and $\kappa_n(\hat{t})$ is the signed normal curvature in direction $\hat{t}$. A spherical surface has equal directional curvatures, whereas cylindrical and toroidal surfaces can have direction-dependent curvature. The radius of a spectral image surface is a distinct quantity described by [spectral surface curvature of optical element](name:spectral_surface_curvature_of_optical_element).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the center of curvature lies on the designated positive side of the surface normal.

NAMES.name: back_surface_curvature_of_optical_element
NAMES.short: Signed radius of curvature of a diagnostic optical element’s rear surface measured along its first local tangential aperture direction.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the rear-surface component of [curvature of optical element](name:curvature_of_optical_element), resolved along the first local tangential direction of the aperture frame. It describes surface shape rather than the optical element’s aperture size or the curvature of a spectral image surface.

The signed radius is defined from the signed normal curvature of the rear-surface curve:

$$
R_1 = \frac{1}{\kappa_1}, \qquad \kappa_1 = \frac{d^2\mathbf{r}}{ds^2} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}
$$

where $R_1$ is the signed radius of curvature in m, $\kappa_1$ is the signed normal curvature in m$^{-1}$, $\mathbf{r}$ is the surface-curve position in m, $s$ is arc length in m along the first local tangential direction, and $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ is the chosen unit surface normal. This component is distinct from the corresponding second local tangential direction represented by [vertical back-surface curvature of optical element](name:vertical_back_surface_curvature_of_optical_element).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the rear-surface curve bends toward the chosen positive surface-normal side.

NAMES.name: deuterium_density
NAMES.subject: deuterium
NAMES.short: Deuterium density is the number density of ionized deuterium in the fuel-ion population. It is the local density of deuterons, excluding neutral atoms, molecules, and line- or volume-averaged deuterium densities.
NAMES.long:
Deuterium density is the number density of ionized deuterium in the fuel-ion population. As a species-level density it is charge-state-summed over ionized atomic charge states; for deuterium this reduces to the singly ionized deuteron population.

The local deuterium density is defined by the charge-state sum

$$
n_D = \sum_{q>0} n_{\mathrm{D}^{q+}}
$$

where $n_D$ is the deuterium density, $q$ is the positive atomic charge state, and $n_{\mathrm{D}^{q+}}$ is the number density of deuterium ions in charge state $q$.

Neutral deuterium atoms, molecular deuterium, and non-deuterium species are excluded. This quantity is local; spatial aggregations such as [line-averaged deuterium density](name:line_averaged_deuterium_density) and [volume-averaged deuterium density](name:volume_averaged_deuterium_density) are distinct quantities.

sources.leaf_definition: Radio of densities nT/nD

NAMES.name: efficiency_of_filter
NAMES.short: Dimensionless probability, bounded from 0 to 1, that a photon incident on a diagnostic filter produces a registered detection event, combining filter transmission, relay optics throughput, detector quantum efficiency, and all other losses in the detection chain.
NAMES.long:
The efficiency of a diagnostic filter is the overall probability that a photon arriving at the filter aperture is ultimately registered as a detection event, accounting for every source of attenuation and conversion loss between the optical input and the readout electronics. Contributing factors include the wavelength-dependent transmission of the filter material, the geometric and optical throughput of any relay optics, and the quantum efficiency of the detector element. The quantity is dimensionless and bounded between 0 and 1, where 0 indicates complete attenuation or detector insensitivity and 1 indicates perfect detection of every incident photon.

The spectrally resolved form is given by the [spectral efficiency of filter](name:spectral_efficiency_of_filter), which tracks detection probability as a function of wavelength across the filter passband and is the primary input for absolute photon-flux calibrations. A band-integrated effective efficiency may be derived by weighting the spectral form by the incident spectrum and integrating over the filter passband. The [absorptivity of filter](name:absorptivity_of_filter) isolates the photon-absorption component of the loss budget, while [efficiency of spectrometer channel](name:efficiency_of_spectrometer_channel) provides the analogous combined throughput descriptor for a full dispersive detection channel.

This efficiency is determined experimentally through absolute photometric calibration using a source of known spectral irradiance, or assembled from independently measured component efficiencies across the detection chain.

NAMES.name: efficiency_of_spectrometer_channel
NAMES.short: Efficiency of a spectrometer channel is a bounded dimensionless fraction, between zero and one, of photons already within the channel acceptance that reach the active detector area after optical-path losses.
NAMES.long:
Efficiency of a spectrometer channel is a bounded dimensionless fraction, between zero and one, of photons already within the channel's geometrical and spectral acceptance that reach the active detector area after propagation through the channel optical path. It characterizes the channel efficiency after acceptance, not the acceptance itself.

The channel efficiency is defined by the ratio of photon rates for the same accepted spectral interval:

$$
\eta_\mathrm{ch} = \frac{\dot{N}_\mathrm{det}}{\dot{N}_\mathrm{acc}}
$$

where $\dot{N}_\mathrm{det}$ is the photon rate arriving at the active detector area and $\dot{N}_\mathrm{acc}$ is the photon rate within the channel acceptance before optical-path losses. Both rates are expressed in the same units, for example photons per second for an interval-integrated rate or photons per second per meter for a wavelength-resolved rate.

This quantity is distinct from [spectral etendue of a spectrometer channel](name:spectral_etendue_of_spectrometer_channel), which defines the accepted geometrical and spectral phase-space extent rather than a loss probability. It excludes [detector quantum efficiency], detector gain, and electronic registration probability after photons reach the active detector area. Component filter properties such as [absorptivity of a filter](name:absorptivity_of_filter) and [transmissivity of a filter] describe individual optical elements; they may contribute to, but are not synonyms for, the aggregate spectrometer-channel efficiency.

sources.leaf_definition: Values of the light collection efficiencies

NAMES.name: emissivity_due_to_fusion
NAMES.short: Local volumetric rate of neutron production from thermonuclear fusion reactions, giving the spatial distribution of fusion neutron emission per unit volume at each point in the plasma.
NAMES.long:
The neutron emissivity due to fusion quantifies the number of fusion-born neutrons generated per unit volume per unit time at a given plasma location. This volumetric source term encodes the combined effect of local fuel-ion densities and the thermally-averaged fusion reactivity, and drives the global neutron field from which plasma performance is diagnosed.

For a binary fusion reaction between ion species $a$ and $b$, the emissivity is given by:

$$
\epsilon_{ab} = \frac{n_a \, n_b}{1 + \delta_{ab}} \langle \sigma v \rangle_{ab}
$$

where $n_a$ and $n_b$ are the number densities of the reacting ions, $\langle \sigma v \rangle_{ab}$ is the fusion reactivity (velocity-averaged fusion cross-section) at the local ion temperature, and $\delta_{ab} = 1$ for identical-species reactions to avoid double-counting.

The emissivity profile is inferred from measurements by neutron camera arrays and collimated detector systems via Abel inversion or tomographic reconstruction. The two principal reaction channels are resolved as [deuterium_deuterium_emissivity_due_to_fusion](name:deuterium_deuterium_emissivity_due_to_fusion), covering the neutron-emitting D-D branch, and [deuterium_tritium_emissivity_due_to_fusion](name:deuterium_tritium_emissivity_due_to_fusion), which dominates in D-T operation due to the much larger fusion cross-section. Integrating this emissivity over the plasma volume and weighting by the per-reaction neutron energy connects to the [total_neutron_power](name:total_neutron_power).

NAMES.name: deuterium_deuterium_emissivity_due_to_fusion
NAMES.subject: deuterium_deuterium
NAMES.short: Local volumetric rate of neutron production from deuterium-deuterium fusion reactions, giving the spatial distribution of DD neutron emission per unit volume across the plasma.
NAMES.long:
The deuterium-deuterium neutron emissivity $\varepsilon_{DD}$ is the local number of neutrons produced per unit volume per unit time from D-D fusion reactions. Of the two equally probable D-D reaction branches, only the neutron-producing channel $^2\text{H} + ^2\text{H} \rightarrow {^3\text{He}} + n$ (releasing a 2.45 MeV neutron) contributes to this quantity; the proton-producing branch $^2\text{H} + ^2\text{H} \rightarrow T + p$ does not.

The emissivity is related to the local fuel conditions by:

$$
\varepsilon_{DD} = \frac{n_D^2}{2} \langle \sigma v \rangle_{DD,n}
$$

where $n_D$ is the local deuterium number density and $\langle \sigma v \rangle_{DD,n}$ is the velocity-averaged reaction rate coefficient for the neutron-producing branch; the factor $1/2$ prevents double-counting of identical reactants.

The spatial profile of $\varepsilon_{DD}$ is reconstructed from chord-integrated signals recorded by multiple neutron detectors distributed around the device, using tomographic inversion to recover the local distribution. Volume integration of $\varepsilon_{DD}$ yields the global neutron emission rate characterized by deuterium_deuterium_flux_due_to_thermal_fusion for the purely thermal component and includes beam-related contributions captured by deuterium_deuterium_flux_due_to_beam_thermal_fusion. The D-T plasma analog is [deuterium_tritium_emissivity_due_to_fusion](name:deuterium_tritium_emissivity_due_to_fusion), and the corresponding local fusion power density from all D-D channels is [deuterium_deuterium_power_density_due_to_fusion](name:deuterium_deuterium_power_density_due_to_fusion).

NAMES.name: deuterium_tritium_emissivity_due_to_fusion
NAMES.subject: deuterium_tritium
NAMES.short: Local volumetric rate of neutron production from deuterium-tritium fusion reactions, giving the spatial distribution of D-T neutron emission per unit volume at each point in the plasma.
NAMES.long:
The deuterium-tritium neutron emissivity $\varepsilon_{DT}$ is the local number of neutrons produced per unit volume per unit time from D-T fusion reactions. Each D-T fusion reaction produces exactly one neutron, so this quantity is equal to the local D-T fusion reaction-rate density.

For reacting deuterium and tritium ion populations, the emissivity is given by:

$$
\varepsilon_{DT} = n_D \, n_T \, \langle \sigma v \rangle_{DT}
$$

where $n_D$ and $n_T$ are the local deuterium and tritium number densities and $\langle \sigma v \rangle_{DT}$ is the D-T fusion reactivity, the velocity-averaged fusion cross-section evaluated over the relative-velocity distribution of the reacting ion populations; for thermal reactants it is the thermally averaged reactivity at the local ion temperature. No symmetry factor appears because the reactants are distinct species.

This quantity counts neutron production, not fusion energy deposition or neutron power. It is the D-T channel of the parent [emissivity_due_to_fusion](name:emissivity_due_to_fusion) and the counterpart of [deuterium_deuterium_emissivity_due_to_fusion](name:deuterium_deuterium_emissivity_due_to_fusion), which covers the neutron-emitting D-D branch. Its energy-weighted counterpart is [deuterium_tritium_power_density_due_to_fusion](name:deuterium_tritium_power_density_due_to_fusion), and integrating the emissivity over the plasma volume and weighting by the per-reaction neutron energy connects to the [total_neutron_power](name:total_neutron_power).

NAMES.name: energy_of_detector_pixel
NAMES.short: The energy of a detector pixel is the central or representative photon energy assigned to that pixel's spectral bandpass in an X-ray crystal spectrometer. It is distinct from the lower and upper bandpass-edge energies.
NAMES.long:
The energy of a detector pixel is the central or representative photon energy assigned to that pixel's spectral bandpass in an X-ray crystal spectrometer. It is the energy counterpart of the [wavelength of detector pixel](name:wavelength_of_detector_pixel) and identifies the pixel's spectral-channel assignment rather than the finite width of its accepted band.

For diffraction order $n$, the representative pixel energy is related to the pixel Bragg angle by Bragg's law and the photon energy-wavelength relation:

$$
E_\mathrm{pix} = \frac{n h c}{2 e d \sin\theta_\mathrm{pix}}
$$

where $E_\mathrm{pix}$ is the energy of the detector pixel, $n$ is the diffraction order, $h$ is Planck's constant, $c$ is the speed of light in vacuum, $e$ is the elementary-charge magnitude, $d$ is the spacing of the diffracting crystal planes, and $\theta_\mathrm{pix}$ is the Bragg angle associated with the pixel.

This representative energy is the calibrated spectral-channel value selected by the spectrometer energy scale; it need not equal the arithmetic midpoint between the [lower bound energy of detector pixel](name:lower_bound_energy_of_detector_pixel) and the [upper bound energy of detector pixel](name:upper_bound_energy_of_detector_pixel), which define the edges of the pixel's accepted photon-energy interval.

NAMES.name: etendue_of_spectrometer_channel
NAMES.short: Etendue of a spectrometer channel is the linear optical phase-space acceptance of that channel. It represents geometric throughput set by effective entrance-aperture extent and accepted ray directions, not the channel efficiency or spectral weighting.
NAMES.long:
Etendue of a spectrometer channel is the linear optical phase-space acceptance of that channel. It is the channel-specific reduced form of optical etendue for slit-like or otherwise channelized spectrometers, using an effective entrance aperture extent rather than an aperture area.

The etendue is defined by integrating the channel geometric acceptance over effective entrance position and ray direction:

$$
G_\ell = \int_\ell \int_\Omega A(\ell', \hat{s}) \, d\Omega \, d\ell'
$$

where $G_\ell$ is the etendue of the spectrometer channel, $\ell'$ is position along the effective entrance aperture, $\hat{s}$ is ray direction, $d\Omega$ is differential solid angle, and $A(\ell', \hat{s})$ is the geometric acceptance weight of the channel. For uniform acceptance this reduces to $G_\ell = L_\mathrm{eff}\Omega_\mathrm{eff}$, where $L_\mathrm{eff}$ is the effective entrance length and $\Omega_\mathrm{eff}$ is the effective collection solid angle.

This quantity excludes wavelength-dependent detector response, grating or filter transmission, and spectral-line-shape weighting. The [spectral etendue of a spectrometer channel](name:spectral_etendue_of_spectrometer_channel) is the normalized-spectral-response-weighted wavelength density associated with this throughput, while the [effective spectral etendue of a spectrometer channel](name:effective_spectral_etendue_of_spectrometer_channel) is the corresponding acceptance integrated over the effective spectral width. It is distinct from [efficiency of a spectrometer channel](name:efficiency_of_spectrometer_channel), which represents transmission or detection probability rather than phase-space acceptance.

NAMES.name: exposure_time_of_spectrometer_channel
NAMES.short: Temporal duration over which a spectrometer channel accumulates incident photons to form one spectral measurement.
NAMES.long:
The integration duration is the elapsed time between the start and end of the photon-accumulation interval for a spectrometer channel. It defines the temporal window contributing to one spectral measurement and is distinct from the channel's spectral response, including its [effective spectral width](name:effective_spectral_width_of_spectrometer_channel).

It is defined by

$$
\Delta t = t_{\mathrm{end}} - t_{\mathrm{start}}
$$

where $\Delta t$ is the integration duration, and $t_{\mathrm{start}}$ and $t_{\mathrm{end}}$ are the times at which photon accumulation begins and ends. The accumulated signal is determined by the time integral of the [incident spectral flux](name:incident_spectral_flux) over this interval.

sources.enhanced_context: Exposure (integration) time of the filter spectrometer detector for a given channel measurement. Defines the temporal window over which the spectral signal is accumulated.
sources.leaf_definition: Exposure time

NAMES.name: extent_of_detector_pixel
NAMES.short: Extent of a detector pixel is the nonnegative linear size of one pixel footprint along either the first or second local tangential axis in the right-handed local detector frame (first local tangential, second local tangential, detector normal). It excludes optical resolution and spacing or inactive gaps between neighboring pixels.
NAMES.long:
Extent of a detector pixel is the nonnegative linear size of one pixel footprint along a specified in-plane axis of the right-handed local detector frame $(\hat{t}_1,\hat{t}_2,\hat{n})$, where $\hat{t}_1$ and $\hat{t}_2$ are the first and second local tangential directions in the detector plane and $\hat{n}$ is the detector-plane normal. The footprint is the area assigned to that pixel for geometric mapping or active collection, independent of the optical point-spread function.

For a coordinate $s_a$ along the selected local tangential axis, the extent is the separation of the footprint boundaries:

$$
r_a = s_{a,+} - s_{a,-}
$$

where $a$ is either $1$ or $2$ and selects the axis $\hat{t}_a$, $r_a$ is the detector-pixel extent in meters, $s_{a,-}$ and $s_{a,+}$ are the lower and upper footprint-boundary coordinates in meters along $\hat{t}_a$, and $s_{a,+} \ge s_{a,-}$. Consequently $r_a \ge 0$.

This quantity is a footprint-edge separation, not the detector-pixel center location, the center-to-center pitch, the optical point-spread width, or the spacing or inactive gap between neighboring pixels. The detector-pixel center location is described by separate coordinate quantities, such as [horizontal coordinate of detector pixel] and [vertical coordinate of detector pixel](name:vertical_coordinate_of_detector_pixel). The extent equals the pitch along the same selected axis only when adjacent pixel footprints tile the detector plane contiguously with negligible inactive gap; this condition is independent of whether the footprint is square or non-square.

NAMES.name: extent_of_soft_xray_detector
NAMES.short: Full edge-to-edge physical dimension of a soft X-ray detector measured along a specified local detector-plane direction.
NAMES.long:
The extent is the full edge-to-edge physical dimension of a soft X-ray detector along one specified local detector-plane direction. It describes the detector’s overall physical size and is distinct from an individual pixel dimension.

For a detector-plane coordinate $u$, the extent $E$ is defined as

$$
E = u_{\max} - u_{\min}
$$

where $u_{\max}$ and $u_{\min}$ are the maximum and minimum boundary coordinates along the same local direction, and $E$ and $u$ are lengths in m.

The direction is intrinsic to the detector plane rather than a machine-axis projection. The corresponding boundary coordinates may be described using the [first local tangential coordinate](name:first_local_tangential_coordinate_of_soft_xray_detector) or [second local tangential coordinate](name:second_local_tangential_coordinate_of_soft_xray_detector).
