NAMES.name: factor_of_spectrometer
NAMES.short: Factor of spectrometer is the generic multiplicative coefficient associated with a spectrometer response or signal conversion. Its specific qualified form defines what signal is multiplied and what physical observable or corrected signal results.
NAMES.long:
Factor of spectrometer is a parent quantity for multiplicative response coefficients of a spectrometer. It denotes the factor that scales a spectrometer signal or an already defined spectrometer-related quantity into the corresponding quantity specified by a more qualified standard name.

For a purely multiplicative spectrometer response, the defining relation is:

$$
Q = F_{\mathrm{spec}} S
$$

where $S$ is the input spectrometer signal or quantity, $F_{\mathrm{spec}}$ is the spectrometer factor, and $Q$ is the resulting scaled quantity.

This parent name does not by itself fix the target observable, signal convention, spectral dependence, or dimensional character of the factor; those semantics belong to its qualified descendants. The [calibration factor of spectrometer](name:calibration_factor_of_spectrometer) is one concrete specialization, where the factor represents an absolute calibration response rather than the entire parent category.

NAMES.name: calibration_factor_of_spectrometer
NAMES.short: Multiplicative absolute radiometric calibration coefficient for a spectrometer response channel, mapping registered photon count rate to the corresponding photon radiance density. It abstracts calibration factors by their count-rate-to-radiance role rather than by a specific resolved-variable specialization.
NAMES.long:
Calibration factor of a spectrometer is the multiplicative coefficient that places a spectrometer response channel on an absolute photon radiance-density scale. It represents the net radiometric response needed to convert the photon count rate registered in that channel into the corresponding photon radiance density.

The defining relation is:

$$
\mathcal{L}_\gamma = C_\mathrm{cal} \, \dot{N}_\gamma
$$

where $\mathcal{L}_\gamma$ is the photon radiance density represented by the spectrometer response channel, $\dot{N}_\gamma$ is the photon count rate registered in the same channel, and $C_\mathrm{cal}$ is this calibration factor.

This parent quantity is defined by the absolute radiometric count-rate-to-radiance conversion, not by the particular variable used to identify the spectrometer channel. The [spectral calibration factor of a spectrometer](name:spectral_calibration_factor_of_spectrometer) is the wavelength-resolved specialization; non-radiometric spectrometer factors and additive corrections such as background or dark-count offsets are excluded.

NAMES.name: factor_of_visible_camera
NAMES.short: Visible-camera factor is a multiplicative radiometric coefficient associated with visible-band camera measurements. In this dimensional convention, it scales a corrected dimensionless camera signal to band-integrated photon radiance while absorbing throughput, detector response, etendue, and exposure treatment.
NAMES.long:
Visible-camera factor is a parent concept for multiplicative radiometric coefficients used with visible-band camera measurements. It represents the response factor that converts a consistently corrected, dimensionless detector signal into absolute photon radiance integrated over the relevant spectral band, with optical throughput, detector response, electronics, exposure treatment, and viewing etendue condensed into one coefficient. The absolute-calibration specialization [calibration factor of visible camera](name:calibration_factor_of_visible_camera) is one concrete member of this factor family.

When used in the radiance-calibration direction, the defining relationship is

$$
L_\gamma = F_\mathrm{vis} S_\mathrm{corr}
$$

where $L_\gamma$ is the band-integrated photon radiance, $F_\mathrm{vis}$ is the visible-camera factor, and $S_\mathrm{corr}$ is a dimensionless detector signal after the corrections and normalizations specified for the factor. A signal represented as a rate would require a coefficient with different dimensionality, so the treatment of exposure time or frame integration is part of the factor definition.

The factor is determined by radiometric calibration with a source of known photon radiance, by end-to-end modeling of the optical and detector response, or by a hybrid of both. The calibration must be consistent with dark subtraction, background removal, flat-fielding, nonlinearity correction, spectral filtering, and any conversion between camera electronics and corrected signal.

Numerical values are highly instrument-specific because throughput, etendue, exposure duration, gain, and bandpass can vary widely. For visible imaging channels, values of order $10^{12}$-$10^{19}$ per corrected count are common; a single constant factor is not valid for saturated, nonlinear, or configuration-dependent response unless those effects are explicitly included.

NAMES.name: calibration_factor_of_visible_camera
NAMES.short: Multiplicative radiometric coefficient that converts a corrected visible-camera detector signal into absolute photon radiance integrated over the admitted spectral band.
NAMES.long:
A visible-camera radiometric factor converts a consistently corrected detector signal into band-integrated photon radiance. It represents the combined response of the optical throughput, detector sensitivity, pixel etendue, and exposure treatment rather than the radiance itself.

The defining conversion is

$$
L_{\mathrm{vis}} = C_{\mathrm{vis}} S_{\mathrm{corr}}
$$

where $L_{\mathrm{vis}}$ is the [visible-camera brightness](name:brightness_of_visible_camera), $C_{\mathrm{vis}}$ is this visible-camera factor, and $S_{\mathrm{corr}}$ is the corrected detector signal. The spectral dependence is integrated over the relevant visible passband. Unlike the resulting brightness, the factor is a calibration coefficient and must be applied to the corrected signal; it is the camera-specific component of the parent [factor of visible camera](name:factor_of_visible_camera).

sources.enhanced_context: Calibration factor converting raw detector pixel counts to radiance for each pixel of the 2D visible camera detector array. Incorporates relay optics transmission and camera quantum efficiency integrated over the wavelength bandpass.
sources.leaf_definition: Counts to radiance factor, for each pixel of the detector. Includes both the transmission losses in the relay optics and the quantum efficiency of the camera itself, integrated over the wavelength range
sources.parent_definition: Set of detectors

NAMES.name: filter_window_width
NAMES.short: Full opening span of a rectangular filter window measured along its first local tangential axis in the right-handed (X1, X2, X3) frame.
NAMES.long:
The filter-window width is the full separation of the two opposing boundaries measured along the first local tangential direction, X1, of the right-handed aperture frame (X1, X2, X3). The X1 and X2 directions lie in the filter plane, while X3 is normal to that plane.

For opposing window boundaries with first-coordinate values $x_{1,\min}$ and $x_{1,\max}$, the width is defined by

$$
w = x_{1,\max} - x_{1,\min}
$$

where $w$, $x_{1,\min}$, and $x_{1,\max}$ are geometric lengths measured in m.

This quantity describes the clear geometric opening of the rectangular filter window, excluding filter-material thickness and detector active width. The orthogonal window extent is described by the [second local tangential coordinates of the filter window](name:second_local_tangential_coordinate_of_filter_window), while the boundary positions along X1 are given by the [first local tangential coordinates of the filter window](name:first_local_tangential_coordinate_of_filter_window).

sources.enhanced_context: Full width of the X-ray crystal spectrometer filter window in the X1 direction, applicable when the rectangular geometry type (geometry_type=3) is selected. Specifies the physical aperture size in the primary filter axis direction for photon transmission.
sources.leaf_definition: Full width of the filter in the X1 direction, used only if geometry_type/index = 3
sources.parent_definition: Characteristics of the filter window

NAMES.name: first_local_tangential_coordinate_of_bragg_crystal
NAMES.short: Signed coordinate of a Bragg-crystal outline vertex along the first local tangential axis of the right-handed crystal-local (e1, e2, e3) frame, with e1 the more horizontal crystal-tangential direction oriented toward increasing toroidal angle φ in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Signed coordinate of a Bragg-crystal outline vertex along the first local tangential axis is the scalar displacement of that vertex from the crystal-local reference point along the first in-surface direction of the Bragg crystal. The quantity is defined in the right-handed crystal-local $(\hat{\mathbf{e}}_1,\hat{\mathbf{e}}_2,\hat{\mathbf{e}}_3)$ frame tied to the crystal surface.

The coordinate is the projection of the vertex displacement onto the first local tangential unit vector:

$$
X_1 = (\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}_0) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}_1
$$

where $\mathbf{r}$ is the position vector of the Bragg-crystal outline vertex, $\mathbf{r}_0$ is the position vector of the crystal-local reference point, and $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_1$ is the first local tangential unit vector.

The crystal-local triad is fixed geometrically: $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_3$ is the plasma-facing surface normal, $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_1$ is the more horizontal tangent to the crystal surface and is oriented so that its toroidal component points in the $+\hat{\phi}$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, and $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_2 = \hat{\mathbf{e}}_3 \times \hat{\mathbf{e}}_1$. This coordinate is distinct from the [second local tangential coordinate](name:second_local_tangential_coordinate_of_bragg_crystal), which uses $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_2$, and from any coordinate along the surface normal.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the outline vertex is displaced from the crystal-local reference point in the $+\hat{\mathbf{e}}_1$ direction, the more horizontal crystal-tangential direction oriented toward increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

sources.enhanced_context: Positions along the X1 axis of the irregular outline of the crystal in the (X1, X2) coordinate system for an X-ray crystal spectrometer channel. Defines the boundary vertices of the crystal cross-section used in Bragg diffraction geometry.
sources.leaf_definition: Positions along x1 axis
sources.parent_definition: Irregular outline of the object in the (X1, X2) coordinate system, used only if geometry_type/index=1. Do NOT repeat the first point.

NAMES.name: first_local_tangential_coordinate_of_filter
NAMES.short: Signed position of a vertex or sampled point on a diagnostic filter boundary projected onto the filter’s first object-local tangential axis.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the signed position of a vertex or sampled point on a diagnostic filter boundary along the filter’s first local tangential axis. This axis belongs to the filter’s object-local planar basis $(\hat{\mathbf e}_1,\hat{\mathbf e}_2)$ and is distinct from the second local tangential direction.

The coordinate is defined by projection relative to the origin of the filter-local frame:

$$
x_1 = (\mathbf r-\mathbf r_0)\mathbin{\cdot}\hat{\mathbf e}_1
$$

where $\mathbf r$ is the boundary-point position, $\mathbf r_0$ is the local-frame origin, and $\hat{\mathbf e}_1$ is the first local tangential unit vector. Together with the [second local tangential coordinate of filter](name:second_local_tangential_coordinate_of_filter), it specifies the point in the local tangential plane. The owning object is the filter rather than a separately scoped filter window.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the displacement from $\mathbf r_0$ points in the direction of $\hat{\mathbf e}_1$.

sources.enhanced_context: Positions of the filter window outline vertices along the X1 axis in the local (X1, X2) coordinate system. Defines the irregular contour of the soft X-ray filter window for a given detector channel.
sources.leaf_definition: Positions along x1 axis
sources.parent_definition: Irregular outline of the filter in the (X1, X2) coordinate system, used only if geometry_type/index=1. Do NOT repeat the first point.

sources.enhanced_context: Positions of the filter window outline vertices along the x1 axis of the local (X1, X2) coordinate system for an X-ray crystal spectrometer channel. Defines the irregular aperture geometry of the filter window.
sources.leaf_definition: Positions along x1 axis
sources.parent_definition: Irregular outline of the filter in the (X1, X2) coordinate system, used only if geometry_type/index=1. Do NOT repeat the first point.

NAMES.name: first_local_tangential_coordinate_of_filter_window
NAMES.short: Signed position of a filter-window outline point along the first local tangential in-plane basis direction in the object-local frame (e1, e2, e3), chosen as the more-horizontal tangent oriented toward increasing toroidal angle φ in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Signed position of a filter-window outline point along the first local tangential in-plane basis direction is the scalar coordinate of the point in the filter-window object-local planar frame. The object-local frame is the orthonormal triad $(\hat{e}_1,\hat{e}_2,\hat{e}_3)$, with $\hat{e}_1$ the window-plane tangent having the larger projection onto the local horizontal plane spanned by $\hat{R}$ and $\hat{\phi}$ and oriented toward increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

The coordinate is defined by the projection of the outline-point displacement onto the first local tangent:

$$
\xi_1 = (\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}_0) \cdot \hat{e}_1
$$

where $\xi_1$ is the first local tangential coordinate of the filter-window outline point, $\mathbf{r}$ is the outline-point position, $\mathbf{r}_0$ is the filter-window local origin, and $\hat{e}_1$ is the first local tangential unit vector.

The object-local triad $(\hat{e}_1,\hat{e}_2,\hat{e}_3)$ is right-handed: $\hat{e}_3$ is the filter-window normal directed toward the plasma-facing side, and $\hat{e}_2 = \hat{e}_3 \times \hat{e}_1$ is the second local tangential direction. This quantity excludes the coordinate along $\hat{e}_2$, which is the [second local tangential coordinate of a filter-window outline point](name:second_local_tangential_coordinate_of_filter_window).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the outline point lies on the side of the filter-window local origin reached by moving along the more-horizontal in-plane tangent toward increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

sources.enhanced_context: Positions along the X1 axis of the irregular outline of the filter window for an X-ray camera. Together with X2 positions, defines the 2D boundary polygon of the filter aperture in the local (X1, X2) coordinate system.
sources.leaf_definition: Positions along x1 axis
sources.parent_definition: Irregular outline of the filter in the (X1, X2) coordinate system, used only if geometry_type/index=1. Do NOT repeat the first point.

NAMES.name: first_local_tangential_coordinate_of_optical_element
NAMES.short: Signed position of an optical-element outline vertex along the first local tangential coordinate of the optical-element object-local frame. The positive first tangent is the more-horizontal in-surface direction selected toward increasing toroidal angle φ in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, where R is major radius and Z is vertical height.
NAMES.long:
Signed position of an optical-element outline vertex along the first local tangential coordinate of the optical-element object-local frame is the scalar coordinate obtained by projecting the vertex displacement from the local origin onto the first tangent. The object-local frame is the right-handed triad $(\hat{\mathbf{e}}_1,\hat{\mathbf{e}}_2,\hat{\mathbf{e}}_3)$ with $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_3$ the plasma-facing surface normal; $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_1$ is the more-horizontal surface tangent directed toward increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $Z$ is vertical height, and $\phi$ increases counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$.

The coordinate is defined by the projection

$$
q_1 = (\mathbf{r}_v - \mathbf{r}_0) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}_1
$$

where $q_1$ is the first local tangential coordinate of the optical element, $\mathbf{r}_v$ is the position vector of the outline vertex, $\mathbf{r}_0$ is the optical-element local origin, and $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_1$ is the first local tangential unit vector.

It applies only to the in-surface outline of the optical element and excludes displacement along the plasma-facing normal. The companion [second local tangential coordinate](name:second_local_tangential_coordinate_of_optical_element) gives the coordinate along $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_2$, the other surface tangent that completes the right-handed local triad.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the vertex displacement from the optical-element local origin has a component along $+\hat{\mathbf{e}}_1$, the more-horizontal surface tangent directed toward increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

sources.enhanced_context: Positions of the UV spectrometer detector aperture outline vertices along the X1 axis of the local (X1, X2) coordinate system of the detector face. Defines one component of the 2D aperture boundary polygon.
sources.leaf_definition: Positions along x1 axis
sources.parent_definition: Irregular outline of the detector/aperture in the (X1, X2) coordinate system. Do NOT repeat the first point.

sources.enhanced_context: Positions of the optical element outline along the X1 axis in the local (X1, X2) coordinate system, defining the irregular boundary geometry of a detector or aperture for a visible spectrometer channel.
sources.leaf_definition: Positions along x1 axis
sources.parent_definition: Irregular outline of the detector/aperture in the (X1, X2) coordinate system. Do NOT repeat the first point.

NAMES.name: first_local_tangential_coordinate_of_soft_xray_detector
NAMES.short: Signed coordinate of a soft X-ray detector outline vertex along the first local tangential (X1) axis of the detector-local two-dimensional Cartesian frame.
NAMES.long: The first local tangential coordinate specifies the signed displacement of an outline vertex along the first tangential axis (X1) of the detector-local Cartesian frame. Together with [second_local_tangential_coordinate_of_soft_xray_detector](name:second_local_tangential_coordinate_of_soft_xray_detector), it defines the polygonal boundary of the soft X-ray detector's sensitive area projected onto the object-local plane. The two coordinates $(X_1, X_2)$ form a right-handed pair intrinsic to the owning detector object; their orientation is fixed per detector installation and is not in general aligned with the machine cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the vertex displacement is in the direction of the positive first local tangential axis of the detector-local frame.

sources.enhanced_context: Positions of the soft X-ray detector outline vertices along the X1 axis in the local (X1, X2) coordinate system. Defines part of the polygonal boundary of the detector or aperture used for etendue and line-of-sight calculations.
sources.leaf_definition: Positions along x1 axis
sources.parent_definition: Irregular outline of the detector/aperture in the (X1, X2) coordinate system

NAMES.name: flux_of_spectrometer_channel
NAMES.short: Raw photon-equivalent detection-event rate from a spectral observation over a selected line or wavelength passband, before absolute radiometric calibration.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the raw rate of photon-equivalent detection events associated with radiation selected by a spectral line or wavelength passband. It represents detector-response counts rather than absolute photon spectral radiance or radiant power.

The rate is defined by

$$
\dot{N}_{\mathrm{det}} = \frac{dN_{\mathrm{det}}}{dt}
$$

where $N_{\mathrm{det}}$ is the accumulated photon-equivalent detection-event count and $t$ is elapsed time.

The quantity is uncalibrated: it excludes conversion to absolute radiometric units and should not be identified with [spectral radiance](name:spectral_radiance). A concrete spectrometer-channel instance is [spectral flux of a spectrometer channel](name:spectral_flux_of_spectrometer_channel); the corresponding conversion is characterized separately by the [spectrometer calibration factor](name:calibration_factor_of_spectrometer).

NAMES.name: hard_xray_brightness
NAMES.subject: hard_xray
NAMES.short: Band-integrated photon radiance of hard X-ray emission incident on a detector channel, expressed as photon rate per projected area and accepted solid angle.
NAMES.long:
Band-integrated photon radiance is the photon arrival rate from hard X-ray emission per projected collecting area and accepted solid angle, with photon-energy dependence integrated over the channel bandpass.

$$
B = \int_{E_{\min}}^{E_{\max}} L_E(E)\,dE
$$

where $B$ is the band-integrated photon radiance, $L_E(E)$ is the photon spectral radiance at photon energy $E$, and $E_{\min}$ and $E_{\max}$ are the lower and upper accepted photon energies.

The quantity counts photons without weighting them by photon energy. It is therefore distinct from the power radiance defined for a [soft X-ray detector](name:radiance_of_soft_xray_detector), while sharing the photon-radiance meaning of [visible-camera brightness](name:brightness_of_visible_camera).

sources.enhanced_context: Hard X-ray channel radiance defined as photon flux per unit solid angle per unit area (photon flux divided by étendue), resolved across multiple energy bands. Used for absolute calibration of bremsstrahlung emission from suprathermal electrons.
sources.leaf_definition: Photons received by the detector per unit time, per unit solid angle and per unit area (i.e. photon flux divided by the etendue), in multiple energy bands if available from the detector
sources.parent_definition: Set of channels (detector or pixel of a camera)

NAMES.name: hard_xray_emissivity
NAMES.subject: hard_xray
NAMES.short: Band-integrated hard-X-ray photon emissivity: the local photon production rate per volume and solid angle over a specified photon-energy interval, rather than per unit energy.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the local directional production rate of hard-X-ray photons, integrated over a specified photon-energy band. It describes photon emission from plasma radiation processes, including bremsstrahlung from energetic electrons interacting with ions.

The band-integrated emissivity is defined by

$$
J(\mathbf{r},\Omega;E_1,E_2)=\int_{E_1}^{E_2} j_E(\mathbf{r},\Omega;E)\,dE
$$

where $\mathbf{r}$ is position, $\Omega$ is emission direction, $E$ is photon energy, $E_1$ and $E_2$ are the lower and upper band limits, and $j_E$ is the differential photon emissivity per unit volume, solid angle, and photon energy. Unlike [bremsstrahlung spectral emissivity](name:bremsstrahlung_spectral_emissivity), this quantity has no remaining photon-energy differential.

sources.enhanced_context: Radial profile of plasma hard X-ray (HXR) emissivity in a specific energy band, reconstructed from multi-channel brightness measurements. Characterizes the spatial distribution of suprathermal electrons producing bremsstrahlung emission.
sources.leaf_definition: Radial profile of the plasma emissivity in this energy band
sources.parent_definition: Emissivity profile per energy band (assumed common to all channels used in the profile reconstruction)

NAMES.name: height_of_hard_xray_detector
NAMES.short: Full physical extent of a hard X-ray detector aperture along the local X2 axis of the detector coordinate frame, applicable to rectangular aperture geometry.
NAMES.long:
The height of a hard X-ray detector is the full dimension of the detector aperture measured along the local X2 axis of the detector coordinate frame (X1, X2, X3), where X1 and X2 lie in the nominal aperture plane and X3 is normal to the detector surface. This geometric parameter is defined for rectangular aperture geometries and represents one of two orthogonal in-plane dimensions required to fully characterize the aperture opening.

Together with [width_of_hard_xray_detector](name:width_of_hard_xray_detector), which gives the X1 extent, the height defines the total aperture area $A = h \times w$, where $h$ is the X2 extent and $w$ is the X1 extent. The aperture area enters the étendue calculation that determines the photon collection efficiency of the diagnostic channel. The analogous X2 dimension for X-ray diagnostic filter windows is filter_window_height, which follows the same local-frame X2 convention.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the aperture extent is measured in the direction of increasing X2 coordinate in the local detector frame.

sources.enhanced_context: Full width of the hard X-ray detector aperture in the X2 direction, applicable for rectangular aperture geometry (geometry_type=3). A geometric parameter for aperture characterization and etendue calculation.
sources.leaf_definition: Full width of the aperture in the X2 direction, used only if geometry_type = 3
sources.parent_definition: Detector description

NAMES.name: height_of_optical_element
NAMES.short: Height of an optical element is the usable clear-aperture extent along the second local tangential axis in the right-handed local aperture frame (X1, X2, X3), where X1 and X2 span the aperture plane and X3 is the aperture normal. It is distinct from optical-element width, the first-axis aperture extent.
NAMES.long:
Height of an optical element is the full usable clear-aperture dimension along the second local tangential axis in the right-handed local aperture frame $(X_1, X_2, X_3)$, whose unit axes satisfy $\hat{X}_1 \times \hat{X}_2 = \hat{X}_3$. The $X_1$ and $X_2$ axes span the aperture plane, and $X_3$ is the aperture-normal axis. For a rectangular optical element, it is the side length along $X_2$ of the region that can transmit, reflect, or otherwise accept radiation.

If the usable aperture is represented by the set $\mathcal{A}$ of points projected onto the local aperture plane, the height is the range of the second local coordinate over that set:

$$
h_\mathrm{opt} = \max_{\mathbf{p}\in\mathcal{A}} X_2(\mathbf{p}) - \min_{\mathbf{p}\in\mathcal{A}} X_2(\mathbf{p})
$$

where $h_\mathrm{opt}$ is the optical-element height, $\mathbf{p}$ is a point in the usable aperture, and $X_2(\mathbf{p})$ is its coordinate along the second local tangential axis.

It is distinct from [width of an optical element](name:optical_element_width), which is the corresponding extent along the first local tangential axis. For nonrectangular apertures, this quantity is a projected extent along $X_2$, not an equivalent circular diameter or aperture area; opaque mounts, bevels, clamps, and intentionally excluded or inactive regions are outside the usable aperture unless they define the aperture boundary.

sources.enhanced_context: Full width of the optical aperture in the X2 direction for a rectangular aperture geometry (geometry_type=3) of an IR camera optical element. Used to define aperture dimensions for geometric ray-tracing and pixel-to-surface mapping.
sources.leaf_definition: Full width of the aperture in the X2 direction, used only if geometry_type = 3
sources.parent_definition: Further geometrical description of the element

sources.enhanced_context: Full width of the reflector element in the X2 direction for an X-ray crystal spectrometer channel, applicable when geometry_type index is 3 (rectangular). Defines the physical extent of the optical reflector for ray-tracing and throughput calculations.
sources.leaf_definition: Full width of the object in the X2 direction, used only if geometry_type/index = 3
sources.parent_definition: Set of reflectors (optional) reflecting the light coming from the plasma towards the crystal. If empty, means that the plasma light directly arrives on the crystal.

NAMES.name: lower_bound_energy_of_detector_pixel
NAMES.short: The lower bound energy of a detector pixel is the minimum photon energy accepted by its spectral bandpass in an X-ray crystal spectrometer.
NAMES.long:
The lower bound energy of a detector pixel is the minimum photon energy at the low-energy edge of the spectral interval accepted by that pixel in an X-ray crystal spectrometer. It defines the lower endpoint of the pixel's photon-energy acceptance band.

Together with the [upper bound energy of detector pixel](name:upper_bound_energy_of_detector_pixel), it bounds the accepted photon-energy interval. The [energy of detector pixel](name:energy_of_detector_pixel) is the central or representative spectral-channel energy and need not equal the arithmetic midpoint of these two bounds.

sources.enhanced_context: Lower energy bound of the photon detection range for each pixel of the X-ray crystal spectrometer detector. Defines the minimum detectable photon energy per pixel for spectral calibration.
sources.leaf_definition: Lower energy bound for the photon detection, for each pixel (horizontal, vertical)
sources.parent_definition: Measurement channel, composed of a camera, a crystal, and (optional) a set of reflectors. The light coming from the plasma passes through the (optional) set of reflectors, then the crystal and arrives at the camera

NAMES.name: lower_photon_energy
NAMES.short: Minimum photon energy at the lower edge of a defined photon-energy acceptance interval; photons below this boundary lie outside the interval.
NAMES.long:
The lower photon-energy boundary specifies the smallest photon energy included in a defined acceptance interval. It applies to an energy-selective response or emission band and does not represent the energy of an individual detected photon.

The boundary is defined by

$$
E_{\min} = \inf\{E_\gamma \mid E_\gamma \text{ belongs to the accepted photon-energy interval}\}
$$

where $E_\gamma$ is photon energy and $E_{\min}$ is the lower interval boundary. The corresponding upper boundary is represented separately by the [upper photon energy bound](name:upper_photon_energy). Photons below $E_{\min}$ are excluded from the specified interval, regardless of whether they are physically present.

sources.enhanced_context: Lower energy detection threshold per pixel of the X-ray camera detector. Photons are registered only if their energy exceeds this pixel-specific threshold, defining the low-energy cutoff for photon counting.
sources.leaf_definition: Lower energy detection threshold on each pixel of the detector (photons are counted only if their energy is above this value)

sources.enhanced_context: Lower photon energy bound of a hard X-ray detector channel energy band. Defines the minimum photon energy threshold for counting in that band, used with the upper bound to specify the detection energy window.
sources.leaf_definition: Lower bound of the energy band
sources.parent_definition: Set of energy bands in which photons are counted by the detector

sources.enhanced_context: Lower photon energy bound of a hard X-ray emission energy band used in the emissivity profile reconstruction. Defines the lower threshold of the photon energy window for a given energy-resolved emissivity channel.
sources.leaf_definition: Lower bound of the energy band
sources.parent_definition: Emissivity profile per energy band (assumed common to all channels used in the profile reconstruction)

sources.enhanced_context: Lower photon energy bound of a soft X-ray detector channel energy band, defining the minimum photon energy for which the channel is sensitive. Together with the upper bound, it specifies the spectral window for photon detection.
sources.leaf_definition: Lower bound of the energy band
sources.parent_definition: Set of energy bands in which photons are counted by the detector

NAMES.name: neutral_fraction
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Dimensionless fraction of a hydrogen-isotope neutral population component (cold recycled or hot charge-exchange neutrals) relative to the total neutral atom population.
NAMES.long:
The neutral fraction is a dimensionless ratio bounded in $[0, 1]$ expressing the relative abundance of a defined component of the hydrogen-isotope neutral population. In the standard two-component neutral model, cold recycled neutrals and charge-exchange-born hot neutrals partition the neutral atom inventory, and their respective fractions sum to unity.

The fraction for a given component is defined as:

$$
f_{\mathrm{component}} = \frac{n_{\mathrm{component}}}{n_{\mathrm{cold}} + n_{\mathrm{hot}}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{component}}$ is the number density of the specified neutral component and $n_{\mathrm{cold}}$, $n_{\mathrm{hot}}$ are the cold and hot neutral number densities respectively.

The component fractions are inferred from Doppler-broadening analysis of visible hydrogen-isotope spectral emission lines, in which the cold and hot neutral populations contribute distinct narrow and broad Gaussian components to the line shape. The [cold_neutral_fraction](name:cold_neutral_fraction) characterizes the low-energy recycled neutral component, while [hot_neutral_fraction](name:hot_neutral_fraction) gives the charge-exchange-born component; together they form a complete partition of the neutral population. The energy threshold separating the two components must be specified by the diagnostic or population model employed.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the specified neutral component density is greater than zero.

NAMES.name: cold_neutral_fraction
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Dimensionless fraction of low-energy, cold recycled neutral atoms in a hydrogen-isotope population relative to the total cold-plus-hot neutral population.
NAMES.long:
The cold neutral fraction is a dimensionless ratio bounded in $[0, 1]$ expressing the relative abundance of the low-energy cold component of a hydrogen-isotope neutral population. It is a component of the broader [neutral_fraction](name:neutral_fraction) quantity.

For a two-component neutral model, the cold fraction is defined as:

$$
f_{\mathrm{cold}} = \frac{n_{\mathrm{cold}}}{n_{\mathrm{cold}} + n_{\mathrm{hot}}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{cold}}$ is the number density of cold neutral atoms and $n_{\mathrm{hot}}$ is the number density of charge-exchange-born hot neutral atoms.

The cold and hot components are separated by an energy threshold specified by the applicable population model. The complementary [hot_neutral_fraction](name:hot_neutral_fraction) and the cold neutral fraction sum to unity when these two components exhaust the neutral population.

sources.enhanced_context: Fraction of cold neutrals for a given hydrogen isotope, defined as n_cold/(n_cold + n_hot). Quantifies the relative population of cold (low-energy) neutrals compared to the total neutral population of that isotope from visible spectroscopy.
sources.leaf_definition: Fraction of cold neutrals for this isotope (n_cold_neutrals/(n_cold_neutrals+n_hot_neutrals))
sources.parent_definition: Set of isotopes

NAMES.name: hot_neutral_fraction
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Dimensionless fraction of the hot charge-exchange-born component of a hydrogen-isotope neutral population relative to the total neutral atom population.
NAMES.long:
The hot neutral fraction is a dimensionless ratio bounded in $[0, 1]$ expressing the relative abundance of the hot charge-exchange-born component of a hydrogen-isotope neutral population. It is a component of the broader [neutral fraction](name:neutral_fraction), distinct from the low-energy recycled component.

The fraction is defined as:

$$
f_{\mathrm{hot}} = \frac{n_{\mathrm{hot}}}{n_{\mathrm{cold}} + n_{\mathrm{hot}}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{hot}}$ is the number density of charge-exchange-born hot neutral atoms and $n_{\mathrm{cold}}$ is the number density of cold recycled neutral atoms.

Within the two-component population model, the hot and cold fractions sum to unity. The [cold neutral fraction](name:cold_neutral_fraction) represents the complementary low-energy component; the energy threshold separating the components is defined by the applicable population model.

sources.enhanced_context: Fraction of hot neutrals relative to the total neutral population for a given hydrogen isotope, defined as n_hot/(n_cold + n_hot). Used in spectroscopic isotope ratio analysis to account for charge-exchange-born fast neutrals.
sources.leaf_definition: Fraction of hot neutrals for this isotope (n_hot_neutrals/(n_cold_neutrals+n_hot_neutrals))
sources.parent_definition: Set of isotopes

NAMES.name: neutron_energy
NAMES.subject: neutron
NAMES.short: Kinetic energy carried by an individual fusion-born neutron, serving as the energy coordinate for neutron emission and transport descriptions.
NAMES.long:
The neutron kinetic energy is the translational energy carried by one neutron produced in a fusion reaction. It characterizes the energy distribution of emitted neutrons rather than their total production rate or transported power.

$$
E_n = \frac{1}{2}m_n v_n^2
$$

where $E_n$ is the neutron kinetic energy, $m_n$ is the neutron mass, and $v_n$ is the neutron speed; the result is converted from joules to eV. The quantity applies to individual fusion-born neutrons and may vary with reaction channel and emission conditions. The corresponding integrated production rate is [neutron flux](name:neutron_flux), while its local source distribution is described by [emissivity due to fusion](name:emissivity_due_to_fusion).

sources.enhanced_context: Array of discrete neutron energy values within a defined energy band of a neutron detector channel. Each value represents a specific neutron energy sampled within the band's measurement interval of the neutron spectrum.
sources.leaf_definition: Array of discrete energy values inside the band
sources.parent_definition: Set of energy bands in which neutrons are counted by the detector

sources.enhanced_context: Array of source neutron energy bin values defining the energy grid for Green function response calculations in a neutron detector. Specifies the discrete fusion neutron energies used in detector response modelling.
sources.leaf_definition: Array of source neutron energy bins
sources.parent_definition: Green function coefficients used to represent the detector response based on its field of view

NAMES.name: normalized_count_at_detector_pixel
NAMES.short: Normalized count at detector pixel is the detector-pixel count divided by a positive count-equivalent reference from the same acquisition frame. It also covers count rates when numerator and reference use identical exposure normalization.
NAMES.long:
Normalized count at detector pixel is the detector-pixel count divided by a positive count-equivalent reference from the same acquisition frame. The reference is a relative scale for that frame and must be common to the detector pixels whose normalized values are compared.

The defining ratio for detector pixel $p$ is

$$
C_\mathrm{norm}(p) = \frac{C(p)}{C_\mathrm{ref}}, \qquad C_\mathrm{ref} > 0
$$

where $C_\mathrm{norm}(p)$ is the normalized count, $C(p)$ is the [count at detector pixel], and $C_\mathrm{ref}$ is the positive count-equivalent reference for the same acquisition frame.

The same definition applies to count rates or exposure-normalized count-equivalent signals only when $C(p)$ and $C_\mathrm{ref}$ use identical time or exposure normalization. The quantity is a relative normalization; it does not specify whether $C_\mathrm{ref}$ is a total-frame, peak, mean, or externally specified reference count, and it is distinct from an absolute calibration factor.

NAMES.name: optical_element_width
NAMES.short: Full clear-aperture width of a rectangular optical-element aperture measured along its first local tangential axis.
NAMES.long:
The clear-aperture width is the usable transverse extent of a rectangular optical-element aperture measured along its first local tangential axis. The local frame is right-handed $(\hat{X}_1,\hat{X}_2,\hat{X}_3)$, with $\hat{X}_3$ normal to the aperture surface and $\hat{X}_1$, $\hat{X}_2$ tangent to it.

The width is defined by

$$
w_1 = x_{1,\max} - x_{1,\min}
$$

where $w_1$ is the aperture width and $x_{1,\max}$ and $x_{1,\min}$ are the maximum and minimum first local tangential coordinates of the clear aperture boundary.

Only the unobstructed opening is included; the surrounding frame, mounting structure, and extent normal to the aperture are excluded. The corresponding second local tangential extent is the [height of the optical element](name:height_of_optical_element).

NAMES.name: power_density_due_to_fusion
NAMES.short: Local volumetric rate of energy release from all included nuclear-fusion reaction channels, including energy carried by charged particles and neutrons.
NAMES.long:
Fusion power density is the local energy-release rate generated by nuclear-fusion reactions per unit volume. It may represent a specific reaction channel or the channel-summed quantity, with unqualified fusion power density understood as the sum over included channels.

The defining reaction-rate sum is

$$
P_{\mathrm{fus}}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{r \in \mathcal{R}} \frac{n_{a,r}(\mathbf{x})\,n_{b,r}(\mathbf{x})}{1+\delta_{a_rb_r}}\,\langle\sigma v\rangle_r\,E_r
$$

where $r$ indexes fusion channels, $n_{a,r}$ and $n_{b,r}$ are reactant number densities in m$^{-3}$, $\langle\sigma v\rangle_r$ is the reaction-rate coefficient in m$^{3}$ s$^{-1}$, $E_r$ is the energy released per reaction in joules, and $\delta_{a_rb_r}$ is one for identical reactants and zero otherwise. The deuterium–deuterium and deuterium–tritium instances are represented by [deuterium-deuterium fusion power density](name:deuterium_deuterium_power_density_due_to_fusion) and [deuterium-tritium fusion power density](name:deuterium_tritium_power_density_due_to_fusion). This energy-release quantity includes neutron and charged-particle product energy and is distinct from [fusion neutron emissivity](name:emissivity_due_to_fusion).

NAMES.name: deuterium_deuterium_power_density_due_to_fusion
NAMES.subject: deuterium_deuterium
NAMES.short: Local volumetric power density from deuterium-deuterium thermonuclear reactions, including energy carried by both the neutron-producing and proton-producing branches and characterized by their branch-weighted per-reaction Q value.
NAMES.long:
The D-D fusion power density is the local rate at which deuterium-deuterium thermonuclear reactions $D + D \rightarrow {}^3\mathrm{He} + n$ and $D + D \rightarrow T + p$ release energy per unit plasma volume. It includes both the neutron-producing branch and the proton-producing branch, so it represents branch-summed D-D fusion energy release rather than only neutron-branch energy.

For a thermal deuterium population, the branch-summed power density is

$$
P_{\mathrm{DD}}(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{1}{2} n_D(\mathbf{x})^2 \left[\langle\sigma v\rangle_n Q_n + \langle\sigma v\rangle_p Q_p\right]
$$

where $n_D$ is the deuterium ion number density in m$^{-3}$, $\langle\sigma v\rangle_n$ and $\langle\sigma v\rangle_p$ are the thermonuclear rate coefficients in m$^3$ s$^{-1}$ for the helium-3-neutron and tritium-proton branches, $Q_n$ and $Q_p$ are the corresponding branch energies in joules, and the factor $1/2$ avoids double counting identical deuteron pairs. The branch Q-values are $Q_n = 3.27\,\mathrm{MeV}$ for $D + D \rightarrow {}^3\mathrm{He} + n$ and $Q_p = 4.03\,\mathrm{MeV}$ for $D + D \rightarrow T + p$; equal branch probabilities give a branch-weighted $Q_{\mathrm{DD}} \simeq 3.65\,\mathrm{MeV}$ per D-D reaction, to be converted to joules in the equation.

The displayed expression is the thermal-thermal specialization of the definition. For beam-thermal, beam-beam, or otherwise non-Maxwellian deuteron populations, $P_{\mathrm{DD}}$ is still the branch-summed local energy-release rate, with each branch reaction-rate density multiplied by its branch energy rather than using Maxwellian rate coefficients. This quantity is the D-D channel instance of [fusion power density](name:power_density_due_to_fusion); it includes neutron and charged-particle product energy and is distinct from [fusion neutron emissivity](name:emissivity_due_to_fusion), from deposited heating of fusion products, and from [D-T fusion power density](name:deuterium_tritium_power_density_due_to_fusion).

NAMES.name: deuterium_tritium_power_density_due_to_fusion
NAMES.subject: deuterium_tritium
NAMES.short: Local volumetric power density from deuterium-tritium thermonuclear reactions, with each reaction yielding 17.6 MeV distributed between the alpha particle (3.5 MeV) and the neutron (14.1 MeV).
NAMES.long:
The D-T fusion power density is the local rate at which deuterium-tritium reactions $D + T \rightarrow {}^4\mathrm{He} + n$ deposit energy per unit plasma volume, with each event releasing $Q_\mathrm{DT} = 17.6\,\mathrm{MeV}$, partitioned as 3.5 MeV to the alpha particle and 14.1 MeV to the 14.1 MeV neutron.

The volumetric power density is defined by:

$$
P_\mathrm{DT} = n_D \, n_T \, \langle \sigma v \rangle_\mathrm{DT} \, Q_\mathrm{DT}
$$

where $n_D$ and $n_T$ are the local deuterium and tritium number densities, $\langle \sigma v \rangle_\mathrm{DT}$ is the velocity-averaged D-T fusion reactivity (maximized near ion temperature $T_i \approx 65\,\mathrm{keV}$), and $Q_\mathrm{DT} = 17.6\,\mathrm{MeV}$ is the total energy released per reaction.

The spatial distribution of $P_\mathrm{DT}$ is inferred from neutron emissivity tomography: multi-channel neutron detector signals are tomographically inverted to yield the [deuterium_tritium_emissivity_due_to_fusion](name:deuterium_tritium_emissivity_due_to_fusion) (volumetric reaction rate), which is then scaled by $Q_\mathrm{DT}$ to obtain the power density. In a balanced D-T fuel mixture at reactor-relevant temperatures of 10–20 keV, the D-T channel dominates the total [power_density_due_to_fusion](name:power_density_due_to_fusion), exceeding the [deuterium_deuterium_power_density_due_to_fusion](name:deuterium_deuterium_power_density_due_to_fusion) by roughly two orders of magnitude due to the much larger D-T reactivity at these temperatures. Peak on-axis values in near-ignition plasmas are expected to reach several MW m$^{-3}$.

NAMES.name: power_density_due_to_radiation
NAMES.short: Local volumetric rate at which plasma energy is converted into emitted electromagnetic radiation, with positive values denoting energy loss from the plasma.
NAMES.long:
Radiative power density is the local rate of electromagnetic energy emission per unit volume, summed over the radiation mechanisms included by the physical model. It describes energy leaving the plasma as radiation rather than energy transferred through collisional, conductive, or convective channels.

$$
p_{\mathrm{rad}} = \frac{\partial E_{\mathrm{rad}}}{\partial V\,\partial t}
$$

where $p_{\mathrm{rad}}$ is the radiative power density, $E_{\mathrm{rad}}$ is emitted electromagnetic energy, $V$ is plasma volume, and $t$ is time. As a radiative specialization of [power_density](name:power_density), it may include line radiation, continuum radiation, and other modeled emission processes; it excludes energy that remains in the plasma or is transferred by nonradiative channels.
NAMES.sign: Positive when energy leaves the plasma as emitted electromagnetic radiation.

NAMES.name: power_due_to_line_radiation
NAMES.short: Total electromagnetic power emitted in discrete spectral lines by bound-bound transitions of plasma atoms and ions.
NAMES.long:
Line-radiation power is the volume-integrated electromagnetic emission from bound-bound transitions of atomic and ionic populations in the plasma. It represents the energy carried by discrete spectral lines and is a radiative loss from the emitting plasma.

For downward transitions, the emitted power is defined by

$$
P_{\mathrm{line}} = \int_V \sum_s \sum_{i>j} n_{s,i} A_{s,ij} h\nu_{s,ij}\,dV
$$

where $V$ is the emitting plasma volume, $n_{s,i}$ is the population density of upper state $i$ of species $s$ in m$^{-3}$, $A_{s,ij}$ is the transition probability in s$^{-1}$, $h$ is Planck's constant, and $\nu_{s,ij}$ is the emitted-photon frequency in s$^{-1}$. The sums include all specified atomic and ionic emitters and radiative transitions.

This quantity includes line emission from hydrogenic and impurity species, but excludes continuum bremsstrahlung represented by [bremsstrahlung_power](name:bremsstrahlung_power) and other channels such as [power_due_to_synchrotron_radiation](name:power_due_to_synchrotron_radiation). It contributes to [total_plasma_radiated_power](name:total_plasma_radiated_power), while [power_due_to_impurity_radiation](name:power_due_to_impurity_radiation) covers the impurity-specific component.

sources.enhanced_context: Radiated power from atomic line radiation (Pline), representing photon emission from bound-electron transitions in impurity and hydrogen ions. A component of the total radiated power contributing to plasma energy losses.

sources.parent_definition: Radiated power from line radiation

NAMES.name: power_due_to_synchrotron_radiation
NAMES.short: Total electromagnetic power emitted by relativistic electrons as synchrotron radiation while their gyromotion is curved by the plasma magnetic field.
NAMES.long:
Power due to synchrotron radiation is the total electromagnetic power emitted by relativistic electrons as synchrotron radiation while their gyromotion is curved by the plasma magnetic field. It is a mechanism-specific contribution to the plasma radiative power and refers to emitted radiation, not stored electromagnetic energy.

For an emitting plasma volume $V$, the quantity is defined by the volume integral of the local synchrotron volumetric emissivity:

$$
P_{\mathrm{syn}} = \int_V p_{\mathrm{syn}}(\mathbf{x})\,dV
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{syn}}$ is the power due to synchrotron radiation, $p_{\mathrm{syn}}(\mathbf{x})$ is the local synchrotron volumetric emissivity formed from the relativistic electron phase-space distribution and the local magnetic field, $\mathbf{x}$ denotes position, and $dV$ is a volume element.

This quantity includes only synchrotron emission and excludes [bremsstrahlung power](name:bremsstrahlung_power) and [power due to line radiation](name:power_due_to_line_radiation). It denotes gross electromagnetic power emitted by the radiating electrons and is distinct from net synchrotron power escaping a plasma-facing or material boundary after reabsorption or reflection.

NAMES.name: power_of_soft_xray_detector
NAMES.short: Power of a soft X-ray detector is the band-integrated radiant power admitted by a detector channel after its spectral selection. It includes the projected-area factor for rays entering the detector aperture and is not a photon-energy content.
NAMES.long:
Power of a soft X-ray detector is the radiant power admitted by one soft-X-ray detector channel after the channel's photon-energy selection and geometric acceptance. It is an aperture- and direction-integrated scalar formed from the incident soft-X-ray radiance, the channel throughput, and the detector projected-area factor.

A radiometric definition is:

$$
P_\mathrm{SXR} = \int_{\Delta E_\mathrm{SXR}} \int_A \int_{\Omega_A} L_E(\mathbf{x},\hat{\mathbf{s}},E)\,T(\mathbf{x},\hat{\mathbf{s}},E)\,\max\!\left(0,\hat{\mathbf{n}}_d(\mathbf{x})\cdot\hat{\mathbf{s}}\right)\,d\Omega\,dA\,dE
$$

where $\Delta E_\mathrm{SXR}$ is the photon-energy interval admitted by the channel, $A$ is the active entrance aperture, $\Omega_A$ is the set of admitted directions, $L_E$ is the directional soft-X-ray spectral radiance incident on the aperture before channel spectral selection, $T$ is the channel spectral throughput, $\hat{\mathbf{n}}_d$ is the detector entrance normal pointing toward the admitted source half-space, and $\hat{\mathbf{s}}$ is the direction from the aperture point toward the source.

This quantity is a collected radiant power, not a stored photon energy or a spectral-density quantity. The positive-part projection defines the projected-area convention: rays from the non-admitted side of the aperture contribute zero rather than negative collected power. It is distinct from [spectral radiance of a soft-X-ray detector](name:spectral_radiance_of_soft_xray_detector), which denotes radiance rather than aperture-integrated power.

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_aperture
NAMES.short: Radial coordinate of the aperture is the major-radius R coordinate of the geometric center of an aperture in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, where R is the perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis measured outward. It locates the aperture center along the radial axis and is a non-negative distance.
NAMES.long:
Radial coordinate of the aperture is the major-radius coordinate $R$ of the geometric center of an aperture in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis measured outward, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle increasing counter-clockwise viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is the vertical height. As a distance from the symmetry axis, $R \ge 0$.

This is the radial component of the aperture-center position and is paired with [toroidal_coordinate_of_aperture](name:toroidal_coordinate_of_aperture) and [vertical_coordinate_of_aperture](name:vertical_coordinate_of_aperture), which give the other two coordinates of the same geometric center. It encodes only the radial position of the center: two aperture centers at different toroidal angles but the same distance from the symmetry axis share the same radial coordinate. It is distinct from the signed horizontal Cartesian component x_coordinate_of_aperture, and it does not encode aperture size, which is represented separately by [radius_of_diagnostic_aperture](name:radius_of_diagnostic_aperture).

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_detector_pixel
NAMES.short: Major-radius coordinate of a detector pixel’s geometric center, locating the pixel relative to the machine symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The major-radius coordinate of a detector pixel is the perpendicular distance from the machine symmetry axis to the pixel’s geometric center. It is the pixel-specific counterpart of the general [radial coordinate](name:radial_coordinate).

In the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$ basis, with $\hat{z}=\hat{Z}$, it is defined by

$$
R_{\mathrm{pix}} = \sqrt{x_{\mathrm{pix}}^2+y_{\mathrm{pix}}^2}
$$

where $R_{\mathrm{pix}}$ is the major radius and $x_{\mathrm{pix}}$ and $y_{\mathrm{pix}}$ are the horizontal Cartesian coordinates of the pixel center, each measured in m. Equivalently, it is the $R$ coordinate in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

The quantity refers to the pixel center and does not represent the pixel width, radial extent, or the position of the complete detector.

NAMES.name: radial_coordinate_of_filter_window
NAMES.short: Radial coordinate of a filter window is the non-negative major-radius coordinate of the window's geometric center in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Radial coordinate of a filter window is the major-radius coordinate of the geometric center of that window in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is distance from the toroidal symmetry axis, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. The geometric center is the center of the filter-window element itself, not the center of another aperture or support structure.

For a filter-window center with Cartesian coordinates $(x_\mathrm{fw}, y_\mathrm{fw}, z_\mathrm{fw})$ in the right-handed Cartesian $(x, y, z)$ frame with $\hat{z}=\hat{Z}$, the radial coordinate is

$$
R_\mathrm{fw} = \sqrt{x_\mathrm{fw}^2 + y_\mathrm{fw}^2}
$$

where the Cartesian origin lies on the toroidal symmetry axis and $R_\mathrm{fw}$ is non-negative.

$R_\mathrm{fw}$ specifies only the major-radius component of the filter-window position. The paired angular and vertical position coordinates are [toroidal coordinate of filter window] and [vertical coordinate of filter window](name:vertical_coordinate_of_filter_window); size quantities such as [radius of filter](name:radius_of_filter) describe spatial extent rather than center position.

NAMES.name: radiance_at_spectral_line
NAMES.short: Directional radiative power associated with an identified spectral transition, integrated over its line interval and normalized by projected area and accepted solid angle.
NAMES.long:
Spectral-line radiance is the directional radiative output associated with one identified transition, integrated over the wavelength interval assigned to that line and resolved by projected area and solid angle.

The energy-basis line radiance is defined by

$$
L_\ell = \int_{\Delta\lambda_\ell} L_\lambda(\lambda)\,d\lambda = \frac{dP_\ell}{dA_\perp\,d\Omega}
$$

where $L_\ell$ is line radiance, $L_\lambda$ is spectral radiance, $\Delta\lambda_\ell$ is the assigned line interval, $P_\ell$ is radiant power from the transition, $A_\perp$ is projected area normal to the viewing direction, and $\Omega$ is solid angle. The energy-basis quantity is distinct from photon-number [spectral radiance](name:spectral_radiance); a resolved component such as [motional-Stark radiance at a spectral line](name:motional_stark_radiance_at_spectral_line) may use the photon-count representation and is not numerically interchangeable with this energy basis.

NAMES.name: radiance_of_soft_xray_detector
NAMES.short: Band-integrated electromagnetic radiance incident on a soft X-ray detector, equal to radiant power per projected detector area per incident solid angle over the detector photon-energy acceptance. It names the common non-energy-differential detector radiance, independent of how the accepted band is represented.
NAMES.long:
Radiance of a soft-X-ray detector is the band-integrated electromagnetic radiance incident on the detector aperture over the detector photon-energy acceptance. It is the radiant power carried by accepted soft-X-ray photons per projected detector area normal to the incident ray bundle and per incident solid angle.

The defining differential relation is

$$
L = \frac{d^2 P_{\mathcal{B}}}{dA_\perp \, d\Omega}
$$

where $L$ is the detector-incident radiance, $P_{\mathcal{B}}$ is the radiant power in the detector photon-energy acceptance $\mathcal{B}$, $A_\perp$ is the detector area projected perpendicular to the incident ray bundle, and $\Omega$ is the incident solid angle.

This quantity is an accepted-band radiance, not a photon-energy-differential spectral density, detector responsivity, count rate, or electronic signal. Related names such as [spectral radiance of a soft-X-ray detector](name:spectral_radiance_of_soft_xray_detector) may indicate that an energy-dependent radiance has been integrated over the detector acceptance; because the detector type is already soft-X-ray, that qualifier is not an additional soft-X-ray specialization.

NAMES.name: radius_of_bragg_crystal
NAMES.short: Geometric distance from the center of a circular Bragg-crystal aperture to the edge of its active diffracting surface.
NAMES.long:
The Bragg-crystal aperture radius is the transverse geometric extent of the circular active diffracting surface, measured from its center to its circumferential edge. It describes aperture size rather than the curvature of the crystal substrate.

For a boundary point of the aperture, the radius is defined by

$$
r_{\mathrm{ap}} = \left\lVert \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{edge}} - \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{center}} \right\rVert
$$

where $r_{\mathrm{ap}}$ is the aperture radius, and $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{edge}}$ and $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{center}}$ are position vectors in the aperture plane, with $r_{\mathrm{ap}}$ expressed in meters.

For an ideal circular aperture, this distance is the same for every boundary point. It is analogous to the [radius of a diagnostic aperture](name:radius_of_diagnostic_aperture), but must not be confused with the [toroidal curvature of the Bragg crystal](name:toroidal_curvature_of_bragg_crystal) or its [vertical curvature](name:vertical_curvature_of_bragg_crystal).

NAMES.name: radius_of_filter
NAMES.short: Geometric radius of the circular aperture associated with a diagnostic filter window, measured from its center to the circumferential edge.
NAMES.long:
The filter-window aperture radius is the Euclidean distance from the aperture center to any point on its circular boundary. It characterizes the opening geometry of the filter window and is non-negative.

$$
r = \left\|\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{edge}}-\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{center}}\right\|
$$

where $r$ is the aperture radius, and $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{edge}}$ and $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{center}}$ are the position vectors of a boundary point and the aperture center, respectively.

This quantity applies specifically to a circular filter-window aperture and is distinct from the [radius of a diagnostic aperture](name:radius_of_diagnostic_aperture) when that aperture is not part of a filter window.

NAMES.name: reference_calibration_wavelength_of_spectrometer_channel
NAMES.short: Reference calibration wavelength of a spectrometer channel is the vacuum-wavelength intercept of the channel's linear detector-pixel dispersion relation at pixel coordinate k = 0.
NAMES.long:
Reference calibration wavelength of a spectrometer channel is the vacuum wavelength assigned by a linear wavelength calibration to detector-pixel coordinate $k=0$. It is the intercept term of the affine relation between detector-pixel coordinate and vacuum wavelength for that channel.

The linear calibration relation is

$$
\lambda(k) = g k + \lambda_0
$$

where $\lambda(k)$ is the vacuum wavelength at detector-pixel coordinate $k$, $k$ is a dimensionless detector-pixel coordinate, $g$ is the signed dispersion coefficient in $\mathrm{m}$ per pixel-coordinate unit, and $\lambda_0$ is the reference calibration wavelength.

This quantity is the intercept $\lambda_0$, not the dispersion coefficient $g$ and not the wavelength evaluated at any nonzero detector-pixel coordinate. The sign of $g$ encodes whether vacuum wavelength increases or decreases with increasing $k$; the reference calibration wavelength itself is a wavelength value at the chosen coordinate origin.

NAMES.name: roughness_of_optical_element
NAMES.short: Roughness of an optical element is an optical roughness parameter that quantifies redistribution of reflected radiation between ideal specular and ideal diffuse behavior: 0 denotes ideal specular reflection and 1 denotes ideal diffuse reflection.
NAMES.long:
Roughness of an optical element is an optical roughness parameter that quantifies how the element partitions reflected radiation between a specular component and a diffuse component. The endpoint value zero denotes ideal specular reflection, and the endpoint value one denotes ideal diffuse reflection.

The parameter is defined from the reflected-power partition as

$$
P_{\mathrm{refl}} = P_{\mathrm{spec}} + P_{\mathrm{diff}}, \qquad r = \frac{P_{\mathrm{diff}}}{P_{\mathrm{refl}}} = 1 - \frac{P_{\mathrm{spec}}}{P_{\mathrm{refl}}}, \qquad 0 \le r \le 1
$$

where $r$ is the roughness parameter, and $P_{\mathrm{refl}}$, $P_{\mathrm{spec}}$, and $P_{\mathrm{diff}}$ are radiant powers in watts for the total reflected, ideal-specular, and diffuse reflected components under the same incident radiation and optical state.

This quantity is not a metrological surface-height roughness such as an rms height or correlation length. Intermediate values specify the diffuse fraction of reflected power in the stated partition; they do not by themselves prescribe the angular distribution of the diffuse component, require Lambertian scattering, or include transmitted or absorbed power.

NAMES.name: second_local_tangential_coordinate_of_bragg_crystal
NAMES.short: Signed coordinate of a Bragg-crystal outline vertex along the second local tangential axis of the crystal-local Cartesian (X1, X2) frame.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the signed position of a vertex on the Bragg-crystal outline, resolved along the crystal-local second tangential direction. It describes the crystal geometry in the local planar Cartesian frame $(X_1, X_2)$ rather than in the machine cylindrical frame.

For a vertex position vector $\mathbf{r}$ and local-frame origin $\mathbf{r}_0$, the coordinate is defined by:

$$
x_2 = (\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}_0) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}_2
$$

where $x_2$ is the second local tangential coordinate, $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_2$ is the unit vector along the second local tangential axis, and $\mathbf{r}_0$ is the origin of the crystal-local frame. Together with the [first local tangential coordinate of the Bragg crystal](name:first_local_tangential_coordinate_of_bragg_crystal), it specifies the in-plane location of the outline vertex.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the vertex displacement from the crystal-local origin has a positive projection along the second local tangential unit vector $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_2$.

NAMES.name: second_local_tangential_coordinate_of_diagnostic_aperture
NAMES.short: Signed position of a vertex on a diagnostic-aperture boundary along the second tangent of the object-local (X1, X2) aperture-plane frame.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the signed second local tangential coordinate of a vertex on a diagnostic-aperture boundary. It locates the vertex within the aperture plane and, together with the first local tangential coordinate, defines the boundary geometry.

The coordinate is defined by

$$
x_2 = (\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}_0) \cdot \mathbf{e}_2
$$

where $\mathbf{r}$ is the vertex position, $\mathbf{r}_0$ is the origin of the local aperture frame, and $\mathbf{e}_2$ is the second local tangential unit vector. The right-handed object-local basis $(\mathbf{e}_1, \mathbf{e}_2, \mathbf{e}_3)$ uses $\mathbf{e}_3$ as the plasma-facing normal, $\mathbf{e}_1$ as the more-horizontal tangent directed toward increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, and $\mathbf{e}_2 = \mathbf{e}_3 \times \mathbf{e}_1$.

The quantity applies only to the diagnostic-aperture boundary and is distinct from corresponding coordinates of filters, detector outlines, or other optical objects. The same local-axis convention is used by [second local tangential coordinate of filter](name:second_local_tangential_coordinate_of_filter).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the vertex lies from the local origin in the direction of $\mathbf{e}_2 = \mathbf{e}_3 \times \mathbf{e}_1$.

NAMES.name: second_local_tangential_coordinate_of_filter
NAMES.short: Second local tangential coordinate of a filter boundary point is the signed position of that point along the filter's second in-plane basis direction in the object-local planar frame attached to the filter.
NAMES.long:
Second local tangential coordinate of a filter boundary point is the signed scalar coordinate obtained by projecting the point's displacement from the filter local-frame origin onto the filter's second local tangential direction. It is paired with the [first local tangential coordinate of a filter](name:first_local_tangential_coordinate_of_filter) to locate points in the filter plane.

The coordinate is defined by the projection

$$
u_{2,f} = (\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}_{0,f}) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{t}}_{2,f}
$$

where $u_{2,f}$ is this coordinate, $\mathbf{r}$ is the position vector of the filter boundary point, $\mathbf{r}_{0,f}$ is the filter local-frame origin, and $\hat{\mathbf{t}}_{2,f}$ is the second local tangential unit vector of the filter.

The filter local frame is object-local: $\hat{\mathbf{t}}_{1,f}$ and $\hat{\mathbf{t}}_{2,f}$ lie in the filter plane. The first local tangential unit vector is chosen with positive projection along increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame; the second local tangential unit vector completes the oriented in-plane basis with the filter normal, so that $\hat{\mathbf{t}}_{1,f} \times \hat{\mathbf{t}}_{2,f}$ points along the positive filter normal. This quantity refers to the filter boundary itself, not to the [second local tangential coordinate of a filter window](name:second_local_tangential_coordinate_of_filter_window).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the displacement from the filter local-frame origin to the point has positive projection on the second local tangential unit vector of the filter.

NAMES.name: second_local_tangential_coordinate_of_filter_window
NAMES.short: Signed position of a filter-window outline vertex along the second local tangential axis, which completes the window-local (X1, X2) frame.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the signed position of a filter-window outline vertex projected onto the second local tangential axis. Together with the [first local tangential coordinate of the filter window](name:first_local_tangential_coordinate_of_filter_window), it specifies the window aperture boundary in the object-local planar $(X_1,X_2)$ frame.

The coordinate is defined by

$$
x_2 = (\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}_0)\mathbin{\cdot}\hat{\mathbf{e}}_2
$$

where $\mathbf{r}$ is the outline-vertex position, $\mathbf{r}_0$ is the origin of the window-local frame, and $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_2$ is the second local tangential unit vector. The vector $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_2$ completes the right-handed window-local triad $(\hat{\mathbf{e}}_1,\hat{\mathbf{e}}_2,\hat{\mathbf{e}}_3)$, with $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_1$ the first local tangential direction and $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_3$ the window-normal direction. This quantity describes the filter window rather than the corresponding filter boundary, whose analogous coordinate is [second local tangential coordinate of the filter](name:second_local_tangential_coordinate_of_filter).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the displacement from $\mathbf{r}_0$ points along $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_2$.

NAMES.name: second_local_tangential_coordinate_of_hard_xray_detector
NAMES.short: Signed coordinate of a hard X-ray detector outline vertex along the second local tangential axis of the right-handed detector-local Cartesian basis (first local tangential, second local tangential, local normal).
NAMES.long:
Second local tangential coordinate of a hard X-ray detector is the signed scalar coordinate of a detector outline vertex along the detector-local second tangential direction. It is defined in the right-handed object-local Cartesian basis $(\hat{\mathbf e}_1, \hat{\mathbf e}_2, \hat{\mathbf e}_3)$, where $\hat{\mathbf e}_1$ is the first local tangential unit vector, $\hat{\mathbf e}_3$ is the detector-local normal unit vector, and $\hat{\mathbf e}_2 = \hat{\mathbf e}_3 \times \hat{\mathbf e}_1$.

The coordinate $q_2$ of a vertex at position $\mathbf r$ is the signed projection of its displacement from the detector-local origin:

$$
q_2 = (\mathbf r - \mathbf r_0) \cdot \hat{\mathbf e}_2
$$

where $\mathbf r_0$ is the detector-local origin and $\hat{\mathbf e}_2$ is the second local tangential unit vector.

Only the component along $\hat{\mathbf e}_2$ is included. The companion coordinate along $\hat{\mathbf e}_1$ is the [first local tangential coordinate of a hard X-ray detector]; neither quantity is a radial, toroidal, or vertical component in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the vertex displacement from the detector-local origin is toward $\hat{\mathbf e}_3 \times \hat{\mathbf e}_1$.

NAMES.name: second_local_tangential_coordinate_of_optical_element
NAMES.short: Second local tangential coordinate of an optical element is the signed coordinate of a point on the optical-element surface along the second in-plane tangential axis, measured from the aperture vertex. It belongs to the element-local frame formed by the first local tangential, second local tangential, and plasma-facing surface-normal axes.
NAMES.long:
Second local tangential coordinate of an optical element is the signed coordinate of a point on the optical-element surface along the second in-plane tangential axis, measured from the aperture vertex. It is one of the two surface-tangent coordinates of the optical-element local triad and is distinct from the [first local tangential coordinate of the optical element](name:first_local_tangential_coordinate_of_optical_element).

The coordinate is the projection of the surface-point displacement from the aperture vertex onto the second local tangential unit vector:

$$
\eta_2 = (\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}_\mathrm{v}) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}_2
$$

where $\eta_2$ is the second local tangential coordinate of the optical element, $\mathbf{r}$ is the position vector of the surface point, $\mathbf{r}_\mathrm{v}$ is the position vector of the aperture vertex, and $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_2$ is the second local tangential unit vector.

The object-local triad $(\hat{\mathbf{e}}_1, \hat{\mathbf{e}}_2, \hat{\mathbf{e}}_3)$ is right-handed. For a steered optical element, $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_3$ is the plasma-facing surface-normal unit vector, $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_1$ is the first local tangential unit vector oriented with positive projection along increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ increases counterclockwise when viewed from $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height; the second local tangential unit vector is $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_2 = \hat{\mathbf{e}}_3 \times \hat{\mathbf{e}}_1$. This coordinate is not a coordinate along $Z$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame unless the optical-element orientation makes the second local tangential axis coincide with that direction.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the displacement from the optical-element aperture vertex has a positive projection in the $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_3 \times \hat{\mathbf{e}}_1$ direction.

NAMES.name: second_local_tangential_coordinate_of_soft_xray_detector
NAMES.short: Signed coordinate of a soft X-ray detector outline vertex along the second local tangential (X2) axis of the detector-local right-handed Cartesian frame.
NAMES.long: The second local tangential coordinate $x_2$ locates a vertex of the soft X-ray detector outline along the X2 axis of the detector-local frame. In this right-handed Cartesian triad, X3 is the detector's outward plasma-facing surface normal, X1 is the first local tangential axis directed more horizontally toward the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$, and X2 = X3 $\times$ X1 completes the right-handed triad. The ordered set of $(x_1, x_2)$ vertex pairs defines the detector boundary polygon in the X1–X2 plane; $x_1$ is given by [first local tangential coordinate](name:first_local_tangential_coordinate_of_soft_xray_detector). Together the two tangential coordinates fully specify the detector aperture geometry in the object-local frame, distinct from the aperture outline given by [second local tangential coordinate of a diagnostic aperture](name:second_local_tangential_coordinate_of_diagnostic_aperture).

NAMES.name: spectral_absorptivity_of_filter
NAMES.short: Wavelength-resolved fraction of incident photon flux absorbed within filter material at each photon wavelength, excluding transmitted and reflected photons.
NAMES.long:
Spectral absorptivity of a filter is the fraction of incident photons at a specified wavelength that are absorbed within the filter material. It describes absorption alone, rather than transmission, reflection, scattering, or detector registration.

The spectral absorptivity is defined by

$$
\alpha(\lambda) = \frac{\Phi_{\mathrm{abs}}(\lambda)}{\Phi_{\mathrm{inc}}(\lambda)}
$$

where $\alpha(\lambda)$ is the absorptivity, $\Phi_{\mathrm{abs}}(\lambda)$ is the absorbed spectral photon-flux density, $\Phi_{\mathrm{inc}}(\lambda)$ is the incident spectral photon-flux density, and $\lambda$ is photon wavelength measured in meters; the two flux densities have units of photons per square meter per second per meter. The value lies between zero and one wherever the incident flux is nonzero.

The broadband [absorptivity of a filter](name:absorptivity_of_filter) is the incident-flux-weighted average of $\alpha(\lambda)$. This quantity is distinct from [spectral efficiency of a filter](name:spectral_efficiency_of_filter), which includes the probability that an incident photon produces a registered detection event.

NAMES.name: spectral_calibration_factor_of_spectrometer
NAMES.short: Wavelength-channel calibration coefficient that converts a spectrometer photon count rate into absolute photon spectral radiance density at the channel’s selected wavelength.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the wavelength-specific component of the [calibration factor of a spectrometer](name:calibration_factor_of_spectrometer). It converts a dark-corrected photon count rate from one channel into absolute photon spectral radiance density at that channel's wavelength.

For channel wavelength $\lambda_c$, the calibrated spectral radiance density is defined by

$$
L_\lambda(\lambda_c) = C(\lambda_c) S(\lambda_c)
$$

where $L_\lambda$ is photon spectral radiance density, $C(\lambda_c)$ is this calibration factor, and $S(\lambda_c)$ is the dark-corrected count rate in s$^{-1}$. The wavelength $\lambda_c$ is the channel value defined by [wavelength of spectrometer channel](name:wavelength_of_spectrometer_channel). The coefficient includes the channel's wavelength-dependent optical throughput, detector response, etendue, and effective spectral-width normalization; its spectral response is related to the [effective spectral width of a spectrometer channel](name:effective_spectral_width_of_spectrometer_channel).

NAMES.name: spectral_efficiency_of_filter
NAMES.short: Wavelength-resolved probability that a photon incident on a diagnostic filter produces a registered detection event after wavelength-dependent transmission and detection losses.
NAMES.long:
The wavelength-resolved filter efficiency is the conditional probability that a photon arriving at the filter input with wavelength $\lambda$ produces a registered detection event. It includes the wavelength-dependent transmission and conversion losses of the filter, optical path, detector, and readout chain, and is distinct from material absorptivity alone.

$$
\eta_{\mathrm{filter}}(\lambda)=P(\mathrm{registered\ detection}\mid\mathrm{photon\ incident\ at\ wavelength\ }\lambda)
$$

Here, $\lambda$ is the photon wavelength and $P$ denotes a conditional probability. The parent [efficiency of filter](name:efficiency_of_filter) is the incident-spectrum-weighted average of this response, with weighting supplied by the [incident spectral flux](name:incident_spectral_flux) over the relevant wavelength range. Consequently, this quantity is dimensionless and bounded from 0 to 1.
