NAMES.name: spectral_etendue_of_spectrometer_channel
NAMES.short: Response-weighted linear optical phase-space acceptance of a spectrometer channel, retaining its aperture extent and accepted ray directions while incorporating the channel’s wavelength response.
NAMES.long:
Spectral etendue is the wavelength-response-weighted linear optical phase-space acceptance of a spectrometer channel. It extends the parent [etendue of a spectrometer channel](name:etendue_of_spectrometer_channel) by incorporating the channel’s spectral response without changing the linear-aperture basis.

$$
G_{\mathrm{spec}} = \frac{\int G(\lambda)\,R(\lambda)\,d\lambda}{\int R(\lambda')\,d\lambda'}
$$

where $G(\lambda)$ is the channel etendue at wavelength $\lambda$, $R(\lambda)$ is the spectral response, and $\lambda'$ is a dummy wavelength variable used for normalization. This response-weighted quantity is distinct from [effective spectral etendue of a spectrometer channel](name:effective_spectral_etendue_of_spectrometer_channel), which represents the corresponding area-solid-angle acceptance.

NAMES.name: spectral_flux_of_spectrometer_channel
NAMES.short: Raw photon-equivalent detection-event rate from a spectrometer channel observing a selected spectral line or wavelength passband, before absolute radiometric calibration.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the uncalibrated photon-equivalent count rate produced by a spectrometer channel for a selected spectral line or wavelength passband. It is the raw detection rate represented by [flux of spectrometer channel](name:flux_of_spectrometer_channel), before conversion to absolute spectral radiance.

The rate is defined by

$$
F = \frac{dN}{dt}
$$

where $N$ is the accumulated photon-equivalent detection count and $t$ is time. The quantity includes the channel response and detection-chain efficiency implicit in the registered count, but it is not an absolute radiometric flux or spectral radiance; those require a separate calibration factor.

NAMES.name: spectral_radiance
NAMES.short: Photon-number spectral radiance of plasma emission, giving the photon rate per projected collecting area, solid angle, and wavelength interval along a viewing direction.
NAMES.long:
Photon-number spectral radiance quantifies the wavelength-resolved photon emission received from plasma along a specified viewing direction. Each photon contributes one count, independent of its energy.

It is defined by

$$
L^{(N)}_\lambda = \frac{\mathrm{d}^4 N_\gamma}{\mathrm{d}t\,\mathrm{d}A_\perp\,\mathrm{d}\Omega\,\mathrm{d}\lambda}
$$

where $N_\gamma$ is photon number, $t$ is time, $A_\perp$ is projected collecting area normal to the viewing direction, $\Omega$ is solid angle, and $\lambda$ is wavelength. Unlike [brightness of visible camera](name:brightness_of_visible_camera), which is integrated over an admitted band, this quantity retains spectral dependence; [radiance at spectral line](name:radiance_at_spectral_line) instead represents radiative power integrated over an identified line interval.

NAMES.name: spectral_radiance_of_soft_xray_detector
NAMES.short: Power radiance of soft X-ray emission incident on a detector channel, defined as detected power per unit area per unit solid angle and integrated over the detector energy band.
NAMES.long:
Soft X-ray spectral radiance is the detected electromagnetic power from plasma emission per unit detector area per unit solid angle, integrated over one or more energy bands defined by the detector channel's filter or spectral response. It quantifies the power flux delivered along a specific line of sight through the plasma and is distinct from photon radiance; the companion quantity brightness_of_soft_xray_detector expresses the same measurement in photons per second rather than in power units.

The defining relation is:

$$
L = \frac{d^2 P}{dA \, d\Omega}
$$

where $P$ is the detected power, $dA$ is the active detector area element, and $d\Omega$ is the solid-angle element subtended by the field of view; integration over the detector energy passband is implicit in this band-integrated form.

Soft X-ray power radiance is measured with semiconductor photodiodes placed behind metallic foil filters that select an effective energy passband, commonly in the range 0.1–10 keV. Fan arrays of such channels enable tomographic inversion to recover the volumetric soft X-ray emissivity profile, supporting impurity transport studies, MHD mode tracking, and sawtooth monitoring. Multiplying by the detector étendue (area times solid angle) recovers the total channel power given by [power_of_soft_xray_detector](name:power_of_soft_xray_detector). The hard X-ray power radiance analog following the same spatial radiance definition at higher photon energies is spectral_radiance_of_hard_xray_detector.

NAMES.name: spectral_wavelength_of_optical_element
NAMES.short: Wavelength coordinate axis defining the spectral sampling grid at which the optical properties or instrument response of a diagnostic optical element are characterized.
NAMES.long:
This quantity specifies the set of photon wavelength values constituting the spectral axis used to sample the wavelength-resolved properties of a diagnostic optical element, such as its transmission, reflectivity, absorption, refractive index, or instrument response function. It applies across a wide range of diagnostic types, from crystal X-ray spectrometers and soft or hard X-ray filter windows to visible-band filter spectrometers, wherever the element's spectral behavior must be characterized on a defined wavelength grid.

The photon wavelength $\lambda$ relates to photon energy $E$ by

$$
\lambda = \frac{hc}{E}
$$

where $h$ is Planck's constant and $c$ is the speed of light in vacuum. For hard X-ray filter materials the grid spans roughly 0.001–0.1 nm; for soft X-ray diagnostics, 0.1–50 nm; for visible-band spectrometers, 380–780 nm.

This spectral coordinate is the companion axis to wavelength-resolved material properties such as [spectral_refractive_index_of_optical_element](name:spectral_refractive_index_of_optical_element) and feeds into the derivation of quantities like [effective_spectral_width_of_spectrometer_channel](name:effective_spectral_width_of_spectrometer_channel). For identifying individual spectral features resolved within this grid, the central rest-frame vacuum wavelength of a transition is given by [wavelength_of_spectral_line](name:wavelength_of_spectral_line).

NAMES.name: surface_area_of_filter
NAMES.short: Geometric area of the actual filter-window surface that intercepts or transmits incoming radiation, including surface curvature rather than only its projected aperture.
NAMES.long:
The filter-window surface area is the geometric area of the actual material surface associated with a radiation filter and participating in interception or transmission of incoming radiation. It is the window-specific component of the parent [filter area](name:area_of_filter).

The area is defined by integrating the surface-area element over the filter-window surface:

$$
A_w = \int_{S_w} dS
$$

where $A_w$ is the filter-window area, $S_w$ is the actual window surface, and $dS$ is an infinitesimal surface-area element.

This quantity includes curvature of the material surface and excludes a planar projected aperture area or areas belonging to other filter components.

NAMES.name: surface_roughness_of_optical_element
NAMES.short: Dimensionless parameter describing how microscopic texture on an optical element redistributes reflected radiation between specular and diffuse scattering.
NAMES.long:
Surface roughness of an optical element is a phenomenological parameter describing the scattering behavior of its material surface. It quantifies the partition of reflected radiation between an ideal specular component and an ideal diffuse component.

The parameter is bounded by $0 \leq r_s \leq 1$, where $r_s$ is the surface roughness parameter: $r_s=0$ denotes perfectly specular reflection and $r_s=1$ denotes perfectly diffuse reflection. Its value may depend on wavelength when the surface scattering behavior is wavelength-dependent.

This quantity is the surface-specific component of the broader [roughness of an optical element](name:roughness_of_optical_element) parameter and must not be interpreted as a geometric surface height, curvature, or texture amplitude.

NAMES.name: thickness_of_bragg_crystal
NAMES.short: Physical thickness of a Bragg crystal is the normal material thickness measured between its opposing surfaces along the local surface normal. It excludes the X-ray ray-path length through the crystal, which depends on incidence geometry.
NAMES.long:
Physical thickness of a Bragg crystal is the geometric separation of its opposing crystal surfaces measured along the local surface normal. It is a property of the crystal body, independent of the direction taken by an incident or diffracted X-ray ray.

The local normal thickness is defined by

$$
t = \left| (\mathbf{x}_2 - \mathbf{x}_1) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}} \right|
$$

where $t$ is the Bragg-crystal thickness in meters, $\mathbf{x}_1$ and $\mathbf{x}_2$ are corresponding points on the two opposing crystal surfaces in meters, and $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ is the unit normal to the local surface at $\mathbf{x}_1$.

This quantity excludes the oblique material path length of an X-ray through the crystal; for an ideal flat slab that path length also depends on the ray angle relative to the local normal. It is distinct from [bragg_crystal_width](name:bragg_crystal_width) and height_of_bragg_crystal, which are tangential dimensions of the crystal element.

NAMES.name: thickness_of_filter
NAMES.short: Physical thickness of a diagnostic filter window material, which governs the energy-dependent photon attenuation and the effective spectral passband of X-ray detector channels.
NAMES.long:
The filter window thickness is the geometric extent of the absorbing filter material measured along the direction normal to the filter surface, coinciding with the photon beam propagation path. Together with the material composition, it sets the Beer-Lambert transmission spectrum of the filter, controlling the low-energy photon cutoff and shaping the spectral sensitivity of the detector channel.

The photon transmission through a filter of thickness $d$ at photon energy $E$ follows:

$$
T(E) = \exp(-\mu(E)\, d)
$$

where $\mu(E)$ is the energy-dependent linear attenuation coefficient of the filter material in m$^{-1}$ and $d$ is the filter thickness. Increasing $d$ suppresses low-energy photons more strongly, raising the effective energy cutoff of the diagnostic.

The thickness is a fixed hardware parameter established at instrument construction and determined by the required spectral selection. In soft X-ray diagnostics, filter foils span from tens of nanometers to tens of micrometers; hard X-ray diagnostics may use material layers from tens of micrometers to millimeters. The wavelength-resolved photon absorption that results from this thickness is captured by [spectral absorptivity of the filter](name:spectral_absorptivity_of_filter), while the lateral extent of the filter opening is characterized by [radius_of_filter](name:radius_of_filter). The analogous geometric parameter for the dispersing element is [thickness_of_bragg_crystal](name:thickness_of_bragg_crystal).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the filter material thickness is measured from the beam-entry face to the beam-exit face along the direction of photon propagation.

NAMES.name: thickness_of_optical_element
NAMES.short: Perpendicular separation between the opposing optical surfaces of an optical element, measured along the local surface normal as its physical material thickness.
NAMES.long:
The physical thickness of an optical element is the separation between corresponding points on its opposing optical surfaces, measured along the local surface normal. It describes the material dimension of the element rather than its optical path length, focal length, or clear-aperture dimensions.

For corresponding front- and back-surface position vectors, the thickness is defined by

$$
t = \left|\left(\mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{back}}-\mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{front}}\right)\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}}\right|
$$

where $t$ is the thickness in m, $\mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{front}}$ and $\mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{back}}$ are the surface position vectors, and $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ is the local unit normal. For a nonuniform or curved element, the definition applies locally along the corresponding surface normal.

This geometric definition is specialized for a [Bragg crystal](name:thickness_of_bragg_crystal) or a [diagnostic filter](name:thickness_of_filter) when those components are the optical element.

NAMES.name: time_derivative_of_bremsstrahlung_count_at_detector_pixel
NAMES.short: Detected visible-bremsstrahlung count rate accumulated by a single detector pixel, representing photoelectron-equivalent events rather than plasma photon emissivity.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the detected visible-bremsstrahlung count rate associated with one detector pixel. It represents photoelectron-equivalent detection events produced by the accepted bremsstrahlung continuum, not the local photon emissivity of the plasma.

The rate is defined from the accumulated bremsstrahlung count by

$$
r_{\mathrm{brem}} = \frac{dN_{\mathrm{brem}}}{dt}
$$

where $N_{\mathrm{brem}}$ is the accumulated photoelectron-equivalent count, $t$ is elapsed time measured in seconds, and $r_{\mathrm{brem}}$ is the corresponding detection rate. The count is the accumulated quantity being differentiated; this name does not denote the derivative of an already defined rate.

The pixel-local detected rate is distinct from the plasma source quantity [bremsstrahlung spectral emissivity](name:bremsstrahlung_spectral_emissivity), which describes photon emission per volume, spectral interval, and solid angle. It is analogous in detection semantics to the [photon-equivalent count rate](name:flux_of_spectrometer_channel) of a spectrometer channel.

NAMES.name: toroidal_angular_width_of_camera
NAMES.short: Full angular span of a camera field of view in the toroidal direction of the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, equal to the non-negative difference between the largest and smallest unwrapped toroidal viewing angles.
NAMES.long:
Full angular span of a camera field of view in the toroidal direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame is the non-negative difference between the largest and smallest limiting signed toroidal viewing angles subtended by the camera acceptance. In this frame $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ increases counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height.

Let $\phi_{\min}$ and $\phi_{\max}$ be the minimum and maximum unwrapped signed toroidal viewing angles of the limiting accepted rays. The toroidal angular width is defined by:

$$
\Delta\phi_\mathrm{cam} = \phi_{\max} - \phi_{\min}
$$

where $\Delta\phi_\mathrm{cam}$ is the toroidal angular width of the camera and the extrema are taken over the camera field-of-view boundary after choosing a continuous branch of $\phi$.

This quantity describes only the toroidal extent of the field of view. It excludes the central toroidal pointing angle, the detailed field-of-view footprint or optical distortion, and the complementary [vertical angular width](name:vertical_angular_width_of_camera).

NAMES.name: toroidal_coordinate_of_optical_element
NAMES.short: Toroidal angular coordinate of an optical element’s geometric reference center, locating it around the machine symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal coordinate $\phi$ gives the azimuthal location of an optical element’s geometric reference point around the machine symmetry axis. It is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height.

For a reference point with horizontal Cartesian coordinates $x$ and $y$ in the right-handed $(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$ basis, with the $x$ direction aligned to $\phi=0$, the angular coordinate is

$$
\phi = \operatorname{atan2}(y,x)
$$

The reference point is the geometric center of a circular optical element or the origin of the local coordinate system describing a planar detector or aperture. Its vertical counterpart is the [vertical coordinate of the optical element](name:vertical_coordinate_of_optical_element).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the reference point lies in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$, counter-clockwise when viewed from above along $+\hat{Z}$.

NAMES.name: total_plasma_radiated_power
NAMES.short: Total electromagnetic power lost from the plasma as radiation, integrated over the full plasma volume and all emission channels including impurity line emission, bremsstrahlung, and recombination.
NAMES.long:
The total plasma radiated power $P_\mathrm{rad}$ is the rate at which electromagnetic energy escapes the plasma via all radiation processes — impurity line radiation, electron-ion bremsstrahlung continuum, recombination radiation, and synchrotron emission — integrated over the entire plasma volume. It constitutes the radiation-loss channel in the global power balance, alongside conductive and convective energy transport.

The defining relation connects $P_\mathrm{rad}$ to the local volumetric emissivity $\epsilon_\mathrm{rad}(\mathbf{r})$:

$$
P_\mathrm{rad} = \int_V \epsilon_\mathrm{rad}(\mathbf{r}) \, dV
$$

where the integral is taken over the full plasma volume $V$.

Measurement relies on bolometry: broadband multi-chord detectors sensitive from infrared to soft X-ray wavelengths collect line-integrated emission signals, which are tomographically inverted to reconstruct $\epsilon_\mathrm{rad}(\mathbf{r})$ and then volume-integrated. The radiation fraction $f_\mathrm{rad} = P_\mathrm{rad} / P_\mathrm{heat}$, where $P_\mathrm{heat}$ is the [total plasma heating power](name:total_plasma_heating_power), quantifies the confinement efficiency and guides impurity-seeding strategies for divertor detachment. In present-day tokamaks, $P_\mathrm{rad}$ spans 0.1–50 MW depending on density, impurity content, and heating level; in impurity-seeded reactor scenarios it can account for 50–80% of $P_\mathrm{heat}$. The bremsstrahlung continuum contribution alone is captured by [bremsstrahlung_power](name:bremsstrahlung_power), while [total neutron power](name:total_neutron_power) tracks the kinetic energy channel that exits via particle transport rather than electromagnetic emission.

NAMES.name: tritium_density
NAMES.subject: tritium
NAMES.short: Local number density of tritium ions in the plasma, the foundational fuel-ion parameter underlying chord-averaged, volume-averaged, and isotopic ratio child quantities.
NAMES.long:
Tritium ion number density $n_T$ quantifies the local concentration of hydrogen-3 fuel ions in the plasma. It serves as the common physical basis for a family of derived quantities: the chord-integrated mean [line_averaged_tritium_density](name:line_averaged_tritium_density), the confined-volume mean [volume_averaged_tritium_density](name:volume_averaged_tritium_density), and dimensionless isotopic ratios such as ratio_of_tritium_density_to_electron_density and [ratio_of_tritium_density_to_deuterium_density](name:ratio_of_tritium_density_to_deuterium_density).

In deuterium-tritium (DT) fusion plasmas the local volumetric reaction rate is:

$$
R_{DT} = n_T \, n_D \langle \sigma v \rangle_{DT}
$$

where $n_D$ is the deuterium ion number density and $\langle \sigma v \rangle_{DT}$ is the Maxwellian-averaged DT fusion reactivity. The combined DT fuel-ion purity relative to the electron population is tracked by ratio_of_deuterium_tritium_density_to_electron_density.

Tritium density is inferred from active charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, neutron emission measurements in DT plasmas, or pellet injection and fueling diagnostics.
NAMES.sign: Positive when tritium ions are present in the plasma.

NAMES.name: ratio_of_tritium_density_to_deuterium_density
NAMES.short: Local ratio of tritium-ion to deuterium-ion number densities, expressing fuel-isotope composition independently of the total fuel-ion density.
NAMES.long:
The local tritium-to-deuterium density ratio expresses the relative abundance of the two hydrogen-isotope fuel-ion populations at the same location. It is derived from the local [tritium density](name:tritium_density) and [deuterium density](name:deuterium_density).

$$
R_{T/D} = \frac{n_T}{n_D}
$$

where $R_{T/D}$ is the tritium-to-deuterium density ratio, and $n_T$ and $n_D$ are the local number densities of tritium and deuterium ions, respectively. The densities include the relevant isotope populations summed over their charge states unless a charge-state-resolved quantity is explicitly specified.

This ratio is dimensionless and does not represent the total fuel-ion density; multiplying it by the deuterium density gives the tritium density.

NAMES.name: upper_bound_energy_of_detector_pixel
NAMES.short: Maximum photon energy accepted by a detector pixel in an X-ray crystal spectrometer, defining the high-energy edge of the pixel's spectral bandpass.
NAMES.long:
The upper bound energy of a detector pixel is the maximum photon energy in the spectral interval accepted by that pixel in an X-ray crystal spectrometer. Together with the [lower bound energy of a detector pixel](name:lower_bound_energy_of_detector_pixel), it defines the pixel bandpass around the central [energy of a detector pixel](name:energy_of_detector_pixel).

The accepted photon-energy interval is defined by

$$
E_{\mathrm{lower}} \leq E \leq E_{\mathrm{upper}}
$$

where $E$ is photon energy, $E_{\mathrm{lower}}$ is the lower bound energy, and $E_{\mathrm{upper}}$ is the upper bound energy of the pixel. Photons with energies above $E_{\mathrm{upper}}$ are outside this pixel's defined spectral acceptance interval.

sources.enhanced_context: Upper energy bound of the photon detection range for each pixel of the X-ray crystal spectrometer detector, defining the high-energy edge of the sensitivity window per pixel. Complements the lower energy bound to specify the per-pixel spectral bandpass.

sources.parent_definition: Measurement channel, composed of a camera, a crystal, and (optional) a set of reflectors. The light coming from the plasma passes through the (optional) set of reflectors, then the crystal and arrives at the camera

NAMES.name: upper_photon_energy
NAMES.short: Upper photon energy bound defining the high-energy threshold of an X-ray detector channel spectral sensitivity window.
NAMES.long:
The upper photon energy bound marks the maximum photon energy at which a detector channel registers photon counts, defining the high-energy edge of the band over which photon flux is integrated. Together with [lower_photon_energy](name:lower_photon_energy), it fully specifies the energy band used for spectrally resolved X-ray bremsstrahlung measurements in both soft and hard X-ray diagnostics.

The photon energy $E_\gamma$ relates to radiation frequency $\nu$ and wavelength $\lambda$ through:

$$
E_\gamma = h\nu = \frac{hc}{\lambda}
$$

where $h \approx 4.136 \times 10^{-15}$ eV·s is Planck's constant and $c$ is the speed of light in vacuum.

The upper energy limit is set by detector material properties, filter transmittance, and electronic discriminator thresholds in the pulse-height analyzer. Soft X-ray channel upper bounds span roughly 0.1–10 keV; hard X-ray diagnostic channels extend to tens to hundreds of keV depending on detector type. The analogous threshold for crystal spectrometer cameras is [upper_bound_energy_of_detector_pixel](name:upper_bound_energy_of_detector_pixel).
NAMES.sign: Positive for all physical photon energies, as $E_\gamma = h\nu > 0$ for any non-zero photon frequency.

NAMES.name: vertical_angle_of_detector_pixel
NAMES.short: Signed elevation angle of a camera pixel’s line of sight relative to the camera optical axis, specifying its vertical position within the field of view.
NAMES.long:
The vertical viewing angle of a camera pixel is the signed elevation offset of its line of sight from the camera optical axis. It specifies angular position in the camera’s vertical image direction, rather than the full vertical field-of-view span described by [vertical angular width of camera](name:vertical_angular_width_of_camera).

In the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$ frame, let $\hat{\ell}$ be the pixel line-of-sight unit vector, $\hat{o}$ the optical-axis unit vector, and $\hat{v}$ the camera image-up unit vector. The angle is defined by

$$
\alpha_v = \operatorname{atan2}(\hat{\ell}\cdot\hat{v},\hat{\ell}\cdot\hat{o})
$$

where $\alpha_v$ is the signed vertical viewing angle and the three hatted quantities are dimensionless unit vectors. The image-up orientation determines the vertical angular direction.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the pixel line of sight has a positive projection onto the camera image-up direction relative to the optical axis.

NAMES.name: vertical_angular_width_of_camera
NAMES.short: Angular extent of a camera’s imaging coverage along the vertical Z direction of the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Vertical angular width is the total angular span covered by a camera’s imaging region in the detector plane along the physical vertical direction. It is a non-negative field-of-view quantity, independent of the signs of the individual viewing angles.

The width is defined by the difference between the largest and smallest covered vertical viewing angles:

$$
\Delta\theta_{\mathrm{vert}} = \theta_{\mathrm{vert,max}} - \theta_{\mathrm{vert,min}}
$$

where $\Delta\theta_{\mathrm{vert}}$ is the vertical angular width and $\theta_{\mathrm{vert,max}}$ and $\theta_{\mathrm{vert,min}}$ are the upper and lower signed vertical viewing-angle limits, expressed in radians. The vertical direction is $+Z$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

This full-span quantity is distinct from the signed [vertical angle of a detector pixel](name:vertical_angle_of_detector_pixel). Its directional counterpart is the [toroidal angular width of a camera](name:toroidal_angular_width_of_camera).

NAMES.name: vertical_back_surface_curvature_of_optical_element
NAMES.short: Vertical back-surface curvature of an optical element is the signed directional radius of curvature of the rear optical surface along the second local tangential aperture direction. Here vertical means object-local aperture vertical, not the Z direction of the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Vertical back-surface curvature of an optical element is the signed directional radius of curvature of the back optical surface in its second local tangential aperture direction. The right-handed local optical-surface frame is $(\hat{\mathbf{e}}_1, \hat{\mathbf{e}}_2, \hat{\mathbf{n}}_b)$ with $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_1 \times \hat{\mathbf{e}}_2 = \hat{\mathbf{n}}_b$, where $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_1$ and $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_2$ are the first and second surface-tangential aperture directions and $\hat{\mathbf{n}}_b$ is the positive normal of the back surface; this quantity uses $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_2$, the object-local aperture vertical direction.

The defining relation is the reciprocal of the signed normal curvature of the back-surface normal section tangent to $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_2$:

$$
R_{b,2} = \frac{1}{\kappa_{n,b}(\hat{\mathbf{e}}_2)}
$$

where $R_{b,2}$ is the vertical back-surface curvature of the optical element and $\kappa_{n,b}(\hat{\mathbf{e}}_2)$ is the signed normal curvature of the back surface in the $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_2$ direction.

This is a local directional radius, not the scalar parent [optical-element curvature](name:curvature_of_optical_element) and not the direction-agnostic [back-surface curvature](name:back_surface_curvature_of_optical_element). It equals the first-direction radius only for locally spherical or otherwise direction-independent curvature, and it is not a principal, sagittal, or meridional radius unless the surface definition aligns $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_2$ with that direction. Together with an orthogonal directional radius it may characterize simple aligned toroidal curvature, but it does not fully characterize a general aspherical surface.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the center of curvature of the normal section tangent to $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_2$ lies in the $+\hat{\mathbf{n}}_b$ half-space of the back-surface local frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_bragg_crystal
NAMES.short: Vertical Z coordinate of the geometric center of a Bragg crystal, measured from the machine midplane in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Vertical Z coordinate of the geometric center of a Bragg crystal is the $Z$ coordinate of the crystal's geometric center in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, measured from the machine midplane $Z=0$. It specifies the vertical location of that center, not the coordinate of another point on the crystal.

For a geometric-center position vector $\mathbf{r}_c$ taken from the coordinate origin, the coordinate is the projection onto the vertical basis direction:

$$
Z_c = \mathbf{r}_c \cdot \hat{Z}
$$

where $Z_c$ is the vertical coordinate of the Bragg-crystal geometric center and $\hat{Z}$ is the vertical basis vector of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

This quantity refers only to the geometric center of the Bragg crystal as a diffracting optical element. It excludes the vertical coordinate of crystal surface vertices, mounts, apertures, detectors, or any other associated component.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the Bragg-crystal geometric center lies above the machine midplane $Z=0$.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_detector_pixel
NAMES.short: Vertical Z coordinate of the geometric center of a detector pixel in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, measured from the machine midplane and independent of detector-local indexing or pixel span.
NAMES.long:
Vertical Z coordinate of the geometric center of a detector pixel is the $Z$ component of the center point of an individual radiation-detector pixel in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ increases counter-clockwise when viewed from above along $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height measured from the machine midplane. It is an absolute geometry coordinate of the pixel center, not a detector-local row coordinate or the vertical extent of the pixel.

The coordinate is defined by projecting the pixel-center position onto the vertical basis direction:

$$
Z_\mathrm{pixel} = \mathbf{r}_\mathrm{center} \cdot \hat{Z}
$$

where $\mathbf{r}_\mathrm{center}$ is the geometric center position of the detector pixel and $\hat{Z}$ is the vertical basis vector of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

Together with the corresponding radial coordinate and toroidal angle of the same pixel center, this quantity fixes the pixel-center location. It excludes detector-local indexing, active-height coordinates, pixel pitch, and the full vertical span of the pixel.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the pixel center lies above the machine midplane in the $+\hat{Z}$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_filter_window
NAMES.short: Signed vertical coordinate of the geometric center of a diagnostic filter window in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate identifies the height of the geometric center of the filter window in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It is a geometric location, not a photon-interaction or optical-response quantity.

For a window surface $S$ with area $A$, the centroidal vertical coordinate is defined by

$$
Z_c = \frac{1}{A}\int_S Z\,dA
$$

where $Z_c$ and $Z$ are vertical coordinates measured in m, $dA$ is the surface-area element, and $A=\int_S dA$ is the window area. The corresponding radial location is given by [radial coordinate of filter window](name:radial_coordinate_of_filter_window); this quantity is distinct from the vertical coordinate of a diagnostic aperture, such as [vertical coordinate of diagnostic aperture](name:vertical_coordinate_of_diagnostic_aperture).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the window center lies in the $+Z$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_soft_xray_detector
NAMES.short: Vertical Z coordinate of the geometric center of a soft X-ray detector in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Vertical Z coordinate of the geometric center of a soft X-ray detector is the height coordinate of that detector center in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. The origin of $Z$ is the machine midplane, so $Z=0$ lies on that midplane.

Together with the corresponding major-radius and toroidal-angle coordinates, this quantity specifies the absolute geometric position of the detector center. It is distinct from a detector-pixel coordinate, an aperture position, a line-of-sight direction, and any measured soft-X-ray signal.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the detector center is above the machine midplane in the $+\hat{Z}$ direction.

NAMES.name: vertical_curvature_of_bragg_crystal
NAMES.short: Radius of curvature of the diffracting surface of a Bragg crystal along its local vertical (X2) direction, defining one axis of its focusing geometry.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the local radius of curvature of the Bragg crystal's diffracting surface along its local vertical, or X2, tangent direction. It characterizes the crystal bending used for Bragg-diffraction focusing in a doubly curved geometry.

$$
R_v = \frac{1}{|\kappa_v|}
$$

where $R_v$ is the radius of curvature in m and $\kappa_v$ is the signed normal curvature in m$^{-1}$ along the local vertical tangent direction. A planar surface corresponds to zero curvature and an unbounded radius.

This quantity describes the diffracting surface, not the geometric aperture radius given by [radius of Bragg crystal](name:radius_of_bragg_crystal). Together with the [toroidal curvature of the Bragg crystal](name:toroidal_curvature_of_bragg_crystal), it specifies the directional curvature scales of a doubly curved crystal.

sources.parent_definition: Characteristics of the crystal used

NAMES.name: vertical_front_surface_curvature_of_optical_element
NAMES.short: Vertical front surface curvature of an optical element is the signed principal radius of curvature of the front, beam-entry surface along X2, the second local tangential aperture direction in the right-handed local aperture frame (X1, X2, z).
NAMES.long:
Vertical front surface curvature of an optical element is the signed principal radius of curvature of the element's front, beam-entry surface along the second local tangential aperture direction. The direction is $X_2$ in the right-handed local aperture frame $(X_1, X_2, z)$, where $X_1$ and $X_2$ are local tangential aperture coordinates at the surface vertex and $z$ is the local sag coordinate along the chosen surface-normal or optical-axis direction.

For a differentiable front-surface sag function $z_s(X_1,X_2)$ expressed in that frame, the radius $R_{2,\mathrm{front}}$ is defined by the second derivative at the vertex:

$$
\left.\frac{\partial^2 z_s}{\partial X_2^2}\right|_{X_1=0,\,X_2=0} = \frac{1}{R_{2,\mathrm{front}}}
$$

where $z_s$ is the displacement of the front surface along $z$, $X_1=X_2=0$ is the surface vertex, and $R_{2,\mathrm{front}}$ is this quantity. The reciprocal local curvature is $\kappa_{2,\mathrm{front}}=1/R_{2,\mathrm{front}}$.

The quantity is the signed-radius form of the second-direction front-surface curvature, not the reciprocal curvature magnitude. It uses the same local-frame convention as [vertical front surface radius](name:vertical_front_surface_radius_of_optical_element); [vertical back surface curvature](name:vertical_back_surface_curvature_of_optical_element) is the corresponding quantity for the back surface. The word vertical denotes the aperture $X_2$ direction in the local aperture frame $(X_1, X_2, z)$ and not the $Z$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the center of curvature of the front-surface normal section in the second local tangential aperture direction lies on the $+z$ side of the surface vertex in the local aperture frame $(X_1, X_2, z)$.

NAMES.name: vertical_front_surface_radius_of_optical_element
NAMES.short: Radius of curvature of an optical element's beam-entry front surface along the local second tangential direction (X2, the optical-element vertical direction) in the right-handed local optical-element frame (X1, X2, z).
NAMES.long:
Radius of curvature of an optical element's beam-entry front surface along the local second tangential ($X_2$, optical-element vertical) direction is the signed radius of the front-surface normal section spanned by $\hat{X}_2$ and $\hat{z}$ in the right-handed local optical-element frame $(\hat{X}_1,\hat{X}_2,\hat{z})$. The coordinates $x_1$ and $x_2$ lie in the local tangent plane at the surface vertex, and $z$ is the local front-surface-normal sag coordinate. This is a radius of curvature, not a reciprocal curvature.

At the surface vertex, after subtracting planar tilt so that $\partial z/\partial x_2=0$ there, the signed radius is defined by the second derivative of the sag in the $X_2$ normal section:

$$
\frac{1}{R_2} = \left.\frac{\partial^2 z}{\partial x_2^2}\right|_{x_2=0}
$$

where $z(x_2)$ is the front-surface sag along $\hat{z}$, $x_2$ is displacement along $\hat{X}_2$, and $R_2$ is this signed radius; $z$, $x_2$, and $R_2$ are in meters. For small sag this definition implies $z(x_2)-z(0)\simeq x_2^2/(2R_2)$ near the vertex, and a flat section is the limiting case $1/R_2=0$.

For spherical surface models the first- and second-local-tangential radii of the front surface are equal. For cylindrical, toroidal, or separably curved surface models they may differ, so this quantity is distinct from the orthogonal first-local-tangential front-surface quantity x_front_surface_curvature_of_optical_element and from the rear-surface quantity [vertical_back_surface_curvature_of_optical_element](name:vertical_back_surface_curvature_of_optical_element); [vertical_front_surface_curvature_of_optical_element](name:vertical_front_surface_curvature_of_optical_element) uses the same second-local-tangential front-surface radius convention.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the center of curvature of the front surface in the normal section spanned by $\hat{X}_2$ and $\hat{z}$ lies on the $+\hat{z}$ side of the local tangent plane.

NAMES.name: voltage_of_spectrometer
NAMES.short: Voltage of a spectrometer is the signed electric potential difference between two designated electrical terminals of a spectrometer. It is the spectrometer-level quantity, not a voltage assigned to an individual spectrometer channel.
NAMES.long:
Voltage of a spectrometer is the signed electric potential difference between two designated electrical terminals of a spectrometer. The terminal pair may define a control, bias, supply, or signal-output voltage, provided the locus is the spectrometer as an instrument rather than an individual channel.

For designated terminals $a$ and $b$, the voltage is defined by the electric-potential difference:

$$
V = \varphi_a - \varphi_b
$$

where $V$ is the voltage of the spectrometer and $\varphi_a$ and $\varphi_b$ are the electric potentials, each expressed in volts, at the positive and reference terminals respectively.

This spectrometer-level quantity is distinct from [voltage of a spectrometer channel](name:voltage_of_spectrometer_channel), which applies to a designated terminal pair of one spectrometer channel. It denotes an electrical potential difference only; photon flux, spectral radiance, and other calibrated optical quantities are separate physical quantities.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the designated positive terminal of the spectrometer is at a higher electric potential than the designated reference terminal.

NAMES.name: requested_voltage_of_spectrometer
NAMES.short: Commanded bias potential between a spectrometer detector or electrode and its supply return, specifying the intended setpoint rather than the measured detector-output voltage.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the commanded electrical bias setpoint applied by a spectrometer high-voltage supply between a detector or electrode terminal and the supply return or reference terminal. It specifies the intended operating potential, not a detector readout signal.

The commanded voltage is defined by

$$
V_{\mathrm{set}} = \phi_{\mathrm{terminal,set}} - \phi_{\mathrm{return}}
$$

where $V_{\mathrm{set}}$ is the commanded voltage, $\phi_{\mathrm{terminal,set}}$ is the requested electric potential of the detector or electrode terminal, and $\phi_{\mathrm{return}}$ is the electric potential of the supply return or reference terminal. A positive value therefore commands a terminal potential above the return potential.

This setpoint is distinct from the raw detector signal represented by [voltage of a spectrometer](name:voltage_of_spectrometer), which can include detector response, bias, dark signal, gain, and electronic offset. It does not represent the actual measured supply output or calibrated radiometric signal.

NAMES.name: voltage_of_spectrometer_channel
NAMES.short: Electrical output signal from a spectrometer channel before offset correction or conversion to calibrated radiometric quantities.
NAMES.long:
The channel voltage is the electrical potential difference delivered by a spectrometer detector channel relative to its electronics reference. It represents the raw detector and front-end response associated with that channel, not calibrated radiance, irradiance, photon flux, or optical power.

$$
V_{\mathrm{ch}} = \Phi_{\mathrm{sig}} - \Phi_{\mathrm{ref}}
$$

where $V_{\mathrm{ch}}$ is the channel voltage in V, and $\Phi_{\mathrm{sig}}$ and $\Phi_{\mathrm{ref}}$ are the electrical potentials of the signal and reference terminals, respectively. The polarity follows this reference definition; positive voltage means that the signal-terminal potential exceeds the reference-terminal potential. Offset or dark-signal subtraction and radiometric calibration are excluded. The quantity provides the common physical context for [measured voltage of a spectrometer channel](name:measured_voltage_of_spectrometer_channel) and is distinct from the calibrated [calibration factor of a spectrometer](name:calibration_factor_of_spectrometer).

NAMES.name: width_of_diagnostic_aperture
NAMES.short: Width of a diagnostic aperture is the full clear-opening span of a rectangular diagnostic aperture measured along X1, the first local tangential axis, in the right-handed local aperture frame (X1, X2, X3). X2 is the second local tangential axis and X3 is normal to the aperture plane.
NAMES.long:
Width of a diagnostic aperture is the full clear-opening span of a rectangular diagnostic aperture measured along $X_1$, the first local tangential axis of the right-handed local aperture frame $(X_1, X_2, X_3)$. The axes $X_1$ and $X_2$ span the aperture plane, with $X_2$ the second local tangential axis, and $X_3$ is normal to that plane.

For a rectangular clear opening, the width is the coordinate extent of the transmitting interval along $X_1$:

$$
w = x_{1,\max} - x_{1,\min}
$$

where $w$ is the aperture width, and $x_{1,\max}$ and $x_{1,\min}$ are the maximum and minimum transmitting-boundary coordinates along $X_1$, measured in meters.

The width is a clear-opening dimension: opaque supports, masks, bevels, housing material, and other non-transmitting parts of the aperture plane are excluded. It is the rectangular first-local-tangential size of a diagnostic aperture, distinct from [diameter of diagnostic aperture](name:diameter_of_diagnostic_aperture) for a circular opening and from [width of aperture](name:width_of_aperture) for the corresponding non-diagnostic aperture concept.

NAMES.name: width_of_filter
NAMES.short: Wavelength span between the two selected boundaries of an optical filter’s transmitted passband, independent of the boundary criterion used.
NAMES.long:
Spectral passband width is the full wavelength extent between the lower and upper boundaries selected to define an optical filter’s transmitted band. It describes an edge-to-edge span rather than the passband center or peak wavelength.

The width is defined by

$$
\Delta\lambda = \lambda_{\rm high} - \lambda_{\rm low}
$$

where $\Delta\lambda$ is the passband width, $\lambda_{\rm high}$ is the higher-wavelength boundary, and $\lambda_{\rm low}$ is the lower-wavelength boundary.

The boundary criterion is part of the quantity’s definition and must be stated when the boundaries are not intrinsic. For example, [spectral_width_of_filter](name:spectral_width_of_filter) uses the wavelengths at which transmission falls to 90% of its peak. This edge-to-edge width is distinct from the [reference_wavelength_of_filter](name:reference_wavelength_of_filter), which characterizes the passband center or peak.

NAMES.name: spectral_width_of_filter
NAMES.short: Full wavelength span of a filter’s transmitted passband between the two wavelengths where transmission reaches 90% of its peak value.
NAMES.long:
The 90%-transmission width is the edge-to-edge spectral span of an optical filter’s passband, using the two transmission crossings at 90% of the maximum transmission. It is a specific boundary criterion for [width of filter](name:width_of_filter), not the passband center or peak wavelength.

The width is defined by

$$
\Delta\lambda_{90} = \lambda_{\mathrm{high},90} - \lambda_{\mathrm{low},90}
$$

where $\lambda_{\mathrm{low},90}$ and $\lambda_{\mathrm{high},90}$ are the lower and upper wavelengths satisfying $T(\lambda)=0.9T_{\mathrm{max}}$, $T(\lambda)$ is the filter transmission, and $T_{\mathrm{max}}$ is its peak transmission. The value is non-negative and applies when two such passband crossings define the transmitted band.

NAMES.name: width_of_hard_xray_detector
NAMES.short: Full physical width of a rectangular hard X-ray detector aperture measured along the first local axis of the detector frame (X1, X2, X3).
NAMES.long:
The hard X-ray detector aperture width is the full physical extent of the rectangular aperture along the first local detector axis, X1, in the local frame (X1, X2, X3). It is the width dimension orthogonal to the aperture height.

The width is defined by the separation of the two opposite aperture edges along X1:

$$
W_{X1} = x_{1,\mathrm{max}} - x_{1,\mathrm{min}}
$$

where $x_{1,\mathrm{max}}$ and $x_{1,\mathrm{min}}$ are the X1 coordinates of those edges, and $W_{X1}$ is the full aperture width.

This quantity describes the geometric aperture dimension and excludes the orthogonal extent represented by [height of hard X-ray detector](name:height_of_hard_xray_detector), as well as detector response or radiation throughput.

NAMES.name: width_of_optical_element
NAMES.short: Full non-negative clear-aperture extent of a rectangular optical element along X1, the first local tangential axis of its right-handed frame.
NAMES.long:
The optical-element width is the full clear-aperture extent of a rectangular optical element along the first local tangential axis $X_1$. The aperture plane is spanned by $X_1$ and $X_2$, while $X_3$ is its normal in the right-handed local frame $(X_1, X_2, X_3)$.

It is defined by the difference between the two opposing aperture-edge coordinates:

$$
W = X_{1,\max} - X_{1,\min}
$$

where $W$ is the aperture width and $X_{1,\max}$ and $X_{1,\min}$ are the maximum and minimum edge coordinates along $X_1$. The quantity is non-negative and applies to the usable clear opening, excluding opaque mounts or other structures outside the aperture. The corresponding extent along the second local tangential axis is [height of the optical element](name:height_of_optical_element).

NAMES.name: width_of_spectrometer_channel
NAMES.short: Wavelength-domain measure of a spectrometer channel’s response spread, quantifying instrumental broadening around its characteristic response wavelength.
NAMES.long:
A spectral width is a wavelength-domain measure of the spread of a spectrometer channel’s instrument response to monochromatic radiation. It describes the broadening of the response about the channel’s [reference wavelength](name:reference_wavelength_of_spectrometer_channel).

For the Gaussian representation used by [spectral_width_of_spectrometer_channel](name:spectral_width_of_spectrometer_channel), the response is modeled as

$$
R(\lambda) = R_0 \exp\left[-\frac{(\lambda-\lambda_{\rm ref})^2}{2\sigma_\lambda^2}\right]
$$

where $R(\lambda)$ is the response at wavelength $\lambda$, $R_0$ is the peak response, $\lambda_{\rm ref}$ is the reference wavelength, and $\sigma_\lambda$ is the spectral width.

The width parameter must be distinguished from [effective_spectral_width_of_spectrometer_channel](name:effective_spectral_width_of_spectrometer_channel), which is the equivalent-width bandwidth for a response profile and is not generally a Gaussian standard deviation.

NAMES.name: spectral_width_of_spectrometer_channel
NAMES.short: Spectral width of a spectrometer channel is the Gaussian standard deviation of the channel spectral response to monochromatic radiation about its reference vacuum wavelength. It specifies instrumental broadening and is distinct from an effective full-response width or a passband interval.
NAMES.long:
Spectral width of a spectrometer channel is the Gaussian standard deviation of the channel response in vacuum wavelength about the channel reference wavelength. It characterizes the instrumental spectral broadening produced by the channel for a monochromatic input, excluding the physical line width of the radiation source.

For a Gaussian spectral response component $G(\lambda)$ centered at $\lambda_0$, the spectral width $\sigma_\lambda$ is defined by the second central moment:

$$
\sigma_\lambda^2 = \frac{\int (\lambda - \lambda_0)^2 G(\lambda)\, d\lambda}{\int G(\lambda)\, d\lambda}
$$

where $\lambda$ is vacuum wavelength, $\lambda_0$ is the [reference wavelength of the spectrometer channel](name:reference_wavelength_of_spectrometer_channel), both are expressed in meters, and $G(\lambda)$ is the non-negative Gaussian spectral response component. The normalization of $G(\lambda)$ cancels in the ratio.

This name denotes the Gaussian $\sigma_\lambda$ convention. It excludes the Gaussian full width at half maximum, related to this quantity by $2\sqrt{2\ln 2}\,\sigma_\lambda$, and excludes the equivalent full-response or rectangular-bandwidth measure denoted by [effective spectral width of spectrometer channel](name:effective_spectral_width_of_spectrometer_channel). The valid physical domain is $\sigma_\lambda \ge 0$; $\sigma_\lambda = 0$ is the ideal limit of no instrumental spectral broadening by that Gaussian component.

NAMES.name: effective_spectral_width_of_spectrometer_channel
NAMES.short: Response-equivalent wavelength interval of a spectrometer channel, defined from the full spectral instrument function rather than a Gaussian approximation.
NAMES.long:
Effective spectral width is the wavelength interval equivalent to the area of the spectrometer channel's normalized instrument-function response. It captures the integrated response of non-Gaussian line shapes and is distinct from the Gaussian standard-deviation measure named by [spectral width of a spectrometer channel](name:spectral_width_of_spectrometer_channel).

$$
W_{\mathrm{eff}} = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{R(\lambda)}{R_{\max}}\,d\lambda
$$

where $R(\lambda)$ is the channel response to monochromatic radiation at wavelength $\lambda$, and $R_{\max}$ is its peak response. For a Gaussian response with standard deviation $\sigma$, the equivalent width is $W_{\mathrm{eff}} = \sqrt{2\pi}\,\sigma$; therefore, this quantity is not numerically identical to the Gaussian spectral width.

NAMES.name: cold_neutral_temperature
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Translational kinetic temperature, expressed as energy per particle, of the low-energy neutral atom component in the plasma edge or scrape-off layer.
NAMES.long:
Cold neutral temperature is the translational kinetic temperature of the low-energy neutral atom component in the plasma edge or scrape-off layer, representing random kinetic energy after removal of mean flow. It characterizes the thermal energy of recycled or otherwise low-energy neutral atoms and is the cold component of [neutral temperature](name:neutral_temperature).

For the cold neutral component, the temperature is defined from the second central moment of its velocity distribution:

$$
T_c = \frac{m_c}{3 e n_c}\int \left|\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{u}_c\right|^2 f_c(\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $T_c$ is the cold neutral temperature, $m_c$ is the neutral particle mass, $e$ is the elementary charge, $f_c(\mathbf{v})$ is the cold-neutral velocity distribution, $n_c$ is its density, and $\mathbf{u}_c$ is its mean velocity. The definition excludes the energetic neutral component; [cold neutral velocity](name:cold_neutral_velocity) describes the corresponding bulk-flow component.

NAMES.name: cold_neutral_velocity
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Cold neutral velocity is the line-of-sight component of the bulk flow of low-energy neutral atoms, identified from the Doppler shift of their emission.
NAMES.long:
Cold neutral velocity is the line-of-sight component of the bulk drift vector of a cold neutral particle population. It represents convective neutral motion after averaging over particle velocities and over the contributing cold-neutral population states.

The component is defined from the parent [neutral velocity](name:neutral_velocity) by

$$
v_{n,c,ell} = \mathbf{v}_{n,c} \cdot \hat{\ell}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_{n,c}$ is the bulk velocity of the cold neutral population, $\hat{\ell}$ is the selected line-of-sight unit vector, and $v_{n,c,\ell}$ is the signed projected velocity. The projection is the velocity represented by the Doppler centroid of the corresponding cold-neutral emission component.

This quantity is distinct from [hot neutral velocity](name:hot_neutral_velocity), which describes the energetic neutral population, and from [neutral internal state velocity](name:neutral_internal_state_velocity), which is resolved for a specified internal state. It excludes thermal speed and velocity spread, which are higher moments of the velocity distribution.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the cold-neutral bulk velocity points along the chosen positive line-of-sight unit vector $\hat{\ell}$.

sources.enhanced_context: Line-of-sight projected velocity of cold neutral atoms measured via Doppler spectroscopy in a polarization spectroscopy channel. Positive values indicate motion from the first to the second point of the line of sight.
sources.leaf_definition: Projection of the cold neutral velocity along the line of sight, positive when going from first point to second point of the line of sight
sources.parent_definition: Physics quantities measured from polarized light spectroscopy

NAMES.name: hot_neutral_temperature
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Translational kinetic temperature, expressed as energy per particle, of the energetic neutral-atom component in the plasma edge or scrape-off layer.
NAMES.long:
Energetic neutral temperature is the translational kinetic temperature of the energetic neutral-atom component in the plasma edge or scrape-off layer, representing random kinetic energy after removal of mean flow. It is the component-specific counterpart of [neutral temperature](name:neutral_temperature) and is distinct from the low-energy population described by [cold neutral temperature](name:cold_neutral_temperature).

For the included energetic neutral states, the density-weighted temperature is defined by

$$
T_{\mathrm{en}} = \frac{\sum_s m_s \int \left|\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{u}_s\right|^2 f_s(\mathbf{v})\,d^3v}{3e\sum_s n_s}, \qquad n_s=\int f_s(\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $T_{\mathrm{en}}$ is the energetic neutral temperature, $s$ indexes the included neutral states, $m_s$ is the particle mass, $e$ is the elementary charge, $f_s(\mathbf{v})$ is the state velocity distribution, $n_s$ is its number density, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity, and $\mathbf{u}_s$ is the state mean velocity.

Only the energetic neutral-atom component is included; cold neutral atoms and populations outside the specified energetic selection are excluded. State contributions are combined by number-density weighting rather than equal weighting.

NAMES.name: hot_neutral_velocity
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Line-of-sight projected velocity of the energetic (hot) neutral atom population, inferred from the Doppler centroid shift of the broad emission component in visible polarization spectroscopy.
NAMES.long:
The hot neutral population consists of energetic neutral atoms — produced primarily by charge-exchange reactions between fast ions and cold neutrals or by beam-neutral interactions — whose velocity distribution yields a broad Doppler profile overlaid on the narrower thermal (cold) component. The line-of-sight component $v_\mathrm{hot}$ represents the bulk flow of this energetic neutral ensemble along the diagnostic chord, distinguishing it from [cold_neutral_velocity](name:cold_neutral_velocity) for the thermal population; the associated kinetic spread is captured by [hot_neutral_temperature](name:hot_neutral_temperature).

The centroid velocity is extracted from the observed wavelength shift of the emission line:

$$
v_\mathrm{hot} = c \, \frac{\lambda_\mathrm{obs} - \lambda_0}{\lambda_0}
$$

where $c$ is the speed of light, $\lambda_\mathrm{obs}$ is the centroid wavelength of the hot neutral spectral component, and $\lambda_0$ is the rest wavelength of the observed line.

Measurement requires fitting the observed line profile from a visible polarization spectrometer with a multi-Gaussian model that separates the broad hot and narrow cold neutral contributions; the centroid shift of the broad component yields $v_\mathrm{hot}$. Hot neutrals sourced from fast-ion charge exchange carry line-of-sight velocities spanning tens to hundreds of km/s, substantially exceeding those of cold recycled neutrals.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the hot neutral atoms are moving from the first to the second point along the line of sight.

NAMES.name: neutron_flux_due_to_beam_beam_fusion
NAMES.subject: neutron
NAMES.short: Total neutron count rate from neutron-producing beam-beam fusion reactions, summed over represented fast-ion fuel channels in which both reactants are nonthermal ions from neutral beam injection.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the volume-integrated neutron count rate from fusion reactions between two nonthermal fast fuel ions generated by neutral beam injection. It includes only neutron-producing reaction branches and aggregates the represented isotope channels. It is the neutron-count component of [beam-beam fusion flux](name:flux_due_to_beam_beam_fusion), distinct from beam-thermal and thermonuclear neutron production.

$$
\dot{N}_{n}^{\mathrm{bb}} = \sum_{(a,b)\in\mathcal{C}} \int_{V} \nu_{ab}^{(n)}(\mathbf{r})\,R_{ab}^{\mathrm{bb}}(\mathbf{r})\,\mathrm{d}V
$$

Here $\dot{N}_{n}^{\mathrm{bb}}$ is the total neutron count rate, $\mathcal{C}$ is the set of included fast-ion reaction channels, $a$ and $b$ label the fast-ion fuel species, $R_{ab}^{\mathrm{bb}}(\mathbf{r})$ is the local beam-beam reaction rate density, $\nu_{ab}^{(n)}$ is the neutron multiplicity of the reaction branch, $V$ is the active plasma volume, and $\mathbf{r}$ is position. Channel-specific entries such as [deuterium-deuterium neutron flux due to beam-beam fusion](name:deuterium_deuterium_neutron_flux_due_to_beam_beam_fusion) and [deuterium-tritium neutron flux due to beam-beam fusion](name:deuterium_tritium_neutron_flux_due_to_beam_beam_fusion) resolve the aggregate by fuel channel.

NAMES.name: neutron_flux_due_to_beam_thermal_fusion
NAMES.subject: neutron
NAMES.short: Neutron flux due to beam-thermal fusion is the global neutron emission rate from fusion reactions in which fast injected beam ions react with thermal plasma ions. It is the channel-summed beam-thermal neutron flux, excluding thermal-thermal and beam-beam fusion.
NAMES.long:
Neutron flux due to beam-thermal fusion is the global neutron emission rate from fusion reactions in which fast ions originating from injected neutral beams react with thermal plasma ions. It is integrated over the plasma volume and summed over all neutron-emitting beam-thermal reaction channels.

For resolved fast-ion and thermal-ion velocity distributions, the channel-summed neutron emission rate is defined by:

$$
\Phi_n^{\mathrm{BT}} = \sum_{(a,b)\in \mathcal{C}_n} \int_V \int \int f_a^{\mathrm{beam}}(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{v}_a) f_b^{\mathrm{th}}(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{v}_b) \sigma_{ab}(v_{\mathrm{rel}}) v_{\mathrm{rel}} Y_{ab}(v_{\mathrm{rel}}) \, d^3v_a \, d^3v_b \, dV
$$

where $\Phi_n^{\mathrm{BT}}$ is the beam-thermal neutron emission rate, $V$ is the plasma volume over which the reactions are counted, $\mathcal{C}_n$ is the set of ordered neutron-emitting beam-thermal reaction pairs, $a$ labels the fast beam-ion isotope, $b$ labels the thermal target isotope, $f_a^{\mathrm{beam}}$ and $f_b^{\mathrm{th}}$ are velocity-space density distributions normalized so that velocity integration gives the corresponding number density, $\sigma_{ab}$ is the fusion cross-section, $v_{\mathrm{rel}}=|\mathbf{v}_a-\mathbf{v}_b|$ is the relative speed, and $Y_{ab}$ is the neutron yield per reaction.

This quantity is the neutron-yield-weighted sum of channel-resolved beam-thermal fusion rates, including [deuterium-deuterium beam-thermal neutron flux](name:deuterium_deuterium_neutron_flux_due_to_beam_thermal_fusion) and [deuterium-tritium beam-thermal neutron flux](name:deuterium_tritium_neutron_flux_due_to_beam_thermal_fusion) when those channels are present. It excludes thermal-thermal fusion, beam-beam fusion, and non-fusion neutron sources. It counts emitted neutrons rather than reaction events, so neutron-branching fractions and neutron multiplicities are included in $Y_{ab}$.

NAMES.name: radiated_power_density
NAMES.short: Power density due to radiation is the local volumetric rate at which plasma energy is converted into emitted electromagnetic radiation.
NAMES.long:
Power density due to radiation is the local volumetric rate at which plasma energy is converted into emitted electromagnetic radiation. It is the non-negative magnitude of radiative energy loss from the emitting plasma volume.

The radiated power density is defined by

$$
P_{\mathrm{rad}} = \frac{\mathrm{d}P_{\mathrm{emit}}}{\mathrm{d}V}
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{emit}}$ is the emitted electromagnetic power and $V$ is the emitting volume. This quantity represents radiative emission rather than the signed source term in the plasma energy balance; radiation contributes negatively to that balance. It is a volumetric quantity and is distinct from the incident surface flux represented by [flux at wall due to radiation](name:flux_at_wall_due_to_radiation). The broader [power density](name:power_density) includes radiative and non-radiative source or loss mechanisms.

NAMES.name: ratio_of_volume_averaged_krypton_density_to_volume_averaged_electron_density
NAMES.short: Ratio of volume-averaged krypton density to volume-averaged electron density compares the krypton number density, summed over all charge states and averaged over the plasma volume, with the electron number density averaged over the same volume.
NAMES.long:
Ratio of volume-averaged krypton density to volume-averaged electron density is the abundance ratio formed from the volume average of krypton number density and the volume average of electron number density over the same plasma volume. The krypton density is the species-level krypton number density summed over all charge states, including neutral through fully stripped krypton.

The ratio is defined by the quotient of the two volume averages:

$$
f_{\mathrm{Kr},V} = \frac{\langle n_{\mathrm{Kr}} \rangle_V}{\langle n_e \rangle_V} = \frac{V_p^{-1}\int_{V_p}\sum_{q=0}^{Z_{\mathrm{Kr}}} n_{\mathrm{Kr},q}(\mathbf{x})\,dV}{V_p^{-1}\int_{V_p} n_e(\mathbf{x})\,dV}
$$

where $\langle n_{\mathrm{Kr}} \rangle_V$ is the [volume-averaged krypton density](name:volume_averaged_krypton_density), $\langle n_e \rangle_V$ is the [volume-averaged electron density](name:volume_averaged_electron_density), $V_p$ is the averaging plasma volume, $n_{\mathrm{Kr},q}$ is the krypton number density in charge state $q$, $q=0$ denotes neutral krypton, $q=Z_{\mathrm{Kr}}$ denotes fully stripped krypton, $Z_{\mathrm{Kr}}$ is the nuclear charge of krypton, $n_e$ is the electron number density, and $\mathbf{x}$ is position.

This quantity uses the same volume-averaging operation in the numerator and denominator. It is not normalized by the maximum local electron density and is not a local krypton-to-electron density ratio at a particular position.

NAMES.name: ratio_of_volume_averaged_neon_density_to_volume_averaged_electron_density
NAMES.short: Dimensionless abundance ratio of charge-state-summed neon nuclei to electrons, with both number densities averaged over the plasma volume bounded by the last closed flux surface.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the volume-averaged abundance of neon nuclei relative to the volume-averaged electron population. The neon numerator includes neutral through fully stripped neon and is summed over all ionization states.

$$
A_{\mathrm{Ne}} = \frac{\langle n_{\mathrm{Ne}} \rangle_V}{\langle n_e \rangle_V}
$$

where $\langle n_{\mathrm{Ne}} \rangle_V$ is the [volume-averaged neon density](name:volume_averaged_neon_density), $\langle n_e \rangle_V$ is the [volume-averaged electron density](name:volume_averaged_electron_density), and the volume average is taken over the plasma volume bounded by the last closed flux surface. This ratio is distinct from the local [neon density](name:neon_density) and does not resolve neon ionization states.

NAMES.name: ratio_of_volume_averaged_nitrogen_density_to_volume_averaged_electron_density
NAMES.short: Dimensionless abundance ratio of volume-averaged nitrogen nuclei to volume-averaged electrons, with nitrogen summed over all ionization states inside the last closed flux surface.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the abundance of nitrogen nuclei relative to electrons in the plasma volume enclosed by the last closed flux surface. The nitrogen population includes neutral and charged nitrogen, summed over all ionization states, while the electron density provides the reference population.

$$
f_{\mathrm{N/e}} = \frac{\langle n_{\mathrm{N}} \rangle_V}{\langle n_e \rangle_V}
$$

where $\langle n_{\mathrm{N}} \rangle_V$ is the [volume-averaged nitrogen density](name:volume_averaged_nitrogen_density), $\langle n_e \rangle_V$ is the [volume-averaged electron density](name:volume_averaged_electron_density), and $V$ is the plasma volume enclosed by the last closed flux surface. This is a ratio of separate volume averages, not the volume average of a local nitrogen-to-electron ratio.

NAMES.name: refractive_index_of_optical_element
NAMES.short: Dimensionless wave-propagation quantity relating electromagnetic phase propagation in a medium to vacuum propagation, including vector and scalar forms.
NAMES.long:
The refractive index is the dimensionless relation between an electromagnetic wave’s phase propagation in a medium and in vacuum. It describes the wave-vector direction and magnitude relative to vacuum propagation, while material-specific forms describe the corresponding phase-velocity ratio.

The defining relation is:

$$
\mathbf{n} = \frac{\mathbf{k}}{k_0}, \qquad k_0 = \frac{\omega}{c}
$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ is the refractive-index vector, $\mathbf{k}$ is the wave vector, $k_0$ is the vacuum wave number, $\omega$ is angular frequency, and $c$ is the speed of light in vacuum. For a scalar bulk-medium index, the corresponding relation is $n = c/v_{\rm ph}$, where $v_{\rm ph}$ is phase velocity. Directional plasma projections include [parallel refractive index](name:parallel_refractive_index), while wavelength-resolved optical-material behavior is represented by [spectral refractive index of optical element](name:spectral_refractive_index_of_optical_element).
NAMES.sign: Positive when a signed wave-vector projection points along its stated positive direction; cylindrical directions use the right-handed $(R, \phi, Z)$ basis.

NAMES.name: spectral_refractive_index_of_optical_element
NAMES.short: Wavelength-dependent refractive index of an optical-element material, defined by the ratio of vacuum light speed to phase velocity and expressing material dispersion.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the phase refractive index of the optical-element material resolved as a function of wavelength. It describes how the material changes electromagnetic phase propagation relative to vacuum.

For vacuum wavelength $\lambda$, the refractive index is defined by

$$
n(\lambda) = \frac{c}{v_p(\lambda)}
$$

where $n(\lambda)$ is the dimensionless refractive index, $c$ is the vacuum speed of light, $v_p(\lambda)$ is the material phase velocity, and $\lambda$ is the vacuum wavelength; $c$ and $v_p$ are measured in m s$^{-1}$ and $\lambda$ in m.

The wavelength dependence represents material dispersion and distinguishes this quantity from the wavelength-independent abstraction [refractive index of the optical element](name:refractive_index_of_optical_element). It describes phase propagation only and does not represent absorptive loss or a complex extinction component. The wavelength coordinate is the spectral axis defined by [spectral wavelength of optical element](name:spectral_wavelength_of_optical_element).

NAMES.name: total_neutron_source_rate_due_to_thermal_fusion
NAMES.subject: neutron
NAMES.short: Total neutron production rate from thermonuclear neutron-producing deuterium-deuterium, deuterium-tritium, and tritium-tritium reaction branches among Maxwellian bulk ions, excluding beam-target and beam-beam fast-ion contributions.
NAMES.long:
The total neutron source rate due to thermal fusion is the number of neutrons produced per unit time by the neutron-producing thermal deuterium-deuterium, deuterium-tritium, and tritium-tritium reaction branches between bulk ions with locally Maxwellian velocity distributions. It is the channel-summed member of [neutron source rate due to thermal fusion](name:neutron_source_rate_due_to_thermal_fusion), equal to the sum of [deuterium-deuterium neutron source rate due to thermal fusion](name:deuterium_deuterium_neutron_source_rate_due_to_thermal_fusion), [deuterium-tritium neutron source rate due to thermal fusion], and [tritium-tritium neutron source rate due to thermal fusion](name:tritium_tritium_neutron_source_rate_due_to_thermal_fusion).

The channel-summed thermal neutron source rate is defined by

$$
S_{n,\mathrm{tot}}^{\mathrm{th}} = \int_V \sum_{c \in \{DD,DT,TT\}} \nu_{n,c}\,\frac{n_{a_c} n_{b_c}}{1+\delta_{a_c b_c}}\,\langle\sigma v\rangle_c(T_{a_c},T_{b_c})\,dV
$$

where $S_{n,\mathrm{tot}}^{\mathrm{th}}$ is the total source rate, $V$ is the emitting plasma volume, $c$ labels a neutron-producing thermal fusion branch, $\nu_{n,c}$ is the neutron multiplicity of branch $c$, $a_c$ and $b_c$ are its reactant ion species, $n_{a_c}$ and $n_{b_c}$ are their local bulk number densities, $\delta_{a_c b_c}$ is one for identical reactants and zero otherwise, $\langle\sigma v\rangle_c$ is the Maxwellian-averaged reactivity, $T_{a_c}$ and $T_{b_c}$ are the local reactant temperatures, and $dV$ is a volume element. The denominator prevents double counting of identical reactant pairs.

Only reactions among locally Maxwellian bulk ions are included; beam-target, beam-beam, fusion-product, and other nonthermal fast-ion contributions are excluded. For deuterium-deuterium fusion, only the D(d,n)$^3\mathrm{He}$ neutron branch contributes; the D(d,p)T proton branch is not counted. For deuterium-deuterium and deuterium-tritium neutron branches $\nu_{n,c}=1$, while for tritium-tritium fusion $\nu_{n,c}=2$.

NAMES.name: wavelength_of_camera
NAMES.short: Spectral wavelength characterizing a camera detector channel's optical response band, encompassing characteristic wavelengths such as band-edge cutoffs that define the channel's sensitivity range.
NAMES.long:
Wavelength of a camera is the spectral coordinate, expressed as vacuum wavelength, that identifies a characteristic position within a camera detector channel's spectral sensitivity band. As a parent quantity, it encompasses any fiducial wavelength associated with the camera's optical response, including upper and lower sensitivity cutoffs.

For a monochromatic wave in vacuum, wavelength relates to optical frequency by

$$
\lambda = \frac{c}{\nu}
$$

where $\lambda$ is the vacuum wavelength in meters, $c$ is the speed of light in vacuum in meters per second, and $\nu$ is the optical frequency in hertz.

The specific instance [upper_bound_wavelength_of_camera](name:upper_bound_wavelength_of_camera) identifies the long-wavelength (red-side) cutoff above which photons fall outside the detector response. This parallels [wavelength_of_filter](name:wavelength_of_filter), which similarly encompasses passband edge and center wavelengths for optical filters; both quantities share the same physical definition of vacuum wavelength but differ in the optical element and response characteristic they describe.

NAMES.name: upper_bound_wavelength_of_camera
NAMES.short: Long-wavelength boundary of a visible-camera detector channel’s spectral sensitivity band; photons at longer wavelengths fall outside the defined response interval.
NAMES.long:
The red-side cutoff is the long-wavelength boundary of a visible-camera detector channel’s spectral sensitivity band. It identifies the upper endpoint of the characteristic wavelength range represented by [wavelength of camera](name:wavelength_of_camera).

For a band with short-wavelength boundary $\lambda_{\rm blue}$ and long-wavelength boundary $\lambda_{\rm red}$, the sensitivity interval is represented by

$$
\Lambda_{\rm camera} = [\lambda_{\rm blue},\lambda_{\rm red}]
$$

where $\Lambda_{\rm camera}$ is the defined vacuum-wavelength sensitivity interval and both boundary wavelengths are measured in m.

This quantity is a band edge, not a central wavelength or bandwidth. Photons with vacuum wavelength greater than $\lambda_{\rm red}$ lie beyond the defined detector response interval.

sources.enhanced_context: Upper bound of the detector wavelength sensitivity range for a visible camera channel. Defines the long-wavelength cutoff of the spectral window used for photon detection.
sources.leaf_definition: Upper bound of the detector wavelength range
sources.parent_definition: Set of detectors

NAMES.name: wavelength_of_detector_pixel
NAMES.short: Wavelength of a detector pixel is the vacuum spectral coordinate assigned by Bragg diffraction geometry to its representative X-ray response.
NAMES.long:
Wavelength of a detector pixel is the vacuum spectral coordinate assigned to a detector pixel by the Bragg diffraction geometry of an X-ray crystal spectrometer. It identifies a characteristic photon wavelength associated with the pixel's response.

The assigned wavelength follows Bragg's relation:

$$
n\lambda_0 = 2d\sin(\theta_B)
$$

where $\lambda_0$ is the vacuum wavelength, $d$ is the spacing of the diffracting crystal lattice planes, $\theta_B$ is the Bragg angle between the incident beam and those planes, and $n$ is the diffraction order.

This pixel-level assignment is a specialization of [wavelength](name:wavelength) and is distinct from the channel-level response coordinate [wavelength_of_spectrometer_channel](name:wavelength_of_spectrometer_channel). The corresponding photon-energy representation is [energy_of_detector_pixel](name:energy_of_detector_pixel), while the accepted spectral bounds are given by [lower_bound_energy_of_detector_pixel](name:lower_bound_energy_of_detector_pixel) and [upper_bound_energy_of_detector_pixel](name:upper_bound_energy_of_detector_pixel).

sources.enhanced_context: Bragg wavelength (λ_Bragg) of the diffracting crystal in an X-ray crystal spectrometer channel, satisfying the Bragg diffraction condition for the crystal's lattice spacing and orientation. Determines the central wavelength of the spectral passband.
sources.leaf_definition: Bragg wavelength of the crystal
sources.parent_definition: Characteristics of the crystal used

sources.enhanced_context: 2D map of photon wavelength across each detector pixel of the X-ray crystal spectrometer frame. Primarily varies horizontally due to Bragg dispersion, with a full 2D map capturing the elliptical curvature of iso-wavelength surfaces in the vertical direction.
sources.leaf_definition: Wavelength of incoming photons on each pixel of the frames, mainly varying accross the horizontal dimension of the frame. However a 2D map of the wavelength is given since it is not constant vertically due to the elliptical curvature of the photon iso-surfaces
sources.parent_definition: Measurement channel, composed of a camera, a crystal, and (optional) a set of reflectors. The light coming from the plasma passes through the (optional) set of reflectors, then the crystal and arrives at the camera

NAMES.name: wavelength_of_filter
NAMES.short: Wavelength of a filter is the spectral coordinate, expressed as vacuum wavelength, that identifies a characteristic point or boundary of a diagnostic filter's transmitted spectral band.
NAMES.long:
Wavelength of a filter is the spectral coordinate, expressed as vacuum wavelength, that identifies a characteristic point or boundary of a filter's transmitted spectral band. It is a property of the filter transmission response, rather than the rest-frame wavelength of a spectral line or the wavelength inside a material medium.

For a filter characteristic associated with temporal frequency $\nu_f$, the vacuum wavelength is defined by:

$$
\lambda_f = \frac{c}{\nu_f}
$$

where $\lambda_f$ is the filter characteristic vacuum wavelength, $c$ is the speed of light in vacuum, and $\nu_f$ is the corresponding temporal frequency.

This parent quantity includes passband-edge wavelengths such as the [lower wavelength of a filter](name:lower_wavelength_of_filter) and [upper wavelength of a filter](name:upper_wavelength_of_filter), and nominal response wavelengths such as the [reference wavelength of a filter](name:reference_wavelength_of_filter). It excludes the full transmission function and any medium-dependent wavelength convention.
