sources.leaf_definition: Central wavelength of the filter
sources.parent_definition: Filter description

NAMES.name: lower_wavelength_of_filter
NAMES.short: Lower wavelength boundary of the spectral passband transmitted by a diagnostic filter window, marking the short-wavelength edge below which transmission is attenuated.
NAMES.long:
The lower wavelength of a filter is the short-wavelength boundary of the passband transmitted by a diagnostic filter window. It marks the high-frequency edge of the transmitted spectral interval.

The wavelength corresponding to this passband boundary is related to photon frequency by

$$
\lambda_{\mathrm{lower}} = \frac{c}{\nu_{\mathrm{lower}}}
$$

where $\lambda_{\mathrm{lower}}$ is the lower passband wavelength, $\nu_{\mathrm{lower}}$ is the photon frequency at that boundary, and $c$ is the speed of light in vacuum.

The lower wavelength is the short-wavelength counterpart of the [upper wavelength of a filter](name:upper_wavelength_of_filter), with the transmitted interval bounded by these two wavelengths. It is one component of the overall [wavelength of a filter](name:wavelength_of_filter) and is distinct from the [reference wavelength of a filter](name:reference_wavelength_of_filter), which identifies the nominal center or designated peak-transmission wavelength.

NAMES.name: upper_wavelength_of_filter
NAMES.short: Upper wavelength boundary of the spectral passband transmitted by a diagnostic filter window, marking the long-wavelength edge above which transmission is attenuated.
NAMES.long:
The upper wavelength of a filter, $\lambda_\mathrm{upper}$, is the long-wavelength boundary of the passband transmitted by a diagnostic filter window. It marks the low-frequency, low-photon-energy edge of the transmitted spectral interval.

The photon energy corresponding to this boundary is the minimum photon energy admitted at the upper edge:

$$
E_\mathrm{min} = \frac{hc}{\lambda_\mathrm{upper}}
$$

where $E_\mathrm{min}$ is the photon energy at the upper wavelength boundary, $h$ is Planck's constant, and $c$ is the speed of light in vacuum.

For a finite passband, [lower_wavelength_of_filter](name:lower_wavelength_of_filter) and $\lambda_\mathrm{upper}$ bound the transmitted wavelength interval, with $\lambda_\mathrm{lower} \le \lambda_\mathrm{upper}$ under the same passband acceptance criterion. The [width_of_filter](name:width_of_filter) is related to their difference only when the width and both edge wavelengths are defined using the same transmission criterion; [reference_wavelength_of_filter](name:reference_wavelength_of_filter) instead denotes the nominal center or designated peak-transmission wavelength, not a passband edge.

NAMES.name: wavelength_of_spectral_line
NAMES.short: Central rest-frame vacuum wavelength of an atomic, ionic, molecular, or nuclear spectral emission or absorption line. It is set by the transition energy between quantum states and identifies the unshifted physical line.
NAMES.long:
Wavelength of a spectral line is the central vacuum wavelength $\lambda_0$ of the photon associated with a transition between two quantum states, evaluated in the rest frame of the emitting or absorbing species. It is a property of the transition itself, separate from observed wavelength shifts, broadening, field-induced splitting, and instrumental response.

The rest wavelength is set by the transition energy:

$$
\lambda_0 = \frac{h c}{|E_u - E_l|}
$$

where $\lambda_0$ is the vacuum wavelength in meters, $h$ is the Planck constant in joule seconds, $c$ is the speed of light in meters per second, and $E_u$ and $E_l$ are the upper- and lower-state energies in joules.

In spectroscopy, $\lambda_0$ is usually taken from evaluated atomic, molecular, or nuclear transition data, or from fitted line centers after wavelength calibration and correction to vacuum wavelength. For an observed line center $\lambda_{\mathrm{obs}}$ in meters, the non-relativistic Doppler relation is $(\lambda_{\mathrm{obs}}-\lambda_0)/\lambda_0 \approx v_{\mathrm{los}}/c$ for $|v_{\mathrm{los}}| \ll c$, where $v_{\mathrm{los}}$ is in meters per second and is positive when the source recedes from the observer, increasing the observed wavelength. Thermal Doppler Gaussian width scales as $\sigma_\lambda/\lambda_0 \approx \sqrt{k_B T_s/(m_s c^2)}$, where $\sigma_\lambda$ is in meters, $T_s$ is the species temperature in kelvin, and $m_s$ is the particle mass in kilograms; equivalently use $\sqrt{T_s/(m_s c^2)}$ when $T_s$ is expressed as an energy.

The quantity is not limited to a particular spectral band. Lines used in plasma spectroscopy commonly span about $1\times10^{-11}$-$1\times10^{-5}$ m, including soft-x-ray lines near $1\times10^{-10}$-$1\times10^{-9}$ m, extreme-ultraviolet and ultraviolet lines near $1\times10^{-8}$-$4\times10^{-7}$ m, visible lines near $4\times10^{-7}$-$7\times10^{-7}$ m, and near-infrared lines near $7\times10^{-7}$-$1\times10^{-5}$ m; other atomic, molecular, or nuclear transitions can lie outside these ranges.

NAMES.name: wavelength_of_spectrometer_channel
NAMES.short: Wavelength of a spectrometer channel is the spectral coordinate, expressed as vacuum wavelength, that identifies a characteristic point of the channel's spectral response. It covers channel-response wavelengths such as the reference wavelength at maximum instrument-function response.
NAMES.long:
Wavelength of a spectrometer channel is the spectral coordinate, expressed as vacuum wavelength, that assigns a characteristic wavelength to a spectrometer channel's optical response. It is a property of the channel response, rather than the rest-frame wavelength of a physical spectral transition.

When represented by its corresponding vacuum frequency, the channel wavelength obeys:

$$
\lambda_{\mathrm{ch}} = \frac{c}{\nu_{\mathrm{ch}}}
$$

where $\lambda_{\mathrm{ch}}$ is the vacuum wavelength assigned to the spectrometer channel, $c$ is the speed of light in vacuum in m s$^{-1}$, and $\nu_{\mathrm{ch}}$ is the corresponding vacuum frequency in s$^{-1}$.

This parent quantity is limited to wavelength coordinates assigned to spectrometer channels through their spectral response. The attested concrete specialization is the [reference wavelength of a spectrometer channel](name:reference_wavelength_of_spectrometer_channel), the vacuum wavelength at which the channel's spectral instrument function has maximum response; the quantity excludes channel bandwidths and in-medium wavelengths unless a separate medium-dependent convention is explicitly defined.

NAMES.name: reference_wavelength_of_spectrometer_channel
NAMES.short: Vacuum wavelength at which a spectrometer channel’s spectral instrument function has its maximum response, identifying the channel’s response peak rather than a physical spectral line.
NAMES.long:
The reference wavelength of a spectrometer channel is the vacuum wavelength corresponding to the maximum of that channel’s spectral instrument function. It is the peak-position specialization of [wavelength of a spectrometer channel](name:wavelength_of_spectrometer_channel), not the wavelength of a plasma emission line or an independently selected calibration reference.

The reference wavelength is defined by

$$
\lambda_{\mathrm{ref}} = \underset{\lambda}{\operatorname{arg\,max}}\; \mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{ch}}(\lambda)
$$

where $\lambda$ is vacuum wavelength and $\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{ch}}(\lambda)$ is the spectral instrument function of the channel as a function of wavelength. The value identifies the response maximum; the response spread is described separately by quantities such as [spectral width of a spectrometer channel](name:spectral_width_of_spectrometer_channel).

sources.enhanced_context: Central wavelength of the instrument function for a given vertical bin of the X-ray crystal spectrometer, representing the absolute wavelength at the centre of the detector response function for that bin.

The resulting image on the detector will be a 2-D distribution of pixel values, for each wavelength. It can be given as explicit values for each detector pixel (values node) or as a parametric function of wavelength (described by the other nodes)

NAMES.name: area_of_first_wall
NAMES.short: Total geometric area of the material surface forming the plasma-facing first wall, including installed wall armor and bare vessel surface where applicable.
NAMES.long:
The first-wall area is the geometric measure of the material surface exposed toward the plasma and forming the innermost plasma-facing boundary. It includes installed wall armor and bare vessel surface where no armor is present, but excludes backing structures and surfaces that are not plasma-facing.

$$
A_{\mathrm{FW}} = \int_{\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{FW}}} \mathrm{d}A
$$

where $A_{\mathrm{FW}}$ is the total first-wall area, $\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{FW}}$ is the plasma-facing first-wall surface, and $\mathrm{d}A$ is an elemental surface area. This surface measure is distinct from the enclosed [volume of the first wall](name:volume_of_first_wall) and provides the geometric basis for integrating areal loads such as [energy flux at the wall](name:energy_flux_at_wall).

sources.enhanced_context: Total surface area of the first wall (A_fw), the plasma-facing inner surface of the vacuum vessel. A global device geometry parameter relevant to plasma-wall interaction and heat load analysis.
sources.leaf_definition: First wall surface area

NAMES.name: fraction_of_breeder_blanket_layer
NAMES.short: Fraction of breeder blanket layer is the part-to-whole share of a specified constituent material, phase, void, or subregion within a defined breeder-blanket layer. It abstracts composition fractions formed on a stated basis, such as volume, mass, chemical amount, or atom count, for homogenized layer properties.
NAMES.long:
Fraction of breeder blanket layer is the composition share of a specified constituent material, phase, void, or subregion within a defined breeder-blanket layer. It is an abstract part-to-whole fraction; each concrete specialization defines which extensive geometrical or material measure is used to form the share.

For a constituent $\alpha$ and a chosen fraction basis $Q$, the fraction is defined by

$$
f_\alpha^{(Q)} = \frac{Q_\alpha}{Q_\mathrm{layer}}
$$

where $Q_\alpha$ is the selected extensive measure associated with constituent $\alpha$ in the breeder-blanket layer, and $Q_\mathrm{layer}$ is the corresponding total measure for that same layer on the same basis.

Fractions formed on different bases, such as volume basis, mass basis, chemical-amount basis, or atom-count basis, are distinct quantities and are not generally interchangeable. The [volumetric fraction of breeder blanket layer](name:volumetric_fraction_of_breeder_blanket_layer) is the volume-basis specialization of this parent concept. A set of such fractions sums to unity only when the listed constituents form a complete, non-overlapping decomposition of the same layer on the same basis.

NAMES.name: heating_power_of_breeder_blanket
NAMES.short: Heating power of a breeder blanket is the rate at which thermal energy is deposited or generated in breeder-blanket materials, integrated over the whole blanket and independent of deposition mechanism. Mechanism-qualified names such as nuclear heating power are contributions to this aggregate.
NAMES.long:
Heating power of a breeder blanket is the total rate of conversion of any energy source into thermal energy within the materials of the breeder blanket. It is a mechanism-independent source power for the blanket as a component, summed over all breeder-blanket modules and materials.

The integrated heating power may be written as the sum of volumetric and absorbed surface contributions:

$$
P_\mathrm{heat} = \int_{V_\mathrm{bb}} q_V(\mathbf{r})\,dV + \int_{\partial V_\mathrm{bb}} q_S(\mathbf{r})\,dA
$$

where $V_\mathrm{bb}$ is the breeder-blanket material volume, $\partial V_\mathrm{bb}$ denotes its heat-receiving boundary surfaces, $q_V$ is the local volumetric heating-rate density, and $q_S$ is the absorbed surface heat-flux density.

Only energy deposited in or converted to heat by the breeder-blanket materials is included. Incident power not absorbed in those materials, heat generated in neighboring structures, and power removed by coolants after deposition are not part of this source quantity. Mechanism-qualified quantities, such as [nuclear heating power of a breeder blanket](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket), are specific contributions to this mechanism-independent quantity rather than duplicate definitions.

NAMES.name: heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_layer
NAMES.short: Rate at which energy is deposited as heat within a defined breeder-blanket material layer, integrated over the layer and independent of deposition mechanism.
NAMES.long:
Heating power of a breeder-blanket layer is the total rate of energy converted to heat within a specified material layer. It is an extensive quantity integrated over the layer, rather than a local volumetric heat source.

$$
P_{\mathrm{layer}} = \int_{V_{\mathrm{layer}}} \dot{q}_{\mathrm{dep}}(\mathbf{r})\,\mathrm{d}V
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{layer}}$ is the layer-integrated heating power, $\dot{q}_{\mathrm{dep}}(\mathbf{r})$ is the local volumetric rate of energy deposition at position $\mathbf{r}$, and $V_{\mathrm{layer}}$ is the volume of the defined material layer. The quantity is distinct from [power density of a breeder blanket layer](name:power_density_of_breeder_blanket_layer), which is local; [nuclear heating power of a breeder blanket layer](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_layer) is a mechanism-specific specialization involving neutron and photon energy deposition.

NAMES.name: heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_shield
NAMES.short: Rate of energy deposition as heat within the breeder blanket shield, integrated over the full shield volume and independent of the specific deposition mechanism.
NAMES.long:
The heating power of the breeder blanket shield is the volume-integral of all local power-deposition rates within the shield structural materials, encompassing every mechanism by which incident radiation transfers energy to the shield.

The total shield heating power $P_\mathrm{shield}$ is defined as:

$$
P_\mathrm{shield} = \int_{V_\mathrm{shield}} q'''(\mathbf{r}) \, dV
$$

where $q'''(\mathbf{r})$ is the local volumetric power deposition rate and $V_\mathrm{shield}$ is the total shield volume.

In a fusion blanket, the shield primarily attenuates the neutron and photon fluxes emerging from the breeding zone, making nuclear interactions — neutron scattering, neutron capture, and secondary gamma absorption — the dominant heating channel, as detailed by [nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_shield](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_shield). This total power sets the thermal load on shield coolant circuits and constrains peak material temperatures critical for structural integrity. The layer-resolved analog [nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_layer](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_layer) and the module-integrated quantity [nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_module](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_module) provide complementary views of the power distribution within the broader blanket system. Shield heating powers are obtained by integrating neutron and photon transport solutions over the shield volume, summing contributions from all interaction channels.

NAMES.name: nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket
NAMES.short: Total rate of heat generation in all breeder-blanket materials from neutron and photon interactions, excluding plasma-facing surface heat loads and external incident power.
NAMES.long:
Nuclear heating power of the breeder blanket is the total rate at which neutron and photon interactions deposit energy as heat throughout all included blanket materials. It is the blanket-wide nuclear component of [heating power of the breeder blanket](name:heating_power_of_breeder_blanket).

The defining relation is

$$
P_{\mathrm{nuc}} = \int_{V_{\mathrm{BB}}} q_{\mathrm{nuc}}(\mathbf{r})\,dV
$$

where $q_{\mathrm{nuc}}(\mathbf{r})$ is the local nuclear heating power density in W m$^{-3}$, $\mathbf{r}$ is position within the blanket, $dV$ is differential volume in m$^3$, and $V_{\mathrm{BB}}$ is the union of the included blanket-module and constituent-material volumes.

The integral includes energy deposited by neutron scattering, neutron capture, and photon interactions, including secondary gamma absorption, without double-counting overlapping material descriptions. It excludes power carried by neutrons or photons crossing into the blanket before deposition and separate plasma-facing surface loads. Module- and layer-restricted integrals are represented by [nuclear heating power of the breeder blanket module](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_module) and [nuclear heating power of the breeder blanket layer](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_layer), respectively.

sources.enhanced_context: Nuclear heating power deposited in the breeding blanket modules by neutron and gamma interactions (P_nuclear,blanket). A key performance metric governing tritium breeding and energy multiplication in a fusion reactor.
sources.leaf_definition: Nuclear heating power on the blanket
sources.parent_definition: Dynamic quantities for a set of time_slices

NAMES.name: nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_layer
NAMES.short: Total rate of heat generated within one breeder-blanket material layer by neutron and photon interactions, excluding external and surface heat loads.
NAMES.long:
Nuclear heating power of a breeder-blanket layer is the volume-integrated rate at which neutron and photon interactions convert radiation energy into heat within that material layer. It is the nuclear component of [heating power of a breeder-blanket layer](name:heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_layer), rather than the local volumetric quantity [nuclear power density of a breeder-blanket layer](name:nuclear_power_density_of_breeder_blanket_layer).

The defining relation is

$$
P_{\mathrm{nuc,layer}} = \int_{V_{\mathrm{layer}}} \dot{q}_{\mathrm{nuc}}\,\mathrm{d}V
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{nuc,layer}}$ is the layer-integrated nuclear heating power, $\dot{q}_{\mathrm{nuc}}$ is the local nuclear energy-deposition rate per unit volume, and $V_{\mathrm{layer}}$ is the volume of the specified material layer.

The integral includes energy deposited by neutron interactions and absorption of primary or secondary photons within the layer. It excludes plasma-facing radiative heat loads, incident energy that is not deposited, and energy deposited outside the layer; the result is non-negative.

sources.enhanced_context: Total nuclear power deposited in a specific breeding blanket layer by neutron heating. Represents the volumetric nuclear heat load from fusion neutron interactions with the blanket material.
sources.leaf_definition: Nuclear power heating this layer
sources.parent_definition: Dynamic quantities at various time slices

NAMES.name: nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_module
NAMES.short: Rate of nuclear energy deposited throughout one breeder blanket module by neutron interactions and associated photon absorption, excluding incident and externally applied heat.
NAMES.long:
Nuclear heating power of a breeder blanket module is the rate of nuclear energy deposited within the material volume of one module by neutron interactions and the absorption of primary or secondary photons. It is an integrated deposition quantity, not incident radiation power or local power density.

The module-integrated power is defined by

$$
P_{\mathrm{nuc,module}} = \int_{V_{\mathrm{module}}} q_{\mathrm{nuc}}(\mathbf{r})\,\mathrm{d}V
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{nuc,module}}$ is the integrated nuclear heating power, $V_{\mathrm{module}}$ is the module material volume, $q_{\mathrm{nuc}}(\mathbf{r})$ is the local nuclear heating power density in W m$^{-3}$, $\mathbf{r}$ is position in the module in m, and $\mathrm{d}V$ is differential material volume in m$^{3}$.

The integration includes energy deposited in module materials by neutron and photon interactions. It excludes unde posited incident radiation, plasma-facing surface heat loads, and heat subsequently transferred to coolant. It is distinct from the local [nuclear power density of a breeder blanket module](name:nuclear_power_density_of_breeder_blanket_module), the layer-resolved [nuclear heating power of a breeder blanket layer](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_layer), and the blanket-wide [nuclear heating power](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket).

sources.enhanced_context: Total neutron power (deposited plus generated) in a breeding blanket module, combining incident fusion neutrons and neutrons from multiplication reactions. A key quantity for nuclear heating and tritium breeding assessments.
sources.leaf_definition: Total neutron power (deposited + generated) in the blanket module
sources.parent_definition: Dynamic quantities at various time slices

NAMES.name: nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_shield
NAMES.short: Nuclear heating power deposited in the breeding blanket shield by neutron and gamma radiation interactions with shield structural materials.
NAMES.long:
The breeder blanket shield absorbs residual neutron and gamma radiation that penetrates the breeding zone, converting particle energy to heat through neutron scattering, capture reactions, and Compton scattering of secondary photons. This thermal load determines the cooling circuit requirements for the shield structure and is a principal design constraint for protecting superconducting magnets from radiation-induced heating.

The total nuclear heating power is the volume integral of the local nuclear power density $q'''(\mathbf{r})$ over the shield volume $V_\mathrm{shield}$:

$$
P_\mathrm{shield} = \int_{V_\mathrm{shield}} q'''(\mathbf{r}) \, dV
$$

where $q'''(\mathbf{r})$ is in W m$^{-3}$ and sums contributions from both neutron and secondary gamma interactions throughout the shield material.

This quantity is evaluated via neutron transport analysis using validated nuclear cross-section libraries for the shield material composition, benchmarked against integral activation experiments. It is the shield-level analog of the layer-resolved [nuclear heating power of a breeder blanket layer](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_layer) and the blanket-wide integral [nuclear heating power of the full breeding blanket](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket); the volumetric counterpart [nuclear power density of a breeder blanket module](name:nuclear_power_density_of_breeder_blanket_module) provides the spatially resolved distribution used in detailed thermal-hydraulic analyzes.

NAMES.name: power_of_breeder_blanket_module
NAMES.short: Power quantity associated with a single breeder blanket module, abstracting over incident neutron surface loads, volumetric nuclear energy deposition, plasma radiation, and total thermal output as distinct energy-budget components.
NAMES.long:
A breeder blanket module participates in multiple distinct energy-exchange pathways between the fusion plasma and the blanket structure. The principal power channels resolved at the module level include the neutron surface load characterized by [incident_power_of_breeder_blanket_module](name:incident_power_of_breeder_blanket_module), the volumetric nuclear energy deposited inside the module through scattering and capture reactions described by neutron_power_of_breeder_blanket_module, and the electromagnetic photon flux from plasma bremsstrahlung and line radiation quantified by [radiated_power_of_breeder_blanket_module](name:radiated_power_of_breeder_blanket_module).

The total power delivered to the module coolant combines these channels:

$$
P_\mathrm{module} = P_n + P_\mathrm{rad,abs} + P_\mathrm{aux}
$$

where $P_n$ is the deposited neutron power, $P_\mathrm{rad,abs}$ is the absorbed fraction of incident plasma radiation after surface reflection, and $P_\mathrm{aux}$ covers auxiliary heating contributions; nuclear multiplication reactions in the tritium-breeding material can amplify $P_n$ above the incident neutron surface load.

Module-level power quantities are computed from neutronics transport simulations for nuclear deposition channels, coupled with plasma radiation models for photon loads, and validated against calorimetric measurements of coolant enthalpy rise, the latter captured by [net_thermal_power_of_breeder_blanket_module](name:net_thermal_power_of_breeder_blanket_module). The blanket-wide integral summed over all modules is given by [nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket).

NAMES.name: incident_power_of_breeder_blanket_module
NAMES.short: Fusion-born neutron power crossing onto a single breeder blanket module before energy deposition within its materials, defining an incident neutron surface load.
NAMES.long:
The incident neutron power of a breeder blanket module quantifies the energy rate carried by fusion-born neutrons crossing onto the module's neutron-intercepting surface. It is a surface-load quantity, distinct from volumetric nuclear heating and electromagnetic photon power.

The incident power is defined by the surface integral

$$
P_{n,\mathrm{inc}} = \int_{S_\mathrm{module}} q_{n,\mathrm{inc}}(\mathbf{r})\,\mathrm{d}A
$$

where $P_{n,\mathrm{inc}}$ is incident neutron power, $S_\mathrm{module}$ is the module surface receiving the neutrons, $q_{n,\mathrm{inc}}(\mathbf{r})$ is the inward neutron energy-flux density at surface position $\mathbf{r}$, and $\mathrm{d}A$ is a surface-area element. The surface integral includes neutron energy entering the module before subsequent scattering, capture, or nuclear multiplication within its materials.

This quantity is one component of the broader [power associated with a breeder blanket module](name:power_of_breeder_blanket_module). It excludes deposited energy, represented by [nuclear heating power of a breeder blanket module](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_module), and electromagnetic radiation, represented by [incident radiated power of a breeder blanket module](name:incident_radiated_power_of_breeder_blanket_module).

NAMES.name: power_of_limiter_tile
NAMES.short: Component-integrated rate at which energy is deposited in a limiter tile, with the physical power channel and deposition mechanism specified by each specialization.
NAMES.long:
Power of a limiter tile is the total energy-deposition rate attributed to the material of the complete tile for a specified physical channel. It is a component-integrated quantity rather than a local value.

For volume-deposited power, the defining relation is

$$
P = \int_{V} q(\mathbf{r})\,dV
$$

where $P$ is the tile power, $V$ is the tile-material volume, and $q(\mathbf{r})$ is the local volumetric power-deposition rate at position $\mathbf{r}$. The nuclear specialization [nuclear power of limiter tile](name:nuclear_power_of_limiter_tile) applies this relation to energy deposited by neutron and photon interactions; its local counterpart is [nuclear power density of limiter tile](name:nuclear_power_density_of_limiter_tile).

NAMES.name: nuclear_power_of_limiter_tile
NAMES.short: Total nuclear energy-deposition rate within limiter-tile material from neutron interactions and absorption of primary and secondary gamma radiation.
NAMES.long:
Nuclear heating power of a limiter tile is the volume-integrated rate at which neutron and gamma interactions deposit energy as heat throughout the tile material. It is the nuclear component of the complete tile power, rather than a local heating density or incident radiation power.

$$
P_{\mathrm{nuc}} = \int_{V_{\mathrm{tile}}} q_{\mathrm{nuc}}(\mathbf{r})\,dV
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{nuc}}$ is the tile nuclear heating power, $V_{\mathrm{tile}}$ is the volume occupied by tile material, $q_{\mathrm{nuc}}(\mathbf{r})$ is the local nuclear heating power density at position $\mathbf{r}$, and $dV$ is a material-volume element. The deposition includes energy from elastic and inelastic neutron scattering, neutron capture, and absorption of primary and secondary gamma radiation. It is the volume integral of [nuclear power density of a limiter tile](name:nuclear_power_density_of_limiter_tile) and specializes [power of a limiter tile](name:power_of_limiter_tile) to the nuclear-heating channel; incident energy that is not deposited in the tile is excluded.

NAMES.name: pressure_at_cooling_circuit_inlet
NAMES.short: Absolute static pressure of a coolant or working fluid at a defined hydraulic location, referenced to perfect vacuum and independent of flow-speed effects.
NAMES.long:
Absolute static pressure is the isotropic thermodynamic pressure of a coolant or working fluid at a defined hydraulic location, referenced to perfect vacuum. It describes the local fluid state rather than a pressure contribution associated with bulk-flow motion.

The quantity is the static component only: it excludes gage pressure as a reference convention, dynamic pressure, and stagnation pressure. A concrete inlet instance is [coolant pressure at cooling-circuit inlet](name:coolant_pressure_at_cooling_circuit_inlet), while [coolant pressure](name:coolant_pressure) applies the same physical definition at a plant-system component port.

NAMES.name: coolant_pressure_at_cooling_circuit_inlet
NAMES.short: Coolant pressure at a cooling-circuit inlet is the absolute static pressure of the coolant where it enters a hydraulically defined cooling circuit or component. It is the coolant-specific inlet pressure boundary and excludes gage, dynamic, and stagnation pressure.
NAMES.long:
Coolant pressure at a cooling-circuit inlet is the absolute static thermodynamic pressure of the coolant where it enters a hydraulically defined cooling circuit or component. It denotes the scalar upstream boundary pressure of the coolant and excludes gage pressure, dynamic pressure, and stagnation pressure.

For the same hydraulic flow path, the associated static pressure drop is related to this inlet pressure by:

$$
p_{\mathrm{coolant,in}} = p_{\mathrm{coolant,out}} + \Delta p_{\mathrm{coolant}}
$$

where $p_{\mathrm{coolant,in}}$ is this inlet absolute static coolant pressure in pascals, $p_{\mathrm{coolant,out}}$ is the corresponding outlet absolute static coolant pressure in pascals, and $\Delta p_{\mathrm{coolant}}$ is the total static pressure drop in pascals, defined positive when the outlet static pressure is lower than the inlet static pressure.

This quantity is the coolant-specific specialization of [pressure at a cooling-circuit inlet](name:pressure_at_cooling_circuit_inlet): when the working fluid is coolant, both names denote the same inlet absolute static pressure. It is also the cooling-circuit-inlet value of [coolant pressure](name:coolant_pressure), and it is distinct from pressure loss, pump head, and mechanical stress in the surrounding structure.

NAMES.name: radiated_power_of_breeder_blanket_module
NAMES.short: Radiated power associated with a single breeder blanket module, abstracting over plasma electromagnetic power incident on the module surface, the reflected portion, and the absorbed portion retained as a module heat load as distinct radiation energy-budget components.
NAMES.long:
Radiated power of a breeder blanket module quantifies the rate at which plasma electromagnetic emission, chiefly bremsstrahlung continuum and atomic line radiation, is assigned to the module-level radiation channel. It is the umbrella scalar for the incident photon power crossing onto the module surface and the absorbed photon power retained after surface reflection, represented by [incident_radiated_power_of_breeder_blanket_module](name:incident_radiated_power_of_breeder_blanket_module) and [absorbed_radiated_power_of_breeder_blanket_module](name:absorbed_radiated_power_of_breeder_blanket_module).

The radiated-power component for a single module is defined by integrating the corresponding radiative surface energy flux over the module surface:

$$
P_{\mathrm{rad},c} = \int_{A_m} \Phi_{\mathrm{rad},c}\, dA,\qquad c \in \{\mathrm{inc},\mathrm{abs}\}
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{rad},c}$ is the module-level radiated-power component in watts, $A_m$ is the module plasma-facing surface, $dA$ is a surface element, $\Phi_{\mathrm{rad},\mathrm{inc}}$ is the incident photon energy flux density onto that surface, and $\Phi_{\mathrm{rad},\mathrm{abs}}$ is the retained photon energy flux density after reflection.

The incident and absorbed components are related by the surface-reflection balance $P_{\mathrm{rad},\mathrm{abs}} = P_{\mathrm{rad},\mathrm{inc}} - P_{\mathrm{rad},\mathrm{ref}}$, equivalently $P_{\mathrm{rad},\mathrm{abs}} = (1-\mathcal{R})P_{\mathrm{rad},\mathrm{inc}}$ for an effective reflectance $\mathcal{R}$. The parent quantity is not a sum of incident and absorbed terms; it identifies the module radiation channel, while the component qualifier identifies which surface-budget term is represented. Neutron surface loads, volumetric nuclear energy deposition, auxiliary heating, and thermal radiation emitted by the module itself are outside this radiated-power channel; the absorbed part contributes to [thermal_power_of_breeder_blanket_module](name:thermal_power_of_breeder_blanket_module) within [power_of_breeder_blanket_module](name:power_of_breeder_blanket_module).

NAMES.name: absorbed_radiated_power_of_breeder_blanket_module
NAMES.short: Net photon power retained by a breeding blanket module after reflection of incident plasma radiation at its plasma-facing surface.
NAMES.long:
The absorbed radiated power of a breeding blanket module is the net electromagnetic photon power retained by the module after plasma radiation interacts with its plasma-facing surface. It includes absorbed bremsstrahlung and atomic line radiation and is the absorbed component of the broader [radiated power of a breeder blanket module](name:radiated_power_of_breeder_blanket_module).

The absorbed power is related to the [incident radiated power of a breeder blanket module](name:incident_radiated_power_of_breeder_blanket_module) by:

$$
P_\text{abs} = (1 - \mathcal{R}) P_\text{inc}
$$

where $P_\text{inc}$ is the incident radiative power, $\mathcal{R}$ is the effective hemispherical surface reflectance averaged over the incident photon spectrum, and $P_\text{abs}$ is the absorbed radiated power. This quantity excludes photon power reflected from the surface and nuclear energy deposited within the module.

NAMES.name: incident_radiated_power_of_breeder_blanket_module
NAMES.short: Total electromagnetic radiative power from the plasma arriving at the outer surface of a breeding blanket module, including bremsstrahlung and line radiation contributions, before accounting for surface reflection losses.
NAMES.long:
The incident radiated power of a breeding blanket module is the total electromagnetic power from the surrounding plasma that arrives at the module's outer surface, integrated over that surface per unit time. Plasma radiation sources contributing to this load include bremsstrahlung from electron-ion Coulomb collisions, impurity line radiation, and synchrotron emission, all transported across the scrape-off layer to the first-wall and blanket boundary.

The incident radiative load is defined as:

$$
P_\mathrm{inc,rad} = \int_S \mathbf{q}_\mathrm{rad} \cdot \hat{n} \, dA
$$

where $\mathbf{q}_\mathrm{rad}$ is the local incident radiative heat-flux vector, $\hat{n}$ is the inward surface unit normal, and the integral extends over the total module surface area $A$.

This quantity represents the gross radiative power before surface reflection; the net thermally retained fraction is captured by [absorbed_radiated_power_of_breeder_blanket_module](name:absorbed_radiated_power_of_breeder_blanket_module), which subtracts the reflected component. Together with nuclear heating quantified by [total_neutron_power_of_breeder_blanket_module](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_module), this term enters the full surface thermal balance of the blanket and is a key input for coolant circuit design and blanket lifetime assessment.

NAMES.name: resistance_of_cryostat
NAMES.short: Resistance of a cryostat passive-conductor element is its lumped ohmic opposition to current flow in the conducting vessel or thermal-shield structure. It sets Joule dissipation and, with inductance, induced-current decay timescales in passive electromagnetic response.
NAMES.long:
Resistance of a cryostat passive-conductor element is the scalar branch resistance assigned to a localized conducting part of the cryostat passive structure. It characterizes the ohmic voltage drop associated with current through the conducting vessel or thermal-shield structure.

The defining relation for a lumped ohmic element is:

$$
R = \frac{V}{I}
$$

where $R$ is the resistance, $V$ is the voltage across the element in volts, and $I$ is the current through the element in amperes, with $V$ and $I$ referenced to the same chosen branch direction.

This quantity is an element-level passive-conductor parameter, not a bulk material property; for a homogeneous current path it is related to [resistivity of cryostat](name:resistivity_of_cryostat) by the element geometry, such as the inline relation $R = \eta \ell/A$ with resistivity $\eta$, current-path length $\ell$, and cross-sectional area $A$. It is distinct from [resistance of vacuum vessel](name:resistance_of_vacuum_vessel), which applies to passive-conductor elements of the vacuum vessel rather than the cryostat.

NAMES.name: resistance_of_vacuum_vessel
NAMES.short: Lumped ohmic opposition to current flow through a discrete passive-conductor element of the vacuum vessel.
NAMES.long:
Electrical resistance of a discrete passive-conductor element is the proportionality between the voltage drop across the element and the current through it, representing irreversible ohmic dissipation.

$$
R = \frac{\Delta V}{I}
$$

where $R$ is the resistance, $\Delta V$ is the potential difference across the element, and $I$ is the through-current. For an approximately homogeneous element, resistance is determined by the material resistivity and the element geometry, as described by [resistivity of the vacuum vessel](name:resistivity_of_vacuum_vessel) and [resistivity of wall material](name:resistivity_of_wall_material). This lumped quantity excludes inductive opposition and represents only the ohmic component; it is distinct from the total resistance of a closed [passive loop](name:resistance_of_passive_loop).

NAMES.name: resistivity_of_cryostat
NAMES.short: Electrical resistivity of the cryostat structural material, encompassing both the vessel body and the thermal shield, used as the primary electromagnetic material property in eddy-current analyzes.
NAMES.long:
Electrical resistivity is an intrinsic material property quantifying resistance to electrical current flow per unit length and unit cross-sectional area of a conducting medium. For the cryostat — which comprises the main structural vessel and the surrounding thermal shield — this property governs the amplitude of eddy currents induced during transient plasma events such as disruptions and vertical displacement events, and the resulting ohmic heating and electromagnetic forces on the structure.

The resistance $R$ of a cryostat structural element is related to its resistivity $\rho$ through element geometry:

$$
R = \rho \frac{L}{A}
$$

where $L$ is the element length along the current path and $A$ is its cross-sectional area perpendicular to current flow.

This material constant is applied in electromagnetic finite-element analyzes to model induced current distributions and compute $\mathbf{J} \times \mathbf{B}$ forces and ohmic power deposition during disruptions. Metallic cryostat materials span a wide range: austenitic stainless steel yields roughly $7 \times 10^{-7}$ Ω·m, while aluminum alloys are lower at approximately $3 \times 10^{-8}$ Ω·m at ambient temperature; both values increase with temperature. The companion [resistance_of_cryostat](name:resistance_of_cryostat) gives the total resistance of a discrete structural element, while [resistivity_of_vacuum_vessel](name:resistivity_of_vacuum_vessel) is the analogous property for the vacuum vessel wall.

NAMES.name: resistivity_of_limiter_tile
NAMES.short: Nonnegative electrical resistivity of limiter-tile material, relating the local electric field to current density and governing ohmic losses in the tile.
NAMES.long:
Electrical resistivity of a limiter tile is the intrinsic material property that measures opposition to electrical current and determines the electric field required to sustain a current density. For this scalar quantity, the material response is represented as isotropic or as an effective value for the specified material state.

The defining local constitutive relation is:

$$
\mathbf{E} = \rho\,\mathbf{J}
$$

where $\mathbf{E}$ is electric field in V/m, $\mathbf{J}$ is current density in A/m$^2$, and $\rho$ is electrical resistivity in $\Omega\,\mathrm{m}$. The corresponding volumetric ohmic heating is $\mathbf{J}\cdot\mathbf{E}$.

This quantity describes the limiter-tile material itself and excludes contact resistance, geometric resistance, and the integrated resistance of the complete tile. It is the limiter-tile counterpart of [resistivity of a plasma-facing component](name:resistivity_of_plasma_facing_component) and is distinct from [power density of a limiter tile](name:power_density_of_limiter_tile), which describes deposited energy rather than material resistance.

NAMES.name: resistivity_of_plasma_facing_component
NAMES.short: Electrical resistivity of limiter-unit material, relating local electric field to current density and governing induced and eddy-current response.
NAMES.long:
Electrical resistivity of a limiter unit is the intrinsic material property that characterizes opposition to electric current in the plasma-facing component and governs its electromagnetic response.

Under the effective isotropic-material approximation, Ohm's law is

$$
\mathbf{E} = \rho\mathbf{J}
$$

where $\mathbf{E}$ is the local electric-field vector, $\mathbf{J}$ is the local current-density vector, and $\rho$ is the electrical resistivity. The scalar value is nonnegative and represents the limiter material itself; geometry-dependent total resistance is a separate quantity determined by the component dimensions and current paths. Its role is analogous to the material property defined for a [limiter tile](name:resistivity_of_limiter_tile) and a [passive structure](name:resistivity_of_passive_structure).

NAMES.name: resistivity_of_vacuum_vessel
NAMES.short: Effective isotropic electrical resistivity of vacuum-vessel material, relating local electric field to current density and governing transient passive-current response.
NAMES.long:
Electrical resistivity of vacuum-vessel material is the effective isotropic constitutive coefficient that opposes electric current and determines ohmic dissipation during transient electromagnetic events. It governs induced eddy and halo currents in the vessel material.

For isotropic material, the constitutive relation is

$$
\mathbf{E} = \rho\,\mathbf{J}
$$

where $\mathbf{E}$ is the local electric-field vector, $\rho$ is electrical resistivity, and $\mathbf{J}$ is current-density vector. The associated ohmic power density is $\mathbf{J}\cdot\mathbf{E} = \rho |\mathbf{J}|^2$.

This is a local material property of the vessel and excludes conductor geometry, interfaces, and contact effects. Consequently, it is distinct from the total [resistance of the vacuum vessel](name:resistance_of_vacuum_vessel), which also depends on current path and geometry.

NAMES.name: resistivity_of_wall_material
NAMES.short: Electrical resistivity of the wall material, governing eddy current amplitudes and ohmic dissipation induced during disruptions and other electromagnetic transient events.
NAMES.long:
Electrical resistivity $\rho$ of the wall material is the intrinsic scalar property of the conducting medium that relates the local electric field to the induced current density via Ohm's law in differential form.

$$
\mathbf{E} = \rho \, \mathbf{J}
$$

where $\mathbf{E}$ is in V m$^{-1}$ and $\mathbf{J}$ is in A m$^{-2}$. It is the reciprocal of the local electrical conductivity $\sigma = 1/\rho$. In fusion device wall structures, this property governs the amplitude of eddy currents induced during disruptions, vertical displacement events, and other rapid electromagnetic transients, directly controlling ohmic heating and the resulting electromagnetic loads on the wall.

Values are derived from material-property databases or direct laboratory measurement, often as a function of temperature; resistivity increases with temperature in metallic conductors. For fusion-relevant materials, $\rho$ spans roughly $10^{-8}$ $\Omega\cdot\text{m}$ for high-conductivity copper alloys to $\sim 10^{-6}$ $\Omega\cdot\text{m}$ for austenitic stainless steels at room temperature. Analogous quantities for other structural components include [resistivity_of_vacuum_vessel](name:resistivity_of_vacuum_vessel) and [resistivity_of_limiter_tile](name:resistivity_of_limiter_tile); the corresponding property for plasma-facing surface layers is described by [resistivity_of_plasma_facing_component](name:resistivity_of_plasma_facing_component).

NAMES.name: thermal_power_of_breeder_blanket_module
NAMES.short: Thermal power quantity associated with a single breeder blanket module, abstracting over module-level thermal-output quantities for heat transferred from the module to its coolant, including net coolant-transfer accounting.
NAMES.long:
Thermal power of a breeder blanket module quantifies the rate at which energy retained as heat in a single breeder blanket module is assigned to the module-level thermal-output channel. It is a module-integrated heat-output quantity, not a local material temperature, stored thermal energy, or surface power load.

This parent name does not by itself prescribe a particular thermal-accounting convention. A qualified child name supplies that convention; [net thermal power of a breeder blanket module](name:net_thermal_power_of_breeder_blanket_module) denotes the net transfer from the module to its coolant summed over all coolant branches as an enthalpy increase.

Thermal power is distinct from input or deposition channels such as neutron surface load and plasma radiation before their absorbed energy is accounted as module heat output. It belongs to the broader [power of a breeder blanket module](name:power_of_breeder_blanket_module) family of module-level energy-budget quantities.

NAMES.name: net_thermal_power_of_breeder_blanket_module
NAMES.short: Net thermal power transferred from a single breeder blanket module to its coolant, summed over all coolant branches as an enthalpy increase.
NAMES.long:
Coolant thermal power of a single breeder blanket module is the net rate at which heat leaves the module through its coolant circuits. It aggregates the thermal energy carried by every coolant branch serving that module, regardless of whether the heat originated from nuclear deposition or absorbed incident radiation.

The defining branch balance is

$$
P_{\mathrm{cool}} = \sum_b \dot{m}_b\left(h_{b,\mathrm{out}} - h_{b,\mathrm{in}}\right)
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{cool}}$ is the coolant-transferred power, $b$ indexes coolant branches, $\dot{m}_b$ is the mass flow rate in branch $b$, and $h_{b,\mathrm{in}}$ and $h_{b,\mathrm{out}}$ are its inlet and outlet specific enthalpies. The quantity is the coolant-transferred component of [thermal power of a breeder blanket module](name:thermal_power_of_breeder_blanket_module), distinct from source-specific quantities such as [nuclear heating power of a breeder blanket module](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_module) and [absorbed radiated power of a breeder blanket module](name:absorbed_radiated_power_of_breeder_blanket_module).

NAMES.name: thickness_of_breeder_blanket_layer
NAMES.short: Non-negative geometric separation between the inner and outer material interfaces of a breeder blanket layer along the specified thickness direction.
NAMES.long:
Non-negative geometric separation between the inner and outer material interfaces of a breeder blanket layer is the local through-thickness of that layer along the specified thickness direction. The quantity applies to a single material or functional layer within the blanket, not to the total breeder blanket module build.

The layer thickness is defined by the separation of the two bounding interfaces along the thickness coordinate:

$$
d_\ell = \left|s_{\ell,\mathrm{out}} - s_{\ell,\mathrm{in}}\right|
$$

where $d_\ell$ is the layer thickness in m, and $s_{\ell,\mathrm{in}}$ and $s_{\ell,\mathrm{out}}$ are the signed coordinates in m of the inner and outer layer interfaces along the specified thickness direction.

It is not the toroidal width, poloidal height, surface extent, or volume-equivalent thickness of the layer. It is distinct from module-level quantities such as [thickness_of_breeder_blanket_module](name:thickness_of_breeder_blanket_module), [lower_thickness_of_breeder_blanket_module](name:lower_thickness_of_breeder_blanket_module), and [upper_thickness_of_breeder_blanket_module](name:upper_thickness_of_breeder_blanket_module). For a radially stacked layer, the thickness direction is the cylindrical $\hat{R}$ direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

NAMES.name: thickness_of_breeder_blanket_module
NAMES.short: Non-negative geometric separation across a breeder blanket module or one of its structural subregions, measured along the specified thickness direction.
NAMES.long:
Thickness is the non-negative geometric extent between two bounding surfaces or interfaces of a breeder blanket module or a defined module subregion. The direction is the local thickness direction appropriate to those boundaries, so the definition covers cap and other structural dimensions.

For corresponding points on the bounding surfaces, the projected separation is defined by

$$
t = \left|\left(\mathbf{r}_2-\mathbf{r}_1\right)\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}}\right|
$$

where $t$ is the thickness in m, $\mathbf{r}_1$ and $\mathbf{r}_2$ are position vectors of the corresponding boundary points, and $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ is the specified unit thickness direction.

The parent quantity includes the cap-specific dimensions represented by [lower thickness of a breeder blanket module](name:lower_thickness_of_breeder_blanket_module) and [upper thickness of a breeder blanket module](name:upper_thickness_of_breeder_blanket_module). It describes structural geometry, excluding the thickness of an individual breeder material layer when that layer is treated as a separate subcomponent.

NAMES.name: lower_thickness_of_breeder_blanket_module
NAMES.short: Lower thickness of a breeder blanket module is the non-negative geometric separation through the lower cap, measured normal to its exterior boundary and main-body interface.
NAMES.long:
Lower thickness of a breeder blanket module is the geometric thickness of the cap that closes the module at its lower end. The reference surfaces are the lower exterior boundary of the cap and the interface where the lower cap joins the main module body. It is distinct from the overall [thickness of a breeder blanket module](name:thickness_of_breeder_blanket_module) and the corresponding [upper thickness of a breeder blanket module](name:upper_thickness_of_breeder_blanket_module).

The lower-cap thickness is the normal projection of the separation between the reference surfaces:

$$
t_{\mathrm{lower}} = \left|\left(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{ext}} - \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{int}}\right) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}\right|
$$

where $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{ext}}$ and $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{int}}$ are corresponding points on the lower exterior boundary and cap-to-body interface, $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ is the local unit normal directed through the cap, and $t_{\mathrm{lower}}$ is the lower-cap thickness. The quantity is a non-negative geometric magnitude; it is not a signed vertical coordinate or displacement and excludes the thicknesses of internal breeder, coolant, or shielding layers.

NAMES.name: thickness_of_cryostat
NAMES.short: Local through-wall distance across the cryostat structural vessel, measured along the wall normal between its inner and outer material faces.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the geometric thickness of the cryostat structural vessel at a specified location. It is the separation through the wall material between corresponding inner and outer faces, measured along the local wall-normal direction.

At the corresponding inner and outer face points, the thickness is defined by

$$
t = (\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{out}}-\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{in}})\mathbin{\cdot}\hat{\mathbf{n}}
$$

where $t$ is the thickness in m, $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{in}}$ and $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{out}}$ are the face position vectors in m, and $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ is the unit normal directed from the inner face toward the outer face.

The value is a non-negative material separation and excludes gaps, insulation, and attached components. It is distinct from [thickness of the vacuum vessel](name:thickness_of_vacuum_vessel), which describes the vacuum-vessel wall rather than the cryostat structural wall.

NAMES.name: thickness_of_plasma_facing_component
NAMES.short: Through-material geometric separation between a plasma-facing component’s exposed surface and its opposite material boundary, evaluated at the component midplane.
NAMES.long:
The thickness is the through-material dimension of a plasma-facing component at its midplane, separating the plasma-exposed surface from the opposite material boundary. It is measured along the local thickness direction normal to the exposed surface.

$$
t_{\mathrm{PFC}} = d_{\perp}\left(S_{\mathrm{plasma}}, S_{\mathrm{back}}\right)\big|_{\mathrm{midplane}}
$$

Here, $t_{\mathrm{PFC}}$ is the component thickness, $d_{\perp}$ is the through-material normal separation, and $S_{\mathrm{plasma}}$ and $S_{\mathrm{back}}$ are the exposed and opposite material surfaces, respectively.

This is a geometric material dimension for the specified midplane section; it is not a plasma-to-wall separation such as the [gap at the plasma boundary](name:gap_at_plasma_boundary), nor a surface thermal quantity.

NAMES.name: thickness_of_vacuum_vessel
NAMES.short: Local through-wall distance between the inner and outer faces of the vacuum vessel, measured along the wall-normal direction.
NAMES.long:
Vacuum-vessel wall thickness is the material distance separating the vessel's inner and outer faces at corresponding locations. It describes the vessel wall itself, excluding separate internal components, armor, and external structures.

At a given wall location, the thickness is defined by

$$
d = \left|\left(\mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{out}}-\mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{in}}\right)\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}}\right|
$$

where $\mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{in}}$ and $\mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{out}}$ are corresponding positions on the inner and outer faces, and $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ is the local unit normal directed from the inner face toward the outer face. The quantity is non-negative and is distinct from [thickness of cryostat](name:thickness_of_cryostat), which describes a separate structural enclosure.

NAMES.name: toroidal_current_of_cryostat
NAMES.short: Net electric current carried by a conducting cryostat element in the toroidal direction of the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the signed net electric current carried by a conducting cryostat element along the toroidal direction. It represents current in the passive cryostat structure, including induced eddy current, rather than current carried by the plasma or another component.

$$
I_\phi = \int_{S_\perp} J_\phi\,\mathrm{d}S
$$

where $I_\phi$ is the net toroidal current in A, $J_\phi = \mathbf{J}\cdot\hat{\phi}$ is the toroidal component of the local electric current density in A m$^{-2}$, $\mathbf{J}$ is the current-density vector, and $S_\perp$ is the cryostat element cross-section normal to the toroidal direction. The unit vector $\hat{\phi}$ belongs to the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height.

This quantity is distinct from [toroidal current of vacuum vessel](name:toroidal_current_of_vacuum_vessel), which is confined to the vacuum vessel, and from [toroidal halo current](name:toroidal_halo_current), which is carried by halo plasma. It is a component of the broader current represented by [current of passive structure](name:current_of_passive_structure).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the electric current flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: tritium_breeding_ratio
NAMES.short: Tritium breeding ratio is the blanket-level ratio of tritium atoms produced in breeder-blanket breeding regions to the incident fusion-neutron count over the same normalization interval. Compatible module contributions share this denominator and add to the blanket value.
NAMES.long:
Tritium breeding ratio is the blanket-level ratio of tritium atoms produced inside the breeding regions of a breeder blanket to the incident fusion-neutron count used to normalize the same neutronics balance. It is a tritium production figure of merit for the blanket as a whole, distinct from nuclear heating or power deposition.

The ratio is defined over a specified normalization interval by

$$
\mathrm{TBR} = \frac{N_{T,\mathrm{blanket}}}{N_{n,\mathrm{inc}}}
$$

where $N_{T,\mathrm{blanket}}$ is the number of tritium atoms produced in the blanket breeding regions during that interval, and $N_{n,\mathrm{inc}}$ is the incident fusion-neutron count for the same interval.

Breeding regions are the blanket material volumes designated for neutron-induced tritium production; tritium produced outside those volumes is excluded unless that material is part of the breeder blanket breeding region. The denominator is the common incident-neutron denominator, not the number of neutrons absorbed in the blanket and not a module-specific denominator. Compatible non-overlapping module values of [tritium_breeding_ratio_of_breeder_blanket_module](name:tritium_breeding_ratio_of_breeder_blanket_module) that use this same denominator are additive and sum to the blanket-level ratio.

The quantity differs from [power_of_breeder_blanket](name:power_of_breeder_blanket) and [power_of_breeder_blanket_module](name:power_of_breeder_blanket_module), which describe energy deposition rates rather than tritium atom yield. Because both counts are non-negative and the denominator must be positive, negative values are outside the physical domain; values greater than one mean more tritium atoms are produced than the tritium atoms consumed by the fusion reactions that generated the same incident-neutron population, which is the breeding condition for tritium self-sufficiency.

sources.enhanced_context: Tritium breeding ratio (TBR), the number of tritium atoms produced per fusion neutron absorbed in the breeding blanket. A key figure of merit for tritium self-sufficiency in fusion reactor design.

sources.parent_definition: Dynamic quantities for a set of time_slices

NAMES.name: tritium_breeding_ratio_of_breeder_blanket_module
NAMES.short: Dimensionless tritium-production contribution from one breeder-blanket module, normalized by the common incident fusion-neutron count used for the blanket balance.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the contribution of one breeder-blanket module to the blanket-level [tritium breeding ratio](name:tritium_breeding_ratio). It counts tritium atoms produced within that module's breeding regions and uses the common incident fusion-neutron normalization for the complete blanket.

$$
TBR_{\mathrm{module}} = \frac{N_{T,\mathrm{module}}}{N_{n,\mathrm{incident}}}
$$

where $N_{T,\mathrm{module}}$ is the number of tritium atoms produced in the module's breeding regions and $N_{n,\mathrm{incident}}$ is the incident fusion-neutron count used for the blanket balance.

For modules that partition the blanket breeding regions and share this denominator, the module contributions add to the blanket tritium breeding ratio. The quantity excludes tritium production outside the specified module and is not a separate normalization of the module's incident neutron count.

sources.enhanced_context: Tritium breeding ratio (TBR) of a breeding blanket module, defined as tritium atoms produced per fusion neutron. A key figure of merit for tritium self-sufficiency and blanket performance in fusion reactor design.
sources.leaf_definition: Number of tritium atoms created for each fusion neutron (TBR)
sources.parent_definition: Dynamic quantities at various time slices

NAMES.name: upper_thickness_of_breeder_blanket_module
NAMES.short: Upper thickness of a breeder blanket module is the non-negative projected separation between the module's upper exterior end boundary and the interface where the upper cap joins the main module body, measured along the specified upper-cap thickness direction. It characterizes the geometric thickness of the upper end cap.
NAMES.long:
Upper thickness of a breeder blanket module is the geometric thickness of the upper cap that closes the module at its upper end. The reference surfaces are the upper exterior end boundary of the cap and the cap-to-module interface where the cap joins the main blanket body; the thickness is measured as a projected separation along the specified upper-cap thickness direction, not as an arbitrary point-to-point distance between inner and outer surfaces.

For a local cap-thickness direction $\hat{\mathbf{n}}_\mathrm{u}$, the projected thickness is

$$
t_\mathrm{u} = \left|\left(\mathbf{x}_\mathrm{end} - \mathbf{x}_\mathrm{int}\right) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}_\mathrm{u}\right|
$$

where $t_\mathrm{u}$ is the upper cap thickness, $\mathbf{x}_\mathrm{end}$ is a point on the upper exterior end boundary, $\mathbf{x}_\mathrm{int}$ is the corresponding point on the cap-to-module interface, and $\hat{\mathbf{n}}_\mathrm{u}$ is the unit direction used to define the upper-cap thickness. The absolute value reflects that this scalar is a non-negative length.

In engineering definitions the value is taken from the module geometry or design specification. For a tapered or spatially varying upper cap, the scalar denotes the specified nominal projected thickness, commonly the representative average over the cap region or the value at the design reference section; local maxima, minima, and detailed shape variations are separate geometric information.

This quantity is related to the overall [breeder blanket module thickness](name:thickness_of_breeder_blanket_module), to the analogous [lower cap thickness](name:lower_thickness_of_breeder_blanket_module), and to individual [breeder blanket layer thicknesses](name:thickness_of_breeder_blanket_layer). It is reported in meters and is design-specific; no universal device-independent numerical range is implied.

NAMES.name: vertical_outline_of_limiter_tile
NAMES.short: Signed vertical coordinate of each contour point defining the poloidal cross-sectional boundary of a limiter tile.
NAMES.long:
This quantity gives the vertical placement of a point on the geometric boundary outline of a limiter tile in a poloidal section. It is the coordinate counterpart of the related [vertical outline of a divertor tile](name:vertical_outline_of_divertor_tile), but applies specifically to a limiter tile.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame with basis $(\hat{R}, \hat{\phi}, \hat{Z})$, the coordinate is defined by

$$
Z = \mathbf{r} \cdot \hat{Z}
$$

where $\mathbf{r}$ is the position vector of the contour point, $\hat{Z}$ is the vertical unit vector, and $Z$ is the signed vertical coordinate in m.

The values describe the tile boundary contour and do not represent tile thickness, a surface-normal displacement, or a volumetric property.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the contour point lies in the direction of increasing vertical coordinate $Z$.

sources.enhanced_context: Vertical (Z) coordinate of outline.
sources.leaf_definition: Height
sources.parent_definition: Irregular outline of the limiting surface. Do NOT repeat the first point for closed contours

NAMES.name: vertical_outline_of_vacuum_vessel
NAMES.short: Signed vertical position of a point on a vacuum-vessel element outline, measured along the vertical axis of the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the vertical coordinate of a specified point on the geometric outline of a vacuum-vessel element. It identifies the point's height relative to the cylindrical coordinate origin, rather than an element center, thickness, or surface-normal displacement.

The coordinate is defined by projection of the point position onto the vertical basis vector:

$$
Z_{\rm point}=\mathbf{r}_{\rm point}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{Z}}
$$

where $\mathbf{r}_{\rm point}$ is the position vector of the outline point, $\hat{\mathbf{Z}}$ is the vertical unit vector, and $(R,\phi,Z)$ is the right-handed cylindrical frame with $R$ the major radius, $\phi$ the toroidal angle, and $Z$ the vertical coordinate.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the outline point lies in the direction of increasing $Z$.

sources.enhanced_context: Vertical (Z) coordinate of outline.
sources.leaf_definition: Height
sources.parent_definition: Outline of the block element. Do NOT repeat the first point for closed contours

NAMES.name: vertical_outline_of_wall_material
NAMES.short: Signed vertical coordinate of each contour point defining the poloidal cross-sectional boundary of a wall-material component.
NAMES.long:
Signed vertical coordinate of each contour point defining the poloidal cross-sectional boundary of a wall-material component is the $Z$ coordinate of that point in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius measured from the symmetry axis, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. The contour is the component boundary in a plane of constant $\phi$ and is independent of the material composition assigned to the component.

Together with radial_outline_of_wall_material, it locates the same contour point on the poloidal boundary. It is distinct from horizontal_outline_of_wall_material, which denotes a horizontal outline coordinate rather than the vertical $Z$ coordinate.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the contour point lies in the direction of increasing $Z$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.
