NAMES.name: volume_of_breeder_blanket
NAMES.short: Geometric volume occupied by a defined material constituent or structural subregion within a breeder blanket assembly, bounded by the specified blanket scope.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the geometric volume occupied by a specified constituent or structural subregion of a breeder blanket assembly. It is an extensive measure of the portion of the assembly assigned to that entity.

The volume is defined by integrating the differential volume element over the specified domain:

$$
V_{\Omega} = \int_{\Omega} dV
$$

where $V_{\Omega}$ is the occupied volume, $\Omega$ is the defined material or structural domain within the breeder blanket assembly, and $dV$ is the differential volume element.

The domain excludes regions outside the stated blanket scope and does not represent a part-to-whole volume ratio, which is defined by [fraction of breeder blanket layer](name:fraction_of_breeder_blanket_layer). [Coolant volume of breeder blanket](name:coolant_volume_of_breeder_blanket) is a constituent-specific specialization for the coolant or breeder material and excludes external coolant loops and other blanket materials.

NAMES.name: coolant_volume_of_breeder_blanket
NAMES.short: Total geometric volume occupied by lead-lithium coolant/breeder throughout the breeder blanket assembly, excluding external coolant loops and other blanket materials.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the total volume occupied by the lead-lithium coolant/breeder constituent within the complete breeder blanket assembly. It is a material-specific component of the broader [volume of breeder blanket](name:volume_of_breeder_blanket) and is distinct from the volume of an individual module or layer.

$$
V_{\mathrm{PbLi}} = \int_{\Omega_{\mathrm{blanket}}} \chi_{\mathrm{PbLi}}(\mathbf{r})\,\mathrm{d}V
$$

where $V_{\mathrm{PbLi}}$ is the PbLi volume, $\Omega_{\mathrm{blanket}}$ is the volume of the complete breeder blanket assembly, $\chi_{\mathrm{PbLi}}$ is one inside the PbLi region and zero elsewhere, and $\mathrm{d}V$ is an elemental volume. The integral excludes external coolant loops, structural materials, voids, and other non-PbLi constituents.

sources.enhanced_context: Volume of lead-lithium (PbLi) coolant/breeder contained within the breeding blanket. A key engineering parameter for tritium breeding and nuclear heating assessments in fusion reactor design.
sources.leaf_definition: Volume of PbLi contained in the blanket

NAMES.name: volume_of_first_wall
NAMES.short: Volume enclosed by the first-wall surface, representing the interior region inside the innermost plasma-facing boundary rather than the wall material itself.
NAMES.long:
The first-wall volume is the total interior volume enclosed by the innermost plasma-facing surface of the vacuum vessel. It includes the space available to the confined plasma, edge and scrape-off-layer regions, and neutral gas, but excludes the material volume of the wall.

For an axisymmetric first-wall contour in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, the volume is defined by

$$
V_{\rm FW}=2\pi\iint_A R\,dR\,dZ
$$

where $A$ is the poloidal cross-sectional area enclosed by the first-wall contour, $R$ is major radius in meters, and $Z$ is vertical height in meters. For non-axisymmetric geometry, the complete three-dimensional enclosed region, including bounded ports and recesses, defines the volume.

This enclosed volume is distinct from [volume enclosed by the plasma boundary](name:volume_of_flux_surface), which is limited by the last closed flux surface, and from [area of the first wall](name:area_of_first_wall), which measures the wall's material surface rather than an enclosed region.

sources.enhanced_context: Volume enclosed by the first wall contour, representing the space available to gas or plasma within the vacuum vessel. A key geometric device parameter for global particle balance and fuelling calculations.
sources.leaf_definition: Volume available to gas or plasma enclosed by the first wall contour

NAMES.name: volumetric_force
NAMES.short: Electromagnetic Lorentz body-force density vector acting locally on plasma, conducting wall, or structural material, with components resolved in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The volumetric force is the local electromagnetic Lorentz force density acting on plasma and current-carrying conducting or structural material. Its projections include the [radial volumetric force](name:radial_volumetric_force), [toroidal volumetric force](name:toroidal_volumetric_force), and [vertical volumetric force](name:vertical_volumetric_force).

The electromagnetic force density is defined by

$$
\mathbf{f}_{\mathrm{vol}} = \rho_e \mathbf{E} + \mathbf{J} \times \mathbf{B}
$$

where $\mathbf{f}_{\mathrm{vol}}$ is the volumetric force vector, $\rho_e$ is charge density, $\mathbf{E}$ is electric field, $\mathbf{J}$ is current density, and $\mathbf{B}$ is magnetic field. The quantity is local and is distinct from the net force obtained by integrating it over a material volume.
NAMES.sign: Positive when a force component points along its corresponding positive basis direction—increasing $R$, increasing toroidal angle $\phi$, or increasing $Z$—in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: radial_volumetric_force
NAMES.short: Radial component of the electromagnetic body-force density vector, projected onto the direction of increasing major radius R in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The radial volumetric force is the $\hat{R}$-projection of the local electromagnetic body-force density $\mathbf{f} = \mathbf{J} \times \mathbf{B}$ acting on plasma volumes or conducting wall and structural elements. It characterizes the net radial push or pull arising from the interaction of local current density with the magnetic field, driving stress and displacement in the major-radial direction.

The defining relation is the radial projection of the Lorentz force density in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame with basis $(\hat{R}, \hat{\phi}, \hat{Z})$:

$$
f_R = (\mathbf{J} \times \mathbf{B}) \cdot \hat{R} = J_\phi B_Z - J_Z B_\phi
$$

where $\mathbf{J}$ is the current density vector, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field, and $J_\phi$, $J_Z$, $B_\phi$, $B_Z$ are the toroidal and vertical components respectively.

This component is computed in magnetohydrodynamic equilibrium analyzes and disruption-load assessments to quantify radial electromagnetic stresses on plasma-facing components, wall tiles, and blanket structures. Together with [toroidal_volumetric_force](name:toroidal_volumetric_force) and [vertical_volumetric_force](name:vertical_volumetric_force), it resolves the complete local electromagnetic body-force density vector described by [volumetric_force](name:volumetric_force).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the electromagnetic force points in the direction of increasing major radius $R$.

sources.enhanced_context: Major radius (R) coordinate of em force density.
sources.leaf_definition: Component along the major radius axis, one scalar value is provided per element in the grid subset.
sources.parent_definition: Electromagnetic force density computed by the cross-product of j_total x b_field and given on various grid subsets

NAMES.name: toroidal_volumetric_force
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the electromagnetic body-force density vector acting on plasma volumes or conducting wall and structural elements, projected onto increasing toroidal angle φ in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal volumetric force is the $\hat{\phi}$-projection of the local electromagnetic body-force density vector acting on plasma volumes or conducting wall and structural elements. It characterizes the local mechanical load per unit volume directed around the torus in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

For the magnetic Lorentz body force, the toroidal projection is:

$$
f_\phi = \mathbf{f}\cdot\hat{\phi} = (\mathbf{J}\times\mathbf{B})\cdot\hat{\phi} = J_Z B_R - J_R B_Z
$$

where $f_\phi$ is the toroidal volumetric force, $\mathbf{f}$ is the electromagnetic body-force density vector, $\mathbf{J}$ is current density, $\mathbf{B}$ is magnetic field, and $J_R$, $J_Z$, $B_R$, and $B_Z$ are the corresponding projections in the same right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The magnetic-field vector entering this relation is the quantity represented by [magnetic field](name:magnetic_field).

This quantity is one signed projection of [volumetric force](name:volumetric_force), complementary to [radial volumetric force](name:radial_volumetric_force) and [vertical volumetric force](name:vertical_volumetric_force). It excludes the magnitude of the body-force density vector and any force integrated over a finite volume.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the force density points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

sources.enhanced_context: Toroidal angle (φ) coordinate of em force density.
sources.leaf_definition: Toroidal component, one scalar value is provided per element in the grid subset.
sources.parent_definition: Electromagnetic force density computed by the cross-product of j_total x b_field and given on various grid subsets

NAMES.name: vertical_volumetric_force
NAMES.short: Vertical (Z) component of the electromagnetic body-force density vector, giving the net upward or downward force per unit volume on current-carrying material in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The vertical volumetric force is the $Z$-component of the local electromagnetic body-force density vector, expressing the net mechanical load per unit volume directed along the vertical axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It is the vertical projection of the full [volumetric_force](name:volumetric_force) vector, completing the cylindrical triad alongside the [radial_volumetric_force](name:radial_volumetric_force) and [toroidal_volumetric_force](name:toroidal_volumetric_force) components.

In electromagnetic contexts — the dominant application in tokamak structural engineering — the vertical component is the $Z$-projection of the Lorentz body force:

$$
f_Z = (\mathbf{J} \times \mathbf{B}) \cdot \hat{Z}
$$

where $\mathbf{J}$ is the local current density, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field, and $\hat{Z}$ is the unit vector pointing in the $+Z$ direction. Integrating $f_Z$ over a conductor or blanket volume yields the total vertical force on that component, analogous to the globally integrated vertical_force.

The vertical force density is evaluated from electromagnetic field solutions by computing the local cross product of the current density and magnetic field distributions across the material domain. In tokamak structural components subject to disruption-induced halo currents, electromagnetic force densities can reach $10^6$–$10^8$ N m$^{-3}$ near highly loaded conductor regions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the force points in the $+Z$ direction (vertically upward in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame).

sources.enhanced_context: Vertical (Z) coordinate of em force density.
sources.leaf_definition: Component along the height axis, one scalar value is provided per element in the grid subset.
sources.parent_definition: Electromagnetic force density computed by the cross-product of j_total x b_field and given on various grid subsets

NAMES.name: volumetric_fraction_of_breeder_blanket_layer
NAMES.short: Volumetric fraction of a breeder blanket layer is the share of a specified constituent material or phase in the layer's bulk volume. It is a dimensionless effective-medium composition parameter for homogenized breeder-blanket layer properties.
NAMES.long:
Volumetric fraction of a breeder blanket layer is the part-to-whole volume ratio for one specified constituent material, phase, void region, coolant region, or gas region within a breeder blanket layer. It describes the layer composition used for homogenized material properties over the same geometric region.

For constituent $i$, the fraction is defined by:

$$
f_i = \frac{V_i}{V_\mathrm{layer}}
$$

where $f_i$ is the volumetric fraction, $V_i$ is the volume of constituent $i$ in cubic meters, and $V_\mathrm{layer}$ is the total bulk volume of the same breeder blanket layer in cubic meters over the homogenization region.

The numerator and denominator must refer to the same layer region. For an exhaustive non-overlapping partition of that region, $0 \le f_i \le 1$ and $\sum_i f_i = 1$; separately represented voids, coolant, or gas regions are included as their own constituents. This quantity is distinct from mass fraction, atomic fraction, porosity, and selected-solid packing factor, and its layer denominator differs from the whole-blanket volume described by [volume of breeder blanket](name:volume_of_breeder_blanket).

sources.enhanced_context: Volume fraction of each constituent material in a breeding blanket layer, describing the relative proportion of each material component within the composite layer. Used in neutronics and thermal-hydraulic calculations.
sources.leaf_definition: Volume fraction of each material entering the composition of this layer
sources.parent_definition: Set of layers in the blanket module

NAMES.name: y_coordinate_of_ferritic_element_centroid
NAMES.short: Signed y coordinate of the geometric centroid of a ferritic element in the right-handed Cartesian (x, y, z) frame, with z aligned to vertical Z.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the signed Cartesian y position of the geometric centroid of one ferritic element. The coordinate is defined in the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ basis, with coordinate values $(x,y,z)$ and $\hat{z}=\hat{Z}$.

$$
y_c = \frac{1}{V_e}\int_{V_e} y\,dV
$$

where $y_c$ and $y$ are Cartesian y coordinates measured in m, $V_e$ is the ferritic-element volume measured in m$^3$, and $dV$ is a differential volume element. The integration covers the entire element, so this is a volume centroid rather than a surface centroid or a selected-point coordinate. The corresponding orthogonal centroid coordinates are [x coordinate of the ferritic element centroid](name:x_coordinate_of_ferritic_element_centroid) and [z coordinate of the ferritic element centroid](name:z_coordinate_of_ferritic_element_centroid).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the centroid displacement from the coordinate origin has a positive projection onto $\hat{y}$.

sources.enhanced_context: Y coordinate of centroid.
sources.leaf_definition: List of Y coordinates
sources.parent_definition: List of positions of the centroids, in Cartesian coordinates

NAMES.name: power_density_of_breeder_blanket_layer
NAMES.short: Power density of a breeder blanket layer is the net local rate at which energy is transferred to or from material within a specified breeder blanket layer per unit material volume, independent of the volumetric mechanism specified by a more specialized quantity.
NAMES.long:
Power density of a breeder blanket layer is the net local rate at which energy is transferred to or from material within a specified breeder blanket layer per unit material volume. It is the material-region specialization of [power density](name:power_density) for a layer of a breeder blanket, with the layer defining the recipient material region in the local energy balance.

For a differential material volume of the layer, the volumetric power density is defined by

$$
p_\mathrm{layer} = \frac{dE_\mathrm{layer}}{dt\,dV_\mathrm{layer}}
$$

where $E_\mathrm{layer}$ is the energy transferred to the layer material, $t$ is time, and $V_\mathrm{layer}$ is the material volume within that layer.

This quantity is not mechanism-specific unless qualified by a more specialized standard name; [nuclear power density of breeder blanket layer](name:nuclear_power_density_of_breeder_blanket_layer) restricts the transfer to nuclear energy deposition in the same material layer. It is distinct from surface heat flux at a layer interface, volume-integrated power of the layer, and [power density of a breeder blanket module](name:power_density_of_breeder_blanket_module) defined for a larger blanket material region.
NAMES.sign: Positive when energy is transferred to the material of the breeder blanket layer.

NAMES.name: nuclear_power_density_of_breeder_blanket_layer
NAMES.short: Local rate of nuclear energy deposition within the material volume of one breeder blanket layer, generated by neutron interactions and associated photon absorption.
NAMES.long:
Nuclear power density is the local volumetric heat-generation rate within one defined breeder blanket material layer. It includes energy deposited by neutron interactions and by absorption of primary or secondary photons, rather than surface heat loads or externally applied heating.

The volume integral gives the corresponding layer-integrated nuclear heating power:

$$
P_{\mathrm{nuc,layer}} = \int_{V_{\mathrm{layer}}} q_{\mathrm{nuc}}(\mathbf{r})\,\mathrm{d}V
$$

where $q_{\mathrm{nuc}}(\mathbf{r})$ is the local nuclear power density, $P_{\mathrm{nuc,layer}}$ is the integrated nuclear heating power, $\mathbf{r}$ is position, and $V_{\mathrm{layer}}$ is the material volume of the layer. This quantity is the nuclear-deposition component of [power density of a breeder blanket layer](name:power_density_of_breeder_blanket_layer) and integrates to [nuclear heating power of a breeder blanket layer](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_layer).

sources.enhanced_context: Nuclear heating power density (volumetric) in a breeding blanket layer evaluated at the outboard midplane. Quantifies local neutron-induced heat deposition at the midplane position within the blanket material.
sources.leaf_definition: Nuclear heating power density in the layer, evaluated at midplane
sources.parent_definition: Dynamic quantities at various time slices

NAMES.name: power_density_of_breeder_blanket_module
NAMES.short: Net volumetric rate of energy transfer to or from material within a single breeder blanket module, encompassing the mechanisms included in its local material energy balance.
NAMES.long:
Power density of a breeder blanket module is the net local rate at which energy is transferred to or from material within a single breeder blanket module per unit material volume. It is the material-region specialization of [power density](name:power_density), with the transfer mechanism left unqualified.

The local volumetric power density is defined by

$$
p_E = \frac{dE}{dt\,dV}
$$

where $E$ is the energy transferred to the material, $t$ is time, and $V$ is the material volume. Positive values denote net energy gain by the material, while negative values denote net energy loss.

This is a local quantity, not a module-integrated power or a module average. Mechanism-specific quantities such as [nuclear power density of breeder blanket module](name:nuclear_power_density_of_breeder_blanket_module) are specializations, while [power of breeder blanket module](name:power_of_breeder_blanket_module) is the corresponding integrated module-level quantity; [power density of breeder blanket layer](name:power_density_of_breeder_blanket_layer) applies the same local concept to a layer locus.

NAMES.name: nuclear_power_density_of_breeder_blanket_module
NAMES.short: Volumetric nuclear heating power density deposited in breeder-blanket module materials by neutron interactions and associated photon absorption. It is a local material quantity, not a module average or total module heating power.
NAMES.long:
Volumetric nuclear heating power density deposited in a breeder blanket module is the local rate of nuclear energy deposition per material volume within the module material. It represents nuclear heating from neutron-induced reactions, recoil and charged-particle products, and associated photon energy absorption in the local material mixture.

The total nuclear heating power of the module is the material-volume integral of the local density:

$$
P_\mathrm{nuc}^{\mathrm{module}} = \int_{V_\mathrm{module}} q_\mathrm{nuc}(\mathbf{r})\,dV
$$

where $P_\mathrm{nuc}^{\mathrm{module}}$ is the [nuclear heating power of the breeder blanket module](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket_module), $q_\mathrm{nuc}(\mathbf{r})$ is the local nuclear power density at material point $\mathbf{r}$, $V_\mathrm{module}$ is the material volume of the breeder blanket module, and $dV$ is a material-volume element.

This quantity is local to breeder-blanket module material and is not a module-volume average, not the layer-restricted [nuclear power density of a breeder blanket layer](name:nuclear_power_density_of_breeder_blanket_layer), and not the total module nuclear heating power. A layer-specific density restricts the same local physical quantity to an individual functional layer of the module.

sources.enhanced_context: Nuclear heating power density profile in a breeding blanket module, evaluated at the midplane. Represents the volumetric power deposition from neutron and gamma interactions in the blanket material.
sources.leaf_definition: Nuclear heating power density in the module, evaluated at midplane
sources.parent_definition: Dynamic quantities at various time slices

NAMES.name: power_density_of_limiter_tile
NAMES.short: Net volumetric rate of energy transfer to or from material within a limiter tile, independent of the mechanism producing the local gain or loss.
NAMES.long:
Power density of a limiter tile is the net rate at which energy is transferred to or from material within the tile per unit material volume. It is the local source or sink in the tile's energy balance and is independent of the contributing mechanism. This material-region specialization of [power density](name:power_density) applies to the net energy balance of the tile.

For a differential material volume, the volumetric power density is defined by

$$
p_E = \frac{dE}{dt\,dV}
$$

where $E$ is the energy transferred to the tile material, $t$ is time, and $V$ is material volume.

The quantity is local and per unit material volume, not the volume-integrated [nuclear power of a limiter tile](name:nuclear_power_of_limiter_tile). Positive values denote net energy gain by the tile material, while negative values denote net energy loss. [Nuclear power density of a limiter tile](name:nuclear_power_density_of_limiter_tile) is a mechanism-specific specialization.

NAMES.name: nuclear_power_density_of_limiter_tile
NAMES.short: Local volumetric rate of nuclear energy deposition in limiter-tile material from neutron interactions and associated absorption of primary and secondary gamma radiation.
NAMES.long:
Nuclear power density of a limiter tile is the local volumetric energy deposition rate within the material of one limiter tile caused by neutron interactions and associated gamma-radiation absorption. It is the nuclear contribution to the broader [power density of a limiter tile](name:power_density_of_limiter_tile), not the total local energy source.

$$
P_{\mathrm{nuc}} = \int_{V_{\mathrm{tile}}} q_{\mathrm{nuc}}(\mathbf{r})\,\mathrm{d}V
$$

where $q_{\mathrm{nuc}}(\mathbf{r})$ is the nuclear power density at position $\mathbf{r}$, $V_{\mathrm{tile}}$ is the material volume of the limiter tile, and $P_{\mathrm{nuc}}$ is the corresponding [nuclear power of a limiter tile](name:nuclear_power_of_limiter_tile).

The quantity includes energy deposited volumetrically by neutron scattering and capture and by absorption of primary and secondary gamma radiation. Surface heat loads, externally applied heating, and nonnuclear energy-transfer mechanisms are excluded.

sources.enhanced_context: Nuclear power density deposited in a limiter wall unit at the midplane. Represents volumetric nuclear heating from neutron and gamma interactions at that toroidal location.
sources.leaf_definition: Nuclear power density heating this unit evaluated at the midplane (whenever relevant)
sources.parent_definition: Set of limiter units

NAMES.name: argon_density
NAMES.subject: argon
NAMES.short: Charge-state-summed number density of argon ions, including Ar+ through Ar18+ and excluding neutral argon; local and averaged forms share this definition.
NAMES.long:
Argon density is the number of argon ions per unit volume, summed over all ionization stages from singly charged Ar+ through fully stripped Ar18+. Neutral argon is excluded.

$$
n_{\mathrm{Ar}} = \sum_{Z=1}^{18} n_{\mathrm{Ar}^{Z+}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{Ar}}$ is the total argon-ion number density, $Z$ is the integer argon charge state, and $n_{\mathrm{Ar}^{Z+}}$ is the number density of argon ions in that charge state.

The definition applies to a local value and to averages over a specified chord or confined plasma volume, including the [line-averaged argon density](name:line_averaged_argon_density) and [volume-averaged argon density](name:volume_averaged_argon_density). It is distinct from [argon count](name:argon_count), which represents an equivalent-electron inventory rather than particles per volume.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the counted argon-ion population contributes positively to the particle number.

NAMES.name: atomic_mass
NAMES.short: Atomic mass of a particle species, identifying its isotope or composition and setting the inertial mass scale for collisional and transport calculations.
NAMES.long:
Atomic mass is the rest-mass scale assigned to a specified particle species, determined by its isotope and elemental or molecular composition. The common definition applies to both ion and neutral species.

The numerical atomic mass is represented by

$$
m_s = A_s\,u
$$

where $m_s$ is the atomic mass of species $s$ expressed in unified atomic mass units, $A_s$ is its dimensionless numerical atomic mass, and $u$ is the unified atomic mass unit, defined as one-twelfth of the mass of a neutral carbon-12 atom. This mass sets the particle inertia used in transport, collisionality, momentum, and gyroradius relations.

The ion and neutral cases are represented by [ion atomic mass](name:ion_atomic_mass) and [neutral species atomic mass](name:neutral_species_atomic_mass). Atomic mass is distinct from [ion mass number](name:ion_mass_number), which is the integer nucleon count, and from [volume-averaged effective mass](name:volume_averaged_effective_mass), which is an aggregate over multiple species.

NAMES.name: atomic_number
NAMES.short: Integer nuclear charge number identifying an element by its proton count, invariant under ionization state and isotope.
NAMES.long:
The nuclear charge number identifies an atomic species by the number of protons in its nucleus. It is unchanged when the species is ionized or when its isotope changes.

The defining relation is

$$
Z_n = N_p
$$

where $Z_n$ is the nuclear charge number and $N_p$ is the integer proton count. The quantity applies to neutral and charged species, including injected species and their fragments. The ion-specific and neutral-beam-specific instances are [ion atomic number](name:ion_atomic_number) and [neutral-beam atomic number](name:neutral_beam_atomic_number); neither should be confused with [ion charge](name:ion_charge), which changes with ionization state.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the nucleus contains a positive number of protons.

sources.enhanced_context: Normalized z of species.
sources.leaf_definition: Nuclear charge
sources.parent_definition: Atomic species in the gas composition

NAMES.name: average_charge_number
NAMES.short: Concentration-weighted mean ionic charge number across the constituent charge states of a grouped ion population.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the average ionic charge number of a grouped population containing multiple ion charge states. It characterizes the population's mean ionization level while retaining charge-state concentration weighting.

For included charge states, the mean is defined by

$$
\bar{Z} = \frac{\sum_q n_q q}{\sum_q n_q}
$$

where $q$ is the ionic charge number and $n_q$ is the number density of ions in charge state $q$, represented by the [ion charge-state density](name:ion_charge_state_density). The summation includes the charge states assigned to the group.

This average is distinct from the [ion charge](name:ion_charge), which describes an individual or otherwise specified ionic charge number, and from the [ion upper-bound charge number](name:ion_upper_bound_charge_number), which identifies the maximum charge state in a group. The specific bundled-population instance is [ion charge-state average charge number](name:ion_charge_state_average_charge_number).

sources.enhanced_context: Concentration-weighted mean charge number (⟨Z⟩) of an ion charge-state bundle, volume-averaged over the plasma radius. Computed as Σ(Z·x_z) over all charge states within the bundle; scalar complement to the radial profile z_average_1d.
sources.leaf_definition: Average Z of the charge state bundle, volume averaged over the plasma radius (equal to z_min if no bundle), = sum (Z*x_z) where x_z is the relative concentration of a given charge state in the bundle, i.e. sum(x_z) = 1 over the bundle.
sources.parent_definition: Quantities related to the different states of the species (ionisation, energy, excitation, ...)

NAMES.name: center_of_mass_velocity
NAMES.short: Center-of-mass velocity is the mass-weighted barycentric velocity vector of a multicomponent plasma, equal to total momentum density divided by total mass density. It is the single-fluid bulk plasma velocity whose projections define the radial, poloidal, toroidal, and field-parallel center-of-mass velocity components.
NAMES.long:
Center-of-mass velocity is the mass-weighted barycentric velocity vector of a multicomponent plasma. It is the velocity whose product with total mass density equals the total plasma momentum density of the species included in the plasma mixture.

The center-of-mass velocity $\mathbf{V}_{cm}$ is defined as total momentum density divided by total mass density:

$$
\mathbf{V}_{cm} = \frac{\sum_s m_s n_s \mathbf{v}_s}{\sum_s m_s n_s} = \frac{\sum_s \rho_s \mathbf{v}_s}{\rho}
$$

where $s$ indexes included plasma species, $m_s$ is the particle mass of species $s$, $n_s$ is the number density of species $s$, $\mathbf{v}_s$ is the species fluid velocity entering the [plasma velocity](name:plasma_velocity) aggregate, $\rho_s=m_s n_s$ is the species contribution to [mass density](name:mass_density), and $\rho=\sum_s \rho_s$ is the total [mass density](name:mass_density).

The weighting is by mass density, not by charge, number density alone, or an unweighted species average. When [plasma velocity](name:plasma_velocity) denotes the single-fluid bulk velocity of the same mixture, it is identical to center-of-mass velocity. Projections of this vector define the [radial](name:radial_center_of_mass_velocity), [poloidal](name:poloidal_center_of_mass_velocity), [toroidal](name:toroidal_center_of_mass_velocity), and [field-parallel](name:parallel_center_of_mass_velocity) center-of-mass velocity components.
NAMES.sign: Positive when a vector component is directed along the positive basis vector of the explicitly specified coordinate system used for that component, with right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ components positive along $+\hat{R}$ toward increasing major radius, $+\hat{\phi}$ toward increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ counter-clockwise viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $+\hat{Z}$ upward, and field-parallel projections positive along the magnetic-field direction.

NAMES.name: charge_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.short: Charge at an internal transport barrier is a dimensionless descriptor of the ionic charge content of a plasma evaluated at the internal transport barrier. The specific charge moment, weighting, or averaging rule is defined by a more specific child quantity.
NAMES.long:
Charge at an internal transport barrier is a dimensionless member of the family of ion-charge descriptors evaluated at the spatial locus of an internal transport barrier. It fixes the evaluation locus and the general physical subject, namely ionic charge content, without selecting a particular charge moment or averaging convention.

This parent quantity has no single governing equation because different child quantities define different charge weightings and normalizations. A representative specialization is [effective charge at the internal transport barrier](name:effective_charge_at_internal_transport_barrier), which specifies the effective-charge aggregation of the ion mixture; other specializations would define their own charge descriptor rather than inheriting that aggregation from this parent.

This quantity is not a net electric charge density, particle density, or electrostatic potential. It is a structural abstraction for dimensionless descriptors of ion charge state at the internal-transport-barrier locus, so the child name supplies the operative definition of the charge statistic.

NAMES.name: charge_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.short: Charge at the magnetic axis is a local charge-related scalar evaluated at the plasma magnetic axis. The parent quantity identifies the on-axis charge measure generically; specific children define the particular charge moment, population, and normalization.
NAMES.long:
Charge at the magnetic axis is a charge-related scalar evaluated locally at the plasma magnetic axis, the central locus of the nested magnetic flux surfaces. This parent quantity fixes the evaluation locus but does not by itself specify which charge measure is used.

The scope is the generic on-axis charge quantity shared by more specific standard names. A child such as [effective charge at magnetic axis](name:effective_charge_at_magnetic_axis) adds the defining ionic charge-state moment and electron-density normalization; those details are not part of this parent definition.

NAMES.name: co_passing_fast_particle_pressure
NAMES.short: Kinetic pressure moment of the suprathermal particle distribution restricted to co-passing guiding-center orbits; it is the flux-surface-averaged co-passing-orbit contribution to fast-particle pressure.
NAMES.long:
Co-passing fast-particle pressure is the scalar trace pressure carried by suprathermal particles on co-passing guiding-center orbits. It is the co-passing-orbit contribution to [fast-particle pressure], complementary to the field-aligned [parallel co-passing fast-particle pressure](name:parallel_co_passing_fast_particle_pressure) and transverse [perpendicular co-passing fast-particle pressure](name:perpendicular_co_passing_fast_particle_pressure).

The flux-surface-averaged pressure is defined by the co-passing-particle second velocity moment:

$$
P_{\mathrm{co,fast}}(\psi) = \left\langle \frac{1}{3}\sum_s m_s \int_{\Omega_{\mathrm{co},s}(\mathbf{x})} v^2 f_{\mathrm{fast},s}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\,d^3v \right\rangle_{\psi}
$$

where $\psi$ labels the magnetic flux surface, $\langle\cdot\rangle_{\psi}$ denotes its flux-surface average, $s$ labels fast-particle species, $m_s$ is particle mass, $v=|\mathbf{v}|$ is particle speed, $f_{\mathrm{fast},s}$ is the distribution function, and $\Omega_{\mathrm{co},s}$ contains only co-passing guiding-center orbits. The factor one-third gives the scalar trace; with the same orbit selection, $P_{\mathrm{co,fast}}=(P_{\parallel,\mathrm{co,fast}}+2P_{\perp,\mathrm{co,fast}})/3$. [Counter-passing fast-particle pressure](name:counter_passing_fast_particle_pressure) and [trapped fast-particle pressure](name:trapped_fast_particle_pressure) populations are excluded.

NAMES.name: co_passing_torque_density
NAMES.short: Co-passing torque density is the local vector source density of angular momentum for passing particles whose parallel motion is in the co-current sense. It fixes the orbit class to co-passing while leaving the spatial component or projection unspecified.
NAMES.long:
Co-passing torque density is the local vector source density of angular momentum transferred to the co-passing particle population. Co-passing denotes passing particles whose motion parallel to the magnetic field is in the same sense as the plasma current, so the orbit-class qualifier is fixed by this quantity.

The source contribution to the local angular-momentum balance is defined by:

$$
\left.\frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\ell}_{\mathrm{co,p}}}{\partial t}\right|_{\mathrm{source}} = \boldsymbol{\tau}_{\mathrm{co,p}}
$$

where $\boldsymbol{\ell}_{\mathrm{co,p}}$ is the local angular-momentum density of the co-passing population and $\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\mathrm{co,p}}$ is the co-passing torque density.

This parent quantity does not choose a spatial component or projection. Direction-resolved quantities, such as the [toroidal co-passing torque density](name:toroidal_co_passing_torque_density), are projections of this vector; a toroidal projection is along $\hat{\phi}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. Torque densities for counter-passing, trapped, or orbit-class-summed populations are outside this scope.
NAMES.sign: Positive when a resolved component of $\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\mathrm{co,p}}$ acts along the positive sense of the basis vector or projection direction used for that component.

NAMES.name: conductivity
NAMES.short: Local directional electrical conductivity coefficients relating conductive current-density components to corresponding electric-field components in a plasma.
NAMES.long:
Electrical conductivity characterizes the local linear response of conductive plasma current to the electric field. The parent quantity covers directional coefficients expressed in cylindrical, flux-coordinate, or magnetic-field-aligned directions.

The conductivity tensor is defined by

$$
\mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{cond}} = \boldsymbol{\sigma}\cdot\mathbf{E}, \qquad J_{\mathrm{cond},i}=\sum_j\sigma_{ij}E_j
$$

where $\mathbf{J}_{\mathrm{cond}}$ is the conductive current-density vector, $\mathbf{E}$ is the electric-field vector, and $\sigma_{ij}$ is the conductivity coefficient coupling electric-field direction $j$ to current direction $i$. Directional children such as [radial conductivity](name:radial_conductivity) and [parallel conductivity](name:parallel_conductivity) represent same-direction projections; off-diagonal couplings may contribute to the resulting current component and are not excluded by a diagonal coefficient. Cylindrical directions use the right-handed $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, while parallel conductivity uses the magnetic-field-aligned basis $(\mathbf{b},\mathbf{e}_{\perp 1},\mathbf{e}_{\perp 2})$.

NAMES.name: coulomb_logarithm
NAMES.short: Dimensionless logarithm of the ratio of the Debye screening length to the minimum Coulomb impact parameter, appearing as a multiplicative factor in all classical collision frequencies and resistivity expressions.
NAMES.long:
The Coulomb logarithm $\ln \Lambda$ is a dimensionless factor encoding the effective range of impact parameters that contribute to cumulative small-angle Coulomb scattering in a plasma. It arises because the Debye-shielded potential introduces a maximum effective impact parameter $b_{\max}$, while quantum or classical mechanics sets a minimum $b_{\min}$, producing a well-defined logarithmic ratio.

The defining expression is

$$
\ln \Lambda = \ln\!\left(\frac{b_{\max}}{b_{\min}}\right)
$$

where $b_{\max} = \lambda_D$ is the Debye screening length, and $b_{\min}$ is the larger of the classical distance of closest approach $e^2/(m_e v_e^2)$ and the thermal de Broglie wavelength $\hbar/(m_e v_e)$, with $e$ the elementary charge, $m_e$ the electron mass, and $v_e$ the electron thermal speed.

The collision frequency scales as $\nu \propto \ln \Lambda$ and the Spitzer resistivity as $\eta \propto \ln \Lambda \, T_e^{-3/2}$, where $T_e$ is the electron temperature. In tokamak core conditions ($T_e \sim 5$–$10$ keV, $n_e \sim 10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$), $\ln \Lambda \approx 17$–$19$; in the cooler edge ($T_e \sim 10$–$100$ eV), values fall to approximately $10$–$14$. The pedestal-localized value is captured by [coulomb_logarithm_at_pedestal_top](name:coulomb_logarithm_at_pedestal_top).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the Debye length exceeds the minimum Coulomb impact parameter, a condition satisfied in all weakly coupled plasmas where $\Lambda > 1$.

NAMES.name: counter_passing_density
NAMES.short: Number density of particles on counter-passing guiding-center orbits, summed over thermal and suprathermal populations.
NAMES.long:
Counter-passing particle density is the local number density carried by guiding-center trajectories that circulate in the direction opposite to the plasma current. It includes both thermal and suprathermal particles and excludes trapped and co-passing orbit classes.

$$
n_{\mathrm{cp}}(\mathbf{x}) = \int f(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\,\mathbb{1}_{\mathrm{cp}}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{cp}}$ is the counter-passing density, $f$ is the total particle velocity distribution at position $\mathbf{x}$, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity, and $\mathbb{1}_{\mathrm{cp}}$ selects particles whose guiding-center parallel motion is counter-current. The fast suprathermal subset is represented by [counter-passing fast particle density](name:counter_passing_fast_particle_density), while the complementary circulating class is [total co-passing particle density](name:total_co_passing_particle_density).

NAMES.name: counter_passing_fast_particle_pressure
NAMES.short: Kinetic pressure moment of the suprathermal distribution restricted to counter-passing guiding-center orbits; it is the flux-surface-averaged counter-passing contribution to fast-particle pressure.
NAMES.long:
Counter-passing fast-particle pressure is the scalar trace pressure carried by suprathermal particles on counter-passing guiding-center orbits. It is the counter-passing-orbit contribution to [fast-particle pressure], complementary to the field-aligned [parallel counter-passing fast-particle pressure](name:parallel_counter_passing_fast_particle_pressure) and transverse [perpendicular counter-passing fast-particle pressure](name:perpendicular_counter_passing_fast_particle_pressure).

The flux-surface-averaged pressure is defined by the counter-passing second velocity moment:

$$
P_{\mathrm{cp,fast}}(\psi) = \left\langle \frac{1}{3}\sum_s m_s \int_{\Omega_{\mathrm{cp},s}(\mathbf{x})} v^2 f_{\mathrm{fast},s}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\,d^3v \right\rangle_{\psi}
$$

where $\psi$ labels the magnetic flux surface, $\langle\cdot\rangle_{\psi}$ denotes its flux-surface average, $s$ labels fast-particle species, $m_s$ is particle mass in kg, $v=|\mathbf{v}|$ is particle speed in m s$^{-1}$, $f_{\mathrm{fast},s}$ is the distribution function, and $\Omega_{\mathrm{cp},s}$ contains guiding-center orbits that pass in the direction opposite to the plasma-current direction. The factor one-third gives the scalar trace, with $P_{\mathrm{cp,fast}}=(P_{\parallel,\mathrm{cp,fast}}+2P_{\perp,\mathrm{cp,fast}})/3$ for the same orbit selection. Trapped and co-passing populations are excluded.

NAMES.name: counter_passing_torque_density
NAMES.short: Vector density of angular-momentum transfer from counter-passing particles, defined by their local momentum-exchange force density and its lever arm.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the local torque-density vector associated with momentum exchange involving counter-passing particles. It retains the full torque direction rather than selecting a particular axis projection.

The torque-density vector is defined by

$$
\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\mathrm{cp}} = \mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{f}_{\mathrm{cp}}
$$

where $\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\mathrm{cp}}$ is the angular-momentum source density, $\mathbf{r}$ is the lever-arm vector relative to the torque axis, and $\mathbf{f}_{\mathrm{cp}}$ is the net force density associated with the counter-passing particle population. The [toroidal counter-passing torque density](name:toroidal_counter_passing_torque_density) is the corresponding toroidal projection, formed with the major-radius lever arm.
NAMES.sign: Positive toroidal torque increases angular momentum in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$; vector components follow the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ basis.

NAMES.name: current_density_due_to_anomalous_transport
NAMES.short: Vector conventional electric-current density attributed to turbulence-driven anomalous transport in a plasma.
NAMES.long:
Current density due to anomalous transport is the vector conventional electric-current density associated with turbulent, nonclassical transport processes that produce a net charge flow. It denotes only the anomalous-transport contribution to the plasma current, not the total current density.

This is a phenomenological transport-current contribution; no universal closed-form constitutive identity is part of its definition. The vector may be resolved into [radial_current_density_due_to_anomalous_transport](name:radial_current_density_due_to_anomalous_transport), [toroidal_current_density_due_to_anomalous_transport](name:toroidal_current_density_due_to_anomalous_transport), and [vertical_current_density_due_to_anomalous_transport](name:vertical_current_density_due_to_anomalous_transport) in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, and into [parallel_current_density_due_to_anomalous_transport](name:parallel_current_density_due_to_anomalous_transport) along the local magnetic-field direction $\hat{b} = \mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$, where $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field. It is distinct from [current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity](name:current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity), which represents a perpendicular-viscous transport-current contribution.
NAMES.sign: Positive when a resolved conventional-current component due to anomalous transport points in the positive direction of the projection used: $+\hat{R}$, $+\hat{\phi}$, or $+\hat{Z}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, or along $\hat{b}$ for the magnetic-field-parallel projection.

NAMES.name: current_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.short: Electric current density vector arising from collisional momentum exchange between plasma particle populations, including ion-neutral friction in partially ionized edge and scrape-off-layer plasmas.
NAMES.long:
Collisional momentum exchange between plasma species — ions, electrons, and background neutrals — imparts species-dependent velocity perturbations; the resultant differential flows of the charged species constitute a nonzero net current density $\mathbf{j}_\mathrm{coll}$.

The collisional current density follows from the multi-fluid species momentum equations. For each charged species $s$ with charge $q_s$, number density $n_s$, and collisionally induced velocity perturbation $\delta\mathbf{u}_s$ arising from the net friction force $\mathbf{R}_s$ exerted by all other populations:

$$
\mathbf{j}_\mathrm{coll} = \sum_s q_s n_s \, \delta\mathbf{u}_s
$$

where the sum runs over all charged species and $\delta\mathbf{u}_s$ is the velocity perturbation driven by collisional friction alone.

In partially ionized edge and scrape-off-layer plasmas, ion-neutral friction is the dominant contribution to this quantity; the full vector encompasses all spatial projections, including the [poloidal component](name:poloidal_current_density_due_to_collisions) along increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in flux coordinates $(\psi, \theta, \varphi)$. For the case where ion-neutral friction is the sole collisional mechanism, see [current_density_due_to_ion_neutral_friction](name:current_density_due_to_ion_neutral_friction) and its [parallel projection](name:parallel_current_density_due_to_ion_neutral_friction). This vector is evaluated in multi-fluid transport models coupling neutral and charged-particle populations; it is not directly measured but inferred from combined neutral-particle and ion-flow diagnostics with collision-rate models.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the current vector points in the direction of the respective unit vector $\hat{R}$, $\hat{\phi}$, or $\hat{Z}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is the major radius, $\phi$ is the toroidal angle increasing counter-clockwise viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is the vertical height.

NAMES.name: current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift
NAMES.short: Vector electric current-density contribution associated with pressure-gradient diamagnetic drift, including its perpendicular drive and field-aligned closure contributions.
NAMES.long:
The diamagnetic drift current density is the conventional electric-current contribution associated with pressure gradients in a magnetized plasma. The parent vector includes the pressure-gradient-driven perpendicular term and field-aligned return-current contributions required by current continuity; its projections include the [radial diamagnetic-drift current density](name:radial_current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift) and [vertical diamagnetic-drift current density](name:vertical_current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift).

The isotropic-pressure diamagnetic contribution is defined by

$$
\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{dia},\perp}=\frac{\mathbf{B}\times\nabla p}{B^2}
$$

where $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field in tesla, $B=|\mathbf{B}|$ is its magnitude, and $p$ is the plasma pressure in pascals. This relation gives the perpendicular drive; field-aligned components such as the [parallel diamagnetic-drift current density](name:parallel_current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift) and [Pfirsch–Schlüter diamagnetic-drift current density](name:pfirsch_schlueter_current_density_due_to_diamagnetic_drift) are included when required by the current-density decomposition. The vector quantity retains direction, unlike the [diamagnetic current density](name:diamagnetic_current_density) magnitude.
NAMES.sign: Positive when a current-density component points along the corresponding positive direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ basis.

NAMES.name: current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity
NAMES.short: Vector electric current density arising from heat-viscosity terms in the collisional plasma fluid closure, where the divergence of the heat-viscosity stress tensor drives net charge transport in a magnetized plasma.
NAMES.long:
The heat-viscosity current density is the electric current density vector generated when heat-viscosity contributions in a collisional plasma fluid model (such as the Braginskii closure) induce net species motion that results in charge transport. In a magnetized plasma, the viscous stress tensor $\overset{\leftrightarrow}{\pi}$ contains a heat-viscosity part $\overset{\leftrightarrow}{\pi}_\mathrm{hv}$ that couples heat transport to bulk plasma momentum; the divergence of this tensor enters the fluid momentum equation for each species and drives flows carrying net electric current.

The heat-viscosity current density vector $\mathbf{j}_\mathrm{hv}$ is expressed as:

$$
\mathbf{j}_\mathrm{hv} = \sum_s q_s n_s \mathbf{v}_{s,\mathrm{hv}}
$$

where $q_s$ is the charge of species $s$, $n_s$ is its number density, and $\mathbf{v}_{s,\mathrm{hv}}$ is the flow velocity component driven by heat-viscosity forces in the species momentum balance.

This vector is decomposed into geometric projections, including the [radial component](name:radial_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity) along $\hat{R}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. The companion quantity current_density_due_to_collisions captures the distinct inter-species collisional friction mechanism, while radial_current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity represents the analogous contribution from field-aligned (parallel) viscosity. Heat-viscosity current contributions are most significant in the edge plasma where the collisionality is high enough for fluid closures to remain valid.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the net charge flow points in the direction of increasing coordinate of the respective projection axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: current_density_due_to_ion_inertia
NAMES.short: Vector current density arising from the inertial force terms of the ion fluid in the two-fluid plasma model, principally through the polarization drift generated by ion acceleration in the momentum equation.
NAMES.long:
The current density due to ion inertia represents the net electric current produced by the inertial acceleration terms in the ion fluid momentum equation. In a two-fluid plasma description, ions with finite mass contribute to net charge transport whenever they are accelerated — through flow convergence, curvature forces, or time-varying electric fields — giving rise to a polarization-type current that is absent in the massless-electron fluid.

The dominant contribution is the ion polarization drift current:

$$
\mathbf{J}_{inertia} = \frac{m_i n_i}{e B^2} \mathbf{B} \times \frac{d_i \mathbf{v}_{\perp i}}{dt}
$$

where $m_i$ is the ion mass, $n_i$ is the ion number density, $e$ is the elementary charge, $B$ is the magnetic field magnitude, and $d_i/dt = \partial/\partial t + \mathbf{v}_i \cdot \nabla$ is the ion convective derivative applied to the perpendicular ion velocity $\mathbf{v}_{\perp i}$.

The divergence of this current feeds the vorticity equation and contributes to the radial current balance, making it particularly significant in edge and scrape-off-layer transport modeling where large ion flows develop. In multi-fluid transport codes, the vector is evaluated on generalized geometry grids and decomposed into cylindrical components — [radial_current_density_due_to_ion_inertia](name:radial_current_density_due_to_ion_inertia), [toroidal_current_density_due_to_ion_inertia](name:toroidal_current_density_due_to_ion_inertia), [vertical_current_density_due_to_ion_inertia](name:vertical_current_density_due_to_ion_inertia) — and a field-aligned component [parallel_current_density_due_to_ion_inertia](name:parallel_current_density_due_to_ion_inertia). The analogous turbulent contribution is given by [current_density_due_to_anomalous_transport](name:current_density_due_to_anomalous_transport).
NAMES.sign: Positive when each vector component points in the positive $\hat{R}$, $\hat{\phi}$, or $\hat{Z}$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, or along the local magnetic field direction for the parallel component.

NAMES.name: current_density_due_to_ion_neutral_friction
NAMES.short: Mechanism-resolved electric current-density vector attributable to ion–neutral frictional momentum exchange in a partially ionized plasma.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the vector contribution to electric current density attributed to momentum exchange between plasma ions and neutral particles. It excludes current contributions assigned to other mechanisms and does not represent the total plasma current density.

The mechanism-resolved current density is defined from the corresponding charged-particle velocity contributions:

$$
\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{in}} = \sum_s q_s n_s \mathbf{v}_{s,\mathrm{in}}
$$

where $q_s$ is the charge of charged species $s$ in C, $n_s$ is its number density in m$^{-3}$, and $\mathbf{v}_{s,\mathrm{in}}$ is the velocity contribution attributed to ion–neutral friction. Neutral particles have zero charge and do not contribute directly to the sum.

The vector may be projected onto cylindrical, poloidal, field-aligned, or other specified directions, including the [radial current-density component](name:radial_current_density_due_to_ion_neutral_friction), [toroidal current-density component](name:toroidal_current_density_due_to_ion_neutral_friction), and [parallel current-density component](name:parallel_current_density_due_to_ion_neutral_friction). Unlike [current density due to collisions](name:current_density_due_to_collisions), its mechanism attribution is restricted to ion–neutral friction.
NAMES.sign: Positive when a specified component points along its declared positive direction; in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, these directions are increasing $R$, increasing $\phi$, and increasing $Z$, respectively.

NAMES.name: current_density_due_to_non_inductive_current_drive
NAMES.short: Vector electric current-density contribution sustained by non-inductive mechanisms, including bootstrap and externally driven sources, with inductive electric-field drive excluded.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the vector contribution to plasma electric current density produced by current-drive mechanisms that do not rely on an inductive electric field. It includes contributions such as bootstrap current and externally driven non-inductive current, while excluding the inductive or Ohmic contribution.

The total non-inductive contribution is defined by

$$
\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{NI}} = \sum_k \mathbf{j}_k
$$

where $\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{NI}}$ is the non-inductive current-density vector and $\mathbf{j}_k$ is the contribution from each included non-inductive current-drive mechanism. The [parallel current density due to non-inductive current drive](name:parallel_current_density_due_to_non_inductive_current_drive) is a field-aligned, flux-surface-averaged instance of this general quantity, while [current density due to wave-driven current drive](name:current_density_due_to_wave_driven_current_drive) identifies one particular drive mechanism.
NAMES.sign: Positive when a current-density component points along the corresponding positive direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(\hat{R},\hat{\phi},\hat{Z})$ basis, with $\hat{R} \times \hat{\phi} = \hat{Z}$.

NAMES.name: current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity
NAMES.short: Full current-density vector arising from the divergence of the parallel viscous stress tensor in a magnetized plasma.
NAMES.long:
Full current-density vector arising from the divergence of the parallel viscous stress tensor in a magnetized plasma. It is the current-density contribution associated with the parallel part of viscous momentum transport, where parallel refers to the magnetic-field direction in the stress tensor rather than to the direction of the resulting current.

The perpendicular force-balance drift produced by the parallel-viscous force density is

$$
\mathbf{J}_{\Pi_\parallel} = \frac{(\nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\Pi}_\parallel) \times \mathbf{B}}{B^2}
$$

where $\mathbf{J}_{\Pi_\parallel}$ is this current-density vector, $\boldsymbol{\Pi}_\parallel$ is the parallel viscous stress tensor, $\nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\Pi}_\parallel$ is the corresponding viscous force density, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic-field vector, and $B=|\mathbf{B}|$ is the magnetic-field magnitude. Only the full tensor divergence enters this relation; it is not a scalar-viscosity definition. The vector direction is governed by the right-hand rule applied to the parallel-viscous force density and the magnetic field, and the contribution is locally perpendicular to $\mathbf{B}$.

This quantity excludes current density due to [perpendicular viscous stress](name:current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity), including its [field-aligned projection](name:parallel_current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity), and the separate [heat-viscosity contribution](name:current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity). Directional projections include the [radial](name:radial_current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity), [toroidal](name:toroidal_current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity), and [vertical](name:vertical_current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity) components along $\hat{R}$, $\hat{\phi}$, and $\hat{Z}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle increasing counter-clockwise when viewed from above $+\hat{Z}$, and $Z$ is vertical height, and the [poloidal component](name:poloidal_current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity) in the plane spanned by $\hat{R}$ and $\hat{Z}$. Aggregate viscous-current components such as [radial_current_density_due_to_viscosity](name:radial_current_density_due_to_viscosity) and toroidal_current_density_due_to_viscosity combine this contribution with perpendicular-viscosity contributions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when a signed component of $\mathbf{J}_{\Pi_\parallel}$ is aligned with the positive direction of the basis vector defining that component, with the vector direction set by $(\nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\Pi}_\parallel)\times\mathbf{B}$ according to the right-hand rule.

NAMES.name: current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity
NAMES.short: Vector electric current-density contribution generated by the divergence of perpendicular viscous stress in a magnetized charged plasma.
NAMES.long:
Perpendicular-viscosity current density is the vector electric-current contribution attributed to perpendicular viscous stress acting on charged plasma. The word “perpendicular” identifies the viscous-stress mechanism, not a restriction of the resulting current vector to directions perpendicular to the magnetic field.

The current-density contribution is defined by

$$
\mathbf{J}_{\perp,\nu}=\sum_s q_s n_s\mathbf{u}_{s,\perp,\nu}
$$

where $q_s$ is the signed charge of species $s$ in coulombs, $n_s$ is its number density in m$^{-3}$, and $\mathbf{u}_{s,\perp,\nu}$ is the species-velocity response attributed to the divergence of perpendicular viscous stress. The vector may be resolved into radial, toroidal, vertical, poloidal, parallel, or diamagnetic components, including the [parallel current-density component](name:parallel_current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity) and [diamagnetic current-density component](name:diamagnetic_current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity). It is distinct from the analogous [current density due to parallel viscosity](name:current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity).
NAMES.sign: Positive when a projected component points along its designated positive direction: increasing $R$, $\phi$, or $Z$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, or the defined positive local direction for poloidal, parallel, and diamagnetic projections.

NAMES.name: current_density_due_to_viscosity
NAMES.short: Current density due to viscosity is the vector part of the electric current density associated with viscous-stress terms in plasma species momentum balance. It represents charge transport produced when the divergence of viscous stress changes the species particle fluxes.
NAMES.long:
Current density due to viscosity is the vector part of the electric current density associated with viscous-stress terms in plasma species momentum balance. The divergence of each species viscous stress tensor is a force density; by changing the species particle fluxes, it produces a charge-weighted current contribution.

A defining species decomposition is:

$$
\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{visc}} = \sum_s q_s \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{s,\mathrm{visc}} = \sum_s q_s n_s \mathbf{u}_{s,\mathrm{visc}}
$$

where $s$ labels a plasma species, $q_s$ is the species electric charge, $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{s,\mathrm{visc}}$ is the species particle-flux contribution caused by the viscous force density $\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol{\pi}_s$, $n_s$ is the species number density, $\mathbf{u}_{s,\mathrm{visc}}$ is the corresponding species velocity contribution, and $\boldsymbol{\pi}_s$ is the species viscous stress tensor. The constitutive relation for $\boldsymbol{\pi}_s$ may represent collisional, gyroviscous, neoclassical, or turbulent viscosity, but this quantity is the resulting current-density contribution, not the stress tensor itself.

This parent vector is not restricted to the perpendicular drift part proportional to $(\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol{\pi}_s)\times\mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|^2$; it may include field-aligned and cross-field parts generated by viscous terms in the full momentum balance. It excludes [current density due to heat viscosity](name:current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity), the distinct contribution in which heat-viscosity coupling is identified as the cause of charge transport, and is distinct from [current density due to anomalous transport](name:current_density_due_to_anomalous_transport), whose cause is nonclassical transport not specifically attributed to viscous stress.

Projected and channel-resolved quantities inherit this parent meaning with an explicit projection or stress-tensor subset: [radial current density due to viscosity](name:radial_current_density_due_to_viscosity) is the $\hat{R}$ projection in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame with basis $(\hat{R}, \hat{\phi}, \hat{Z})$, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height; [radial current density due to parallel viscosity](name:radial_current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity) and [radial current density due to perpendicular viscosity](name:radial_current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity) separate that radial projection by parallel- and perpendicular-viscosity contributions; [parallel current density due to perpendicular viscosity](name:parallel_current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity) projects the perpendicular-viscosity contribution along $\hat{b}=\mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$; and [diamagnetic current density due to perpendicular viscosity](name:diamagnetic_current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity) selects the corresponding diamagnetic channel.
NAMES.sign: Positive when a resolved component of $\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{visc}}$ points along the positive direction of its explicitly stated projection basis, such as $+\hat{R}$ for a radial component in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame with basis $(\hat{R}, \hat{\phi}, \hat{Z})$ or $+\hat{b}=\mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$ for a component parallel to the local magnetic field.

NAMES.name: current_due_to_non_inductive_current_drive
NAMES.short: Net toroidal electric current sustained by non-inductive current-drive mechanisms, excluding the contribution from inductive electric-field drive.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the net toroidal electric current carried by the plasma as a result of non-inductive current-drive mechanisms. It excludes current produced by the transformer-induced electric field and includes the algebraic sum of the included non-inductive contributions. The plasma-specific realization is [plasma current due to non-inductive current drive](name:plasma_current_due_to_non_inductive_current_drive).

The current is defined by the flux of non-inductive current density through a poloidal cross-section:

$$
I_{\mathrm{NI}} = \int_{S_p} \mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{NI}} \cdot d\mathbf{S}
$$

where $I_{\mathrm{NI}}$ is the non-inductive current, $\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{NI}}$ is the corresponding electric-current density, and $d\mathbf{S}$ is the oriented area element of the poloidal cross-section. Contributions such as [current due to electron-cyclotron current drive](name:current_due_to_electron_cyclotron_current_drive) and [current due to ion-cyclotron current drive](name:current_due_to_ion_cyclotron_current_drive) are instances of this quantity, whereas [plasma current due to ohmic induction](name:plasma_current_due_to_ohmic_induction) is excluded.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the net current flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: current_due_to_ohmic_induction
NAMES.short: Current due to ohmic induction is the net current component generated by the collisional Ohmic response of a conducting medium to an inductive electric field or loop-voltage drive along the current path. It excludes bootstrap and externally driven non-inductive current contributions.
NAMES.long:
Current due to ohmic induction is the scalar current component produced by an inductive electric field acting through the Ohmic conductivity of a conducting medium. The drive mechanism is changing magnetic flux, equivalently the loop voltage around the current path, not pressure-gradient-driven bootstrap current or externally applied non-inductive current drive.

The current is the flux of the Ohmic current-density component through an oriented surface that cuts the current channel:

$$
I_\mathrm{Ohm} = \int_S \mathbf{j}_\mathrm{Ohm} \cdot d\mathbf{A}
$$

where $S$ is the oriented cutting surface, $d\mathbf{A}$ is its vector area element, and $\mathbf{j}_\mathrm{Ohm}$ is the current density produced by the inductive electric field. In a magnetized plasma, the constitutive Ohmic transport component is field-parallel, with $j_{\mathrm{Ohm}\parallel} = \sigma_\parallel E_{\mathrm{ind}\parallel}$.

This quantity is a drive-mechanism component and equals the total current only when Ohmic induction is the only current source. It excludes [current due to non-inductive current drive](name:current_due_to_non_inductive_current_drive); [plasma current due to ohmic induction](name:plasma_current_due_to_ohmic_induction) is the toroidal plasma-current specialization, and [parallel plasma current due to ohmic induction](name:parallel_plasma_current_due_to_ohmic_induction) denotes the field-parallel plasma specialization.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $\mathbf{j}_\mathrm{Ohm}$ flows through the oriented surface in the direction of $d\mathbf{A}$.

NAMES.name: density_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.short: Particle number density of a specified plasma population evaluated on the flux surface assigned to an internal transport barrier, with charge-state aggregation determined by the population.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the local number density of a selected plasma population at the flux-surface location assigned to an internal transport barrier. It applies to electrons, individual ion species, and compound fuel populations treated as effective species.

The number density is defined by

$$
n = \lim_{\Delta V\to 0}\frac{\Delta N}{\Delta V}
$$

where $n$ is the number density in m$^{-3}$, $N$ is the number of counted particles, and $V$ is volume in m$^{3}$. For an ion species, the count is summed over its ionic charge states and excludes neutral atoms; electrons are counted directly. The [ion density at the internal transport barrier](name:ion_density_at_internal_transport_barrier) and [electron density at the internal transport barrier](name:electron_density_at_internal_transport_barrier) are specific population instances, while the [deuterium-tritium density at the internal transport barrier](name:deuterium_tritium_density_at_internal_transport_barrier) treats the fuel mixture as one effective population. The internal transport barrier is the designated flux-surface location where reduced cross-field turbulent transport permits steep density gradients.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the counted particle population is present at the internal transport barrier.

NAMES.name: beryllium_density_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: beryllium
NAMES.short: Particle number density of beryllium ions evaluated on the flux surface assigned to an internal transport barrier, summed over all beryllium ion charge states and excluding neutral beryllium.
NAMES.long:
Particle number density of beryllium ions evaluated on the flux surface assigned to an internal transport barrier is the local density of the beryllium-ion population at that flux-surface location. Beryllium has atomic number $Z = 4$; unless a charge state is specified separately, this quantity is the elemental beryllium ion density, summed over all beryllium ion charge states and excluding neutral beryllium atoms. The internal transport barrier is the designated flux-surface location where locally reduced cross-field turbulent transport can sustain steep density gradients.

The charge-state aggregation is defined by

$$
n_{\mathrm{Be,ITB}} = \sum_{q=1}^{4} n_{\mathrm{Be}^{q+},\mathrm{ITB}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{Be,ITB}}$ is the beryllium ion number density on the internal-transport-barrier flux surface, $n_{\mathrm{Be}^{q+},\mathrm{ITB}}$ is the number density of beryllium charge state $q$ on the same flux surface, and $q$ runs over positive beryllium ion charge states. The lower limit excludes neutral beryllium.

This is an unweighted particle density, not the charge-weighted impurity charge density or the electron density contributed by beryllium. It is a species-specific instance of [density at the internal transport barrier](name:density_at_internal_transport_barrier) and differs from [ion density at the internal transport barrier](name:ion_density_at_internal_transport_barrier), which may represent a broader ion population.

NAMES.name: boron_density_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: boron
NAMES.short: Number density of boron ions at the radial location of the internal transport barrier, where suppressed cross-field turbulent transport enables steep impurity density gradients to develop.
NAMES.long:
Boron density at the internal transport barrier is the local number density of boron ions ($Z = 5$) on the flux surface designated as the internal transport barrier reference location. Unless a charge state is specified separately, this quantity represents the elemental boron ion density summed over all ionization states (B$^{1+}$ through B$^{5+}$), excluding neutral boron atoms.

The local particle number density is the zeroth velocity moment of the boron-ion distribution function $f_\mathrm{B}$:

$$
n_\mathrm{B}(\rho_\text{ITB}) = \int f_\mathrm{B}(\mathbf{v},\, \rho_\text{ITB})\, d^3v
$$

where $\mathbf{v}$ is the particle velocity and $\rho_\text{ITB}$ is the normalized minor radius identifying the ITB flux surface. The ITB is a confined-plasma region where locally reduced cross-field transport coefficients permit steep radial gradients in density and temperature to be sustained; the parent concept is described in [density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:density_at_internal_transport_barrier). For the analogous boron density at the innermost confined flux surface, see [boron_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:boron_density_at_magnetic_axis).
NAMES.sign: Positive when boron ions are present at the barrier reference flux surface.

NAMES.name: carbon_density_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: carbon
NAMES.short: Number density of carbon ions at the radial location of the internal transport barrier, where suppressed cross-field turbulent transport enables steep impurity density gradients to develop.
NAMES.long:
Carbon density at the internal transport barrier is the local number density of carbon ions ($Z = 6$) evaluated at the flux surface designated as the internal transport barrier reference location. Unless a charge state is specified separately, this quantity is summed over all carbon ionization states from $\mathrm{C}^{1+}$ through $\mathrm{C}^{6+}$, providing the total elemental impurity concentration at the barrier, consistent with the parent [density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:density_at_internal_transport_barrier).

The total carbon number density at the ITB is defined as:

$$
n_{\mathrm{C,ITB}} = \left. \sum_{k=1}^{6} n_{\mathrm{C}^{k+}} \right|_{r = r_\mathrm{ITB}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{C}^{k+}}$ is the number density of carbon ions in charge state $k$ and $r_\mathrm{ITB}$ is the radial coordinate of the barrier reference surface.

Carbon enters fusion plasmas through erosion of carbon-based plasma-facing components such as graphite limiters and divertor tiles. At an ITB, where cross-field turbulent transport is locally suppressed, neoclassical impurity transport can drive steep radial carbon density gradients — local accumulation or depletion depending on the sign of the radial electric field and density-gradient scale lengths. This quantity is inferred from charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy or soft X-ray continuum emission combined with atomic-physics modeling.

Carbon density evaluated at other plasma locations includes [carbon_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:carbon_density_at_magnetic_axis), [carbon_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:flux_surface_averaged_carbon_density_at_plasma_boundary), and [carbon_density_at_divertor_target](name:carbon_density_at_divertor_target); the total ion number density at the same barrier position is given by [total_ion_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:total_ion_density_at_internal_transport_barrier).

NAMES.name: density_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.short: Local particle number density of a specified plasma population evaluated at the magnetic axis, with species and charge-state aggregation defined by that population.
NAMES.long:
Particle number density at the magnetic axis is the local number of particles belonging to a specified population per physical volume at that location. The population may be an electron, ion, neutral, isotope mixture, or other explicitly defined plasma population, with its charge-state aggregation included in the definition.

The defining relation is

$$
n_{\mathcal{P}} = \frac{dN_{\mathcal{P}}}{dV}
$$

where $n_{\mathcal{P}}$ is the number density of population $\mathcal{P}$, $N_{\mathcal{P}}$ is its particle count, and $V$ is physical volume.

This parent quantity does not specify the population, charge-state aggregation, or neutral internal-state selection. These distinctions are resolved by specific quantities such as [ion density at the magnetic axis](name:ion_density_at_magnetic_axis), [electron density at the magnetic axis](name:electron_density_at_magnetic_axis), [neutral density](name:neutral_density), and [neutral internal-state number density](name:neutral_internal_state_number_density). For ion and species densities, aggregation over charge states is specified by the population definition.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the local counted particle population has positive number density.

NAMES.name: argon_density_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: argon
NAMES.short: Particle number density of argon ions evaluated at the magnetic axis, the innermost location of nested closed poloidal magnetic-flux surfaces where the poloidal-flux gradient vanishes, summed over all argon ionic charge states.
NAMES.long:
Particle number density of the argon ion population evaluated at the magnetic axis is the local argon-ion count per physical volume at the innermost point of nested closed poloidal magnetic-flux surfaces, summed over all argon ionic charge states. The magnetic axis is the locus where the gradient of the poloidal magnetic flux vanishes. Argon (Ar) has atomic number 18; this species-level ion population excludes neutral argon.

The charge-state-summed on-axis density is defined by

$$
n_{\mathrm{Ar,axis}} = \sum_{q=1}^{18} n_{\mathrm{Ar}^{q+},\mathrm{axis}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{Ar,axis}}$ is the particle number density of the argon ion population at the magnetic axis, $q$ indexes the positive argon ionic charge state, and $n_{\mathrm{Ar}^{q+},\mathrm{axis}}$ is the particle number density of argon ions in charge state $q$ evaluated at the magnetic axis.

This is the magnetic-axis evaluation of [argon density](name:argon_density) and the argon-specific realization of [density at magnetic axis](name:density_at_magnetic_axis). It is a local value, distinct from a radially varying argon-density field, [argon density at the plasma boundary](name:flux_surface_averaged_argon_density_at_plasma_boundary), and [volume-averaged argon density](name:volume_averaged_argon_density). It contributes to [ion density at the magnetic axis](name:ion_density_at_magnetic_axis) through the argon term in the ion-population sum.
