NAMES.name: beryllium_density_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: beryllium
NAMES.short: Number density of beryllium ions at the magnetic axis, the innermost point of the confined plasma where the gradient of the poloidal magnetic flux vanishes, summed over all beryllium ionization states.
NAMES.long:
Beryllium ($Z = 4$) density at the magnetic axis is the local number density of beryllium ions at the innermost flux-surface singular point of the confined plasma, where $\nabla\psi = 0$ with $\psi$ denoting the poloidal magnetic flux, at position $(R_\mathrm{axis}, Z_\mathrm{axis})$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. This is the beryllium-specific realization of [density_at_magnetic_axis](name:density_at_magnetic_axis), summed over all ionization stages from $\mathrm{Be}^{1+}$ to the fully stripped $\mathrm{Be}^{4+}$.

$$
n_\mathrm{Be} = \sum_{k=1}^{4} n_{\mathrm{Be}^{k+}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{Be}^{k+}}$ is the number density of beryllium ions in ionization stage $k$. In the hot plasma core beryllium is nearly fully stripped, so the sum is dominated by $\mathrm{Be}^{4+}$.

Beryllium is a low-$Z$ metallic impurity that enters the confined plasma primarily through sputtering or erosion of beryllium plasma-facing components. The on-axis density is inferred from charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy or passive emission line analysis; transport modeling constrained by line-integrated measurements can also provide radial profiles from which the axis value is extracted. The profile counterpart at arbitrary radial positions is [beryllium_density](name:beryllium_density); locus-specific values at the pedestal or separatrix are given by [beryllium_density_at_pedestal_top](name:beryllium_density_at_pedestal_top) and [beryllium_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:flux_surface_averaged_beryllium_density_at_plasma_boundary).

NAMES.name: boron_density_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: boron
NAMES.short: Number density of boron ions at the magnetic axis, the innermost point of the confined plasma where the gradient of the poloidal magnetic flux vanishes.
NAMES.long:
Boron (B, atomic number $Z = 5$) is a low-$Z$ impurity introduced into fusion plasmas through boronization of first-wall surfaces or erosion of boron-containing plasma-facing materials. This quantity gives the local particle number density of boron ions, summed over all ionization states ($\mathrm{B}^{1+}$ through $\mathrm{B}^{5+}$), as the boron-specific realization of [density_at_magnetic_axis](name:density_at_magnetic_axis).

The magnetic axis is located at coordinates $(R_\mathrm{axis}, Z_\mathrm{axis})$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, at the singular innermost point of the nested closed flux surfaces where $\nabla\psi = 0$ and $\psi$ is the poloidal magnetic flux. In the hot plasma core, fully stripped boron $\mathrm{B}^{5+}$ dominates the ionization balance, so the charge-state-summed density closely approximates the $\mathrm{B}^{5+}$ concentration; together with [ion_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:ion_density_at_magnetic_axis), it contributes to the central effective ionic charge $Z_\mathrm{eff}$.

The on-axis boron density is inferred from charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy of boron line emission or from impurity transport modeling constrained by soft X-ray brightness profiles. Comparison with the edge value [boron_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:flux_surface_averaged_boron_density_at_plasma_boundary) characterizes the radial peaking of the boron impurity profile, which is sensitive to neoclassical inward convection and turbulent diffusion in the core. Related impurity on-axis densities follow the same definition pattern, including [nitrogen_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:nitrogen_density_at_magnetic_axis) and [neon_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:neon_density_at_magnetic_axis).

NAMES.name: carbon_density_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: carbon
NAMES.short: Number density of carbon ions at the magnetic axis, the innermost point of the confined plasma where the gradient of the poloidal magnetic flux vanishes, summed over all carbon ionization states.
NAMES.long:
Carbon density at the magnetic axis is the local number density of carbon impurity ions at the innermost point of the nested closed flux surfaces, summed over all ionization states. This is the carbon-specific realization of [density_at_magnetic_axis](name:density_at_magnetic_axis), evaluated at the point $(R_\mathrm{axis}, Z_\mathrm{axis})$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame where the poloidal magnetic flux $\psi$ satisfies $\nabla\psi = 0$.

The defining relation aggregates contributions from each carbon charge state:

$$
n_\mathrm{C} = \sum_{j=1}^{6} n_{\mathrm{C}^{j+}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{C}^{j+}}$ is the number density of carbon ions in ionization state $j$, and $j$ runs from 1 to 6 (the atomic number of carbon, with fully stripped $\mathrm{C}^{6+}$ dominating in the hot core).

Carbon ($Z = 6$) enters confined plasmas primarily through physical and chemical sputtering of graphite or carbon-fiber composite plasma-facing components. On-axis values are inferred from charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy combined with radial profile fitting, or from soft X-ray emission tomography calibrated against spectroscopic charge-state distributions.

In ohmically or NBI-heated tokamaks, the central carbon fraction $n_\mathrm{C}/n_e$ spans $10^{-3}$–$10^{-2}$; for core electron densities of order $10^{19}$–$10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$, on-axis carbon densities fall in the range $10^{16}$–$10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$. The total [ion_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:ion_density_at_magnetic_axis) includes contributions from carbon alongside all other ion species, while [boron_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:boron_density_at_magnetic_axis) and [argon_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:argon_density_at_magnetic_axis) are analogous siblings for other impurity species.

NAMES.name: deposited_power
NAMES.short: Volume-integrated net power transferred to a specified plasma particle population by a source or sink, with positive values denoting energy gain by that population.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the net energy-transfer rate to a specified plasma particle population from a specified source or sink, integrated over the confined plasma volume. It may represent either deposition into the population or removal from it.

$$
P_{\mathrm{dep}} = \int_V p_{\mathrm{dep}}(\mathbf{x})\,\mathrm{d}V
$$

where $P_{\mathrm{dep}}$ is the integrated power, $p_{\mathrm{dep}}(\mathbf{x})$ is the local net power-transfer density at position $\mathbf{x}$, and $V$ is the integration volume. A positive value denotes net energy gain by the population, while a negative value denotes net energy loss. The [electron deposited power](name:electron_deposited_power) quantity is the electron-population instance of this general definition; collisional contributions are represented by [power due to collisions](name:power_due_to_collisions) or, for a fast-particle channel, [particle power due to collisions](name:particle_power_due_to_collisions).

sources.enhanced_context: Total power of a volume-integrated source or sink in Fokker-Planck modelling of the particle distribution function. Represents the net energy input rate from a wave or particle source process acting on the distribution.

NAMES.name: deposited_power_density_due_to_fast_particle_source
NAMES.short: Local volumetric energy-source term from injection or production of fast particles, representing energy deposited into the relevant particle-energy balance.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the energy deposited per unit volume by a fast-particle source, such as fast-particle injection or production. It represents an energy source for the relevant particle population rather than a particle-number source rate.

The defining relation is

$$
S_E = dP_s/dV
$$

where $P_s$ is source-associated deposited power in watts, $V$ is volume in cubic meters, and $S_E$ is the resulting energy-source density in watts per cubic meter.

Positive values denote energy added to the relevant particle-energy balance. The beneficiary population and fast-particle species are determined by the source definition; this quantity does not by itself imply deposition into thermal particles. Energy transferred from fast particles to thermal particles by collisions is represented separately by [thermal particle power density due to thermalization](name:thermal_particle_power_density_due_to_thermalization).

sources.enhanced_context: Volumetric energy source term for the energy transport equation from a particle distribution source (e.g., NBI, fusion reactions), given as a 1D radial profile. Represents the energy deposition rate per unit volume from the specified source in kinetic modelling.
sources.leaf_definition: Source term for the energy transport equation
sources.parent_definition: Source radial profiles (flux surface averaged quantities) for various time slices

sources.enhanced_context: Flux-surface-averaged source rate of energy density contributed by a specific wave or particle process to the distribution function. Represents power deposition per unit volume entering the kinetic (Fokker-Planck) equation.
sources.leaf_definition: Source rate of energy density

NAMES.name: deuterium_density_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: deuterium
NAMES.short: Number density of deuterium ions at the radial location of the internal transport barrier, where suppressed turbulent cross-field transport enables steep fuel-species density gradients to develop.
NAMES.long:
Deuterium density at the internal transport barrier is the local number density of deuterium ions on the flux surface assigned as the barrier reference location. Deuterium ($^2$H, mass number $A = 2$) is the heavier hydrogen isotope used as primary fuel in magnetic-confinement fusion and is fully ionized to D$^+$ in the hot plasma core, requiring no summation over charge states.

An internal transport barrier is a radially localized region of reduced cross-field turbulent transport within the confined plasma, enabling steep radial gradients in particle density and temperature to be sustained. The deuterium density at the barrier is the point value of the local number density $n_D(\rho)$ evaluated at the normalized minor radius $\rho_\mathrm{ITB}$ of the barrier:

$$
n_D^\mathrm{ITB} = n_D(\rho_\mathrm{ITB})
$$

where $\rho_\mathrm{ITB}$ is identified by the location of the maximum logarithmic gradient in the density or temperature profile.

This quantity is inferred from main-ion charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, or derived from transport analysis constrained by Thomson scattering and interferometry, with the steep gradients at the ITB making precise radial localization critical. It is the deuterium-isotope counterpart to [hydrogen_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:hydrogen_density_at_internal_transport_barrier); together they represent the two lightest hydrogenic fuel species. The full family of species-specific barrier densities is described by [density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:density_at_internal_transport_barrier), and [electron_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:electron_density_at_internal_transport_barrier) provides the quasi-neutral electron counterpart.

NAMES.name: deuterium_density_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: deuterium
NAMES.short: Particle number density of deuterium ions evaluated at the magnetic axis, summed over all deuterium ionic charge states.
NAMES.long:
Particle number density of deuterium ions evaluated at the magnetic axis is the local deuterium-ion count per physical volume at the innermost point of nested closed poloidal magnetic-flux surfaces, summed over all deuterium ionic charge states. The magnetic axis is the locus where the gradient of poloidal magnetic flux vanishes.

The on-axis density is defined by the limiting value of the local deuterium-ion density field:

$$
n_{\mathrm{D}}^{\mathrm{axis}} = \lim_{\mathbf{x}\to\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{axis}}} \sum_{q\in\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{D}}} n_{\mathrm{D},q}(\mathbf{x})
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{D},q}(\mathbf{x})$ is the local number density of deuterium ions in charge state $q$, $\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{D}}$ is the set of deuterium ionic charge states included in the aggregation, $\mathbf{x}$ is position, and $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{axis}}$ is the magnetic-axis position.

This isotope-specific quantity is a specialization of [density_at_magnetic_axis](name:density_at_magnetic_axis) and the selected-ion quantity [ion_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:ion_density_at_magnetic_axis). It excludes neutral deuterium and is distinct from [helium_4_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:helium_4_density_at_magnetic_axis), which applies to helium-4 ions.

NAMES.name: deuterium_tritium_density
NAMES.subject: deuterium_tritium
NAMES.short: Deuterium-tritium density is the local ion number density of the deuterium-tritium fuel-ion pseudo-species, treating deuterium and tritium as one effective species.
NAMES.long:
Deuterium-tritium density is the local ion number density of the deuterium-tritium fuel-ion pseudo-species, treating deuterium and tritium ions as one effective species. It is a species-level per-volume particle count summed over all ion charge states.

The defining relation is the sum of the component fuel-ion number densities:

$$
n_{DT} = n_D + n_T
$$

where $n_{DT}$ is the deuterium-tritium density, $n_D$ is the [deuterium density](name:deuterium_density), and $n_T$ is the [tritium density](name:tritium_density). Each component density is charge-state-summed over the corresponding ion charge states; the dimensionless tritium fraction, where used, is $f_T = n_T/n_{DT}$.

This quantity includes only deuterium and tritium fuel ions represented by the effective deuterium-tritium species. Neutral deuterium or tritium atoms, neutral molecules such as D$_2$, T$_2$, and DT, reaction products, and impurity ions are excluded. As a number density, its value domain is $n_{DT} \ge 0$.

NAMES.name: deuterium_tritium_density_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: deuterium_tritium
NAMES.short: Particle number density of the combined deuterium-tritium fuel-ion pseudo-species evaluated on the flux surface assigned to an internal transport barrier, where locally reduced cross-field turbulent transport can sustain steep fuel-density gradients; deuterium and tritium ions are treated as one effective population.
NAMES.long:
Particle number density of the combined deuterium-tritium fuel-ion pseudo-species at the internal transport barrier is the local number density of deuterium and tritium fuel ions treated as one effective population on the flux surface selected as the barrier reference location. The internal transport barrier is a confined-plasma flux-surface location where locally reduced cross-field turbulent transport permits steep fuel-density gradients across neighboring flux surfaces.

The combined density is defined as the sum of the isotope ion densities at the barrier flux surface:

$$
n_{\mathrm{DT,ITB}} = n_{\mathrm{D,ITB}} + n_{\mathrm{T,ITB}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{DT,ITB}}$ is the deuterium-tritium pseudo-species density at the internal transport barrier, and $n_{\mathrm{D,ITB}}$ and $n_{\mathrm{T,ITB}}$ are the deuterium and tritium ion densities at the same barrier flux surface. This species-level number density is summed over all charge states of deuterium and tritium ions and excludes neutral deuterium and tritium atoms.

The deuterium-tritium pseudo-species denotes a fuel-state quantity, not a fusion reaction rate or reaction-product population. If represented by mean mass number $A = 2.5$, it corresponds to an equal deuterium-tritium number-density mixture; for unequal isotope mixtures the density remains the isotope sum, while the effective mass number is composition-weighted. It is distinct from the isotope-resolved [deuterium density at the internal transport barrier](name:deuterium_density_at_internal_transport_barrier) and [tritium density at the internal transport barrier](name:tritium_density_at_internal_transport_barrier), and from spatially aggregated deuterium-tritium quantities such as [volume-averaged deuterium-tritium density](name:volume_averaged_deuterium_tritium_density).

NAMES.name: deuterium_tritium_density_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: deuterium_tritium
NAMES.short: Particle number density of the deuterium-tritium fuel pseudo-species evaluated at the magnetic axis, treating the mixture as one ion population and summing over all ionic charge states of both isotopes.
NAMES.long:
Particle number density of the deuterium-tritium fuel pseudo-species evaluated at the magnetic axis is the local deuterium-tritium ion count per physical volume at the innermost point of nested closed poloidal magnetic-flux surfaces, summed over all ionic charge states of both isotopes. The magnetic axis is the locus where the gradient of poloidal magnetic flux vanishes.

The on-axis density is defined by the limiting value of the local deuterium-tritium ion density field:

$$
n_{\mathrm{DT}}^{\mathrm{axis}} = \lim_{\mathbf{x}\to\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{axis}}} \sum_{s\in\{\mathrm{D},\mathrm{T}\}}\sum_{q\in\mathcal{Q}_s} n_{s,q}(\mathbf{x})
$$

where $n_{s,q}(\mathbf{x})$ is the local number density of isotope $s$ in ionic charge state $q$, $\mathcal{Q}_s$ is the set of included ionic charge states for isotope $s$, $\mathbf{x}$ is position, and $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{axis}}$ is the magnetic-axis position.

This fuel-mixture quantity is a specialization of [density_at_magnetic_axis](name:density_at_magnetic_axis), treats deuterium–tritium as one effective ion population rather than a fusion-reaction channel, and excludes neutral atoms. It is distinct from the local [deuterium_tritium_density](name:deuterium_tritium_density) and the volume-averaged [volume_averaged_deuterium_tritium_density](name:volume_averaged_deuterium_tritium_density).

NAMES.name: diamagnetic_current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity
NAMES.short: Diamagnetic current density due to parallel viscosity is the signed projection onto the local diamagnetic direction of the current-density contribution generated by field-aligned viscous stress. The diamagnetic direction is defined by the magnetic field and plasma-pressure gradient.
NAMES.long:
Diamagnetic current density due to parallel viscosity is the component along the local diamagnetic direction of the current-density contribution associated with the field-aligned part of the plasma viscous stress tensor. The diamagnetic direction is the unit direction of $\mathbf{B}\times\nabla p$, where $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field and $p$ is the plasma pressure.

The defining projection is:

$$
j_{\Pi_\parallel,\mathrm{dia}} = \hat{\mathbf{e}}_{\mathrm{dia}}\cdot\frac{\mathbf{B}\times(\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol{\Pi}_\parallel)}{B^2},\qquad \hat{\mathbf{e}}_{\mathrm{dia}} = \frac{\mathbf{B}\times\nabla p}{|\mathbf{B}\times\nabla p|}
$$

where $j_{\Pi_\parallel,\mathrm{dia}}$ is the diamagnetic current-density component due to parallel viscosity, $\boldsymbol{\Pi}_\parallel$ is the parallel viscous stress tensor, $\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol{\Pi}_\parallel$ is the associated viscous force density, $B=|\mathbf{B}|$, and $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{\mathrm{dia}}$ is defined where $|\mathbf{B}\times\nabla p|$ is nonzero.

This quantity is the diamagnetic projection of [current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity](name:current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity). It excludes diamagnetic projections of currents due to perpendicular viscous stress or heat-viscosity effects, which are represented by [diamagnetic_current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity](name:diamagnetic_current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity) and [diamagnetic_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity](name:diamagnetic_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the parallel-viscosity-driven current density has a component in the direction of $\mathbf{B}\times\nabla p$.

NAMES.name: diamagnetic_current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity
NAMES.short: Diamagnetic component of the current density generated by perpendicular viscous stress in a magnetized plasma, projected along the local diamagnetic direction.
NAMES.long:
The diamagnetic current density due to perpendicular viscosity is the signed projection of the electric-current contribution generated by the divergence of perpendicular viscous stress onto the local diamagnetic direction. The perpendicular-viscosity mechanism does not require the resulting current vector to be perpendicular to the magnetic field.

The component is defined by

$$
J_{\mathrm{dia},\perp,\nu}=\mathbf{J}_{\perp,\nu}\cdot\hat{\mathbf e}_{\mathrm{dia}}
$$

where $J_{\mathrm{dia},\perp,\nu}$ is this scalar component, $\mathbf{J}_{\perp,\nu}$ is the vector [current density due to perpendicular viscosity](name:current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity), and $\hat{\mathbf e}_{\mathrm{dia}}$ is the local diamagnetic unit vector. The unit vector is oriented along $\mathbf{B}\times\nabla p$, where $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic-field vector, $p$ is plasma pressure, and $\nabla p$ is its spatial gradient, when this cross product is nonzero. This quantity is distinct from the [diamagnetic current density due to parallel viscosity](name:diamagnetic_current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the projected current points along $\hat{\mathbf e}_{\mathrm{dia}}$, oriented with $\mathbf{B}\times\nabla p$.

NAMES.name: diamagnetic_energy
NAMES.short: Volume-integrated plasma energy associated with pressure perpendicular to the local magnetic field, including thermal and fast-particle populations while excluding electromagnetic and bulk-flow energy.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the plasma stored energy associated with the total pressure perpendicular to the local magnetic field. It includes thermal and fast-particle populations and excludes electromagnetic-field energy and bulk-flow kinetic energy.

The diamagnetic stored energy is defined by

$$
W_{\mathrm{dia}} = \frac{3}{2}\int_V p_\perp\,dV
$$

where $W_{\mathrm{dia}}$ is the diamagnetic stored energy, $p_\perp$ is the total plasma pressure perpendicular to the local magnetic-field direction, and $V$ is the plasma volume over which the energy is evaluated.

This quantity is distinct from [thermal plasma energy](name:thermal_plasma_energy), which excludes fast-particle contributions, and from [total plasma energy](name:total_plasma_energy), whose pressure scope is defined by the corresponding total internal-energy convention. Its time rate of change is represented by [tendency of diamagnetic energy](name:tendency_of_diamagnetic_energy).

NAMES.name: effective_charge_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.short: Effective charge Zeff of the plasma ion mixture evaluated at the internal transport barrier, defined as the charge-squared-weighted mean charge number over all ion species.
NAMES.long:
The effective charge $Z_\text{eff}$ characterizes the ionic composition of a magnetically confined plasma by weighting each ion species by the square of its charge number relative to the first charge moment, yielding a single dimensionless index of impurity content.

The defining relation is

$$
Z_\text{eff} = \frac{\sum_s n_s Z_s^2}{\sum_s n_s Z_s}
$$

where $n_s$ is the number density of ion species $s$ (summed over all charge states) and $Z_s$ is its charge number. A pure single-species hydrogenic plasma gives $Z_\text{eff} = 1$; the presence of higher-$Z$ impurities always raises $Z_\text{eff}$ above unity.

Evaluated at the internal transport barrier (ITB), this quantity captures the local effective charge where turbulent transport is suppressed and kinetic profile gradients are steep — the same reference location used by [electron density at the ITB](name:electron_density_at_internal_transport_barrier) and [electron temperature at the ITB](name:electron_temperature_at_internal_transport_barrier). Local impurity accumulation or expulsion near the ITB can shift the local $Z_\text{eff}$ considerably from its volume-averaged value.

The effective charge is inferred spectroscopically from the free-free bremsstrahlung continuum, whose radiated intensity scales as $n_e^2 Z_\text{eff} T_e^{-1/2}$ where $n_e$ is the electron number density and $T_e$ is the electron temperature, or from charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy summed over resolved ion species. In clean deuterium discharges $Z_\text{eff}$ approaches 1.0, rising to 3–5 in high-impurity or metallic-wall scenarios.
NAMES.sign: Positive when any ionized species populate the plasma, which is always the case in a magnetically confined discharge; the lower bound $Z_\text{eff} = 1$ is attained only for a hypothetically impurity-free single-species plasma.

NAMES.name: effective_charge_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.short: Effective charge at the magnetic axis is the local charge-squared-weighted ion charge sum divided by the electron density, evaluated at the magnetic axis. It equals 1 for a plasma containing only singly charged hydrogen-isotope ions and increases with impurity charge content.
NAMES.long:
Effective charge at the magnetic axis is the local charge-squared-weighted ion charge sum divided by the electron density, evaluated at the magnetic axis. It is the on-axis value of [effective charge](name:effective_charge). It equals unity for a plasma containing only singly charged hydrogen-isotope ions, and higher-charge impurity ions contribute disproportionately because the charge number is squared.

For a local ion mixture, the on-axis effective charge is defined by:

$$
Z_{\mathrm{eff,axis}} = \frac{\sum_s n_s(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{axis}}) Z_s^2}{n_e(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{axis}})}
$$

where $s$ indexes ion species or ionization states present at the magnetic-axis location, $n_s$ is the corresponding ion number density in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, $Z_s$ is the positive ion charge number, $n_e$ is the electron number density in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, and $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{axis}}$ denotes the magnetic-axis location.

The sum includes charged ions and excludes neutral atoms, neutral molecules, and electrons. For a locally quasineutral plasma, $n_e = \sum_s n_s Z_s$, so the same quantity may be interpreted as the ion-density-weighted ratio $\langle Z^2 \rangle / \langle Z \rangle$. This locus-specific value is distinct from [effective charge at the plasma boundary](name:effective_charge_at_plasma_boundary).

NAMES.name: effective_neutral_internal_state_energy_diffusivity
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Effective neutral internal-state energy diffusivity is the scalar coefficient for diffusive thermal-energy transport by neutral particles in a specified internal state. It is the direction-independent temperature-gradient coefficient used in a Fickian energy-flux closure.
NAMES.long:
Effective neutral internal-state energy diffusivity is the scalar transport coefficient for the diffusive thermal-energy flux carried by neutral particles of a specified species and internal state. It represents the direction-independent Fickian response to the local temperature gradient of that neutral-state population.

In a scalar effective closure for the conductive part of the energy flux, the defining relation is:

$$
\mathbf{q}^{\mathrm{diff}}_{E,a,s} = - n_{a,s}\,\chi^{\mathrm{eff}}_{E,a,s}\,\nabla T_{a,s}
$$

where $\mathbf{q}^{\mathrm{diff}}_{E,a,s}$ is the diffusive thermal-energy flux carried by neutral species $a$ in internal state $s$, $n_{a,s}$ is the [neutral internal-state number density](name:neutral_internal_state_number_density), $\chi^{\mathrm{eff}}_{E,a,s}$ is the effective neutral internal-state energy diffusivity, and $T_{a,s}$ is the [neutral internal-state temperature](name:neutral_internal_state_temperature). The minus sign denotes down-gradient diffusive transport in this closure.

This is a scalar effective coefficient, not the full anisotropic diffusivity. In an anisotropic formulation a second-rank tensor $\boldsymbol{\chi}_{E,a,s}$ maps $\nabla T_{a,s}$ to $\mathbf{q}^{\mathrm{diff}}_{E,a,s}$; this quantity is the direction-independent value used in place of that tensor, such as through $\boldsymbol{\chi}_{E,a,s}=\chi^{\mathrm{eff}}_{E,a,s}\mathbf{I}$ or another specified scalar contraction. A projection along a particular direction vector, $\hat{\mathbf{e}}\cdot\boldsymbol{\chi}_{E,a,s}\hat{\mathbf{e}}$, is a directional component and is not this quantity unless it is explicitly adopted as the scalar effective representation.

It includes only the energy flux represented by the temperature-gradient term; convective energy transport associated with neutral particle flow and local source or loss terms are excluded. It is the effective scalar counterpart of [neutral internal-state energy diffusion coefficient](name:neutral_internal_state_energy_diffusion_coefficient) and is distinct from [neutral internal-state heat diffusivity](name:neutral_internal_state_heat_diffusivity), which denotes the heat-diffusion coefficient for the same neutral-state population when the heat channel is specified separately from the energy channel.

NAMES.name: effective_neutral_internal_state_velocity_due_to_convection
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Effective advective drift velocity of neutral particles in a specified internal state due to convective transport, representing the full vector quantity of which spatial projections such as the radial component are instances.
NAMES.long:
The effective convective velocity of a neutral internal state is the distribution-function-weighted advective drift velocity responsible for particle-number transport of neutrals occupying a specified internal quantum state (such as an electronic excitation level, vibrational level, or rotational state). It differs from the bare [neutral_internal_state_velocity_due_to_convection](name:neutral_internal_state_velocity_due_to_convection) in that the effective form incorporates weighting corrections needed to close the neutral transport equations at the internal-state level, yielding a single representative drift per state rather than a simple fluid velocity.

As a vector, its components resolve the convective flux along each spatial direction; the radial projection is given by [radial_effective_neutral_internal_state_velocity_due_to_convection](name:radial_effective_neutral_internal_state_velocity_due_to_convection). It is distinct from [effective_neutral_internal_state_momentum_velocity_due_to_convection](name:effective_neutral_internal_state_momentum_velocity_due_to_convection), which is weighted by momentum density rather than particle number density and governs momentum rather than particle-number convection.

NAMES.name: effective_neutral_internal_state_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Effective fluid velocity of a neutral species in a specific internal quantum state attributable to the diamagnetic drift in the edge plasma, driven by the pressure gradient of the internal-state population perpendicular to the magnetic field.
NAMES.long:
The effective neutral internal-state diamagnetic drift velocity is the fluid-level velocity of a neutral species population occupying a defined internal quantum state (such as a vibrational, rotational, or electronic excitation level) that arises from the diamagnetic mechanism in the magnetized edge plasma. Analogous to the [bulk plasma diamagnetic drift velocity](name:bulk_plasma_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift) but restricted to a single neutral internal-state population, this contribution is part of the E×B drift family in drift-fluid edge transport models and is directed perpendicular to both the pressure gradient $\nabla p_s$ and the magnetic field $\mathbf{B}$, where $p_s$ is the partial pressure of the neutral internal state and $B = |\mathbf{B}|$.

Unlike the diamagnetic drift for charged species, which follows from single-particle guiding-center theory, the effective neutral variant arises through fluid-model pressure-gradient terms and collisional coupling to the charged-particle components rather than from direct electromagnetic forcing. The [parallel component](name:parallel_effective_neutral_internal_state_velocity_due_to_diamagnetic_drift) gives this velocity projected along the local magnetic field direction $\hat{\mathbf{b}} = \mathbf{B}/B$.

NAMES.name: effective_thermal_ion_charge_state_energy_velocity_due_to_convection
NAMES.subject: ion_charge_state
NAMES.short: Effective velocity vector for convective transport of thermal energy by a specified ion charge-state population.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the effective vector velocity associated with convective transport of thermal energy by a specified thermal ion charge-state population. It retains transport direction rather than selecting a particular spatial projection.

The effective velocity is defined through the convective thermal-energy flux:

$$
\mathbf{Q}_{s,\mathrm{conv}} = w_{s,\mathrm{th}}\,\mathbf{v}_{s,\mathrm{eff,conv}}
$$

where $\mathbf{Q}_{s,\mathrm{conv}}$ is the convective thermal-energy flux, $w_{s,\mathrm{th}}$ is the thermal-energy density of the population, and $\mathbf{v}_{s,\mathrm{eff,conv}}$ is this effective velocity. The quantity is the thermal specialization of [ion charge-state energy velocity due to convection](name:ion_charge_state_energy_velocity_due_to_convection) and provides the parent context for the [radial effective thermal ion charge-state energy velocity due to convection](name:radial_effective_thermal_ion_charge_state_energy_velocity_due_to_convection). It excludes diffusive and conductive energy transport contributions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when a component points along the corresponding positive direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ basis.

NAMES.name: electric_field
NAMES.short: Local vector electric field equal to the force per unit charge on a positive stationary test charge, including electrostatic, inductive, and electromagnetic-wave contributions.
NAMES.long:
The electric field $\mathbf{E}$ is the local force per unit positive charge on a stationary test charge. It is the complete vector quantity from which projections such as the [vertical electric field](name:vertical_electric_field) and field-parallel electric field are formed.

In terms of electromagnetic potentials, the field is defined by

$$
\mathbf{E} = -\nabla\Phi - \frac{\partial\mathbf{A}}{\partial t}
$$

where $\Phi$ is the electrostatic potential, $\mathbf{A}$ is the magnetic vector potential, and $t$ is time. The first term is electrostatic and the second is inductive; their sum also describes wave fields, including the [wave electric field](name:wave_electric_field). The electrostatic contribution is related to the [electrostatic potential](name:electrostatic_potential). Cylindrical projections use the right-handed $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is increasing toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.
NAMES.sign: Positive when a resolved cylindrical component points toward increasing $R$, $\phi$, or $Z$, or when a field-parallel component points along the local magnetic field.

NAMES.name: critical_electric_field
NAMES.short: Electric-field threshold giving the force-per-charge level at which collisional drag is overcome and charged particles enter sustained runaway acceleration.
NAMES.long:
The critical electric field is the threshold field strength at which electric acceleration reaches the collisional-drag limit separating drag-dominated motion from runaway acceleration. It is a derived scalar threshold associated with the [electric field](name:electric_field), not a vector component or an independently defined local field.

At threshold, the electric force balances collisional drag at the boundary between the two regimes:

$$
|q|E_{\mathrm{crit}} = F_{\mathrm{coll}}(v_{\mathrm{crit}})
$$

where $q$ is the particle charge in C, $E_{\mathrm{crit}}$ is the critical field in V m$^{-1}$, $F_{\mathrm{coll}}$ is the collisional drag force in N, and $v_{\mathrm{crit}}$ is the boundary particle speed in m s$^{-1}$.

The threshold depends on the particle population, collision model, and acceleration direction. The [runaway-electron critical electric field](name:runaway_electron_critical_electric_field) is its parallel-field specialization, while [runaway-electron critical electric-field magnitude](name:runaway_electron_critical_electric_field_magnitude) represents the corresponding nonnegative magnitude.

NAMES.name: electron_collisionality
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Electron collisionality is an electron-specific collisionality parameter comparing an electron collision frequency with a characteristic electron transit, bounce, or orbital frequency, including any defined geometric normalization.
NAMES.long:
Electron collisionality is the electron-specific collisionality parameter that measures electron Coulomb collision rates relative to a characteristic electron orbital motion. It denotes the collisionality of the electron population, not a species-neutral, ion, or impurity collisionality.

A generic electron-collisionality definition has the form:

$$
C_e = N_e\,\frac{\nu_e}{\omega_e}
$$

where $C_e$ is the electron collisionality, $\nu_e$ is the electron collision frequency specified by the definition, $\omega_e$ is the characteristic electron transit, bounce, or orbital frequency used as the comparator, and $N_e$ is the specified geometric normalization factor.

This parent covers electron collisionality definitions with or without additional normalization factors. The [normalized electron collisionality](name:normalized_electron_collisionality) is a more specific member that fixes a neoclassical normalization, while [normalized collisionality](name:normalized_collisionality) does not by itself impose the electron-specific scope.

NAMES.name: electron_density_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Particle number density of electrons evaluated on the flux surface assigned to an internal transport barrier, where reduced cross-field turbulent transport can sustain steep electron-density gradients.
NAMES.long:
Particle number density of electrons evaluated on the flux surface assigned to an internal transport barrier is the local density of the electron population at that flux-surface location. Electrons are counted directly as mobile negative charge carriers; no ion charge-state aggregation is involved.

The number density is defined by

$$
n_e = \lim_{\Delta V\to 0}\frac{\Delta N_e}{\Delta V}
$$

where $n_e$ is the electron number density in m$^{-3}$, $\Delta N_e$ is the dimensionless number of electrons in the volume element, and $\Delta V$ is the volume element in m$^{3}$.

This is the electron-specific member of [density at the internal transport barrier](name:density_at_internal_transport_barrier). It is distinct from [ion density at the internal transport barrier](name:ion_density_at_internal_transport_barrier), which counts ions rather than electrons; in a quasineutral plasma the electron density is related to ion charge densities at the same flux surface by charge balance. The internal transport barrier is the designated flux-surface location where reduced cross-field turbulent transport permits steep density gradients.

NAMES.name: electron_density_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Particle number density of the electron population evaluated at the magnetic axis is the local electron count per physical volume at the innermost point of nested closed poloidal magnetic-flux surfaces.
NAMES.long:
Particle number density of the electron population evaluated at the magnetic axis is the local electron count per physical volume at the innermost point of nested closed poloidal magnetic-flux surfaces. The magnetic axis is the locus where the gradient of poloidal magnetic flux vanishes.

The on-axis electron density is defined by the limiting value of the local density field:

$$
n_e^{\mathrm{axis}} = \lim_{\mathbf{x}\to\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{axis}}} n_e(\mathbf{x})
$$

where $n_e(\mathbf{x})$ is the electron number-density field, $\mathbf{x}$ is position, and $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{axis}}$ is the magnetic-axis position.

This is the electron-specific realization of [density_at_magnetic_axis](name:density_at_magnetic_axis). It counts free electrons directly and is not summed over ionic charge states or combined with ion populations; [ion_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:ion_density_at_magnetic_axis) describes the corresponding ion population.

NAMES.name: electron_deposited_power
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Volume-integrated net power transferred to the electron population by a specified plasma source or sink, including electron heating and energy removal.
NAMES.long:
The electron deposited power is the net energy-transfer rate to the electron population, integrated over the confined plasma volume. It is the electron-specific component of [deposited power](name:deposited_power), rather than a local power density.

For local net deposited-power density $p_{e,\mathrm{dep}}(\mathbf{x})$, the integrated power is defined by

$$
P_{e,\mathrm{dep}} = \int_V p_{e,\mathrm{dep}}(\mathbf{x})\,d^3\mathbf{x}
$$

where $P_{e,\mathrm{dep}}$ is the electron deposited power, $V$ is the confined plasma volume, and $\mathbf{x}$ is position.

The specified source or sink may represent auxiliary heating, fusion reactions, ohmic dissipation, ionization, or another plasma energy-transfer channel. Unlike [electron absorbed wave power](name:electron_absorbed_wave_power), this quantity is not restricted to coherent-wave absorption; [total ion power](name:total_ion_power) applies the analogous definition to ions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when net energy is transferred into the electron population.

NAMES.name: electron_diffusion_coefficient
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Fickian diffusion coefficient for electron particle transport, relating the diffusive electron flux to the local electron density gradient in magnetized plasma transport models.
NAMES.long:
The electron diffusion coefficient $D_e$ characterizes irreversible diffusive transport of the electron particle population, entering the Fickian constitutive relation between the electron particle flux and the local electron density gradient. This is specifically a particle transport quantity — distinct from electron energy transport, which is captured by a separate energy diffusion coefficient such as [poloidal_electron_energy_diffusion_coefficient](name:poloidal_electron_energy_diffusion_coefficient).

In the Fick-law formulation, the diffusive electron particle flux density satisfies:

$$
\mathbf{J}_e^{\rm diff} = -D_e \nabla n_e
$$

where $n_e$ is the electron number density. In magnetized plasmas, the strong transport anisotropy between cross-field and along-field directions means directional components are resolved independently: the radial component describes transport across magnetic flux surfaces while the [poloidal_electron_diffusion_coefficient](name:poloidal_electron_diffusion_coefficient) describes transport along the poloidal direction.

The coefficient is specified within edge plasma fluid transport models on general geometry grids. Anomalous (turbulence-driven) cross-field values in the edge region range from 0.1–10 m² s⁻¹ in present-day tokamaks, substantially exceeding neoclassical particle diffusion. The companion convective transport channel is characterized by the [electron_particle_flux](name:electron_particle_flux).

NAMES.name: electron_diffusivity
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Directional electron particle diffusion coefficient linking the diffusive electron flux to the electron density gradient in a magnetized plasma.
NAMES.long:
Electron particle diffusivity is the effective transport coefficient governing the diffusive part of electron number transport, with direction-specific entries for anisotropic magnetized-plasma transport.

The constitutive relation is

$$
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_e^{\mathrm{diff}} = -\mathbf{D}_e \cdot \nabla n_e
$$

where $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_e^{\mathrm{diff}}$ is the diffusive electron particle-flux vector, $\mathbf{D}_e$ is the electron diffusivity tensor, $n_e$ is electron number density, and $\nabla n_e$ is its spatial gradient. The minus sign denotes transport down the density gradient.

This parent quantity includes directional forms such as [parallel electron diffusivity](name:parallel_electron_diffusivity) and [poloidal electron diffusivity](name:poloidal_electron_diffusivity). It describes diffusive transport only and excludes convective fluxes, particle sources, and sinks. The corresponding unprojected Fickian quantity is [electron diffusion coefficient](name:electron_diffusion_coefficient).

NAMES.name: electron_power
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Volume-integrated rate of energy exchange involving the electron population, serving as the parent concept over thermal, fast, and total electron power channels.
NAMES.long:
The electron population power is the volume-integrated rate at which energy is transferred to or from electrons in a fusion plasma. Depending on the context in which a child quantity is defined, this exchange may include contributions from auxiliary wave or beam heating absorbed by electrons, collisional energy exchange between electrons and ions, and radiative or conductive losses — making the assignment of source channels explicit in each child name.

The defining integral is:

$$
P_e = \int_V Q_e(\mathbf{r})\, dV
$$

where $Q_e(\mathbf{r})$ is the local electron power density at position $\mathbf{r}$ and $V$ is the plasma volume over which the integration is performed.

Children of this parent discriminate by electron population: [thermal_electron_power](name:thermal_electron_absorbed_wave_power) captures only the bulk Maxwellian component absorbing wave energy, fast_electron_power resolves the suprathermal channel, and [total_electron_power](name:electron_deposited_power) aggregates both for a given source. The related electron_deposited_power names the volume-integrated deposition from a plasma source. In power-balance analysis these terms are inferred from electron temperature profile evolution combined with transport modeling.
NAMES.sign: Positive when energy flows into the electron population.

NAMES.name: electron_pressure
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Kinetic pressure associated with the electron population, defined as the isotropic second central velocity-space moment and applicable to thermal and suprathermal contributions.
NAMES.long:
Electron pressure is the isotropic kinetic part of the electron pressure tensor, representing random electron momentum transport and allowing thermal and suprathermal populations to be included under a common definition.

For an electron distribution function, its defining relation is

$$
p_e = \frac{m_e}{3} \int |\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{u}_e|^2 f_e(\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $p_e$ is electron pressure, $m_e$ is electron mass, $\mathbf{v}$ is electron velocity, $\mathbf{u}_e$ is mean electron velocity, and $f_e(\mathbf{v})$ is the electron velocity distribution function normalized so its velocity integral gives electron number density.

The quantity denotes the one-third trace of the pressure tensor; anisotropic stress components are excluded from this scalar isotropic part. Population scope may be thermal, suprathermal, or their sum, as in [fast electron pressure](name:fast_electron_pressure) and [total electron pressure](name:total_electron_pressure). A spatial derivative such as [gradient of electron pressure](name:gradient_of_electron_pressure) acts on this underlying quantity without changing its definition.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the isotropic electron stress is compressive rather than tensile.

NAMES.name: electron_source_rate
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Volume-integrated rate of net electron production or removal by specified particle sources and sinks within a plasma volume.
NAMES.long:
Electron source rate is the volume-integrated rate at which a specified electron population is created or removed by particle processes.

$$
S_e = \int_V s_e(\mathbf{x})\,dV
$$

where $S_e$ is the integrated electron source rate, $s_e(\mathbf{x})$ is the local source density at position $\mathbf{x}$, and $V$ is the specified plasma volume. Positive $s_e$ denotes net production and negative $s_e$ denotes net removal.

This parent quantity includes production-only components such as [fast electron source rate](name:fast_electron_source_rate) and aggregate net rates such as [total electron source rate](name:total_electron_source_rate). Particle-production and removal mechanisms are included according to the defined population scope; transport losses represented by the divergence of a particle flux are excluded unless explicitly treated as a source process.

NAMES.name: electron_torque_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Total collisional torque on the electron population, combining contributions from both thermal and fast electron sub-populations through Coulomb momentum exchange with other plasma constituents.
NAMES.long:
The electron collisional torque quantifies the net rate of angular momentum transferred to electrons through Coulomb collisions with ions and other plasma species in the plasma. It serves as the parent quantity spanning the [fast electron](name:fast_electron_torque_due_to_collisions) and [thermal electron](name:thermal_electron_torque_due_to_collisions) sub-populations, which differ in their velocity-distribution shape and the resulting collision-operator weighting.

The quantity enters the toroidal angular momentum balance for the electron fluid:

$$
\frac{\partial L_{e,\phi}}{\partial t} = T_{e,\mathrm{coll}} + T_{e,\mathrm{EM}} + T_{e,\nabla p}
$$

where $L_{e,\phi}$ is the electron toroidal angular momentum density integrated over the plasma volume, $T_{e,\mathrm{coll}}$ is the collisional torque, and $T_{e,\mathrm{EM}}$ and $T_{e,\nabla p}$ are the electromagnetic and pressure-gradient contributions respectively.

In transport modeling, this torque is evaluated by taking the toroidal moment of the Coulomb collision operator over the electron distribution function and integrating over the plasma volume; it couples directly to the total species-summed [torque_due_to_collisions](name:torque_due_to_collisions). The separation into fast and thermal electron contributions is physically important when suprathermal populations from electron cyclotron heating or runaway generation carry non-negligible angular momentum distinct from the bulk Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution. The related volume-integrated formulation is complemented by the [torque_density_due_to_collisions](name:torque_density_due_to_collisions) per-unit-volume counterpart.
NAMES.sign: Positive when angular momentum is transferred to electrons in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: electron_velocity
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Local bulk-flow velocity of the electron fluid, defined by the density-weighted first moment of its velocity distribution and distinct from random thermal motion.
NAMES.long:
Electron fluid velocity is the local bulk translational velocity of the electron population, describing collective advective motion rather than the random thermal motion of individual electrons.

At position $\mathbf{x}$, the velocity is defined by the first moment of the electron distribution:

$$
\mathbf{u}_e(\mathbf{x})=\frac{1}{n_e(\mathbf{x})}\int \mathbf{v}\,f_e(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\,d^3v,\qquad n_e(\mathbf{x})=\int f_e(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $\mathbf{u}_e$ is the electron fluid velocity in m s$^{-1}$, $\mathbf{x}$ is position in m, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity in m s$^{-1}$, $f_e$ is the electron velocity distribution, and $n_e$ is electron number density in m$^{-3}$.

This is the complete vector before directional projection. Its projections include [radial electron velocity](name:radial_electron_velocity), [toroidal electron velocity](name:toroidal_electron_velocity), [vertical electron velocity](name:vertical_electron_velocity), [poloidal electron velocity](name:poloidal_electron_velocity), and [parallel electron velocity](name:parallel_electron_velocity). It is distinct from the bulk velocities of ions and neutrals, such as [ion velocity](name:ion_velocity) and [neutral velocity](name:neutral_velocity).
NAMES.sign: Positive when a resolved component points along its declared positive direction—$+\hat R$, $+\hat\phi$, or $+\hat Z$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, or along the local magnetic-field direction for a parallel projection.

NAMES.name: energy_confinement_time
NAMES.short: Characteristic timescale for loss of confined plasma thermal energy, defined as stored thermal energy divided by the net power leaving that energy reservoir.
NAMES.long:
Energy confinement time is the characteristic timescale on which the confined plasma loses its stored thermal energy through net outward energy transport and other thermal-energy loss channels. The stored energy is the volume-integrated quantity defined by [thermal plasma energy](name:thermal_plasma_energy), not a particle confinement time or the duration of plasma confinement.

$$
\tau_E = \frac{W_{\mathrm{th}}}{P_{\mathrm{loss}}}
$$

where $\tau_E$ is the energy confinement time, $W_{\mathrm{th}}$ is the stored thermal energy in J, and $P_{\mathrm{loss}}$ is the net power loss from that thermal-energy reservoir in W. In a stationary power balance, $P_{\mathrm{loss}}$ equals the net heating power deposited in the plasma. It is distinct from [plasma confinement time](name:plasma_confinement_time), which denotes the elapsed duration of confinement rather than an energy-loss timescale.

NAMES.name: energy_convection_velocity
NAMES.short: Effective advection coefficient for non-diffusive thermal-energy transport, appearing as the convective velocity in the energy flux term of plasma transport equations for any plasma species or spatial projection.
NAMES.long:
The energy convection velocity is the effective advection coefficient $V_E$ that parameterizes the convective (non-diffusive) component of the energy flux in plasma transport equations. It is distinct from the bulk plasma fluid velocity: it encapsulates contributions from drift flows, turbulent heat pinch effects, and other mechanisms that advect thermal enthalpy across magnetic flux surfaces without requiring a temperature gradient.

The convective energy flux for a species is expressed as:

$$
Q_\mathrm{conv} = \tfrac{3}{2}\, n T \, V_E
$$

where $n$ is the particle number density, $T$ is the temperature expressed as an energy, and $V_E$ is the energy convection velocity. This relation defines $V_E$ operationally as the prefactor linking the observed convective heat flux to the local thermal enthalpy density $\tfrac{3}{2} n T$.

In transport analyzes, $V_E$ is inferred by decomposing the total energy flux from experimental profile measurements into diffusive and convective contributions, or it emerges directly from fluid and gyrokinetic transport models as a sum of drift and turbulent pinch velocities. Species-resolved instances include [electron_energy_convection_velocity](name:electron_energy_convection_velocity) and total_ion_energy_convection_velocity; spatial projections include the [radial_energy_convection_velocity](name:radial_energy_convection_velocity) and poloidal_energy_convection_velocity. The purely diffusive counterpart is the energy diffusion coefficient, which multiplies the negative temperature gradient in the complementary flux term.
NAMES.sign: Positive when directed outward in the direction of increasing major radius $R$ for the radial projection.

NAMES.name: energy_density
NAMES.short: Energy density is the kinetic energy per unit volume of a specified plasma particle population, including the thermal, suprathermal, relativistic, or bulk-flow content represented by its distribution.
NAMES.long:
Energy density is the kinetic energy per unit volume of a specified plasma particle population. It is a non-negative scalar phase-space moment whose population scope determines whether thermal random motion, directed bulk flow, suprathermal particles, relativistic particles, or a combination of these contributions is included.

For a momentum-space distribution function, the kinetic energy density excluding rest-mass energy is defined by the moment:

$$
\mathcal{E}(\mathbf{x}) = \int \left[\gamma(\mathbf{p}) - 1\right] m c^2 f(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{p}) \, d^3p
$$

where $\mathcal{E}$ is the energy density, $\mathbf{x}$ is position, $\mathbf{p}$ is particle momentum, $m$ is particle rest mass, $c$ is the speed of light, $f$ is the momentum-space particle distribution function, and $\gamma(\mathbf{p}) = \sqrt{1 + |\mathbf{p}|^2/(m^2 c^2)}$ is the Lorentz factor.

This quantity is a local density, not a volume-integrated energy such as [electron energy](name:electron_energy), [fast-particle energy](name:fast_particle_energy), or [fast-electron energy](name:fast_electron_energy). In the non-relativistic fluid limit, the same kinetic-energy content separates into a directed bulk-flow term and a random-motion term, with the random-motion contribution proportional to the trace of the pressure tensor; rest-mass energy is excluded unless a quantity explicitly defines total mass-energy content.

NAMES.name: energy_diffusivity
NAMES.short: Energy diffusivity is the scalar Fickian coefficient that maps the spatial gradient of thermal-energy density to the local diffusive thermal-energy flux. It is defined for an energy-density-gradient closure, not for a temperature-gradient heat-transport coefficient unless the density and heat-capacity factors have been specified.
NAMES.long:
Energy diffusivity is the scalar local transport coefficient for diffusive smoothing of thermal-energy density. It represents only the Fickian, down-gradient part of thermal-energy transport for the population to which the quantity is applied.

The defining closure relates the diffusive thermal-energy flux to the gradient of thermal-energy density:

$$
\mathbf{q}_E^{\mathrm{diff}} = -\chi_E \nabla w
$$

where $\mathbf{q}_E^{\mathrm{diff}}$ is the diffusive thermal-energy flux, $\chi_E$ is the energy diffusivity, and $w$ is the thermal-energy density. The minus sign defines the down-gradient convention: positive $\chi_E$ gives a diffusive flux from larger $w$ toward smaller $w$.

This quantity excludes convective energy transport, explicitly nonlocal transport, and source or sink terms. Species-resolved variants such as [ion_energy_diffusivity](name:ion_energy_diffusivity) and charge-state-resolved variants such as [ion_charge_state_energy_diffusivity](name:ion_charge_state_energy_diffusivity) retain the energy-density-gradient meaning. Quantities named as energy diffusion coefficients, such as [internal_state_energy_diffusion_coefficient](name:internal_state_energy_diffusion_coefficient), may instead denote temperature-gradient closures and are not equivalent to $\chi_E$ unless the heat-capacity and density factors relating $\nabla w$ to the temperature gradient are part of the definition.

NAMES.name: electron_energy_diffusivity
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Electron energy diffusivity is the scalar Fickian coefficient that maps the spatial gradient of electron thermal-energy density to the local diffusive electron thermal-energy flux. It is defined for an electron energy-density-gradient closure, not for a temperature-gradient heat-transport coefficient unless the electron density and heat-capacity factors have been specified.
NAMES.long:
Electron energy diffusivity is the scalar local transport coefficient for diffusive smoothing of electron thermal-energy density. It represents only the Fickian, down-gradient part of electron energy transport for the electron population.

The defining closure relates the diffusive electron thermal-energy flux to the gradient of electron thermal-energy density:

$$
\mathbf{q}_{E,e}^{\mathrm{diff}} = -\chi_{E,e} \nabla w_e
$$

where $\mathbf{q}_{E,e}^{\mathrm{diff}}$ is the diffusive electron thermal-energy flux, $\chi_{E,e}$ is the electron energy diffusivity, and $w_e$ is the electron thermal-energy density. The minus sign defines the down-gradient convention: positive $\chi_{E,e}$ gives a diffusive flux from larger $w_e$ toward smaller $w_e$.

This quantity excludes convective electron energy transport, explicitly nonlocal transport, and electron energy source or sink terms. It is the electron-population specialization of [energy diffusivity](name:energy_diffusivity). It is not equivalent to temperature-gradient electron heat-transport coefficients such as [electron energy diffusion coefficient](name:electron_energy_diffusion_coefficient), [parallel electron energy diffusivity](name:parallel_electron_energy_diffusivity), or [poloidal electron energy diffusivity](name:poloidal_electron_energy_diffusivity) unless the heat-capacity and density factors relating $\nabla w_e$ to the electron-temperature gradient are part of the definition.

NAMES.name: energy_flux
NAMES.short: Energy flux is the signed component of energy flux density normal to an oriented surface, for energy carried by a specified particle, neutral, plasma, wave, radiation, or field reservoir. It includes convective and conductive contributions when those channels are in scope.
NAMES.long:
Energy flux is the signed component of energy flux density normal to an oriented surface, for energy carried by a specified particle, neutral, plasma, wave, radiation, or field reservoir. It gives the rate per unit area at which that reservoir crosses the surface, including convective, conductive, collisional, radiative, wave, or field transport channels only when those channels are part of the stated reservoir definition.

For an oriented surface with chosen unit normal $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$, the scalar energy flux $F_E$ is the normal projection of the corresponding energy-flux-density vector $\mathbf{q}_E$:

$$
F_E = \mathbf{q}_E \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}
$$

where $\mathbf{q}_E$ is the vector density of energy transport for the selected reservoir and $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ defines the positive normal direction.

Energy flux is a parent quantity for more specific transport channels. [Heat flux](name:heat_flux) is the thermal-energy specialization; [neutral energy flux](name:neutral_energy_flux) and [internal-state energy flux](name:internal_state_energy_flux) restrict the carried energy reservoir; [flux due to radiation](name:flux_due_to_radiation) denotes the radiative channel. The scalar flux is distinct from an energy density, a volumetric source or sink, and from any carrier velocity because it already combines transported energy content with the normal transport rate.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the energy-flux-density vector has a component in the direction of the chosen unit normal to the oriented surface.

NAMES.name: electron_energy_flux
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Net power per unit area carried by the electron population across a surface element, encompassing both conductive and convective contributions to electron thermal energy transport.
NAMES.long:
The electron energy flux density quantifies the net rate at which thermal energy is transported per unit area across any oriented surface by the electron population. Both the conductive channel — driven by electron temperature gradients through the electron thermal conductivity — and the convective channel — carried by bulk electron motion — contribute to the total flux.

The electron energy flux density vector $\mathbf{q}_e$ is expressed as:

$$
\mathbf{q}_e = \frac{5}{2} n_e T_e \mathbf{v}_e - \boldsymbol{\kappa}_e \cdot \nabla T_e
$$

where $n_e$ is the electron number density, $T_e$ is the electron temperature, $\mathbf{v}_e$ is the electron bulk velocity, and $\boldsymbol{\kappa}_e$ is the electron thermal conductivity tensor.

In transport modeling, the flux is resolved along specific geometric axes. The [parallel electron energy flux](name:parallel_electron_energy_flux) captures the strongly anisotropic conduction along magnetic field lines, which dominates in collisional plasmas; the [poloidal electron energy flux](name:poloidal_electron_energy_flux) and [radial electron energy flux](name:radial_electron_energy_flux) characterize cross-field transport relevant to scrape-off layer and divertor physics. The [energy convection velocity](name:energy_convection_velocity) offers a complementary convective closure when multiplied by local electron pressure. Sign conventions for scalar projections are defined separately for each directional component.

NAMES.name: fast_electron_pressure
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Kinetic pressure contribution from suprathermal (fast) electrons, forming the non-Maxwellian component of the total electron pressure tensor that is generally anisotropic in a magnetized plasma.
NAMES.long:
The fast electron pressure quantifies the kinetic stress contributed by the suprathermal electron population — those with energies well above the bulk thermal energy $k_B T_e$ — and represents the non-Maxwellian component of the total [electron_pressure](name:electron_pressure). In a magnetized plasma this pressure is anisotropic with respect to the local magnetic field direction, with the field-aligned projection described by [parallel_fast_electron_pressure](name:parallel_fast_electron_pressure) and the transverse projection by the perpendicular component; the two can differ substantially when wave-particle resonances preferentially energize electrons perpendicular to the field.

The fast electron pressure is the second velocity moment of the suprathermal part of the electron distribution function $f_{fe}(\mathbf{v})$:

$$
p_{fe} = \frac{m_e}{3} \int v^2 \, f_{fe}(\mathbf{v}) \, d^3v
$$

where $m_e$ is the electron mass and $v = |\mathbf{v}|$; this isotropic scalar form is valid when the suprathermal population is nearly isotropic, while in general the parallel and perpendicular components must be treated separately to capture the full anisotropic stress tensor.

Fast electron pressure is inferred from hard X-ray bremsstrahlung spectra or non-thermal electron cyclotron emission diagnostics, or computed from kinetic simulations of the electron velocity distribution function. When combined with the thermal bulk contribution, it yields the [total_electron_pressure](name:total_electron_pressure), entering the pressure-gradient force $-\nabla p_e$ in the plasma momentum equation and contributing to MHD stability through the fast-particle pressure drive.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the suprathermal electron population exerts outward kinetic stress on a confining surface, consistent with the thermodynamic definition of pressure as a non-negative mechanical stress.

NAMES.name: fast_electron_source_rate
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Total volumetric generation rate of fast, suprathermal electrons, summed over all relevant production mechanisms. It counts creation into the fast-electron population and excludes transport losses or explicit sink terms in the number-density balance.
NAMES.long:
The fast-electron source rate $S_\mathrm{fast}$ is the local volumetric rate at which electrons enter the fast, suprathermal population. It measures how rapidly the population is created before transport, slowing-down, or other sink processes are applied. It is the sum of production mechanisms such as Dreicer acceleration, avalanche multiplication, hot-tail survival after rapid cooling, Compton scattering, and tritium beta-decay injection.

In a local fast-electron number-density balance, the production role of $S_\mathrm{fast}$ can be written as

$$
\frac{\partial n_\mathrm{fast}}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_\mathrm{fast} = S_\mathrm{fast} - L_\mathrm{fast}
$$

where $n_\mathrm{fast}$ is the [fast_electron_density](name:fast_electron_density) in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$, $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_\mathrm{fast}$ is the fast-electron particle flux in $\mathrm{m}^{-2}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, $S_\mathrm{fast}$ is this production rate in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, and $L_\mathrm{fast}$ represents explicit loss, slowing-down, or reclassification terms in $\mathrm{m}^{-3}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$. A signed production-minus-removal residual is therefore a net balance term, not this source rate.

The rate is usually obtained from kinetic or integrated transport modeling by summing mechanism-specific contributions, including quantities such as [fast_electron_source_rate_due_to_hot_tail](name:fast_electron_source_rate_due_to_hot_tail). It can also be constrained indirectly by combining time-resolved estimates of fast-electron density or current with transport and loss models, using diagnostics sensitive to suprathermal electrons such as hard-x-ray emission, synchrotron radiation, electron-cyclotron emission, and current evolution. The closely related [runaway_electron_source_rate](name:runaway_electron_source_rate) applies the same aggregate-production concept to the runaway-electron subset.

Representative magnitudes are highly scenario-dependent and should be interpreted as order-of-magnitude scales rather than universal constants. With no active accelerating or seed mechanism the rate is effectively $0\ \mathrm{m}^{-3}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$; creating $10^{14}$-$10^{18}\ \mathrm{m}^{-3}$ fast electrons over $1\ \mathrm{ms}$-$1\ \mathrm{s}$ corresponds to an average source-rate scale of about $10^{14}$-$10^{21}\ \mathrm{m}^{-3}\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, with stronger disruption or avalanche phases potentially exceeding this scale.
