NAMES.name: runaway_electron_diffusivity
NAMES.subject: runaway_electron
NAMES.short: Effective transport coefficient that quantifies gradient-driven particle diffusion, with directional components describing how a population spreads through a plasma.
NAMES.long:
Diffusivity characterizes the gradient-driven component of particle transport. It relates a population’s diffusive flux to the spatial gradient of its number density and may be represented by directional coefficients or an anisotropic tensor.

For number density $n$ and diffusive particle flux $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{\mathrm{diff}}$, the defining relation is

$$
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{\mathrm{diff}} = -\mathbf{D} \cdot \nabla n
$$

where $n$ is the particle number density, $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{\mathrm{diff}}$ is the diffusive particle flux, and $\mathbf{D}$ is the diffusivity tensor or its directional representation. The minus sign expresses transport down the density gradient. The [perpendicular runaway-electron diffusivity](name:perpendicular_runaway_electron_diffusivity) is a cross-field instance of this general quantity. Diffusivity describes diffusive transport and is distinct from directed transport represented by [runaway-electron convection velocity](name:runaway_electron_convection_velocity).

NAMES.name: perpendicular_runaway_electron_diffusivity
NAMES.subject: runaway_electron
NAMES.short: Cross-field diffusion coefficient governing the perpendicular spread of runaway electrons across magnetic flux surfaces.
NAMES.long:
The perpendicular diffusivity $D_\perp$ of runaway electrons quantifies how rapidly the runaway electron population spreads across magnetic flux surfaces due to stochastic magnetic field perturbations, collisional pitch-angle scattering, and turbulent transport processes. It is the perpendicular projection of the full runaway_electron_diffusivity tensor, characterizing the diffusive part of cross-field transport for this suprathermal population.

The diffusive contribution to the perpendicular particle flux is defined as:

$$
\Gamma_{\perp}^{\text{diff}} = -D_\perp \nabla_\perp n_r
$$

where $n_r$ is the [runaway electron number density](name:runaway_electron_density). Combined with the convective contribution from [perpendicular_runaway_electron_convection_velocity](name:perpendicular_runaway_electron_convection_velocity), this constitutes the net [perpendicular_runaway_electron_particle_flux](name:perpendicular_runaway_electron_particle_flux).

The value of $D_\perp$ is inferred from runaway electron density evolution measurements or prescribed in disruption transport models based on the estimated level of magnetic field stochasticity. During disruptions with significant stochastic magnetic field perturbations, $D_\perp$ can reach $10^{-2}$–$1\;\text{m}^2\,\text{s}^{-1}$; under quiescent magnetohydrodynamic conditions cross-field stochasticity is substantially weaker. Larger values of $D_\perp$ enhance runaway electron losses to the first wall and suppress the growth of the post-disruption runaway current.

NAMES.name: runaway_electron_energy_density
NAMES.subject: runaway_electron
NAMES.short: Kinetic energy per unit volume of the runaway electron population, incorporating their characteristically relativistic energies reached through electric-field acceleration beyond the Dreicer threshold.
NAMES.long:
The runaway electron energy density is the local kinetic energy stored per unit volume by the runaway electron (RE) population on a given flux surface. Unlike thermal electrons, runaway electrons are accelerated to suprathermal and relativistic energies by a parallel electric field exceeding the critical (Dreicer) threshold, so their energy density must account for relativistic kinematics. It is the electron-population analog of [ion_species_kinetic_energy_density](name:ion_kinetic_energy_density) but for the non-thermal, suprathermal runaway component.

The defining expression integrates the relativistic kinetic energy over the RE momentum-space distribution:

$$
\mathcal{E}_{RE} = \int (\gamma - 1) \, m_e c^2 \, f_{RE}(\mathbf{p}) \, d^3p
$$

where $\gamma = (1 + p^2/m_e^2 c^2)^{1/2}$ is the Lorentz factor, $m_e$ is the electron rest mass, $c$ is the speed of light, and $f_{RE}(\mathbf{p})$ is the runaway electron distribution function in momentum space $\mathbf{p}$.

This quantity is computed from kinetic Fokker–Planck solvers or fluid-moment RE models that evolve the runaway population. Volumetrically integrating $\mathcal{E}_{RE}$ over the confined plasma yields the total [runaway electron kinetic energy](name:runaway_electron_kinetic_energy), while averaging over the plasma volume gives the [volume-averaged energy density](name:volume_averaged_runaway_electron_kinetic_energy_density). The current density carried by the same population is characterized by [parallel runaway electron current density](name:parallel_runaway_electron_current_density).

Post-disruption runaway beams in tokamaks can accumulate MeV-range electrons at number densities of $10^{16}$–$10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$, producing local energy densities of order $10^3$–$10^6$ J m$^{-3}$.

NAMES.name: runaway_electron_kinetic_energy
NAMES.subject: runaway_electron
NAMES.short: Relativistic kinetic energy summed over the entire runaway-electron population, giving the total energy carried by runaway electrons.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the total kinetic energy carried by all electrons classified as runaway, integrated over the complete population and its occupied plasma volume. It excludes electron rest-mass energy and energy carried by non-runaway populations.

The total energy is defined from the runaway-electron distribution function by

$$
E_{\mathrm{RE}} = \int_V \int \left[\gamma(\mathbf{p})-1\right]m_e c^2 f_{\mathrm{RE}}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{p})\,d^3p\,d^3x
$$

where $E_{\mathrm{RE}}$ is the total kinetic energy in J, $V$ is the plasma volume, $\mathbf{x}$ is position in m, $\mathbf{p}$ is electron momentum in kg m s$^{-1}$, $m_e$ is the electron rest mass, $c$ is the speed of light, $f_{\mathrm{RE}}$ is the runaway-electron phase-space number distribution, and $\gamma(\mathbf{p})=\sqrt{1+p^2/(m_e^2c^2)}$ is the Lorentz factor. The corresponding local density is [runaway electron energy density](name:runaway_electron_energy_density), while volume averaging gives [volume-averaged runaway electron kinetic energy density](name:volume_averaged_runaway_electron_kinetic_energy_density).

NAMES.name: runaway_electron_particle_flux
NAMES.subject: runaway_electron
NAMES.short: Runaway electron particle flux is the directed number of runaway electrons crossing a unit area per unit time through an oriented surface, the full vector particle-transport flux of the suprathermal runaway electron population.
NAMES.long:
Runaway electron particle flux quantifies the directed flow of runaway electrons across an oriented reference surface, capturing particle transport for the suprathermal electron population that has decoupled from the bulk through acceleration by parallel electric fields or avalanche multiplication.

For a runaway electron population with number density $n_{RE}$ and mean fluid velocity $\mathbf{v}_{RE}$, the particle flux vector is:

$$
\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{RE} = n_{RE} \mathbf{v}_{RE}
$$

where the surface-normal projection satisfies the runaway electron continuity equation $\partial n_{RE} / \partial t + \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{RE} = S_{RE}$, with $S_{RE}$ the local runaway source or sink rate density.

The [perpendicular_runaway_electron_particle_flux](name:perpendicular_runaway_electron_particle_flux) is the component of this vector projected onto the outward flux-surface normal, governing cross-field runaway transport described by the associated [perpendicular_runaway_electron_diffusivity](name:perpendicular_runaway_electron_diffusivity). This quantity is a species-specific specialization of the general [particle_flux](name:particle_flux) restricted to the runaway electron sub-population.
NAMES.sign: Positive when runaway electrons flow in the direction of the outward surface normal, away from the enclosed plasma volume.

NAMES.name: perpendicular_runaway_electron_particle_flux
NAMES.subject: runaway_electron
NAMES.short: Cross-field number flux of runaway electrons through magnetic flux surfaces, obtained by projecting their particle-flux vector onto the outward flux-surface normal.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the cross-field component of runaway-electron particle transport through magnetic flux surfaces. It describes the directed rate at which the suprathermal runaway-electron population crosses those surfaces, rather than transport along magnetic field lines.

The component is defined by

$$
\Gamma_{\mathrm{RE},\perp}=\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{\mathrm{RE}}\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}_{\mathrm{FS}}
$$

where $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{\mathrm{RE}}$ is the [runaway electron particle flux](name:runaway_electron_particle_flux) vector and $\hat{\mathbf n}_{\mathrm{FS}}$ is the unit normal to the magnetic flux surface, directed toward increasing flux label. The subscript $\perp$ denotes the cross-field projection.

This is a signed normal component, not the magnitude of the full particle-flux vector and not a field-aligned flux. It is distinct from cross-field transport coefficients such as [perpendicular runaway electron diffusivity](name:perpendicular_runaway_electron_diffusivity) and from [perpendicular runaway electron convection velocity](name:perpendicular_runaway_electron_convection_velocity).
NAMES.sign: Positive when runaway-electron particle transport is directed toward increasing flux label, outward from the magnetic axis.

NAMES.name: runaway_electron_source_rate
NAMES.subject: runaway_electron
NAMES.short: Volumetric rate at which active mechanisms add electrons to the runaway population, summed over mechanisms and applicable locally or as a plasma-volume average.
NAMES.long:
Runaway-electron source rate is the volumetric rate at which active physical mechanisms add electrons to the runaway population. It is an aggregate production quantity; removal by collision, radiation, deconfinement, or other loss processes is excluded.

The aggregate source is defined as

$$
S_{\mathrm{RE}}(\mathbf{x},t)=\sum_k S_{\mathrm{RE},k}(\mathbf{x},t)
$$

where $S_{\mathrm{RE}}$ is the total source rate, $S_{\mathrm{RE},k}$ is the contribution from mechanism $k$, $\mathbf{x}$ is position, and $t$ is time. In the runaway-electron continuity balance, it appears as $\partial n_{\mathrm{RE}}/\partial t+\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{\mathrm{RE}}=S_{\mathrm{RE}}-L_{\mathrm{RE}}$, where $n_{\mathrm{RE}}$ is runaway-electron number density, $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{\mathrm{RE}}$ is its transport flux, and $L_{\mathrm{RE}}$ is the loss rate.

A volume-averaged realization, such as [volume-averaged runaway-electron source rate](name:volume_averaged_runaway_electron_source_rate), is $V^{-1}\int_V S_{\mathrm{RE}}\,dV$ over the specified plasma volume. Mechanism-resolved forms include [runaway-electron source rate due to Compton scattering](name:runaway_electron_source_rate_due_to_compton_scattering) and [runaway-electron source rate due to hot tail](name:runaway_electron_source_rate_due_to_hot_tail).

NAMES.name: safety_factor
NAMES.short: Safety factor is the field-line winding number on a magnetic flux surface, giving the number of toroidal turns made during one complete poloidal turn. It is the reciprocal of rotational transform.
NAMES.long:
Safety factor is the magnetic-field-line winding number associated with a magnetic flux surface. It counts toroidal turns of a field line per complete poloidal turn around the plasma core on that surface.

The safety factor is defined from neighboring nested flux surfaces by the ratio of the toroidal magnetic-flux increment to the poloidal magnetic-flux increment divided by $2\pi$:

$$
q = \frac{d\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}}{d\left(\Phi_{\mathrm{pol}}/2\pi\right)}
$$

where $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the toroidal magnetic flux enclosed by the flux surface, $\Phi_{\mathrm{pol}}$ is the poloidal magnetic flux linked by the same surface, and the derivative is taken across the flux-surface label.

It is a flux-surface quantity, not a local magnetic pitch angle or local field-direction component. It is the multiplicative inverse of the [rotational transform](name:rotational_transform), so $q = 1/\iota$ when both are evaluated on the same flux surface with the same orientation convention, where $\iota$ denotes rotational transform.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the toroidal magnetic-field direction and the toroidal plasma-current direction are parallel in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: safety_factor_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.short: Safety factor at the internal transport barrier is the field-line winding number on the flux surface assigned to the barrier, giving toroidal turns per poloidal turn.
NAMES.long:
The safety factor at the internal transport barrier is the value of the [safety factor](name:safety_factor) on the flux surface assigned to the internal transport barrier. It characterizes magnetic-field-line winding by the number of toroidal turns per complete poloidal turn on that surface, where cross-field turbulent transport is locally reduced.

The safety factor is defined from neighboring nested flux surfaces by the ratio of toroidal magnetic-flux increment to poloidal magnetic-flux increment divided by $2\pi$:

$$
q_{\mathrm{ITB}} = \frac{d\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}}{d\left(\Phi_{\mathrm{pol}}/2\pi\right)}
$$

where $q_{\mathrm{ITB}}$ is the safety factor at the internal transport barrier, $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is toroidal magnetic flux, $\Phi_{\mathrm{pol}}$ is poloidal magnetic flux, and the derivative is taken across nested flux surfaces. Its radial variation is related to [magnetic shear at the internal transport barrier](name:magnetic_shear_at_internal_transport_barrier).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the toroidal magnetic-field direction and the toroidal plasma-current direction are parallel in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: source_due_to_diamagnetic_drift
NAMES.short: A source due to diamagnetic drift is a local contribution to a plasma transport balance produced by pressure-gradient-driven diamagnetic drift transport. The mechanism is fixed as diamagnetic drift; the balanced quantity is the one identified by the more specific source, such as momentum.
NAMES.long:
A source due to diamagnetic drift is the local source term in a plasma transport balance attributable to pressure-gradient-driven diamagnetic drift. The mechanism is fixed as diamagnetic drift; the balanced quantity is set by the concrete specialization, for example momentum in [momentum source due to diamagnetic drift](name:momentum_source_due_to_diamagnetic_drift).

When the diamagnetic contribution is represented as transport of a balanced density $q$, the source is the negative divergence of the corresponding diamagnetic-drift flux:

$$
S_q^{\mathrm{dia}} = -\nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_q^{\mathrm{dia}}
$$

where $S_q^{\mathrm{dia}}$ is the source due to diamagnetic drift, $q$ is the density of the balanced quantity, and $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_q^{\mathrm{dia}}$ is its flux density carried by the diamagnetic-drift contribution. For quantities whose flux has tensor rank, $\nabla \cdot$ denotes the appropriate contraction over the spatial flux index.

This quantity excludes source terms from other transport mechanisms, external forcing, and the diamagnetic drift velocity itself. It also excludes selecting a species, component, projection, or normalization unless that qualification is present in the concrete specialization.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the diamagnetic-drift contribution increases the balanced quantity.

NAMES.name: momentum_source_due_to_diamagnetic_drift
NAMES.short: Diamagnetic-drift contribution to an area-normalized momentum-balance source, representing pressure-gradient-driven transport of a specified projected linear momentum.
NAMES.long:
Diamagnetic-drift contribution to an area-normalized momentum-balance source is the part of the source for a specified projected linear momentum caused by pressure-gradient-driven diamagnetic transport in a magnetized plasma. It represents the net effect of the diamagnetic projected-momentum stress on the momentum balance after normalization by the area through which the balance is written.

An area-normalized source is defined from the corresponding volumetric projected-momentum source density over a balance volume:

$$
S_{\mathrm{mom,dia}} = \frac{1}{A}\int_V q_{\mathrm{mom,dia}}\,dV,\qquad q_{\mathrm{mom,dia}}=-\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol{\Pi}_{\mathrm{dia}}
$$

where $S_{\mathrm{mom,dia}}$ is the area-normalized diamagnetic-drift momentum source, $A$ is the normalizing area, $V$ is the balance volume, $q_{\mathrm{mom,dia}}$ is the volumetric projected-momentum source density with dimensions of force per volume, and $\boldsymbol{\Pi}_{\mathrm{dia}}$ is the diamagnetic projected-momentum flux tensor with dimensions of force per area. The division by $A$ makes this quantity area-normalized rather than a volumetric force density; the minus sign follows the conservation-law convention that an outward divergence of momentum flux is a sink.

This quantity is the momentum-specific member of [source_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:source_due_to_diamagnetic_drift). It differs from [momentum_flux_due_to_diamagnetic_drift](name:momentum_flux_due_to_diamagnetic_drift), which is the flux or stress before taking its divergence and area normalization, and it is not the effective transport coefficient [diamagnetic_momentum_diffusivity](name:diamagnetic_momentum_diffusivity). The scalar projection is a projected linear-momentum component; an angular-momentum moment arm or torque normalization is not implied.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the diamagnetic-drift term increases the projected linear momentum in the positive direction of the momentum projection used in the balance.

NAMES.name: ion_momentum_source_due_to_diamagnetic_drift
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Ion momentum source due to diamagnetic drift is the area-normalized force on the represented scalar projection of ion linear momentum caused by pressure-gradient-driven diamagnetic transport. The ion contribution is summed over all charge states, and the projection is left unspecified unless fixed by a more specific name.
NAMES.long:
Ion momentum source due to diamagnetic drift is the area-normalized force on a represented scalar projection of ion linear momentum caused by pressure-gradient-driven diamagnetic transport. The represented projection is left open at this name level; a more specific child name fixes the projection when a direction or component is part of the name. Because this is a species-level extensive source, the ion contribution is summed over all ion charge states.

For a region $V$ with boundary $\partial V$, the area-normalized flux-convergence definition for projection $a$ is

$$
S_{i,\mathrm{dia}}^{(a)} = -\frac{1}{A_\mathrm{ref}} \sum_{\chi} \int_{\partial V} \boldsymbol{\Pi}_{i\chi,\mathrm{dia}}^{(a)} \cdot \hat{\boldsymbol{n}} \, dA_b
$$

where $S_{i,\mathrm{dia}}^{(a)}$ is this quantity, $a$ identifies the represented scalar momentum projection, $A_\mathrm{ref}$ is the normalizing area for the region, $\chi$ labels ion charge states, $\boldsymbol{\Pi}_{i\chi,\mathrm{dia}}^{(a)}$ is the diamagnetic-drift contribution to the [ion charge-state momentum flux](name:ion_charge_state_momentum_flux), $\hat{\boldsymbol{n}}$ is the outward normal to the boundary, and $dA_b$ is the boundary area element.

This is the ion momentum member of [source due to diamagnetic drift](name:source_due_to_diamagnetic_drift) and is more specific than the generic [momentum source due to diamagnetic drift](name:momentum_source_due_to_diamagnetic_drift). It excludes momentum sources assigned to non-diamagnetic mechanisms and differs from [parallel net ion momentum source](name:parallel_net_ion_momentum_source), which denotes the net source for the magnetic-field-parallel projection rather than a single process contribution with an open projection.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the charge-state-summed diamagnetic momentum flux carrying positive represented projected ion momentum converges into the considered region.

NAMES.name: source_rate_due_to_compton_scattering
NAMES.short: Local volumetric production rate of electrons sourced by Compton scattering of high-energy gamma-ray photons off free plasma electrons, generalizing over the receiving electron population.
NAMES.long:
Compton scattering deposits kinetic energy and momentum into free plasma electrons when energetic gamma-ray photons collide with them, acting as a volumetric source of electrons across one or more population channels. This quantity is the general production rate, per unit volume and unit time, without specifying whether the recoiling electrons remain in the bulk thermal distribution or cross the critical momentum threshold to enter the runaway population; the child quantities [electron_source_rate_due_to_compton_scattering](name:electron_source_rate_due_to_compton_scattering) and [runaway_electron_source_rate_due_to_compton_scattering](name:runaway_electron_source_rate_due_to_compton_scattering) resolve those respective channels.

The source rate $S_C$ is proportional to the local electron number density $n_e$, the incident gamma-ray photon flux $\Phi_\gamma$, and the Klein–Nishina Compton cross section $\sigma_C$:

$$
S_C = n_e \, \sigma_C \, \Phi_\gamma
$$

where $\sigma_C$ approaches the classical Thomson cross section $\sigma_T \approx 6.65 \times 10^{-29}\,\mathrm{m}^2$ at photon energies much less than the electron rest-mass energy and decreases for higher-energy gamma rays per the Klein–Nishina formula. The recoil electron energy then determines which population the scattered electron enters.

In deuterium–tritium burning plasmas, the dominant gamma-ray source is neutron capture in first-wall and blanket materials, so this source rate scales with the local neutron flux and electron density profile. It is evaluated by integrating the Compton recoil-electron production spectrum over the incident gamma-ray energy distribution obtained from neutronics calculations. The source is particularly relevant for runaway electron seeding during disruptions, where even a modest Compton-generated population can initiate an avalanche multiplication.

NAMES.name: electron_source_rate_due_to_compton_scattering
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Local volumetric production rate of electrons sourced by Compton scattering of high-energy gamma-ray photons off free plasma electrons, abstracting over which electron population sub-channel receives the scattered electrons.
NAMES.long:
Electron source rate due to Compton scattering is the local rate at which scattering of high-energy gamma-ray photons adds electrons to the free-electron population per unit plasma volume per unit time, without specifying which energy sub-population the recoiling electrons enter. It is the electron-species specialization of [source_rate_due_to_compton_scattering](name:source_rate_due_to_compton_scattering) and acts as a structural parent over population-resolved contributors; [fast_electron_source_rate_due_to_compton_scattering](name:fast_electron_source_rate_due_to_compton_scattering) resolves the sub-channel for electrons that gain enough energy to join the fast-electron population, while [runaway_electron_source_rate_due_to_compton_scattering](name:runaway_electron_source_rate_due_to_compton_scattering) captures electrons that exceed the critical runaway momentum threshold.

The total scattered-electron production rate follows:

$$
S_e = n_e \, \sigma_C(\varepsilon_\gamma) \, \Phi_\gamma
$$

where $n_e$ is the free electron number density, $\sigma_C(\varepsilon_\gamma)$ is the energy-dependent Klein–Nishina Compton cross section (approaching the Thomson value $\sigma_T \approx 6.65 \times 10^{-29}\,\mathrm{m}^2$ for photon energies $\varepsilon_\gamma \ll m_e c^2$, and decreasing at higher energies), and $\Phi_\gamma$ is the incident gamma-ray photon flux integrated over the photon-energy spectrum. The recoil energy transferred to each electron then determines which population sub-channel it enters.

In deuterium–tritium burning plasmas, the dominant gamma-ray source is neutron capture in first-wall and blanket structures, making this rate proportional to the local neutron flux and electron density profile. It is evaluated by folding the differential Compton recoil cross section with the incident gamma-ray energy distribution from neutronics calculations and integrating over photon energy. This aggregate electron source is particularly relevant to disruption mitigation studies, where Compton-seeded populations in either the fast or runaway channel can initiate avalanche multiplication.

NAMES.name: fast_electron_source_rate_due_to_compton_scattering
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Volumetric production rate of fast electrons created when high-energy gamma rays Compton-scatter from free plasma electrons; subsequent losses and evolution are excluded.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the local production rate of fast electrons generated by Compton scattering of high-energy gamma-ray photons from free plasma electrons. Only recoiling electrons that enter the defined fast-electron population are included; losses and subsequent evolution are excluded.

The rate is defined by

$$
S_{\rm fast}^{\rm C} = \left.\frac{\partial n_{\rm fast}}{\partial t}\right|_{\rm Compton,\ production}
$$

where $S_{\rm fast}^{\rm C}$ is the source rate, $n_{\rm fast}$ is the number density of fast electrons, and $t$ is time. It is the fast-electron component of the [electron source rate due to Compton scattering](name:electron_source_rate_due_to_compton_scattering), whereas [runaway electron source rate due to Compton scattering](name:runaway_electron_source_rate_due_to_compton_scattering) includes only electrons classified as runaway. The quantity is a source term, not a net rate after subtracting losses.

NAMES.name: runaway_electron_source_rate_due_to_compton_scattering
NAMES.subject: runaway_electron
NAMES.short: Local volumetric production rate of runaway electrons sourced by Compton scattering of high-energy gamma-ray photons off free plasma electrons, restricted to recoils above the runaway threshold.
NAMES.long:
Runaway-electron source rate due to Compton scattering is the local rate at which high-energy gamma-ray photons add recoiling electrons to the runaway population after scattering from free plasma electrons. It is the runaway-channel component of the general [source rate due to Compton scattering](name:source_rate_due_to_compton_scattering), distinct from the broader [electron source rate due to Compton scattering](name:electron_source_rate_due_to_compton_scattering).

The rate of above-threshold Compton recoils is

$$
S_C^{\mathrm{RE}} = n_e \int dE_\gamma\, \Phi_\gamma(E_\gamma) \int_{p_c}^{\infty} dp\, \frac{d\sigma_C(E_\gamma)}{dp}
$$

where $n_e$ is the free-electron number density, $\Phi_\gamma(E_\gamma)$ is the spectral flux of incident gamma-ray photons, $d\sigma_C/dp$ is the differential Compton-scattering cross section for recoil momentum $p$, and $p_c$ is the critical momentum defining entry into the runaway population. Recoils below $p_c$ are excluded from this quantity and remain part of the non-runaway channel.

NAMES.name: source_rate_due_to_dreicer
NAMES.short: Volumetric production rate of electrons generated by the Dreicer mechanism, where a parallel electric field accelerates thermal-tail electrons past the critical velocity at which Coulomb collisional friction can no longer confine them.
NAMES.long:
The Dreicer source rate is the local volumetric rate at which a parallel electric field continuously accelerates electrons from the high-energy tail of the thermal distribution past the runaway critical velocity $v_c$, above which Coulomb collisional drag — scaling as $v^{-2}$ — can no longer balance the electric force. The net acceleration then becomes self-reinforcing, feeding particles irreversibly into a runaway population. The specific destination population (total electrons, runaway sub-population, or fast electrons) is resolved by child quantities.

The generation rate is exponentially sensitive to the ratio of the local parallel electric field $E_\parallel$ to the Dreicer field $E_D$:

$$
\dot{n}_\mathrm{RE}^D \propto n_e \nu_{ee} \left(\frac{E_\parallel}{E_D}\right)^{-h} \exp\!\left(-\frac{E_D}{4E_\parallel} - \sqrt{\frac{E_D}{E_\parallel}}\right)
$$

where $n_e$ is the electron number density, $\nu_{ee}$ is the electron–electron collision frequency, $E_D = n_e e^3 \ln\Lambda / (4\pi\epsilon_0^2 m_e v_{te}^2)$ defines the Dreicer field with $\ln\Lambda$ the Coulomb logarithm and $v_{te}$ the thermal electron velocity, and $h$ is a numerical factor depending on $Z_\mathrm{eff}$.

Dreicer generation dominates runaway seeding in quiescent discharges and moderate disruptions, while the [source_rate_due_to_hot_tail](name:source_rate_due_to_hot_tail) mechanism becomes important during rapid thermal quenches when surviving suprathermal electrons escape collisional thermalization. Child quantities distinguish the target population: [electron_source_rate_due_to_dreicer](name:electron_source_rate_due_to_dreicer) covers the total electron source, [runaway_electron_source_rate_due_to_dreicer](name:runaway_electron_source_rate_due_to_dreicer) isolates the runaway sub-population, and [fast_electron_source_rate_due_to_dreicer](name:fast_electron_source_rate_due_to_dreicer) the fast-electron channel. Rates are computed from profiles of $n_e$, $T_e$, $E_\parallel$, and $Z_\mathrm{eff}$ using semi-analytic Connor–Hastie expressions or Fokker–Planck kinetic solvers.

NAMES.name: electron_source_rate_due_to_dreicer
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Volumetric production rate of electrons generated by the Dreicer mechanism for an electron population, where a parallel electric field accelerates thermal-tail electrons past the critical velocity at which Coulomb collisional friction can no longer confine them.
NAMES.long:
The Dreicer source rate for electrons is the local volumetric rate at which a parallel electric field accelerates electrons from the high-energy tail of the thermal distribution past the critical velocity $v_c$, above which Coulomb collisional drag — scaling as $v^{-2}$ — can no longer balance the electric force. The net acceleration then becomes self-reinforcing, feeding electrons into a nonthermal population. This quantity is not restricted to a more specific electron subset unless a child quantity states that subset explicitly.

The generation rate is exponentially sensitive to the ratio of the magnitude of the local parallel electric field $|E_\parallel|$ to the Dreicer field $E_D$:

$$
S_e^D \propto n_e \nu_{ee} \left(\frac{|E_\parallel|}{E_D}\right)^{-h} \exp\!\left[-\frac{E_D}{4|E_\parallel|} - \sqrt{\frac{E_D}{|E_\parallel|}}\right]
$$

where $S_e^D$ is the electron source rate due to Dreicer generation, $n_e$ is the electron number density, $\nu_{ee}$ is the electron-electron collision frequency, $E_\parallel$ is the electric-field component parallel to the magnetic field, $E_D = n_e e^3 \ln\Lambda / (4\pi\epsilon_0^2 m_e v_{te}^2)$ is the Dreicer field with $e$ the elementary charge, $\ln\Lambda$ the Coulomb logarithm, $\epsilon_0$ the vacuum permittivity, $m_e$ the electron mass, and $v_{te}$ the thermal electron velocity, and $h$ is a numerical factor depending on the effective ion charge $Z_\mathrm{eff}$.

This electron source rate includes only production caused by direct Dreicer acceleration of thermal-tail electrons. Relative to the generic [Dreicer source rate](name:source_rate_due_to_dreicer), it makes the electron destination explicit; relative to [fast-electron source rate due to Dreicer generation](name:fast_electron_source_rate_due_to_dreicer), it does not restrict the destination to the fast-electron subset. It excludes electrons attributed to avalanche multiplication or [hot-tail generation](name:source_rate_due_to_hot_tail).

NAMES.name: fast_electron_source_rate_due_to_dreicer
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Fast-electron source rate due to Dreicer generation is the local volumetric production rate of electrons assigned to the fast-electron population when the electric field parallel to the magnetic field drives suprathermal electrons past the critical velocity where electric acceleration overcomes collisional friction. It excludes avalanche and hot-tail production.
NAMES.long:
Fast-electron source rate due to Dreicer generation is the local volumetric production rate of electrons entering the fast-electron population through Dreicer acceleration. The mechanism is acceleration by the electric-field component parallel to the magnetic field, opposed by collisional friction, so that sufficiently suprathermal electrons cross the critical velocity boundary into the fast-electron region.

The kinetic definition is the velocity-space flux across that critical boundary assigned to the fast-electron population:

$$
S_{\mathrm{D,fast}} = \int_{\Sigma(v_c)} \boldsymbol{\Gamma}^{\mathrm{D}}_v \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}_v \, dA_v
$$

where $S_{\mathrm{D,fast}}$ is the fast-electron source rate due to Dreicer generation, $\Sigma(v_c)$ is the velocity-space surface at the critical speed $v_c$, $\hat{\mathbf{n}}_v$ points into the fast-electron region, $dA_v$ is an element of that surface, and $\boldsymbol{\Gamma}^{\mathrm{D}}_v$ is the Dreicer velocity-space flux caused by parallel electric acceleration and collisional friction. The critical speed is set by $e|E_\parallel| = F_\mathrm{coll}(v_c)$, where $E_\parallel = \mathbf{E}\cdot\mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$, $e$ is the elementary charge, and $F_\mathrm{coll}$ is the magnitude of the collisional friction force.

This quantity is a contribution to [fast_electron_source_rate](name:fast_electron_source_rate) and a population-specific member of the Dreicer source family represented by [source_rate_due_to_dreicer](name:source_rate_due_to_dreicer). It is distinct from [runaway_electron_source_rate_due_to_dreicer](name:runaway_electron_source_rate_due_to_dreicer), unless the fast-electron population is defined to coincide with the runaway-electron region, and it excludes avalanche multiplication, hot-tail production, and non-Dreicer secondary sources.

NAMES.name: runaway_electron_source_rate_due_to_dreicer
NAMES.subject: runaway_electron
NAMES.short: Volumetric production rate of runaway electrons generated by the Dreicer mechanism, where a parallel electric field accelerates thermal-tail electrons past the critical velocity at which Coulomb collisional friction can no longer confine them.
NAMES.long:
The Dreicer source rate for runaway electrons is the local volumetric rate at which a parallel electric field accelerates electrons from the high-energy tail of the thermal distribution past the critical velocity $v_c$, above which Coulomb collisional drag can no longer balance the electric force. It is the contribution of primary Dreicer generation to the runaway-electron population.

The local source rate is the Dreicer contribution to the time derivative of the runaway-electron number density:

$$
S_\mathrm{RE}^{D} = \left.\frac{\partial n_\mathrm{RE}}{\partial t}\right|_{D}
$$

where $S_\mathrm{RE}^{D}$ is the runaway-electron Dreicer source rate, $n_\mathrm{RE}$ is the runaway-electron number density, $t$ is time, and the subscript $D$ denotes the part of the evolution due to the Dreicer mechanism.

This quantity is the runaway-population specialization of [source_rate_due_to_dreicer](name:source_rate_due_to_dreicer). It excludes other runaway-generation mechanisms, including hot-tail seeding described by [source_rate_due_to_hot_tail](name:source_rate_due_to_hot_tail) and avalanche multiplication. It also excludes sink or loss terms, so it is a source-only contribution rather than a signed net balance; [electron_source_rate_due_to_dreicer](name:electron_source_rate_due_to_dreicer) denotes the corresponding electron-population source and [fast_electron_source_rate_due_to_dreicer](name:fast_electron_source_rate_due_to_dreicer) denotes the fast-electron channel.

NAMES.name: source_rate_due_to_hot_tail
NAMES.short: Volumetric production rate of electrons by the hot-tail mechanism during rapid thermal quench, in which suprathermal electrons failing to rethermalize with the cooling bulk may cross the runaway momentum threshold.
NAMES.long:
During a rapid thermal quench — when the bulk electron temperature collapses on a timescale shorter than the electron–electron collision time — electrons in the suprathermal tail of the pre-quench distribution fail to rethermalize with the cooling bulk. These surviving hot-tail electrons retain momenta that can exceed the critical runaway momentum, making the hot-tail mechanism one of the dominant seed sources for runaway electrons in disruption scenarios.

The volumetric source rate $S_\mathrm{ht}$ is defined by the time rate of change of the electron population above a threshold momentum $p_c$:

$$
S_\mathrm{ht} = \frac{\partial}{\partial t} \int_{p > p_c} f(\mathbf{p},t) \, d^3p
$$

where $f(\mathbf{p}, t)$ is the electron momentum distribution function and $p_c$ is the local critical momentum at which the accelerating electric force exceeds collisional drag. This source is non-negative by construction, as the hot-tail mechanism only promotes electrons upward across $p_c$.

This parent quantity spans both [electron_source_rate_due_to_hot_tail](name:electron_source_rate_due_to_hot_tail), which captures all suprathermal-electron generation by this mechanism, and [runaway_electron_source_rate_due_to_hot_tail](name:runaway_electron_source_rate_due_to_hot_tail), which counts only electrons promoted above the runaway threshold. In contrast to [runaway_electron_source_rate_due_to_dreicer](name:runaway_electron_source_rate_due_to_dreicer), which operates in quasi-steady state under a parallel electric field, the hot-tail mechanism is inherently transient and tied to rapid cooling events. The contribution of all active generation mechanisms is summed in [runaway_electron_source_rate](name:runaway_electron_source_rate).

NAMES.name: electron_source_rate_due_to_hot_tail
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Volumetric production rate of electrons by the hot-tail mechanism during a rapid thermal quench, in which suprathermal electrons failing to rethermalize with the cooling bulk cross a momentum threshold into the counted electron population.
NAMES.long:
Volumetric production rate of electrons by the hot-tail mechanism is the local rate at which electrons are added to an electron population by survival of a suprathermal tail during a rapid thermal quench. The mechanism applies when the bulk electron temperature collapses on a timescale shorter than the electron-electron collision time, so high-momentum electrons from the pre-quench distribution fail to rethermalize with the cooling bulk and cross the threshold defining the counted population.

The source rate $S_{\mathrm{ht},e}$ is defined as the hot-tail contribution to the time rate of change of the local electron population above a threshold momentum $p_\mathrm{thr}$:

$$
S_{\mathrm{ht},e} =
\left.\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\right|_{\mathrm{ht}}
\int_{p > p_\mathrm{thr}} f_e(\mathbf{p}, t) \, d^3p
$$

where $f_e(\mathbf{p}, t)$ is the local electron momentum distribution function, $p_\mathrm{thr}$ is the momentum threshold defining the counted electron population, and the derivative selects only the hot-tail contribution.

This parent quantity is specialized by the [fast-electron source rate due to hot-tail generation](name:fast_electron_source_rate_due_to_hot_tail), which restricts the counted population to fast electrons. The parent does not impose a runaway-electron criterion; losses, slowing down, and source terms from mechanisms other than hot-tail generation are excluded.

NAMES.name: fast_electron_source_rate_due_to_hot_tail
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Volumetric production rate of fast electrons due to hot-tail generation during a rapid thermal quench is the local production into the fast-electron population when an initially hotter high-energy tail does not rethermalize with the cooling bulk. It is not restricted to electrons satisfying a runaway-electron criterion.
NAMES.long:
Volumetric production rate of fast electrons due to hot-tail generation during a rapid thermal quench is the local rate at which electrons enter the fast-electron population because the high-energy tail of an initially hotter distribution does not rethermalize with the cooling bulk. The quantity represents production by hot-tail survival of suprathermal electrons, not subsequent acceleration or losses.

A kinetic definition is the hot-tail source part of the time derivative of the electron density contained in the fast-electron momentum-space domain:

$$
S_{\mathrm{fe,ht}}(\mathbf{x},t) =
\left[\frac{\partial}{\partial t}
\int_{\Omega_{\mathrm{fe}}(\mathbf{x},t)}
f_e(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{p},t)\,d^3p
\right]_{\mathrm{hot\ tail\ source}}
$$

where $S_{\mathrm{fe,ht}}$ is the local hot-tail fast-electron source rate, $\mathbf{x}$ is position, $t$ is time, $\mathbf{p}$ is electron momentum, $f_e$ is the electron distribution function, and $\Omega_{\mathrm{fe}}$ is the momentum-space region assigned to the fast-electron population. The bracketed subscript means that only production caused by incomplete rethermalization of the hot tail is retained.

This source is a component of [fast_electron_source_rate](name:fast_electron_source_rate). It excludes [fast_electron_source_rate_due_to_dreicer](name:fast_electron_source_rate_due_to_dreicer), avalanche multiplication, external injection, and sink terms; it is therefore not a signed net balance term. The fast-electron domain need not coincide with the runaway-electron domain; if it is chosen to be the runaway-electron domain, the same hot-tail mechanism reduces to [runaway_electron_source_rate_due_to_hot_tail](name:runaway_electron_source_rate_due_to_hot_tail).

NAMES.name: runaway_electron_source_rate_due_to_hot_tail
NAMES.subject: runaway_electron
NAMES.short: Volumetric production rate of runaway electrons by the hot-tail mechanism during a rapid thermal quench, in which suprathermal electrons failing to rethermalize with the cooling bulk cross the critical runaway momentum threshold.
NAMES.long:
Volumetric production rate of runaway electrons by the hot-tail mechanism is the local rate at which suprathermal electrons are added to the runaway-electron population during a rapid thermal quench. The mechanism applies when the bulk electron temperature collapses faster than suprathermal electrons can collisionally rethermalize, leaving part of the pre-quench tail above the critical runaway momentum.

The source rate $S_{\mathrm{RE,ht}}$ is defined as the hot-tail contribution to the time rate of change of the electron population above the local runaway threshold:

$$
S_{\mathrm{RE,ht}} = \left.\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\int_{p>p_{c,\mathrm{RE}}} f(\mathbf{p},t)\,d^3p\right|_{\mathrm{hot\text{-}tail}}
$$

where $f(\mathbf{p},t)$ is the electron momentum distribution function, $p=|\mathbf{p}|$ is momentum magnitude, and $p_{c,\mathrm{RE}}$ is the local critical runaway momentum at which electric acceleration exceeds collisional drag. The qualifier on the derivative retains only the one-sided production associated with hot-tail electrons crossing into the runaway population.

This quantity is the runaway-electron member of [source_rate_due_to_hot_tail](name:source_rate_due_to_hot_tail). It differs from [electron_source_rate_due_to_hot_tail](name:electron_source_rate_due_to_hot_tail) by restricting the counted population to electrons promoted above the runaway threshold, and it excludes losses, radial transport, avalanche multiplication, and the quasi-steady field-driven production represented by [runaway_electron_source_rate_due_to_dreicer](name:runaway_electron_source_rate_due_to_dreicer). Contributions from all active runaway-electron generation mechanisms are combined in [runaway_electron_source_rate](name:runaway_electron_source_rate).

NAMES.name: source_rate_due_to_thermal_fusion
NAMES.short: Source rate due to thermal fusion is the volume-integrated production rate of a specified fusion-reaction product or source term generated by thermonuclear reactions among thermal bulk ions. More specific names define the emitted product or channel aggregation; the thermal qualifier excludes fast-ion fusion contributions.
NAMES.long:
Source rate due to thermal fusion is the volume-integrated production rate of a specified fusion-reaction product or source term generated by thermonuclear reactions among thermal, approximately Maxwellian ion populations in the plasma. It is a parent concept for source rates whose child names identify the produced particle or source component.

The source rate is defined by integrating the corresponding local source-rate density over the plasma volume:

$$
S_{\mathrm{tf}} = \int_{V_{\mathrm{p}}} s_{\mathrm{tf}}(\mathbf{x})\, dV
$$

where $S_{\mathrm{tf}}$ is the source rate due to thermal fusion, $s_{\mathrm{tf}}$ is the local source-rate density due to thermal fusion for the same specified product or source term, and $V_{\mathrm{p}}$ is the plasma volume.

This parent does not by itself specify the reaction-product species, fusion-reaction channel, or channel aggregation. For example, the [neutron source rate due to thermal fusion](name:neutron_source_rate_due_to_thermal_fusion) specializes this concept to neutron production. The thermal-fusion qualifier restricts the contributing reactions to thermal bulk-ion fusion and excludes beam-target, beam-beam, and other fast-ion fusion contributions.

NAMES.name: neutron_source_rate_due_to_thermal_fusion
NAMES.subject: neutron
NAMES.short: Global neutron production rate from thermonuclear reactions among Maxwellian bulk ions, applicable to individual neutron-producing reaction channels or their aggregate total, excluding fast-ion fusion contributions.
NAMES.long:
The neutron source rate due to thermal fusion is the global rate at which neutrons are generated by thermonuclear reactions between plasma ion species whose velocity distributions are Maxwellian. It encompasses both per-channel rates for a single neutron-producing reaction (DD, DT, or TT) and the aggregate sum over all channels, and is an instance of the general [source_rate_due_to_thermal_fusion](name:source_rate_due_to_thermal_fusion) restricted to the neutron product.

For each neutron-producing reaction channel $c$ between reactant species $a$ and $b$, the channel source rate is:

$$
S_{n,c}^{\rm th} = \frac{1}{1 + \delta_{ab}} \int n_a \, n_b \, \langle \sigma v \rangle_c \, dV
$$

where $n_a$ and $n_b$ are the number densities of the two reactant species, $\langle \sigma v \rangle_c$ is the Maxwell-averaged reaction-rate coefficient for channel $c$, $\delta_{ab} = 1$ when the two reactants are identical (as in DD and TT channels) and 0 otherwise, and the integral extends over the confined plasma volume. The aggregate quantity sums contributions from all neutron-producing channels.

This quantity excludes neutrons from beam-target fusion (see [flux_due_to_beam_thermal_fusion](name:flux_due_to_beam_thermal_fusion)), beam-beam fusion, fusion-product reactivation, and radio-frequency-tail ion populations. Per-channel instances include [deuterium_deuterium_neutron_source_rate_due_to_thermal_fusion](name:deuterium_deuterium_neutron_source_rate_due_to_thermal_fusion) and [tritium_tritium_neutron_source_rate_due_to_thermal_fusion](name:tritium_tritium_neutron_source_rate_due_to_thermal_fusion); the channel-summed total is [total_neutron_source_rate_due_to_thermal_fusion](name:total_neutron_source_rate_due_to_thermal_fusion).

NAMES.name: deuterium_deuterium_neutron_source_rate_due_to_thermal_fusion
NAMES.subject: deuterium_deuterium
NAMES.short: Total neutron production rate from the thermonuclear deuterium-deuterium reaction branch among Maxwellian bulk deuterons, excluding beam-target and beam-beam fast-ion contributions.
NAMES.long:
The total neutron source rate due to thermal fusion is the number of neutrons produced per unit time by the thermal deuterium-deuterium reaction branch between bulk deuterons with locally Maxwellian velocity distributions. It is the deuterium-deuterium channel member of [neutron source rate due to thermal fusion](name:neutron_source_rate_due_to_thermal_fusion), distinct from the channel-summed [total neutron source rate due to thermal fusion](name:total_neutron_source_rate_due_to_thermal_fusion).

The deuterium-deuterium thermal neutron source rate is defined by

$$
S_{n,DD}^{\mathrm{th}} = \int_V \frac{1}{2} n_D^2\,\langle\sigma v\rangle_{DD,n}(T_D)\,dV
$$

where $S_{n,DD}^{\mathrm{th}}$ is the source rate, $V$ is the emitting plasma volume, $n_D$ is the local bulk deuteron number density, $\langle\sigma v\rangle_{DD,n}$ is the Maxwellian-averaged reactivity for the neutron-producing deuterium-deuterium branch, $T_D$ is the local bulk deuteron temperature, and $dV$ is a volume element. The factor $1/2$ prevents double counting of identical deuteron pairs.

Only the neutron-producing D-D branch is included; the proton-producing D(d,p)T branch, beam-target fusion, beam-beam fusion, fusion-product reactions, and other nonthermal fast-ion contributions are excluded.

NAMES.name: suprathermal_neutral_internal_state_pressure
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Kinetic pressure of suprathermal neutral particles occupying a specified internal quantum or excitation state, arising from the anisotropic velocity distribution of the non-Maxwellian fast-neutral population.
NAMES.long:
The suprathermal neutral internal state pressure is the kinetic pressure associated with neutral particles in a specified internal quantum or excitation state whose velocity distribution departs significantly from a local Maxwellian — the suprathermal population. Such populations originate from charge exchange with energetic ions or from neutral beam injection, and their pressure is generally anisotropic with respect to the local magnetic field direction.

As a vector quantity, it encodes directional components of this anisotropic fast-neutral pressure. For the suprathermal neutral distribution $f_s(\mathbf{v})$ in internal state $s$, the pressure component along direction $\hat{e}_\alpha$ is:

$$
P_{\alpha,s} = m_n \int (v_\alpha - u_\alpha)^2 f_s(\mathbf{v}) \, d^3v
$$

where $m_n$ is the neutral particle mass and $u_\alpha$ is the local mean flow velocity component along $\hat{e}_\alpha$. The [perpendicular_suprathermal_neutral_internal_state_pressure](name:perpendicular_suprathermal_neutral_internal_state_pressure) gives the specific component perpendicular to the magnetic field.

This quantity excludes the near-Maxwellian thermal contribution and appears as a sub-component of the total [neutral_internal_state_pressure](name:neutral_internal_state_pressure), which covers the full kinetic pressure of neutrals in a specified internal state. The more general [neutral_pressure](name:neutral_pressure) aggregates over all internal states.

NAMES.name: perpendicular_suprathermal_neutral_internal_state_pressure
NAMES.subject: neutral
NAMES.short: Gyrotropic kinetic pressure perpendicular to the local magnetic field for fast (suprathermal) neutral particles in a specified internal quantum or excitation state. It is the central second velocity moment transverse to the local magnetic field for that selected population.
NAMES.long:
Gyrotropic kinetic pressure perpendicular to the local magnetic field for fast (suprathermal) neutral particles in a specified internal quantum or excitation state is the transverse component of the state-resolved kinetic pressure tensor. It represents the central second velocity moment in the two directions orthogonal to the magnetic-field unit vector and is the perpendicular complement of [parallel fast-neutral internal-state pressure](name:parallel_fast_neutral_internal_state_pressure).

For a state-resolved suprathermal neutral distribution, the perpendicular pressure is defined by the central moment

$$
p_{\perp,\chi}^{\mathrm{sup}}(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{m}{2}\int c_\perp^2 f_{\chi}^{\mathrm{sup}}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $\chi$ labels the internal quantum or excitation state, $m$ is the neutral-particle mass, $f_{\chi}^{\mathrm{sup}}$ is the suprathermal neutral velocity distribution for that internal state, $\mathbf{x}$ is position, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity, $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume element, $\mathbf{c}=\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{u}_{\chi}^{\mathrm{sup}}$ is velocity relative to the state-resolved mean flow, $\hat{\mathbf{b}}$ is the local magnetic-field unit vector, and $c_\perp=|\mathbf{c}-(\mathbf{c}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{b}})\hat{\mathbf{b}}|$ is the magnitude of the central velocity component perpendicular to the local magnetic field.

This quantity is not the scalar trace pressure of the selected population; in a gyrotropic tensor, the scalar pressure is related to the parallel and perpendicular components by $p=(p_\parallel+2p_\perp)/3$. It excludes thermal neutral particles and excludes summation over internal states; the corresponding state-summed perpendicular fast-neutral pressure is [perpendicular fast-neutral pressure](name:perpendicular_fast_neutral_pressure).

NAMES.name: temperature_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.short: Kinetic temperature of a specified plasma particle population evaluated on the flux surface assigned to an internal transport barrier.
NAMES.long:
The quantity is the kinetic temperature of a designated plasma particle population evaluated at the flux-surface location assigned to an internal transport barrier. It may represent one population, such as electrons, or an explicitly species-averaged population.

For the scalar kinetic-temperature convention, the defining relation is:

$$
T = \frac{2}{3}\langle E_{\mathrm{kin}}\rangle
$$

where $T$ is the kinetic temperature represented as an energy and $\langle E_{\mathrm{kin}}\rangle$ is the mean random kinetic energy per particle.

The value is evaluated on the assigned flux surface, not spatially averaged over that surface. The [electron temperature at an internal transport barrier](name:electron_temperature_at_internal_transport_barrier) applies the definition to electrons, while the [average temperature at an internal transport barrier](name:average_temperature_at_internal_transport_barrier) uses an arithmetic mean over constituent species.

NAMES.name: average_temperature_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.short: Kinetic temperature of a species-averaged plasma particle population evaluated at the flux-surface location of an internal transport barrier. The average is an arithmetic mean over constituent species, not a spatial average over the flux surface.
NAMES.long:
Kinetic temperature at an internal transport barrier is the energy-equivalent measure of random motion for a species-averaged plasma particle population on the barrier's assigned flux surface. It is the averaged-population member of the temperature family.

For an arithmetic species average, the defining relation is:

$$
\bar{T}_{\mathcal{S}} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{S}|}\sum_{s \in \mathcal{S}} T_s
$$

where $\bar{T}_{\mathcal{S}}$ is the average kinetic temperature of the particle-population set $\mathcal{S}$, $T_s$ is the kinetic temperature of constituent species $s$, and $|\mathcal{S}|$ is the number of species included in the average.

The averaging is over the population set specified by the concrete member, not over positions on the flux surface or over a radial interval. The charged-ion realization is [ion average temperature at an internal transport barrier](name:ion_average_temperature_at_internal_transport_barrier), in which $\mathcal{S}$ is the set of charged-ion species and electrons and neutral species are excluded. The broader family quantity is [temperature at an internal transport barrier](name:temperature_at_internal_transport_barrier); this name adds the averaged-population qualifier.

NAMES.name: electron_temperature_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Kinetic temperature of the electron population evaluated on the flux surface assigned to an internal transport barrier.
NAMES.long:
Kinetic temperature at an internal transport barrier is the energy-equivalent measure of random motion for the electron population on the barrier’s assigned flux surface. It is the electron-specific member of the temperature family.

For an isotropic electron population, the defining relation is:

$$
T_e = \frac{2}{3}\langle E_e\rangle
$$

where $T_e$ is the electron kinetic temperature and $\langle E_e\rangle$ is the mean random kinetic energy per electron. The quantity applies only to electrons and is distinct from the ion-population [average temperature at an internal transport barrier](name:average_temperature_at_internal_transport_barrier). It is a local value on the assigned core flux surface, not an integral across the barrier; the population-unspecified parent is [temperature at an internal transport barrier](name:temperature_at_internal_transport_barrier).

sources.enhanced_context: Electron temperature (Te) at the internal transport barrier (ITB) location. Represents the thermal energy of the electron population at this specific transport-relevant radial position.
sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Electron temperature

NAMES.name: ion_average_temperature_at_internal_transport_barrier
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Kinetic temperature of the charged-ion population at an internal transport barrier, defined as the arithmetic mean of charged-ion species temperatures, excluding electrons and neutral species.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the arithmetic mean of the kinetic temperatures of all charged ion species on the flux surface assigned to an internal transport barrier. It retains the locus and population scope of [average temperature at an internal transport barrier](name:average_temperature_at_internal_transport_barrier).

$$
T_{i,\mathrm{avg}} = \frac{1}{N_i}\sum_{s\in\mathcal{C}} T_{i,s}
$$

where $\mathcal{C}$ is the set of included charged ion species, $N_i$ is the number of species in that set, and $T_{i,s}$ is the kinetic temperature of species $s$. For each species, $T_{i,s}$ is the density-weighted mean over its charge-state temperatures, using $T_{i,s}=\sum_Z n_{s,Z}T_{s,Z}/\sum_Z n_{s,Z}$, where $n_{s,Z}$ is the number density of charge state $Z$ and $T_{s,Z}$ is its [ion charge-state temperature](name:ion_charge_state_temperature). Charge-state weighting is therefore applied within each species, but distinct ion species are averaged equally; electrons and neutral species are excluded.

sources.leaf_definition: Value
sources.parent_definition: Ion temperature (average over ion species)

NAMES.name: temperature_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.short: Thermal energy per particle for a plasma population, or the corresponding temperature-equivalent radiation energy scale, evaluated at the magnetic axis.
NAMES.long:
Thermal energy per particle for a plasma population, or the corresponding temperature-equivalent radiation energy scale, evaluated at the magnetic axis. The magnetic axis is the degenerate innermost magnetic surface of the equilibrium, the locus in the poloidal cross-section where the gradient of the [poloidal magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux) vanishes; evaluation at this locus does not imply that the temperature has an extremum there.

When the population possesses a well-defined absolute thermodynamic temperature, the quantity is its energy-equivalent form:

$$
T = k_\mathrm{B}\,\Theta
$$

where $T$ is the temperature expressed as an energy per particle, $\Theta$ is the absolute thermodynamic temperature of the population, and $k_\mathrm{B}$ is the Boltzmann constant.

This is the species-agnostic parent quantity: it does not by itself select a species, charge state, or kinetic versus radiative interpretation. Population-resolved children include the [electron temperature at the magnetic axis](name:electron_temperature_at_magnetic_axis), the [average temperature at the magnetic axis](name:average_temperature_at_magnetic_axis), the [ion average temperature at the magnetic axis](name:ion_average_temperature_at_magnetic_axis), and the [radiative temperature at the magnetic axis](name:radiative_temperature_at_magnetic_axis). It is the axis-locus counterpart of [plasma temperature](name:plasma_temperature) and of the same-locus companion [density at the magnetic axis](name:density_at_magnetic_axis), and parallels the loci-qualified siblings [temperature at the plasma boundary](name:temperature_at_plasma_boundary) and [temperature at the outboard midplane](name:temperature_at_outboard_midplane).

NAMES.name: average_temperature_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.short: Thermal energy per particle of a specified plasma population, formed as a density-weighted average over its components and evaluated at the magnetic axis, the innermost singular point of the confined plasma where the poloidal magnetic flux gradient vanishes.
NAMES.long:
Average temperature at the magnetic axis is the local density-weighted thermal energy per particle of a specified plasma population at the central singular point of the confined plasma, where the gradient of the poloidal magnetic flux $\psi$ vanishes. The population set is defined by the concrete child quantity and may aggregate species, charge states, or other physically defined plasma components without the parent name selecting any one of them.

For a component set $A$ evaluated at the magnetic axis, the average temperature is defined by

$$
T_{\mathrm{avg}} = \frac{\sum_{a \in A} n_a T_a}{\sum_{a \in A} n_a}
$$

where $T_{\mathrm{avg}}$ is the population-averaged temperature, $a$ labels a component of $A$, $n_a$ is the local number density of component $a$, and $T_a$ is its local temperature at the same locus.

Because temperature is an intensive per-particle quantity, aggregation over species or charge states is a density-weighted mean, not a sum of temperatures. The concrete child [ion_average_temperature_at_magnetic_axis](name:ion_average_temperature_at_magnetic_axis) applies this definition to all ion species and charge states; this parent remains population-agnostic within the broader [temperature_at_magnetic_axis](name:temperature_at_magnetic_axis) family. The quantity is a local on-axis value, not a flux-surface average, volume average, or maximum value in the confined plasma.

NAMES.name: electron_temperature_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Thermal energy per particle of the electron population evaluated at the magnetic axis, where the poloidal magnetic flux gradient vanishes.
NAMES.long:
Electron temperature at the magnetic axis is the local thermal energy per particle of the electron population at the central singular point of the confined plasma, where the gradient of the poloidal magnetic flux $\psi$ vanishes. It is the electron-specific member of the broader [temperature at the magnetic axis](name:temperature_at_magnetic_axis) family.

For an isotropic electron velocity distribution, the energy-valued temperature at the magnetic axis is defined by

$$
T_{e,\mathrm{axis}} = \frac{2}{3}\langle E_{e,\mathrm{axis}}\rangle
$$

where $T_{e,\mathrm{axis}}$ is the electron temperature at the magnetic axis and $\langle E_{e,\mathrm{axis}}\rangle$ is the mean random kinetic energy per electron at that same locus.

This quantity applies only to electrons and is not a sum or density-weighted mean over ion species or other plasma components. Unlike [average temperature at the magnetic axis](name:average_temperature_at_magnetic_axis), it does not aggregate multiple species; it is a local on-axis value rather than a flux-surface or volume average.

NAMES.name: ion_average_temperature_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.subject: ion
NAMES.short: Density-weighted effective temperature of the combined thermal ion population at the magnetic axis, with all ion species and charge states contributing according to their number densities. The magnetic axis is the geometric center of the nested closed magnetic flux surfaces, where the poloidal magnetic flux is stationary.
NAMES.long:
Density-weighted effective temperature of the combined thermal ion population at the magnetic axis is the local ion temperature obtained by weighting each thermal ion species and charge state by its local number density. The magnetic axis is the geometric center of the nested closed magnetic flux surfaces, equivalently the locus where the poloidal magnetic flux is stationary.

For resolved ion populations, the effective temperature is defined by the density-weighted average at the magnetic axis:

$$
T_{i,\mathrm{avg}}^{\mathrm{axis}} = \frac{\sum_s \sum_\zeta n_{s,\zeta}^{\mathrm{axis}} T_{s,\zeta}^{\mathrm{axis}}}{\sum_s \sum_\zeta n_{s,\zeta}^{\mathrm{axis}}}
$$

where $s$ labels ion species, $\zeta$ labels charge state, $n_{s,\zeta}^{\mathrm{axis}}$ is the local number density of that species and charge state at the magnetic axis, and $T_{s,\zeta}^{\mathrm{axis}}$ is its local temperature at the magnetic axis. The sums include the same thermal ion populations in the numerator and denominator.

This is a local on-axis quantity, not a volume average and not the temperature of a single species unless the included ion population is effectively single-component or all included components have the same temperature. It is the magnetic-axis counterpart of [total ion temperature](name:total_ion_temperature) and is distinct from [volume-averaged total ion temperature](name:volume_averaged_total_ion_temperature). It excludes electrons, neutral particles, and nonthermal energetic-ion components that are not part of the thermal ion population, and it does not imply the maximum ion temperature in the plasma.

NAMES.name: thermal_electron_power_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Signed local volumetric rate of Coulomb-collisional energy transfer from fast particle populations to the bulk thermal electron population.
NAMES.long:
Thermal-electron collisional power density is the net local volumetric energy exchange received by the bulk thermal electron population from Coulomb collisions with fast or otherwise non-Maxwellian particle populations.

The quantity is defined by

$$
P_{e,\mathrm{th}}^{\mathrm{coll}} = \sum_a \sum_o Q_{e,\mathrm{th}\leftarrow a,o}^{\mathrm{coll}}
$$

where $P_{e,\mathrm{th}}^{\mathrm{coll}}$ is the thermal-electron collisional power density in W m$^{-3}$, $Q_{e,\mathrm{th}\leftarrow a,o}^{\mathrm{coll}}$ is the collisional energy-transfer rate per unit volume from source population $a$ in orbit class $o$, and the sums include the specified fast populations and orbit classes.

This is the thermal-target component of [electron collisional power density](name:electron_power_density_due_to_collisions), resolved over classes such as co-passing, counter-passing, and trapped populations. Its volume integral gives [thermal-electron collisional power](name:thermal_electron_power_due_to_collisions), while [trapped thermal-electron collisional power density](name:trapped_thermal_electron_power_density_due_to_collisions) is one orbit-resolved instance.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the bulk thermal electron population gains energy from the collision partners.

NAMES.name: co_passing_thermal_electron_power_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Volumetric Coulomb-collisional energy transfer rate from co-passing fast particles to the bulk thermal electron population, positive for net thermal-electron heating.
NAMES.long:
Co-passing thermal electron power density due to collisions is the local rate per unit volume at which Coulomb collisions transfer kinetic energy from the co-passing part of a fast or otherwise non-Maxwellian particle population to bulk thermal electrons. It is the co-passing orbit-class contribution to the [thermal electron power density due to collisions](name:thermal_electron_power_density_due_to_collisions).

The quantity is defined by the negative kinetic-energy moment of the fast-particle collision operator for collisions with thermal electrons:

$$
p_{e,\mathrm{co}}^{\mathrm{coll}}(\mathbf{x})=-\int \frac{1}{2}m_fv^2 C_{fe}[f_{f,\mathrm{co}}](\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $p_{e,\mathrm{co}}^{\mathrm{coll}}$ is this power density, $m_f$ is the fast-particle mass, $v$ is particle speed, $f_{f,\mathrm{co}}$ is the co-passing fast-particle distribution, $C_{fe}$ is its Coulomb-collision operator for thermal-electron interactions, and $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume element. The quantity includes only the co-passing guiding-center source-orbit class; trapped and counter-passing contributions are excluded and form separate components such as [counter-passing thermal electron power density due to collisions](name:counter_passing_thermal_electron_power_density_due_to_collisions).
NAMES.sign: Positive when Coulomb collisions transfer energy from co-passing fast particles to the bulk thermal electron population.

NAMES.name: counter_passing_thermal_electron_power_density_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Volumetric Coulomb-collisional energy transfer rate from counter-passing fast particles to the bulk thermal electron population, positive for net thermal-electron heating.
NAMES.long:
Counter-passing thermal electron power density due to collisions is the local rate per unit volume at which Coulomb collisions transfer kinetic energy from the counter-passing part of a fast or otherwise non-Maxwellian particle population to the bulk thermal electron population. It is the counter-passing orbit-class contribution to electron-channel collisional heating.

The quantity is defined as the negative kinetic-energy moment of the fast-particle collision operator associated with collisions against thermal electrons:

$$
p_{e,\mathrm{th}}^{\mathrm{coll,cp}}(\mathbf{x}) = -\int \frac{1}{2}m_f v^2 C_{fe}[f_{f,\mathrm{cp}}](\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $p_{e,\mathrm{th}}^{\mathrm{coll,cp}}$ is this power density, $m_f$ is the fast-particle mass in kg, $v$ is particle speed in m s$^{-1}$, $f_{f,\mathrm{cp}}$ is the counter-passing fast-particle distribution, $C_{fe}$ is its rate of change from Coulomb collisions with thermal electrons, and $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume element. The minus sign converts fast-particle energy loss into thermal-electron energy gain.

This contribution excludes trapped and co-passing orbit classes. Its full orbit-class sum is [thermal electron collisional power density](name:thermal_electron_power_density_due_to_collisions); the corresponding co-passing contribution is [co-passing thermal electron collisional power density](name:co_passing_thermal_electron_power_density_due_to_collisions). The fast-particle energy change has the opposite sign in [fast-particle collisional power density](name:fast_particle_power_density_due_to_collisions).
NAMES.sign: Positive when Coulomb collisions transfer net kinetic energy from counter-passing fast particles to the bulk thermal electron population.

NAMES.name: thermal_electron_power_due_to_collisions
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Volume-integrated Coulomb-collisional power transferred from fast non-Maxwellian particles to bulk thermal electrons across trapped and passing orbit classes, with positive values indicating electron heating.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the net Coulomb-collisional energy-transfer rate into the bulk thermal-electron population from fast non-Maxwellian particles. It is the thermal-electron component of [electron power due to collisions](name:electron_power_due_to_collisions), including the represented trapped and passing orbit classes.

$$
P_{e,\mathrm{th}}^{\mathrm{coll}} = \int_V p_{e,\mathrm{th}}^{\mathrm{coll}}(\mathbf{x})\,dV
$$

where $P_{e,\mathrm{th}}^{\mathrm{coll}}$ is the volume-integrated power, $p_{e,\mathrm{th}}^{\mathrm{coll}}(\mathbf{x})$ is the local [thermal-electron collisional power density](name:thermal_electron_power_density_due_to_collisions), $V$ is the integration volume, and $\mathbf{x}$ is position. The quantity includes energy received by thermal electrons and excludes the corresponding donor-side energy change represented by [fast-particle collisional power](name:fast_particle_power_due_to_collisions). Positive values denote net heating of the bulk thermal-electron population.

NAMES.name: thermal_electron_pressure_at_post_sawtooth_crash
NAMES.subject: electron
NAMES.short: Isotropic pressure associated with random motion of the bulk thermal electron population, evaluated in the plasma state immediately after a sawtooth crash.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the isotropic pressure produced by random thermal motion of bulk electrons in the plasma state immediately following a sawtooth crash. It is evaluated at the event-defined post-crash state rather than at an arbitrary later time.

For an isotropic thermal electron population, the pressure is defined by

$$
p_{e,\mathrm{th}} = n_{e,\mathrm{th}} k_B T_{e,\mathrm{th}}
$$

where $p_{e,\mathrm{th}}$ is the thermal electron pressure, $n_{e,\mathrm{th}}$ is the thermal electron number density, $k_B$ is Boltzmann's constant, and $T_{e,\mathrm{th}}$ is the thermal electron temperature.

The quantity excludes fast and suprathermal electron contributions. It is the post-crash, thermal-population counterpart of [electron pressure](name:electron_pressure), whereas [total electron pressure](name:total_electron_pressure) includes all electron populations.
